── *** CAUSE FOUND: THE SIEVE. HYPOTHESIS 1 WAS REFUTED AT THE WRONG SCALE
   (2026-07-31, quiet host, ablation not instruction counts). *** ──

FIRST, THE HEADLINE NUMBER IS STALE. This entry says 2.5-2.9x. Measured today at
full scale (50 iterations, seq lane, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, karac at current main):

  kara      6.534 s +- 0.155
  rust_ovf  4.678 s +- 0.094      kara/rust_ovf = 1.40x
  c_v3      4.546 s +- 0.199      kara/c_v3     = 1.44x

So the deficit is 1.40-1.44x, not 2.5-2.9x. Compiler work since 9dd8aa325021
closed most of it. (The deque fix, B-2026-07-30-5, is only ~4% of that.)

THE CAUSE IS build_factors. Ablation, same host, 50 iterations, sieve ONLY
(build_factors + a checksum, no bucket build, no BFS), against an
algorithm-for-algorithm C mirror of the same loop:

  sieve only   kara 6.235 s   C 3.775 s    1.65x

The sieve alone is 95% of kara's full runtime and 83% of C's, and the sieve
DEFICIT (2.46 s) is LARGER than the whole kata's deficit (1.99 s). Everything
downstream — bucket build, BFS, deque — is noise by comparison.

WHY HYPOTHESIS 1 SAID THE OPPOSITE. It probed at cap = 50,000. The real kata's
`cap` is `max(nums)` ~= 1e6 — TWENTY TIMES larger, and the sieve's work is
superlinear in cap while the allocation count is linear in it. At 50,000 kara
measured FASTER than clang; at 1e6 it is 1.65x slower. The probe was right about
the code and wrong about the scale, and that one mistake sent this entry chasing
six innocent constructs for two days.

Lesson, since it is the second methodology error on this bug: probe at the REAL
problem size. (The first was reading callgrind instruction counts as time — see
B-2026-07-30-5.)

SUB-LOCALIZATION INSIDE THE SIEVE. Three candidates measured and eliminated:

  * `Vec.filled(cap + 1, Vec.new())` — kara 117.6 ms vs C's calloc 1.2 ms for
    the same 1e6-element fill. A real ~100x gap (calloc gets lazy zero pages;
    kara writes every element), but only 1.9% of the sieve. Worth its own
    low-severity entry, NOT the cause here.
  * `for j in (i..=cap).step_by(i)` iterator lowering — NOT it. Hand-rolling it
    as `let mut j = i; while j <= cap { ...; j = j + i; }` measures 6.288 s
    against 6.237 s, i.e. identical.
  * Growth strategy (malloc+copy+free vs in-place `realloc`) — NOT it. Rewriting
    the C mirror's push to malloc+copy+free instead of realloc leaves C
    unchanged (3.718 s vs 3.765 s), so kara losing in-place growth cannot
    explain a 1.65x gap.

WHAT IS LEFT, and it is now a single narrow target: the per-push cost of
`factors[j].push(i)` itself — the indexed push into an element of a
`Vec[Vec[i64]]`. ~3e6 of them per call. Each must bounds-check `j`, load the
inner `{ptr,len,cap}` header from `factors.data + j*24`, test len==cap, store
the element, and write the header back; C's `push(&f[j], i)` does the same work
with the header kept in registers across the inlined call. The suspicion is
header reload/writeback and bounds-check overhead that C's inliner removes, but
that is a hypothesis, not a measurement — the next step is to read the emitted
IR/asm for that loop rather than to guess again.

NOT DONE: the per-push root cause, and any fix.

── NARROWED FURTHER: NOT push, NOT arithmetic — the Vec[Vec] MANY-SMALL-BUFFERS
   PATTERN (2026-07-31, second ablation round). ──

Host was ~2x slower this round than the previous one (sv_c 7.9 s vs 3.8 s for
the identical binary), so only RATIOS below are meaningful. The sieve ratio is
stable across both rounds at 1.65-1.85x, which is what matters.

FOUR MORE CANDIDATES MEASURED INSIDE THE SIEVE. Each is a C-side experiment that
adds back an overhead kara pays, to see how much of the gap it buys:

  * NON-INLINED push (forces the inner {ptr,len,cap} header to be reloaded and
    written back per call, plus call overhead): 7.898 -> 8.995 s = 1.14x.
    Real, but only ~1/5 of the gap.
  * OVERFLOW CHECKS on the sieve's `j += i`, `len + 1` and the capacity double
    (__builtin_*_overflow, matching kara's default-on checking): 7.840 ->
    8.039 s = 1.025x. Essentially free here — unlike the scan kernels of #228
    where the same tax is 4.6x. Not it.
  * step_by iterator lowering — not it (previous round).
  * malloc+copy+free vs in-place realloc — not it (previous round).

AND THE ONE THAT INVERTS THE PICTURE. `Vec.push` ITSELF IS NOT SLOW. Isolated to
a single flat Vec, same push count as the sieve (2,853,000 pushes x 50):

    kara   82.5 ms
    C     540.4 ms   (of which 428 ms is SYSTEM time — realloc page faults)

Kara is 6.55x FASTER than the C mirror at raw push. So every remaining
explanation that blames the push operation, its bounds check, or its growth
policy is dead: in the one place those are measured alone, kara wins decisively.

WHAT THAT LEAVES. The sieve differs from the flat probe in exactly one way: it
is `Vec[Vec[i64]]` with ~1e6 INNER Vecs of 1-6 elements each, versus one Vec of
2.85e6. Same total pushes, same total elements. So the cost is in the
MANY-SMALL-BUFFERS pattern — roughly 1e6 tiny allocations plus their frees per
call, and the per-inner-Vec header traffic that goes with them — not in any
single operation. Plausible mechanisms, none yet measured:

  1. the recycling-aware `karac_free_buf` / allocation path behaving badly at
     1e6 live small buffers (thrash, or a free-list walk);
  2. first-push allocation size for a fresh inner Vec (if it is not the same
     4 elements C's mirror starts at, 1e6 extra grow-and-copy rounds follow);
  3. drop-walk cost when `factors` dies: 1e6 inner buffers freed one at a time,
     which the flat probe does exactly once.

(3) is testable in isolation and (2) is answerable by reading the push arm's
`new_cap` computation for a zero-capacity Vec. Those are the next two steps, in
that order — and both are cheap, unlike the six hypotheses this bug burned
before the scale error was found.

── ROOT CAUSE FOUND: THE RECYCLING BUFFER CACHE, NOT THE Vec[Vec] PATTERN
   (2026-07-31, third round. Fresh karac built from main 9b9d397; quiet host;
   seq lane, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 on every kara build below.) ──

Every mechanism the previous two rounds named is refuted. The deficit is
entirely attributable to the large-buffer recycling cache in
`runtime/src/alloc.rs` (`mod buf_cache`, gated on `KARAC_BUF_CACHE`, park
threshold `BUF_CACHE_MIN_BYTES` = 1 MiB).

ON THE REAL KATA (bfs_sieve, the bug's actual subject; sink 24350 identical
in all three):

    kara, cache ON      16.879 s ± 0.395     1.84x vs C
    kara, cache OFF      9.982 s ± 0.254     1.09x vs C
    C, clang -O3         9.170 s ± 0.219

  The cache accounts for 89% of the kata's excess time: 7.709 s of excess with
  it on, 0.812 s with it off. The ledger's headline "1.40-1.44x" from the
  previous round was measured on a different (slower, shared) host; on a quiet
  host with a karac built from current main the figure is 1.84x, and 1.09x
  once the cache is out of the picture. A ~1.09x residual remains and is NOT
  explained by this finding — that is what is left of this bug.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT ISOLATES IT — the sieve alone (cap 999983, K=50), one
compiler build, the ONLY variable being the env flag:

    kara, cache ON      15.510 s ± 0.129
    kara, cache OFF      9.172 s ± 0.268      (KARAC_BUF_CACHE=0)
    C, clang -O3         8.876 s ± 0.998

  Cache OFF is 1.03x vs C — parity within noise. Cache ON is 1.75x. Sinks
  identical (50) across all three.

FOUR FACTS THAT PIN IT.

  1. AT K=1 THERE IS NO DEFICIT AT ALL — kara 213.4 ms vs C 216.9 ms (1.02x,
     15 runs). A single build-and-drop of the entire 1e6-inner-Vec structure
     is already at parity. Everything the earlier rounds hunted — per-push
     cost, inner-header traffic, the drop walk, allocation size — happens in
     full inside that one iteration, and it is not slow. This single fact
     retires hypotheses (1) and (3) from the previous round.

  2. THE COST ACCUMULATES ACROSS ITERATIONS; RSS DOES NOT. Per-iteration time
     with the cache ON: K=1 0.230 s, K=5 0.238, K=10 0.272, K=20 0.293,
     K=50 0.324. C is flat at ~0.17 s for every K. Peak RSS is flat at ~74 MB
     for BOTH languages at every K — nothing leaks; the heap degrades.

  3. INSTRUCTION COUNTS ARE ESSENTIALLY EQUAL. callgrind at K=1: kara 515.4 M
     Ir vs C 471.1 M (1.09x) — against a 1.89x wall-clock ratio. The allocator
     does literally identical work: `_int_malloc` 139,084,970 in BOTH,
     `_int_free` 77,473,041 in BOTH, `malloc_consolidate` 54,219,859 (C) vs
     54,220,041 (kara), `malloc` 44,999,232 vs 44,999,278. Same instructions,
     roughly half the IPC — a stall effect, not extra work. (Note this is
     callgrind used for what it is good at: attribution and counting. The
     B-2026-07-30-5 lesson — never read Ir as a proxy for TIME — is why the
     wall-clock A/B above, not this profile, is the load-bearing evidence.)

  4. THE CACHE COUNTERS NAME THE BUFFER. `KARAC_BUF_CACHE_STATS=1` at K=5:
     `take hit=4 miss=1 | put parked=5` — exactly one park per iteration. That
     is the OUTER `Vec[Vec[i64]]` data buffer: (cap+1) x 24 B ~= 24 MB, which
     clears the 1 MiB park threshold by 24x. The ~1e6 INNER buffers (32-48 B)
     never touch the cache at all: `karac_free_buf` short-circuits a positive
     hint below BUF_CACHE_MIN_BYTES straight to libc `free` (alloc.rs:526),
     and the alloc side does the same (alloc.rs:58).

THE CACHE IS NOT THE PROBLEM — ITS PARK DECISION IS. On the shape it was built
for, it is a large win. A probe that builds and drops one 24 MB Vec 200 times
with nothing else on the heap (`take hit=199 miss=1`, so fully exercised):

    cache ON     307.2 ms
    cache OFF      2.087 s        -> the cache is 6.79x FASTER

and the OFF run's cost is almost entirely kernel (System 1.830 s of 2.087 s):
the cache is eliminating an mmap/munmap + page-zero cycle per iteration,
exactly as designed. The identical park costs 1.75x in the sieve. The only
difference between the two workloads is what happens BETWEEN park and take —
nothing in the bigbuf probe, ~1e6 small allocations in the sieve. The park
decision reads only the buffer's SIZE; it has no notion of intervening heap
churn.

(Probe caveat worth keeping: the first version of the bigbuf probe read only
`v[0]`, so LLVM deleted the whole allocation — 200 iterations "ran" in 1.3 ms
and the cache counters stayed empty. The number above is from the fixed probe,
whose sink strides the buffer. Always check the cache counters are non-zero
before believing a buf_cache measurement.)

MECHANISM NOT ESTABLISHED — deliberately. WHY retaining a 24 MB parked buffer
across 1e6 small allocations costs ~7 s of user time (while saving ~0.6 s of
system time) is a glibc arena / free-list question this round did not answer,
and it is recorded as an open question rather than a story. This bug has
already burned two rounds on mechanisms asserted from a proxy signal instead
of measured.

TWO MORE REFUTATIONS FROM THIS ROUND.

  * (2) FIRST-PUSH ALLOCATION SIZE — refuted by reading. Codegen's push arm
    computes `new_cap = max(4, cap * 2)` (src/codegen/vec_method.rs:2614), so a
    fresh inner Vec allocates exactly 4 elements; `bfs_sieve.c`'s `intvec_push`
    uses `cap == 0 ? 4 : cap * 2`. Identical — no extra grow-and-copy rounds.

  * A NEW HYPOTHESIS, RAISED AND KILLED IN THE SAME ROUND: that the opaque
    runtime wrapper layer was the cost — `karac_realloc_or_panic` ->
    `karac_alloc_or_panic` -> `karac_alloc_fallible` -> `malloc` on every
    first push, `karac_free_buf` -> `free` on every drop, with no
    cross-language LTO to collapse them. A C sieve calling faithful copies of
    all four wrappers in a SEPARATE translation unit linked WITHOUT LTO ran
    8.054 s against plain C's 8.570 s — not slower at all. The wrapper layer
    costs nothing measurable at this scale.

WHAT A FIX LOOKS LIKE (untested, and the reason this stays open). The park
decision needs a second input beyond size: some signal of whether the buffer
is likely to be re-taken before the heap churns underneath it. Unevaluated
options — evict a parked buffer back to the allocator once N unrelated
allocations pass without a take; or decline to park while the small-allocation
rate is high. Any such change has two oracles, and must satisfy both:
`bigbuf.kara` must stay ~6.8x faster than cache-off (the win the cache
exists for), and `sieve_only.kara` must reach C parity (the loss it causes).

SCOPE — this is not a #3629 fact. Any program that repeatedly builds and drops
a >= 1 MiB buffer while allocating many small ones in between pays it. #3629
is simply the first kata whose shape exposed it.

PROBES PRESERVED: docs/spikes/buf-cache-park-pessimization.md
(sieve_only.kara/.c and bigbuf.kara, with the measurement tables and the
LLVM-elided-probe caveat). The scratchpad they were developed in is ephemeral.

── FIXED (507a446, 2026-07-31) — AND THE FRAMING ABOVE IS CORRECTED. ──

THE EARLIER "kara defect" FRAMING WAS WRONG. This entry previously called the
cause "the cache's size-only park decision", implying a kara defect. A pure-C
reproduction refutes that reading: `sieve_only.c` with the factors array
RETAINED across iterations (the exact park analogue, same allocator, same
access pattern) costs 8.312 s -> 15.153 s = 1.82x, with no kara involved at
all. And kara tracked C in BOTH configurations to within 5 ms:

    C, free-each        8.312 s        kara, cache OFF   9.104 s
    C, HOLD            15.153 s        kara, cache ON   15.148 s

So kara's codegen and runtime were never underperforming. Retaining a large
buffer across many small allocations is slow for EVERY language on glibc; the
cache's only role is to steer programs into it.

LOCALIZED: it is the SMALL allocations that degrade, not the zeroing or the
freeing. Per-phase timing of the two C variants (50 rounds):

    phase        free-each     hold
    zero/alloc     0.164 s   0.127 s
    sieve build    5.283 s  11.385 s   <- the entire 6.1 s gap, 2.15x
    free inner     2.618 s   3.036 s

THE FIX: `malloc_trim` on park, asking glibc for the consolidation
housekeeping a large `free` would have prompted. Three gates:

  * SMALL_CHURN — a load-then-store flag set by karac_free_buf's small-buffer
    fast path, swapped-and-cleared at park. Only programs that interleave
    small allocations with the parked buffer pay the trim. Without this gate
    the pure large-buffer ping-pong loses ~30% (306 -> 398 ms) trimming an
    arena with nothing in it. Load-then-store (never an unconditional store)
    so the line stays shared-clean and multi-threaded hot paths do not
    ping-pong a cacheline.
  * `target_env = "gnu"` — musl has no malloc_trim and CI builds this crate
    under rust:alpine.
  * called AFTER the cache spinlock is released, so glibc's arena lock is
    never taken while holding ours.

TRIM_PAD = 64 MiB rather than 0: the consolidation is what fixes the
small-alloc path, while actually releasing the pages only buys a re-fault
storm next round (sieve system time 0.04 s -> 1.17 s at pad 0, 0.92 s at
pad 64 MiB; wall 9.705 s -> 9.420 s).

BOTH ORACLES GREEN AT ONCE:

    sieve_only   15.510 s -> 9.420 s     1.75x -> 1.14x vs C
    bigbuf       cache win 6.79x -> 7.22x (no cost to the shape the cache
                 exists for)
    sinks byte-identical: 50 / 1025000 / 24350

VERIFIED: cargo fmt clean; cargo clippy --all --all-targets clean; 360
karac-runtime unit tests; codegen E2E 2693 passed / 0 failed; memory_sanitizer
883 passed / 0 failed (Linux, LSan active).

FOUR HYPOTHESES DIED BEFORE THIS ONE, all measured not argued: the
mmap-threshold / mallopt nudge (MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_ and
MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_ change nothing — bigbuf stays ~2.1 s with the cache off
either way); eviction keyed on cache operations (park and take alternate once
per iteration, so a parked buffer is never "stale" by that measure); THP (set
to `madvise` on this host, so neither config gets huge pages); and the opaque
wrapper-call layer (refuted by the no-LTO C ablation, 8.054 s vs 8.570 s).

STILL OPEN, TRACKED SEPARATELY BELOW THIS LINE:

  1. The ~1.09x residual between kara-cache-off and C is UNCHANGED by this fix
     and remains unexplained. It is small, and it is not the buffer cache.
  2. PLATFORM GAP: `malloc_trim` is glibc-only. macOS and musl keep the old
     behaviour, so the pessimization persists there. Gated rather than guessed
     at a portable equivalent — no measurement exists for what those
     allocators need, and this bug has already cost two rounds to unmeasured
     mechanism claims.

title: VecDeque.pop_front is O(n) (memmove per pop), making a DEEP queue drain O(n^2) — fixed by a head-index lowering for eligible locals (767x on a depth-25k queue); NOT the cause of B-2026-07-30-4, whose frontier is shallow
detail:
`VecDeque[T]` shares `Vec[T]`'s `{ptr, len, cap}` codegen layout
(codegen/types_lowering.rs:269) -- there is NO head index -- so `pop_front` cannot just
advance a head. codegen/vec_method.rs:3488 instead emits, and its own comment says so,
`memmove(data, data + 1, (len - 1) * sizeof(elem))` on every pop. Each pop_front is O(n),
so draining a queue of n elements is O(n^2). A VecDeque's entire reason to exist is O(1)
push_back/pop_front, so this is a silent algorithmic-complexity trap: the code looks right,
the asymptotics are wrong, and nothing warns.

MEASURED (scratchpad dq.kara -- push_back n tuples, then drain; single round):
  n= 2000    14 ms
  n= 4000    45 ms   (3.2x)
  n= 8000   173 ms   (3.8x)
  n=16000   666 ms   (3.85x)
Time quadruples per doubling of n. Textbook O(n^2). A 2.5M push+pop probe did not finish
inside 120 s; O(1) pops would put it near 25 ms.

THIS IS THE ROOT CAUSE OF B-2026-07-30-4 (#3629 bfs_sieve, 2.89x vs rust_ovf / 2.45x vs
c_v3 -- the corpus's largest genuine deficit and the only kata trailing C). That kata is a
BFS over n=50000 with `queue: VecDeque[(i64,i64)]`, run 50 times. Rust's VecDeque and C's
hand-rolled ring buffer are both O(1); Kara's queue drain alone is ~n^2/2 = 1.25e9 element
moves per BFS. The four hypotheses ruled out in B-2026-07-30-4 (the sieve, nested-Vec push,
Map entry/or_insert/push, index-into-index reads) were all correct to rule out -- the cost
was never in them.

BLAST RADIUS, corrected by measurement -- NARROWER than the asymptotics suggest. 10 katas
reference VecDeque; 3 use it as a real queue (#226 invert-binary-tree, #133 clone-graph,
#3629). Only #3629 is actually hurt:
  #226 iterative/recursive   0.89x / 0.90x vs rust_ovf   (Kara AHEAD)
  #133 clone_bfs seq         0.95x         vs rust_ovf   (Kara AHEAD)
  #3629 bfs_sieve seq        2.89x         vs rust_ovf   (the only victim)
The quadratic only bites once the queue gets DEEP. #226 is a tree BFS and #133 a graph BFS
whose frontiers stay small, so n^2 on a short queue is invisible; #3629 queues up to n=50000.
So this is a latent trap that scales into a wall, not a broad current regression -- which is
an argument for fixing it before a deeper-queue kata lands, not for treating it as urgent
across the corpus.

FIX IS A LAYOUT CHANGE, NOT A ONE-LINER. Making pop_front O(1) needs a head offset, i.e. a
4th field, which would stop VecDeque sharing Vec's 24-byte shape. The comment at
types_lowering.rs:269 documents why that sharing is load-bearing: without it the baked
`struct VecDeque[T] {}` falls through to `llvm_type_for_name`'s unknown-name arm, sizes an
escaped-binding parent slot at 8 bytes, and the par branch then stores a 24-byte aggregate
there and corrupts the neighbouring alloca (the known Map+VecDeque co-existence repro).
So the options are (a) give VecDeque its own 32-byte {ptr,len,cap,head} layout and audit
every site that currently assumes Vec-compatibility, or (b) keep the layout and amortize --
e.g. drain-from-the-back semantics or a periodic compaction -- which is cheaper but does not
give true O(1). (a) is the correct fix. Do NOT try to make pop_front O(1) by advancing the
data pointer in place: the allocation base is needed for free, and push_back would realloc
from the wrong address.

Found by probe bisection, not profiling -- the measurement container has no perf.

PAYOFF MEASURED (2026-07-30), so the layout refactor can be costed against a real
number rather than a guess. Same workload, same sink (2500000000): push 50,000 pairs
then drain, VecDeque vs a manual head-index queue (two Vec[i64] + an integer head,
which is what an O(1) ring-buffer VecDeque would cost):
  VecDeque (memmove per pop)   6.282 s +- 0.066
  head-index queue (O(1))      2.0 ms  +- 0.1
= 3141x. The quadratic term is the entire runtime of this shape at n=50k; there is
essentially nothing else in it.

Sanity bound for #3629: that kata's Kara total is 24.9 s against Rust's 8.6-10.1 s, its
sieve accounts for ~0.8 s, and the other three probed constructs are all fast, so the
deque drain plausibly accounts for the great majority of the 24.9 s. Expect the fix to
move #3629 from 2.89x-behind to at or ahead of Rust -- but that is an inference from the
bound, not a measurement; re-bench the kata after the fix rather than quoting a
predicted figure.

── INVESTIGATION 2026-07-30 (reproduction confirmed; cost estimate corrected) ──

1. REPRODUCTION THRESHOLD — this entry's own numbers cannot be reproduced as written, and
a re-prober who tries will wrongly conclude NOT-REPRODUCED. Two traps:

   (a) A probe with a LITERAL argument measures nothing. `drain(2000)` is closed-formed by
   LLVM to n(n-1)/2 -- the deque, the mallocs and the memmoves are all optimized away. My
   first probe printed the four correct sums in 0.018 s TOTAL. The loop bound must come
   from an opaque source; `Env.args().len()` works.

   (b) With `i64` elements the quadratic is invisible at this entry's n. Defeating the fold
   and re-running n=2000/4000/8000/16000 still gives 0.022 s total. Measured with an opaque
   bound:  n=50000 -> 0.200 s,  n=100000 -> 0.772 s  = 3.86x for a 2x input. Textbook
   O(n^2), but you need n>=50k to see it. This entry's 14/45/173/666 ms at n=2000..16000
   must come from the TUPLE element type (bigger memmove per pop); state the element type
   when quoting them.

2. THE FIX IS NOT A LAYOUT REFACTOR — IT IS A REPRESENTATION PROJECT. This entry says
`VecDeque[T]` shares `Vec[T]`'s layout, which is true but understates the cost. Codegen has
NO VecDeque IDENTITY AT ALL: the string `deque` does not appear anywhere in `src/codegen/`.
`extract_vec_elem_type` (types_lowering.rs:895) files `Vec` and `VecDeque` into the SAME
`vec_elem_types` map, and `llvm_type_for_type_expr` / `llvm_type_for_name` return
`vec_struct_type()` for `String | str | StringSlice | VecDeque | Vec | CString` alike.
`pop_front` reaches its arm by METHOD NAME, not by receiver type, so codegen never needed
the distinction and never recorded it. Consequently "add a head index" requires FIRST
threading VecDeque identity through binding / param / struct-field / closure-capture /
mono-substitution registration, and only THEN changing the layout -- with 199
`vec_struct_type()` call sites as the blast radius and silent heap corruption as the
failure mode (precisely what the types_lowering.rs:264 comment warns about for the
mis-sizing direction). Cost this as an architectural slice, not a bug fix.

3. A DESIGN THAT SIDESTEPS BOTH. This entry rejects advancing the data pointer because
"the allocation base is needed for free, and push_back would realloc from the wrong
address". Both objections are escapable WITHOUT changing the layout, by keeping the head
offset OUTSIDE the value:

   - Advance `ptr` on pop_front and decrement `cap` with it, so `ptr` is always the live
     head and `ptr + cap*sz` is an invariant (the allocation end). Every shared Vec read
     path -- index, iterate, len, pop_back, contains, sort -- then stays correct BY
     CONSTRUCTION, which is what makes this cheap: no shared site changes.
   - Keep `head` in a codegen-side ALLOCA, one per eligible binding, never in the struct.
     Nothing about the value's 24-byte shape changes, so no copy/size site can lose it.
   - Gate on a local ESCAPE CHECK: eligible = a VecDeque local with `pop_front` called on
     it that is never passed by value, returned, stored into an aggregate, captured by a
     closure or par block, or aliased by ref. An escaping deque keeps today's memmove, so
     the fallback is the current (correct) behaviour.
   - Two interception points, both bounded: (i) free -- scope-exit drop for an eligible
     binding frees `ptr - head*sz`; (ii) growth -- compact to base and reset head before
     any realloc. Growth is NOT a shared helper (it is inlined per arm at vec_method.rs
     :2615 and :2750, plus the String grow at :104), so the arms are enumerable.
   - Growth interception is REQUIRED, not optional: #3629's BFS interleaves push_back with
     pop_front, so an eligible deque will hit the grow path with head > 0.

   This is sound for the non-escaping case and covers the reported workload. It does NOT
   retire the general trap -- an escaping deque stays O(n^2) -- so closing this entry on
   the gated fix must leave a follow-up for the escaping case, or say plainly that the
   trap survives outside the gate.

"baked-stdlib impl bodies are neither resolved nor type-checked — only the signatures
are the contract"; 354 of 439 stdlib fns are `#[compiler_builtin]` placeholders. Real
executing Kara lives in `GATED_STDLIB_SOURCES`, keyed by module path and reached only
via an explicit `import std.x` (that is what `embeddings.kara` is). There is no
auto-import or always-splice mechanism. Moving VecDeque there would make
`import std.vec_deque` MANDATORY — a breaking change for every existing user. Viable
only bundled with new always-splice infrastructure, which is its own slice.

THE SHAPE THAT WORKS — a FIELD-COMPATIBLE SUPERSET: `{ ptr, len, cap, head }`, where
ptr/len/cap are at their Vec offsets and describe exactly the LIVE elements, and `head`
is the element offset from the allocation base. The invariant that makes it cheap:
`ptr` ALWAYS points at the live head, so GEP indices 0/1/2 mean what every shared Vec
arm already assumes and the entire Vec read surface — index, iterate, len, pop_back,
contains, sort, Slice coercion — keeps working BY CONSTRUCTION, unmodified. Contiguity
is preserved, which is also why a true wrapping ring buffer is the wrong answer here
despite being the textbook one: wrapping breaks contiguity and takes the whole shared
surface down with it.

  pop_front:  ptr += sz; len -= 1; cap -= 1; head += 1        -- O(1)
  push_front: head > 0 ? (ptr -= sz; head -= 1; len += 1; cap += 1) : compact/grow
  free:       base = ptr - head*sz
  growth:     compact to base (reclaiming the head gap), reset head = 0, then grow

Only free and growth read `head`; nothing else in the compiler needs to know. Growth
interception is REQUIRED not optional — #3629's BFS interleaves push_back with
pop_front, so an in-use deque reaches the grow path with head > 0.

DESIGN NOTE — the tempting contained fix is UNSAFE. RULED OUT (2026-07-30).
The obvious way to get O(1) pop_front WITHOUT changing the {ptr,len,cap} layout is to
keep a head counter in a header inside the allocation: malloc(cap*sz + 16), keep `ptr`
pinned at base+16 so free is `free(ptr - 16)`, store head at base+0, and address element
i as ptr[head + i]. pop_front then becomes head++ / len--, genuinely O(1), and the struct
shape is untouched so no slot sizing changes.
It does not work. Vec, VecDeque and String all lower to the SAME LLVM struct
({ptr,i64,i64}), and `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct` discriminates by LLVM type identity, so the
GENERIC recursive-drop path cannot tell a deque buffer from a vec buffer. It would emit
free(ptr) where the deque needs free(ptr - 16) -- freeing 16 bytes into a live
allocation. That is heap corruption on every deque drop reached through generic cleanup
(Vec[VecDeque[T]] elements, struct fields, escaped bindings), and it is silent.
Every free site would have to know the static type, and the generic drop path by
construction does not.
So the distinct 4-field {ptr,len,cap,head} layout is not merely the cleaner option, it is
the only correct one: the discriminating LLVM type is what lets drop/cleanup do the right
thing. Budget the refactor accordingly (~171 VecDeque references in codegen, and
llvm_ty_is_vec_struct plus every `"Vec" | "VecDeque"` match arm needs auditing).

── DESIGN LANDED, LOWERING PENDING (2026-07-31). ──

The eligibility gate is implemented, tested and on main (`src/deque_head.rs`,
`deque_head::eligible_deque_locals`). No lowering change yet, so this is still a
no-op at runtime — the gate went first because a rule that is too loose there is
a miscompile, not a slow program. 10 unit tests, 7 of them rejections.

WHY NOT THE 4-FIELD LAYOUT, settled by inspection rather than estimate. With
three fields you provably cannot have both ends O(1) — you need two independent
indices plus cap. But `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct` (types_lowering.rs:621) decides
"is this a Vec/String buffer" by LLVM TYPE IDENTITY, and Vec, VecDeque and
String are the same type today. Adding a field forks that: either the 69
`llvm_ty_is_vec_struct` sites stop recognizing deques (their drops silently
skip — a leak), or they keep matching and every generic element walk reads
`data[0..len]` when the live range starts at `head` (a UAF for element types
with drop glue). Plus 199 `vec_struct_type()` construction sites. That is a
whole-backend change and it is why this stayed open.

THE CONTAINED ALTERNATIVE. Keep the layout; give codegen a private `head`
counter (an i64 alloca beside the deque's slot) for locals where it is provably
invisible. Eligibility: a `let mut` local declared directly in the function body
and initialized in place by `VecDeque.new` / `with_capacity`; POD element type
(so the untouched scope-exit cleanup stays a bare `free(ptr)` — this is what
avoids the generic-drop surgery entirely); used ONLY as receiver of
push_back / pop_front / len / is_empty; never mentioned inside a closure or
`par` region (those copy the aggregate to a frame where the head does not
exist). Everything else keeps today's memmove lowering, so the optimization can
only cost performance, never correctness.

THE REMAINING STEP, and it is smaller than it first looks. Re-interpret `len`
for an eligible deque as the END INDEX rather than the count — live range is
`data[head..len]`, count is `len - head`. Then:

  * push_back      UNCHANGED. It already writes at `len` and bumps it, and
                   already grows when `len == cap`. This is the whole reason to
                   pick this formulation.
  * pop_front      read at `head`; `head += 1`. No memmove. <- the fix
  * len/is_empty   return `len - head` / `len == head`
  * scope exit     UNCHANGED (`free(ptr)`; ptr is still the allocation base)
  * grow path      one added branch: when `len == cap` and `head > 0`, compact
                   (memmove the live range to 0, `len -= head`, `head = 0`)
                   instead of doubling. Amortized O(1), and it is what bounds
                   memory by live depth rather than by total enqueues — without
                   it a long-running queue would grow without bound.

So the codegen delta is: a `head_slots: HashMap<String, PointerValue>` side
table, an entry-block alloca + zero-store per eligible local, three method arms

on #3629. That is the honest shape of it: this bug is real, worth fixing, and
was never #3629's problem.

RETRACTION. The 2026-07-31 entry above ("RESTORED TO PRIMARY CAUSE ... the
14f99d7 falsification was wrong") is itself wrong, and 14f99d7 was right. Its
estimate was 2.7% of #3629's excess; the measured answer is ~4%. I overturned a
correct conclusion.

THE ERROR, so it is not repeated: I read INSTRUCTION COUNTS as a proxy for time.
Callgrind attributes 41.82% of #3629's instructions to memcpy, and the ablation
removes 406M of them (-41.6%) — both facts are true and reproducible. But
valgrind counts the ERMS `rep movsb` path per BYTE, so a bandwidth-bound,
L1-resident copy inflates to a huge instruction count while costing very little
wall clock. 41.6% of instructions turned out to be 4% of time. The supporting
wall-clock number I quoted (1.779 s -> 1.300 s, 1.37x) came from a heavily
loaded container AND compared two different karac vintages; neither survives a
clean A/B on one build.

Rule of thumb worth keeping: callgrind is excellent for LOCALIZING a cost and
useless for SIZING one when the cost is a bulk memory operation. Confirm with
wall clock, on a quiet host, toggling one variable.

INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION (session 01P2Hq5ojJ2qxkMoRq31zTQU, same build, quiet host): the QUADRATIC-DRAIN class this bug was filed about is decisively fixed — a 400k-element push-then-drain went 26.6 s -> 9 ms wall clock and scales linearly across 50k/100k/200k/400k (5/5/6/8-9 ms) under the default auto-par build, so the retraction above (bandwidth-bound memcpy on #3629, ~4% of time) and the drain win are both true: callgrind mis-SIZED the kata cost, but deep FIFO drains really were O(n^2) and are now O(n) amortized. Nine probe shapes (full/partial/interleaved drains, pop-to-empty-then-push, two-deque, ineligible returned/param/indexed, read-only-group) valgrind 0 errors with three-way interp/JIT/AOT parity. Test battery landed with the B-2026-07-31-35 fix commit: e2e_deque_head_fifo_semantics + e2e_deque_ineligible_shapes_slow_path (+ interp twins), asan_deque_head_frees_base_once. CAVEAT cross-ref: as first landed, 60733f7 ICE'd `karac build` for eligible deques in auto-par-split functions — filed and fixed as B-2026-07-31-35.

title: CRASH (run-vs-build): an `Array[T, N]` REF PARAM forwarded to a `Slice[T]` parameter segfaults under `karac build` while the interpreter is correct. `fn via(a: ref Array[String, 3]) -> String { first(a) }` with `fn first(s: ref Slice[String]) -> String { s[0] }` prints the element under `--interp` and SIGSEGVs (139) built; the JIT fails too (exit 1, no diagnostic). NOT generic-specific and NOT part of B-2026-07-30-3 — it reproduces with a CONCRETE `ref Slice[String]` callee on the non-generic path that has carried B-2026-06-19-1's fix since June, which is why it is filed separately. ROOT CAUSE: that fix synthesizes the `{ptr,len}` header for Array sources, but its gate tested only `variables[name].ty` for an LLVM `ArrayType`. That holds for an owned Array LOCAL and is FALSE for an Array `ref` param, whose alloca holds a `ptr` — the declared array type lives in `ref_params` instead. So the forward fell through to `get_data_ptr`, handing the callee a pointer to the raw elements, and it read `ptr = elem0, len = elem1` — the same bogus slice -06-19-1 documents. `coerce_to_slice` already had a correct `ref_params` ArrayType arm, so only the GATE was wrong. FIX: both call sites (call_dispatch.rs and the mono path in mono.rs) now share one `arg_is_array_source` predicate that accepts either spelling, so the two gates cannot drift apart again.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-07-30-3's fix against shapes beyond the original probe matrix — an Array param forwarding to a generic `ref Slice[T]` still crashed after both of that entry's defects were fixed, and reducing it to a concrete callee showed the fault was never generic-specific. Confirmed to reproduce on plain `main` with no change of mine involved. Regression test `e2e_array_ref_param_forwarded_to_slice_param_gets_a_real_header` covers the generic callee, the concrete callee, and a `len()` read (the silent-wrong- answer direction: len comes back as elem1); confirmed failing at baseline. INVESTIGATION NOT DONE: no ASan run. Unknown whether a `mut ref Array[T, N]` param, or an Array param forwarded through TWO hops, behave the same way — both plausible given the gate was purely about how the array's type is spelled, but neither was probed.

title: A PLAIN type alias whose base is not `i64`-shaped, used as a parameter or return type, lowers to the `i64` unknown-name fall-through in codegen: `type Plain = Vec[i64]; fn total(xs: Plain)` passes `karac check` and `karac run --interp` but fails LLVM module verification under `karac build` / `karac run` (JIT). A REFINEMENT alias over the same base works.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO (three files; `check` accepts all of them):

  // (a) generic plain alias — BUILD FAILS
  type Plain[T] = Vec[T];
  fn total(xs: Plain[i64]) -> i64 { let mut t = 0; for x in xs { t = t + x; } t }
  fn main() { let v = vec![1, 2, 3]; println(total(v)); }
  // error: codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Call parameter type
  //   does not match function signature!  %v1 = load { ptr, i64, i64 } ...
  //   i64  %call = call i64 @total({ ptr, i64, i64 } %v1)"

  // (b) NON-generic plain alias — SAME FAILURE, so this is not about generics
  type Plain = Vec[i64];
  fn total(xs: Plain) -> i64 { ... }

  // (c) plain alias over String — same class, hits the return position too
  type Name = String;
  fn shout(n: Name) -> String { n }
  // error: "Function return type does not match operand type of return inst!"

CONTROLS THAT PASS, which localize it precisely:
  * `type Count = i64; fn bump(n: Count) -> i64 { n + 1 }` BUILDS and runs —
    the alias base is already `i64`-shaped, so the fall-through happens to be
    the right layout. That is why this has stayed invisible: the aliases people
    write in tests are mostly newtype-ish integer aliases.
  * `type NonEmpty[T] = Vec[T] where self.len() > 0;` — the REFINEMENT sibling
    of (a) — builds and runs correctly. Codegen resolves refinement aliases
    through its `refinement_base` / `refinement_generic_params` maps
    (`src/codegen.rs` ~1164-1193, and `tests/codegen.rs::test_ir_refinement_
    over_string_matches_base_layout` pins exactly the non-`i64`-base layout arm
    that this bug is missing). Plain aliases have NO equivalent map, so the
    paradox is that adding a `where` clause FIXES the program.
  * `karac run --interp` prints the right answer for every case above.

So the failure axis is (plain alias) x (non-`i64` base) x (param/return
position), and the likely fix is the plain-alias twin of the existing
refinement-base map: populate an alias->base layout map before
`build_struct_types` / signature lowering, the same ordering fix the
refinement arm already needed.

SEVERITY high on divergence, not on blast radius of a wrong ANSWER: it is a
loud LLVM verification failure, never a silent miscompile. But `karac check`
reporting 'All checks passed' on a program `karac build` cannot compile is the
run-vs-build class this repo treats as high, and `type Name = String` is an
entirely ordinary thing to write.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced as the CONTROL in B-2026-07-29-26's own repro — the
`where`-free `type Plain[T] = Vec[T]` arm that was supposed to demonstrate
correct behavior type-checked but would not build. Pre-existing and untouched
by that fix (no `Type::Refinement` is involved); confirmed against 5445e85.

FIXED (b528fa2). Root cause exactly as filed: codegen kept a base map for the
REFINEMENT arm of `Item::TypeAlias` and none for the plain arm, so a plain
alias name fell through to `llvm_type_for_name`'s unknown-name `i64` default.
The fix is the plain-alias twin of that map, populated from the same
`populate_type_alias_bases` pass — which already runs before
`register_struct_metadata` / `build_struct_types`, so the ordering the
refinement arm once needed was in place.

  1. `plain_alias_bases` / `plain_alias_generic_params` (`src/codegen.rs`) —
     the `where`-free siblings of `refinement_bases` /
     `refinement_generic_params`, filled from the same loop's `else` arm.
     TAIT aliases (`type X = impl Trait;`) are excluded: the RHS has no
     layout to project and is still `E_TAIT_NOT_IMPLEMENTED_YET` at
     witness-required use sites, so peeling to it would only obscure that
     diagnostic.
  2. All four sites that peeled a refinement now peel a plain alias too, and
     were renamed to say so: `llvm_type_for_type_expr`, `llvm_type_for_name`,
     `refinement_base_name` -> `type_alias_base_name`, and
     `resolve_refinement_alias_te` -> `resolve_type_alias_te`. The
     `TypeExpr`-level arm additionally SUBSTITUTES the use-site generic args
     into the base (`Plain[i64]` -> `Vec[i64]`) rather than lowering the
     uninstantiated base — a strict improvement the refinement arm inherits.
  3. `register_struct_metadata` (`src/codegen/declarations.rs`) peels the
     alias before writing `struct_field_type_names` /
     `struct_field_type_exprs`. Found while widening the repro: the reported
     param/return failure is only half the surface — a FIELD declared through
     an alias recorded the ALIAS name, so `h.pt.x` (field `pt: Pt`,
     `type Pt = Point;`) died in `field_index_for` with "cannot resolve field
     'x' on this receiver", and an alias-typed `String`/`Vec` field was
     invisible to drop synthesis. A struct's own generic params shadow a
     same-named global alias here (`type T = String;` next to
     `struct S[T] { v: T }`), matching the `type_subst`-first precedence
     `llvm_type_for_name` already applied.
  4. `prune_cyclic_type_aliases` — a guard the peel newly requires, not part
     of the reported defect. Nothing upstream rejects `type A = A;`,
     `type A = B; type B = A;`, or `type Vec = Vec[i64];`, and peeling those
     recurses forever. Entries on a base-name cycle are dropped at population
     time, so such a program falls back to the bounded (wrong) unknown-name
     layout instead of overflowing the compiler's stack. Covers refinements
     too, where the same hazard was already latent.

VERIFIED: all three filed arms (generic alias, non-generic alias, `String`
alias reaching the return position) build and run, AOT output byte-identical
to `--interp`. Widened checks agree across both lanes for aliases over
struct / tuple / Map, alias CHAINS, enum-variant payloads, `shared struct`
fields, `Vec[Alias]` iteration, method dispatch on an alias-typed receiver,
and the generic-param shadowing case.

PINNED: `tests/codegen.rs` — `test_ir_plain_alias_over_string_matches_base_
layout` and `test_ir_plain_alias_over_vec_matches_base_layout` (IR-level, the
plain twins of `test_ir_refinement_over_string_matches_base_layout`),
`test_e2e_plain_alias_param_and_return` (the filed repro),
`test_e2e_plain_alias_struct_field_and_nested_access` (the field leg), and
`test_e2e_plain_alias_chain_and_cycle_are_bounded` (chain peel + cycle
guard). `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_plain_alias_struct_fields_no_leak`
covers the leak / double-free pair on either side of the struct-field peel.

title: Auto-par's early-exit gate declines a reduction for a `break`/`continue` that targets a NESTED loop and therefore cannot exit the reduction body at all -- the idiomatic `loop { match cur { Some(n) => ..., None => break } }` list walk never fans out
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while building the probe for B-2026-07-30-1. The first probe used the
idiomatic list-walk shape and did not fan out even after that bug's analyzer fix; rewriting
the walk as `while cur.is_some() { let n = cur.unwrap(); ... }` -- semantically identical, no
`break` -- made it fire. The analyzer had already recognized the reduction in both versions;
the decline is in CODEGEN.

MECHANISM. `try_emit_reduction_lowering` bails on `block_has_early_exit(&shape.body)`
(src/codegen/reduce.rs). The rationale is sound as stated: "early exits in the (post-stripped)
body would cross the worker-fn boundary and generate `ret <T>` inside a void worker fn ->
invalid IR." But `expr_has_early_exit` returns true for `Return | Break | Continue` at its
FIRST arm, and separately RECURSES into nested `While` / `For` / `Loop` bodies. So a `break`
that belongs to a loop nested inside the reduction body -- one that provably cannot transfer
control out of the body -- is counted as an early exit of the body.

REPRO (both bodies compute the same thing over the same `shared` list; only the walk differs):
  loop { match cur { Some(n) => { acc = acc + n.val; cur = n.next } None => break } }   0 karac_par_* DECLINES
  while cur.is_some() { let n = cur.unwrap(); acc = acc + n.val; cur = n.next }         1 karac_par_* FIRES
Measured on the second form: 400000 iterations x 12-node list, 0.10 s -> 0.04 s wall, 100% ->
~330% CPU. The first form gets none of that.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS ONE SHAPE: `loop { ... break }` is how you write a walk over an
`Option`-linked structure in Kara today (`while cur.is_some()` costs an extra `unwrap`), and
the whole point of B-2026-07-30-1 was to unblock exactly the per-iteration-list-build-and-fold
family. The two gates compose to leave the most idiomatic member of that family sequential.

LIKELY FIX: make the classification control-flow aware rather than shape-blind. An unlabeled
`break` / `continue` is an early exit of the BODY only if it is not enclosed by a nested loop
within the body; a LABELED one is an early exit iff its label is bound outside the body.
`Return` stays unconditional. The nesting depth is already available at the recursion site --
`expr_has_early_exit`'s `While` / `For` / `Loop` arms are where a nested-loop flag would be
set. Strictly a precision improvement; keep the current behaviour as the fallback for anything
the label analysis cannot resolve, since the failure mode it guards is invalid IR.

Related: B-2026-07-30-1 (the analyzer-side gate that had to be fixed before this one became
observable), B-2026-07-16-6 (the soundness gate that started the family).

── FIXED 2026-07-30 (3993c2e) ──
As the entry's LIKELY FIX predicted: made the classification control-flow-aware rather than shape-blind. `block_has_early_exit`/`expr_has_early_exit` (src/codegen/reduce.rs) now thread `(depth, labels)` — `depth` counts loops nested WITHIN the reduction body, `labels` the labels those nested loops bind. A `break`/`continue` is a BODY escape iff it targets the reduction loop: unlabeled at `depth == 0`, or labeled with a label NOT bound by a nested loop (so `break 'reduction` from inside a nested loop still escapes). `Return` stays unconditional; loop headers (`while` condition / `for` iterable) check at the current depth since a break there targets the enclosing loop. The idiomatic `loop { match cur { … None => break } }` walk now fans out. Verified: the nested-loop-break reduction emits `karac_par_reduce` and prints byte-identical to sequential (interp / auto-par ON / OFF all agree), valgrind identical to a pre-existing firing reduction (thread-pool baseline, definitely-lost 0); a break DIRECTLY in the body still declines. par_codegen 202 / codegen 2632 / memory_sanitizer 867 green; fmt + clippy clean. Tests `test_ir_reduction_fires_with_break_in_nested_loop` + `test_ir_reduction_declined_for_direct_break_in_body`. NOTE: kept as the deliberate fallback — a labeled break/continue whose label the walk cannot resolve to a nested loop still counts as an escape, since the failure it guards (a body escape emitting `ret` in a void worker fn → invalid IR) is loud.

title:
`println` is not line-atomic across tasks: it emits TWO separate `write_console` calls (payload, then the newline), so two spawned tasks printing concurrently interleave into `12

` instead of `1
2
` -- makes tests/spawn_e2e.rs::test_spawn_fan_out_five_tasks_all_join flaky (~1 in 3 on a 4-core container)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by a full `cargo test --features llvm` run while working B-2026-07-30-1.
Unrelated to that change -- the failing program has no `shared` type and no reduction loop.

OBSERVED. `tests/spawn_e2e.rs::test_spawn_fan_out_five_tasks_all_join` spawns five tasks, each
`println(n)` for n in 1..=5, and asserts the printed set is {1,2,3,4,5}. Failing run printed:

  12
  <blank>
  3
  5
  4

parsed as {12, 3, 4, 5}. Re-ran the test three times in isolation: pass / FAIL / pass.

MECHANISM, CONFIRMED IN CODEGEN (not inferred from the output). `emit_nul_safe_write`
(src/codegen/control_flow.rs) writes the payload with one `write_console` call and then, when
`nl` is non-empty, emits a SECOND `write_console` call for the newline global. Each call locks
stdout on its own (`std::io::stdout().lock()` per call in the runtime), so the lock is
released between the two. Two tasks racing there produce payload-A, payload-B, newline-A,
newline-B -- exactly `12\n\n`. A single `println` is therefore atomic only for its payload,
never for the line.

WHY IT IS LOW AND NOT MEDIUM: it garbles interleaved output, it does not corrupt memory or
change computed results, and the auto-par paths that matter most already avoid it -- the
parallel-branch arm of `write_console` CAPTURES bytes for ordered replay at the join rather
than writing inline (the "auto-par never changes what your program prints" invariant). It is
the EXPLICIT-concurrency surface (`spawn` / `TaskGroup`) that writes straight through.

LIKELY FIX: make the line one write. Either append the newline into the payload buffer before
the single `write_console` (cheap for the f-string/Display arms, which already render into an
owned accumulator -- the literal-backed `cap == 0` case would need a copy), or give
`write_console` a `trailing_newline: bool` parameter so the runtime emits both under ONE
stdout lock. The second is smaller and covers every arm uniformly, at the cost of a runtime
signature change (all five archives rebuild).

NOTE the test would still be correct under the fix -- it asserts a SET, deliberately not an
order, since spawn order is not output order. The flake is purely the mid-line interleave.

── ATTEMPTED 2026-07-30, REVERTED — fix WORKS but exposes a latent leak that turns a green ASAN test red ──

MECHANISM CORRECTION. This entry says each call takes `std::io::stdout().lock()`. It does NOT. `karac_runtime_write_console` (runtime/src/lib.rs) calls raw `fwrite` on a `FILE*`; the lock is glibc's internal per-`FILE` lock, held for the duration of ONE `fwrite` and released between calls. Same race, different primitive — and it rules out the entry's suggested runtime-signature fix in favour of making the line ONE write.

SECOND CORRECTION, and the one that decides the design: a runtime-side fix would not even be REACHED by the flaking program. `finalize_write_console_wrapper` (src/codegen.rs) emits `__karac_write_console` as an inline `fwrite` whenever the program uses no `par` — the runtime chokepoint is only called when auto-par capture is needed. `spawn`/`TaskGroup` does not trip that, so the spawn test takes the inline path. The fix has to be in CODEGEN.

WHAT WAS BUILT, AND IT WORKS. A `__karac_write_console_line(data, len, nl, nl_len, stream)` internal wrapper: stage payload+newline into one function-scoped uninitialised 4 KiB alloca (two `memcpy`s, no allocation), then ONE `__karac_write_console` call — which feeds both the inline-`fwrite` path and the capture path unchanged. Lines over the buffer fall back to the original two writes. `emit_nul_safe_write` routes there only when `nl` is non-empty, so `print` keeps its single plain call. MEASURED: the five-spawned-task probe went from 14 garbled runs in 60 to 0 in 60. Oversized (4500-byte) lines, `print` vs `println`, and interp/AOT parity all verified; valgrind clean. Suites: codegen 2634, spawn_e2e 3, par_codegen 202, cli 507, interpreter 1327 — all green. Two IR regression tests written.

WHY IT WAS REVERTED. It makes `memory_sanitizer::asan_fnret_drop_temp_arg_passthrough_and_discard_single_fire` fail with a 47-byte leak. Investigated to root cause, and the leak is NOT in the println path — see the new entry B-2026-07-30-12. In short: before the change that test's program performs ONE heap allocation in total (the 4 KiB stdio buffer); the `Guard.name` strings are never allocated, because LLVM elides the whole malloc/free set. Staging adds a `memcpy` that reads the payload, which blocks that elision for this shape, so the allocations materialise — 3 × 47 bytes for 2 Guards, one of them never freed. The test has therefore been passing VACUOUSLY for this allocation class.

STATUS: the fix is ready to re-land as-is the moment B-2026-07-30-12 is fixed. Nothing about the println design needs to change; it was reverted only because landing it would turn a green test red, and a red suite on main is worse than a known cosmetic flake.

── FIXED 2026-07-30 (36a7fa5). Re-landed unchanged the moment its blocker cleared. ──

The reverted design needed no revision. B-2026-07-30-12 was fixed in 3ee768a and
`memory_sanitizer` went green (868/868) with this change applied, exactly as the
revert note predicted. Re-measured after re-landing rather than trusted: the
five-task fan-out probe went 10 garbled runs in 60 -> 0 in 60 (the earlier
attempt measured 14/60; same order, the rate is container- and load-dependent).

SHIPPED SHAPE. `__karac_write_console_line(data, len, nl, nl_len, stream)`,
internal linkage: two `memcpy`s into one function-scoped 4 KiB uninitialised
alloca, then a SINGLE `__karac_write_console`. `emit_nul_safe_write` routes there
only when the newline is non-empty, so `print` keeps its single plain call.
Over-buffer lines fall back to the original two writes -- correct, not atomic.
Emitted by `finalize_write_console_line_wrapper`, which MUST run after
`finalize_write_console_wrapper` (it calls that wrapper, whose body first has to
decide inline-`fwrite` vs capture from whether `par` is used anywhere).

THE LOAD-BEARING DESIGN POINT, restated because it is the one a re-reader will
want to undo: this belongs in CODEGEN, not the runtime. A `trailing_newline`
parameter on `karac_runtime_write_console` is smaller and DOES NOT WORK --
`finalize_write_console_wrapper` inlines `fwrite` directly whenever the program
uses no `par`, so the runtime chokepoint is never reached on precisely the
spawn-only programs that flake. Staging in front of that wrapper covers the
inline arm and the auto-par capture arm both, and needs no runtime-ABI change,
so none of the five archives rebuild.

A fixed alloca rather than a malloc because this is on every `println`; a
heap allocation per line would be a real cost on print-heavy paths.

VERIFIED BEYOND THE PROBE: a 4502-byte line takes the fallback and round-trips
byte-identically; interp and AOT output are md5-identical across print, println,
empty-line and oversized cases; valgrind clean. Suites: codegen 2636,
memory_sanitizer 868, spawn_e2e 3, cli 545, par_codegen 202, interpreter 1329,
concurrency 134, coro_e2e 34, wasm_codegen 3, typechecker 2105, ownership 381,
drop_differential 13, selfhost_codegen.

TESTS: `test_ir_println_fuses_payload_and_newline_into_one_write` and
`test_ir_print_without_newline_keeps_plain_write`, asserted on the emitted CALL
SHAPE rather than by running the program -- deliberately. The bug is a race: a
passing run proves nothing, and the pre-fix program passes most of the time
(50 of 60). The call shape is the invariant; the flake was only ever a symptom.

The entry's original "LIKELY FIX" text is left above for provenance but is
superseded on both counts -- the `stdout().lock()` mechanism was wrong (it is
glibc's per-`FILE` lock inside `fwrite`) and the runtime-signature option it
preferred is the one that cannot work.

title: `Result[T, E].clone()` is still rejected at typecheck (`no method 'clone' on type 'Result'`) after B-2026-07-29-31 gave `Option[T]` a callable one — codegen has no in-place deep-copy helper for Result's inline payload, so admitting it would emit a SHALLOW copy that aliases the source buffer.
detail:
Held back DELIBERATELY while closing B-2026-07-29-31, not overlooked.

REPRO:
  fn main() {
      let r: Result[String, i64] = Result.Ok("x");
      let c = r.clone();          // no method 'clone' on type 'Result'
  }
`Option[String]` in the same position now works.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST AN ALLOWLIST ENTRY. `Result` shares `Option`'s `{tag, w0, w1, w2}` inline-payload overlay, and `type_supports_clone` already answers TRUE for it — so the typechecker half is a one-line change. The backend half is not there: `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`'s `Option` arm routes to `emit_option_value_clone_fn`, which is `Option`-specific (it reads the `Option` layout and its `Some` tag, and calls `deep_copy_option_inline_payload_in_place`). `Result` falls to the generic enum arm, whose `emit_enum_clone_fn` returns None on the TYPE-ERASED layout — `field_drop_kinds` records no heap for the erased payload — and the dispatcher then takes `emit_primitive_clone_fn`, a plain load+store. For `Result[String, _]` that aliases the source's `{ptr,len,cap}`: both drops free it. The `Option` arm's own comment already records this ('`Result` has the same shape but no in-place deep-copy helper yet — it stays on the shallow path').

FIX SHAPE: a `emit_result_value_clone_fn` twin of `emit_option_value_clone_fn` (tag-guarded deep copy of whichever half is live, reusing `deep_copy_result_inline_heap_halves_in_place`, which already exists for the param entry-copy), then add `Result` back to `clone_receiver_self_type`'s allowlist and to the codegen aggregate arm in `try_compile_clone`. Interpreter needs nothing — `deep_clone_value` already covers `Value::EnumVariant`, so `Result.clone()` would work under `--interp` the moment typecheck admits it, which is exactly why the typecheck gate must stay until codegen catches up.

SEVERITY low: the workaround is a fresh `let` binding or a `match` + rebuild, and nothing miscompiles today — the gate is a clean rejection on every surface.

── FIXED 2026-07-30 (4b5f811) ──
Codegen half: `emit_result_value_clone_fn` (clone_drop.rs), the Result twin of `emit_option_value_clone_fn` — shallow-copy the whole `{tag,w0,w1,w2}` value, then rewrite the live half in place via the existing `deep_copy_result_inline_heap_halves_in_place`. Self-gates on `result_field_direct_vecstr_halves_ok`: returns None for a heap-free or uncovered-half Result so the shallow path (exact only when heap-free) is taken.
