title: let-else with a moved Drop-bearing enum payload: the interpreter runs the payload's Drop body TWICE (once BEFORE the binding is even used) while AOT runs it once with the wrong owner — a live cross-backend divergence, not a silent-in-parity residual.
detail: PROBE (scratchpad b3011_letelse.kara): `struct Res { id } impl Drop; enum Box2 { Full(Res), Empty }; let w = Box2.Full(Res { id: 52 }); let Full(r2) = w else { println("nope"); return }; println(f"bound {r2.id}"); println("end")`. Interp prints a / drop 52 / bound 52 / drop 52 / end (body twice, the first BEFORE the binding use); AOT prints a / drop 52 / bound 52 / end (once, but fired by w's enum-payload walk at w's NLL while r2 — the payload's new owner — is still live; r2's own slot never fires). Baseline-verified with the overnight session's src/ changes stashed: PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by the B-2026-07-30-11 legs. Both backends are wrong differently: the let-else destructure-move should retract w's payload walk (the disarm the match/if-let sites run) and give r2 a real Drop slot firing at r2's NLL end — after `bound 52`. Correct output: a / bound 52 / drop 52 / end. WHERE: codegen compile_let_else (src/codegen/control_flow.rs ~513) lacks both the disarm and the current_variant_payload_bindings hook the match/if-let sites have; interp's let-else path apparently runs the source walk AND some binding-side fire without retraction (hence the double) — trace which two channels fire when taking this. The bindings ESCAPE into the enclosing scope (no arm frame), so the adoption mechanism differs from match/if-let: the binding must join the ENCLOSING block's cleanup slots. SOURCE NOTE: found while probing the if-let leg, 2026-08-01 overnight session; b3011_letelse.kara + b3011_wletelse.kara in the session scratchpad. FIXED 2a8f4a7: interp LetElse arm gains the disarm_moved_out_enum_payload_one call (retracts the source's walk; the escaped binding's existing slot is the single, correctly-placed fire); codegen compile_let_else gains the owned-variable suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup arm (match-edge only) + the current_variant_payload_bindings hook around bind_pattern_values. Both backends now print a / bound 52 / drop 52 / end; miss edges verified; tests e2e/test_let_else_moved_payload_single_drop (proven failing pre-fix). RESIDUAL NOTED on B-2026-07-30-11's list, not here: an enum-CTOR call argument's Drop payload (check(E2.B(Res { id: 55 })) whose callee drops the enum whole on the divergent edge) stays silent in parity — the arg-position sibling shape.

title: Chained get/first().unwrap() then len() on a fresh-temp Vec[Vec[scalar]] receiver double-frees the borrowed row: let n = mk_rows().first().unwrap().len(); aborts (free(): double free detected) under AOT while the interpreter prints the length.
detail: mk_rows() -> Vec[Vec[i64]] (two pushed rows); let n = mk_rows().first().unwrap().len(); AOT aborts with glibc 'free(): double free detected in tcache 2' (exit 134); interp prints 3. PRE-EXISTING: reproduced on ff3c218 with the B-2026-07-31-43 fix stashed, and the -43 fix neither worsens nor masks it (scalar row-elements are deliberately not recorded in temp_recv_len_elem_types, so the new path never fires here). MECHANISM (two independent trackers free the same row buffer): (1) the typechecker records the fresh-temp receiver's element type (Vec[i64], pod-vec) for first() in temp_recv_elem_types, so codegen's try_compile_freshtemp_vec_read_method materializes mk_rows() and drop-tracks it with the per-element vec-struct recursion — outer buffer plus EACH ROW buffer freed at frame exit; (2) .unwrap() reconstructs the borrowed row as a {ptr,len,cap} value (cap>0, aliasing the tracked storage), the len intercept's expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp admits the chain (MethodCall, not a borrow-returning Call — is_borrow_returning_call_expr only knows free fns), owned_temp_drops has no entry (span-collided chain), and materialize_owned_temp's degrade path track_vec_var(slot, None) frees the SAME row buffer again. Candidate fixes: teach the len-family intercept (and materialize_owned_temp callers generally) to refuse a receiver whose chain already routed through the freshtemp-read materialization (e.g. a span-keyed 'receiver already tracked' set), or classify unwrap-of-borrow chains as borrow-returning in expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp. NOTE the sibling shape Vec[Vec[String]] fails closed instead (first() on the non-recorded element type loud-bails 'no handler for method first on non-identifier receiver') — documented deferral, no UB. SOURCE NOTE: found probing hazard shapes for the B-2026-07-31-43 fix, 2026-08-01 overnight session; probe scratchpad/b43_chain1.kara. FIXED 54ac148: narrow structural gate at the len-family intercept — new expr_is_unwrap_of_borrow_accessor(expr) (MethodCall unwrap|expect whose object satisfies the existing scrutinee_is_borrow_call classification: get/first/last, non-Client) short-circuits the drop-track branch, so the unwrapped borrow is never materialized as an owned temp; the get-family materialization's per-element walk remains the single owner of the row storage (valgrind: 0 errors, 0 leaks — the walk frees outer + both rows exactly once). Sibling positions were probed and are ALREADY clean, confirming the intercept was the only borrow-blind consumer: let-binding of the unwrapped row (prints 3, valgrind clean), wildcard discard (clean), and the arg position is REJECTED by the typechecker (expected Vec[i64], found ref Vec[i64] — the checker knows the unwrap result is a borrow, which is also why the codegen-side structural gate is faithful to the type system rather than a heuristic). unwrap_or* variants deliberately excluded from the gate (miss arm substitutes an owned default — branch-dependent ownership, no proven double-free shape). Tests: e2e_len_of_unwrapped_borrow_row_single_free (first/last/get legs, proven ABORTING pre-fix with src/ stashed), asan_len_of_unwrapped_borrow_row_freed_once (200-iteration loop, proven failing pre-fix). Full B-43 probe battery re-verified valgrind-clean post-fix (no interaction with the -43 element-walk tracking).
tracker: src/codegen/method_call.rs (len/is_empty/count intercept, try_compile_freshtemp_vec_read_method, expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp interplay), src/codegen/runtime.rs (materialize_owned_temp)

title: wildcard-let user-enum discard fires the Drop payload body under karac run but not karac build (+ own-Drop-enum and erased-generic sibling divergences)
detail: Probe after the -30-11 user-method leg: `fn mk_enum(n: i64) -> Box2 { return Box2.Full(Res { id: n }); }` (Res has a user impl Drop) with `let _ = mk_enum(21);` — karac run prints 'drop 21', karac build prints NOTHING (bare `mk_enum(22);` was silent in both, an in-parity gap). Root cause: codegen's try_track_discarded_user_drop_temp resolved the enum return type and then returned at the deliberate 'SHAPE 1 stays out of scope' exclusion (the struct field-body walk GEPs parent fields and cannot reach an enum payload), while the interpreter's run_discarded_value_user_drops walked EnumVariant payloads VALUE-driven. The same pre-fix probe matrix surfaced two sibling wildcard-let divergences from that value-driven walk: an own-impl-Drop enum discard fired own body + payload bodies under interp vs own body only under AOT, and an erased-generic payload (enum MyBox[T] { Wrap(T) } instantiated at a Drop struct) fired under interp while codegen structurally cannot see through the erasure. FIXED 6915b47: codegen now registers __karac_dropelems_enum_<E> (declared-type-driven, BODIES ONLY) on the one-shot discard frame for a user-enum return — free fns AND user impl methods (the method arm's struct-only return filter widened to enum_layouts, closing the residual the -30-11 user-method leg recorded); the enum drop switch (track_enum_var) is pushed BEFORE the UserDrop body so the LIFO drain runs the body before the payload's heap is freed — the reverse order was caught IN-SLICE printing garbage ('drop 41 dro' instead of 'drop 41 h41') with valgrind Invalid reads on a String-carrying payload, the same ordering rule the ctor arm documents ('pushed AFTER the battery so the LIFO drain runs them before the battery's frees'). Interp: run_discarded_value_user_drops' EnumVariant arm split three ways — Option/Result keep the value-driven recursion (codegen twin: track_discarded_optres_payload_bodies, instantiation-driven), own-impl-Drop enums run their OWN body only (matching codegen's karac_drop_<E> wrapper and the enum-assign leg's exclusion), all other user enums take the extracted declared-type-driven run_enum_payload_user_drops_value walk — and the bare-statement StmtKind::Expr arms (Call + MethodCall) gained the enum leg. Post-fix all four quadrants (wildcard-let x bare, run x build) match the struct behavior: concrete payloads fire everywhere, erased generics are silent everywhere (their heap is still freed — valgrind 'all heap blocks freed' via the mono enum drop switch), own-Drop enums are own-body-only everywhere. user_method_returns_owned_struct renamed user_method_returns_owned_type (admits enum returns). Tests: e2e_enum_return_discard_runs_payload_body + test_enum_return_discard_runs_payload_body twins (identical source and expected string covering all shapes incl. the String payload that pins the LIFO ordering; both proven failing with src/ stashed); six-probe three-way parity sweep (interp/AOT/JIT identical) with valgrind zero-error on every AOT binary. SOURCE NOTE: self-directed session probe (b154 family), 2026-08-01 overnight session.

title: enum reassign never frees the displaced payload's interior heap — Full(Res{name: String}) leaks the old String on every assignment (DCE-masked until the payload bodies walk made the value live)
detail: Found while probing the own-Drop enum reassign leg of B-2026-07-30-11: `let mut a = mk(1); a = mk(2);` over `enum SBox { Full(Res), Empty }` with `Res { id: i64, name: String }` leaked the displaced payload's String (valgrind: definitely lost, one block per reassign). The Assign arm's eager-free ladder had Vec/String, Map/Set, tensor and struct legs but NO enum leg, so the old value's interior heap was orphaned by the store. Masked two ways until now: (1) in trivial probes LLVM DCE deletes the dead allocation chain entirely, so valgrind reports nothing — the earlier enum-assign leg's memory probe ('SBox.Full(String) reassign: all heap blocks freed') was this mask, its DIRECT String payload never being read after displacement; (2) once the enum-assign bodies walk (97712c2) made the old payload live, the leak surfaced in any Drop-struct-payload shape. FIXED fff43cb: the assign-site block runs the tag-dispatched `__karac_drop_<E>` switch (emit_enum_drop_switch) on the old slot AFTER the payload bodies, BEFORE the store — cap-guarded, so a moved-out (cap-zeroed) payload and a payload-free variant both no-op, and the binding's scope-exit EnumDrop reads the slot after the store, covering only the new value. Verified: sbox/m1 probes 'all heap blocks freed', 5-shape matrix valgrind zero errors, no double-free with the bodies reads (bodies run first). RESIDUAL, pre-existing and in-parity: the pass-roundtrip shape `e = pass(e)` (arg move disarms the binding's EnumDrop; the mentions-guard correctly skips displacement; nothing re-arms the memory action for the returned value) still leaks one payload String — probe b155_m4, 2 bytes/run, output identical on both backends. Tests: memory_sanitizer asan_enum_reassign_displaced_payload_heap_freed (LSan leak gate on Linux, proven failing with src/ stashed) + the e2e sequencing twins above. SOURCE NOTE: self-directed session probe (b155 family), 2026-08-01 overnight session. PASS-ROUNDTRIP RESIDUAL CLOSED (6d95ba7): `e = pass(e)` no longer leaks — the leak was one corner of the wider caller-retained roundtrip class, filed and fixed as B-2026-08-01-9 (memory-only eager free of the old slot when the RHS is an owned-returning user call; struct twins and field/ref-mention shapes leaked identically and are covered).

title: fresh Drop-bearing call-arg temp in let position fires its body at scope exit (owned param) or never (ref param) under karac build; the interpreter fires at statement end
detail: Probe family b156 (while sweeping the -30-11 receiver-temp residual): `let x = consume(mk(1));` — the interpreter runs the fresh arg temp's Drop body as the call returns (run_fresh_temp_arg_drops, the statement-end placement design.md's temps-die-at-statement-end rule implies), but karac build registered the __owned_agg_tmp UserDrop on the enclosing SCOPE frame, so the body printed after every later statement's output (after 'end'); and `let y = peek(mk(2));` (fresh rvalue to a `ref` param) never fired at all — queue_ref_rvalue_arg_cleanup had Vec/String and Map/Set legs but no struct/enum leg, so no body was ever registered. Bare-statement shapes were already correct (the one-shot discard frame). FIXED d88686c: (1) drain_statement_temp_user_drops — compile_block and the auto-par sequential arm snapshot the scope frame's length before each statement and, after it, fire+retire exactly the temp-named UserDrop actions pushed during it (__owned_agg_tmp / __refarg_tmp), LIFO, before the NLL fires; firing a wrapper early is safe for the same reason fire_due_user_drops' NLL placement is (the temp is dead; passthrough registrars never register an escaping value). Memory-channel actions and named bindings are untouched. (2) queue_ref_rvalue_arg_cleanup gains the struct/enum leg: a fresh owned Drop-bearing rvalue borrowed by the callee registers under __refarg_tmp (wrapper for own-impl-Drop, field-bodies walk for transitive, declared-type payload walker + EnumDrop for value enums, plus track_struct_var memory). RESIDUALS, recorded: a STRUCT LITERAL rvalue to a ref param (`peek(Res { .. })`) still fires under interp only — it routes around the patched path (silent under AOT, next leg); and the RECEIVER-temp class is B-2026-08-01-5 (open). Tests: e2e_fresh_arg_temp_drop_fires_at_statement_end (proven failing with src/ stashed — pre-fix output had drop 1 r1 trailing after 'end' and no drop 2 r2 at all) + test_fresh_arg_temp_drop_fires_at_statement_end (interp parity pin, passes pre-fix by design). Probes: b156_ref three-way parity (interp/AOT/JIT) + valgrind zero errors, all heap freed. SOURCE NOTE: self-directed session probe (b156 family), 2026-08-01 overnight session. RESIDUAL CLOSED (7f6db7e): the struct-LITERAL rvalue to a ref param (`peek(Res { .. })`, let and bare) now fires on karac build too — the refarg leg's freshness gate used expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp, which only admits Call/MethodCall shapes; a literal is fresh by construction and is now admitted explicitly. Three-way parity (interp/AOT/JIT), valgrind zero errors, all heap freed. Tests: e2e_struct_literal_ref_param_arg_drop (proven failing with src/ stashed — pre-fix fully silent) + test_struct_literal_ref_param_arg_drop (interp parity pin).

title: fresh method-RECEIVER Drop temps: interp never fires their bodies, karac build fires them at scope exit — and owned-self passthrough chains DOUBLE-fire with stale slots
detail: Probes b156_recvtemp/b156_chain (2026-08-01 session; full design notes in the session state file). `let x = mk(1).ident();` (ref-self method on a fresh Drop-bearing receiver): the interpreter fires NO receiver-temp body ever (run_fresh_temp_arg_drops has no method-receiver sibling), while karac build's __urecv_tmp materialization (method_call.rs try_compile_user_method_on_fresh_temp region, track_user_drop_var registered unconditionally for fresh owned receivers) fires it at SCOPE EXIT — after 'end'. Worse, owned-self methods whose result flows onward multiply: `mk(3).me().ident()` where `fn me(self) -> Res { return self; }` printed 'drop 3 r3' TWICE at exit (receiver temp + result temp both tracked over the same conceptual value), `let y = mk(2).me();` printed r2's body at y's death AND again at exit, and `mk(1).plus(10)` (rebuild) printed a STALE-slot body ('drop 1 r1' after the value had become id 11). Memory is valgrind-clean throughout — the divergence is body observability. HAZARDS for the implementer, probed this session: (a) the karac_drop_<T> wrapper is body+MEMORY for structs, so any statement-end drain of __urecv_tmp must exclude borrow-RETURNING methods (user_ref_method_names) — freeing the receiver at statement end dangles a returned borrow that today survives to scope exit; (b) the owned-self registration needs a returns-self/passthrough guard (the fn_returns_param analog for receivers) or must be dropped entirely — the interpreter's silent-for-owned-self behavior is the current parity direction; (c) any interp receiver hook must admit exactly the codegen-registrable shapes (declared-type rule). Suggested target semantics (struct twin + design.md): ref-self fresh receivers fire at statement end on both backends; owned-self receiver temps stay silent on both (the callee consumed the value); passthrough results covered by the result consumer only. SOURCE NOTE: self-directed session probe (b156 family), found while probing the -30-11 receiver-temp residual. FIXED 79f99b0 (struct receivers): the target semantics landed exactly as designed above. Codegen: the __urecv_tmp tracking is now self-mode-gated via impl_method_self_and_borrow_return (program-snapshot scan, impl target head + method name -> (SelfParam, returns-borrow)) — only a ref self / mut ref self method that does not return a borrow registers the user-Drop body, under the drain-eligible __urecv_drop_tmp name (fires at statement end via drain_statement_temp_user_drops); owned-self and borrow-returning methods are memory-only (track_struct_var), which removes ALL three chain pathologies (double fire, re-fire after the binding's own death, stale-slot fire). Interp: new run_fresh_recv_temp_drop hook in try_eval_impl_method's success path — fresh receiver shapes (Call to user fn / ctor, struct literal), ref-self only, borrow-return excluded (new method_returns_borrow helper), STRUCT values only. RESIDUALS, deliberate and in-parity: chain-link receivers (MethodCall objects) stay body-silent on both backends; ENUM receivers stay out of the hook entirely — a ref-self method that matches on self and binds the payload fires the interpreter's match-arm channel already, an interp-only fire now filed as B-2026-08-01-6 (adding the walk here double-fired interp-side, caught in-slice by probe b157_enum); generic-impl receivers resolve to no SelfParam and stay memory-only. Tests: e2e+test_fresh_recv_temp_drop_semantics and e2e+test_owned_self_chain_no_double_drop (3 of 4 proven failing with src/ stashed; the interp chain twin passes pre-fix by design — parity pin). Probes: b156_recvtemp/b156_chain/b157_test all interp/AOT/JIT identical, valgrind zero errors.

title: match on a borrowed `ref self` enum receiver binding the Drop payload fires the payload body under karac run only (arm channel treats the borrowed view as owning)
detail: Probe b157_enum (found in-slice while landing B-2026-08-01-5): `enum Box2 { Full(Res), Empty }` with `fn tag(ref self) -> i64 { match self { Box2.Full(r) => { return 1; } ... } }` called on a FRESH receiver (`mk_e(5).tag()`) — the interpreter prints 'drop 5 e5' once (the B-2026-07-30-11 match-arm channel fires the bound payload r's body at arm end, treating the binding as an owning move-out even though the scrutinee is a BORROWED self view), karac build prints nothing. Pre-existing on both sides of the -5 work (verified by stash: identical divergence before the receiver-temp legs). Note the same borrowed-self match shape presumably fires for a ref-self method called on a NAMED binding too (the arm channel keys on the value, not the receiver's freshness) — scope the fix at the arm channel's scrutinee classification: a match on `self` under a ref/mut-ref receiver is a borrow, its arm bindings are views, and the body belongs to the receiver's real owner. The -5 fix deliberately keeps ENUM receivers out of both backends' receiver-temp hook until this is settled, so fixing this row unlocks that leg too. SOURCE NOTE: self-directed session probe (b157 family), 2026-08-01 overnight session. FIXED 1881798: scrutinee_expr_is_consuming is now receiver-mode-aware — a `self` scrutinee is consuming only under an OWNED receiver, read from the new Interpreter::self_param_stack (pushed/popped around each impl-method body in try_eval_impl_method via the existing method_self_param lookup; empty outside method context, where `self` cannot occur). Under `ref self` / `mut ref self` the match arm's payload bindings are borrowed views whose bodies the receiver's real owner fires, matching karac build exactly: the fresh-receiver shape (mk_e(5).tag()) is now silent on both backends and the named-binding shape (let bx = mk_e(8); bx.tag()) fires exactly once via bx's own walk (pre-fix interp printed drop 8 e8 TWICE — stash + walk). While probing the owned-self arm of the gate, found a SEPARATE in-parity double-fire filed as B-2026-08-01-7. Tests: test_ref_self_match_borrowed_payload_silent (proven failing with src/ stashed — pre-fix output had the spurious drop 5 e5 and the doubled drop 8 e8) + e2e_ref_self_match_borrowed_payload_silent (codegen parity pin, passes pre-fix by design). Probes: b157_enum/b158_test three-way parity, valgrind clean; b155/b156/b157 probe sweeps unchanged.

title: owned-self method matching its payload out double-fires the payload Drop body — on BOTH backends (receiver binding's walk + the arm channel each fire once)
detail: Probe b158_ownmatch (found while fixing B-2026-08-01-6): `fn into_id(self) -> i64 { match self { Box2.Full(r) => { return r.id; } ... } }` called on a named binding (`let b = mk_e(7); let v = b.into_id();`) prints 'drop 7 e7' TWICE under karac run AND karac build alike — the receiver binding b's let-site payload walk fires once (nothing disarms it when the value moves into the owned-self method), and the arm-channel stash inside the method fires the bound r once more. In-parity (class `other`, not run-vs-build — the defect is a double Drop-body observation, memory is valgrind-clean since the walks are bodies-only). Correct behavior: exactly one fire — the move into an owned-self method should disarm b's walk the same way `let c = b;` does (disarm_container_bodies_move_sources / the codegen retraction twin), leaving the arm channel as the sole owner. Fix wants BOTH backends' receiver-move disarm extended to owned-self method calls on Drop-payload enum bindings; keep the B-2026-08-01-6 gate (self consuming under Owned) so the arm channel keeps firing. SOURCE NOTE: self-directed session probe (b158 family), 2026-08-01 overnight session. FIXED a598112: exactly the fix direction the row proposed — the move into an owned-self method now disarms the named enum receiver's payload-bodies walk on both backends, leaving the method-internal arm channel as the payload's sole owner (kept consuming under Owned by the B-2026-08-01-6 gate). Codegen: at the identifier-receiver user-method dispatch (`Type.method` resolution in compile_method_call), an Owned self mode (impl_method_self_and_borrow_return) on a value-enum receiver calls suppress_container_elem_bodies_for_var — the same retraction `let c = b;` takes. Interp: try_eval_impl_method inserts the receiver into moved_out_container_bodies_bindings at dispatch when self_param is Owned and the receiver value is an EnumVariant (the reassign rearm hook clears it as usual). Post-fix: `b.into_id()` fires 'drop 7 e7' exactly once (the arm), and a NON-consuming owned-self method (`c.just_three()`) is silent on both — the consumed value's drop is the documented owned-self residual, consistent with the fresh-receiver convention from B-2026-08-01-5. STRUCT receivers deliberately untouched: probe b159_ownstruct shows the established in-parity single fire via the binding's walk. Tests: e2e+test_owned_self_enum_receiver_single_fire (BOTH proven failing with src/ stashed — the pre-fix output shows the double 'drop 7 e7' and the walk-only 'drop 8 e8'). title: reassigning a struct/enum binding from a call that mentions it (`e = pass(e)`, `s = mk(s.id + 1)`) orphans the old value's heap under karac build — the mentions-guard assumed a move the caller-retains convention never makes
detail: Probe family b163 (chasing B-2026-08-01-3's recorded pass-roundtrip residual, which turned out to be one corner of a wider class): for `x = f(...x...)` over a heap-carrying non-shared STRUCT or value ENUM, the Assign arm's displacement legs skip the old value's eager free whenever the RHS mentions the target (expr_mentions_name_deep — 'moved into the callee, uncertain => silent'). But the old value never moves: an owned arg is deep-copied at CALLEE ENTRY (the caller-retains convention — IR shows the p14e dcopy region cloning the payload and the callee freeing its copy), a ref arg only borrows, and a scalar field read consumes nothing. The store then overwrites the only pointer to the original buffers — a hard leak, one block per reassign, on EVERY mention shape probed: owned-arg roundtrip `e = pass(e)` (enum, 2 bytes/run — the recorded -3 residual), struct `s = pass_res(s)` (with AND without impl Drop), ref-param mention `s = peekmk(s)`, scalar-field mention `s = mk(s.id + 1)`. DCE-masked in probes whose old payload is never read (constant f-strings lower to cap==0 statics — probe hygiene note: interpolate to force real heap). Vec/Map/Set/tensor LHS shapes are NOT affected (their reassign legs free the old handle without a mentions gate — probed clean). Output was already in three-way parity (the NLL channel fires the bodies once at the binding's last-use statement on both backends); only memory diverged. FIXED 6d95ba7: the struct and enum displacement legs admit the mentions case when the RHS is a free-fn Call to a top-level USER function returning an owned value (assign_rhs_is_owned_user_call — declines borrow-returning callees, whose result could alias the old heap, and names shadowed by locals), and fire MEMORY ONLY: emit_struct_drop_synthesis for structs (never the body+memory wrapper — the NLL fire already covers the body) and the cap-guarded __karac_drop_<E> switch for enums (bodies section skipped). Cap-guards make the eager free robust against RHS-internal moves: a legitimately moved heap field was cap-zeroed by the move machinery, so the free no-ops on exactly what left. Post-fix: three-way parity (interp/AOT/JIT) with output unchanged on all 9 b163 probes + valgrind 'all heap blocks freed / 0 errors' on every one; b154-b162 probe corpus re-swept (2 pre-existing flags recorded separately — bare user-enum ctor discard divergence and bare struct-call discard leak, see the b164 follow-up). RESIDUALS, recorded: MethodCall RHS (`s = other.build(s)`) and non-call mention shapes (if/match tails) keep the conservative silence — leak-side. Tests: asan_roundtrip_reassign_frees_displaced_original (LSan gate, proven failing with src/ stashed — LeakSanitizer detected the orphaned buffers) + e2e/test_roundtrip_reassign_single_nll_fire (output pins on both backends). title: struct destructure of an owned param (`let Holder { r } = h;` in the callee) fires the bound field's Drop body a second time under karac run only
detail: Probes b165_c7/c9 (found mapping the -30-11 ctor-arg landscape): a callee that destructures its OWNED by-value struct param fired the bound field's Drop body TWICE under the interpreter — once at the destructured binding's death inside the callee, once via the caller's own fire (identifier arg: the caller binding's NLL fire; fresh literal arg: the fresh-arg temp fire) — while karac build fired exactly once, caller-side. title: Assign-based param rebind (`h2 = h;` onto a pre-declared local) double-fires the Drop body on both backends and silently skips the displaced value's body under karac build
detail: Probe b169_assign_rebind (the second recorded B-2026-08-01-15 residual — the b168 param-view rebind gate covers Let/LetElse only, and this probe confirms Assign escapes it): callee `fn take(h: Holder) { let mut h2 = Holder { r: Res { id: 9, .. } }; h2 = h; println(f"held {h2.r.id}"); }` where Res has a Drop body. AOT actual: 'a|held 5|drop 5 y5|take done|drop 5 y5|end' — TWO defects: the displaced 'drop 9 z9' NEVER fires (the struct-assign displacement channel loses the old value's body when the RHS is a param identifier), and the same double body. Backends also diverge from each other (interp fires the displacement, AOT doesn't), so `karac run` vs `karac build` disagree twice over. Memory is BALANCED on both backends (valgrind: 5 allocs 5 frees, 0 in use at exit; no leak, no double-free) — this is purely Drop-body observability, sibling of the -15 class. Not affected: whole-move LET rebinds (let h2 = h) and enum-param LET rebinds both verified clean same-session (probe b169_enum_rebind: single caller fire, parity OK, heap clean). SOURCE NOTE: 2026-08-01 overnight session, probing the -15 residual list immediately after closing it. FIXED e0fc863 (two legs, and the displaced-body leg turned out GENERAL — a plain local reassign `a = Holder{5}` over `Holder{9}` also freed z9's heap silently under AOT while the interpreter printed the body; probe b169_local_displace). Tests (both proven failing with src/ stashed): e2e_assign_param_rebind_and_displaced_bodies (tests/codegen.rs), test_assign_param_rebind_and_displaced_bodies (tests/interpreter.rs). title: SortedSet[DropT] element Drop bodies drain in INSERTION order under karac build, sorted order under the interpreter (plain Set diverges too)
detail: Found by the b169 drop-arc parity sweep (probes b151_set / b152_set / b152_sset, retained from the B-2026-07-30-11 Set-elements leg, 854ccef): `let mut s: SortedSet[Res] = SortedSet.new(); s.insert(Res{id:6}); s.insert(Res{id:5});` at scope exit prints 'drop 5|drop 6' under the interpreter (sorted order — the container's defined iteration order) but 'drop 6|drop 5' under karac build (insertion order — the AOT element-bodies walk drains the backing storage, not the sorted view). Proven PRE-EXISTING: reproduced identically with b169's src/ changes stashed, so it dates from the 854ccef Set-elements leg or earlier — the landed tests evidently assert line SETS, not order. Plain Set[T] shows the same run-vs-build divergence (drop 5|drop 6 interp vs drop 6|drop 5 AOT), though for an UNSORTED container the order is arguably unspecified — the divergence itself is still observable behavior. Suggested fix: the AOT SortedSet element-bodies walk should traverse in sorted order (the container's public iteration order); for plain Set, either match the interpreter's order or document element-drop order as unspecified and normalize the interpreter. Low severity: bodies all fire exactly once, memory balanced — ordering observability only. SOURCE NOTE: 2026-08-01 overnight session, b169 sweep. FIXED 96ad40a (both sorted legs, plus a missing-feature unlock the SortedSet leg required). Leg 1, walker order: __karac_dropelems_map_<T> (synth_drop.rs) gains a sorted-order arm for SortedMap/SortedSet — it walks the same karac_map_sorted_keys buffer the for-in lowering uses (SortedSet: bodies run directly on the sorted key copies; SortedMap: each value fetched by key via karac_map_get into a val_size scratch — bodies only, so the copy is exactly as observable as the slot), freeing kbuf+scratch after. Probes b170_smap (i64 keys, insert 6,5,7 → drop 5,6,7) and b170_smap_str (String keys) confirm ascending drains, PARITY OK, valgrind clean. Leg 2, the blocker: every Drop-bearing Set ELEMENT is necessarily a struct, and emit_sorted_key_cmp_fn supported only integer/String keys — struct keys were a loud codegen error ('only integer and String keys sort in codegen'), which also made `for x in sortedset_of_structs` REJECT under karac build. New emit_sorted_struct_key_cmp_fn (collections.rs): field-wise lexicographic in declaration order (derived-Ord semantics, matching the interpreter), int-family + String fields, short-circuit per field; floats/nested structs/enums/generics/ shared still decline with the (reworded) actionable error. b152_sset now drains sorted on both backends — the title shape fixed — and struct-key SortedSet ITERATION compiles and matches interp incl. String tie-breaks (probes b170_sset_iter, b170_multifield: '1 aa1|1 bb1|2 zz2'). JIT verified on the composite twin (no new runtime symbols — archives unaffected). Plain Set/Map keep bucket order BY DESIGN: their iteration order is already backend-divergent/unspecified (the walker's documented rule), so drop order follows; the interpreter's insertion-order drain for plain Set stays a documented, order-insensitive-test surface. Tests: e2e_sorted_container_drop_bodies_key_order (proven failing pre-fix with src/ stashed — bucket order 'drop 7|drop 5|drop 6' + 'tag 6|tag 5'), e2e_sortedset_struct_key_iteration (compile-gated pre-fix; non-vacuity rides the order twin), interp pin test_sorted_container_drop_bodies_key_order. title: Set/SortedSet element with a String field leaks the field buffer at scope exit under karac build (element blob freed, fields never walked)
detail: Found during b170 verification (probe b170_plainset_leak): `let mut set: Set[P] = Set.new(); set.insert(P { a: 2, s: f"zz{2}" }); ...` where `#[derive(Hash, Eq)] struct P { a: i64, s: String }` — valgrind reports one definitely-lost block per inserted element (the String field buffers; 2 elements → 6 bytes in 2 blocks, malloc'd in main). Pre-existing — NOT introduced by the b170 comparator (reproduced with a plain Set and no sorted machinery in play); it only became visible because struct-keyed sets with heap fields were rare before struct keys could sort/iterate under build. Suggested fix: extend the Set/SortedSet scope-exit free to run the per-element struct field-heap synthesizer over the key half (occupied buckets), mirroring the Map value-half field cleanup; the interpreter frees these fine (GC'd values), so this is codegen-only. tracker: src/parser/exprs.rs:379-385 (the `Token::PipePipe` / `Token::AmpAmp` arms of the Pratt infix match), src/parser.rs:635 (`fn error` — the no-replacement helper) vs src/parser/exprs.rs:487 (a sibling site that DOES set `replacement`)
title: `&&` / `||` diagnostics are emitted 2-3x per occurrence and carry NO `replacement`, so `karac fix` cannot apply a one-token substitution the message itself spells out. 11 real mistakes rendered as 24 JSON diagnostics, none machine-applicable.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found on the FIRST `karac check` of examples/sigv4.kara — writing `&&`/`||` out of Rust habit is exactly the mistake a fresh LLM author makes, which is what makes this a wedge issue rather than a cosmetic one.

MEASURED (examples/sigv4.kara, first pass):
  total diagnostics : 24
  distinct sites    : 11
  multiplicity      : every site >= 2x; three sites 3x
  with `replacement`: 0

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS, same two lines of source.

(1) DUPLICATE EMISSION, scaling with expression nesting. Both arms live in the Pratt parser's infix loop, keyed off `self.peek_token()`:
      Token::PipePipe => { self.error("the `||` operator is not used…"); (BinOp::Or, 6, 7) }
      Token::AmpAmp   => { self.error("the `&&` operator is not used…"); (BinOp::And, 8, 9) }
PEEK does not consume, so a given operator token is re-examined once per precedence level the climb unwinds through, and each visit re-emits. The multiplicity therefore tracks chain length: a lone `a && b` doubles, while the 4-operand `||` chain at line 301 of the source that found this emitted THREE copies of each of its four operators. The fix is to emit once per token position — a seen-set keyed on the operator's span, or emitting at the consume site rather than the peek site.

(2) NO MACHINE-APPLICABLE FIX, for the most mechanical substitution in the language. The message already names the replacement verbatim ("use `and` instead"); it is a single-token, context-free rewrite with no ownership or type consequences. But the site calls the plain `self.error(msg)` helper, so the JSON carries no `replacement` key and `karac fix` is a no-op — confirmed by running it: `fix` reprints the errors and changes nothing. The parser HAS the channel (src/parser.rs:157 documents edits hung there; src/parser/exprs.rs:487 is a sibling site that populates `replacement`), so this is an unconverted call site, not missing infrastructure.
This is the B-2026-07-31-31 class — 'mechanical diagnostics that name their own replacement carry no `karac fix`' — which was fixed for the diagnostics that leg enumerated. These two were not in that set. Worth an audit pass over the remaining `self.error(` call sites for others that name a literal replacement in prose.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE WEDGE: the Mend loop feeds structured diagnostics to an LLM and counts what the compiler fixes FOR it. Here the compiler hands back 24 items for 11 mistakes, tells the author the exact answer in prose, and then declines to apply any of it — so a trivially mechanical class lands in the 'fixed-by-llm' bucket instead of 'fixed-by-karac', understating the machine-fix rate while inflating the diagnostic volume the model has to read. Both halves push the measurement the wrong way.

REPRO: any file with a `&&` or `||`. `fn f(a: bool, b: bool) -> bool { a && b }` → two identical diagnostics, neither fixable.

FIXED 28438e8. Both defects, both at the parser's Pratt infix match (src/parser/exprs.rs). (1) DUPLICATE EMISSION: exactly as the row diagnosed — the `Token::PipePipe`/`Token::AmpAmp` arms emitted inside the PEEK-driven operator match, which re-examines the same token once per precedence level the climb unwinds through. The emission now lives at the CONSUME site (after the `l_bp < min_bp` break, immediately before `self.advance()`), which runs exactly once per source token — one diagnostic per occurrence, no seen-set needed. (2) MACHINE-APPLICABLE FIX: the same consume-site block registers a `fix_edits` TextEdit keyed on the operator token's span (the same span `error()` stamps on the diagnostic, so `collect_diagnostics`' span-join attaches it as `replacement`): `&&` -> `and`, `||` -> `or`, with the word-operator spacing rule from the `!` -> `not` sibling generalized to BOTH sides — a side that abuts its neighbor token gains one space (`a == 1&&b` fixes to `a == 1 and b`), a side with existing whitespace reuses it. title: Vec.filled's calloc fast path only recognises a SCALAR constant zero, so Vec.filled(n, Vec.new()) store-loops an all-zero aggregate instead of calloc'ing it — measured ~100x (117.6 ms vs 1.2 ms on a 1e6-element fill)
detail:
`Vec.filled(n, v)` has a calloc fast path (B-2026-07-08-7) that turns a
statically all-zero fill into ONE lazily-zeroed allocation instead of a
per-element store loop. It fires only for a SCALAR constant zero, so the very
common `Vec.filled(n, <empty collection>)` misses it and writes every element
by hand.

MEASURED (during the B-2026-07-30-4 sub-localization, karac 79757f5d70a6):

    Vec.filled(cap + 1, Vec.new())   kara 117.6 ms
    calloc(cap + 1, sizeof(IntVec))  C       1.2 ms

for the same 1e6-element fill -- a ~100x gap. calloc gets lazily-zeroed pages
from the kernel; kara touches all 24 MB. (In that kata it was only 1.9% of
total runtime, which is why it was set aside rather than chased -- it is a
real gap, not the cause of that bug.)

WHY IT MISSES -- TWO guards in `build_vec_filled`
(src/codegen/collections.rs:1401-1422), and BOTH reject this case, so relaxing
either one alone is not a fix:

  1. `val_is_zero_bits` matches only `IntValue` / `FloatValue` constants:

         let val_is_zero_bits = match val {
             BasicValueEnum::IntValue(iv)   => iv.get_zero_extended_constant() == Some(0),
             BasicValueEnum::FloatValue(fv) => fv.get_constant().is_some_and(|(v,_)| v.to_bits()==0),
             _ => false,          // every struct/aggregate lands here
         };

     `Vec.new()` lowers to the aggregate `{ptr: null, len: 0, cap: 0}` -- all
     zero BYTES, but not an int/float constant, so it falls to `_ => false`.

  2. `needs_clone = !is_trivially_copyable_te(elem_te)` is TRUE for a `Vec`
     element (it owns a heap buffer), and the fast path requires `!needs_clone`.

SUGGESTED FIX (untested). Recognise a statically all-zero-bits AGGREGATE, and
note that the `needs_clone` guard is over-strict for exactly that value: the
per-element "clone" of an all-zero collection handle is the identity -- cloning
an empty Vec/String/Map/Set allocates nothing and copies `{null,0,0}` to
`{null,0,0}` -- so calloc is sound even when the element type is not trivially
copyable, PROVIDED the fill value is statically all-zero.

Guard the relaxation on that provability rather than on the element type: it
holds for empty collections and for `Option::None`, and should NOT be extended
to a bare `shared` handle (all-zero would be a null RC pointer, and a retain on
null is not the identity) -- though no surface syntax constructs that value
today.

SCOPE. Any `Vec.filled(n, <empty collection>)`, which is the natural way to
build an adjacency list / bucket table / grid of rows -- `Vec[Vec[T]]`,
`Vec[String]`, `Vec[Map[K,V]]`. The larger `n`, the larger the gap.

NOT MEASURED SINCE the karac that produced the numbers above; the figures are
from a loaded shared container and are indicative of the ratio, not precise.
A clean re-measure is the first step for whoever takes this. FIXNOTE (2026-08-02): fixed in 0872d65. Re-measure first (per the row): the gap had already narrowed from the filed 117ms to ~20ms vs Rust ~6ms for 1e6 Vec.filled(n, Vec.new()) -- the store loop improved in the interim -- but the per-slot clone loop was still the bottleneck. Fix in build_vec_filled (src/codegen/collections.rs): val_is_zero_bits gains a StructValue arm (ConstantAggregateZero detection via as_value_ref() == const_zero() ref-compare -- runtime-built values never match the uniqued constant, so the arm only fires for statically-all-zero aggregates like Vec.new()/String.new()/Map.new() literals in fill position), and the calloc gate relaxes from `!needs_clone && val_is_zero_bits` to `val_is_zero_bits && !elem_is_shared` -- an all-zero aggregate needs no per-slot clone even when the elem type is heap-bearing, since every slot starts as the same all-zero control block. shared elements stay excluded (RC headers must be per-slot). After: ~6ms, at parity with the Rust baseline. Slot independence + drop pairing pinned by test_e2e_vec_filled_empty_vec_elements_independent + asan_vec_filled_empty_aggregate_fill_and_drop; the calloc lowering itself pinned by test_ir_vec_filled_empty_aggregate_uses_calloc (stash-proven FAILED pre-fix). SPLIT: Vec.filled(n, Map.new()) segfaults under AOT -- stash-verified PRE-EXISTING (crashes identically without this change; interp fine) -- filed separately as B-2026-08-02-12.

THE REJECTION IS CORRECT AND INTENDED, per design.md § Rc vs Arc — Two-Phase
Algorithm, quoted in `src/ownership/concurrent_shared.rs`: `live_range(v) ∩
parallel_region ≠ ∅` AND reachable from > 1 concurrent branch → compile error.
Rc→Arc promotion covers a sole-ownership move into exactly ONE branch. The
reason is refcount traffic, not payload mutation: `emit_rc_inc` is a plain
load/add/store, so even pure READS race on the refcount (this is what B-2026-
07-28-13's SIGSEGV was, from a stale pre-gate binary).

THE GAP. There is no way to express "share this immutable structure across
tasks, read-only, without locks". The two available answers both overshoot:

  * `par struct` + `Mutex[T]` on every `mut` field — the migration the
    diagnostic prescribes. Correct and safe, but it buys mutual exclusion for a
    structure nobody mutates, and every read pays a lock.
  * restructure so each branch owns its own copy — sound, but it means building
    N copies of a read-only structure purely to satisfy the checker.

For the benchmark corpus this has a concrete cost: the C mirror shares the same
read-only graph across pthreads with NO locking, because C has no refcount to
race. So there is no Kāra formulation of this kata that is both legal and
algorithm-matched to its own C mirror — the parity rule and the language rule
cannot both be satisfied. The kata's par lane is withdrawn rather than
published with a lock Kāra conceptually does not need (see the kata README).

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT (all unexplored, listed so nobody re-derives them):

  * An immutable/frozen `shared` handle whose reads emit no RC traffic, hence
    nothing to race. Needs a freeze point in the type system.
  * Admitting the read-only case in `concurrent_shared.rs` when every branch use
    is provably a read AND the retain/release for those uses is elided. NOTE:
    the existing `src/rc_elide.rs` machinery does NOT already do this — it is a
    per-FUNCTION param analysis (`nonescaping_param_names`, fail-closed), not a
    par-capture analysis. It is cited here as precedent for "read-only + non-
    escaping ⇒ RC traffic is skippable", not as an implementation that covers
    this case.
  * An arena / index-pool representation (`Vec[Vec[i64]]` adjacency, indices
    instead of handles) sidesteps RC entirely and is trivially shareable. This
    is the corpus's existing idiom for the same problem (#222 index-pool tree,
    #234 index-pool list) and is the recommended user-level answer TODAY — but
    it is a different program, not a fix to the restriction.

SEVERITY. Low as a correctness matter (the gate is sound and the diagnostic is
good, carrying a machine-applicable fix_diff). It is filed because it is a real
expressiveness hole that costs a benchmark lane and has no non-overshooting
workaround.

IMMUTABLE fields is exactly that mechanism, it is lock-free, and the compiler
says so in the diagnostic for a `mut` field:

    error[typecheck]: `mut` field `x` of `par struct Pt` must be `Atomic[T]` or
    `Mutex[T]`: a `par struct`'s concurrent-safety guarantee is structural, so
    plain mutable fields are not permitted. Wrap the field type in `Atomic[...]`
    for lock-free access or `Mutex[...]` for locked compound mutation, or drop
    `mut` to make the field immutable (IMMUTABLE FIELDS ARE FREELY READABLE
    ACROSS TASKS)

VERIFIED (scratchpad parimmut.kara): a `par struct Pt { x: i64, y: i64 }` read
by FOUR concurrent `par` branches — no Mutex, no Atomic, no annotation at the
use site — checks clean and produces identical correct output on interp and
AOT. So the "both available answers overshoot" framing was wrong: only the
`mut`-field case needs a lock, and `Atomic[T]` covers the lock-free scalar case
even then.

WHY THE `shared struct` GATE IS RIGHT, which this entry also under-explained.
RC atomicity is a property of the TYPE, not of a binding: codegen picks
`emit_rc_inc` (plain load/add/store) vs `emit_arc_inc` (atomic) from the type.
`ownership/par_capture_classify.rs`'s `SharedRc` mode already emits one ATOMIC
inc per branch with a balancing atomic dec, so the captured ROOT handle could be
made safe by relaxing the gate — but that is not sufficient. A branch traversing
the structure retains/releases the NESTED handles it walks, and those are
ordinary `shared struct` values whose inc/dec are non-atomic. Two branches
walking one graph therefore race on the interior nodes' refcounts regardless of
how the root was captured. That is precisely B-2026-07-28-13's SIGSEGV. Making
this safe requires the whole reachable graph to be atomically refcounted, which
IS what `par struct` means. Relaxing the gate alone would reintroduce the race.

WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS — a much narrower gap: there is NO FREEZE POINT. A type
that needs post-construction mutation to be BUILT (a cyclic graph must link its
nodes after they exist, so `mut neighbors: Vec[Node]`) cannot afterwards be
declared immutable. It must carry `Mutex[Vec[Node]]` for its whole lifetime,
including a purely read-only phase, and `Atomic[T]` does not help because the
field is compound. A `freeze`/`finalize` operation transitioning a value from
mutable-construction to immutable-shared is the missing piece — and only for
COMPOUND fields, since scalar mut fields already have the lock-free `Atomic[T]`
answer.

CONSEQUENCE FOR #133, unchanged in outcome but for a corrected reason: its par
lane stays withdrawn not because "Kāra cannot share read-only" (it can) but
because THIS type needs construction-time mutation of a compound field, so the
only legal form carries a Mutex its lock-free C mirror does not. The
recommended user-level answer is still an index-pool representation, which
sidesteps the whole question by not making the graph a `shared struct` at all.

SEVERITY: stays low, and is now better justified — this is a missing
convenience for one shape (compound-mut-then-frozen), not a hole in cross-task
sharing.

THE CONSTRAINT THAT DECIDES THE DESIGN, and it is not the one this row's
"WHAT SHOULD CLOSE IT" list assumed: #133's traversal is IN A CALLEE
(`sum_clones(root, 28)` -> `clone_graph(root)`). So any freeze that is not
expressed IN THE TYPE must infer, across function boundaries, that the callee
never writes through the handle and that the handles it materializes are safe --
which IS mechanism 1, and inherits mechanism 1's failure mode. A freeze point
spelled as a local annotation or a statement-scoped fact is therefore not a
cheaper third option at all; it is mechanism 1 wearing a hat. This is why the
call is a TYPE-LEVEL MODE.

THE CALL: `frozen T` as a mode beside `ref T` / `mut ref T` -- a non-owning,
NON-COUNTING handle to a deeply-immutable `shared` value whose lifetime spans
the region. Four properties, each load-bearing: non-counting (removes the raced
header rather than making it atomic -- the same argument `rc_elide.rs` already
ships default-ON for read-only non-escaping `ref` params, B-2026-07-15-21);
DEEP/sticky through projection (without it the interior handles a traversal
materializes are ordinary `shared` values and the race returns -- the same
reason mechanism 2 had to close over the whole reachable type set); NON-ESCAPING
(the fail-closed condition that pays for non-counting; a non-counting handle
outliving its owner is a use-after-free); and CROSSES SIGNATURES (the property
that makes #133 reachable). Created by an explicit `let g = freeze graph;` --
declared, never inferred.

Stage 1's winning move was to keep the mode out of the type tree and reuse the borrow vocabulary (`frozen T` -> `ref T`, and codegen emits no refcount traffic for a borrow). A `ref`-typed LOCAL is not a borrow at codegen level — it still materialises a counted handle. The parameter case works because the lowering rides the CALLING CONVENTION (caller keeps ownership, callee's slot holds a pointer-to-handle); a local has no caller to borrow from, so the annotation buys nothing. Worth recording because `let r: ref N = g;` typechecks, builds, runs, and passes to a `frozen` parameter today, so the route looks viable until the traffic is counted. That is the same capability mechanism 1 would need — the freeze statement does not avoid that work, it only makes the CHECK local once the work exists. That materially resizes stage 3, which the staging list called 'much smaller' than stage 2. AND TWO GUARDS MUST MOVE TOGETHER, deliberately independent by stage 2's design: the freeze-site check (E0512) refuses any type whose reachable closure holds a `mut` field, and stage 2's place walk refuses a `mut` field at every projection step. #133 needs BOTH relaxed — `Node.neighbors` is `mut` AND is the traversal path — so neither relaxes alone.

Removing the retain IS what was needed, but NOT mechanism 1's interprocedural elision: for a place rooted at a `frozen` parameter the owner is known WITHOUT ANY ANALYSIS — it is the caller's value and its lifetime is the whole call. So a `let` bound from a frozen place now compiles as a NON-COUNTING ALIAS (codegen skips the Vec-element clone, the receive-inc and the scope-exit dec) and the ownership pass adds the local to the frozen set, so it inherits every restriction the parameter has. WHAT THIS IS, in the staging's own vocabulary: the "codegen binding class whose slot aliases an existing owner without retaining" that the stage-3 note names as the capability the freeze STATEMENT needs. Stage 2.5 builds it for the case where the owner is known by construction; what stage 3 still has to add is the harder half — a frozen local whose owner is an ordinary local in the same frame, where the owner's lifetime is a real question rather than a given. MEASURED, per-function traffic in `outer`'s own frame (module-wide counts cannot see this — `main` and the drop helpers carry traffic in every variant): `let k = o.inner; k.v` frozen 0/0; `let k = o.kids[0]; k.v` frozen 0/0; `let k = o.inner; readi(k)` frozen 0/0; all three written `ref` 2/3. Mutation-checked: disabling the codegen guard turns the assertion red with left: (2, 3). STILL REFUSED, each for a stated reason rather than by omission: `let mut k` (a mutable alias could be repointed; the assignment would report on its own, but refusing the DECLARATION makes the alias immutable by construction rather than by an argument a later change to the assignment walk could break); `for k in n.kids` (the loop lowers an element copy, not an alias); a place that is not a `shared struct` (a Vec/String place is a {ptr,len,cap} aggregate whose binding codegen registers as a buffer owner, and a generic type resolves fields through unsubstituted parameter names — neither is a single refcounted pointer, both fail closed); and EVERY ESCAPE — returning the alias, storing it in a struct/tuple/Vec literal, a user method receiver, a non-`frozen` slot, a closure capture. That last group is unchanged and is what pays for the non-counting representation: the alias is IN the frozen set, so the same whitelist judges it. Its diagnostics now say "`frozen` ALIAS `k`" rather than "parameter", because the line to change is the `let`, not the signature. BOTH HALVES WERE WRONG. (1) THE VARIABLE WAS AUTO-PAR, WHICH THE MEASUREMENT DID NOT CONTROL FOR: it was taken "at the default opt level", i.e. auto-par ON, whereas the stage-2 3.7x table it was implicitly compared against was taken with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. STAGE 2.6 LANDED — `for k in <frozen place>`, AND IT RETRACTS A CLAIM STAGE 2.5 MADE WITHOUT MEASURING. Stage 2.5's note above lists `for k in n.kids` among the shapes "still refused, each for a stated reason rather than by omission", and gives the reason as "the loop lowers an element copy, not an alias". THAT REASON IS WRONG. Measured, the emitted loop is `%for.v.elem = load ptr, ptr %for.v.elem.ptr` followed by `store ptr %for.v.elem, ptr %k` — a pointer load out of the Vec and a store into the loop variable's slot, with NO clone, NO retain, NO release and NO cleanup at `for.exit` — and it is that in BORROW mode and in `frozen` mode alike (both (0,0,0) for rc_inc / rc_dec / karac_clone_ calls, against (2,3,0) for the `let`-alias shape in `ref` mode). There was never any refcount traffic here to remove; only the ownership walk was refusing. So stage 2.6 is an OWNERSHIP-ONLY slice: one admission arm in frozen_escape.rs, zero codegen change. WHAT IS ADMITTED: a `for` whose ITERABLE is a place rooted at a frozen root and whose element type is either (a) a non-generic `shared struct`, in which case the loop variable joins the frozen set exactly as a `let` alias does and is judged by the same whitelist thereafter, or (b) a SCALAR (`is_copy_type_basic`), in which case the loop variable is left an ordinary binding — a register copy of an `i64` has nothing to escape with. Anything else falls through to the ordinary walk and reports: a `Map`/`Set` (which `element_type` deliberately does not model), an element that is neither a handle nor a scalar (a `Vec[Vec[i64]]` element, whose binding codegen registers as a buffer owner), a destructuring loop pattern, and the whole surface inside a closure. Classification happens BEFORE the iterable is consumed, so a rejection falls through to exactly one walk rather than reporting the index operands twice. NEGATIVES VERIFIED INDIVIDUALLY: the element passed to an OWNED slot, returned, or captured by a closure all still report, and they name the loop variable as a `frozen` ALIAS (the stage-2.5 noun fix carries over, which is right — the line to change is the `for`, not the signature). THE AUTO-PAR SURFACE IS UNTOUCHED, and the reason is the loop FORM rather than anything about `frozen`: `karac query concurrency` reports `loop_reductions: []` for a container-iterating `for` in BOTH `frozen` and `ref` mode, while the same body written `for j in 0..64` over an indexed element IS recognized and fans out. So container iteration is simply not an auto-par candidate shape today; the two modes agree, and there is no surface asymmetry to fix. Recorded as a measured fact, not filed as a defect. STAGE 2.7 LANDED — `frozen self`, AND A HOLE FOUND IN ITS OWN FIRST DRAFT. The two halves (a `frozen self` receiver form, and admitting a METHOD CALL on a frozen place) are one slice because neither is sound alone: admitting `place.m()` requires the callee's BODY to be checked — a `ref self` method may store or return `self`, and doing that with a non-counting handle is a use-after-free — and only a declared receiver mode gets it checked. So a method call is admitted exactly when the resolved declaration says `frozen self`. THE HOLE, recorded because it is the kind that ships: `self` is its OWN `ExprKind::SelfValue`, not an `Identifier` whose name happens to be "self", so the first draft's `frozen_place_root` never matched a receiver. `frozen self` parsed, type-checked, ownership-checked CLEAN, and protected nothing — and every accept-row test I had written passed VACUOUSLY, because the pass was not looking at `self` at all. Found by probing the one case whose expected answer was "must report": a closure capturing `self`. Now pinned by that exact row in `frozen_self_receiver_is_checked_like_a_frozen_parameter`, mutation-checked (stubbing the `SelfValue` arm to `None` turns it red). The general lesson is the one this row keeps re-learning from the other direction: an accept-only battery cannot tell "admitted" from "never examined". NO CODEGEN CHANGE, and the measurement is why the ownership rule is keyed on the DECLARED MODE rather than on emitted traffic: a `ref self` receiver on a `shared struct` measures 0 rc_inc / 0 rc_dec in the CALLER's frame, the CALLEE's frame, and a nested `ref self` call — so `frozen self` (which lowers to `ref self`, the same trick `frozen T` uses) is indistinguishable in the IR from the mode that must be REFUSED. What differs is only whether the body was checked. The par_codegen test asserts BOTH zeros on purpose and says so, and its discriminating leg is an alias bound off the receiver (frozen 0/0 vs ref 2/3). Ten construction sites needed the field; trait methods get `false` (stage 2.7 is impl-only). `frozen` stays a CONTEXTUAL keyword, disambiguated by one token of lookahead (`frozen` followed by `self`), so `fn frozen(ref self)` still parses as a method named `frozen` — pinned. Method resolution needs NO typechecker callee map: the pass already computes the receiver PLACE's type, so `(type, method)` names exactly one declaration; keyed by that pair and never by method name alone, so two types with a same-named method cannot borrow each other's guarantee. The freeze-site check (E0512) covers the receiver through the SAME classifier the parameter uses, with the impl target as its type — verified on a non-shared type, a `par struct`, a `mut`-bearing type, and a type whose mutable state is reachable only THROUGH a field. Diagnostics gained a third noun: `self` is a "receiver", not a "parameter" or an "alias", because all three name a different line to go change. KNOWN LIMIT, measured and NOT introduced here: passing `self` to a borrow parameter (`frz(self)` where `frz(i: frozen Inner)`) is a TYPE error — and so is `byref(self)` from a plain `ref self` method, and from an owned `self` one. The typechecker types `self` as `T` regardless of receiver mode while a `ref T` / `frozen T` parameter wants `ref T`. Filed separately as B-2026-08-07-8.       may not be stored in a non-`frozen` container -- property 3, the

      `queue.push_back(root)` is refused. Isolated repro:

          fn bfs(root: frozen Node) -> i64 {
              let mut queue: VecDeque[Node] = VecDeque.new();
              queue.push_back(root);        // refused
              return queue.len();

happened to sit on the permitted side of it. The fixture is still worth keeping
-- it pins a real capability that did not exist before -- but it is NOT the
kata, and the step-3 note should not have implied the gap was closed.

title: A module-level `let` whose name starts with a LOWERCASE letter is not recognized as a module binding at all — it falls through to a top-level statement and the author is told to "move the statements into `main`, or remove the explicit `main`", two suggestions that both destroy the intent. `E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING` never fires.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found building canned LLM responses for the Mend corpus — the iteration-0 attempt for `link_registry` deliberately used lowercase module bindings, which is the mistake its notes.md predicts. Instead of the naming diagnostic, it produced one misdirecting parse error.

THE BOUNDARY IS THE FIRST LETTER'S CASE. Same three-line program each time, only the binding's name changes:

  let mut <NAME>: i64 = 0;
  fn bump() { <NAME> = <NAME> + 1; }
  fn main() { bump(); println(<NAME>.to_string()); }

  COUNT      -> All checks passed          (recognized as a module binding)
  MY_COUNT   -> All checks passed          (recognized)
  Count      -> E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING    (recognized; correct, actionable, machine-fixable)
  C          -> E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING    (recognized; correct)
  myCount    -> "file contains both top-level statements and an explicit `fn main()`"
  my_count   -> same
  c          -> same

An uppercase FIRST letter is what makes the parser treat the `let` as a module binding. Anything starting lowercase is parsed as a top-level (script-mode) statement, collides with the explicit `fn main()`, and produces an error about a completely different subject.

WHY THE DIAGNOSTIC IS WORSE THAN MERELY WRONG. It is confidently actionable and both of its actions are destructive:
  "move the statements into `main`"  — impossible by construction; the binding exists precisely
                                       because SEVERAL functions share it. Moving it into main
                                       breaks every reader.
  "remove the explicit `main`"       — deletes the program's entry point to silence a naming
                                       problem.
Neither mentions capitalisation. An author who follows either suggestion ends up further from a working program than when they started, and the actual one-token fix (rename to SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE) is never surfaced.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A TYPICAL DIAGNOSTIC GAP:
 * Lowercase is the DEFAULT habit for a variable name in every mainstream language. This is not
   an exotic mistake; it is the first thing a new author types.
 * Module-level mutable state is how a service holds state — `examples/shortener/` needed exactly
   this shape (LINKS / HITS / SEQ), so it is on the main path, not a corner.
 * It lands squarely on the AI-first wedge. A fresh LLM author gets a diagnostic that is
   confidently wrong about the subject, with no `replacement`, and whose prose actively steers
   toward a worse program. That is the failure mode `karac fix` exists to prevent.

THE GOOD DIAGNOSTIC ALREADY EXISTS. `E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING` handles the uppercase-initial cases correctly today — it names the rule, and since B-2026-07-31-31/-32/-33 it carries a machine-applicable rename that also rewrites use sites. So the fix is to widen the RECOGNIZER so a lowercase-initial module-level `let` is still parsed as a module binding, and let the existing naming diagnostic do its job. That converts this from a misdirecting parse error into an auto-fixable rename.

OPEN QUESTION for whoever takes it: script mode is the reason the recognizer is case-keyed at all — a bare `let x = 1;` at top level is a legitimate script-mode statement. Disambiguating will need a rule (perhaps: a top-level `let` in a file that ALSO defines `fn main()` is a module binding, since script mode and explicit main are already mutually exclusive). Worth confirming that reading against design.md § Module-Level Bindings before implementing.

title: The Mend scorer counts a CORRECT `karac fix` as having "broken the build" whenever it unmasks errors a earlier-phase failure was hiding. Because the compiler is phased, any fix to a parse error that reveals a typecheck error is scored as a regression — systematically understating fix precision on exactly the multi-layer programs that are most realistic.
detail:
SURFACE NOTE: the defect is in the measurement harness, not a compiler phase, so `surface` is `other`.

SOURCE NOTE: found running the first full 9-task dry-run batch after backfilling the missing canned_responses.json files. The new `canonical_request` fixture is deliberately LAYERED — a parse error hiding a type error hiding an ownership error — which is what exposed this.

MEASURED (batch_20260801T235833, canonical_request/iter_000):
  BEFORE fix : E0001  parse      the `&&` operator is not used in Kāra; use `and` instead
  AFTER  fix : E0210  typecheck  E_INT_AS_CHAR: cannot cast `i64` to `char` directly
               E0500  ownership  value 'h' moved here, used again here

The fix was CORRECT — `&&` → `and` is exactly right, and the run went on to converge cleanly. The two "new" codes were always present in the source; the parse failure simply meant the compiler never reached typecheck or ownership to report them. Fixing the parse error is what let it get further.

THE DEFECT. `fix_introduced_new_error` is computed as set-difference on diagnostic CODES across the fix boundary: any code present after and absent before counts as the fix introducing an error. In a PHASED compiler that is the normal, desirable outcome of any early-phase fix. The predicate conflates two opposite things:
  (a) the fix genuinely broke the program — a real regression, the thing worth catching;
  (b) the fix removed a blocker and later phases finally ran — progress.

CONSEQUENCES, both on headline numbers:
  * "fixes that broke the build : 1 run(s)" — reported for a run in which nothing broke.
  * fix precision 75.0% (6 resolved / 8 applied) — understated, since the unresolved count
    includes a fix that did its job.
The bias is not random: it fires precisely on programs with mistakes in more than one phase, which are the realistic ones. A corpus of single-mistake fixtures would never show it, so the metric looks fine right up until the fixtures get good.

SUGGESTED FIX SHAPE (unverified): make the comparison phase-aware rather than code-set-based. The diagnostics already carry a `phase` field. A fix should only be charged with a regression when a NEW diagnostic appears at or BEFORE the phase of the diagnostic it fixed — a parse fix that yields typecheck errors is progress, while a parse fix that yields a DIFFERENT parse error is suspect. An alternative, cheaper rule: charge a regression only when the after-set contains a code from a phase that had already run clean before the fix. Either way, keep a real regression detectable — the metric is worth having, it is just measuring the wrong difference.

WORTH CHECKING WHILE IN THERE: whether `fixes_resolved` has the same phase-blindness, since it feeds `fix_precision_pct` from the same comparison.

title: No implicit `*mut T` -> `*const T` weakening at call sites — every consume-direction binding that passes a malloc'd (or otherwise mut) buffer to a `*const` foreign param needs an explicit `as *const T` cast (the cast is SAFE — earlier premise that it was unsafe-gated was wrong)
detail:
Found authoring examples/interop-zlib: `uncompress(back, ptr.mut(back_len), dest, dest_len)` where `dest: *mut u8` (we malloc'd and filled it) and the declared param is `source: *const u8` → E0200 TYPE_MISMATCH expected '*const u8', found '*mut u8'. The weakening direction is always sound (dropping write permission on the same allocation; Rust coerces *mut T → *const T implicitly at coercion sites for exactly this reason), and the natural shape of C bindings hits it immediately — compress-then-use, fill-then-hash, any produce-into-then-read-from buffer. Workaround is `unsafe { dest as *const u8 }` per call site (raw-to-raw casts are unsafe-gated), which taxes the flagship additive-adoption surface with unsafe blocks that assert nothing beyond what the type system already knows. DESIGN FORK to settle before fixing: either (a) add the implicit weakening coercion at call sites (matches Rust; zero soundness cost), or (b) keep the explicitness but make the raw-to-raw mut→const cast SAFE (it introduces no capability), so the workaround at least sheds its unsafe block. Current behavior may be intent (design.md § Unsafe Escape Hatch lists raw-to-raw casts as unsafe-block-legal and never discusses call-site pointer coercion) — if so, document the pattern in § FFI; the gap today is that natural binding code fails with a bare type error and no guidance.

title: A BUILTIN function name in ANY non-call position — `spawn;`, `let f = println;`, `spawn { … }` — passes `karac check` and then panics the interpreter with an internal `unreachable!` whose own message says "should be caught by resolver". USER-defined functions are fine as values, so this is builtins-only.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found writing the S3-client dogfood. I wrote `spawn { … }` to run a server alongside a client — the wrong syntax (the real form is `spawn(|| …)`) — and `karac check` told me the program was fine.

REPRO (one line):
  fn main() { spawn { println("x"); }; }

  karac check          -> All checks passed.
  karac run --interp   -> thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs:170:17:
                          internal error: entered unreachable code: variable 'spawn' not found
                          at 8:5; should be caught by resolver
                          + a full Rust stack backtrace
  karac build          -> error: codegen failed: Undefined variable 'spawn'

SCOPE — it is every builtin FUNCTION name, not just spawn:
  spawn { … }         check passes -> interpreter panic
  println { … }       check passes -> interpreter panic
  print { … }         check passes -> interpreter panic
  assert { … }        check passes -> interpreter panic
  len { … }           correctly rejected at resolve (not a global builtin; it is a method)
  notafunction { … }  correctly rejected: "undefined name 'notafunction'"

So the resolver resolves the NAME (it is a real builtin) and never checks that it is being USED as a call. The block form sails through resolve and typecheck, and the interpreter then tries to evaluate the bare identifier as a variable, finds no binding, and hits an `unreachable!` whose message correctly blames the resolver.

WHY THIS EXACT MISTAKE IS LIKELY, NOT EXOTIC. Kāra really does have block-form constructs — `par { }`, `seq { }`, `unsafe { }`, `comptime { }`, `lock { }`. Someone who has just written `par { }` and wants a single background task will write `spawn { }` by analogy. It is the natural wrong guess, and `spawn` is precisely the builtin reached for when writing concurrent code — the language's headline capability.

THREE THINGS WRONG, IN DESCENDING SEVERITY:
 1. `karac check` IS NOT AUTHORITATIVE. It greenlights a program that cannot run on either
    backend. Every consumer that trusts check — the Mend loop above all, which iterates until
    check is clean and then declares the program correct — will accept this program as done.
    An LLM author following the documented loop converges on a program that panics.
 2. The interpreter PANICS WITH A RUST BACKTRACE rather than emitting a diagnostic. CLAUDE.md's
    coding standard is explicit: "Every compiler phase must emit structured diagnostics with
    source spans — never just panic." The user sees compiler internals for a syntax mistake.
 3. Codegen's message (`codegen failed: Undefined variable 'spawn'`) is a raw string with no
    span, no code, and no JSON representation, so it is invisible to `--output=json` consumers.

SUGGESTED FIX SHAPE (unverified): reject a builtin function name in non-call position at resolve, with a diagnostic that names the correct form — for `spawn` specifically, "`spawn` takes a closure: `spawn(|| …)`", which is machine-applicable (wrap the block in `(|| … )`) and would make this a `karac fix` case rather than a crash. The `notafunction` path already produces the right SHAPE of error; builtins just need to reach it. Whoever takes it should also decide whether the `unreachable!` at eval_expr.rs:170 should become a structured internal-error diagnostic regardless, since it is reachable from any future resolver hole of this kind.

── SCOPE CORRECTED (same day, before any fix) ──
The original entry framed this as the BLOCK form (`spawn { … }`). That is narrower than reality and a fix aimed at it would be incomplete. Re-measured on exit codes rather than first-line matching — the panic output begins with a BLANK line, so an earlier `head -1` probe scored several panicking cases as clean and produced a wrong boundary:

  spawn { … };            check passes -> PANIC (exit 101)
  spawn;                  check passes -> PANIC   <- no block involved at all
  spawn; println("a");    check passes -> PANIC
  println { … };          check passes -> PANIC
  let f = println;        check passes -> PANIC   <- ordinary let, no block
  { println("x"); };      check passes -> clean   (a bare block is fine)
  helper;                 check passes -> clean   (USER fn as a value)
  helper { … };           check passes -> clean   (USER fn)

So the rule is: ANY reference to a builtin function name outside call position panics. The block form is simply how I happened to hit it. User-defined functions ARE first-class values — `Server.serve(addr, handle)` in examples/shortener depends on exactly that — so the asymmetry is builtins-only.

That also settles the fix's shape: builtins are NOT first-class values today, so the correct repair is to say so at resolve for every non-call reference, not to special-case the block form. Making builtins first-class would be a feature (and would need a codegen half), not a bug fix.
