fix: a82b4ff (src/codegen/stmts.rs; pins the extended memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box, stash-proven RED against this commit's change alone at 6,400 bytes under LeakSanitizer)

title: `?` PROPAGATING an Err whose payload is a struct wider than THREE words silently drops every word past the third -- the Err mirror of B-2026-08-04-9's second defect, in the error-staging path rather than the Ok-reconstruction one
detail: REPRO (probe b232/e3): `struct Err4 { msg: String, code: i64 }` (4 words, which FITS `Result`'s 5-word payload area, so it is INLINE and never boxed), `fn fail4(i: i64) -> Result[i64, Err4] { return Result.Err(mk4(i)); }`, and a propagating wrapper `fn prop4(i: i64) -> Result[i64, Err4] { let v = fail4(i)?; return Result.Ok(v); }`. Matching `prop4(4i64)`'s Err and printing `{e.msg}:{e.code}` gives `mid-err-4:0` under AOT and `mid-err-4:4` under `karac run`. The `String` survives; `code` -- word 3 -- does not. Probe b232/e1 shows the same value as 32 in a different program, i.e. it is whatever happens to be in that slot, not a consistent zero.  CONTROL: b232/e4 matches the SAME `Result` WITHOUT the `?` wrapper and is correct on both backends, so it is the propagation, not the construction or the match. b232/e2 (a 6-word Err, BOXED) is also correct -- the boxed path stores a pointer in w0 and does not depend on the word cap.  MECHANISM: `compile_question`'s error-staging path calls `rebuild_value_from_payload_words(e_ty, w0_i, w1_i, w2_i)` -- exactly three words, extracted as fields 1..3 of the Result aggregate. Any `E` wider than three words loses the rest. This is the SAME helper and the SAME three-word cap that B-2026-08-04-9's second defect hit on the Ok side, where `Mid { name: String, pad: i64 }` came back with a garbage `pad`; that one was fixed by reading the full payload span and rebuilding through `reconstruct_struct_from_words`. The Err side was not touched.  WHY IT WAS LEFT: the Ok-side fix sat in one function with one caller. The Err staging has at least TWO sites -- the fn-level return path and the `with_provider` return-retarget path just below it -- and both are interleaved with error-trace recording and errdefer draining. That is a bigger surgery than a same-shape patch, and a half-verified change to error propagation is worse than a filed row. Whoever takes it should port the Ok-side shape to BOTH sites and check the errdefer/error-trace interaction explicitly.  PRE-EXISTING and independent of everything landed today: the `?` Ok-side fix (60087fc) does not touch the Err staging, and the shape reproduces with the same values before it.  ORACLE NOTE: parity diffing only -- no leak, no crash, correct-looking output with one wrong field. This is the quiet corner of the family and the reason a wide MIXED payload deserves a fixture axis of its own: a 3-word `E` is immune, and 3 words is what most hand-written error structs happen to be.  SOURCE NOTE: surfaced in the b232 sweep of the `?` ERROR side, run after B-2026-08-04-9 fixed the Ok side.  FIXED (2026-08-04, e6a2eca), and it turned out SMALLER than this row estimated. The row deferred it on the grounds that the Err staging has two sites -- the fn-level return path and the `with_provider` retarget path -- both interleaved with error-trace recording and errdefer draining. That is true of the SITES but not of the DEFECT: both consumers build their Err aggregate from a single `ret_words` vector, and its non-converting branch was the literal `vec![w0_i, w1_i, w2_i]`. Widening that one expression covers both paths and touches neither the trace nor the errdefer drain.  The words are now taken as `min(inner_word_count, outer_word_count).max(1)` -- bounded on BOTH ends so the extract loop cannot index past the source aggregate when an outer `E` is wider than the inner one, which the conversion branch beside it can produce.  VERIFIED: probes b232/e1..e5 all correct, parity-EQUAL, vg=0. Suites: codegen 2780, memory_sanitizer 926, interpreter 1441, drop_differential 13, par_codegen 226 = 5386 passed, 0 failed. The pin is stash-proven RED on the exact wrong value (`b:mid-err-4:32`), which is worth more than a generic assertion here: the failure is one wrong integer field in otherwise correct output.  LESSON FOR THE FIXTURE CORPUS, restated because it is the transferable part: a 3-word error struct is IMMUNE to this whole class, and 3 words -- a lone `String`, or two scalars and a tag -- is what most hand-written error types happen to be. Payload WIDTH deserves an explicit axis (3 / 4-5 / >5) rather than one representative error type, on both the Ok and Err sides. Three separate defects this session (B-2026-08-04-9's two and this one) were all invisible at 3 words.
fix: e6a2eca (src/codegen/exprs.rs; pins codegen.rs::e2e_question_propagates_a_wide_inline_err_payload_whole, stash-proven RED on the exact wrong field value, with a BOXED 6-word control and a no-`?` control)

title: The descending-loop bounds-check skip (B-2026-07-17-1) reads the facts it rests on with `stmt_writes_ident`, which sees only TOP-LEVEL assignment targets. A write one block deep (`if c { i = 50 }`) therefore left every fact reading 'unchanged' while the program changed it, and the skip elided a load-bearing check. Three independent levers reach it: the enclosing counter, the index's init, and the fill counter (which makes the length pin overstate the buffer). Default-ON since 6474a73. Observed as an out-of-range Vec STORE — silent exit 0, `munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer`, and a glibc malloc assertion, depending on the case.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while reading `bce_length_pin.rs` to scope the row-major extension B-2026-08-04-8 asks for. Not hypothesised from the code and then assumed — each of the three levers below was reproduced as a running binary before anything was changed, and the A/B was `KARAC_BCE_DESC_SKIP=0` on the SAME source (the flag exists as the escape hatch for exactly this class).

THE MECHANISM. The skip proves `k <= k_init < B_pin <= v.len()` for an inner descending loop. Each conjunct is read off a region scan, and five of those scans route through one helper, `stmt_writes_ident`. That helper descends into nested blocks via `expr_writes_ident`, which sees each nested statement's VALUE but never its assignment TARGET — so `if c { k = 100 }` answered 'does not write k'. The module already knew this shape of gap: its `region_bindings` collector exists specifically to close it, its section comment names it ('blind to ... assignment targets buried in an inner block'), and `only_monotone_decrement` was converted to use it. The five callers that read the OTHER facts never were.

THREE LEVERS, THREE REPRODUCTIONS. All on a Vec filled to 10, indexed by a descending `k`:
  (1) ENCLOSING COUNTER  `if flag == 1 { i = 50 }` before the inner loop. `i <= u_max` is
      then false where the proof substitutes it, so `k = i + 9` starts at 59. Ran to
      completion printing `len=10` — 60 out-of-range stores, exit 0.
  (2) INDEX INIT         `if flag == 1 { k = 50 }` after `let mut k`. `sole_scalar_init`
      reports a value `k` no longer holds. Aborted with `munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer`.
  (3) FILL COUNTER       `if flag == 1 { j = 5 }` before the counted fill. Here the skip's
      arithmetic is right and its PREMISE is not: the fill runs 5 iterations, so the length
      pin claims a buffer twice the real one. Aborted inside glibc's malloc assertion.
Each panics correctly with `KARAC_BCE_DESC_SKIP=0`, and each panics correctly now.

THIS IS THE SECOND OCCURRENCE OF THE SAME CLASS, and the first one's fix is what should have prevented it. B-2026-07-04-13 (6ca6fe44) found exactly this — 'a GENERIC walker that only inspects statement VALUES ... blind to `let` patterns and assignment TARGETS buried in an inner block' — with two confirmed exploits, one of them a SILENT WRONG ANSWER. Its fix BUILT `region_bindings` for the purpose. But it wired the collector into the call sites it had in hand, the after-fill invariance scans (`vec_readonly_after` / `var_unwritten_after`), rather than into the blind helper itself. `compute_descending_skips` (B-2026-07-17-1, 6474a73) then landed AFTER that fix and added five fresh scans through the still-blind `stmt_writes_ident`. The guard existed and the new code simply did not reach for it.

THE FIX IS ONE PRE-CHECK AT THE SHARED HELPER, not five patched call sites. All five callers want the same predicate ('is this name written anywhere in this statement'), they were all wrong in the same way, and a per-caller fix would leave the next caller to rediscover it. `stmt_writes_ident` now consults `region_bindings`' assignment-target roots first and answers the question its own doc comment always claimed to answer. Only `assigned` is consulted, not `rebound`: a nested `let` shadows an inner name without writing the outer one, and treating that as a write would reject sound programs for nothing.

WHY THE EXISTING TESTS MISSED IT, which is the reusable part. There WAS a negative test for lever (1) — `desc_no_fire_when_counter_rewritten` — and it passed, because it spells the rewrite at the TOP level, which the blind helper does catch. The suite tested the fact, not the fact's reachability: every negative was written in the one syntactic position the analysis handles. So the new tests are built from a SHARED BASE with three empty slots, and the control asserts that base FIRES; each negative differs from a firing program only by the nested write, which is what makes it a test of the nesting rather than of some unrelated gate a longer program tripped. Verified both directions: with the pre-check reverted, all five new tests fail; the two controls pass either way.

THE E2E ASSERTS THE PANIC, NOT THE IR, and deliberately. The failure is a STORE past the end of a buffer, so what it looks like is allocator-dependent — the three cases produced three different symptoms above, one of them a clean exit 0. A clean panic is the only stable oracle; every corruption mode fails it.

THE GENERALISABLE LESSON, given it took two rounds: when a shared helper answers a question WRONG, fixing the callers that happen to be in front of you leaves the helper's doc comment still lying to the next caller — and here the next caller arrived five weeks later and wrote five new scans against it. The durable repair is at the helper, so that reaching for the obvious function is safe by default. Anything in this module still needing the raw structural match can call the inner one deliberately; nothing currently does.

NOT A REASON TO DISTRUST THE SKIP'S ARITHMETIC. The linear-normal-form proof (`init_below_bound`) was right throughout; what failed was the reading of its inputs. The Pascal-row and exclusive-bounds wins are unchanged, and `test_ir_descending_loop_bce_skip_wiring` still asserts the elision.

COMPILE-TIME COST, MEASURED (the pre-check adds a `region_bindings` walk per
statement, inside helpers that are themselves called in nested loops, so this
was an open question rather than an obvious no-op). Interleaved A/B on the same
container, `karac build` of bench/compile_speed/synthetic.kara (10,858 lines),
min of 6 runs each, binaries differing only in this file:

    pre-fix   9.66 s
    with fix  9.80 s      +133 ms, 1.014x

Accepted. The asymptotics are unchanged — `expr_writes_ident` already walked the
same subtree, so the added work is a HashMap/HashSet allocation per statement,
not a new traversal order. 1.4% on a debug-profile compiler is the right trade
for closing a heap-corrupting elision, and if this ever matters the collector
can be memoised per statement rather than the check reverted.

title: The interpreter silently DROPPED an out-of-range index-assign: `v[100] = 7` on a 2-element Vec produced no error, no growth, and no store — while AOT and the JIT both panic with `vec index out of bounds`. The READ path was checked all along; only the store guarded itself with a bare `if i < len` and fell off the end. Compound assign (`v[100] += 7`) was also correct, because it reads first.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while reproducing B-2026-08-04-13. The probe that proved the codegen miscompile was run under `--interp` as a control, expecting the interpreter to name the out-of-range store the AOT binary was performing. It printed the same successful output the MISCOMPILED binary did.

THAT IS WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SEVERITY SUGGESTS. The interpreter is the reference oracle — the thing consulted to decide what a program is supposed to do. Here it agreed with a codegen bug, for an unrelated reason, and its agreement is what a reasonable investigator would have read as 'the AOT output is correct'. A silent oracle does not just miss its own bug; it launders someone else's.

THE SHAPE. `Interpreter::set_index` ended in two arms that each wrapped the store in `if i < len` with no else, so an out-of-range index fell off the end of the function. Characterised before fixing:
  v[100] = 7   (far past end)   -> silently dropped
  v[2]   = 7   (one past end)   -> silently dropped
  v[-1]  = 7   (negative)       -> silently dropped
  v[100] += 7  (compound)       -> correct error   <- reads first, and the READ is checked
  let x = v[100]                -> correct error
AOT and JIT panic on all of them. The compound-assign and read rows are what localise it: the gap is the store path specifically, not index bounds in the interpreter generally.

The fix reports through `record_runtime_error` with the READ path's exact message and the index's span, so the two directions are indistinguishable in output. Negative indices arrive already wrapped by `i as usize` and so are reported the way the read path has always reported them (`index 18446744073709551615 out of bounds`) — odd-looking, but pre-existing, shared, and deliberately not changed here; making the store nicer than the read would just be a new divergence.

STILL SILENT, and left that way on purpose: `set_index`'s `_ => {}` arm (a store through a receiver that is not an Array/Slice/Map/Tensor) and its `let Value::Int(i) = idx_val else { return }` guard (a non-integer index). Both are unreachable for type-checked programs, and this same `_ => return` has twice been found swallowing a REAL shape (kata-133-audit's field-rooted store; B-2026-07-20-3's tuple-rooted store) — so the arm deserves its own audit rather than a catch-all error bolted on next to an unrelated fix.

title: AUTO-PAR SILENTLY DROPS STORES through a tuple-element receiver: `t.0.push(x)` recorded NO write in the dependency walk, so two pushes to the same Vec (and the read after them) were grouped as 'no data or effect dependencies' and the stores vanished — `t.0.len()` returns 0 after two pushes under `karac build`, 2 under the interpreter, then an out-of-bounds abort on the read. `collect_assign_target_defines` walked FieldAccess/Index/Deref/MethodCall to the place root but let TupleIndex fall through its `_ => {}`, so the MethodCall arm recursed onto `t.0` and recorded nothing. Contained to the tuple spelling: identifier and struct-field receivers were always correct
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while auditing `set_index`'s `_ => {}` arm, the follow-up B-2026-08-04-14 deliberately left open. The audit probed every receiver spelling against the interpreter as oracle; the tuple row diverged, and the trail led out of the interpreter entirely.

REPRO, and it is small:
    let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new();
    let mut t: (Vec[i64], i64) = (v, 3);
    t.0.push(10); t.0.push(20);
    println(f"len {t.0.len()} v0 {t.0[0]} v1 {t.0[1]}");
  interp      -> len 2 v0 10 v1 20
  karac build -> panic: vec index out of bounds   (len was 0)
  karac run   -> same panic (JIT shares the pipeline)
A loop-free seven-line program. `KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1` makes it correct, which is the A/B that localises it to auto-par rather than to tuple-element codegen.

THE SMOKING GUN was `karac query concurrency`, which reported the decision outright:
    parallel_groups: [{statements: [2,3,4,5], reason: 'no data or effect dependencies'}]
Statements 2 and 3 are the two pushes; 4 and 5 are the printlns that READ the vec. The analysis had correctly found 1->2 and 1->3 (RAW on `t`), so it saw the pushes READ `t` — it just never recorded that they WRITE it.

BLAST RADIUS, measured on all three receiver spellings of the identical program:
    v.push(10); v.push(20)              -> serialized correctly (no group)
    h.items.push(10); h.items.push(20)  -> serialized correctly (no group)
    t.0.push(10); t.0.push(20)          -> WRONGLY grouped -> stores lost
The `FieldAccess` sibling arm being present is exactly why only the tuple spelling broke.

THE ARM'S OWN HISTORY IS THE FINDING. `collect_assign_target_defines` accumulated its cases one bug at a time: `SelfValue` for self-hosting #8 ('a `mut ref self` method call recorded no write'), `Unary{Deref}` for B-2026-06-20-16 ('the auto-par dependency check saw a histogram body as not writing the map, then parallelized the loop against a later `m.keys()` read'), `MethodCall` for method-chain places. Three prior single-variant additions, each after a miscompile with the same signature, none of which asked what ELSE the walk was missing. TupleIndex was the fourth. Fixed by folding FieldAccess/Index/TupleIndex into one place-projection arm with an explicit completeness requirement naming `place_root` (same file) as the canonical list of forms — `place_root` had TupleIndex right all along, which is what makes the omission a gap rather than an unknown.

The sibling `collect_assign_target_reads` had the identical hole and is fixed with it: a target spelled `t.0[i] = v` stopped at the TupleIndex and never reached the `Index` arm that contributes the read of `i`. No repro is filed for that half — it is the same walk and the same one-line omission, and leaving it for a future bug report would be choosing to be surprised twice.

WHY THE SUITE WAS GREEN, and this is the part worth carrying: `tests/codegen.rs`'s `run_program` passes `None` for the concurrency analysis, so NOTHING it runs is auto-parallel. `tests/par_codegen.rs`'s harness threads `Some(&analysis)` the way the CLI does. B-2026-08-02-10 had already written `e2e_tuple_elem_method_receivers` over this EXACT source — and it passed, throughout, while `karac build` on a byte-identical file aborted. The test was not weak; it was in the harness that cannot see auto-par. Any bug that only manifests under auto-par is invisible to the whole ~2780-test codegen suite, and the obvious home for a codegen test is precisely the harness that cannot catch it. Regression accordingly went into `par_codegen`: one E2E plus one analysis-level assertion that the group is not formed.

A TEST-SHAPE MISTAKE, recorded because it nearly shipped. The first E2E draft appended a struct-field control to the SAME `main` — and it PASSED against the unfixed compiler. The extra statements changed the grouping enough to hide the miscompile. A regression test that does not fail on the bug is worse than none, so the control moved to its own program and the regression source stays minimal. Both were then verified in BOTH directions: with the TupleIndex arm reverted the E2E and the analysis test fail, the control passes either way. This is the second time today that an unrelated statement in a test program moved the analysis off the shape under test (cf. B-2026-08-04-13's negatives, which had to be built from a shared base whose control asserts the base FIRES).

fix: e986284 (src/codegen/stmts.rs tuple-assign arm; src/codegen/expr_ops.rs tuple_index_elem_type_expr). Pins codegen.rs::e2e_named_source_moved_into_a_tuple_element_is_disarmed, memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_named_source_moved_into_a_tuple_element_is_disarmed (floored at 500 allocations against ~1.8k), interpreter.rs::test_named_source_moved_into_a_tuple_element_is_disarmed. Both codegen tests are stash-proven RED against the unfixed compiler (the E2E aborts to empty output, the ASAN case reports a memory error); the interpreter twin passes both ways, as the oracle should. Verified across 16 probe shapes -- both element positions, Vec / String / Vec[String] elements, both-Vec tuples, fresh-temp vs named sources, and the struct-field control -- all clean on both backends with matching alloc/free counts. cargo test --features llvm: 12974 passed, 0 failed.
title: Moving a Vec OUT of a tuple element, mutating it, and moving it BACK (`let mut e = t.0; e.push(x); t.0 = e;`) aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` under both AOT and the JIT; the interpreter runs it. The struct-field analogue (`let mut e = h.items; ...; h.items = e;`) is correct, so this is again the TUPLE spelling of a walk that handles the field spelling. Independent of auto-par (`KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1` reproduces it) and independent of B-2026-08-04-15, which is fixed
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced in the same receiver-spelling audit that produced B-2026-08-04-15, and kept as its own row because the mechanism is different — that one was a missing WRITE in the auto-par dependency walk, this one is a double FREE with auto-par disabled.

REPRO:
    let mut t: (Vec[i64], i64) = (Vec.new(), 3i64);
    let mut e = t.0;      // move the Vec out of the tuple element
    e.push(10i64);
    t.0 = e;              // move it back
    println(f"{t.0.len()}");
  interp                 -> 1
  karac build            -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2
  KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1     -> same abort (so: not auto-par)
CONTROL, the same program through a struct field rather than a tuple element:
    let mut e = h.items; e.push(10i64); h.items = e;  -> 1, correct
The move-out presumably does not disarm the tuple element's cleanup, so the buffer is freed once for the element and once for `e` (or for the re-assigned element) — but that is a reading of the symptom, NOT a diagnosis: no IR was disassembled and no drop-tracking code was read. Treat it as unlocated.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ONE MORE TUPLE ROW: this is one of the two workarounds B-2026-08-02-10's diagnostic actively recommends. That diagnostic tells an author to 'annotate the tuple binding with its full element types ... or bind the element to a local first'. As of today the FIRST path is correct (it was broken by B-2026-08-04-15 until that fix landed) and the SECOND path is this double-free. The advice should not be shipped pointing at a heap corruption; either this is fixed or that suggestion drops the second clause. Both legs were verified against the current build, so the diagnostic's status is known rather than assumed.

NEXT STEP when picked up: check whether the tuple-element move-out marks the source place as moved-from in the same way the field move-out does (B-2026-08-01-31 covers a deep-chain field MOVE-OUT followed by a reassign, which is the working analogue and the natural place to start), then confirm under ASAN rather than glibc's tcache message, which names the symptom and not the site.  RESOLVED, and the characterization above needed correcting first. The row framed this as a move-out/move-BACK round trip; it is neither round-trip- nor move-out-dependent. A plain `t.0 = <named source>` with NO move-out anywhere aborts identically, and the move-out on its own (`let mut e = t.0; e.push(x);` with no store back) is clean. What matters is only that the RHS is a NAMED heap-owning binding: a fresh-temp RHS (`t.0 = mkvec(n)`) was always correct, because there is no source binding to disarm.  CAUSE: `compile_tuple_index_store` drops the old element and then MOVES the RHS header into the slot, but the tuple-assign arm (added by B-2026-08-02-5) never got the sibling of B-2026-07-15-25's field-assign move-suppression. The source binding was left owning nothing with its scope-exit cleanup still armed, so it and the tuple's element drop freed one buffer. The struct-FIELD spelling has carried that suppression since B-2026-07-15-25, which is exactly the asymmetry the row observed and the thing that located the missing arm.  ELEMENT KINDS: general, not Vec-specific. `String` and `Vec[String]` elements abort too -- `Vec[String]` is a TRIPLE free (11 allocations, 13 frees: the element buffer plus the Strings inside it). An earlier reading of this probe recorded String as clean; that was a dead-allocation artifact of the kind B-2026-08-04-17 describes (7 allocations, the payload never materialized), and it inverted once the fixture read the buffer's bytes.  FIX: the element-type resolution is factored out of `compile_tuple_index_store` into `tuple_index_elem_type_expr` and shared with the assign arm's new suppression, so the displaced-value drop and the source disarm cannot resolve the element differently -- that drift is what this bug was.  SPIN-OFF: the report's own `let mut e = t.0; …; t.0 = e;` spelling draws an ownership warning (`value 't' moved here, used again here`), so it could not go in the regression tests without tripping the harness's ownership gate. It fires on the struct-field spelling equally, so it is not another tuple asymmetry -- filed as B-2026-08-04-18.  DIAGNOSTIC FOLLOW-UP the row asked for: B-2026-08-02-10's suggestion ("bind the element to a local first") no longer produces heap corruption, so the advice can stand on the memory-safety ground it was failing on. It does still produce B-2026-08-04-18's warning, which is worth settling before considering that suggestion fully clean.

title: memory-fixture authoring hazard: a payload whose content is compile-time constant, or that is read only through `.len()`, is a DEAD allocation LLVM deletes at -O2 -- so an E2E/ASAN fixture for an ownership bug can pass against a compiler that aborts on the same shape
detail:
PROVEN TWICE, both in landed tests rather than hypothetically. (1) B-2026-08-04-11 leg (a)'s fixture (codegen.rs::e2e_fstring_interpolation_of_a_payload_heap_field_is_a_move) carries an arm `Result.Err(e) => { println("d:unused"); }` whose payload is built `Wrap { msg: f"err-payload-{i}" }` and called as `g(4i64)`. That is EXACTLY the shape leg (b) aborts on, and the test passed throughout leg (b) being open: with a literal argument the f-string const-folds, the payload is never allocated, and the double free has nothing to hit. (2) The first draft of leg (b)'s own fixture used a `String.new()`+`push_str` payload (so the content was NOT foldable) and read it back through `.len()` only -- it also passed against the unfixed compiler, because a buffer whose bytes are never read is a provably dead allocation and LLVM deletes the malloc outright.  MEASURED, same program shape, valgrind `total heap usage` over ~1200 intended payload allocations: constant-seeded loop + `.len()`-only = 1 alloc (the whole loop folds to its final total); opaque seed + `.len()`-only = 6 allocs (loop survives, mallocs are DCE'd); opaque seed + a `contains` byte read = 3,206 allocs. Only the third exercises anything, and only the third aborts against the unfixed compiler.  SCOPE -- this is a SHAPE hazard, not a corpus-wide defect, and the difference was checked rather than assumed. memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box has the same constant-seeded-loop structure and is NOT affected: 601 allocs as written vs 606 with an opaque seed and runtime-varying payload content, so its coverage is real. No claim is made here that other existing fixtures are vacuous; what is claimed is that nothing currently stops the next one from being so, and that two have already been.  RULE for any new memory fixture: (a) seed from something the optimizer cannot see through -- `env.args().len()` is 1 under both the codegen E2E harness and assert_clean_asan_run, since both exec the binary with no extra argv; (b) read the payload's BYTES, not just its length -- `contains` against a runtime-derived needle works and stays borrow-only, which matters when the bug shape requires a NON-consuming arm (printing the field would consume it and change the shape under test); (c) confirm `total heap usage` shows the buffers were actually allocated before trusting a clean run. An interpreter ORACLE twin should keep a literal seed instead: there is no optimizer to defeat, and `env.args()` inside an in-process interpreter test reports the TEST binary's argv (program_args is None, so resource_method.rs falls back to std::env::args), which varies with the filter.  WORTH DOING, not done here: a cheap harness-side guard. assert_clean_asan_run could assert a minimum allocation count, or the E2E harness could fail a fixture whose binary performs fewer allocations than a declared floor -- either turns this from a reviewer-discipline problem into a mechanical one.  RESOLVED as far as a mechanical guard can take it. `assert_clean_asan_run_min_allocs` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) runs the program with `print_stats=1:atexit=1`, parses the malloc count off ASAN's exit stats, and fails with a VACUOUS FIXTURE message naming both likely causes when the count falls under a caller-supplied floor. The ASAN option was verified to mask nothing: a leaky program still exits 23 with `ERROR: LeakSanitizer` and a double free still exits 23 with `ERROR: AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free`. It is off unless a floor is requested, so the other 928 cases keep their quiet stderr. The assertion is proven LIVE rather than inert -- temporarily raising the floor fails with the real measured count (3208), which is what distinguishes a working parse from one that silently returns None and skips the check. When the runtime prints no stats line at all the check is skipped with a note, since that is "cannot measure", not "measured zero".  WHAT IS NOT COVERED, deliberately: (1) the plain codegen E2E harness (`run_program`) has no equivalent floor -- it does not link ASAN, so there is no allocation counter to read, and adding one would mean running every fixture under valgrind. The E2E half of this hazard is still reviewer discipline, and the leg (b) E2E fixture documents the two rules in its own doc comment. (2) No existing fixture was retrofitted. The one that was spot-checked (asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box) is NOT vacuous -- 601 allocs as written vs 606 with an opaque seed -- so a blanket retrofit is not obviously worth its churn; the floor is there for new fixtures and for any old one that a future measurement implicates.  MEASUREMENT CORRECTION worth recording, since the opposite was assumed for part of this session: `push_str("<literal>")` onto a `String.new()` DOES allocate -- measured 106 allocs over 100 iterations, i.e. one buffer per call. It is not a cap-0 static. The two things that actually make a payload disappear are the two named above (foldable content, and a buffer whose bytes are never read), not the literal-ness of the pushed argument.  SCOPE CORRECTION (same day, after the guard landed) -- the paragraph above saying this is a shape hazard rather than a corpus-wide defect is WRONG, and the reasoning behind it was bad: it generalized from ONE spot-check (asan_question_deboxed_ok_payload_frees_the_box) that happens to be Vec-heavy and therefore unaffected. Sweeping the whole corpus with the counter that 49e126a made available says otherwise. Across all 864 counted `assert_clean_asan_run` fixtures: 102 allocate NOTHING, and 296 sit at or below a 7-alloc baseline. "Nothing" is exact, not inferred -- an allocation-free run reports 3 (the ASAN runtime's own startup allocations) and `asan_baseline_no_allocations` pins that value, so 3 means the program did no heap work of its own.  PROVEN INSTANCE, not an inference from the count: `asan_vec_with_capacity_push_past_n_grows_once`. Its own comment says it exists so that "both the original `with_capacity` malloc'd buffer AND the grown buffer need to be tracked correctly" and to catch "a double-free if the grow path doesn't free the original before swapping the data pointer". At -O2 it performed exactly ONE allocation -- the println buffer. The literal loop bound let the entire loop fold to the constant 16, and reading the result back through `v.len()` alone left the buffer a dead allocation LLVM deletes. A test for the Vec GROW path that never grew a Vec. At -O0 the same source allocates 3, which is the behaviour the comment describes. Fixed in dee8b8a (opaque bound + two ELEMENT reads + a floor of 6; 10 allocations now).  REMAINING WORK, which is why this row is open again: the other 101 zero-allocation fixtures are un-audited. Each needs the same three-way judgement rather than a blanket rewrite -- (a) genuinely heapless by design, so the count is correct and nothing is owed; (b) intends heap work that folds away, like the Vec-grow case, and needs an opaque seed plus a byte/element read; (c) allocates but only through a path the fixture does not assert on. Sweep with `KARAC_ASAN_ALLOC_AUDIT=1 cargo test --features llvm --test memory_sanitizer -- --nocapture`, which prints one `ALLOCAUDIT\t<n>\t<label>` line per fixture. Start with the ones whose NAMES promise heap work (grep the 3-alloc list for vec_ / string_ / map_ / drop / leak / double_free) -- that is how the Vec-grow case surfaced. Adopt `assert_clean_asan_run_min_allocs` as each is fixed, so it cannot drift back.  PROGRESS + A REFINEMENT THAT CHANGES THE REMAINING WORK'S SHAPE. Nine fixtures de-vacuumed so far (dee8b8a, 2467458): the Vec-grow case plus vec_growth_multiple_reallocs, vec_with_capacity_push_exact_n_no_grow, vec_with_capacity_unused_buffer_freed, struct_with_vec_field_freed_on_scope_exit, struct_with_string_field_freed_on_scope_exit, struct_with_multiple_vec_fields_freed_on_scope_exit, method_chain_intermediate_vec_freed and string_new_push_str -- each 0 program allocations before, 9-17 after, all now floored. Zero-allocation population 102 -> 93. None of the nine surfaced a codegen bug once they really ran, which is its own (weak but real) signal.  THE REFINEMENT: the standard recipe -- opaque seed plus a byte/element read -- provably does NOT apply to the DISCARD-shaped family (`make_vec();` as a bare statement, `let x = mk(n);` with x unused, `option_string_discarded_freed`, `result_{ok,err}_string_undestructured_freed`, `discarded_*`). Measured with a runtime-opaque seed and no other change: baseline for `env.args()` + a literal println is 6 allocations, and all three discard shapes tested come in at exactly 6 -- zero program allocations. That is not a fixture defect that better seeding fixes. A discarded value is by construction never read, so a CORRECTLY freed one is a dead malloc/free pair the optimizer is entitled to delete; the same program with the value RETAINED (pushed into a live Vec) allocates 8, which confirms the elision is about deadness rather than folding.  WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THEIR COVERAGE, stated at the confidence the evidence supports: the DOUBLE-FREE direction is still caught, and that is directly observed rather than argued -- B-2026-08-04-11 leg (b)'s probe allocated 9 while buggy and 8 once fixed, i.e. the second free is what kept the allocation alive. The LEAK direction is UNTESTED here and should not be assumed either way: LLVM can delete an unpaired malloc whose result is unused, so a fixture named for the freed/no-leak direction (option_string_discarded_freed and the two undestructured ones are named exactly that way) may be dark in the direction it advertises. Someone should settle it before rewriting that family.  SUGGESTED HANDLING for discard-shaped fixtures once that is settled: do not contort them into reading a value they exist to discard. Pair each with a RETAINED control in the same program -- build the same value, keep one alive and assert on it, discard the other -- so the fixture allocates for a reason adjacent to what it pins, and the floor has something real to measure.  THE LEAK-DIRECTION QUESTION IS NOW SETTLED, and the answer is the pessimistic one. LLVM at -O2 deletes an allocation whose result is never read REGARDLESS of whether it is freed. Measured directly at the C level, same host toolchain, `malloc(64 * argc)` with the pointer never read: freed -> 0 allocations, NEVER freed -> also 0 allocations. So a discard-shaped fixture is dark in BOTH directions for a fully dead buffer -- it would not catch a leak either, not just the ambiguity noted above. The only reason the double-free direction survives is that the SECOND free makes the pattern non-removable, which is exactly what B-2026-08-04-11 leg (b) showed (9 allocations while buggy, 8 once fixed). CAVEAT on transferring this: the C measurement is about LLVM's policy for a known allocator. Kara allocates through `karac_malloc_or_panic`, a runtime function, so the removal depends on LLVM seeing through it -- which it evidently does, since the paired Kara discard shapes measured 0 program allocations. The unpaired Kara case was not measured directly (producing a genuine leak needs a compiler bug or an RC cycle), so treat it as strongly indicated rather than proven.  CONSEQUENCE for the remaining work: the RETAINED-CONTROL suggestion above is not a stylistic preference, it is the only thing that can work for this family. Seeding cannot help, and neither failure direction is currently covered.

withdrawn. A retained control makes the FIXTURE allocate, but it does not

while the shape under test stayed elided: coverage-shaped, not coverage.

SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while writing B-2026-08-04-16's regression tests. The warning is what kept that bug's own reported spelling out of the test suite -- `tests/common/mod.rs`'s ownership gate treats it as an error, so the fixture covers the equivalent `t.0 = <named source>` shape instead.

REPRO (warning only; `karac check` still reports "All checks passed", and both backends run it correctly now that -16 is fixed):
    let mut t: (Vec[i64], i64) = (Vec.new(), 3i64);
    let mut e = t.0;      // partial move OUT of the element
    e.push(10i64);
    t.0 = e;              // re-initializes the element
    println(f"{t.0.len()}");
  warning[ownership]: value 't' moved here, used again here (moved at line 3:17)
  help: clone 't' at the move site (`t.clone()`), declare the callee parameter `ref` if it only reads, or restructure to avoid reuse

NOT A TUPLE-ONLY SHAPE -- checked rather than assumed. The struct-field analogue warns identically:
    let mut e = h.items; e.push(10i64); h.items = e;  -> same warning on 'h'
So this is not another instance of the tuple/field asymmetry that B-2026-08-04-16 was; it is one rule applying to both spellings.

WHY IT LOOKS WRONG: moving out of `t.0` is a PARTIAL move of one element, and the subsequent `t.0 = e` re-initializes exactly the element that was moved. The use-after-move the warning points at is the reassignment itself. Rust accepts the same pattern for both tuple elements and struct fields. Two things to confirm before treating it as a plain false positive, neither of which was checked here: whether the checker models partial moves of aggregate elements at all (it may be collapsing `t.0` to `t`), and whether the design intends element-granular move tracking -- design.md Feature 4 is the place to look.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: B-2026-08-02-10's diagnostic actively recommends this shape ("bind the element to a local first"). Until B-2026-08-04-16 landed that advice produced a double free; it now produces a warning telling the author to clone. If the warning is correct, the suggestion should stop recommending the shape; if it is a false positive, it should be silenced for the move-out-then-reassign pattern. Either way the two should agree.  DESIGN CALL SETTLED (owner, 2026-08-04): assigning to a moved-from aggregate element SHOULD re-initialize it, making that element usable again -- Rust's rule. So the warning IS a false positive and the CHECKER is the side to change; B-2026-08-02-10's "bind the element to a local first" advice stands as written.  SPEC CONTEXT, which pointed the other way and had to be read before asking: design.md is explicit that "the root binding becomes inaccessible once any sub-field is consumed" (7919) and that a consume of `v.field` "is a consume of `v`" pushed back to the root (7860, 8136). Re-INITIALIZATION is simply not specified anywhere -- grep for re-initializ/reinitializ finds nothing -- so this was a spec gap rather than a contradiction, and the owner's call fills it.  IMPLEMENTATION IS NOT OVER-BROAD -- measured, not assumed. The checker already tracks element granularity correctly: reading the untouched `t.1` after moving `t.0` is accepted (as is the struct-field twin `h.n` after moving `h.items`), and re-READING the moved-out `t.0` is correctly flagged. Only the ASSIGNMENT case misfires, so nothing needs unwinding -- just one behavior added.  EXACT SITE: `src/use_classifier.rs:429-445`, the `StmtKind::Assign` arm. A bare-identifier LHS is recorded as `UseKind::Reassign` (which `first_uam_witness` already skips as a "used again" partner and `reassign_kills` already treats as a kill); a field / tuple-index / slice-index LHS deliberately falls to `walk_expr(target, Mode::Reading)` instead, on the stated rationale that those are "partial mutations of the projection root, not rebindings of the binding". True for `t.0.push(x)`, false for a whole-element `t.0 = e`.  FIX SHAPE, two COUPLED changes -- and the second is required for soundness, not tidiness: (1) in the Assign arm, record a STATIC projection target (FieldAccess / TupleIndex rooted at an identifier, at any depth) as `UseKind::Reassign` carrying its PlacePath, via the existing `walk_place` / `record_place_at_root` machinery. Do NOT include `Index` targets -- `v[i] = x` is a dynamic element and cannot statically kill anything. (2) make `reassign_kills` (`src/rc_predicate.rs:119`) place-aware: a Reassign of place P kills a consume of place C only when P is a prefix of (or equal to) C. Without (2), change (1) silently ACCEPTS a genuine use-after-move: `let a = t; t.0 = e; println(t.1);` -- the whole-`t` consume would be killed by the `.0` reassign and the `t.1` read would pass. Existing bare-identifier reassigns carry an empty place, which is a prefix of everything, so they keep today's behavior exactly. `reassign_kills_by_reachability` (same file, ~158) needs the same predicate for consistency.  VERIFICATION THIS NEEDS, and the reason it was not attempted in a low-context window: `reassign_kills` is not only a diagnostics gate -- it feeds the RC-fallback boxing decision, and its own doc records that boxing a reassigned Option/enum local miscompiles (B-2026-07-10-4). A place-awareness change there must clear the full `--features llvm` suite plus the rc_predicate unit tests, not just an ownership probe. Probes are in scratchpad/b238 (a: surviving-element read, b: the reassign case, c: genuine re-read, d: struct-field twin).

FIXED 2026-08-05, along the fix shape this row specified, plus ONE CHANGE THE SHAPE DID NOT
CALL FOR that turned out to be load-bearing (below).

WHAT LANDED, the two coupled changes as written:
  (1) `src/use_classifier.rs` Assign arm -- a STATIC whole-element projection target
      (FieldAccess / TupleIndex chain rooted at a bare identifier, any depth) is now recorded as
      `UseKind::Reassign` at the ROOT binding's span, carrying its PlacePath via the existing
      `record_place_at_root`. `Index` targets are excluded as the row instructed (`v[i] = x`
      names a dynamic element and can statically kill nothing), as is any non-identifier root.
  (2) `place_rebind_covers(reassigned, consumed)` (new, `src/cfg.rs`) -- a rebind of place P
      kills a consume of place C only when P is a prefix of, or equal to, C. Threaded through
      `reassign_kills` AND `reassign_kills_by_reachability` as the row required, and also
      through the loop-of-consume rebind suppression (`loop_of_consume_candidates`), which the
      row did not name but is the same `Reassign | Define` filter and would otherwise let a
      `t.0 = e` in a loop suppress a consume of the whole `t`.

THE ADDITION: the partner-skip in `first_witness` AND `first_uam_witness` also needed the
covers check. Both skip a `Reassign | Define` as the "used again" U partner unconditionally.
With (1) alone that silently DROPS a genuine diagnostic: `let a = t; t.0 = e;` with no later
read of `t` writes into an aggregate that owns nothing, and the assignment is the only site
left to report -- before this change it was a Read partner and got flagged, after it became a
Reassign and got skipped. Scoping the skip by the same predicate keeps it: `[0]` does not cover
the whole-binding empty path, so the marker stays reportable. Verified to be load-bearing
rather than assumed -- reverting just this refinement (keeping everything else) fails
`element_assign_into_a_wholly_moved_aggregate_is_itself_an_error` and nothing else.

NET EFFECT vs. before, stated precisely because the direction matters for RC soundness: every
Reassign the classifier recorded before this change carries the EMPTY place, which is a prefix
of everything, so all of them behave exactly as they did. The predicate only scopes the NEW
projection reassigns -- sites that were previously Reads, contributing nothing to suppression.
Suppression can therefore only grow relative to today, never shrink, which is the safe
direction for the B-2026-07-10-4 miscompile the row warned about (that one came from too
LITTLE suppression -- boxing a reassigned local).

PROBE MATRIX, run against both the fixed and unfixed compiler (scratchpad/b238, extended from
the four the row left with two soundness controls):

                            before   after
  a surviving-element read  clean    clean   (element granularity was already right)
  b THE BUG: reassign back  WARNS    clean   <- fixed
  c genuine re-read         WARNS    WARNS   (no reassign, so nothing re-inits)
  d struct-field twin       WARNS    clean   <- fixed, same rule both spellings
  e whole-move + .0 assign  WARNS    WARNS   <- the row's soundness trap
  f assign into moved, no
    later read              WARNS    WARNS   <- what the addition above preserves

(b) and (d) also RUN correctly on both backends, printing 1 under `--interp` and `karac
build` alike.

TESTS: seven in `tests/ownership.rs` -- three accept (tuple, struct-field, and a two-step
nested projection) and four controls. The three accept tests are stash-proven RED against the
unfixed compiler; the controls pass both ways, which is what a control should do. Three unit
tests in `src/use_classifier.rs`: the placed-Reassign for a field target, the tuple twin, and
the `v[i] = x` exclusion. Round 12.19's `field_assign_target_does_not_emit_reassign` pinned the
OPPOSITE behavior and is REPLACED, not deleted -- its replacement asserts the marker exists AND
carries the right place, since the place is what makes the marker safe.

VERIFICATION the row asked for, in full: `cargo test --features llvm` 12992 passed / 0 failed
across 102 suites; `rc_predicate` unit tests 40/40; `tests/rc_fallback.rs` 48/48; fmt and
`clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm -D warnings` clean.

DIAGNOSTIC FOLLOW-UP now closed: B-2026-08-02-10's "bind the element to a local first"
suggestion produces neither heap corruption (since B-2026-08-04-16) nor a warning (since this),
so it is clean on both grounds the two rows were tracking.

title: Double-free (masked at -O2, hard at -O0/JIT): an owned struct/enum binding moved by an ASSIGNMENT — `o.h = h` into a heap-owning user-struct field, or `w2 = w` param-view rebind onto a value enum — left its SOURCE armed, so both the destination and the source ran the value's memory drop at scope exit and freed the shared heap twice. `karac run` (unoptimized JIT) aborted with `free(): double free detected` where `karac build` (-O2, DSE drops the dead source store) was fine. A leg B-2026-08-01-16/19 left open: those retracted the moved binding's Drop BODIES, but the name-blind memory drop survived.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the JIT run==build parity leg (`KARAC_TEST_JIT=1`, `tests/codegen.rs`) on `e2e_param_field_store_single_caller_fire` and `e2e_assign_param_rebind_and_displaced_bodies` after the owning session's leg-a/leg-b fixes (375dd77, 98335fc8) cleared the f-string sibling. CONFIRMED the -O2 masking directly: `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 karac build` double-frees, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=2` is clean; interp is clean. IR proof: for `o.h = h` the take() epilogue emits both `__karac_drop_struct_Outer(%o)` (owns the moved value) AND `__karac_drop_struct_Holder(%h)` over the un-nulled source. TWO shapes: (1) the field-store source-suppression at the FieldAccess-target Assign only fired for String/Vec (`is_string_type_expr`) and Map/Set fields, never a user-struct field, so nothing cap-zeroed the source struct; (2) the param-view rebind retraction dropped only the LHS bodies, leaving a value ENUM's payload caps live. The struct rebind `h2 = h` and `d = <fresh>` were already clean; the struct-literal move `Outer { h: h }` disarms the free but has a separate body double-fire (out of scope).
resolution: FIXED in 06bf3145. (1) FieldAccess-target Assign: extend the source-suppression to a non-shared user-struct field — `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg(value)` (already struct-aware: it walks var_type_names and zero_struct_move_caps_mono the source) + `suppress_user_drop_for_var(src)` for the bodies, leaving the destination struct the sole owner. (2) Param-view rebind onto a value enum (`rhs_is_param_view && lhs_is_tracked_value_enum`): also `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg(value)` so the source enum's live-variant payload caps zero and its EnumDrop no-ops; scoped to the enum arm since the struct sibling is disarmed upstream. Verified across interp / AOT-O0 / AOT-O2 / JIT (identical output, no crash): codegen 2785/0 on BOTH the AOT and JIT legs, memory_sanitizer 929/0 (ASAN+LSan, no leak from the disarm), clippy --features llvm --all-targets + fmt clean.

title: The `KARAC_TEST_JIT=1` codegen parity leg did not set KARAC_PROGRAM_ARGS, so `env.args().len()` returned 2 (the `karac_jit_runner` argv `[runner, <ir>.ll]`) instead of the AOT-oracle 1 (`[argv0]`). A codegen test folding `env.args().len()` into its output as a deliberate not-a-constant diverged from the AOT oracle by that off-by-one and failed only under JIT.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-04-19 under the full JIT leg — two NON-param-view tests failed (`e2e_named_source_moved_into_a_tuple_element_is_disarmed`, `e2e_freshtemp_result_arm_binding_a_struct_payload_owns_it_once`, both added after the last JIT-leg CI run in e986284/98335fc8). The `left`/`right` diff was a uniform +1 shift on exactly the env.args-derived values (non-derived values matched), and both PASS under AOT — ruling out the drop change and pinning it to `env.args().len()`=2 under the harness. `karac_runtime_env_args_into` (runtime/src/lib.rs) prefers KARAC_PROGRAM_ARGS and falls back to process argv; `karac run` sets it (cli.rs) but the harness's `jit_dispatch` did not. Same class of harness gap as the arrow-JIT routing fix.
resolution: FIXED in 39b0c294. `jit_dispatch` now sets `KARAC_PROGRAM_ARGS` to a single synthetic argv0 element (the IR path) so `env.args().len()` is 1, matching an AOT binary; the value is unread (the tests use `.len()`). B-2026-07-29-18 built this channel for exactly this run==build parity. Verified: full codegen suite 2785/0 on the JIT leg (was 2 failing), still 2785/0 on AOT.

title: `karac fmt` silently deleted every declaration modifier it had no printer for (`unsafe fn`, `comptime fn`, `comptime` param prefix)
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found while adding the `frozen` parameter printer for B-2026-08-01-33 stage 1, which is the same shape — a modifier that lives BESIDE the type rather than inside it has to be written back explicitly by the item/param printer, and three of them never were. REPRO: `karac fmt` on `pub unsafe fn danger() -> i64 { 1 }` emits `pub fn danger() -> i64`; on `comptime fn twice(comptime n: i64)` emits `fn twice(n: i64)`. Confirmed on free functions, impl methods (they share `format_function`), and trait-method signatures (`format_trait_method`, which has its own printer and dropped `unsafe` too). WHY IT MATTERS TODAY vs LATER: `unsafe fn` is not yet enforced at call sites and `comptime` is surface-only (slice 1 records the marker; the typechecker rule lands with the evaluator), so the deletion is currently INERT — a formatted program still compiles and behaves identically. It stops being inert the moment either rule lands, at which point `karac fmt` becomes a silent semantic edit of the user's source. Filed at medium rather than low because the tool corrupts input it was asked only to reformat, and because the failure is invisible: no diagnostic, no diff the user would read as suspicious. FIX: print `comptime` / `unsafe` in `format_function` (in the parser's accepted order, `pub comptime unsafe fn`), `unsafe` in `format_trait_method`, and `comptime` in `format_fn_params`. TEST: `declaration_modifiers_round_trip_through_the_formatter` (tests/parser.rs) asserts all four spellings survive AND that reformatting is a fixpoint — verified RED against the unfixed formatter. NOT AUDITED: whether other AST modifier bits have the same gap. The three found here were the ones reachable from a function signature; a sweep of every `is_*` flag against its printer is a separate task.

title: Passing a TUPLE ELEMENT to a `ref` parameter (`peek(t.0)` where `fn peek(v: ref Vec[i64])`) double-frees the element buffer under AOT; the struct-field twin `peek(h.a)` is clean and the interpreter is correct on both
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by a systematic tuple-vs-struct-field PARITY SWEEP (probe dir b240), not accidentally. Motivation for the sweep: 15 tuple rows were filed between 2026-08-01 and 2026-08-04, four of them high, and every one reads "the tuple spelling of a walk that handles the struct-field spelling" -- yet not one was found by looking. The sweep pairs each operation's struct-field spelling (the reference implementation, and a free oracle) against its tuple-element twin with identical semantics, and runs both on the interpreter and AOT under valgrind. 13 operations covered: destructure, method-on-element, index-of-element, compound assign, owned arg, ref arg, mut ref arg, scope drop, in Vec, in Option, element move-out, String element, nested projection.

SWEEP RESULT: 9 of 13 at parity, 3 divergences (this row is one), and one REVERSE-direction gap that is not a bug -- `h.inner.a[0]` loud-bails with "chained field receivers (`a.b.c`) are deferred to v1.x" while the tuple `t.0.0[0]` works, so the tuple spelling is AHEAD there.

NON-VACUITY: the field twin allocates 8 and frees 8; the counts below differ from that, which is what makes the divergence real rather than an optimizer artifact (B-2026-08-04-17). Seeded from `env.args().len()` with element reads throughout.

SHARED PRELUDE for every repro:
    fn mkv(k: i64) -> Vec[i64] { let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(k); v.push(k + 1i64); return v; }
    struct H { a: Vec[i64], b: i64 }
  and `let n: i64 = env.args().len();` as the first line of main.

REPRO:
    fn peek(v: ref Vec[i64]) -> i64 { return v[0i64]; }
  FIELD (correct):  let h: H = H { a: mkv(n), b: 5i64 };
                    println(f"{peek(h.a)}:{h.a.len()}");   -> 1:2, 8 allocs / 8 frees
  TUPLE (BROKEN):   let t: (Vec[i64], i64) = (mkv(n), 5i64);
                    println(f"{peek(t.0)}:{t.0.len()}");   -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2
                    valgrind: Invalid free, 8 allocs / 9 frees
  interpreter: 1:2 on BOTH spellings, so this is AOT-only.

READING OF THE SYMPTOM, explicitly NOT a diagnosis -- no IR was dumped and no codegen path was read. A `ref` parameter must NOT take ownership, so the callee should register no cleanup for it; the extra free suggests the tuple-element argument is being treated as an owned/temporary value somewhere the field spelling is not. The natural first place to look is whether the ref-arg path recognizes a TupleIndex place the way it recognizes FieldAccess -- the same shape of omission as B-2026-08-04-16, where the tuple-assign arm simply never got the field arm's suppression.

RELATED: B-2026-08-05-2 is the `mut ref` sibling found in the same sweep and is probably the same missing place-recognition; check whether one fix covers both before treating them as independent.  RESOLVED, and the two rows really were one bug -- the shared-fix guess on both rows held. CAUSE: B-2026-07-12-1 taught the ref-argument path to pass a POINTER to a struct FIELD instead of letting it reach the rvalue path, which shallow-copies the `{ptr,len,cap}` header into a temp and queues a scope-exit free of a buffer the owner still holds. That fix's own comment describes `scan(self.names, q)` aborting with `free(): double free detected` under AOT while the interpreter was correct. The TUPLE-element spelling never got the sibling arm, so it fell through and reproduced the identical abort one spelling over.  WHY ONE ARM FIXES BOTH SYMPTOMS: the `ref` case frees the temp (double free); the `mut ref` case MUTATES the temp, so `v.push(42)` grew a copy the tuple never saw -- `t.0.len()` stayed 2 and the following `t.0[2]` panicked. Same missing pointer, two failure modes. Worth noting which is the more dangerous: the panic is loud, but a lost `mut ref` write on a shape with no bounds-checked read after it is a SILENT wrong answer.  GATED exactly like the field arm -- only a `{ptr,len,cap}` element, so scalar and enum elements keep the existing path. Reuses `field_chain_place_ptr`, which already walks a tuple-index hop.  VERIFIED by re-running the full 13-case parity sweep that found these: `ref_arg` and `mutref_arg` now sit at 8 allocs / 8 frees, byte-identical to their struct-field twins. `in_option` (B-2026-08-05-3) is unchanged, confirming it is a separate site as that row predicted.
fix: 99d27f7 (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs — a TupleIndex arm in the ref-argument path, sibling to B-2026-07-12-1's FieldAccess arm). ONE arm closes both rows. Pins codegen.rs::e2e_tuple_element_borrowed_in_place_for_ref_params, memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_tuple_element_borrowed_in_place_for_ref_params (floored at 300 against ~800 allocations), interpreter.rs::test_tuple_element_borrowed_in_place_for_ref_params. Both codegen tests are stash-proven RED against the unfixed compiler (E2E panics with `vec index out of bounds`, ASAN reports a memory error); the interpreter twin passes both ways. cargo test --features llvm: 12980 passed, 0 failed.

title: `Option[(Vec[T], ...)]` leaks the tuple payload's heap element when the Some arm binds and reads it -- 32 bytes definitely lost; the struct payload twin `Option[H]` is clean and the interpreter is correct on both
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by a systematic tuple-vs-struct-field PARITY SWEEP (probe dir b240), not accidentally. Motivation for the sweep: 15 tuple rows were filed between 2026-08-01 and 2026-08-04, four of them high, and every one reads "the tuple spelling of a walk that handles the struct-field spelling" -- yet not one was found by looking. The sweep pairs each operation's struct-field spelling (the reference implementation, and a free oracle) against its tuple-element twin with identical semantics, and runs both on the interpreter and AOT under valgrind. 13 operations covered: destructure, method-on-element, index-of-element, compound assign, owned arg, ref arg, mut ref arg, scope drop, in Vec, in Option, element move-out, String element, nested projection.

SWEEP RESULT: 9 of 13 at parity, 3 divergences (this row is one), and one REVERSE-direction gap that is not a bug -- `h.inner.a[0]` loud-bails with "chained field receivers (`a.b.c`) are deferred to v1.x" while the tuple `t.0.0[0]` works, so the tuple spelling is AHEAD there.

NON-VACUITY: the field twin allocates 8 and frees 8; the counts below differ from that, which is what makes the divergence real rather than an optimizer artifact (B-2026-08-04-17). Seeded from `env.args().len()` with element reads throughout.

SHARED PRELUDE for every repro:
    fn mkv(k: i64) -> Vec[i64] { let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(k); v.push(k + 1i64); return v; }
    struct H { a: Vec[i64], b: i64 }
  and `let n: i64 = env.args().len();` as the first line of main.

REPRO:
  FIELD (correct):  let o: Option[H] = Option.Some(H { a: mkv(n), b: 5i64 });
                    match o { Option.Some(x) => { println(f"{x.a[0i64]}"); }
                              Option.None => { println("none"); } }
                    -> 1, 8 allocs / 8 frees
  TUPLE (BROKEN):   let o: Option[(Vec[i64], i64)] = Option.Some((mkv(n), 5i64));
                    match o { Option.Some(x) => { println(f"{x.0[0i64]}"); }
                              Option.None => { println("none"); } }
                    -> 1 (correct value), but 8 allocs / 7 frees
                    valgrind: 32 bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost
  interpreter: 1 on BOTH. AOT-only, and the VALUE is right -- this is a pure
  leak, not a miscompile.

SCOPE NOTE: this is adjacent to but distinct from the already-fixed B-2026-08-02-22 (`Vec[(T, ...)]` element: no element memory drop and no bodies walk) and B-2026-08-03-3 (a tuple-held Option/Result payload is never freed). Those cover a tuple CONTAINING an Option/Result, or a Vec containing a tuple; this is an Option CONTAINING a tuple, matched and bound. Confirm against those two fixes before assuming a new site -- it may be the same walk missing one more carrier.

The 32 bytes is the `Vec[i64]` data buffer (two i64 elements plus header rounding), i.e. the tuple element's heap, not the tuple itself. — FUZZER COVERAGE (2026-08-05): drop_fuzz now reaches this automatically; it was found on the first run after the grammar gained nested containers (a tuple inside an Option). 2 of 30 programs, on BOTH the seq and autopar surfaces, as `memory-leak`. Seed-reproducible: `drop_fuzz --count 1 --seed 4250` (also 4257), and the built-in shrinker reduces it to the two-line core:  let mut o: Option[(Vec[String], i64)] = Some((Vec["<40+ bytes>"], 30i64));  match o { Some(x) => { acc = acc + tup_vec_len(x); }, None => {} }  — wrapped in a 40-round loop so the leak accumulates past LSan's noise floor, with `tup_vec_len` reading the element so DCE cannot elide it. NOT pinned in drop_fuzz's KNOWN_OPEN: that mechanism is signature-KIND granular, and `memory-leak` is the single highest-value signature the fuzzer has — pinning it to silence one bug would disarm the whole leak class for every new bug too. So the nightly fuzz job stays RED on this until it is fixed. That is the intended trade, but it does mean this row is now gating a CI signal.

RESOLVED 2026-08-05 (commit 18a4084). THREE independent gaps, each uncovered by fixing the one before it; the row's own framing ("when the Some arm binds and reads it") named only the symptom of the first.

GAP 1 -- the let-site drop never registered at all. `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok` (src/codegen/runtime.rs) bails at `let TypeKind::Path(p) = &payload_te.kind else { return false; }`, and a tuple is `TypeKind::Tuple`, so NOTHING queued a scope-exit drop. The arm binding was a red herring: an `Option[(Vec[i64], i64)]` that is bound and NEVER MATCHED leaks identically (probe n2), which is what places this on the let-site walk. Everything downstream already handled tuples -- `te_recursive_drop_fully_supported` recurses through `TypeKind::Tuple`, and `emit_option_drop_fn` defers to `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr`, which synthesizes the same tuple drop `compile_tuple_index_store` already uses on a tuple element. Only the gate was missing the arm. Fix: a Tuple arm in that gate (requiring at least one non-trivially-copyable element, so `Option[(i64, i64)]` gets no no-op drop), plus a new narrow `option_payload_is_droppable_tuple` predicate gating a fourth registrar call (`track_inline_option_agg_payload_var`) at the simple-let site in stmts.rs.

GAP 2 -- the `Result` carrier still leaked after gap 1. A consuming arm ran `suppress_inline_result_payload_cleanup` unconditionally, disarming the source for a binding that has NO OWNER OF ITS OWN. A struct payload is `track_struct_var`'d and a direct `String`/`Vec` payload is `track_vec_var`'d, but `bind_pattern_values` never `track_tuple_var`s a match binding -- so the buffer was handed to nobody. `Option` has been consumption-gated since B-2026-07-03-31 (`arm_only_borrows_option_agg_payload`); `Result` never was. Fix: the missing sibling `arm_only_borrows_result_tuple_payload` / `block_only_borrows_result_tuple_payload`, wired at the match-arm, if-let, and while-let sites (let-else stays unconditional, mirroring the Option twin), narrowed to a whole-TUPLE binding so struct and direct-heap payloads keep their unconditional suppression.

GAP 3 -- a GUARDED arm still leaked, on BOTH carriers, and only when the guard mentioned the binding. `Some(x) if x.1 == 5i64` leaked; `Some(x) if n == 1i64` was clean -- that pair is what isolated it. `a == b` on scalars does NOT stay a surface `Binary`: the lowering pass rewrites it to `Call { callee: Path(["i64", "eq"]), args: [a, b] }`, and `consume_class::has_consuming_sink` reads any non-`Identifier` callee as a path-callee CONSTRUCTION, scoring every derived argument a transfer. Those calls reroute straight to an LLVM binary/unary op (assoc_call.rs's `is_primitive` arm) that reads its operands and stores nothing. Fix: `is_lowered_primitive_operator` in consume_class.rs classifies them free-fn-shaped. This is a general classifier correction, not a tuple-specific one -- it was invisible for a struct payload only because the binding owns itself there, so the spurious suppression was harmless.

TWO REGRESSIONS CAUGHT DURING THE FIX, both now pinned as controls in the fixture:
  * Registering the aggregate payload unconditionally at the let-site DOUBLE-registers a struct payload (it is already on another channel): `Option[H]` went 8 allocs / 8 frees -> 11 / 12 and aborted. Hence the tuple-only gate.
  * Admitting a tuple PATTERN destructure (`Some((v, k))`) to gap 2's borrow-only gate is a DOUBLE FREE: that pattern binds the ELEMENTS, each of which does get a `track_vec_var` owner, so the source must still suppress. `option_agg_payload_binds` now returns None for a `PatternKind::Tuple` sub-pattern -- safe by construction, since a tuple payload only entered that channel with this fix.

VERIFICATION: 35 hand probes (dir b242) across both carriers x match / if-let / never-matched / guarded / borrow-only / move-to-owned-param / move-out-of-fn / tuple-destructure / String element / Vec[String] element / Err-half heap / all-scalar, plus the struct-payload controls. All valgrind-clean, all at interpreter parity. Tests: `asan_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` (the RED one -- 1,807 allocs / 1,007 frees pre-fix, 1,807 / 1,807 after), with codegen and interpreter value-parity twins `e2e_`/`test_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once`. The E2E and interpreter twins PASS pre-fix by construction: this was a pure leak and the printed answer was always correct, which their doc comments state so nobody mistakes them for leak coverage.

FUZZER: this unblocks the deliberately-RED nightly drop_fuzz job (16d929c). Seeds 4250 and 4257 were the reproducers.

REOPENED 2026-08-05 (dd30778) -- the OPTION leg only. 18a4084 claimed all three legs; the Option leg's fix was WRONG and drop_fuzz caught it within the hour (seed 4272: `free(): double free detected`, one extra free per loop round). It is withdrawn. The Result leg and the guard leg stay fixed and verified.

WHAT REMAINS OPEN: exactly the shape this row was filed for -- `Option[(Vec[T], ...)]` leaks the tuple payload's heap element. Both when matched and when NEVER matched (probe n2), so it is the scope-exit walk, not arm binding. Also leaks with a guarded arm, an if-let, a String element, and a move-to-owned-param arm (probes n2 n3 n4 n6 m1 q12 r1 r2 r3 base in scratchpad/b242).

WHY THE FIRST ATTEMPT WAS UNSOUND, which is the useful part. It registered a SECOND, independent scope-exit drop (`track_inline_option_agg_payload_var`) at the simple-let site. A droppable tuple payload is at least FOUR words, so it never fits the inline payload area -- it is ALWAYS heap-boxed at pack time, and `track_boxed_enum_var` has already registered a `BoxedEnumDrop` owning it. Two owners, one buffer. `track_inline_result_payload_var` guards against precisely this (`if self.boxed_enum_payload_vars.contains(var_name) { return; }`); the new registrar had no such guard. All 35 hand probes passed anyway, because the box drop is box-ONLY (`inner_drop_fn` derives from a struct NAME and is `None` for a tuple), so in isolation the second action only freed what the first left behind. It takes a program where the tuple's own drop is ALSO synthesized -- which the fuzzer's larger corpus produces and a two-line probe does not -- for both to free the same pointer.

WHERE THE FIX BELONGS, and how far it was taken. Give the EXISTING `BoxedEnumDrop` the tuple's recursive drop -- the B-2026-07-12-4 pattern: in stmts.rs's boxed-payload registration (the `for (enum_name, variant, inner) in &boxed` loop, ~line 4688), resolve `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr(payload_te)` for a `TypeKind::Tuple` payload that passes `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok`, and pass it through `track_boxed_enum_var_with_inner_drop` instead of the struct-name-derived `inner`. MEASURED: that fixes seed 4272 AND every leak probe. It is NOT sufficient alone -- two probes then DOUBLE-FREE instead, because the consuming-arm suppressors do not clear a box's `inner_drop_fn` for a tuple payload:
  * p3  `let g = match o { Option.Some(x) => x.0, Option.None => Vec.new() };`   (element moved out)
  * q9  `match o { Option.Some((v, k)) => ... }`                                 (tuple PATTERN destructure -- the elements get their own `track_vec_var`)
So the remaining work is extending B-2026-08-04-2's channel (`suppress_boxed_payload_move` / `suppress_boxed_payload_struct_destructure`, which already clears `inner_drop_fn` for a whole-payload binding) to the tuple move-out and tuple-destructure arms. Start there, not from scratch. Note this also requires widening `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok` with a Tuple arm again -- that half was correct and is only reverted because nothing consumed it.

PROCESS NOTE, and the reason this row was closed prematurely: a hand-probe sweep is NOT sufficient evidence for a drop-OWNERSHIP change. 35 probes, interpreter parity on all of them, a 1,807-allocation looped fixture, both clippy gates and the full `--features llvm` suite were all green on a change that double-frees. Re-verify any next attempt against `scripts/drop-fuzz.sh --count 300 --seed 4230`, which is what caught it.

The nightly drop_fuzz job stays RED on this row's leak signature, as 16d929c intended.

STILL FIXED (18a4084, unchanged by the withdrawal): the RESULT carrier and the GUARD leg. `Result[(Vec[T], ...), E]` is clean on every probed shape -- match / if-let / never-matched / guarded / borrow-only / move-to-owned-param / move-out-of-fn / tuple-destructure / String element / Vec[String] element / Err-half heap / all-scalar, plus the struct controls. And a guarded arm no longer leaks on EITHER carrier: `x.1 == 5i64` lowers to `Call { callee: Path(["i64", "eq"]) }` and the consumption classifier was reading that as a path-callee CONSTRUCTION, scoring the operand a transfer; `is_lowered_primitive_operator` in consume_class.rs corrects it. That correction is carrier-independent and benefits every consumer of `binding_only_borrowed`. Regression coverage: `asan_optres_tuple_payload_is_owned_exactly_once` (+ codegen/interpreter value twins), scoped to the Result legs.

RESOLVED 2026-08-05 (f0aadd9) — the Option leg, second attempt. All three legs of this row are now closed.

THE FIX: `Option[(Vec[T], ...)]`'s payload is at least four words, so it never fits the inline payload area — it is heap-BOXED at pack time and `track_boxed_enum_var` already registers a `BoxedEnumDrop` for it. That action's `inner_drop_fn` is derived from a struct NAME and is `None` for a tuple, so the free was box-ONLY: the box came back, the tuple's elements did not. Two coupled halves:
  1. stmts.rs's boxed-payload registration resolves the tuple's own `emit_drop_fn_for_type_expr` and hands it to that SAME action (`track_boxed_enum_var_with_inner_drop`) — the B-2026-07-12-4 pattern, and the named-binding peer of what B-2026-07-18-3 already does for a fresh-temp scrutinee (that site picks its inner drop from the PATTERN, which a let-site cannot see yet).
  2. A CONSUMING arm retracts it back to box-only (`clear_boxed_enum_inner_drop`, mutating not removing — the box allocation must still be reclaimed). Half 1 alone is NOT sufficient: `match o { Some(x) => x.0 }` (element escapes) and `match o { Some((v, k)) => ... }` (per-element destructure, leaf bindings each `track_vec_var`'d) both DOUBLE-FREE without it. WHY THE FIRST ATTEMPT (18a4084, withdrawn dd30778) WAS WRONG, kept because it is the transferable lesson: it registered a SECOND, independent drop action at the let-site instead of using the owner that was already there. `track_inline_result_payload_var` guards against exactly that (`if self.boxed_enum_payload_vars.contains(var_name) { return; }`); the new registrar had no such guard. It passed 35 hand probes, interpreter parity on all of them, a 1,807-allocation looped fixture, both clippy gates and the full `--features llvm` suite — and double-freed one allocation per loop round in the wild.

That seed range is where every reproducer lived: 4231, 4236, 4250, 4257 (the row's own, named in 16d929c) and 4272 (the double-free the first attempt introduced). Plus 21 hand probes across both carriers x match / if-let / never-matched / guarded / borrow-only / move-to-owned-param / move-out-of-match / tuple-destructure / String element / Vec[String] element / Err-half / all-scalar / struct controls, all valgrind-clean and all at interpreter parity.

Both passed on a change that double-freed. drop-fuzz is the gate; run it before closing, and the regression showed up 42 programs in, so `--count 60` is enough for the routine check.
