title: PERF-REGRESSION introduced by B-2026-07-31-21's fix (75a3a928): a remove-heavy Map runs 1.76x slower because the same-width compacting rehash re-fires on every eviction where the old code doubled once -- kata:146 LRU cache 231.7ms -> 422.9ms on the M5 host lane, ROOT-CAUSED by archive swap, sinks identical
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the 15-kata M5 Pro host-lane re-bench of 2026-08-04 (kara-katas c47be47, karac 9b43809a), not by a targeted probe. Fourteen of the fifteen deltas were explained by the honest-C-mirror rewrites of 2026-07-31; this one was not.

WHAT 75a3a928 DID. B-2026-07-31-21 fixed unbounded capacity ratcheting (297 MB RSS for 1024 live entries) by making next_capacity() pick the width when the growth trigger fires: SAME capacity when the live count is at or below ~3/8 of it -- rehash_from drops every tombstone -- else double. That is correct and the RSS win is real (297 MB -> 10 MB).

THE UNPRICED COST. An LRU cache is the canonical remove-heavy map: every insert past capacity evicts, so live count sits permanently near the same-width threshold and the compacting rehash fires again and again, each one O(len). The old code paid one doubling and then stopped rehashing entirely. The commit measured the RSS it bought but not the wall-time it spent, and no bench in the corpus covered a churn-dominated map at the time.

MEASUREMENT (controlled, same machine, same session). git worktree at 75a3a928^ (c4dd6169), `cargo rustc -p karac-runtime --release --crate-type staticlib` there, then the SAME installed karac 9b43809a compiling the SAME kata:146 bench source against each archive via KARAC_RUNTIME. Only the runtime archive differs:
    pre-75a3a928 runtime : 241.0 ms +- 2.7 (hyperfine, 20 runs)
    current runtime      : 424.8 ms +- 6.6
    ratio                : 1.76x
Sinks byte-identical (65640802092) on both, so this is real work, not skipped work. The pre-fix time reproduces the 2026-07-28 recorded 231.7 ms, which closes the loop on the historical number. Both rows are honest single-threaded (cpu 99.6% / 99.7%); user_ms 229.8 -> 418.9, so the cost is compute, not scheduling.

SCOPE. Not every Map workload pays it. Ruled OUT by measurement: kata:170 (Map[i64,i64], ~170 adds and NO removals) is 1.03x across the same archive swap -- the tombstone/compaction path needs removals to fire. kata:219 (sliding-window Set, the LARGEST map in the batch at 13.8 MB RSS) is flat at 1.01x. So the trigger is REMOVAL CHURN at a live count near the 3/8 boundary, not map size and not map traffic.

NOT A REVERT CANDIDATE. Unbounded RSS growth was the worse bug and the 3/8 headroom bound is reasoned (gating same-width on merely fitting under the 3/4 trigger would re-fire an O(len) rehash on every insert at the boundary). The gap is that the compaction has no hysteresis: a table that has just been compacted and is immediately churned back to the trigger compacts again for no gain. Candidate directions: track compactions-since-growth and force a double after N, or widen the same-width band's lower bound so a steady-state churning table settles one size up instead of oscillating.

FIXED 2026-08-05 (73237002), verified on the REAL kata:146 workload.

A first pass at this row (committed, then retracted here) concluded that the
regression did not reproduce on x86 and was in fact INVERTED there, and left
the row open on that basis. That conclusion was WRONG and its write-up has been
removed rather than left to mislead; the row's original attribution was right.
The corrected result follows, with the reason the first pass got it backwards,
because the methodological trap is reusable.

THE MEASUREMENT, three archives, same karac, same source, only the runtime
archive differing (kara-katas 4459646, bench/lru_cache.kara, 32M ops, cap=1024,
key_range=4096, sink 65640802092 identical on all three):

  c4dd6169 (pre-75a3a928)      543 ms    peak RSS 2736 KB
  3/8 band (the regression)    882 ms    peak RSS 2728 KB
  3/16 band (this fix)         552 ms    peak RSS 2716 KB

The regression reproduces at 1.62x on x86 Linux -- the same magnitude the row
recorded on the M5 Pro lane (1.76x) -- and widening the band to 3/16 recovers
it to within 1.7% of the pre-75a3a928 baseline. RSS is flat across all three,
so the recovery costs nothing here.

WHY THE FIRST PASS CONCLUDED THE OPPOSITE, and the lesson. kara-katas was not
in the container, so the first pass APPROXIMATED kata:146 with a hand-written
sliding window of EVER-DISTINCT keys. That single detail inverts the
comparison. With distinct keys the pre-fix unconditional doubling ratchets --
that is exactly the B-2026-07-31-21 bug -- so the baseline table blew out to 1M
buckets, stopped being cache-resident, and measured 3-4x SLOWER than the 3/8
policy. The real kata draws keys from a BOUNDED range of 4096, so removed keys
come back, the doubling policy never ratchets, its table stays small and fast,
and the 3/8 compaction is pure added cost with nothing to trade against. The
approximation reproduced the wrong bug's workload and read its result as
evidence about this one.

Rule this earns: when a perf row names a kata, MEASURE THAT KATA. The katas
repo is a public clone away (`git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/karalang/
kara-katas`) and the bench directories carry a results.json recording host,
toolchain, and sink, so a container run is directly checkable against the
recorded lane. A synthetic stand-in for a named workload is a hypothesis about
the workload, not a measurement of it.

WHAT REMAINS TRUE from the first pass, unchanged by the correction:
  * The amortization arithmetic that motivated the fix. At the 3/8 band edge a
    churning table pays L / (0.75*C - L) = 1.00 key re-hashes per operation --
    the whole live set re-hashed once per op, forever -- because `rehash_from`
    cannot skip the per-key `hash_fn` (buckets store no hash). 3/16 drops that
    to 0.33. The 1.62x recovery is that 3x landing in wall time.
  * 3/32 remains rejected: 0.33 -> 0.14 for another doubling of width, measured
    slower as the table stops being cache-resident.
  * The archive swap in the ORIGINAL row still spans five runtime commits
    (75a3a92, 107a364, 507a446, 6580a60, 07bf66e) rather than isolating
    75a3a928. That criticism stands as a methodology note -- but it changes
    nothing about the verdict, since isolating the band alone (3/8 vs 3/16,
    identical archives otherwise) accounts for the entire delta. 507a446 is
    exonerated by that same isolation.
  * Set moves with Map; it lowers to `karac_map_new` and there is no second
    copy of the policy.

The distinct-key ratchet bound B-2026-07-31-21 bought is preserved and still
covered: `churn_with_distinct_keys_keeps_capacity_bounded` pins the steady
state at 8192 buckets for a 1024-live distinct-key window (unconditional
doubling reaches 65536+ there, and measured 38 MB RSS against this fix's
2.4 MB). The two workloads want opposite things from the resize policy --
bounded-key churn wants rare compaction, distinct-key churn wants bounded
width -- and 3/16 satisfies both where 3/8 sacrificed the first.

VERIFICATION: cargo test --features llvm 13004 passed / 0 failed across 102
suites; fmt and `clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm -D warnings` clean;
wasm clippy clean on wasm32-wasip1 and wasm32-wasip1-threads.

=== FOLLOW-ON (45398dd9): the arm64 confirmation this row was left open for, plus a second fix that goes past the baseline ===

ARM64 HOST-LANE CONFIRMATION. 73237002 shipped the 3/16 band on the honest note
that the 1.76x was not reproducible on its x86 container and the arm64 timing was
therefore unverified. It is now verified on the M5 Pro host lane, with a MATCHED
karac (one binary, worktree HEAD) driving four runtime archives via KARAC_RUNTIME
so nothing but runtime/src/map.rs differs, every binary sink-checked at
65640802092 before being timed (hyperfine, 30 runs, quiet machine):
    pre-75a3a928 (unconditional doubling)  237.2 ms +- 1.4
    3/8 band  (the regression)             419.4 ms +- 3.2   1.77x
    3/16 band (73237002, current main)     238.3 ms +- 3.8   recovers fully
    3/16 band + vacate (this commit)       223.3 ms +- 3.2   0.94x of baseline
The 1.77x reproduces the originally-filed 1.76x, and the band recovers all of it.
The x86 non-reproduction stands as an architecture split, not a retraction.

THE SECOND FIX. The band made the compacting rehash rarer; it did not stop the
tombstones that drive it from being created. `remove` marked a tombstone
unconditionally, but a tombstone is only NEEDED when a probe chain can continue
past the bucket -- and when the next bucket is already EMPTY, none can: any probe
reaching this slot stops one step later regardless. `vacate` releases the slot
outright in that case. Compaction re-hash work on the distinct-key churn test,
over both axes (hash_fn calls above one-per-operation, which is exactly the
compaction work since buckets store no hash):
                        vacate off   vacate on
    3/8  band            15.52%        7.06%
    3/16 band             6.29%        1.92%
The two are independent and STACK; neither subsumes the other. kata:146 goes to
223.3 ms, 6% BELOW the pre-regression baseline, because lookups stop walking
tombstone runs -- a win no capacity policy can buy.

REJECTED VARIANT, measured not reasoned. The same argument extends to the
tombstone run BEHIND the released slot (each becomes a run end once its successor
is cleared). Built and measured: 289.7 ms on kata:146, 30% SLOWER than the
one-slot rule. The walk is a backward dependent-load chain the prefetcher cannot
follow, and -- the non-obvious part -- clearing that aggressively holds the table
one doubling smaller (4096 vs 8192), which makes it denser, which makes a removed
slot's successor EMPTY less often, so the rule undercuts its own precondition and
settles at MORE tombstones than the cheap version. Do not re-derive this into the
repo without re-measuring; the doc comment on `vacate` carries the warning.

TEST GAP THIS CLOSED. churn_with_distinct_keys_keeps_capacity_bounded pinned the
steady-state WIDTH (capacity == 8192) as its guard. That width is 8192 whether or
not the rehash storm is happening, so the test reported green through the entire
regression -- it could not have caught this bug and did not. It now also pins the
compaction re-hash WORK as a fraction of the workload (< 4%; shipping state
1.92%, every single-fix regression above 6%). Each of the three regressed
configurations was confirmed to fail an assertion. A second test,
churn_against_reference_map_never_loses_a_key, cross-checks 200k interleaved
insert/remove/get ops against std HashMap under a deliberately collision-heavy
hash, since the failure mode of releasing a bucket too eagerly is a lookup that
misses a PRESENT key -- silent wrong answer, not a crash.

NO COLLATERAL REGRESSION. kata:219 (sliding-window Set, removal-heavy) 111.1 ->
112.2 ms and kata:170 (no removals, so `vacate` never fires) 1.032 -> 1.009 s,
both within noise with identical sinks. Set shares the path -- it lowers to
karac_map_new -- so it moves with Map. cargo test --features llvm green including
the 933-case ASAN memory_sanitizer suite; fmt, clippy --all --all-targets
--features llvm, and wasm clippy on both wasm32-wasip1 and wasm32-wasip1-threads
all clean.

OPEN FOLLOW-UP -- kata:146's README is STALE and needs a re-bench. It still reads
"B-2026-08-05-4 (open)" and carries 422.9 ms in its benchmark table, i.e. the
regressed number and the pre-73237002 status; the cross-language table around it
(C / Rust / Go) was measured in the same 2026-08-04 session and is unaffected by
this fix. Deliberately NOT hand-edited here: README numbers come from the
bench.sh -> results.json -> consolidate pipeline, and re-running that needs karac
reinstalled from main AFTER this lands. Expected new Kara row ~223 ms, which
moves it from 1.73x-slower-than-Rust to roughly 3.3x FASTER than the equal-safety
Rust row, so the prose around the table needs rewriting, not just the cell.
tracker: runtime/src/map.rs::next_capacity (same-width band 3/8 -> 3/16, 73237002) + runtime/src/map.rs::vacate (release the slot when no probe chain runs past it, 45398dd9); guarded by churn_with_distinct_keys_keeps_capacity_bounded (width AND compaction-work assertions) and churn_against_reference_map_never_loses_a_key

title: ARM64 perf regression ATTRIBUTED to 58412d9f (7-bit hash tag in the map bucket control byte); FIX SHAPE REOPENED, was wrongly recorded as settled. The key-type gate this row prescribed is REFUTED on x86 by a tag-only A/B: dropping the tag on kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` executes 13.1% FEWER instructions and runs 1.20x SLOWER (3763.7 -> 4513.2 ms), because the tag rejects a bucket without touching its key while removing it costs a kv load per occupied bucket. The i64-vs-String pair that decided the old shape straddles TWO implementations (`should_use_mono_map_for` admits only i32/i64 keys, so kata:170 is the inlined mono path and kata:127 the erased runtime path), so it never isolated key type. Holding path and key type FIXED, x86 gains 20% from the tag and arm64 loses 27% -- an ISA effect, which reinstates the arch framing this row had retired. Arch-conditional is the surviving candidate and is UNVALIDATED. Separately, arm64 never received the 1.28x x86 speedup in b7ba6ea4..a42b5338.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by the same 15-kata M5 Pro host-lane re-bench as B-2026-08-05-4 (kara-katas c47be47, karac 9b43809a).

OBSERVATION. kata:170's kara row went 771.2 ms (recorded 2026-07-28) -> 997.1 ms (2026-08-04), 1.29x. The kata's .kara source is untouched: the only 2026-07-31 commit in that directory (9f07f73) edited two_sum_iii.c, two_sum_iii.rs and go-seq/main.go and NOT the kara file. Sink verified unchanged at 762965. In the same run C went 2.86x slower (honest hash map) and rust/go ~1.85x FASTER (they gained the kata's early-return) -- both fully explained by 9f07f73, neither touching kara.

RULED OUT (1) -- the map-capacity fix. Same controlled archive swap used to root-cause B-2026-08-05-4: pre-75a3a928 runtime 1.044 s vs current 1.017 s = 1.03x, i.e. no effect (current is marginally FASTER). Consistent with mechanism: kata:170 does ~170 adds and no removals, so there is no tombstone churn for the compaction arm to act on.

RULED OUT (2) -- codegen AFTER 2026-07-30. karac from 2026-07-30 and karac 9b43809a (2026-08-04) compile this source to BYTE-IDENTICAL binaries (sha256 3933899...ce7f, both sink 762965). NOTE the exact scope of this: it eliminates codegen changes after 2026-07-30 ONLY. Codegen changes WITHIN 2026-07-28..07-30 are NOT eliminated -- the 2026-07-30 binary already contains them.

MECHANISM -- AND A CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN HYPOTHESIS. The row argued 58412d9f 'adds a per-bucket `status[capacity]` byte array, so every probe now touches a SECOND cache line', and rested the arch-divergence argument on 64 B vs 128 B line sizes. THAT PREMISE IS WRONG, checked against the diff rather than assumed: `status[capacity]` and `status: *mut u8` ALREADY EXIST at the parent a42b5338 (map.rs module header line 8, field line 46, `BUCKET_OCCUPIED = 1` line 32). The probe ALREADY read the control byte on every step. What 58412d9f changes is what that byte HOLDS (`0x80 | tag7` instead of a bare flag) and how it is TESTED (`status == ctrl`, where `ctrl` is derived from the searched key's hash, instead of `status == 1` against a constant). There is no new array and no second cache line, so the line-size argument for the arch split does not hold. The conclusion it was offered to support survives anyway -- but on measurement, not on that reasoning.

WHAT DOES LINE UP is the commit's OWN justification. It was measured on kata #127 Word Ladder, and its message states that 88% of the win came from eliminating `karac_eq_String` calls (5,124,890 -> 1,189,583): the benefit IS skipping a cold heap dereference for a STRING key, and the message says so explicitly ('which for a `String` key loads a `{ptr,len,cap}` header and then dereferences a scattered heap buffer'). kata:170's map is `Map[i64, i64]`. Its key compare is a register compare of an L1-resident 8-byte load from a ~168-entry key array -- there is NO cold dereference to skip, so NONE of the measured benefit is available to this kata, on either architecture. What is left is the added cost: per-lookup computation of `ctrl_of(hash)` (shift/truncate/and/or) and an occupancy test whose operand is now computed rather than a constant, across ~200M lookups (1.2M queries x ~168 distinct keys, no early return). The HOT PATH IS CODEGEN-EMITTED, not the runtime library -- `mono.rs` emits its own probe loop for a monomorphized `Map[i64,i64]` (`emit_map_ctrl_of` / `emit_map_is_occupied`) -- so a fix lands in codegen, and surface is corrected from `other` to `codegen+runtime` accordingly. The `control_flow_for.rs` half of the commit is NOT implicated: it only turns the `keys()` walk's occupancy test from `st == 1` into a high-bit compare, which is free.

WHY that residual cost is +27% on arm64 and -3% on x86 is NOT ESTABLISHED by this measurement. The arithmetic alone (a few instructions per lookup over ~200M lookups) does not obviously account for a 214 ms delta, so something microarchitectural -- branch behaviour on the now-computed compare operand, or the loss of the key load's memory-level parallelism -- is likely involved. That needs instruction-level profiling on the M5 Pro and is stated here as UNEXPLAINED rather than guessed at. What IS established is where the regression enters, to a single commit, in both archive configurations and both orders.

(B) is cleaner in principle and keeps the String win on BOTH hosts, but it costs x86 the ~3% it gains on this i64 kata, and it is a wider change. An A/A control (same binary benched against itself) measured a 4.5% apparent effect at a ~257 ms workload here, and 0.0% at ~3.8 s, so the noise is real and workload-length dependent. Minimum-of-N over interleaved runs is the statistic that survives it, since contention only ever ADDS time. Whoever owns that lane should re-run min-of-N interleaved before the number is used; if their host is quiet, their mean is fine and the disagreement is real and needs a third measurement. AN INTERNAL-CONSISTENCY CHECK THAT FAVOURS THE FASTER READING: 13.1% fewer instructions AND 1.20x slower together require IPC to collapse by ~31% on x86. arm64 measured a 22.3% IPC collapse for the tag (2.976 -> 2.313) and that produced only a 1.27x swing there; x86's own IPC penalty, derived independently in this row, is 0-3.4%. A 31% x86 collapse would be far outside everything else measured on this architecture. By contrast 'fewer instructions, slightly faster' is internally consistent and is what I measure. WHY IT MATTERS: the fix shape turns on this sign. If tag OFF is slightly FASTER on x86 for primitive keys (my reading), a plain key-type gate is free on x86 and needs no arch condition. If tag OFF is 1.20x SLOWER (their reading), arch-conditional is required. The two readings prescribe different fixes, so this must be settled before anyone implements. IT IS A ONE-RUN QUESTION: same two binaries, interleaved, minimum-of-N, on a host whose A/A control is first shown to be near zero at this workload length. CACHE BEHAVIOUR IS IDENTICAL — THE 1.20x-SLOWER READING HAS NO MEMORY MECHANISM (2026-08-05, x86_64 Linux). cachegrind is DETERMINISTIC, so this host's contention — which is what the timing dispute hinges on — cannot affect it. Same two `KARAC_MAP_TAG` binaries, sinks 762965 under the tool. tag ON: I refs 15,081,020,557, D refs 2,375,542,051, D1 misses 3,098, LLd misses 2,357. tag OFF: I refs 13,106,242,350, D refs 2,221,968,022, D1 misses 3,098, LLd misses 2,357. THE MISS COUNTS ARE BYTE-IDENTICAL and tag OFF also issues FEWER data references. kata:170's ~168-entry table fits in L1 either way, so there is no cache pressure for the tag to relieve or create. A reading in which tag OFF is 1.20x SLOWER while executing 13.1% fewer instructions and 6.5% fewer data refs at identical miss counts has no mechanism left to appeal to on this architecture. SCOPE OF THE REFUTATION, stated honestly: cachegrind models CACHE only — no prefetcher, no TLB, no front-end. It cannot rule out a throughput/back-end effect, which is precisely what the arm64 lane measured (IPC 2.976 -> 2.313 with no mispredict term). So this refutes the MEMORY explanation specifically, not every conceivable one. But x86's own derived IPC penalty is 0-3.4%, and a 31% collapse would be needed for 1.20x; with cache ruled out there is no candidate for one. AND IT SHARPENS THE INSTRUMENT SPLIT, which turns out to be the real story: on the COMMIT PAIR tag ON executes FEWER instructions on BOTH architectures (x86 13,668,698,926 vs 14,617,644,056; arm64 10,465,485,066 vs 12,006,051,874). Under the FLAG on x86 the sign INVERTS: tag ON 15,081,020,557 vs tag OFF 13,106,242,350, i.e. tag ON executes MORE. So the two ARCHITECTURES never disagreed about instruction counts — the two INSTRUMENTS do, and the arm64 figures in this row are commit-pair figures. Current main's tag path is more expensive than 58412d9f's was, or the flag's off-path is better than the pre-commit code; either way `KARAC_MAP_TAG=0` measures 'current main without the tag', which is exactly what the FIX will produce and therefore the right instrument for choosing its shape. WHAT REMAINS: a wall-clock tiebreak on a QUIET host. This container is not one (A/A control: 4.5% apparent effect at a 257 ms workload, 0.0% at 3.8 s; maxima 2.1x their own minima in interleaved runs). Everything measurable here without a clock now points one way — fewer instructions, fewer data refs, identical misses, and min-of-N interleaved timing 2.0% faster with the tag off.

 ARM64 FLAG-INSTRUMENT SWEEP + THE FIX IS IN (2026-08-06, Apple M5 Pro, Darwin 25.5.0, main ca037cb0). SHIPPED: b3e8206d gates the tag compare on (probe shape x target arch) -- primitive-keyed `emit_mono_map_get_body` / `emit_mono_set_contains_body` test occupancy ALONE on aarch64; `emit_mono_map_str_get_body` keeps the tag on every host; x86 is unchanged at every site. `KARAC_MAP_TAG` survives as the A/B lever, now BOTH directions (`=1` restores 58412d9f's behaviour exactly). THIS ROW STAYS OPEN -- see THE RESIDUAL below, which is the part the fix does NOT recover.

METHOD, identical for all seven workloads: ONE karac and ONE archive pair from current main, two binaries per kata differing ONLY by `KARAC_MAP_TAG`, binaries confirmed to differ by sha256 BEFORE timing (the guard against a flag that never reached the code), every sink verified on both sides, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, default (lean) archive resolution = the recorded lane, `hyperfine --shell=none` in BOTH orders, and exact whole-process counters from `scripts/pmc.c` (3 interleaved reps, instruction spread under 0.01%). No commit-to-commit comparison anywhere.

RESULT -- the tag NEVER pays for a primitive key on arm64, across six workloads, and pays for a String key:

  kata:170 `Map[i64,i64]` 168 keys + keys() walk   tag 1.13-1.17x SLOWER   instr 10.468B ON / 12.008B OFF   cyc 4.675B / 3.946B
  kata:219 `Map[i64,i64]` sliding window           tag 1.03x SLOWER (both orders, +/-1.5ms)   instr 3.526B / 3.413B   cyc 500M / 487M
  kata:1   `Map[i64,i64]` get-heavy, scaled x200   tag 1.02-1.03x SLOWER   instr 973.0M / 961.8M   cyc 134.4M / 129.7M
  kata:146 `Map[i64,i64]` LRU, tombstone churn     NEUTRAL (orders disagree)   instr 3.560B / 3.488B   cyc 1.008B / 1.013B
  kata:128 `Set[i64]` 20k keys / 131072 buckets    NEUTRAL   instr 709.0M / 693.9M   cyc 311.9M / 312.5M
  kata:217 `Set[i64]` 800-key windows              NEUTRAL/tie   instr 48.13B / 48.71B   cyc 9.15B / 9.28B
  kata:127 `Map[String,i64]`                       tag 1.07x FASTER   instr 2.531B / 2.580B   cyc 523M / 553M

THE SET PROBE IS NOW MEASURED, closing this row's longest-standing unmeasured item -- and the answer is NEITHER of the two the row expected: `emit_mono_set_contains_body` is NEUTRAL at both a 20k-key and an 800-key table. So the Set site was never the problem. It is included in the fix for consistency with the Map site and because the mechanism is shared, NOT on its own evidence, and the fix comment says so.

WHICH CORRECTS THIS ROW'S OWN 'PRIMITIVE KEYS' FRAMING. The effect is 1.17x on ONE kata, ~3% on two, and nil on three. A fix sized off kata:170 alone would have overstated its own value by ~5x. The DIRECTION is what six workloads agree on, and that is what the fix rests on.

THE INSTRUMENT SPLIT IS SETTLED, AGAINST THE x86 LANE'S INFERENCE. That lane concluded 'the arm64 figures in this row are commit-pair figures' because arm64 reported tag ON executing FEWER instructions while x86 under the flag reported MORE. Re-measured here on current main with the flag and exact counters: tag ON 10,468,328,088 vs OFF 12,007,737,018 -- reproducing this row's earlier arm64 figures (10,465,485,066 / 12,006,051,874) to 0.03%. Those numbers were flag-instrument all along. So the two ARCHITECTURES genuinely disagree on the instruction-count sign for the same flag on the same kata, and that is a real finding, not a mislabeled instrument. NOTE the sign is not an ISA constant either: on arm64 kata:128 and kata:146 have tag ON executing MORE instructions, the opposite of kata:170. It is workload-dependent on both hosts.

kata:170's MECHANISM, sharpened but still not fully explained. The STATIC difference between its two binaries is 9 instructions (3 emission sites x 3: `ldrsb`+`tbz` for the occupancy-only test vs `ldrb`+`cmp`+`b.ne` plus a hoisted `lsr`/`and`/`orr` for the tag), so the 1.54B dynamic delta is entirely `eq_check` work the tag skips. At the kata's measured load factor that saving should be ~0.2 key compares per get, not the ~2 the counts imply -- unmodelled and stated as such. What IS established: the tag executes 12.8% FEWER instructions and burns 18.5% MORE cycles (IPC 3.04 -> 2.24), which is a throughput cost, not a work cost.

VERIFICATION THAT THE MEASUREMENTS ARE THE SHIPPED BINARIES, not a proxy for them: with the fix in, each kata's DEFAULT build is byte-identical (sha256) to whichever pre-fix flag binary the policy selects -- kata:170/128/146 to `tag_off`, kata:127 to `tag_on` -- and `KARAC_MAP_TAG=1` reproduces the pre-fix `tag_on` binary exactly. So every figure above transfers to the default build bit for bit.

THE RESIDUAL -- WHY THIS ROW STAYS OPEN, and it is now MEASURED rather than inferred (2026-08-06, same host, same session, matched karac+archive pairs per side, both sinks 762965, both binaries the recorded lane's 285592 B, both orders):

  a42b5338 (= 58412d9f~1)   770.0 +/- 9.2 ms  |  798.5 +/- 12.6 ms   instr 12.969B  cyc 3.57B  IPC 3.63
  current main + the fix    858.2 +/- 7.2 ms  |  870.2 +/- 24.7 ms   instr 12.005B  cyc 3.94B  IPC 3.05

So the fix recovers the tag-compare share (1.14x) and kata:170 remains 1.09-1.11x ABOVE its pre-58412d9f baseline. The baseline reproduces this row's own earlier figure for that commit (786 ms lean) at 770-798 ms, which anchors the comparison. ATTRIBUTION, by arithmetic on this row's own trajectory rather than by a new bisect: 58412d9f measured 1000 ms and current main 1014 ms in the earlier arm64 lane, i.e. only +1.4% of drift across the ~800 commits between them -- so the residual belongs to 58412d9f's NON-tag-compare half (the encoding change itself, the insert/resize paths, the `mono.rs` restructuring, the `keys()` walk change), each of which remains UNMEASURED. This is exactly the 'MAGNITUDE GAP WORTH KEEPING HONEST' this row flagged and never chased; it is now sized.

AND IT HAS THE SAME SIGNATURE AS THE PART JUST FIXED: current main + fix executes 7.4% FEWER instructions than the a42b5338 baseline yet burns 10.4% MORE cycles (IPC 3.63 -> 3.05). Fewer instructions, worse throughput -- the same shape as the tag compare, which suggests one mechanism with two carriers inside 58412d9f rather than two unrelated costs. That is a hypothesis, not a finding; whoever takes the residual should test it before assuming it.

WHAT THIS ROW NOW NEEDS TO CLOSE: attribute and recover the 1.09-1.11x residual on kata:170. The tag-compare cause is fixed and shipped in b3e8206d; the row's headline number (771 -> 997 ms) is about 55% recovered. Follow-on filed as its own row and since CLOSED: B-2026-08-06-33 settled the x86 primitive-key sign by measurement on 2026-08-07 -- the tag PAYS on x86, so the arch condition stays and is now justified on evidence.

NOT DONE, and deliberately so: kata:170's README timing table and `bench-results.json` still quote the regressed 997.1 ms. Those come from the bench.sh -> results.json pipeline and must not be hand-edited; the kata needs a proper re-bench once the residual is resolved, so that the recorded number moves once rather than twice.

 RESIDUAL ATTRIBUTED, AND THIS ROW'S OWN ATTRIBUTION IS REFUTED (2026-08-06, Apple M5 Pro, arm64). The entry above sized the residual at 1.09-1.11x and assigned it, BY ARITHMETIC RATHER THAN MEASUREMENT, to 58412d9f's non-tag-compare half. Measured directly, that is WRONG: at 58412d9f the non-tag half costs essentially NOTHING, and the live residual belongs to the ~800 commits AFTER it.

METHOD. Four matched karac+archive sides, each built at its own commit, archive configuration held constant (LEAN pinned via `KARAC_RUNTIME` on every side), `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, every binary sink-checked at 762965 before timing, `hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 25 --shell=none` in BOTH orders, plus exact `scripts/pmc.c` counters. The two middle sides did not exist before: `KARAC_MAP_TAG` postdates 58412d9f, so "58412d9f without its tag compare" was previously unmeasurable. It was produced by patching that commit's own `emit_mono_map_get_body` to call `emit_map_is_occupied` -- exactly what the shipped fix does on arm64 -- and, for the fourth side, by ALSO swapping that commit's occupancy test to the flag form described below.

  a42b5338 (= 58412d9f~1)                        768.7 / 767.0 ms
  58412d9f, tag compare removed + FLAG-form test 770.7 / 786.9 ms   <- PARENT LEVEL
  58412d9f, tag compare removed (sign-form test) 894.1 / 908.0 ms   <- 1.16-1.18x
  current main (tag off, sign-form test)         859.0 / 859.3 ms   <- 1.12x

ANSWER 1 -- AT 58412d9f THE NON-TAG REGRESSION IS ENTIRELY THE OCCUPANCY TEST'S LOWERING, and it is fully recoverable there. The commit changed what the control byte holds, which changed how "is this bucket occupied" is written: `status >= 0x80` (a SIGN-BIT test) instead of the parent's `status == 1`. On arm64 those lower differently -- `ldrsb` + `tbz` versus `ldrb` + `cmp` + `b.cc` -- and the three-instruction form with a flag-setting compare is FASTER than the two-instruction test-and-branch. Writing the identical predicate as `status > TOMBSTONE` (exactly equivalent: the only bytes below 0x80 are EMPTY=0 and TOMBSTONE=1) restores the flag form and recovers the parent's time to within noise.

ANSWER 2 -- AND YET THAT FIX IS WORTH NOTHING ON CURRENT MAIN. The same one-line swap, on current main, moves kata:170 from 859.0 to 855.2 ms, i.e. nothing; and on kata:219 it is 1.01-1.03x WORSE. So the mechanism that costs 1.16x at 58412d9f is no longer live: something in the ~800 commits since changed the surrounding code enough that the sign-bit form stopped being penalised. The lowering hazard is therefore LATENT, not current -- worth knowing before anyone "fixes" it, because the obvious fix is measurably useless today.

ANSWER 3 -- WHERE THE LIVE RESIDUAL ACTUALLY IS: the ~800 commits after 58412d9f. Holding the test form constant at the flag form, 58412d9f measures 770 ms and current main measures 855 ms; holding it at the sign form, 58412d9f measures 894-908 ms and current main 859 ms. Either way current main sits ~1.11x above where 58412d9f lands once its own regression is undone. That interval is UNBISECTED and is what this row now needs. NOTE the earlier "+1.4% from 58412d9f to current" figure this row used for its arithmetic was measured with the tag ON, where the tag compare dominated and masked this; it does not survive as an argument once the tag is off.

RULED OUT ALONG THE WAY, both by measurement:
  * THE keys() WALK. This row and its predecessors repeatedly suspected `control_flow_for.rs`'s occupancy test in the `keys()` iteration, since kata:170 runs it ~1.23B times. An ablation that keeps the walk and drops the gets measures a42 471M cycles vs current main 476M -- equal -- while instructions FALL 8.3%. The walk is also only ~12% of the kata's cycles, not the majority this row assumed.
  * THE BUCKET LAYOUT. Diffed rather than assumed: 58412d9f changes no allocation, no stride, no alignment. `status[capacity]` and the kv array are byte-for-byte the same shape as at the parent; only the byte's VALUE and the tests over it change.

A METHOD WARNING WORTH MORE THAN THE ABOVE, because it nearly produced a wrong fix. An ablation of kata:170 that keeps the gets and drops the `keys()` walk -- same map, same key distribution, same 201.6M gets, keys materialised into a `Vec` once outside the timed loop -- reports the flag-form test as a 1.34x WIN. The real kata reports 1.00x for the same change. The probe over-responds by more than twenty times, and it was deliberately built to be faithful. This row already carries one refuted synthetic probe (the high-load-factor one); this is a second, subtler instance, and the rule it argues for is: an ablation may be used to LOCATE a cost, never to SIZE a fix. Every number that decided anything here was taken on the unmodified kata.

WHAT THIS ROW NEEDS TO CLOSE, unchanged in shape but now correctly aimed: bisect kata:170 across 58412d9f..main (~800 commits, arm64, matched karac+archive per step, sink-checked, tag-off held constant on both sides via `KARAC_MAP_TAG=0` so the shipped fix does not confound the comparison). The endpoints are verified: 770 ms and 855 ms with the test form held constant.

 RESIDUAL FULLY ATTRIBUTED — AND IT IS NOT A MAP PROBLEM AT ALL (2026-08-06). Bisected across the 905 commits this row identified, 8 steps, on CYCLES (the endpoints differ 8.3% in cycles and 0.003% in instructions, so the instruction-count method this repo prefers is blind here), with the tag compare patched off and the occupancy test held in the flag form at every step so the range's two opposing effects could not cancel. Every binary sink-checked at 762965.

THE CULPRIT IS 36a7fa5a (2026-07-30, "make println line-atomic by staging payload+newline into one write", B-2026-07-30-9). Parent b84477dd 3.561B cycles / 781 ms; 36a7fa5a 3.958B / 850 ms; 1.09x on wall clock in both orders, and the 777 commits after it all sit on the slow plateau. kata:170 calls `println` ONCE.

The carrier is CODE PLACEMENT, not work: instructions differ by 0.008%, the binaries are EXACTLY the same size (285,592 B both), `main`'s prologue is identical (`sub sp, sp, #0x80`), and the 4 KiB staging alloca lives in the new helper rather than in the caller. What moves is `_main`'s address, 0x7c8 -> 0x860.

FILED AS B-2026-08-07-10, which owns it from here.

SO THIS ROW'S ARITHMETIC IS COMPLETE: the 7-bit tag compare (1.14x, fixed by the arch x key-type gate) times the placement effect (1.09x) is 1.24x, against the 1.29x this row opened with; the remainder is drift across the range. Nothing map-shaped is left unexplained, which is why every map-shaped hypothesis this row chased — the keys() walk, the bucket layout, the load factor, the encoding — measured clean. CLOSING.
fix: c4e6d76e (the tag compare); the placement half is B-2026-08-07-10
tracker: CLOSED 2026-08-06. Two unrelated causes, both now attributed by measurement: the 7-bit tag compare (1.14x) fixed in c4e6d76e by the arch x key-type gate in src/codegen/mono.rs::map_tag_compare, and code placement from 36a7fa5a (1.09x), which is NOT a map issue and is owned by B-2026-08-07-10. Follow-on B-2026-08-06-33 is also CLOSED (2026-08-07): the x86 primitive-key sign was measured on a quiet x86_64 host and the tag PAYS there (kata:170 +12.2% to drop it, distributions disjoint, A/A control 0.2%; kata:128 Set +5.4%; kata:217/219 neutral), so the arch condition is load-bearing on evidence rather than on an unresolved dispute, and the x86 Set probe is no longer unmeasured.

title: Bounds checks survive in a CALLEE that walks a caller-owned buffer at a caller-chosen offset — `fn f(v: ref Vec[u8], base: i64, len: i64) { while lo <= hi { v[base+lo] .. v[base+hi] } }`. The bound holds only ACROSS the call boundary (every caller passes `base = k*len` with `k < n`, and `v.len() == n*len`), and every BCE analysis in bce_length_pin.rs is per-function by construction, so no local fact exists to prove. Carries the whole of kata #246's residual 1.28x vs equal-safety C. Survives INLINING (measured), and LLVM's IRCE does not reach it either (measured, byte-identical assembly). Split off B-2026-08-04-8, whose intra-function shape is fixed.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the residual half of B-2026-08-04-8 (closed e94e6bd9 + 55f3d4a3),
carved out when that entry's named shape — the converging base-offset scan
written INLINE — was finished. Everything below was measured on the x86
container while working that entry; none of it is hypothesised.

THE SHAPE. Kata #246's punch loop, verbatim:

    fn is_strobogrammatic(corpus: ref Vec[u8], base: i64, len: i64) -> bool {
        let mut lo = 0i64;
        let mut hi = len - 1i64;
        while lo <= hi { .. corpus[base + lo] .. corpus[base + hi] .. }
    }

There is no fill loop, no enclosing counter, and no length pin in this function.
`base + lo < corpus.len()` is TRUE at run time only because of a caller
invariant. This is the ordinary 'hand a helper a row of a flat buffer' shape —
matrix row operations, fixed-stride record scans, per-row palindrome and
two-pointer checks — so it is not specific to #246.

WHY THE PARENT'S FIX CANNOT BE EXTENDED TO IT. `compute_converging_skips`,
`compute_descending_skips` and `compute_vec_length_pins` all take `&Block` and
scan `func.body`. Each of the three facts they compose (a length pin on `v`, an
enclosing counter bounding the row index, a linear `base` in that counter) is
established by a STATEMENT in the same function. Here all three arrive as
parameter values. No amount of strengthening the per-function analysis reaches
this; it needs a fact that crosses the call.

TWO MEASUREMENTS THAT CLOSE OFF THE CHEAP ROUTES, both worth recording because
both look like they should work:

(1) INLINING DOES NOT RESCUE IT. B-2026-08-04-8's EVIDENCE 2 already proves this
    though it does not draw the conclusion: `is_strobogrammatic` is FULLY
    INLINED into `main` in both binaries, and adding Kara-equivalent bounds
    checks to the C mirror makes clang -O3 emit a loop instruction-for-
    instruction isomorphic to kara's — 21 instructions, checks intact. That is
    clang with full post-inline visibility declining to eliminate them. So
    'emit it and let LLVM see through the call' is not a plan.

(2) IRCE IS NOT THE ANSWER EITHER. LLVM ships inductive range-check elimination
    and it is NOT in the `default<O2>` pipeline karac runs, which makes enabling
    it look like a one-line win. Tested directly on #246's pre-opt IR with
    opt-18: `default<O2>` versus
    `default<O2>,function(loop-simplify,lcssa,irce),default<O2>` produce
    BYTE-IDENTICAL assembly — same md5, same 8 `$640000` compares. IRCE does not
    match this shape: the index is a SUM `base + j` whose range is fixed JOINTLY
    by two co-moving induction variables, not by one affine IV against a
    loop-invariant bound. Recorded so the pipeline-flag idea is not re-derived
    by the next person who notices IRCE is off.

FIX DIRECTIONS, both real features rather than extensions:

  (A) INTERPROCEDURAL PRECONDITION. Infer `base + len <= v.len()` as a callee
      precondition from the index sites, discharge it at every call site with
      the machinery that already exists per-function (the call sites in #246 DO
      have the pin, the counter and the linear base locally), and skip the check
      only when every reachable call site discharges it. Fails closed on any
      address-taken / externally-callable function. This is the direct fix and
      it is the first interprocedural analysis in the compiler, which is the
      reason it is scoped separately rather than tacked on.

  (B) LOOP VERSIONING. Emit a checked and an unchecked copy of the loop, chosen
      by ONE widened test in the preheader. Note this is the semantics-preserving
      form: naive PREDICATION — hoisting the widened check and deleting the
      per-iteration ones — would move WHERE a panicking program panics (a
      program that reads 3 valid elements and then goes out of range must
      produce those 3 iterations' effects before panicking), so it is not a
      legal rewrite for Kara's checked semantics. Versioning costs code size and
      needs a profitability gate.

SIZING, so this is not mistaken for a small job: (A) touches the analysis
pipeline's shape, not just codegen, and needs a call-graph pass plus a
conservative escape/visibility rule; (B) is contained in codegen but needs the
duplication machinery and a heuristic. Neither is a slice.

WHAT IT IS WORTH. On #246, the full 1.28x — the entire remaining gap to
equal-safety C, since B-2026-08-04-8's EVIDENCE 2 showed karac's codegen is at
clang -O3 parity on this kata once safety is equalized. On a work-identical
minimal probe the missing elision alone measured 1.93x. NOT a correctness issue:
the checks are sound, just not elided. The kata is NOT written around it and
must not be — it stays the natural converging two-pointer.

METHOD NOTE, carried over from the parent because it cost real time: timing this
shape is corpus-size dependent in a way that INVERTS the result. At n=400000
(12.8 MB, memory-bound) the 2-check probe measured FASTER than the 0-check one —
the checks are free when the loop is waiting on DRAM. The 1.93x is a
cache-resident measurement (640 KB), and only that regime is informative here.

RESOLVED by direction (A), the interprocedural precondition — implemented as
`src/codegen/bce_interproc.rs`, a new whole-PROGRAM analysis that runs once in
`compile_program` and is merged into the existing per-function
`converging_skips` map at `compile_function`.

CORRECTION TO THIS ENTRY'S SIZING. The claim above that (A) "is the first
interprocedural analysis in the compiler" is WRONG, and it is what made the
job look larger than it was. `src/call_graph.rs` already exists (backing
`karac query affected-by`), and `effectchecker/inference.rs` already does
SCC-based interprocedural effect inference over a call graph it builds itself.
Neither was reusable here — the affected-by graph is name-keyed and
deliberately over-approximates method calls, and neither carries the argument
EXPRESSIONS a precondition has to substitute — but "the compiler has no
interprocedural machinery" was not the obstacle it was recorded as.

WHAT MADE IT A CONTAINED CHANGE, and the part worth reusing. The new pass
emits the SAME plain-data `ConvergingSkip` record `compute_converging_skips`
already produces, keyed by the same inner-loop condition `SpanKey`. So
`compile_while` cannot tell the two provenances apart and needed no change at
all: the entire codegen-side cost is one `entry().or_insert_with()` merge.
Framing an interprocedural result as "the existing intra-function fact, proven
a different way" is what kept this off the IR surface. Codegen containment
holds — the pass is AST-only plain data, no LLVM type crosses it.

THE TWO HALVES.
  1. INFER (`infer_precondition`): recognise the converging two-pointer in a
     callee whose `base` is a PARAMETER (the one structural difference from
     the intra path, which requires a local `sole_scalar_init`), and record
     `base + hi_init < v.len()` plus `base + lo_init >= 0` over the callee's
     PARAMETER names.
  2. DISCHARGE (`discharge_call_site`): substitute the caller's actual
     argument terms for those names and re-prove with the caller's own facts,
     through the SAME `init_below_bound` / `sum_nonneg_at_min` linear
     cancellation the intra path uses. All-or-nothing: one undischarged site
     disqualifies the callee, because one body is emitted so one fact must
     cover every call.

WHY "EVERY CALL SITE" IS KNOWABLE. Checked in src/cli.rs rather than assumed:

CONFIRMED THROUGH THE ORDINARY CLI, not just the ASAN harness. Reduced from
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_option_ok_or_string_err_no_leak`, verbatim
fixture body in a file, built with `karac build`:

  fn main() {
      let mut i: i64 = 0;
      let mut errs: i64 = 0;
      while i < 6 {
          let o: Option[i64] = if i % 2 == 0 { Some(i * 10) } else { None };
          let r: Result[i64, String] = o.ok_or(f"absent-{i}-padded-well-past-inline-width");
          match r {
              Ok(v) => println(v),
              Err(e) => { errs = errs + e.len(); },
          }
          i = i + 1;
      }
      println(errs);
  }

  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=2 (default) -> prints 0 / 20 / 40 / 114, exit 0
  KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0           -> `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`,
                                 SIGABRT, exit 134

So codegen emits TWO frees for the `ok_or` String Err payload. At -O2 the
payload is read only through `.len()`, which makes the buffer a provably
dead allocation LLVM deletes outright -- and a second free of an allocation
that never happened is invisible. The bug is in the emitted ownership, not
in the optimizer; -O2 is masking it, not fixing it.

USER-REACHABLE. `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` is a documented, supported knob (the
"did the optimizer eat my IR construct?" debugging fallback -- see
`read_opt_level_env`'s table in src/codegen/driver.rs), so a user who drops
to -O0 to debug an unrelated problem gets a hard SIGABRT in code that works
at -O2. The masking is also fragile at -O2: the moment a program does
anything with the payload beyond taking its length -- read a byte, print it,
store it -- the allocation stops being dead and the second free lands.

ROOT CAUSE of the `ok_or` leg: `Option.ok_or(e)` evaluates `e` EAGERLY,
packs it into the Result's Err slots, and `build_select`s between
`Ok(payload)` and `Err(e)`. A fresh heap `e` that the statement machinery
temp-tracks (an f-string / collection literal) was then owned TWICE: the
tracked temp's scope-exit `FreeVecBuffer` and the Result's Err-payload
free both released one buffer, so every `None` iteration double-freed. The
mirror-image hole sat on the `Some` path, where `e` is discarded and
NOTHING freed it -- the identical present-discards-the-eager-argument shape
`unwrap_or` has, which is why the fix reuses that emitter's proven gate:
drop the tracked temp's registration, suppress a moved binding's slot cap,
and free the discarded `e` on the present path. A branch rather than a
flag, because a `select` cannot carry a side effect.

SECOND, THE CARRY. Fixture:
`asan_vec_get_unwrap_struct_with_heap_field_no_double_free`. Measured
individually, it is a LEAK at -O0 (not the UAF the tally claimed): 64 bytes in
2 objects of 32 bytes each -- one `Person`-shaped copy (a 24-byte String plus
an i64) per `people.get(0).unwrap()` / `people.first().unwrap()`.

Rewritten with runtime-derived names (`f"person-{i}-padded-name"`), an
`env.args().len()` seed, and the gets moved into a 50-iteration loop, the leak
scales EXACTLY with the loop -- 1600 bytes in 50 allocations, one per
`get(k).unwrap()`. So the missing free is real and it is per-call, not a
two-off. `Vec.get(i).unwrap()` on a struct element materializes a copy of the
element and never frees it.

BUT IT WOULD NOT FIRE AT -O2, across two attempts:
  * 50 gets in a loop, reading `p.name` bytes (`starts_with`) and `p.age`
    -> clean, 63 allocations
  * same, with the read results escaping into a heap `Vec[i64]` that is
    indexed afterwards                                  -> clean, 68 allocations
In both, the 50 copies are never allocated at all. That is the same
ALLOCATION-elimination masking as the two fixed cases -- but here it is
structural rather than incidental: the copy is dead BY CONSTRUCTION, because
every use of a `Vec.get(...).unwrap()` borrow view is a field read that LLVM
forwards straight to the container. Neither attempt made the STRUCT itself
escape (only scalars derived from it did), so a shape where the copy must
materialize at -O2 is not ruled out -- it just was not found.

WHAT THIS ANSWERS, and it is not what the row assumed. The remaining failures
are NOT uniformly like `ok_or` / `unwrap_or`. Those two were real -O2
default-build defects. This one is a real missing free in the EMITTED code
with no demonstrated -O2 impact, because the allocation it leaks is one the
optimizer reliably deletes. Both are worth fixing -- an emitted free that is
missing is a defect whether or not today's optimizer hides it, and it will
surface the moment a caller makes the copy escape -- but they are not the same
PRIORITY, and this row should stop implying a single class. Triage the rest
one at a time: measure the mode per fixture (do NOT trust a bulk scan), then
try the -O2 carry, and sort by whether it lands.

ROOT CAUSE FOUND for the two largest remaining leaks (`generic_enum_*`,
900 allocations between them) — diagnosed, NOT fixed. Handing it over precise.

A generic USER enum whose monomorph binds `T` to a type wider than the
declaration-time payload area leaks the box, once per construction:

    enum Opt[T] { Yes(T), No }
    let o: Opt[String] = Opt.Yes(f"yes{i}");
    let a: String = match o { Opt.Yes(v) => v, Opt.No => f"fb" };
    // -O0: 24 bytes leaked per iteration — the {ptr,len,cap} envelope

The declared enum lays `T` out ERASED (one word), so `coerce_to_payload_words`
heap-boxes the 3-word String at construction. Nothing then frees that box,
because `boxed_enum_payload_variants` (types_lowering.rs) — the predicate that
drives `track_boxed_enum_var` at the let-site — matches on the enum NAME and
handles only the seeded `Option` (area 3) and `Result` (area 5):
`_ => return vec![]`. A user enum returns empty, so no `BoxedEnumDrop` is ever
queued for it.

THE THREE CONTROLS that pin it there, each measured:
  * non-generic `enum Opt { Yes(String), No }`            -> CLEAN. A concrete
    user enum sizes its payload area to the widest variant, so nothing boxes.
  * non-generic user enum with a 6-word struct payload    -> CLEAN, same reason.
  * generic `Opt[i64]` (scalar monomorph)                 -> CLEAN. One word
    fits the erased area, so nothing boxes.
Only the generic-with-wide-monomorph combination boxes, and that is exactly the
combination no drop covers.

SHAPE OF THE FIX, and why it was not attempted here: extend the boxed-payload
drop registration to a user enum, resolving the per-variant payload type
through the ACTIVE MONOMORPH SUBST (the declared `T` is useless — that erasure
is the bug) and taking the area from `enum_layouts[name].llvm_type`'s field
count minus the tag. That is the same mono-aware-resolution shape as
B-2026-07-18-44 / B-2026-07-15-11, and it carries real double-free risk if the
area or the subst is computed wrong — a box freed twice is worse than a box
leaked. It wants its own session with the -O0 sweep as the gate.

DO NOT instead free the box in `reconstruct_payload_value`: that is the
reverted experiment recorded above (-O2 0 -> 31 failures). The box's owner is
the enum VALUE, not the match that reads it.

FIXED (103c518) — the generic-enum box leg, exactly as the root cause above
predicted. Adds a user-enum sibling to `boxed_enum_payload_variants` and
registers a box drop at the THREE sites a box can be owned from:
  * the monomorph's own by-value PARAM (mono.rs) — the one that mattered. The
    boxed value is nearly always a temp handed straight into a generic callee
    (`get(Opt.Yes(f"…"), d)`), so no binding exists anywhere to hang a drop
    on, and mono has its own param loop that `compile_function`'s sibling
    registration never reaches. Fixing only the let-site left the reported
    fixtures leaking unchanged — measured, not assumed.
  * a by-value param of a non-generic fn (functions.rs).

    fn mks(k: i64) -> String { let mut s: String = String.new(); s.push_str(f"pay-{k}"); return s; }
    fn dig(i: i64) -> String { let mut d: String = String.new(); d.push_str(f"{i}"); return d; }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        let r: Result[String, i64] = Result.Ok(mks(n));
        match r { Result.Ok(s) => { if s.contains(dig(n)) { println(f"c3:{s.len()}"); } } Result.Err(e) => { println("c3:err"); } }
    }

  karac check        -> All checks passed.
  karac run --interp -> c3:5   (correct)
  karac build        -> error: codegen failed: Binary op Eq: right operand has non-comparable type
                        StructType({ ptr, i64, i64 }) (likely a typechecker gap -- `assert_eq` and
                        `==` should reject mismatched operand types before reaching codegen)

SO IT IS A RUN-VS-BUILD DIVERGENCE, not a diagnostics nit: the program is accepted by every check and runs correctly on one backend, while the other refuses it with a message that blames the typechecker for an `==` THE SOURCE DOES NOT CONTAIN.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT LOCALIZES IT, checked rather than assumed. The identical call on a TUPLE-ELEMENT String payload compiles and runs clean:
    let r: Result[(String, i64), i64] = Result.Ok((mks(n), 5i64));
    match r { Result.Ok(x) => { if x.0.contains(dig(n)) { ... } } ... }   -> builds, 10 allocs / 10 frees, valgrind-clean
So it is specific to a DIRECT `String` payload binding -- not to `contains`, and not to Result as a carrier.

READING OF THE SYMPTOM, explicitly NOT a diagnosis -- no IR was dumped and no codegen path was read. `contains` presumably lowers through a comparison helper, and the error says one operand arrived as a raw `{ptr,i64,i64}` String struct where a scalar was expected. A direct payload binding is reconstructed differently from a tuple element (the single-word vs multi-word split in `reconstruct_payload_value`), so the natural first place to look is whether the direct-String binding reaches the comparison lowering without the shape the tuple path gives it. The tuple spelling being AHEAD here is the REVERSE of the usual tuple/field asymmetry, which is itself a hint about which path is the reference implementation.

NOT the same bug as B-2026-08-05-3 -- that is a leak with correct output, this is a hard compile failure -- but found on the same fixture, hence the followup source.

INDEPENDENT SECOND SIGHTING, same day, reached from B-2026-08-05-7 rather
than from B-2026-08-05-3 -- `contains` was the byte-level read that
B-2026-08-04-17's authoring rule recommends, and it would not compile on the
pattern-bound receiver a heap-payload ownership fixture usually has. Same
error text, same `{ptr,i64,i64}` operand. Adding the coverage matrix, which
widens the shape well past the `Result` Ok arm and narrows the search:

  let-bound String          .contains     -> OK
  for-loop element binding  .contains     -> OK
  struct FIELD access       .contains     -> OK
  Result `Err(e)` arm       .contains     -> FAILS
  Option `Some(e)` arm      .contains     -> FAILS
  user enum arm             .contains     -> FAILS
  `if let Some(e)`          .contains     -> FAILS
  Result `Err(e)` arm       .len()        -> OK
  Result `Err(e)` arm       .starts_with  -> OK

TWO THINGS THAT FOLLOW, one of which corrects a clause above.

(1) It is NOT Result-specific and not Ok-arm-specific: Option, a user enum,
and `if let` all fail the same way. The carrier is irrelevant; what matters is
that the receiver came from a PATTERN BINDING. A `let`, a for-loop element,
and a struct field are all fine.

(2) The row above says it is 'specific to a DIRECT `String` payload binding --
not to `contains`'. The second half of that does not hold: `.len()` and
`.starts_with` on the VERY SAME direct pattern-bound String compile and run
clean. So the defect is the PAIR (pattern-bound receiver x `contains`), not
the binding alone -- which is a tighter target, since whatever `starts_with`
does with that receiver is evidently already correct and `contains` is the
outlier. Consistent with the row's own reading that `contains` lowers through
a comparison helper: it looks like the receiver is not recognised as a String
there and falls through to a COLLECTION membership test that compares elements
with `==`, which is why a whole `{ptr,i64,i64}` arrives where a scalar was
expected. Still a reading, not a diagnosis -- no IR was dumped here either.

SEVERITY NOTE, left for the owner rather than changed unilaterally: this row
is `medium`, but the repo has treated check-passes / build-fails as `high`
elsewhere (B-2026-07-30-7 carries exactly that reasoning). Flagging the
inconsistency, not resolving it. FIXED. ROOT CAUSE, and the row's own matrix is what made it findable: a `String` PAYLOAD BINDING registered `vec_elem_types` but never `string_vars`. Those two sets do different jobs and only one was wired. `vec_elem_types` exists for the SCOPE-EXIT BUFFER FREE (a String payload is tracked as `Vec[u8]`-shaped so `track_vec_var` frees it); `string_vars` is what METHOD DISPATCH consults to pick the String arm for a method name String and Vec SHARE. With the binding in the first set only, it looked like a `Vec[u8]` to dispatch, so `s.contains(other)` fell through to VEC MEMBERSHIP — which compares elements with `==` and therefore handed codegen a whole `{ptr, i64, i64}` String where a scalar was expected. That is the entire explanation for the error text blaming the typechecker for an `==` the source never contained. THE ROW'S MATRIX DID THE HARD PART: recording that `.len()` and `.starts_with` work on the VERY SAME binding is what ruled out pattern binding in general and localized this to shared-name dispatch. Confirmed independently while fixing: rebinding the payload through a `let` (`let mut t = s;`) makes `contains` compile, because the let path is one of the ~10 `string_vars.insert` sites — all of which are in stmts.rs / shadow.rs / method_call.rs, and NONE in pattern_binding.rs or control_flow_match.rs (grep count: 0 in both). FIX: one registration in `bind_pattern_values`, beside the existing `vec_elem_types` line for the same payload. Same intent as the Map/Set arm a few lines below, whose comment already says it registers dispatch side-tables 'so `m.len()` / `s.contains(x)` on a match-arm-bound Map/Set dispatches like a let-bound one' — String was the one payload kind that got the free but not the dispatch. `CString` is deliberately EXCLUDED: its methods route through the `CString.<method>` key, so registering it would aim dispatch at the wrong table. VERIFIED: all five carriers the row listed (Result Ok, Result Err, Option Some, user enum, `if let`) build, and AOT == interpreter on each. Valgrind on the combined program: 22 allocs / 22 frees, 0 errors — the free path is unchanged, which is the thing to check when adding a second registration to a binding that already owns a buffer. A companion test pins `.len()` / `.starts_with` so a bad registration cannot pass by firing the String arm where it should not. GUARD FAMILY, checked not assumed: `push`, `concat`, `sorted`, `sorted_by` share the `string_vars` guard. No second LIVE shape exists today — `push` on a String demands a `Char` (typecheck rejects `u8`) and `concat` is not a String method at all — but the gap was one missing registration for the whole family, so the fix is at the registration rather than in the `contains` arm. SEVERITY QUESTION LEFT OPEN, as the row's author left it: this is `medium` while the repo has treated check-passes/build-fails as `high` elsewhere (B-2026-07-30-7). Not resolved unilaterally here either; now that it is fixed the question is really about how the NEXT such row gets triaged.
tracker: src/codegen (String `contains` lowering for a direct Result/Option payload binding)

title: `unwrap_or` with a FRESH F-STRING default leaks on a DEFAULT -O2 build -- 133 leaked allocations in an existing fixture -- while the byte-identical program with a literal `"...".to_string()` default is clean, because the literal default const-folds away and the f-string one does not
detail:
REPRODUCED AS A TWO-LINE EDIT to an existing, currently-passing fixture,
`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs::asan_unwrap_or_fresh_string_default_no_leak`.
Replace its two `unwrap_or` defaults, changing NOTHING else:

    -  let a = opt(i).unwrap_or("odd-default".to_string());
    +  let a = opt(i).unwrap_or(f"odd-default-{i}");
    -  let b = res(i).unwrap_or("res-default".to_string());
    +  let b = res(i).unwrap_or(f"res-default-{i}");

  before  ->  passes, 503 allocations
  after   ->  `ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks`,
              133 byte(s) leaked in 133 allocation(s)

at the DEFAULT optimization level. Not an -O0 artifact: -O0 reports the same
133. The leak count is EXACTLY the `res(i)` Err-path iteration count
(i % 3 != 0 over 0..199 = 133); the `opt(i)` Option path, which discards a
default on 100 iterations, does not contribute. Enlarging the Err payload
(`Err("e".to_string())` -> `Err(f"eeeeeeeeee-{i}")`) holds the count at 133
and takes the bytes 133 -> 1790, so what leaks scales with the ERROR payload,
one per Err-path iteration.

WHY THE LITERAL SPELLING HIDES IT, which is the B-2026-08-04-17 mechanism
arriving one level up: `"odd-default".to_string()` is literal-derived, so LLVM
constant-folds it and deletes the allocation -- there is then nothing to leak
and the fixture is green. An f-string default is runtime-derived and survives.
The fixture has therefore been GREEN SINCE IT WAS WRITTEN without covering the
case it is named for, and the masking is in the fixture's choice of default
spelling rather than anywhere in the assertion.

NOT ISOLATED -- stated plainly because two attempts failed. Neither standalone
reduction reproduced:
  (a) `Result[i64, String]`, `unwrap_or(0 - 1)`, discarding a String Err
      payload over 30 iterations -> clean.
  (b) `Result[String, String]`, `unwrap_or(f"default-{i}")` plus a
      `starts_with` byte read over 30 iterations -> clean.
So the trigger is NOT simply 'unwrap_or discards a String Err payload' nor
'unwrap_or takes an f-string default'. Something about the full fixture --
the Option and Result receivers sharing a loop, the `as i64` casts, the
iteration count, or the absence of a byte read on `b` (adding one to the
reduction was what made (b) clean) -- is part of the condition. Whoever picks
this up should start from the two-line edit above, which reproduces every
time, and bisect DOWN from it rather than building up from a minimal guess.

RELATION TO B-2026-07-16-22, which this fixture pins: that bug was the
discarded default on the PRESENT path leaking. This leak tracks the ABSENT
path count instead, so it is a different arm and not obviously a regression of
that fix -- but the fixture's literal defaults mean the present-path fix has
also never been exercised against a default the optimizer could not delete.

SOURCE NOTE: found running B-2026-08-05-7's deciding experiment (does an -O0
failure also fire at -O2 once the payload is live?). The first attempt at that
experiment added a byte read but LEFT THE DEFAULT LITERAL, so it still folded
and the fixture still passed at -O2 -- walking straight into the hazard
B-2026-08-04-17 documents while testing for it. Making the CONTENT runtime-
derived is what exposed this.

BISECTED DOWN from the two-line edit, 11 probes in one build. The two
'failed reductions' recorded above FAILED FOR THE WRONG REASON and that entry
should be disregarded: both used a 30-iteration loop, and at n=30 LLVM folds
the ENTIRE loop away (probe p06: `res` half, f-string default, n=30 -> 3
allocations, i.e. zero program allocations, clean). The shapes were right; the
iteration count was too low to survive the optimizer. Same hazard as before,
third time in this investigation.

PROBE MATRIX (all at the default -O2; 'leak' = 133 allocations, 1 byte each):
  p00  both halves, both defaults f-string          LEAK 133
  p01  `res` half ONLY, f-string default            LEAK 133   <- minimal
  p05  `a` literal default, `b` f-string            LEAK 133
  p07  same as p01, no `as i64` cast                LEAK 133
  p08  same as p01, plus a `starts_with` byte read  LEAK 133
  p10  same as p01, inline (no `let b` binding)     LEAK 133
  p02  `opt` half ONLY (Option receiver)            clean, 303 allocs
  p03  `res` half, LITERAL `.to_string()` default   clean, 203 allocs
  p09  `res` half, f-string, but Err payload is i64 clean, 270 allocs
  p06  `res` half, f-string, n=30                   clean, 3 allocs (folded)

MINIMAL REPRODUCING SHAPE, therefore:

    fn res(i: i64) -> Result[String, String] {
        if i % 3 == 0 { Ok("ok-value".to_string()) } else { Err("e".to_string()) }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut total: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 200 {
            let b = res(i).unwrap_or(f"res-default-{i}");
            total = total + (b.len() as i64);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(total);
    }

THREE NECESSARY CONDITIONS, each established by a probe that removes exactly
one of them:
  1. RESULT receiver with a HEAP Err payload. An Option receiver never leaks
     (p02); a `Result[String, i64]` never leaks (p09). What leaks is the
     discarded ERROR payload -- 133 = the Err-path iteration count exactly, at
     1 byte each for `Err("e")`, and enlarging that payload scales the bytes
     133 -> 1790 at a constant 133 allocations.
  2. A FRESH-HEAP default. A literal `.to_string()` default is clean (p03) --
     though see the caveat below, this one may be masking rather than absent.
  3. Enough iterations to survive the optimizer (200 leaks, 30 folds away).
Irrelevant, contrary to the earlier guess: the `as i64` cast (p07), a byte read
on the result (p08), the `let` binding vs inline use (p10), and the presence of
the Option half in the same loop (p01 vs p00).

WHERE IT LIVES: `src/codegen/calls.rs`, the `unwrap_or` emitter (~line 2746,
the block carrying the B-2026-07-16-22 comment). Two observations from reading
it, offered as leads rather than a diagnosis -- no IR was dumped:

  (a) The PRESENT block frees the discarded default. The ABSENT block does
      nothing but `build_unconditional_branch(merge_bb)` -- there is no free of
      the receiver's discarded Err payload anywhere on that path, and
      `suppress_inline_option_result_binding_move(object)` then suppresses the
      receiver's scope-exit free as well. That is consistent with the observed
      leak being the Err payload, one per Err iteration.
  (b) The free condition includes `|| default_is_fstring`, directly beneath a
      comment that explicitly EXCLUDES f-string defaults: 'an f-string /
      collection-literal default is already temp-tracked by the statement
      machinery, so freeing it here would double-free'. Code and comment
      contradict each other. One of them is wrong, and which one it is bears
      directly on why condition 2 above holds -- why the literal-default
      spelling is clean while the f-string spelling leaks.

Note that (a) alone would predict the literal-default case to leak too, and it
does not (p03, 200 program allocations, no leak). So (a) is not the whole
story; the interaction with (b) is the open question.

FIXED (94ec3a9). Root cause exactly as the bisect's lead (a) predicted:
the absent path emitted no free for the discarded Err payload. Confirmed
against the IR before touching anything -- BOTH the clean and the leaking
variant emitted exactly one `karac_free_buf` in `main`, so the Err payload
was never freed in either, and the clean one was clean only because LLVM
folded its literal default away. Lead (b), the `|| default_is_fstring`
clause reading as contradicting its comment, was a RED HERRING: the comment
predates B-2026-07-16-23 leg 3, which added that arm deliberately. A
Call-shaped default (`unwrap_or(mkdef(i))`), which never touches the
f-string cleanup-removal loop, leaks identically -- that probe is what
ruled the clause out.

Also settles condition 2 from the bisect, which was recorded as possibly
'masking rather than absent': it IS masking. With the Err payload held
runtime-derived and only the DEFAULT's spelling varied, the literal form is
clean and the f-string/Call forms leak -- same missing free in all three,
different optimizer outcomes. Post-fix the literal variant's allocation
count rises 203 -> 403, i.e. the fold stops happening once the free exists.

FIX: the typechecker now records `E` in the existing
`method_unwrap_err_types` table for `unwrap_or` on a Result (it was
populated only for the closure combinators, which need `e` to FEED the
absent closure; `unwrap_or` needs it to FREE what it discards), and codegen
reconstructs the payload from the receiver words on the absent path and
frees it. The merge phi had to move from `absent_bb` to `absent_end` --
the free emits a `cap > 0` guard that splits the block, so the edge into
the merge leaves from elsewhere and the old phi fails the LLVM verifier.

KNOWN REMAINING GAP, deliberately not closed: the free covers a DIRECT
(unboxed) String/Vec `E` only. A wide `E` arrives through a box pointer in
`w0` and needs the present path's deboxing plus a free of the box itself,
so an AGGREGATE `E` with heap fields still leaks. Untested territory, left
whole rather than half-handled; the code comment carries the same note.

REGRESSION FIXTURE: `asan_unwrap_or_result_discarded_err_payload_no_leak`,
floored at 200 allocations, with BOTH the Err value and the default
runtime-derived -- a literal anywhere in that chain re-hides the bug, which
is how the sibling fixture stayed green over it. Gates: memory_sanitizer
932 passed, typechecker 2787, codegen 2130, default suite 100 binaries all
ok; clippy --all-targets + fmt clean; interpreter / AOT -O2 / AOT -O0 agree.

title: A `ref`-borrowed `shared` handle captured into a `par` branch reads as ZERO under codegen — silent wrong answer, interpreter disagrees
detail: REPRO (no `frozen` anywhere — this is ordinary Kara): `shared struct N { val: i64 }` / `fn worker(n: ref N, k: i64) -> i64 { n.val + k }` / `fn driver(n: ref N) -> i64 { let (a, b) = par { let a = worker(n, 1); let b = 100; (a, b) }; a + b }` / `fn main() { let g = N { val: 7 }; println(f"{driver(g)}") }`. EXPECTED 108. `karac run --interp` gives 108. `karac build` + run gives 101 — i.e. `n.val` reads as 0 inside the branch, so `worker` returns 0+1 instead of 7+1. `karac check` reports ZERO errors. Silent wrong answer, run-vs-build divergence. SCOPE: ONE branch is enough — this is not a multi-branch conflict and never reaches the `E_CONCURRENT_SHARED_STRUCT` gate, which is why it has gone unnoticed: the gate refuses the TWO-branch shapes loudly, and the one-branch shape it permits is the broken one. NOT A FROZEN BUG — the repro contains no `frozen` token, and it reproduces identically for `frozen N` only because B-2026-08-01-33's suppression lowers `frozen T` to `ref T`. The OWNED spelling of the same program is CORRECT (108), which localizes the defect to how a BORROWED shared handle is materialized into a par branch's task context: an owned capture is retained into the context and read back fine, a borrowed one apparently is not populated at all (payload reads 0). DISCOVERED BY: building B-2026-08-01-33 mechanism 3's `par` admission. The admission itself is written and verified working at the OWNERSHIP layer (the target program passes `karac check` and the interpreter prints the right answer) but is DELIBERATELY NOT LANDED, because admitting more programs onto a silently-miscompiling path is worse than a false rejection. Patch parked at scratchpad/admission.patch; it is ~94 lines and re-appliable once this is fixed. CONSEQUENCE FOR B-2026-08-01-33: mechanism 3 stage 1 is BLOCKED on this. Suppression (e232063) is kept — it is correct on its own (sequential `frozen` is byte-correct and emits 0/0) — but it did move `frozen` params from the working owned-capture path onto this broken borrowed-capture path, so a single-branch `frozen` par capture is now silently wrong too. Impact is latent rather than live (no `frozen` program exists outside tests), but the trap is real and this entry is the reason not to write one until the fix lands. VERIFICATION GAP THAT LET IT THROUGH: the suppression commit's test counted `rc_inc`/`rc_dec` occurrences in the emitted IR and never checked the program's OUTPUT. Traffic-count assertions cannot see a wrong answer. Any future RC-shape test in this family must pair the IR assertion with an E2E run asserting the computed value. FIXED (93b1a81). ROOT CAUSE: the branch prologue's `emit_arc_inc` does `getelementptr %karac.shared.T, <captured>, 0, 0` and atomically adds 1, which assumes the captured value IS the handle. For a borrow the slot holds a POINTER-TO-HANDLE, so the increment did not touch any refcount — it added 1 to the OWNER'S STORED HANDLE POINTER. The callee then dereferenced a pointer one byte off and read 0 instead of 7. The branch-exit `dec` subtracted the 1 back, which is why the corruption left no trace afterwards and the symptom was a merely-wrong answer rather than a crash — the reason this went unnoticed despite being a memory-corruption bug. FIX: exclude borrowed captures (`self.ref_params`) from the `SharedRc` path in `src/codegen/par_blocks.rs`. Correct rather than merely safe: a borrow's referent is kept alive by its owner, and that owner outlives the par run because `karac_par_run` does not return until every branch finishes — the same argument the `SharedRc` doc comment already makes for the parent's own reference. The capture therefore behaves as `Copy`: the pointer threads through the env untouched. NOTE THE CLASSIFIER IS UNCHANGED: `ParCaptureMode` is still chosen from the type name alone, so it still reports `SharedRc` for a borrowed `shared` capture and codegen now overrides it. A cleaner future shape is for the classifier to know borrow-ness and say `Copy` itself; that was not done here because the ownership pass would need parameter-mode information it does not currently thread into `par_capture_classify`. REGRESSION TEST asserts the COMPUTED VALUE across ref/frozen/owned (`borrowed_shared_capture_in_a_par_branch_reads_its_real_payload`, tests/par_codegen.rs) — not an IR traffic count, which is what missed it the first time.

title: `File.read` / `BufReader.read` reject a fixed `Array[u8, N]` buffer that AOT accepts — the blessed `let mut buf: Array[u8, N]; f.read(mut buf)` idiom runs under `karac build` and dies under `karac run --interp`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found on the FIRST file-I/O probe written for the Cumulus app (browser deep-sky stacker, apps/cumulus in kara-katas). Not a synthetic probe — it was the natural way to write a read-a-file round trip.

REPRO:
  let mut buf: Array[u8, 8] = [0u8; 8];
  match f.read(mut buf) { Ok(n) => ... }

  karac build      -> read 8 first=0 last=119   (correct)
  karac run --interp -> runtime error: File.read expects a `mut Slice[u8]` buffer, got `Array`

The idiom is BLESSED, not exotic: examples/relay ships exactly this shape for TcpStream.read (`let mut buf: Array[u8, 4096] = [0u8; 4096]; client.read(mut buf)`), because a `mut Slice[u8]` parameter needs a runtime-sized buffer and a fixed Array is how you make one.

WHY IT IS AN INCONSISTENCY RATHER THAN A MISSING FEATURE: `File.write`, thirty lines below the rejection in the same file, ALREADY accepted a `Value::Array` on purpose, with a comment saying so — 'be permissive at the interpreter level (the typechecker enforces the declared shape)'. Read was the half that never got the same treatment. The two directions of the same file disagreed with each other, and the read half also disagreed with AOT.

DIRECTION MATTERS: the INTERPRETER is the broken side, which is the test/dev path — so a program verified under `karac run` would be the one that fails, and a program shipped via `karac build` silently works. That is the opposite of the usual run-vs-build risk and still a parity break.

FIXED 1caca04: both read arms (method_call_file.rs, method_call_bufreader.rs) accept `Value::Array` as a full-range buffer, mirroring `File.write`. Regression test in tests/interpreter.rs asserts the exact bytes round-tripped through a fixed Array buffer, so a regression surfaces as wrong data rather than as a tolerated error string.
fix: FIXED 1caca04. `File.read` and `BufReader.read` in the interpreter now match `Value::Array` alongside `Value::Slice`, taking the whole array as the buffer window (start 0, len = array len). This mirrors the deliberate permissiveness `File.write` already had. AOT was already correct and is untouched.
tracker: src/interpreter/method_call_file.rs (File.read buffer match), src/interpreter/method_call_bufreader.rs (BufReader.read, identical shape); tests/interpreter.rs::file_read_accepts_a_fixed_array_buffer_like_aot.

title: the `ref` at a call site diagnostic tells the author to remove one token but carries no machine-applicable replacement, so `karac fix` leaves it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit writing apps/cumulus (kara-katas). Passing a borrowed buffer as `u32_at(ref data, 4)` is a natural mistake for anyone arriving from Rust, and it was five of my first six errors in that file.

THE DIAGNOSTIC IS ALREADY GOOD — it is correct, specific, and prescribes the exact edit:

  error[parse]: `ref` is not written at call sites. The parameter's mode is declared on the
  callee's signature. Remove the `ref` keyword.

WHAT IS MISSING is the `replacement`. The fix is a single-token deletion with no ambiguity — delete `ref ` at the marked span — which is about as machine-applicable as a fix gets. In the same file, in the same `karac fix` invocation, `&&` -> `and` and `!` -> `not` were both applied automatically; this one was left for hand editing, so the author is told precisely what to do and then has to do it themselves N times.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND CONVENIENCE: `karac fix` is the wedge. A diagnostic whose prose names an unambiguous single-token edit but ships no replacement is the exact shape the fix loop exists to close, and it is one an LLM author hits early — call-site `ref` is a Rust habit, so it arrives in the first file someone writes, before they have internalised that parameter modes live on the signature.

SEVERITY low: nothing is wrong, nothing is unsafe, and the message is already actionable. This is a fix-coverage gap, not a defect.

SUGGESTED SHAPE (unverified): attach a replacement deleting the `ref ` token span, the same way the operator diagnostics attach theirs. Worth checking whether the sibling call-site-mode errors (`mut` in a position that does not take it, if such a diagnostic exists) have the same gap, since they would share the fix. FIXED (9b17779). Both call-site mode diagnostics now attach a deletion edit through the same `fix_edits` channel the operator diagnostics use, so `karac fix` applies them instead of leaving the author to make the identical single-token edit N times. THE SUGGESTED SHAPE WAS RIGHT, including the hunch about the sibling: `mut ref` had the same gap. It is the more delicate of the two — the diagnostic is anchored at `mut` while the deletion targets `ref`, because `mut` is a legal call-site marker and must survive. `fix_edits` is keyed by the DIAGNOSTIC's span, so the key and the edited span are different tokens there. ONE DETAIL BEYOND THE MINIMUM: the edit covers the keyword AND its trailing whitespace, computed as [keyword.offset, next_token.offset).
