title: a `Slice[T]` / `mut Slice[T]` parameter fed from a PLACE (`f(g.a)`, `f(g.q.a)`, `f(t.0)`, `f(vv[0])`) did not COMPILE — the Vec's 3-word `{ptr,len,cap}` reached the 2-word `{ptr,i64}` slot and LLVM module verification hard-failed; only a bare identifier, a range index, a literal and a fresh rvalue were understood
detail:
SHAPE, minimal:

    struct P { a: Vec[i64] }
    fn setz(s: mut Slice[i64]) { s[0] = 9; }
    fn main() { let mut g = P { a: [1, 2] }; setz(mut g.a); println(g.a[0]); }

    error: codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Call parameter type does not match
    function signature!  %a = extractvalue { { ptr, i64, i64 } } %g1, 0
    { ptr, i64 }  call void @setz({ ptr, i64, i64 } %a)"

The interpreter runs the same program correctly. So this is a build-blocking codegen gap on a shape the language accepts, not a wrong answer.

SCOPE, measured with a clean probe (see the CORRECTION below for why that qualifier matters). Four place spellings, each refused for BOTH by-value `Slice[T]` and `mut Slice[T]`:
  struct field           `f(g.a)`
  nested struct field    `f(g.q.a)`
  tuple element          `f(t.0)`
  Vec element            `f(vv[0])`
A bare identifier argument was fine in every slot shape.

READ-ONLY `ref Slice[T]` WAS NEVER BROKEN, and that asymmetry is the interesting part. Its argument takes the borrow path in `call_dispatch.rs` and never reaches `coerce_to_slice` at all — the field arm passes a POINTER to the argument's Vec header, which is correct because `{ptr,len,cap}` starts with `{ptr,len}`, so the callee reads the right two words. That is also why the naive fix regresses it: a value-producing place arm winning on a ref slot pushes a `{ptr,i64}` VALUE into a `ptr` slot — the identical verification failure, one slot-shape over. Measured as a regression while building the fix, hence the explicit guard.

── CORRECTION TO THIS ROW AS FILED, and to the tool that produced it ──

This row originally said the argument 'writes into a copy under AOT — the caller's Vec is unchanged, while the interpreter mutates it', and quoted `AOT=1 (unchanged), interp=9`. THAT WAS WRONG. The program does not build; there is no AOT run to observe. The quoted AOT value came from a STALE BINARY: the probe shell function used `karac build … && out=$(./p)`, so when the build failed the `&&` short-circuited and the variable kept the PREVIOUS case's output. Every 'AOT=' number that row reported for a non-building program was the value of whatever ran before it.

The same defect briefly produced a phantom FIX, too: a later run of the same helper reported this shape as passing at HEAD, which would have closed the row as 'already fixed by someone else'. It was the control case's 9, held over. Bisecting three candidate commits to find a fix that did not exist is what surfaced the tool bug.

WHAT THE HELPER NOW DOES, and the rule worth keeping: `rm -f` the binary before building, then test `[ -x ./binary ]` rather than the build's exit status, so a failed build is reported AS a failed build and can never be silently attributed to a stale artifact. A probe that can report a result for a program that did not compile is not a measuring instrument.

CROSS-CHECKED AFTERWARDS: B-2026-08-05-39's headline numbers were re-measured with the fixed helper at the pre-fix commit and all held (AOT=2/interp=3, AOT=2/interp=1, AOT=empty/interp=5); B-2026-08-05-37's matrix is independently corroborated by its stash-proven E2E test. Only this row was affected.

FIX 0949f9f (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs `place_vec_header_ptr` + `arg_is_vec_header_place` + `slice_header_from_vec_header`; src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs the ref-slot guard). The place arm rebuilds the `{ptr,len}` header from the place's storage — the same code as the Identifier `Vec` arm, with only the header's ADDRESS differing, factored into a shared helper so the two cannot drift. Positive evidence on both halves: the place's storage must be verified to BE a Vec header (from the containing aggregate's LLVM type) AND `field_chain_place_ptr` must be able to address it, so a shape either half does not model falls through unchanged rather than being guessed at. A `shared` / `par` struct receiver is refused explicitly — its binding slot holds a HANDLE, not the aggregate — the same guard the `mut ref` place arm from B-2026-08-05-37 carries.

NOT RELATED, though it turned up in the same probe: `g.q.a.len()` still bails with 'chained field receivers (`a.b.c…`) are deferred to v1.x'. Confirmed pre-existing and slice-independent — the same bail fires for a plain `.len()` with no slice in sight. A chained-field SLICE ARGUMENT (`f(g.q.a)`) works after this fix.

TESTS: `e2e_slice_param_from_a_place_argument` (tests/codegen.rs) and `test_slice_param_from_a_place_argument` (tests/interpreter.rs, the oracle — passes either way by design) plus `asan_slice_param_from_a_place_argument_no_leak` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs). Four place spellings x by-value and by-ref slots, each MUTATED through a `mut Slice` before it is read: a header built over a COPY would compile and read fine while silently dropping every write, so the mutation is what proves the header points at the caller's real buffer. The ASAN twin gates the memory claim (no copy, no ownership transfer, the callee only borrows). Both codegen tests are STASH-PROVEN RED against the unfixed compiler with the exact verification errors, nine of them, one per call. Expected total DERIVED rather than read off a run: `15i + 31` per round, summed over 200 iterations = 304700.

SUITES: non-llvm 8637 pass, codegen E2E 2810, memory_sanitizer 940 pass / 0 fail / 10 ignored, par_codegen 236, cli 574; clippy and fmt clean.

fix: de799c3 (src/typechecker/fields.rs the `SharedFieldNotMut` gate's `mut ref` argument context; src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs `shared_mut_ref_place_arg_ptr` + `is_pure_field_chain`, replacing `mut_ref_place_arg_ptr`'s explicit shared bail). Pins e2e_mut_ref_place_argument_shared_receiver_writes_back, test_mut_ref_place_argument_shared_receiver_writes_back, asan_shared_field_mut_ref_arg_string_no_leak, and four typechecker gate tests.
title: a `shared struct` field reached through a `mut ref` ARGUMENT bypasses the immutable-field write gate that rejects the assignment spelling, and the write is lost under AOT — `n.val = 5` is refused, `bump(mut n.val)` is accepted and does nothing
detail:
TWO DEFECTS STACKED, both on the same spelling.

1. GATE BYPASS. For an IMMUTABLE field of a `shared struct`:

     shared struct N { val: i64 }
     fn bump(x: mut ref i64) { x = x + 1; }
     fn f(n: ref N) -> i64 { bump(mut n.val); return n.val; }

   checks clean. The SAME write spelled as an assignment is correctly refused:
   `n.val = 5` gives error[typecheck] "shared struct field 'N.val' is not declared mut". So the rule exists and is enforced — just not through the `mut ref` ARGUMENT spelling.

2. LOST WRITE, and a divergence since B-2026-08-05-37. For a DECLARED-`mut` shared field the program is legitimate, and AOT still discards the write while the interpreter now performs it:

     shared struct N { mut val: i64 }
     ... bump(mut g.val); println(g.val);   -> AOT 7, interp 8

   Before B-2026-08-05-37 both printed 7. That commit fixed the plain-struct place class on both backends and, on the interpreter, routed shared places through `write_shared_struct_field` (which correctly refuses the immutable case and performs the `mut` one). Its CODEGEN arm refuses a `shared` / `par` place EXPLICITLY, because a shared binding's slot holds a HANDLE rather than the aggregate — GEPing it as the struct would write past the 8-byte slot into neighbouring stack storage. So the divergence is a deliberate fail-closed choice there, not an oversight: the shared spelling needs a pointer derived from the RC payload, plus the mutability gate, and that is this row.

NOT A MEMORY-SAFETY ISSUE as measured: the write went to a stack temporary, so no shared state was mutated and no `par` branch could race through it. That is what kept this at medium — and it is also why it survived, since the symptom is a missing effect rather than a crash.

NOT `frozen`-SPECIFIC, though that is where it was found: the identical program with the parameter declared owned `N`, `ref N`, or `frozen N` behaves the same in all three modes, so this predates the freeze work (B-2026-08-01-33) entirely. That row's escape checker is correct for what it sees — `n.val` lowers to a scalar read and is admitted as one.

FIX, both halves, as the row specified.

TYPECHECK HALF (src/typechecker/fields.rs). The `SharedFieldNotMut` gate keyed on `is_lhs` alone; it now also fires when the field access sits in a `mut ref` ARGUMENT context. The discriminator is the EXISTING `borrow_context`, set by `borrow_context_for_param`, which yields `Some("mut ref")` only for `Type::MutRef` — so a read-only `ref T` borrow and a `mut Slice[T]` argument are untouched. That scoping is the point: widening to every borrow would make an immutable shared field unreadable through any `ref` callee, and the row asks for parity with the ASSIGNMENT spelling, not for a broader rule than the assignment has. Nested chains behave exactly as the assignment already did — `bump(mut o.inner.v)` with an immutable intermediate `Outer.inner` is refused on `Outer.inner`, which is verbatim what `o.inner.v = 9` does today; whether that pre-existing nested behaviour is right is a separate question this row does not reopen.

CODEGEN HALF (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs). The explicit `shared` / `par` bail in `mut_ref_place_arg_ptr` is replaced by `shared_mut_ref_place_arg_ptr`, which loads the handle and GEPs through the RC payload via `shared_gep_layout` — the same funnel every other shared field site routes through, which is what keeps the headed / headerless / weak-headed layouts from ever mixing on one object. `par` needs no separate arm (identical layout; only the count ops differ, and none are emitted here — a borrow is not an ownership transfer), and a plain `mut` field on a `par struct` is unreachable anyway, since `ParFieldNotConcurrent` requires `Atomic[T]` / `Mutex[T]`.

The bail was safe and wrong, which is the useful part of the story: it fell back to the rvalue path, so the write landed on a shallow COPY and was silently discarded. A fail-closed refusal in a resolver whose caller treats `None` as "use the old path" is not fail-closed at all.

DELIBERATELY NARROW, because this family's history is over-broad widenings that had to be reverted. The receiver must be a PURE FIELD CHAIN (identifier or `self` root, `FieldAccess` hops) because both call sites may already have compiled the argument, so re-evaluating an arbitrary receiver would duplicate its side effects; an `Index` hop is excluded on the same rule. A shared ENUM is excluded (no named fields). A `weak` field and a niche `Option[shared]` field are excluded because neither slot holds the value its source type names — one is a non-owning back-edge that reads as an upgrade, the other a bare pointer standing in for a four-word Option — so handing a callee a raw pointer to either would let it write a value of the wrong shape. All exclusions fall back to the pre-fix rvalue path, i.e. no worse than before.

WHAT WAS AND WAS NOT A WITNESS, measured against the unfixed compiler rather than assumed. Four receiver shapes printed 7 and now print 8: a bare shared local, a shared `ref` PARAMETER, `self` inside a shared method, and a nested shared chain (`o.inner.v`). A STRING field was ALREADY CORRECT — an aggregate `mut ref` reassignment reaches the caller's storage through B-2026-08-05-39's path, not through the argument pointer — so it is carried as a control, not a witness, and the test comment says so. It is kept because the fix newly routes it through the place pointer, and a heap payload must keep reclaiming exactly once on that path: free it twice and the RC box's field dangles, free it never and it leaks per iteration. Neither failure was possible on the copy path, so that guarantee is new and gets its own ASAN evidence rather than an inherited assumption.

TESTS. `e2e_mut_ref_place_argument_shared_receiver_writes_back` (tests/codegen.rs) — five arms, PROVEN RED against the unfixed compiler via a temporary bail-restoring hatch (`a:7 b:7 c:7 d:7` vs the expected 8s). `test_mut_ref_place_argument_shared_receiver_writes_back` (tests/interpreter.rs) pins the reference leg, which was already right, so it cannot silently drift to match a future codegen regression. `asan_shared_field_mut_ref_arg_string_no_leak` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) covers the reclaim leg — 1008 allocations measured, floored at 100 per B-2026-08-04-17. Four typechecker tests pin the gate in both directions: the immutable field refused through a `mut ref` argument, the declared-`mut` field still accepted, a read-only `ref` argument NOT gated, and a plain struct NOT gated.

tracker: src/codegen/synth_drop.rs::emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl -- the subst-driven bare-generic-param reclassification loop, which promotes only to FieldDrop::VecOrString and never to FieldDrop::MapOrSet
title: a generic wrapper's bare `T` field bound to a MAP leaks its whole handle tree: `fn sink(b: Box[Map[i64, String]])` loses 25,830 B / 40 blocks on a DEFAULT -O2 build, because the mono struct drop's bare-`T` reclassification recognises String/Vec/VecDeque heads only -- the concrete twin `Gmap[T] { m: Map[i64, T] }` is clean, since its DECLARED field name is `Map`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while closing B-2026-08-05-33 predicate (a), as a probe one
variable away from the fixture that row fixed. It is the intersection of that
row's predicates (a) generic-erased field and (b) Map-bearing field, and it
survives the fixes to BOTH.

REPRO, default -O2 `karac build`, under valgrind:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    fn sink2(b: Box[Map[i64, String]]) -> i64 { b.v.len() }
    fn main() {
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 40 {
            let mut m: Map[i64, String] = Map.new();
            m.insert(i, f"mapv-{i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer");
            let b = Box { v: m };
            acc = acc + sink2(b);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> prints 40 (correct), 25,830 bytes in 40 blocks definitely lost
       (2,880 direct + 22,950 indirect over 120 blocks). Identical at -O0, so
       this is NOT an optimizer-masking artifact.

MECHANISM, established rather than inferred. B-2026-08-05-33(a) made the
by-value param register its scope-exit drop at the param's DECLARED
instantiation, so `__karac_drop_struct_Box$Map_i64_String` IS now synthesized
for this shape. It frees nothing. `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`'s
name-based classifier reads the declared field `v: T`, matches no arm, and
leaves it `FieldDrop::None`; the subst-driven rescue loop below it then
promotes a bare generic-param field ONLY when the resolved type is a
String/`str` or a `Vec`/`VecDeque` head. A `Map` head falls through and stays
`None`. So the field is classified no-heap at exactly the point where the
subst has already told the compiler it is a Map.

THE ONE-VARIABLE CONTROL that isolates it: `struct Gmap[T] { m: Map[i64, T] }`
passed as `Gmap[String]` is CLEAN. Same generic struct, same Map, same by-value
param -- the difference is that its DECLARED field type is spelled `Map[i64,
T]`, so the name-based classifier sees the head `Map` without needing the subst
at all. Only a field whose declared type is the bare parameter misses.

FIX DIRECTION (deliberately not taken in the row that found it): add the
Map/Set arm to that same reclassification loop --

    Some("Map") | Some("HashMap") | Some("Set") | Some("HashSet")
      | Some("SortedMap") | Some("SortedSet")  ->  FieldDrop::MapOrSet

CAUTION, and it is why this is its own row rather than one more line in
B-2026-08-05-33. That loop is NOT param-specific: it runs for every struct drop
synthesized under a real subst, so the arm changes drop behaviour inside every
MONOMORPH body too, not just for by-value params. This family's history is
three reverted over-broad ownership widenings, and B-2026-08-05-33 records the
method note that the -O2 suite stayed fully green across one that introduced a
double free -- only the -O0 sweep saw it, and only by diffing the failure SET.
So the arm needs both gates in full, plus the specific move-suppression
question below.

THE SPECIFIC QUESTION TO ANSWER FIRST: a Map field freed by a struct drop has no
per-field move-out neutralizer. `zero_struct_field_move_cap` zeroes a Vec/String
cap, an Option tag, a Result payload area -- and for Map/Set does nothing;
`zero_struct_move_caps_mono`'s own comment states Map/Set handles "are NOT
zeroed by this helper today ... they need a `null`-marker convention through
`karac_map_free`". A CONCRETE Map-bearing struct survives that gap because a
whole-struct move retracts the source's entire StructDrop rather than
neutralizing one field (measured: `let g = h; sink(g)` on `struct MapH { m:
Map[i64, String] }` is clean at both opt levels). Whether a bare-`T` Map field
moved out INDIVIDUALLY has the same protection is the thing to establish before
adding the arm -- if it does not, the arm trades this leak for a double free.

NOT A REGRESSION from B-2026-08-05-33: measured against the pre-fix compiler at
8cb7440, where it loses the identical 2,880 B direct + 22,950 B indirect over the same 40 + 120 blocks.

PRECONDITION ANSWERED (2026-08-06), and the answer was NO — filed as B-2026-08-06-6 and FIXED. This row asked, correctly, whether a bare-`T` Map field moved out individually has the same protection a whole-struct move gets. The cheapest decisive experiment turned out to be on the CONCRETE spelling, which already classifies `MapOrSet`: `fn take(h: MapH) -> Map[i64, String] { return h.m; }` SEGFAULTED on a use-after-free. So the per-field neutralizer had no Map arm at all, and the hazard this row predicted was already live for concrete structs. That is now fixed.

THIS ROW STAYS OPEN ANYWAY, and here is the measured reason, so the next reader does not re-derive it. With the neutralizer in place I added the arm this row prescribes. Result:

  FIXED — every READ shape, in full: by-value param (`sink(b)`), plain local
          (`let b = Box { v: m }; b.v.len()` — so this is NOT param-specific,
          which widens the row), and a MID field of a multi-field wrapper.
  BROKE — `fn take2(b: Box[Map[i64, String]]) -> Map[i64, String] { return b.v; }`
          became a SIGSEGV. It is clean today only because nothing frees the field.

WHY THAT SHAPE AND NOT THE STRING ONE. The field-RETURN path (`runtime.rs`, the `te_owns_heap_below_buffer` block) does not neutralize the source — it DEEP-CLONES, so the caller owns an independent buffer and the owner's drop is free to run. Its `single_field_heap_wrapper` gate admits only String / Vec / VecDeque heads, so a Map head falls back to cloning through the bare declared `T`, which is a shallow handle copy, and the returned alias is freed twice.

EXTENDING THAT GATE DOES NOT WORK: there is no `karac_map_clone` in the runtime and no Map arm in `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`, so a Map cannot be deep-cloned at that site today. Closing this row therefore needs ONE OF — (a) a runtime map clone, or (b) that return path switching from clone-the-value to null-the-source, which is what every other move site does. Both are by-value-generic-param machinery, adjacent to B-2026-08-06-2.

The arm was written, measured, and REVERTED rather than landed behind a partial gate; the reason is recorded at the site in `synth_drop.rs` so the next attempt starts from the measurement instead of the idea.

FIXED 2026-08-06, and the row's own CAUTION was right on the substance and wrong
about the remedy. It said the arm 'trades this leak for a double free' unless
the move-suppression question was settled first. It does — measured, 1880
valgrind errors on `let c = b;`. But the settlement is not a runtime map clone
and not a change to the field-RETURN path; both of those were dead ends recorded
here earlier on 2026-08-06 and BOTH ARE NOW SUPERSEDED. The actual defect is
that three sites disagree about what a bare-`T` field IS:

  (1) `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`'s rescue loop — resolves the bare param
      through the struct subst, but promoted only String/Vec/VecDeque heads.
      THE LEAK.
  (2) `zero_struct_field_move_cap` — classifies by the DECLARED field name and
      resolved it through `subst_monomorph_type_params`, i.e. the ACTIVE
      FUNCTION's monomorph subst. A generic wrapper taken at CONCRETE args sits
      in a CONCRETE function, which has no active subst, so the field stayed
      literally `T`, every name arm missed, and a moved-out field left the
      source handle live.
  (3) `zero_struct_move_caps_mono` — the same erased-name problem; its
      bare-param rescue covered only the Vec/String heads, so a whole-struct
      move left one live too.

(1) alone is the double free the row predicted. All three together are the fix:
both neutralizers now resolve a bare param through the SOURCE BINDING's recorded
instantiation (`enum_inst_var_types`) — the same binding the drop is synthesized
against via `track_struct_var_inst`. The invariant is one sentence: whatever the
free list frees, the neutralize list must be able to disarm.

WHY THE EARLIER DEAD END WAS A DEAD END, since it cost a session. The note above

SOURCE NOTE: reached from B-2026-08-05-7's `generic_struct_heap_field_move_out_no_double_free`, one of the five -O0 sweep failures. That fixture SURVIVED B-2026-08-05-33 being closed -- it was predicted to fall with it and did not, which is what prompted the decomposition below.

REPRO, DEFAULT -O2 `karac build`, under valgrind, 40 iterations with a runtime-derived payload so nothing is compile-time dead:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    fn take[T](b: Box[T]) -> T { b.v }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        let mut i: i64 = 0; let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        while i < 40 {
            let s = take(Box { v: "pad-well-past-inline-width".repeat(n) });
            acc = acc + s.len();
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> prints the correct total; `definitely lost: 1,040 bytes in 40 blocks`.
       IDENTICAL at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and at the default -O2, and the
       allocation count is unchanged between them (206 allocs either way on
       the 100-iteration variant), so the optimizer is NOT deleting the
       evidence. This is in the shipped binary.

THREE ONE-VARIABLE CONTROLS, each CLEAN, so the shape needs all three
conditions simultaneously:

  1. NAMED argument instead of the literal
         let bx = Box { v: <String> }; let s = take(bx);        -> CLEAN
  2. CONCRETE param instead of the generic one
         fn take2(b: Box[String]) -> String { b.v }             -> CLEAN
  3. Field NOT moved out (callee returns a scalar)
         fn peek[T](b: Box[T]) -> i64 { 1 }                     -> CLEAN

the surface looks identical. That row's own control section records
"(a) as a FRESH-TEMP arg rather than a local -> leaks too, so the ARGUMENT
FORM is irrelevant here". Here the argument form is the WHOLE thing: control
1 is clean and the literal is not. Opposite asymmetry => different site. -33
is closed and all three of its predicates are fixed; this survives them.

and a `Map` head falls through. The payload here is a STRING -- already
covered by that loop -- and control 2 proves the String classification works
correctly the moment the param is concrete. Adding -06-1's Map/Set arm cannot

HYPOTHESIS, explicitly not a finding. The callee moving the field out disarms
the param's scope drop (that is correct and is what control 3 isolates); the
caller's struct-literal temp then has no binding to own the field; and the
concrete case escapes because B-2026-08-05-33(a) registers the drop at the

where -33(a) landed. Unverified -- no IR was read.

literal "a"). Note the name says double-free and the failure is a LEAK; per

NARROWED (same session, no fix yet). The hypothesis in the section above is

WHAT WAS MEASURED, on the two-line pair `gen.kara` (generic param, leaks
26 B / 1 block) and `con.kara` (concrete param, clean) -- identical except
`fn take[T](b: Box[T]) -> T` vs `fn take(b: Box[String]) -> String`:

  * THE CALLER-SIDE GATE IS IDENTICAL. Instrumenting
    `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`'s StructLiteral arm prints the same
    line for both:
        REACHED literal path=Box in_struct_types=true
        name=Box llvm_heap=true copyable=false sharedown=false
        needs=true flows=false
    So the caller REGISTERS a memory drop in both cases. The literal-arg
    condition is NOT "the registrar declines"; it reaches and fires.

  * NEITHER CALLEE FREES. `objdump --disassemble` of the monomorph
    `take$struct$T_ct_String` and of the concrete `take` shows ZERO calls to

  * THE FREE-INSTRUCTION COUNTS ARE THE SAME. `main` contains 3 free calls in
    both binaries; the whole binary contains 19 in both.

CONCLUSION FROM THAT: this is NOT a missing emission. The same frees are
emitted on both paths; one of them does not RECLAIM at run time. That points
at a runtime GUARD -- the cap/tag test a struct drop wraps its field free in
-- being false on the generic path. The move-out is what would zero it
(`zero_struct_field_move_cap` and friends), which is exactly why control 3
(callee does not move the field out) is clean.

SO THE LIKELY SITE is the move-out cap-zeroing deciding it may neutralize the
CALLER's temp on the generic path but not the concrete one -- i.e. the two
disagree about who was made the owner. That is a DIFFERENT site from the one
the original hypothesis named (it guessed the drop was never registered;
it is registered). Whoever picks this up should start by dumping the guard
value, not by looking for a missing `track_*` call.

NOT ESTABLISHED: which zeroing call does it, and whether the concrete path is

CORRECTION -- THIS ROW WAS FILED WITH A FALSE CONTROL, and the false control
was hiding a DOUBLE FREE. Both earlier sections above ("THREE ONE-VARIABLE
CONTROLS, each CLEAN" and the NARROWED section) called the concrete-param
case CLEAN. It is not. The measurement grepped valgrind for
`definitely lost` ONLY, so an `Invalid free()` printed on the very next line
was never looked at. Re-running the identical binaries with the full error
set:

    1 generic,  literal arg, moves out   ->  definitely lost: 15 bytes
    2 generic,  NAMED   arg, moves out   ->  clean
    3 CONCRETE, literal arg, moves out   ->  INVALID FREE (double free)
    4 CONCRETE, NAMED   arg, moves out   ->  INVALID FREE (double free)
    5 generic,  literal arg, NOT moved   ->  clean

So the argument form is irrelevant to (A) -- both spellings of the concrete
call double-free -- and this row's "needs all three conditions" framing
applies only to the LEAK, (B).

METHOD NOTE, the reusable one: `--leak-check=full` reports leaks AND memory
errors, and a grep for the leak line silently discards the error line. Grep
for `ERROR SUMMARY` (or for `Invalid free|Invalid read|Invalid write`
alongside `definitely lost`) or the "control" that makes a bug look narrow
may be a worse bug. That is what happened here twice in one session.

MECHANISM, now read off the IR (`cargo run --features llvm --example dump_ir`)
rather than inferred. Both spellings share ONE drop, and it is correct:

    __karac_drop_struct_Box$String(ptr %0)
      -> cap-guarded free of field 0    (so the String bare-`T` field IS
                                         reclassified; B-2026-08-06-1's
                                         rescue loop works for a String head)

(A) CONCRETE callee, verbatim:
        %b1 = load ..., ptr %b
        %v  = extractvalue %b1, 0            ; the CALLER's buffer triple
        call void @__karac_drop_struct_Box$String(ptr %b)   ; cap INTACT -> FREES it
        ret { ptr, i64, i64 } %v             ; returns a triple into freed memory
    The caller stores that into `s` and frees it again at scope exit. Two
    frees of one pointer.

(B) GENERIC monomorph `take$struct$T_ct_String`, verbatim: it FIRST
    entry-deep-copies the field (`dcopy.*`: malloc + memcpy, store the copy
    back into %b), THEN
        store i64 0, ptr %sfld.move.cap      ; <- the move-out neutralizer
        call void @__karac_drop_struct_Box$String(ptr %b)   ; no-op, cap==0
        ret %v                               ; returns the COPY
    So the generic path is SAFE (it has the cap-zero the concrete path
    lacks) but leaks: the deep copy means two buffers exist and only the
    copy is ever freed. The caller's original sits in `%__owned_agg_tmp`,
    which `main` stores to and NEVER frees -- confirmed by dumping `main`
    for both spellings, which are otherwise byte-identical.

WHY THE CALLER'S TEMP IS NEVER FREED, and it is a name mismatch worth
checking first: `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg` decides via the MONO
LLVM type (instrumented: `llvm_heap=true needs=true`, identical for both
spellings) and then calls `track_struct_var("Box", slot)` under the BASE
name. The synthesized drop is `__karac_drop_struct_Box$String`. `main`
contains inline cleanup walks for `%s` and `%__owned_tmp` but none for
`%__owned_agg_tmp`, consistent with the base-name lookup resolving `v: T`
to no-heap. UNVERIFIED -- that last step is inference from the emitted
code, not from reading `track_struct_var`.

FIX DIRECTION. (A) is the urgent half and looks small: emit the same
`sfld.move.cap = 0` before the drop on the non-monomorph path -- the
generic path already does exactly this and is the working reference. (B)
then needs either the caller's temp actually freed, or no entry-deep-copy
when the field is immediately moved out. Do (A) first and re-measure (B):
the two interact through who owns the single vs copied buffer, and fixing
(A) alone may change (B)'s accounting.

--- DEFECT (A) FIXED: 933b859 -----------------------------------------------

THE SITE was the caller-side gate in `src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs` (~5540)
that decides whether a moved-out field may be cap-zeroed:

    if let (BasicTypeEnum::StructType(held), Some(st)) = (slot.ty, gep_st) {
        if held == st { self.zero_struct_field_move_cap(slot.ptr, &name, field); }
    }

`gep_st` resolved as "active monomorph subst, else the DECLARED base type".
A CONCRETE fn over a generic struct (`fn take(b: Box[String])`) has no active
subst, so it fell through to the ERASED generic base -- whose bare-`T` field is
a placeholder, not `String` -- and `held == st` was FALSE. The cap-zero was
skipped and the callee's struct drop freed a buffer the caller still returns.
The generic monomorph was correct only because it HAS a subst. This is the
same no-active-subst gap B-2026-08-05-33(a) hit at its own site, which is why
that row's fix did not carry this one (and why this row's fixture survived it).

THE FIX. The slot holding a `StructType` -- rather than a pointer -- is already
proof that this is an OWNED INLINE STRUCT and not a `ref` borrow, which is the
safety property the gate exists for; it does not additionally need type
equality against a separately-resolved layout. So the slot's own layout is
threaded down as the GEP type (`zero_struct_field_move_cap_in`, with the
old entry point delegating), and the vec-ish field classifier gains a fallback
against that concrete layout too -- a bare-`T` type-expr lowers to the
placeholder outside a monomorph, so no existing test could ever have seen the
String through the declared type. Byte-identical for non-generic structs and
for monomorphs; only the concrete-instantiation case changes.

    4 CONCRETE, named,   moves out       CLEAN   (was DOUBLE FREE)

--- DEFECT (B) FIXED: eefe88a -----------------------------------------------

RE-MEASURED after (A), as this row instructed, rather than resumed from the
pre-fix notes: still reproduced at 15 B/block on shape 1, and the IR confirmed
the pre-fix reading exactly. The monomorph `take$struct$T_ct_String`:

    %dcopy.buf = call ptr @malloc(...)   ; entry deep-copy of field 0,
    memcpy; store the COPY back into %b  ; overwriting the caller's triple
    store i64 0, ptr %sfld.move.cap      ; move-out neutralizer
    call void @__karac_drop_struct_Box$String(ptr %b)   ; no-op, cap == 0
    ret %v                               ; returns the COPY

and `main` stores the original into `%__owned_agg_tmp` and never walks it.

WHY THE CALLER REGISTERED NOTHING, now measured rather than inferred (the
earlier UNVERIFIED base-name-vs-mono guess was RIGHT, and this is the proof).
Instrumenting the struct-literal arm of `track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg`:

    name=Box llvm_heap=true  inst=Some(Box[str])
    plain_drop=None                              <- track_struct_var's synthesis
    mono_drop=Some(__karac_drop_struct_Box$str)  <- with the instantiation

`track_struct_var` is name-keyed with an EMPTY subst, so
`emit_struct_drop_synthesis_mono("Box", {})` reads the erased bare-`T` field,
classifies it as no-heap, returns `None`, and the registrar `return`s having
pushed no cleanup action. The gate fired (`needs_memory_drop=true`) and then
silently no-op'd — which is exactly why the earlier instruction-count probe
found the same free count on both paths and concluded "not a missing
emission". It WAS a missing emission; it just wasn't missing from the callee.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS A DOUBLE FREE, and this is the load-bearing part.
Passing the instantiation unconditionally breaks two shapes that are
INDISTINGUISHABLE at the call site:

  * the CONCRETE spelling `fn take(b: Box[String])` — B-2026-08-05-33's
    own-by-transfer arm: no dcopy, the callee's drop owns the buffer;
  * `fn take[U](b: Box[U])` — the SAME generic source with the fn's type
    param named differently from the struct's. `mono_struct_type_from_active_subst`
    looks up the STRUCT's params (`T`) in the FN's subst (`U -> String`),
    finds nothing, falls back to the base layout, and
    `try_make_generic_struct_param_callee_owned` bails — so this monomorph
    ALSO takes own-by-transfer. Verified in IR: `take$struct$U_ct_String`
    has no `dcopy.*` at all.

Both are clean today precisely BECAUSE the caller's registration no-ops. A
caller-side look-alike predicate cannot separate them: the discriminator is
which NAMES the callee's substitution happens to bind, which is invisible
from the call site.

THE FIX. Ask the callee's own predicate instead of predicting it. The
aggregate-arg registration loop in `compile_generic_call` moves down to after
`subst_names` / `subst_type_exprs` are built, installs them briefly, and calls
`mono_entry_copies_aggregate_param` — a thin `pub(super)` wrapper over the
exact `mono_struct_type_from_active_subst` + `aggregate_param_copy_supported_struct_mono`
pair the callee's param prologue runs. Caller and callee cannot disagree.
The instantiation reaches the registrar through a new
`track_inline_owned_aggregate_arg_inst`; the old 3-arg entry point delegates
with `None`, so all six other call sites are byte-identical.

VERIFIED, default -O2 + valgrind, payload from `env.args().len()`:

    generic  literal moves-out   CLEAN  (was 1,040 B / 40 blocks)
    generic  named   moves-out   CLEAN
    CONCRETE literal moves-out   CLEAN
    CONCRETE named   moves-out   CLEAN
    take[U]  literal moves-out   CLEAN  (the divergence control)
    peek[T]  literal not-moved   CLEAN
    peek     concrete not-moved  CLEAN
    non-generic twin             CLEAN

140 B / 4 blocks before, 0 after. fmt + clippy (plain and --features llvm)

the named-arg and `take[U]` controls riding along in the same fixture so a

`asan_concrete_generic_struct_field_move_out_no_double_free` (defect A).

wrong before it closed: the "three clean controls" (one was a double free, hid

so it is inlined generated code rather than an added runtime call.

WHICH PART OF THE COMMIT, and this matters because the commit is named for
something else. 32358cac is "graduate StringSlice to v1", but every codegen hunk
in it is gated on the `StringSlice` type name, which appears NOWHERE in kata #8.
What can touch this kata is its secondary leg, B-2026-06-14-18:

    if matches!(&obj_ty, Type::Ref(i) | Type::MutRef(i) if **i == Type::Str) {
        return self.infer_str_method(method, args, span);
    }

Before it, a borrowed String receiver took the impl-block deref path, which
resolves impl-style methods but does not type the stdlib-only ones -- so
`s.find(' ')` on a `ref String` degraded to `Type::Error` and codegen fell
through. #8's hot function is exactly `fn my_atoi(s: ref String)` calling
`s.bytes()`, so it changed dispatch route.

NOT ESTABLISHED: the instruction-level difference the re-routing produces.
`main`'s STATIC instruction count is IDENTICAL (5,529) on both sides, so the same
code is executing a different number of times rather than more code existing --
which is why an IR diff, not a disassembly diff, is the next step. Until that is
done the fix direction is unknown, which is why this row is severity LOW despite
being fully reproducible: 1.04x on one kata shape, with no known cheap fix.

NOT A REVERT CANDIDATE. B-2026-06-14-18 is a real correctness fix -- stdlib-only
String methods on a borrowed receiver were silently typing to `Type::Error` --
and StringSlice v1 is a shipped feature. The question is whether the borrowed
receiver can reach the same stdlib surface without the per-call cost.

WHERE IT SHOWS UP: proportional to CALL COUNT, not to string size. Worst on code
that calls String methods on a `ref String` parameter inside a hot loop over
short strings; nearly invisible on code that calls a few methods on large
strings. That is the opposite of the intuition "string work scales with string
length", and it is why #8 (8 short inputs, 10M calls) is the kata that caught it.

METHOD NOTE carried from B-2026-08-05-34: the bisect that found this read EXACTLY
one of two values at every one of its 12 steps -- 3,090,000 or 3,215,000, nothing
between, no step skipped -- so the a12a1a69..688865b4 window contains ONE
discrete mover for this probe, not an accumulation. Whoever chases the mirror
question (#9 palindrome OVERSHOOTS its endpoint: a12a1a69 costs it 1.191x while
the endpoint is only 1.146x, so something later GAVE BACK 3.8%) can use the same
harness with the decision inverted. INSTRUCTION-LEVEL DIFFERENCE ESTABLISHED — AND IT IS B-2026-08-05-38'S WIDTH TRAP, SO THIS ROW IS NOT AN INDEPENDENT OPTIMIZATION PROBLEM (2026-08-05, x86_64 Linux). The row closed by saying the instruction-level difference was NOT established and that an IR diff was the next step. It did not need one: callgrind's INSTRUCTION-LEVEL dump (`--dump-instr=yes`) localizes it to four addresses without any IR. REPRODUCED FIRST: matched pair a955c0c7 vs 32358cac (direct parent/child), each with its own karac and its own lean+full archives, sinks 15437323750000 on both. Total I-refs 1,545,303,031 -> 1,607,803,030 = 1.0404 (the row recorded 1.0405), delta 62,499,999 over 10M calls = +6.25 per call EXACTLY. LOCALIZATION: the entire delta is four addresses inside `main`. Before, 0x9085 executed 62,500,000 times; after, BOTH 0x9082 and 0x908e execute 62,500,000 times — one instruction became two in a loop running 6.25x per call. Note 6.25 is the AVERAGE DIGIT COUNT of the eight atoi inputs, which is why padding with 85 leading SPACES left the delta unchanged: spaces are skipped before this loop, so they add per-call work without adding digits. THE DIFFERENCE, disassembled at those addresses. BEFORE: `add $-0x30,%r11` / `cmp %rdx,%r11` / `jge`. AFTER: `add $-0x30,%r10` / `movslq %r10d,%r11` / `cmp %r10,%r11` / `jne`. So a SIGN-EXTENSION is added and the branch changes from a signed bound compare to comparing a value against its own sign-extension — the canonical i32 WIDTH-CHECK idiom (sext the low 32 bits, compare to the full 64-bit value, trap if they differ). IT SITS ON A NARROW-INT OP IN THE SOURCE: `let digit: i32 = (b as i32) - (zero as i32);` — the `add $-0x30` IS that `- '0'`. So the checked op is an i32 subtraction, exactly the class B-2026-08-05-38 describes. SO THE TWO ROWS ARE THE SAME COST, and B-2026-08-05-38 already names kata #8 among its affected shapes. The reconciliation: a12a1a69 INTRODUCED the unconditional width trap; 32358cac then made MORE ops subject to it on this kata — before it, a borrowed String receiver took the impl-block deref path and stdlib-only methods typed to `Type::Error`, so `b` was not a real `u8` and `(b as i32) - (zero as i32)` was not a real i32 op. The correctness fix gave it a real narrow type, and the trap followed. That is why this residual appeared at a commit named for StringSlice. IMPLICATION FOR WHOEVER FIXES -38: their range analysis should eliminate THIS 1.04x too, so this row should be re-checked (and probably closed) against that fix rather than worked separately. `digit` is provably in [0, 9] at that point — the loop only enters on a byte in '0'..'9' — so it is exactly the provably-in-range case -38 says has no elision today. ONE DISCREPANCY WORTH NOTING, not resolved: -38 describes the trap as 'zext/sext to i64, two icmps, an or, and a conditional branch per op', roughly five instructions. What is emitted here nets only ONE extra instruction (sext added; the pre-existing compare and branch are reused with different operands). LLVM appears to fold the full form when one side is already known in-range. So the per-op cost of the trap is SHAPE-DEPENDENT, and -38's 5-instruction figure is an upper bound rather than a constant — worth knowing when sizing that fix's expected win.

── CLOSED — THE ATTRIBUTION IS WRONG, MEASURED AT HEAD (2026-08-06, x86_64) ──

This row's last update said its residual was B-2026-08-05-38's width trap and
that it should be re-checked against that row's range-analysis fix. Half right.
It IS -38's trap. But -38 is now closed `invalid` (651cfe6 — both of its
proposed fixes measured and refuted), so there is no fix to re-check against;
and the op this row names is NOT the one that carries the cost.

WHAT THE ROW CLAIMS: the surviving check sits on
`let digit: i32 = (b as i32) - (zero as i32);`, on the grounds that "the
`add $-0x30` IS that `- '0'`".

WHAT IS ACTUALLY EMITTED AT HEAD, from `--dump-instr=yes` on kata #8's hot loop
(each instruction 125,000x per 20k outer iters):

    movzbl (%rsi,%r8,1),%r10d   ; load b
    lea    -0x3a(%r10),%r11d    ; the '0'..'9' range test
    cmp    $0xf6,%r11b / jb
    cmp    $0xccccccc,%r9d / jg ; the SOURCE guard, result > max_div
    jne
    cmp    $0xf3333333,%r9d / jle
    movslq %r9d,%r9
    lea    (%r9,%r9,4),%r9      ; result*5
    lea    (%r10,%r9,2),%r9     ; b + result*10   <- digit FUSED IN
    add    $0xffffffffffffffd0,%r9   ; ...-48     ->  result*10 + digit
    movslq %r9d,%r10            ; THE width check
    cmp    %r9,%r10 / jne <trap>

LLVM FUSES `(b as i32) - 48` INTO THE ACCUMULATOR. The `add $-0x30` the row
points at is not a standalone digit subtraction in the emitted code — it is the
tail of `result*10 + (b - 48)`, and the `movslq`/`cmp`/`jne` after it is that
FUSED expression's check, not the subtraction's. Adjacency was read as
ownership.

THE DIGIT SUBTRACTION'S OWN CHECK IS ELIMINATED, verified directly rather than
inferred. A probe isolating exactly that op — `let digit: i32 = (b as i32) -
(zero as i32);` over a runtime-seeded `Vec[u8]`, accumulated to a sink —
compiles its hot loop to:

    movzbl (%r15,%rcx,1),%ecx
    add    $0xffffffffffffffd0,%rcx   ; b - 48
    add    %rdx,%rcx / jo             ; the i64 SINK's own overflow check

No `movslq`/`cmp`/`jne` anywhere: no width check on the subtraction. Both
operands are `sext(zext(i8))`, so the result is provably in [-255, 255] and
LLVM's own range reasoning removes the check unaided. This is the same result
-38 recorded ("where interval reasoning suffices, LLVM has already done it"),
now confirmed on this row's specific op.

SO THE TWO SURVIVING CHECKS IN #8 ARE BOTH -38's UNPROVABLE CLASS:
  * `cmp $0xf3333333 / jle` — the multiply's LOWER bound. Provable only from
    the loop invariant `result >= 0` (it starts at 0 and only grows), which is
    an inductive fact, not an interval one.
  * `movslq`/`cmp`/`jne` — the fused add's width check, needing the correlated
    split `result < max_div OR digit <= 7` that an interval domain misses by
    exactly 2 (worked in -38).

WHY THE COST STILL APPEARED AT A StringSlice COMMIT, corrected. The row's own
reconciliation was directionally right: before 32358cac a borrowed `String`
receiver typed stdlib-only methods to `Type::Error`, so `b` was not a real
`u8`. What the correctness fix actually did was give the ACCUMULATOR expression
its correct narrow type — not the subtraction — subjecting `result*10 + digit`
to the width trap. That is -38's dominant op, in -38's own headline kata.

CONSEQUENCE: nothing here is independently fixable. There is no String-receiver
dispatch overhead to remove — the row's title is misleading on that point,
which is why this closes `invalid` rather than as a live-but-deferred item. Any
future attempt belongs to the correlated-predicate question -38 records, under
the `llvm.assume` precondition documented there.

WORTH KEEPING: this row's ONE DISCREPANCY note (that the trap nets ~1 extra
instruction here, not the ~5 -38 describes, because LLVM folds the full form
when one side is known in-range) is CONFIRMED and generalized by the above —
LLVM removes the check outright when BOTH sides are known in range. -38's
5-instruction figure is an upper bound, as that note suspected.
fix: CLOSED AS A DUPLICATE OF B-2026-08-05-38 (itself closed `invalid` at 651cfe6), 2026-08-06, no code change. The 1.04x is real and still reproduces at HEAD (kata #8 = 3,215,000), but it is NOT a String-receiver dispatch cost and NOT on the op this row names: at HEAD LLVM ELIMINATES the digit subtraction's width check entirely and the surviving checks sit on the fused accumulator, which is exactly the correlated-guard case -38 measured as unreachable by interval analysis.

tracker: src/codegen/expr_ops.rs::coerce_to_slice (shared arm) + shared_field_is_vec_header; src/typechecker/exprs.rs::param_mutates_through + TypeChecker::mut_through_param_arg, consumed by src/typechecker/fields.rs::infer_field_access
title: a `shared struct`'s Vec field passed to a `mut Slice[T]` parameter does not COMPILE (LLVM module verification hard-fails) even when the field is declared `mut`, and the immutable case additionally passes `karac check` — the `SharedFieldNotMut` gate cannot see a `Type::Slice` formal
detail:
SHAPES, both minimal, both measured at c0e6700 + the B-2026-08-05-41 fix:

    // (b) LEGAL program — the field IS declared mut
    shared struct H { mut v: Vec[i64] }
    fn zap(s: mut Slice[i64]) { s[0] = 99; }
    fn main() { let h = H { v: [1,2,3] }; zap(mut h.v); println(h.v[0]); }

  `karac check`  -> All checks passed
  `karac run --interp` -> 99   (correct)
  `karac build`  -> error: codegen failed: Module verification failed:
                    "Call parameter type does not match function signature!
                       %v = load { ptr, i64, i64 }, ptr %sh_v
                       call void @zap({ ptr, i64, i64 } %v)"   expected { ptr, i64 }

    // (a) UNSOUND program — the field is NOT declared mut
    shared struct H { v: Vec[i64] }
    fn zap(s: mut Slice[i64]) { s[0] = 99; }
    fn main() { let h = H { v: [1,2,3] }; zap(mut h.v); println(h.v[0]); }

  `karac check`  -> All checks passed          <- the gate bypass
  `karac run --interp` -> runtime error: shared struct field 'H.v' is not declared mut
  `karac build`  -> the same module-verification failure as (b)

TWO LEGS, one shape.

(b) CODEGEN GAP, the visible one: a `shared struct`'s Vec field cannot be coerced to `Slice[T]` at all. B-2026-08-05-40 (0949f9f) taught `coerce_to_slice` to rebuild a 2-word slice header from a PLACE argument, which is exactly this shape — but refused a `shared`/`par` receiver explicitly, on the correct reasoning that its slot holds a HANDLE rather than the aggregate. The refusal returns `None`, and the caller then forwards the raw 3-word `{ptr,len,cap}` against the 2-word formal, so LLVM verification hard-fails. Same structure as B-2026-08-05-41's codegen half: a fail-closed bail in a resolver whose caller treats `None` as "carry on with the old path" is not fail-closed. Here the outcome is at least LOUD (the program does not compile) rather than a silent miscompile.

(a) GATE BYPASS: the `SharedFieldNotMut` gate does not reach a `mut Slice[T]` formal. B-2026-08-05-41 closed the `mut ref T` spelling by keying on `borrow_context`, which `borrow_context_for_param` sets from `Type::Ref` / `Type::MutRef` only; a `mut Slice[T]` formal is a `Type::Slice` and carries no borrow context at all, so it never reaches the check. Confirmed adjacent and NOT bypassed: `zap(s: mut ref Vec[i64])` on the same immutable field IS refused, so this is specific to the Slice coercion, not a hole in the new gate.

The interpreter catches (a) at RUNTIME via `write_shared_struct_field` — defense in depth, the same guard B-2026-06-30-3 promoted to a compile error for the assignment spelling. So the surviving divergence is `karac check` reporting clean on a program the interpreter refuses.

NOT REACHABLE AS A SILENT MISCOMPILE TODAY, which is what keeps this at medium: leg (b) makes every program of this shape fail to BUILD, so the unsound write in (a) never reaches a binary. The exposure is `karac check` — and any tool built on it, including Mend — certifying a program that will not compile and that the interpreter rejects.

WHAT A FIX NEEDS:
  * `coerce_to_slice`'s place arm extended to a shared receiver, deriving the Vec header's address through the RC payload via `shared_gep_layout` — the same recipe B-2026-08-05-41's codegen half uses, so leg (b) compiles;
  * a mutability signal that survives to a `Type::Slice` formal, so leg (a) is refused at typecheck with the message the assignment spelling gets. `borrow_context` is the wrong channel for it, which is why B-2026-08-05-41 deliberately left this alone rather than papering it over.

Both legs must land together: fixing (b) alone would turn a loud compile failure into a silently-accepted unsound write, which is strictly worse than the status quo.

FIXED 2026-08-06 (28ceec6b). Both legs, in one commit, as this row required.

LEG (b), CODEGEN. `coerce_to_slice`'s place arm now resolves a `shared`/`par`
receiver through `shared_gep_layout` -- the funnel every other shared field
site uses -- and rebuilds the slice header exactly as the owned arm does. The
field-is-a-Vec test runs BEFORE any IR is emitted, so a declined field costs
nothing; the receiver re-compile is safe for the same reason B-2026-08-05-41's
is, `is_pure_field_chain` (an identifier or `self` root with FieldAccess hops,
no Index, so re-evaluating has no side effect).

A BONUS FELL OUT that this row under-stated: the READ-ONLY spelling was equally
broken. `fn total(s: Slice[i64])` given the same shared Vec field failed module
verification identically -- the gap was never limited to the mutating form, only
the soundness QUESTION was. Both build now.

LEG (a), TYPECHECK. The signal is a new `mut_through_param_arg`, set from
`param_mutates_through(param_ty)` -- `Type::MutRef(_) | Type::Slice { mutable:
true }` -- at the three call-argument sites that already set `borrow_context`,
and taken alongside it in `infer_field_access` so a nested read inside the same
argument does not inherit the write context.

WHY NOT `borrow_context`, confirming this row's own reading: that field's
contract is which UNION diagnostic applies (`E_UNION_BORROW_REQUIRES_UNSAFE` vs
the read-flavored one), and its doc records that `mut Slice[T]` deliberately
does NOT count there because the slice-assignment contract is write-only. Adding
the slice spelling to it would have changed union diagnostics to close a
shared-struct hole. The two questions are different and now have different
channels.

WHAT THE FIX IS REALLY ABOUT, and it is the same lesson a third time.
B-2026-06-30-3 gated the ASSIGNMENT spelling. B-2026-08-05-41 added the `mut
ref` spelling and its own comment named the flaw -- "the rule was enforced
against the spelling rather than against the operation" -- then keyed the fix on
`borrow_kind == Some("mut ref")`, which is a spelling. `mut Slice[T]` was the
next spelling. `param_mutates_through` asks the operation question once, and is
SHARED with `check_call_site_marker`'s `mut`-marker rule (which had computed the
identical predicate independently all along), so a fourth spelling would have to
be added to both rules at the same definition or to neither.

MEASURED, all three backends agreeing where they should:
  (b) legal   `shared struct H { mut v: Vec[i64] }` / `zap(s: mut Slice[i64])`
              check clean, interp 99, BUILD ok, AOT 99   (was: hard build fail)
  (a) unsound the same with `v` NOT declared mut
              refused at typecheck: "shared struct field 'H.v' is not declared
              mut" -- the identical message the assignment spelling gets
              (was: `karac check` reported All checks passed)

PROBES, each one variable away, all correct:
  * field at index 2 behind a SCALAR and another Vec -- AOT prints `7 1 99 98
    30`, byte-identical to the interpreter, so the header-shifted GEP is
    offset-correct where a plain-struct offset would have read a neighbour
  * a niche `Option[shared]` field PRECEDING the Vec -- also offset-correct
  * `self.v` inside a shared method
  * `par struct` with a read-only slice (a `par` struct cannot have a plain
    `mut` Vec field at all -- an unrelated pre-existing rule refuses it)
  * `mut ref Vec[i64]` on a non-mut shared field -- STILL gated, B-2026-08-05-41
    parity preserved
  * `ref Vec[i64]` read of a non-mut shared field -- NOT gated
  * bare `Slice[i64]` read of a non-mut shared field -- NOT gated, and now builds
  * a SCALAR field to `mut Slice[T]` -- clean type error, not a crash
  * a plain (non-shared) struct -- unchanged, B-2026-08-05-40 control
  * valgrind clean at -O2 AND -O0, output matching the interpreter

TESTS, six, and the split is the point. THREE WITNESSES proven RED against the
unfixed compiler: `shared_struct_non_mut_field_mut_slice_argument_rejected`
(leg a), `e2e_shared_struct_vec_field_coerces_to_slice` (leg b),
`asan_shared_struct_vec_field_slice_coercion_no_leak` (leg b memory, floored at
100 allocations). THREE CONTROLS green either way, which is what a control
should do: the legal program still typechecks, the read-only spelling still does
not gate, and the interpreter parity leg was correct all along -- that last one
is pinned precisely because the interpreter being right while codegen could not
build is what localized this row.

THE ASAN LEG GUARDS SOMETHING NEW, not a re-run of the value test: the slice
header points INTO the Vec buffer inside the shared node's RC box, so it must be
a pure BORROW -- neither making the callee an owner (freeing the box's buffer at
callee scope exit, leaving the reads after the call dangling) nor disarming the
node's own reclaim (one leaked buffer per iteration). Neither failure was
possible on the rvalue-copy path this replaces, and no earlier test can cover it
because no program of this shape could be built at all.

GATES: -O2 13,117 passed / 0 failed / 102 suites; -O0 `memory_sanitizer` failure
SET unchanged (generic_struct_heap_field_move_out,
nested_option_pattern_boxed_payload_lifecycle,
shared_payload_view_optres_field_call_arg_copy, tensor_lifecycle); fmt and
clippy --all-targets --features llvm clean.

title: A cast TO `char` inside an f-string hole is DROPPED by both compiled backends -- `println(f"{b as char}")` prints the integer codepoint (98) where the interpreter prints the glyph (b). Silent wrong answer on code the typechecker accepts; binding the cast to a `let` first is correct, so the bug is invisible in the obvious spelling. Every OTHER cast in the same position is honoured (300 as u8 -> 44, -1 as u8 -> 255, 2.9 as i64 -> 2), which localises it to codegen's `expr_is_char` -- a predicate with one arm per char-yielding form, where `Cast` had no arm.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: LeetCode #249 Group Shifted Strings, found by the kata's own
differential harness rather than by either solver. Both solvers were clean on
all four surfaces from the start; only `differential.kara` builds strings from
computed bytes, which is the shape that trips this.

HOW IT SURFACED, and why the harness is part of the bug-finding surface rather
than scaffolding: the generator emits random words one byte at a time --

    w.push_str(f"{(ch as u8) as char}");

-- so under the compiled backends every generated word became a run of DIGITS
instead of letters. The corpus was still self-consistent, so the differential's
own cross-check ("groupings disagree on 0 of 4000") stayed green; what gave it
away was the four-surface md5 check, and then the group COUNT: 6,135 groups
under `--interp` vs 13,217 under AOT over an identical 14,053 words.

REDUCTION, three lines, and the cast is dropped ONLY in interpolation:

    let n = 97i64; let b = n as u8;
    println(f"A:{b as char}");           // interp a  | JIT+AOT 98
    println(f"B:{(n as u8) as char}");   // interp a  | JIT+AOT 97
    let c = b as char; println(f"C:{c}");// interp a  | JIT+AOT a   <- correct

So the LET-BOUND spelling is right and the inline one is wrong, which is what
makes this dangerous: the author sees a working example next to a broken one and
has no reason to suspect the difference.

SCOPE, established by control rather than assumed -- every other cast in the
same position is honoured under AOT:

    f"{big as u8}"   300 -> 44    OK
    f"{neg as u8}"    -1 -> 255   OK
    f"{f as i64}"    2.9 -> 2     OK
    f"{b as char}"    98 -> 98    WRONG

That rules out "f-string lowering ignores casts" and points at char rendering
specifically.

ROOT CAUSE: `expr_is_char` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) decides whether an
f-string / println part renders as a glyph or as an integer. It matches one arm
per syntactic form that can YIELD a char -- CharLit, Identifier (via
var_type_names), Index (via the element TypeExpr), MethodCall (`clone`, the
ascii case-folds, `unwrap`/`expect` via recorded inner types) -- and had NO arm
for `ExprKind::Cast`. A cast is the most direct char-yielding form there is.

FOURTH INSTANCE OF ONE GAP, which is the part worth keeping. The function's own
comments already record this exact symptom twice for method-call results:
"without this last arm `println(b.get())` for `fn get(self) -> char` formats the
i32 scalar as its integer codepoint (77 instead of 'M')", and again for
`unwrap` ("90 instead of 'Z'"). Each was fixed by adding the one arm in front of
whoever hit it. B-2026-07-24-3 then made `u8 as char` LEGAL at typecheck without
teaching the renderer about it, which is what created this instance. The
durable repair is not another arm -- it is that this predicate is a
denylist-shaped allowlist, and every new char-producing form silently defaults
to the integer rendering. Filed as such; the arm is the fix that ships.

FIX: one `ExprKind::Cast { ty, .. }` arm matching a `char` target path.

TEST: `e2e_cast_to_char_in_fstring_renders_the_glyph` (tests/codegen.rs) asserts
the glyph for both the single and double-cast inline spellings, the let-bound
control, AND the three non-char casts. The non-char casts are controls, not
padding: a regression that re-broke every cast in interpolation would look
identical if only the char line were asserted. Stash-proven RED with the fix
reverted.

NOT A NEW SURFACE FOR run-vs-build: `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` (AOT)
agree with EACH OTHER and both differ from `--interp`, so this is a codegen
miscompile detected by the interpreter oracle, not a JIT/AOT split.

fix: 26b2176 (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs — the Map/Set arm in `zero_struct_field_move_cap`, plus the Sorted variants in `zero_struct_move_caps_mono`'s existing arm). Pins e2e_map_field_move_out_neutralizes_the_source, test_map_field_move_out_transfers_the_handle, asan_map_field_move_out_neutralizes_the_source.
title: a `Map`/`Set` field moved out INDIVIDUALLY left the source handle live, so the owner's struct drop freed storage the destination still owned — `fn take(h: MapH) -> Map[i64, String] { return h.m; }` SEGFAULTS on a use-after-free under AOT while the interpreter is correct; the WHOLE-struct move has nulled the handle since B-2026-07-15-23
detail:
SHAPE, concrete and non-generic — nothing about it is exotic:

    struct MapH { m: Map[i64, String] }
    fn take(h: MapH) -> Map[i64, String] { return h.m; }
    fn main() { … let h = MapH { m: mk(i) }; let m2 = take(h); println(m2.len()); … }

    AOT: Segmentation fault (exit 139). Interpreter: correct.
    valgrind: `Invalid read of size 8` in `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec`,
              address 16 bytes inside a 72-byte block already free'd by main.

MECHANISM, and the asymmetry IS the bug. `zero_struct_move_caps_mono` — the WHOLE-struct move neutralizer — has carried a Map/Set null-store since B-2026-07-15-23, with a comment spelling out exactly this hazard ('a whole-struct move or a struct-field move-out that leaves the SOURCE handle live double-frees the map storage'). The PER-FIELD neutralizer `zero_struct_field_move_cap` never got the same arm: it handles Vec/String (cap-zero), Option (tag), Result (payload area), enums and nested structs, and a Map field falls through its final `else` where both the `enum_layouts` and `struct_types` lookups miss. So the field stays live and `FieldDrop::MapOrSet` frees it.

THE FIX IS A PURE CODEGEN NULL-STORE, because the convention is already the runtime's: `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` early-returns on `map.is_null()`, and both half-walks (`emit_map_key_drop_fn_walk`, `emit_map_shared_half_rc_dec_walk`) null-guard internally. Exactly parallel to the Vec cap-zero beside it.

THREE MOVE-OUT SPELLINGS, all fixed and all tested, because they reach the neutralizer by different routes: returned out of a by-value param, bound to a local (`let m2 = h.m`), and passed to a consuming callee (`eat(h.m)`). TWO CONTROLS that were always correct and must stay so — a field only READ, and a whole-struct move (which retracts the source's entire StructDrop rather than neutralizing one field) — so an over-nulling fix turns them red.

title: shift by >= the bit width is UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR in AOT output — one `let` variable prints two different values in the same run and different values across runs (LLVM shl poison), the JIT disagrees again, and the interpreter raises a raw Rust panic; design.md's `"shift amount out of range"` trap is unimplemented at every width, and narrow `<<` additionally computes at i64 so an `i32` binding can hold 1048576000000
detail:
SHAPE, minimal, and the symptom is NOT a wrong constant — it is POISON:

    fn main() {
        let a: i64 = 1i64;
        let s: i64 = 64i64;
        let r: i64 = a << s;
        println(r);
        println(r);          // SAME variable, printed twice
        let t: i64 = a << s; // SAME expression again
        println(t);
    }

  AOT run 1:  94721897766304 / 0 / 0
  AOT run 2:  94357552725408 / 0 / 0      <- differs BETWEEN RUNS (ASLR-shaped)
  JIT:        0 / -9223372036854775808 / 1
  interp:     thread panicked at src/interpreter/eval_ops.rs:513:
              'attempt to shift left with overflow'

One `let`-bound variable prints two different values in consecutive `println`s
of the same run; the value changes between runs; the three backends disagree;
and the interpreter raises a raw Rust panic instead of a Kāra diagnostic. That
is LLVM `shl`/`ashr` poison (shift >= bit width is UB in LLVM IR, and codegen
emits the raw instruction) leaking into shipped binaries, plus an ICE on the
interpreter — which also violates the repo's own standard that every phase
emits a structured diagnostic and never just panics.

THE RULE IS SPECIFIED AND SIMPLY UNIMPLEMENTED. design.md line 2142: "Shift by
the bit width or more traps. `(x: i32) << 32` panics (`\"shift amount out of
range\"`); `(x: i32) << 31` is legal regardless of whether it flips the sign
bit. Same rule for `>>`." The string "shift amount out of range" does not
appear anywhere in src/ — grep returns nothing. There is no shift-amount check
on any surface at any width.

SECOND, SEPARATE DEFECT ON THE SAME OPERATOR — the narrow width is not
respected, so a narrow-typed binding can hold a value far outside its declared
range with no trap:

    let a: i32 = 1000000i32;
    let s: i32 = a << 20i32;
    println(s);                    // 1048576000000  -- an i32 binding
    println(s > 2147483647i32);    // true           -- typed i32, exceeds i32::MAX
    let u: u8 = 200u8; println(u << 4u8);   // 3200  -- a u8 holding 3200

All three surfaces agree with EACH OTHER here (no run/build divergence) and all
three disagree with the spec. design.md says `<<` is a bit shift at the
declared width — `(1i32) << 31` must be -2147483648 — and codegen instead
computes at i64 and hands back a value the declared type cannot represent.
Measured: `1i32 << 31` yields 2147483648 on interp, JIT and AOT alike.

CAUSE. `compile_narrow_int_binop` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) widens both
operands to i64, computes there, and range-checks ONLY the arithmetic set
`+ - * / %`. Its comment states the exclusion's premise outright -- "Bitwise /
shift results always fit the width (the operands do)" -- which is true for
`& | ^` and FALSE for `<<`. The interpreter mirrors the same split:
eval_ops.rs:513-514 are bare Rust `a << b` / `a >> b` on the i64 carrier, with
neither an amount check nor a `narrow_oob` call, while every arithmetic arm
beside them is `checked_*` + `narrow_oob`.

A THIRD, SMALLER SIBLING found by the same sweep: unary negation of a narrow
minimum does not trap. `let a: i32 = -2147483648i32; println(-a)` prints
2147483648 -- again an out-of-range i32 -- where the i64 equivalent DOES trap
`integer overflow` correctly. Same root: the narrow width is enforced on the
arithmetic binop set and nowhere else.

SEVERITY IS HIGH FOR THE FIRST DEFECT, on the UB alone. It is not merely a
wrong answer: the value is unstable within a single run and across runs, so any
program that shifts by a runtime amount which can reach the width has
nondeterministic behaviour that no test can pin. The narrow-width leg is the
milder half -- deterministic and consistent across backends, just wrong.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, and why it matters beyond correctness: while measuring
B-2026-08-05-38's remaining WIDENING half. That row proposes computing narrow
ops at the declared width instead of widening to i64, which is sound only if a
narrow-typed value always fits its declared width. It does not, and `<<` is why
-- so this row is a hard PREREQUISITE for B-2026-08-05-38's larger half, not
just a correctness item that happens to sit nearby.

INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENT of that half, taken while finding this (x86_64,
callgrind instruction slope over 20k vs 40k iters of kata #9's bench, sinks
verified identical across all three builds):

    i32, current lowering (checked)     1,210,924
    i32, all narrow checks elided       1,178,191   <- the 2.7% ceiling, reproduced exactly
    i64 working variables, same data    1,019,892   <- 1.187x FASTER than i32

The i64 build is equal-safety (its `+`/`*` still trap through the
`llvm.*.with.overflow.i64` intrinsics), takes identical inputs, and prints an
identical sink -- so the 191,032-instruction gap is the narrow lowering itself.
Only 32,733 of it (17%) is the range check; 83% is the widening. That
independently confirms B-2026-08-05-38's 79% figure from a different direction.

WHAT A FIX NEEDS:
  * a shift-amount check on BOTH surfaces at the operand's DECLARED width --
    trap `shift amount out of range` when the amount is negative or >= width,
    for `<<` and `>>` alike, at every width including i64/u64 (the poison leg);
  * narrow `<<` computed at the declared width so the result is representable,
    making `1i32 << 31 == -2147483648` per the spec;
  * narrow unary negation range-checked like the arithmetic binops;
  * the interpreter's raw `a << b` / `a >> b` replaced with the checked form,
    so a shift never raises a Rust panic in place of a Kāra diagnostic.

Once all three hold, "a narrow-typed value always fits its declared width"
becomes a real invariant, and B-2026-08-05-38's widening half can compute at
native width via `llvm.{s,u}{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow.iN`.

── FIXED, the two shift legs, at ee551b8 ─────────────────────────────

BOTH SHIFT LEGS ARE CLOSED and the row stays OPEN for the negation leg alone.

The amount check is ONE unsigned compare: a negative amount reinterpreted as
unsigned is enormous, so `icmp uge amount, bits` catches `< 0` and `>= bits`
together. `bits` is the DECLARED width — 32 for an i32, 64 for an i64 — which
is why narrow shifts are intercepted in `compile_narrow_int_binop` before the
generic dispatch, which would have compared against the i64 carrier's 64 and
let every narrow over-shift through.

Narrow `<<` is re-narrowed after the shift (mask, then sign-extend for a
signed type), which is what makes the result representable in the declared
type. `>>` needed only the amount check: its operand reaches the carrier
already sign- or zero-extended from the declared width, so an i64 shift
smears the correct bit and the re-narrowing is a no-op.

COST IS ZERO for a constant amount, verified by DISASSEMBLY rather than
assumed — a six-shift mix function compiles to bare `sar $0x21` / `sar $0x1d`
/ `sar $0x20`, with no guard in the loop and no trap block anywhere in the
binary; LLVM folds every constant-amount check. Kata #9's callgrind slope is
unchanged to the instruction (1,210,924 before and after). Only a runtime
amount pays a compare, and those are exactly the cases that were undefined.

WHAT IS LEFT — the narrow unary-negation leg, and why it was NOT fixed here.
`-(-2147483648i32)` still yields 2147483648, an out-of-range i32, where the
i64 equivalent traps `integer overflow` correctly. Both surfaces agree with
each other today. The interpreter side is a one-line `narrow_oob` call in
`eval_unary`'s Neg arm, but codegen's `compile_unaryop` receives only a value
— it has no declared width to check against, and the span-keyed maps at its
call site (`tensor_typed_exprs` / `column_typed_exprs`) do not carry integer
widths. Fixing only the cheap side would CREATE a run/build divergence where
none currently exists, which is strictly worse than a consistent wrong answer.
So the leg needs the width plumbed to `compile_unaryop` first, and both sides
must land together.

CONSEQUENCE FOR B-2026-08-05-38: the invariant "a narrow-typed value always
fits its declared width" now holds for every operator EXCEPT narrow negation.
That row's widening half is unblocked for the arithmetic and shift surface and
still needs the negation leg (or an explicit carve-out) to be sound in full.

── FIXED, the negation leg — the row's last open item ─────────────────

ALL THREE LEGS ARE NOW CLOSED. The shift legs went at ee551b8; this closes
narrow unary negation, so the invariant the row set out to establish — "a
narrow-typed value always fits its declared width" — holds for EVERY operator
with no carve-out. B-2026-08-05-38's widening half is unblocked in full.

THE PLUMBING THIS ROW SAID WAS NEEDED TURNED OUT NOT TO BE. The previous pass
recorded "codegen's `compile_unaryop` receives only a value — it has no
declared width to check against", and deferred on that basis. That framing was
looking at the wrong site. `-a` is already lowered by `rewrite_unary`
(src/lowering.rs) into `iN.neg(a)`, exactly as `a + b` becomes `iN.add(a, b)`,
so the assoc-call arm in src/codegen/assoc_call.rs ALREADY has the declared
width in hand as `type_name`. The check goes there. `compile_unaryop` never
needed to learn the width, and nothing was threaded through it.

Worth recording as a method note: the deferral was reasoned from the callee's
signature rather than from the lowered AST, and the lowering had already solved
the problem. Checking what the operator actually lowers to would have found
that immediately.

SHAPE: `emit_narrow_range_check(rv, bits, is_unsigned)` extracted verbatim out
of `compile_narrow_int_binop` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) and called from both
sites, so the negate and the binops emit the IDENTICAL trap rather than two
copies that can drift. Signed-only by construction — `rewrite_unary` gates
`Neg` to `Type::Int`, so a narrow UNSIGNED negate never reaches the arm.

INTERPRETER: one `narrow_oob` call added to `eval_unary`'s Neg arm
(src/interpreter/eval_ops.rs), matching the arithmetic arms directly beside it.
Both surfaces landed together, per this row's own requirement — fixing only the
interpreter would have created a run/build divergence where none existed.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT auto-par / AOT
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), trap and legal-boundary alike:

    let a: i32 = -2147483648i32; -a    ->  integer overflow   (was 2147483648)
    let a: i32 = -2147483647i32; -a    ->  2147483647         (unchanged)
    i8 / i16 minimums                  ->  integer overflow
    i64 minimum                        ->  integer overflow   (already correct)

COST IS ONE NEVER-TAKEN BRANCH, established by DISASSEMBLY rather than
assumed. A negate loop over an i32 compiles to `neg %r8d` / `jo` — LLVM folds
the i64-domain range check into the native 32-bit negate's own overflow flag,
so there is no compare-and-branch pair, just the `jo`. Same shape as the
checked arithmetic already emitted beside it.

TESTS, stash-proven RED against the unfixed compiler (3 of 4 fail without it;
the fourth pins the legal boundary, which was already correct, and guards
against OVER-trapping):
  * test_ir_narrow_negation_emits_range_check   (tests/codegen.rs) — IR-level,
    every narrow width, because the E2E twin can only prove the widths it names
  * e2e_narrow_negation_traps_at_declared_width (tests/codegen.rs)
  * e2e_narrow_negation_of_min_traps            (tests/codegen.rs)
  * test_narrow_negation_of_min_is_runtime_error   (tests/interpreter.rs)
  * test_narrow_negation_inside_range_is_legal     (tests/interpreter.rs)

The E2E trap fixture seeds its operand from `env.args().len()` rather than
writing `-2147483648i32` directly: a constant operand lets the optimizer fold
the check away, and the fixture would then pass without exercising the guard
that actually ships — B-2026-08-04-17's vacuity hazard applied to a trap test.

FOUND WHILE WRITING THE i64 CONTROL, filed separately as B-2026-08-06-13:
`i64::MIN` cannot be written as a literal in ANY spelling (all four probed),
because a negative literal is `Neg(Integer(n))` and 9223372036854775808 does
not fit the i64 the lexer validates against. The interpreter test builds it as
`-9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64` and says why inline.

GATES: fmt clean, clippy clean, interpreter 1461/0, codegen 2822/0,
typechecker 2144/0.
