title: a generic wrapper's bare `T` field bound to a SHARED struct leaks 2,560 B / 80 blocks at -O0 (clean at -O2): `Box[T]` at `T = Node` where `Node` is a `shared struct` -- the third head the bare-param rescue loop does not recognise, after String/Vec (fixed B-2026-07-15-11) and Map/Set (fixed B-2026-08-06-1)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found as a WIDENING CONTROL while fixing B-2026-08-06-1, not as a
regression from it. Measured byte-identical before and after that change, which
is what makes it a separate row rather than a loose end of that one.

REPRO, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 karac build`, under valgrind:

    shared struct Node { s: String }
    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    fn sink(b: Box[Node]) -> i64 { let n = b.v; return n.s.len(); }
    fn main() {
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 40 {
            let b = Box { v: Node { s: f"shrv-{i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer" } };
            let c = b;
            acc = acc + sink(c);
            let b2 = Box { v: Node { s: f"shrv-{i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer" } };
            let n2 = b2.v;
            acc = acc + n2.s.len();
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> prints 3660 (correct, and matching the interpreter), 2,560 bytes direct
       in 80 blocks + 3,660 indirect in 80 blocks definitely lost, 2 valgrind
       errors. CLEAN at the default -O2 — the usual -O0-only signature for this
       family: at -O2 the rc box is provably dead and LLVM deletes the
       allocation along with the evidence. The leak is in the emitted code
       either way.

MECHANISM, by analogy rather than by instrumentation — stated as the hypothesis
it is. The bare-generic-param rescue loop in `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`
resolves the declared `T` through the struct subst and promotes the result to a
`FieldDrop`. It knows String/Vec/VecDeque (B-2026-07-15-11) and, since
B-2026-08-06-1, Map/Set. A `shared` head matches neither, so the field is
classified no-heap and its rc handle is never dec'd — exactly the shape of the
two rows before it. The 80 blocks over 40 rounds (two per round: the rc box and
its String) fit the two shared handles the fixture creates per iteration.

WHY LOW AND NOT MEDIUM, unlike its two predecessors: it is -O0-only, so a
default `karac build` is unaffected today. That is a statement about the
optimizer, not about the emitted code — any change that makes the handle
observable at -O2 promotes this to the severity the Map row carried.

THE FIX IS NOT SIMPLY ONE MORE ARM, which is why this is filed rather than
folded into B-2026-08-06-1. Adding a `shared` promotion to the rescue loop
without the matching neutralizer arms is exactly the trade that row proved turns
a leak into a double free. `zero_struct_move_caps_mono` DOES already have a
`shared_types` arm (B-2026-07-28-9), and B-2026-08-06-1's head resolution now
makes it reachable for a bare param, so the whole-struct-move side may already
be covered — but `zero_struct_field_move_cap`'s corresponding path and the
rc-inc side of the entry copy both need checking first. Establish the
neutralizer coverage BEFORE adding the promotion, in that order, the way
B-2026-08-06-1 eventually had to.

FIXED 2026-08-06 (0928227). The row's instruction — establish the neutralizer
coverage BEFORE adding the promotion — was the right order, and following it
changed the diagnosis: the defect is NOT one more arm in the drop classifier's
rescue loop, which is where this row pointed.

The gate is `track_struct_var_inst`, which decides whether a struct local gets
the COMBINED drop (value drop + shared-field rc-dec walker) or the value drop
alone. It asked the NAME-ONLY `struct_owns_shared_field`, which reads DECLARED
field types, so `Box[T] { v: T }` at `T = Node` answered `false` and nothing
ever rc-dec'd the box. Confirmed by instrumenting the gate rather than reasoning
about it (the B-2026-08-06-1 lesson, applied first this time): the concrete
`Holder` printed `owns_shared=true`, the generic `Box` printed `owns_shared=false`.

Three sites had to learn the instantiation together, since a drop that dec's a
field the walker cannot see is just a differently-shaped bug:
  (1) `struct_owns_shared_field_subst` — the gate;
  (2) `emit_nested_struct_shared_rc_decs_ex_mono` — the walker, whose every arm
      (direct `shared`, `Option[shared]`, `Vec[shared]`, nested-struct
      recursion) keyed off the erased `T`;
  (3) `emit_vec_elem_struct_with_shared_drop_fn_mono` — the combined drop, whose
      symbol needed mono-suffixing (`Box[Node]` and `Box[Other]` are different
      drops on one cached name) and whose VALUE half would otherwise revert to
      the name-keyed drop and lose B-2026-08-06-1's field frees.

THE PREDICTED TRADE HAPPENED TWICE, and both were fixed by neutralizing the
SOURCE rather than inc'ing the copy — which is what the rc-dec walker's existing
`build_is_null` guard was already built to expect:
  * `zero_struct_field_move_cap` gained a `shared` arm, the peer of the Map/Set
    null-store. Chosen over inc'ing the returned alias because an inc has to be
    threaded onto BOTH the explicit-return and tail paths — they diverge,
    `compile_tail_final_expr` is only reached from `return` when the fn returns
    `Option[shared]` — and an over-inc is a silent leak. Attempted the inc route
    first and abandoned it: instrumentation showed the helper was never reached
    for either spelling.
  * `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` gained a FieldAccess arm. It neutralized an
    Identifier tail and fell through on a FIELD tail, while its function-body
    sibling `suppress_cleanup_for_tail_return` hands any shape to the same
    suppressor.

THAT SECOND ARM FIXES A PRE-EXISTING BUG WITH NO GENERICS IN IT:
`let x = { let h = Holder { .. }; h.v }` printed 0 instead of 38 on a DEFAULT
-O2 build with 160 valgrind errors. It was latent for the buffer types (a
moved-out Vec/String tail escapes through its own value copy — the same shape
spelled with a String field is clean at HEAD) and became observable only once an
rc handle, which has no such copy, could reach that path. Found because the fix
routed the generic spelling onto it and turned a correct-but-leaking program
into a wrong answer — i.e. the regression check found someone else's bug.

MEASURED over 24 probe programs at -O2 AND -O0, each cross-checked against the
interpreter. Fixed: move-out from a by-value param, from a plain local, a
whole-struct move, a `ref`-param read, the MID field of a multi-field wrapper,
the field returned out of a by-value param, a consuming callee, the never-moved
control, and the block-tail escape in BOTH spellings. Unchanged controls:
String / Vec[shared] / Option[shared] / Map instantiations of the same wrapper,
and every concrete-spelling shape.

TWO RESIDUALS, measured byte-identical before and after and filed rather than
folded in — neither is generic-specific and neither regressed:
  * B-2026-08-06-14 — a shared field RETURNED out of a by-value param is a
    use-after-free in the CONCRETE path at -O2 (still open; the generic
    spelling is clean because the null-store arm reaches its move site).
  * B-2026-08-06-15 — a shared handle escaping a value-position block is never
    dec'd by its consumer binding: 64 B / 2 blocks at -O0, BOTH spellings.
    This row's block-tail arm fixed the use-after-free half of that shape and
    left the leak half.

TESTS: asan_bare_generic_param_shared_field_is_rc_dec_and_neutralized
(memory_sanitizer), e2e_shared_field_moved_out_of_a_value_block_survives_the_frame_drain
(codegen), test_bare_generic_param_shared_field_transfers_the_handle
(interpreter, the oracle). Both codegen tests are STASH-PROVEN RED against the
half each can observe: the ASAN twin fails at HEAD with `LeakSanitizer: 15870
byte(s) leaked in 398 allocation(s)`, the E2E with `left: "114", right: "152"` —
a WRONG ANSWER, which is why an E2E earns its place beside a leak fixture.

TEST-INFRA NOTE worth carrying forward: the ASAN fixture first tripped the
B-2026-08-04-17 vacuity floor at 48 allocations, because its reads were
`.len()`-only and LLVM folded the payloads away at the default -O2. Adding
byte-level `contains` reads took it to 526. A shared-box fixture needs its
PAYLOAD read, not its length — the box surviving is not the same as the box
being observable.

title: TWO shapes where a heap-BOXED enum payload loses its owner AT A CALL BOUNDARY: (A) [FIXED] a NAMED `Option` binding passed by value has its let-site box drop disarmed by the call site's move-zeroing while the callee's param takes nothing over; (B) [FIXED] a fresh-temp user ENUM passed by value never registered `track_enum_var` at all, because the registrar's gate asked `enum_has_heap_payload` rather than whether the drop switch does any work. 320 B / 10 each
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: both were caught as CONTROLS in the new fixtures written for
B-2026-08-05-7's boxed-payload slice, and both measure IDENTICALLY before and
after that change (320 B / 10 blocks at HEAD and at the fix) -- which is what
makes them a separate row rather than a regression from it. The controls are
kept in those fixtures' doc comments as deliberately-not-covered rather than
deleted, so the gap stays visible where the next reader will be.

LEG A -- a NAMED `Option` binding passed BY VALUE. Reduction, 10 iterations,
KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0:

    fn classify(v: Option[Option[i64]]) -> i64 {
        match v {
            Option.Some(Option.Some(x)) => x,
            Option.Some(Option.None) => -1,
            Option.None => -2,
        }

registration, which is the current behaviour.

of this shape came from `tests/codegen.rs`'s `ir_for`, which calls
`compile_to_ir(program, None, None)` -- ownership is `None`. Every
ownership-derived decision differs from what `karac build` and the ASAN harness
compile, and that IR showed the tag zeroing in BOTH variants with nothing
freeing the box in either, which is consistent with neither measurement. The
`ir_probe_from_env` helper added alongside this entry runs the full pipeline
(desugar, gated-stdlib expansion, resolve, typecheck, lower, ownershipcheck)
and passes ownership in, so what it prints is what runs. Do not read a
drop-ownership question out of `ir_for`.

FIXED. Three sites, and they only work as a set -- each one alone turns the
leak into a different bug, which is why the row's own "measure before fixing"
note was worth following.

  (1) CALLER stays armed. `place_optres_field_move_info_ex`'s whole-move
      admission test now refuses a heap-BOXED `Option` payload, so
      `suppress_place_optres_field_whole_move_source` no longer zeroes the tag
      at a by-value call argument. The premise it was written under -- the
      consumer registers its own free -- is true for the INLINE classes and
      false here: no parameter registers a box drop (caller-retains), and the
      arm binding is a deboxed copy that deliberately registers none either.
  (2) CALLEE mirrors its move-out THROUGH the box. `deboxed_payload_box_ptrs`
      (slot -> box pointer, recorded at the four `reconstruct_payload_value`
      bind sites) lets both move-out neutralizers in
      `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` repeat their zero into the box:
      `zero_struct_field_move_cap_inst` for `x.label`, `zero_struct_move_caps_mono`
      for a whole-payload `x`. Without this, (1) alone is a DOUBLE FREE -- the
      row predicted exactly that, and the prediction held: `Some(x) => x` went
      from a 256 B leak to an ASAN abort with (1) in place and (2) missing.
  (3) The SHARED-VIEW arg clone gets an owner. B-2026-07-28-17 hands the callee
      a private `karac_clone_Option_H` copy when the source is a payload view
      into an RC node, on the same "the callee frees it" premise -- true for its
      inline payload, false for a boxed one. `clone_shared_view_optres_field_arg`
      now registers a caller-scope `BoxedEnumDrop` for the clone when the payload
      is boxed. This was NOT visible in the reduction; it is what the original
      fixture's remaining 64 B / 2 turned out to be after (1) and (2) landed, so
      the reduced probes and the real fixture were measuring two different
      allocations that happened to be the same size.

SCOPE OF (2), stated because it writes into storage the callee does not own:
registration is gated on `pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`, i.e. only
when the box's owner is the CALLER. Every in-frame boxed view is left
byte-identical, which preserves B-2026-08-04-2's deliberate choice to retract
the `BoxedEnumDrop`'s inner walk rather than zero the box's words -- it found
that zeroing them made a user Drop body print an empty string, trading a double
free for a silent wrong value. Across a call there is no action to retract (the
owner is a synthesized drop fn reading DATA), so a data write is the only
channel, and the gate keeps the two techniques from colliding.

MEASURED, 10 iterations each at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, over the row's own four
probes plus two the fix required:

  f1/f7  callee returns `x.k`   (scalar)         CLEAN before, CLEAN after
  f8/f5  callee returns `x.label` (field move)   256 B / 8  ->  0
  f9     callee returns `x` (whole move)         256 B / 8  ->  0
  fx     the original fixture (shared view)      64 B / 2   ->  0

and every one prints its expected total, so this is not a leak traded for a
wrong value.

WHAT THE ROW GOT RIGHT, worth keeping: the recorded mechanism -- caller disarms,
callee writes only to its private copy, naive fix double-frees -- was accurate in
every particular, and the fix is the one it prescribed. It came from IR dumped
through the full pipeline with ownership passed in; the earlier `ir_for` dump
(ownership `None`) had shown the tag zeroing in BOTH variants and would have sent
this somewhere else. The probe helper that produced the good dump is
`codegen_tests::ir_probe_from_env`.

WHAT IT DID NOT SEE: shape (3). The reduction isolated the leak to one variable
(the callee's arm) and was right about that variable, but the ORIGINAL fixture
carried a second, independent leak of the same size behind it. Two 32-byte boxes
are indistinguishable in a total, and "the fixture still leaks 64 B" after a
correct fix reads exactly like "the fix did not work". The general lesson is the
row's own, one level up: a reduction proves what it varies, and re-running the
UNREDUCED fixture is what proves the rest.

title: an owned boxed-payload enum param that ESCAPES -- returned, or forwarded to another by-value param -- is freed by the callee anyway: `fn id(o: Opt[String]) -> Opt[String] { o }` aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` at the DEFAULT -O2, and the forwarding form SIGSEGVs at -O0
detail:
Split out of B-2026-08-05-7 rather than reopening it: that row was closed
(70c15e83 + b359f437) after its last quarantine entry cleared, and this is a
distinct defect in one of the mechanisms it added, still live at de6dfe49.

    enum Opt[T] { Yes(T), No }
    fn get(o: Opt[String], d: i64) -> i64 { match o { Opt.Yes(s) => s.len(), Opt.No => d } }
    fn ident(o: Opt[String]) -> Opt[String] { o }          // returns the box
    fn fwd(o: Opt[String]) -> i64 { get(o, -1) }           // forwards the box

  ident  -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2, at -O2 AND -O0
  fwd    -> freed by both callees, then SIGSEGV (exit 139) at -O0
  get    -> correct, and must stay so: this is the shape the drop is FOR

`Opt[String]` packs a 3-word payload into the erased 1-word area, so
`coerce_to_payload_words` heap-boxes it and the owned-param registration
(compile_function + compile_mono_function) queues a scope-exit `BoxedEnumDrop`.
It queued one for EVERY owned param, including the two above that hand the box
on to someone else.

NOT MASKED AT -O2, unlike most of B-2026-08-05-7's population. The box is live
memory whichever way the pass pipeline goes, so there is no dead allocation for
LLVM to delete and no second free of something that never happened -- the
ordinary `karac build` aborts. That also makes it cheap to gate: a plain
codegen E2E catches it, no ASAN needed
(`e2e_boxed_enum_param_escape_no_double_free`, asserted strictly so an abort
cannot pass as a skip).

FIX: gate the registration on `crate::result_escape::nonescaping_param_names`
-- the escape walk the `Result[shared]` param arm has run since B-2026-07-12-24,
type-agnostic despite its Result-shaped name (a param qualifies when every use
is a match/if-let scrutinee, or it is unused). A forwarded or returned param
falls out and stays unregistered, so the terminal consumer's free remains the
only one and the chain self-balances with no call-site suppression -- exactly
the argument that arm already makes for its own case. The mono site computes
the set locally rather than reading the shared field: a mono body is compiled
INLINE inside its caller's, so that field still holds the CALLER's set there.

SECOND-OWNER HAZARD, measured while fixing this and worth recording because it
is the same trap from the other side. A non-generic enum whose payload is
itself an enum (`enum W { X(Option[String]), Empty }`) boxes too -- the payload
gets a 1-word carve-out instead of being sized to the variant -- and
`user_enum_boxed_payload_variants` skips it, so registering it at the param
looks like the obvious matching fix. It is not: 70c15e83 already owns that box
at CONSTRUCTION, and the param registration makes a second owner that
double-frees as soon as the value arrives from a struct field
(`let h = Holder { o: W.X(Some(s)), n: 1 }; consume(h.o)`, -O0).
`asan_nongeneric_enum_nested_enum_payload_box_no_leak` pins both directions --
red for a second owner as surely as for none -- with a 6-word struct payload
arm alongside for the third edge (area 6, no box, must stay unregistered or the
drop frees a word that was never a pointer).

tracker: ROOT CAUSE IS DEEPER THAN THE SPAN CLOBBER — see the ATTEMPTED FIX section. `impl[T] Box[T]` methods are declared ONCE at the erased layout (`@Box.take({ i64 }) -> i64`), so they are not monomorphized per instantiation the way `fn take[T]` free functions are. The span-clobbered literal layout (src/codegen/types_lowering.rs::struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr) is only the first of two mismatches.
title: a GENERIC struct LITERAL used directly as a METHOD RECEIVER cannot be built: `Box { v: <String> }.take()` passes `karac check`, runs correctly under the interpreter, and then fails `karac build` with an LLVM verifier error -- the literal lowers at the ERASED base layout `{ i64 }` because the outer method call's span CLOBBERS the literal's instantiation record
detail:
SHAPE, minimal and complete:

    struct Box[T] { v: T }
    impl[T] Box[T] { fn take(self) -> T { self.v } }
    fn main() {
        let n: i64 = env.args().len();
        println(Box { v: "payload-past-inline-width-here".repeat(n) }.take().len());
    }

    karac check          -> All checks passed.
    karac run --interp   -> 30            (correct)
    karac build          -> error: codegen failed: Module verification failed:
                            "Invalid InsertValueInst operands!
                               %field = insertvalue { i64 } undef,
                                        { ptr, i64, i64 } %rep.load, 0"

So it is a LOUD failure, not a miscompile, and the workaround is one line
(bind the literal to a local first). That is why this is medium and not high.

ISOLATION -- six variants, each one condition away from the failing one:

    named receiver   `let b = Box { .. }; b.take()`        check ok  interp 30  AOT 30
    LITERAL receiver `Box { .. }.take()`                   check ok  interp 30  AOT FAIL
    literal receiver, field is i64                         check ok  interp 1   AOT 1
    literal receiver, NON-generic struct                   check ok  interp 30  AOT 30
    literal receiver, `ref self`, body ignores the field   check ok  interp 7   AOT FAIL
    same literal as a FREE-FN ARGUMENT `take(Box { .. })`  check ok  interp 30  AOT 30

It needs exactly two conditions -- a GENERIC struct, and a literal in RECEIVER
position with a WIDE instantiated field. It does NOT depend on the self mode
(`self` and `ref self` both fail) nor on the method body touching the field at
all (the `ref self` variant returns a constant 7 and still fails).

MECHANISM, MEASURED rather than inferred. Instrumenting
`struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr`'s span lookup on the two literals that differ
only in position:

    free-fn arg (BUILDS)     span=(122,53)   rec=Some("Box[1 args]")
    method receiver (FAILS)  span=(131,53)   rec=None

Same literal, same length. In the receiver case the record is not WRONG, it is
ABSENT. The chain:

  1. the parser gives a `MethodCall` its RECEIVER's span (the same defect
     B-2026-08-05-28 hit from another direction), so the literal and the call
     share one `expr_types` key;
  2. the method call's type wins that key -- here `i64`, from `.len()`;
  3. lowering.rs builds `enum_inst_type_exprs` by filtering `tc.expr_types` for
     `Named { args } if !args.is_empty()`. A primitive `i64` is not `Named`, so
     the entry is DROPPED ENTIRELY rather than overwritten with something
     wrong;
  4. `struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr` finds nothing, `mono_struct_type_from_
     active_subst` also returns None (there is no active monomorph subst -- we
     are in `main`), so `compile_struct_init` falls back to the pre-built
     all-i64 base layout `{ i64 }`;
  5. inserting a `{ptr,i64,i64}` String into `{ i64 }` fails LLVM verification.

EVERY VARIANT FOLLOWS FROM THAT, which is what makes the mechanism credible:
  * named receiver -- the literal is a `let` RHS with its own uncontested span,
    so the record survives;
  * i64 field -- the erased base layout is COINCIDENTALLY correct at `T = i64`,
    so the missing record costs nothing;
  * non-generic struct -- no instantiation is needed at all;
  * free-fn argument -- the `Call` node has its own span, so no clobber.

AND A THIRD, PREDICTED-THEN-CONFIRMED CASE. If the method returns a type that
IS `Named`-with-args, step 3 no longer drops the entry -- it overwrites it with
the RETURN type. Probed with `fn one(self) -> Vec[T]`: the record then holds
`Vec[String]`, `mono_struct_type("Vec", ..)` returns None because `Vec` is not
a user struct, and the build fails the same way. So the failure survives both
branches of the filter; a surviving entry just fails one step later.

RELATED, SEEN WHILE PROBING, NOT PART OF THIS ROW:
  * `impl[T] Box[T] { fn id(self) -> Box[T] { self } }` -- returning `self`
    from a generic impl is rejected at TYPECHECK with
    "expected 'Box<T>', found 'Box'" (note the `<T>` spelling in a language
    whose generics are `[T]`). Separate surface, not filed yet.
  * the same chained-receiver shape with the literal returning `Box[T]` fails
    AOT differently -- "codegen: cannot resolve field 'v' on this receiver
    (its type was not ...)" -- consistent with the same span clobber losing the
    chain's type, but not separately isolated.

FIX DIRECTION, in increasing order of blast radius:
  1. give the struct-literal path a span-INDEPENDENT way to recover its
     instantiation. The field-init expressions are sub-expressions with their
     OWN uncontested spans, and their types bind the struct's type params
     directly -- this is the same move that closed B-2026-08-05-28 (add a
     span-free signal rather than fight the clobber);
  2. record struct-literal instantiations in a table written ONLY from
     `StructLiteral` nodes, so a method call cannot clobber it (mirrors the
     existing `concrete_named_type_exprs` complement);
  3. give `MethodCall` its own span in the parser. That is the real defect, and
     it has now produced two rows; but many span-keyed tables are calibrated to
     today's behaviour, so it is not a contained change.

METHOD NOTE. The first detector tried here counted `movslq` in the disassembly
as a proxy for a different question and was WRONG -- those were jump tables in
inlined `println` machinery. Caught before it reached a claim, unlike the two
false controls on B-2026-08-06-2. The instrumented span dump above is the
evidence this row rests on; nothing here is read off a proxy.

── ATTEMPTED FIX, REVERTED — AND IT RESIZED THE ROW (same session) ──

Fix direction 1 was implemented and MEASURED, then reverted unlanded. What it
found is worth more than the patch was.

WHAT WAS BUILT: a span-free fallback in `struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr` that
recovers a generic struct literal's instantiation from its OWN FIELD
EXPRESSIONS (which are sub-expressions with uncontested spans) when the
span-keyed record is missing or unusable. Fail-closed at every step: struct
literals only, no spread, only a field whose DECLARED type is exactly a bare
generic param, every param must bind to a non-empty name.

FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WRONG, and the reason generalizes: it used
`infer_arg_elem_te` alone, which resolves an identifier or a literal but yields
an EMPTY name for a METHOD CALL. `Box { v: "…".repeat(n) }` — a fresh heap
value built inline — is precisely the shape the fallback exists for, so the
helper returned None on every case it was written to fix. Instrumented output:
`DBG slmt struct=Box param=T inferred=""`. A chain
(`enum_inst_type_exprs` -> `concrete_named_type_exprs` -> `string_typed_exprs`
-> `infer_arg_elem_te`) resolves it.

WITH THAT IN PLACE THE LITERAL LOWERS CORRECTLY — and the build STILL fails,
one step later:

    Call parameter type does not match function signature!
      %__urecv_tmp_1 = load { { ptr, i64, i64 } }, ptr %__urecv_tmp
      %call = call i64 @Box.take({ { ptr, i64, i64 } } %__urecv_tmp_1)
                        ^ callee declared { i64 } -> i64

So the receiver aggregate is now right and the CALLEE is wrong: `@Box.take` is
emitted ONCE, at the ERASED base layout, for every instantiation. An
`impl[T] Box[T]` method is NOT monomorphized the way a `fn take[T]` free
function is — which is also why the free-function form (v6) was clean all
along, and why the row's isolation table shows every failing variant going
through an impl-block method.

CONSEQUENCE — SEVERITY medium -> high. The row was filed as a span-keyed
lookup gap with a one-line workaround. It is actually a MISSING
MONOMORPHIZATION for generic impl-block methods, of which the span clobber is
a downstream symptom. The workaround (bind the literal to a local) works only
because that path happens to keep both sides consistently erased; it is not
evidence the layout is right.

WHY IT WAS REVERTED RATHER THAN LANDED: the patch makes NO currently-failing
program build correctly. It fixes exactly one probe variant — a `ref self`
method whose body ignores the field and returns a constant — which proves
nothing about layout correctness, and converts the other three shapes from one
LLVM verifier error into a different one. Landing that would add code and
change an error message without moving any program from broken to working.

WHAT THE NEXT ATTEMPT SHOULD START FROM, so the measurement is not redone:
  * the literal-side fallback is a REAL and separable piece and is known to
    work (the receiver aggregate is correctly shaped with it in place); it is
    just not sufficient alone. It is worth re-landing TOGETHER with the callee
    side, not before it.
  * the callee side is the actual work: `impl[T] S[T]` methods need
    per-instantiation monomorphs, keyed and mangled like `compile_generic_call`
    does for free functions.
  * verify with the six-variant table in this row, and treat the `ref self`
    variant as a NON-oracle — its body must be changed to read the field
    before it proves anything.

── FIXED bbb6a9bf — AND THE ROW'S RECORDED DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG ──

The re-classification above ("a MISSING MONOMORPHIZATION for generic impl-block
methods") does not survive measurement. `impl[T] S[T]` methods ARE
monomorphized: a program using `Box[String]` and `Box[i64]` through NAMED
receivers emits `Box.take$i64` AND `Box.take$struct` and runs correctly, and two
instantiations coexist with no mangle collision. The single erased emission the
previous attempt saw was a SYMPTOM of the lost span record, not a separate gap
— with the record restored the failing case emits
`Box.take$struct$T_ct_String` and calls it.

WHY THE PREVIOUS ATTEMPT STALLED, which the note above got right in substance:
TWO consumers read the one missing record, and it only fixed the first.

  1. the literal's own layout, via `struct_inst_mono_type_for_expr`, which fell
     back to the pre-built erased base layout `{ i64 }`;
  2. the CALLEE selection. `materialize_user_method_receiver` spills a
     non-identifier receiver into a synth local and re-enters dispatch with an
     Identifier; the generic-method mono arm then reads `enum_inst_var_types`
     to pick the monomorph. Only `var_type_names` was seeded, so it saw a bare
     `Box`. `let b = Box { .. }; b.take()` works purely because the let-site
     seeds that same record (stmts.rs).

Fix either alone and the verifier error just moves — a correctly shaped
`{ { ptr, i64, i64 } }` receiver handed to a callee still declared `{ i64 }`,
which is exactly the second error the previous attempt hit and read as a
missing monomorph. Both sites now recover from the literal's own FIELD
INITIALIZERS, which are sub-expressions with uncontested spans.

Fail-closed, because a WRONG instantiation silently lowers a struct at another
type's layout and is worse than none: struct literals only, no spread, the
struct must be generic, EVERY param must be pinned by a field whose DECLARED
type is exactly that bare param, and every recovered argument must carry a
non-empty type name. A param reachable only through a container field
(`xs: Vec[T]`) is left to the annotation path (B-2026-07-11-31).

Verified against this row's six-variant table plus the `Pair`/second-field and
`ref self` shapes: all build and match the interpreter.
`e2e_generic_struct_literal_as_method_receiver` carries the table and is red
against the pre-fix compiler.

TWO SHAPES FOUND WHILE ISOLATING, SPLIT OUT RATHER THAN FOLDED IN — this row
has already had one attempt reverted for reaching past its evidence:
  * B-2026-08-06-19 — a chained field access on a generic method's RETURN
    (`w.take().f`) fails where `let x = w.take(); x.f` builds. Same span
    clobber, different consumer.
  * B-2026-08-06-20 — two instantiations of one generic struct reached through a
    MIX of literal and named receivers collide on the unmangled
    `@Type.method` slot. Reproduces identically WITHOUT this change.

title: `i64::MIN` cannot be WRITTEN as a literal in any spelling -- `-9223372036854775808i64` is a parse error (`Invalid integer literal`), because a negative literal parses as `Neg(Integer(n))` and the POSITIVE half must fit i64, which i64::MIN's does not. The value is reachable only by arithmetic (`-9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64`). Same argument applies to every width's minimum, but only i64 is actually unreachable: a narrow minimum's positive half still fits the i64 carrier.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while writing the i64 CONTROL case for B-2026-08-06-7's
narrow-negation regression test -- the test wanted `-9223372036854775808i64`
as the operand that already trapped correctly, and it would not parse.

MEASURED, all four spellings, `karac run --interp`:

    let a: i64 = -9223372036854775808i64;     parse error at the literal
    let a: i64 = -9223372036854775808;        parse error
    let a = -9223372036854775808i64;          parse error
    let a: i64 = (-9223372036854775808i64);   parse error

Every one reports `Expected expression, found Error("Invalid integer literal")`
with the column on the literal, so this is the LEXER rejecting the digits
before the parser ever sees the unary minus.

MECHANISM, and it is the same design note codegen already documents. A negative
literal is `Neg(Integer(n))` with `n` POSITIVE -- src/codegen/exprs.rs says so
explicitly ("Negative integer literals parse as `Neg(Integer(n))` and the
typechecker range-validates them as a UNIT"). That constant-folds correctly for
every value whose positive half is representable. i64::MIN is the one value
where it is not: 9223372036854775808 > i64::MAX, so the lexer rejects it as an
invalid i64 literal and the fold never happens.

WHY ONLY i64. A narrow minimum survives because the positive half is checked
against the i64 CARRIER, not the declared width -- `-2147483648i32` parses
fine (2147483648 fits i64) and the typechecker validates the negated unit
against i32. Only at the carrier's own width does the positive half run out of
room. u64::MAX is unaffected (no sign, fits the unsigned range).

SEVERITY LOW, deliberately. It is a write-ability gap, not a wrong answer:
nothing miscompiles, and the value is reachable as `-9223372036854775807i64 -
1i64` (which does NOT trap -- the result is representable). The cost is that
the most natural spelling of a common constant is a parse error, and the
message ("Invalid integer literal") does not hint at the workaround.

SHAPE OF A FIX, not attempted here: either lex the digit string into a u64 and
let the parser fold `Neg` before range-validating (so the UNIT is checked, as
the typechecker already claims to do), or special-case the exact i64::MIN
magnitude when it is immediately preceded by unary minus. The first is the
principled one and matches how Rust resolves the same problem.

WORKAROUND for anyone hitting it today: `-9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64`.
B-2026-08-06-7's interpreter regression test uses exactly that and says why.

── CORRECTION, before the fix notes: THIS ROW OVERSTATED THE IMPACT ───

The title says the value "is reachable only by arithmetic
(`-9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64`)". THAT IS WRONG, and it was wrong when
filed. `i64.MIN` is an existing primitive const and has been all along —
`tests/interpreter.rs::test_interp_primitive_const_i64_min` pins it, and it
was verified again here on interp and JIT (`let x = i64.MIN` prints
-9223372036854775808 on both). `u64.MAX` works the same way.

Found while writing this row's own regression test, by noticing the
neighbouring pre-existing test. The error came from probing four LITERAL
spellings, concluding "unwritable", and generalising that to "unreachable"
without checking the const surface at all.

What survives the correction: writing the literal — the spelling every other
language accepts and the one a reader reaches for first — was a parse error,
which is a real gap worth closing. What does NOT survive: any suggestion the
value was inaccessible. Severity stays LOW; the justification for LOW is now
"a workaround existed and was idiomatic", not "you had to compute it".

── FIXED ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MECHANISM. The lexer parsed the digit string straight into i64 and rejected
anything that did not fit, so the magnitude never reached a place that could
decide what to do with it. It now hands an out-of-i64-range magnitude up as
`Token::IntegerOutOfRange(u64, suffix)` (all four radix paths — decimal, hex,
binary, octal), and the PARSER decides.

WHY THE PARSER AND NOT THE LEXER, which is the whole design point: the lexer
cannot tell a unary minus from a binary one. `x - 9223372036854775808i64` and
`-9223372036854775808i64` differ only in context, and folding the sign in the
lexer would silently turn the first into `x + 2^63`. The parser knows, because
it is holding the `Token::Minus` prefix arm when it peeks. Exactly
`9223372036854775808` under a unary minus folds to a single, already-negative
`ExprKind::Integer(i64::MIN)`; every other path through
`Token::IntegerOutOfRange` is an error.

THE FOLD, not just the value, is what makes it work downstream. A surviving
`Unary { Neg, Integer(..) }` would re-negate i64::MIN and overflow again at
whichever backend folded it. Emitting one already-negative literal node means
the typechecker's range validation, codegen's constant fold, and the
interpreter's Neg arm all see a plain in-range literal and need no special
case. Zero downstream changes.

VERIFIED, all five spellings on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT auto-par
/ AOT KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), identical output:

    -9223372036854775808i64        -9223372036854775808
    -9223372036854775808           -9223372036854775808
    -9223372036854775808  (inferred)
    (-9223372036854775808i64)      -9223372036854775808
    -0x8000000000000000i64         -9223372036854775808   <- hex too

plus `a == -9223372036854775807i64 - 1i64` -> true, which is the check that
the fold produced the RIGHT value rather than merely a parseable one.

STILL REJECTED, deliberately, and tested as such — these are the cases a
sign-folding lexer would have broken:
    9223372036854775808i64            bare, no minus
    -9223372036854775809i64           one past the negative bound
    y - 9223372036854775808i64        BINARY minus, differs only by context
    99999999999999999999999999i64     past u64 as well; keeps the lexer error

DIAGNOSTIC. The old message was the lexer's bare "Invalid integer literal".
It now names the magnitude, the i64 maximum, and the one legal negative
spelling.

SCOPE HELD, and the discarded attempt is worth recording. The same mechanism
looked like it would make the upper half of u64 writable too (`u64.MAX` as a
literal), and it was implemented — but every integer rides an i64 carrier
downstream, so the literal arrives as a wrapped NEGATIVE value and the
typechecker rejects it: "negative integer literal -1 cannot initialize
unsigned type 'u64'". Making that work is a TYPECHECKER change, not a parser
one. Reverted rather than half-built, and filed as B-2026-08-06-16. The parser
error message is explicit that a `u64` suffix does not help, so nobody is
sent down that path by the diagnostic.

TESTS:
  * test_i64_min_literal_folds_to_a_single_integer_node (tests/parser.rs) —
    asserts the NODE SHAPE, not just that it parses, across all five spellings
  * test_magnitude_above_i64_max_without_unary_minus_is_an_error (parser.rs)
  * test_i64_min_literal_evaluates_to_i64_min (tests/interpreter.rs)

fix: 257630a (src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs — the new `share_direct_shared_field_ref_for_return`, which gates on the caller-retains regime using the SAME name-only predicate the param_own.rs arm gates on so the two cannot drift; src/codegen/exprs.rs — the explicit-`return` hook; src/codegen/stmts.rs — the tail hook, on the early-return side of `compile_tail_final_expr`'s `tail_inner` gate). Pins e2e_shared_field_returned_from_a_caller_retains_param_keeps_its_ref and test_shared_field_returned_from_a_param_transfers_the_handle.
tracker: the CONCRETE-spelling return site for a direct `shared` field of a by-value struct param -- src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs::zero_struct_field_move_cap_impl's `shared` arm (B-2026-08-06-8) is the neutralizer that covers the generic spelling and does not reach this one
title: a `shared` field RETURNED out of a BY-VALUE struct param is a use-after-free on a DEFAULT -O2 build: `fn giveback(b: Holder) -> Node { return b.v; }` frees the 32-byte rc box at the param's scope-exit drop and hands the caller the freed handle -- CONCRETE spelling only, since B-2026-08-06-8's null-store already covers `Box[Node]`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: isolated while fixing B-2026-08-06-8, as a CONTROL on the concrete
spelling rather than a consequence of that fix. Confirmed pre-existing by
building `src/` at d5f2bf2 — before B-2026-08-06-1 or -8 — and measuring the
identical error counts.

REPRO, 7 lines, DEFAULT `karac build` (no -O0 needed):

    shared struct Node { s: String }
    struct Holder { v: Node }
    fn giveback(b: Holder) -> Node { return b.v; }
    fn main() {
        let h = Holder { v: Node { s: "padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap-buffer" } };
        let n = giveback(h);
        println(n.s.len());
    }

    -> prints 38 (correct, matching the interpreter), but valgrind reports
       `Invalid read of size 8` / `Address 0x... is 0 bytes inside a block of
       size 32 free'd` — 1 error at -O2, 2 at -O0. The 32-byte block is the rc
       box. The output is right only because nothing has reused the freed
       memory yet; this is a live use-after-free on a default build.

The TAIL spelling `fn giveback(b: Holder) -> Node { b.v }` reproduces
identically, so it is not an explicit-`return`-only shape.

MECHANISM. `b` is a callee-owned by-value param, so its scope-exit COMBINED drop
rc-dec's the shared field. The field READ loads the rc pointer without inc'ing
(the struct still owns that +1), so the returned handle is the only reference to
a box whose count already reached zero.

WHY IT SURVIVED B-2026-08-06-8, which fixed the GENERIC spelling of this exact
shape: that row's neutralizer is a null-store in `zero_struct_field_move_cap`,
and the generic path reaches that site while the concrete one does not. So
`Box[Node]` is clean here and `Holder` is not — the INVERSE of the usual
asymmetry in this family, and the reason this is a separate row rather than a
residual of that one.

FIX SHAPE, not yet attempted. Either extend the null-store's reach to the
concrete return site, or rc-inc the returned alias. The inc route was tried for
B-2026-08-06-8 and abandoned: `compile_tail_final_expr`'s FieldAccess arm is
only reached from an explicit `return` when the fn returns `Option[shared]`
(exprs.rs), so BOTH the tail and return paths need hooking, and an over-inc is a
silent leak rather than a crash. Prefer the null-store: it is one site and the
rc-dec walker already null-guards every arm.

FIXED 2026-08-06 (257630a), and THIS ROW'S OWN MECHANISM WAS WRONG — recorded
because it is the second time in this family that a plausible story survived on
not being checked.

The row read the generic spelling being clean as "B-2026-08-06-8's null-store
reaches that move site and this one it does not". Instrumenting the neutralizer
refutes that immediately: BOTH spellings emit it, identically, printing
`struct=Holder field=v fname=Node` and `struct=Box field=v fname=Node`. The
neutralizer was never the variable, and the tracker field pointed at it.

THE REAL SPLIT is a REGIME difference one branch away, at the by-value-param arm
in `param_own.rs`:
  * a struct owning NO shared field is owned BY TRANSFER (B-2026-08-05-33) — the
    callee registers the drop, the caller retracts its own, in lockstep — so a
    returned field only needs its SOURCE neutralized, which the null-store does;
  * a struct that DOES own one stays CALLER-RETAINS (B-2026-08-05-32): the
    callee deliberately registers nothing, because rc-dec'ing here as well would
    dec twice.
In the second regime the caller's +1 is still live, so a field handed back out
is an ALIAS and needs its own ref — the discipline `clone_on_extract_view_field`
already applies to a view extract. Null-storing there would be actively WRONG:
it strips the handle from a source the caller still owns. So the inc this row
listed as the fallback is in fact the only correct instrument here, and the
preference it recorded ("prefer the null-store") was backwards.

`Box[Node]` looked clean only because that branch's gate is NAME-ONLY, so a bare
`T` reads as non-shared and the generic wrapper lands in the TRANSFER regime.
That accident is the whole reason the bug presented as generic-vs-concrete.

ISOLATION that produced the diagnosis, one variable at a time: a `ref` param
reproduces too (so it is not about by-value ownership); a direct move-out in the
same scope is clean (so it is the CALL boundary); and the failure persists when
the caller NEVER READS the returned handle (so it is scope-exit accounting, not
a bad load) — that last one is what ruled out every "the load is wrong" theory.

BOTH RETURN SPELLINGS NEEDED HOOKING, because they diverge:
`compile_tail_final_expr` returns early at its `tail_inner` gate for any
non-`Option[shared]` return, so a plain `-> Node` TAIL never reaches the
FieldAccess arm. Fixing only the explicit `return` left the tail form failing —
measured, not assumed. This is the same divergence B-2026-08-06-8 hit and
documented; it has now cost two rows, and the note there about "an inc must be
threaded onto both paths" is exactly what this fix had to do.

MEASURED over 30 probe programs at -O2 AND -O0 against the interpreter. Fixed:
by-value + explicit return, by-value + tail, `ref` param, the never-read variant,
and a 40-round multi-shape fixture that ABORTS at HEAD with `malloc(): unaligned
tcache chunk detected` on every run. Controls an over-inc would have turned into
leaks — the owned-by-transfer generic wrapper and a plain-heap-field struct —
stay clean. Every -O2 probe is clean; the only -O0 leaks remaining are the four
programs carrying B-2026-08-06-15's block-tail shape, at exactly their recorded
sizes.

TEST-INFRA FINDING, and the part most worth carrying forward: THE ASAN HARNESS
CANNOT SEE THIS CLASS. It links a karac-emitted object that carries no ASAN
instrumentation, so the sanitizer catches allocator-level faults (double free,
invalid free, leaks) but NOT a use-after-free READ out of generated code. An
ASAN fixture over this exact program was written and measured GREEN at HEAD —
i.e. it passed against the compiler that aborts on the same input — and was
discarded rather than shipped. The gate that does catch it is the plain E2E run,
where the corrupted heap aborts deterministically. Rule: for a use-after-free
READ, reach for `tests/codegen.rs`, not `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`; valgrind
sees it because it instruments the binary, ASAN here does not.

TESTS: e2e_shared_field_returned_from_a_caller_retains_param_keeps_its_ref
(codegen), stash-proven RED with `left: ""` against `right: "9350"`; and
test_shared_field_returned_from_a_param_transfers_the_handle (interpreter, the
oracle).

the -O0 leg fully GREEN against the now-empty quarantine list; cli 574;
par_codegen 236; interpreter 1463; selfhost_codegen, coro_e2e,
disjoint_differential, drop_differential, shared_ownership_matrix, rc_fallback,

fix: e954652 (src/codegen/stmts.rs — `suppress_block_tail_cleanup`'s FieldAccess arm records the transfer via the new `tail_field_is_direct_shared`, and the let-site receive-inc consumes it; src/codegen.rs — the `block_tail_shared_transfer` channel). Pins asan_shared_field_escaping_a_value_block_transfers_exactly_one_ref and test_shared_field_escaping_a_value_block_transfers_the_handle.
tracker: ORDERING: src/codegen/stmts.rs::compile_naked_block drains the block frame (running the owner's struct drop) BEFORE the consumer's let-site rc-inc can run. Fix by emitting that inc pre-drain for a direct-`shared` tail and dropping the `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` null-store for that shape. NOT an accounting gap and NOT `clone_on_extract_view_field` -- both refuted in the detail.
title: a `shared` handle escaping a VALUE-POSITION BLOCK is never rc-dec'd by its consumer binding: `let x = { let b = Box { .. }; b.v };` leaks 1,280 B / 40 blocks at -O0 (clean at -O2), IDENTICALLY in the generic and concrete spellings -- the leak half of the shape whose use-after-free half B-2026-08-06-8 fixed
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: isolated while fixing B-2026-08-06-8. That row's block-tail
FieldAccess arm fixed the USE-AFTER-FREE half of this shape (which printed a
wrong answer); this row is the LEAK half it left behind. Measured identical in
both spellings, so it is not generic-specific.

REPRO, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`:

    shared struct Node { s: String }
    struct Box[T] { v: T }          // `struct Holder { v: Node }` behaves the same
    fn main() {
        let mut acc: i64 = 0;
        let mut i: i64 = 0;
        while i < 40 {
            let x = { let b = Box { v: Node { s: f"blk-{i}-padded-out-to-force-a-real-heap" } }; b.v };
            acc = acc + x.s.len();
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(acc);
    }

    -> correct output, `definitely lost: 1,280 bytes in 40 blocks` at -O0
       (32 B/round = one rc box). CLEAN at -O2, the usual signature: the box is
       provably dead there and LLVM deletes it along with the evidence.
       Byte-identical for the concrete `Holder` spelling — 1,280 B / 40 blocks.

MECHANISM, by elimination rather than instrumentation — stated as the hypothesis
it is. The block's frame no longer dec's the escaping handle (that is what
B-2026-08-06-8's arm fixed, by null-storing the source), and the consumer
binding `x` never picks up ownership: nothing rc-dec's the box at `x`'s scope
exit. The non-block move-out `let b = Box { .. }; let x = b.v;` IS clean, so the
gap is specific to a handle arriving as a value-position BLOCK's result — the
let-site presumably classifies the block's SSA value without seeing that it is a
shared handle, and so never calls `track_rc_var`.

WHY LOW: -O0-only today, and it is a bounded leak rather than a corruption. That
is a statement about the optimizer, not about the emitted code.

CHECK FIRST, when picking this up: whether `clone_on_extract_view_field`'s bare-
`shared` arm (rc-inc + `track_rc_var`) is the intended owner for this position
and simply is not reached — it was NOT called for either spelling in this shape
(verified by instrumenting it). If so the fix is routing, not new machinery.

INVESTIGATED 2026-08-06, NOT FIXED. Three hypotheses refuted — including both of
this row's own — and the mechanism narrowed to one open question. No compiler
change shipped: every candidate traded this LOW-severity -O0 leak for a
use-after-free, which is a bad trade.

REFUTED (1), this row's stated hypothesis: "the consumer binding never picks up
ownership; nothing rc-dec's the box at `x`'s scope exit". FALSE. Instrumenting
`track_rc_var` shows the consumer IS tracked — `name=x2 in_fn=main` for the
leaking block form, exactly as for the clean non-block form.

REFUTED (2), this row's "CHECK FIRST" pointer at
`clone_on_extract_view_field`'s bare-`shared` arm as the missing owner. It is
not the missing owner; the extract path that DOES run emits an rc-inc, and the
emission counts for the leaking and clean programs are IDENTICAL — 1 inc, 1
dec, 1 `__karac_vec_elem_full_drop_Box$Node` call in `main` for both. So the
fix is NOT routing, which is what this row guessed.

REFUTED (3), the obvious repair: exclude a direct `shared` field from the
block-tail neutralizer that B-2026-08-06-8 added (`suppress_block_tail_cleanup`'s
FieldAccess arm), on the reasoning that nulling the source deletes the dec which
balances the extract's inc. Implemented and measured: the leak does go away, and
is replaced by a USE-AFTER-FREE — 360 valgrind errors over 40 rounds, `Invalid
free()` x2, `Invalid read of size 8` x5, `Invalid write of size 8` x2, in BOTH
spellings. Strictly worse than the leak. Reverted.

SO THE ARM IS A LEVER BETWEEN TWO WRONG STATES, and that is the real finding:
  * arm ON  (main today) — both halves of the combined drop skip the nulled
    field, so nothing frees the escaped payload (safe) and the box's own ref is
    never dec'd (leaks 32 B per evaluation).
  * arm OFF — the combined drop runs on a field the block has handed out, and
    the payload is freed while the escaped handle still names it.

THE OPEN QUESTION, and the next experiment to run. The emitted operations are
the same for the clean non-block form (`let b = mk(); let x = b.v;`) and the
leaking block form, and on paper both balance:
    alloc 1 -> extract inc 2 -> owner drop dec 1 -> consumer dec 0
The only structural difference is WHEN the owner's drop runs — loop-iteration
end vs block end. Yet with the arm OFF the block form behaves as if the inc
never applied to that box. So: verify at RUNTIME whether the extract's inc
actually executes for the block-tail shape and whether it targets the same
allocation (a printf-instrumented `karac_rc_inc`, or a debugger breakpoint on
the box address, will settle it in one run). Everything else here is already
measured; that single fact decides whether the fix is "make the inc apply" or
"split the combined drop's two halves at this site so the rc-dec still runs
while the value half skips the escaped field".

SEVERITY UNCHANGED (low): -O0 only, bounded, correct output. Worth noting for
whoever picks it up that the cheap-looking repair is the dangerous one.

ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-06 (still unfixed, but no longer open-ended). It is an
ORDERING bug, not an accounting one, and the reason it read as accounting is a
measurement mistake worth recording: the earlier emission counts were collected
through `sort | uniq -c`, which destroys the only signal that mattered. The
same trace UNSORTED settles it immediately:

    sh_a  (clean):   rc_INC(v) -> rc_DEC(x1_rc_cleanup) -> StructDrop(b1)
    sh_e  (leaking): StructDrop(b5) -> rc_INC(v) -> rc_DEC(x2_rc_cleanup)

The owner's struct drop is emitted BEFORE the escaping value's ownership inc.
The inc is the LET-SITE inc for the consumer binding, which cannot run until the
block has already returned its value — by which time the block frame has drained
and the owner's drop has run. Same pointer (`v`), same basic block
(`while.body`) in both programs; only the order differs.

That single fact explains every state measured on this row:
  * arm OFF: rc 1 -> owner drop dec -> 0, box FREED -> the let-site inc and the
    consumer's dec then both operate on freed memory. Exactly the invalid
    free/read/write triple observed.
  * arm ON (main today): the owner's dec is skipped by the null-store, so
    rc 1 -> let-site inc 2 -> consumer dec 1. Leaks one ref. Exactly 32 B per
    evaluation.
  * the clean non-block form: the inc precedes both decs, so 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0.

THE FIX, now concrete: the escaping value's inc has to happen while the owner is
still alive — i.e. inside `compile_naked_block`, at the point
`suppress_block_tail_cleanup` runs, BEFORE `drain_top_frame_with_emit`. Then the
owner's drop is left to dec normally (no null-store for this shape) and the
arithmetic is 1 -> inc 2 -> owner dec 1 -> consumer dec 0.

CAUTION for whoever implements it, because this is where a naive attempt leaks
again: the existing let-site inc must not ALSO fire, or the count lands at 1
instead of 0. There is exactly ONE inc emitted today; the change is to move it
earlier for a direct-`shared` block tail, not to add a second one. Verify by
re-running the unsorted trace above and checking the inc now precedes the
StructDrop.

So the earlier framing — "make the inc apply" vs "split the combined drop's two
halves" — resolves to the FIRST, and the drop does not need splitting.

FIXED 2026-08-06 (e954652), and the resolution is the INVERSE of what the
root-cause note above predicted — recorded because the prediction was a coin
flip between two balancing designs and the cheaper one won.

That note said: emit the consumer's inc pre-drain and DROP the null-store. Both
halves turn out to be wrong. The null-store is not incidental — by disarming the
owner's rc-dec it TRANSFERS the box's only ref to the escaping value, so the
correct move is to KEEP it and drop the RECEIVE-INC instead. No ordering change
is needed at all, which is why the fix is a flag rather than surgery on
`compile_naked_block`'s drain.

Final arithmetic, from the emission trace:
    before: 1 (alloc) -> 1 (owner's dec skipped) -> 2 (receive-inc) -> 1 (dec)
    after:  1 (alloc) -> 1 (owner's dec skipped) ------------------> 0 (dec)
and the unchanged non-block control keeps its inc because ITS owner's dec does
run: 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0.

MECHANISM of the fix: the transfer cannot be recognised by `rhs_yields_fresh_ref`,
which runs BEFORE the RHS is compiled — the block's inner binding is not in scope
yet, so the field's type is unresolvable there. It is recorded at the point the
transfer happens (`suppress_block_tail_cleanup`'s FieldAccess arm sets
`block_tail_shared_transfer`) and consumed at the let site, cleared on both sides
so it only ever describes the block immediately to its left. Same shape as the
existing `last_fstr_acc` channel.

THE OTHER DESIGN IS A DOUBLE FREE, and the fixture now covers it: removing the
null-store instead of the inc also balances on paper but frees a payload the
block has already handed out — 360 valgrind errors over 40 rounds (invalid
free/read/write), both spellings. Implemented, measured, rejected.

THIS ROW UNDERSTATED THE SEVERITY, and that is the correction most worth
carrying: it was filed "-O0 only (clean at -O2)". That held only because the
repro read the payload through `.len()`, which lets LLVM delete the box. With a
byte-level read the fixture leaks on a DEFAULT -O2 build too — 5610 B in 120
allocations — so this was a default-build leak whenever the payload is actually
used. The `.len()`-only reproduction is exactly the B-2026-08-04-17 authoring
hazard biting a BUG REPORT rather than a fixture.

MEASURED over 32 probe programs at -O2 AND -O0 against the interpreter: the
whole corpus is clean at both levels, which it had not been at any point across
this cluster (B-2026-08-06-1/-8/-14/-15). Controls that must not move and did
not: the non-block move-out and a String field through the same block shape.

TESTS: asan_shared_field_escaping_a_value_block_transfers_exactly_one_ref
(memory_sanitizer) and test_shared_field_escaping_a_value_block_transfers_the_handle
(interpreter, the oracle). An ASAN fixture rather than an E2E one — the OPPOSITE
of sibling B-2026-08-06-14, whose defect an ASAN run cannot see — because here
the output is correct before and after and only a leak gate can observe it.
Stash-proven RED on BOTH legs: 5610 B / 120 allocations at -O2, 9450 B / 240 at
-O0.

SUITES: non-llvm 8660; codegen E2E 2827; memory_sanitizer 956/0/10 at -O2 and
the -O0 leg 956/0/10 fully green; cli 574; par_codegen 236; interpreter 1465;
selfhost_codegen, coro_e2e, disjoint_differential, drop_differential,
shared_ownership_matrix, rc_fallback, ownership 406, example_corpus, spawn_e2e,
closures. clippy and fmt clean.

title: the upper half of u64 is unwritable as a literal -- `18446744073709551615u64` (and any magnitude above i64::MAX, in any radix) is a parse error, because every integer rides an i64 CARRIER and the literal arrives wrapped NEGATIVE, which the typechecker rejects with `negative integer literal -1 cannot initialize unsigned type 'u64'`. The parser half is already done (B-2026-08-06-13 carries the magnitude); this is the typechecker half.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-06-13 (the i64::MIN literal). That
row's mechanism -- carry the out-of-i64-range magnitude to the parser as
`Token::IntegerOutOfRange(u64, suffix)` -- looked like it would cover this case
for free, and the arm was written. It does not, and the arm was REVERTED rather
than shipped half-working.

WHAT ACTUALLY BLOCKS IT, measured rather than assumed. The parser can emit
`ExprKind::Integer(m as i64, Some(U64))` -- the wrapped bit pattern, which is
exactly how u64 values above i64::MAX are already represented at runtime
(`test_interp_primitive_const_u64_max` pins `u64.MAX` printing as
18446744073709551615 from an all-ones i64 carrier). But the TYPECHECKER
validates the literal before that representation is in play, and rejects:

    let a: u64 = 18446744073709551615u64;
    error[typecheck]: negative integer literal -1 cannot initialize unsigned
                      type 'u64'
    let a: u64 = 9223372036854775808u64;
    error[typecheck]: negative integer literal -9223372036854775808 cannot
                      initialize unsigned type 'u64'

So the fix belongs in the typechecker's literal range-validation: when the
declared / suffixed type is unsigned, the i64 payload must be read as a BIT
PATTERN (u64) rather than as a signed value, and range-checked against the
unsigned bound.

NOT UNREACHABLE, stated up front because B-2026-08-06-13 made exactly this
mistake in the other direction: `u64.MAX` is an existing primitive const and
works today on both interp and JIT. This is a literal-spelling gap, not an
inaccessible value -- which is why it is LOW.

SCOPE NOTE: the same argument applies to `u128`/`i128` suffixes, which the
lexer accepts as tokens; whether those are supported at all is a separate
question this row does not touch.

STATE TODAY: `B-2026-08-06-13` left the parser reporting an explicit message
for this case -- it names the i64 max AND says values above it are unsupported
"including with a `u64` suffix" -- so the diagnostic does not send anyone down
a path that cannot work.

── FIXED ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

TWO SIDES, and this row correctly predicted which one was missing. The parser
half was already in place from B-2026-08-06-13 (the magnitude reaches the parser
as `Token::IntegerOutOfRange`); what was needed was the typechecker reading that
payload back as UNSIGNED.

PARSER: an unsigned-suffixed magnitude past i64::MAX is now admitted as the
wrapped bit pattern on the i64 carrier — the same representation `u64.MAX`
already had at runtime. EVERY unsigned suffix is admitted, not just `u64`, so
`18446744073709551615u8` gets the typechecker's precise "out of range for 'u8'
(expected 0..=255)" rather than a blanket parse error.

TYPECHECKER: `literal_as_i128(n, sfx)` widens the payload through `as u64` when
the suffix is unsigned, instead of sign-extending it back to a negative. Applied
at BOTH check sites — synthesis (`infer_expr_inner`) and the contextual boundary
(`suffixed_int_literal_value`), which is the one that actually fired for
`let x: u64 = ...`.

SAFE TO APPLY TO EVERY UNSIGNED-SUFFIXED LITERAL, not just the wrapped ones, and
the argument matters: the lexer only ever produces a NON-NEGATIVE payload from
digits, so a negative `n` under an unsigned suffix can only have come from the
out-of-range arm. A genuinely negative literal is `Neg(Integer(n))` with `n`
positive — a different AST shape on a different path — so `-5u64` still reports
"negative integer literal -5 cannot initialize unsigned type 'u64'".

A HOLE THIS FIX WOULD HAVE OPENED, caught by writing the REJECTION test
alongside the acceptance one. `int_literal_range` had no `Type::Int(I64)` row.
That was harmless while every literal WAS an i64 — it fit by construction — but
once an unsigned-suffixed literal can carry up to u64::MAX,
`let x: i64 = 18446744073709551615u64` silently bound -1. The row is added, and
its absence is now documented as having been vacuous rather than deliberate. The
acceptance test alone would have passed while the compiler quietly got worse.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT auto-par / AOT
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), byte-identical:
    18446744073709551615u64      -> 18446744073709551615
    9223372036854775808u64       -> 9223372036854775808
    0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFu64        -> 18446744073709551615   (hex too)
    a == u64.MAX                 -> true
    b > 9223372036854775807u64   -> true

STILL REJECTED, tested: a u64-sized magnitude under a `u8` suffix, `-5u64`,
`5000000000u32`, and the i64-binding case above.

A SEPARATE PRE-EXISTING DIVERGENCE FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, filed as
B-2026-08-06-18 (high, run-vs-build): a u64 ARITHMETIC RESULT above i64::MAX
renders SIGNED under both compiled backends — `println(u64.MAX - 1u64)` prints
-2 compiled and 18446744073709551614 interpreted. Established as NOT caused by
this change by reproducing it entirely through `u64.MAX`, with no new literal
involved; the literals added here round-trip identically on all four surfaces.

title: `ref CStr` as an `unsafe extern "C"` PARAMETER type is accepted by the typechecker and then dies at codegen with a raw LLVM module-verification error (`Call parameter type does not match function signature! {ptr, i64} ... ptr`) — the fat two-word CStr reference is passed where the extern lowering expects a thin pointer. Identical failure under `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build`; `--interp` works, so it is also a latent run-vs-build divergence.
detail:
REPRO: `unsafe extern "C" { fn strlen(s: ref CStr) -> usize; }` + `strlen(c"hello")` — the NATURAL first spelling any FFI newcomer writes. Design contract (design.md § C-String Literals, FFI handoff) is `*const u8` + `.as_ptr()`, which works on all three surfaces (verified 2026-08-06: sqrt+strlen example, run == build == KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build). So the correct fix is EITHER a structured typecheck-time rejection of non-FFI-safe types in extern signatures (pointing at `.as_ptr()`, the way rustc's improper_ctypes does) OR lowering `ref CStr` extern params as the thin data pointer. Either way the current unstructured `error: codegen failed: Module verification failed` violates the every-phase-emits-structured-diagnostics rule. SOURCE NOTE: hit while verifying the FFI hello-world for book ch18 + karac.dev FFI guide; the docs use the `.as_ptr()` form.

── FIXED adaa9e34 ──

Taken as a structured typecheck rejection (this row's option 1), not as a
thin-pointer lowering of `ref CStr` (option 2). Option 2 would make a spelling
WORK that design.md does not sanction — the contract is `*const u8` +
`.as_ptr()` — and would owe an answer for every other non-representable type,
not just `CStr`. New kind `ExternSignatureInvalid` (E0805), run-fatal, with the
symbolic code in the message per the `E_REPR_TRANSPARENT_*` convention:

  error[E_EXTERN_REF_PARAM]: `ref` is not a valid parameter type for the
  foreign import 'strlen': pass `*const u8` and hand over the data pointer at
  the call site with `.as_ptr()` — `fn strlen(s: *const u8) …` called as
  `strlen(x.as_ptr())`

THE RULE'S REAL SHAPE, arrived at only after the suite refuted a first attempt:
"a borrow of a KĀRA-REPRESENTABLE type has no C meaning", NOT "a borrow is
never FFI-safe". A blanket rejection of every `ref` broke two legitimate
contracts:

  * `ref Foo` where `Foo` is an OPAQUE foreign type is the canonical Kāra-side
    handle form (design.md § Opaque Foreign Types), and
    `test_opaque_type_through_ref_accepted` exists as an explicit positive
    control for it. It is also exactly the shape this diagnostic recommends: an
    opaque type has no Kāra-visible body, so a reference to it IS the thin
    pointer, with nothing that could make it fat.
  * `host fn` has its own boundary rule with host-specific remedies ("pass an
    opaque handle or a (pointer, length) pair"). Firing here too took that
    test's 5 diagnostics to 7 — one mistake reported twice, the second time
    worse.

Both exemptions are pinned by tests, including the per-referent boundary: an
opaque `ref` and a `ref CStr` in the SAME extern block yield exactly one
diagnostic.

Everything else is still rejected, including the THIN borrows. Measured, only
`ref CStr` and `ref String` trip the verifier — `ref i64` gets through codegen
and fails at link on the undefined symbol like any other extern declaration.
Keying the rule on whether a referent happens to lower fat would put a codegen
layout question in the typechecker, which is the coupling design.md § Codegen
architecture exists to prevent; and a borrow has no C meaning regardless, so
the thin cases build by coincidence of layout rather than by being right.

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN TEXT: "`--interp` works, so it is also a latent
run-vs-build divergence" is FALSE, and not merely for this shape. The
interpreter cannot call ANY foreign function — `unsafe extern "C" { fn abs(n:
i32) -> i32; }` + `abs(-5i32)` fails identically. So there was no divergence to
be latent: `--interp` never ran this program. What it does instead is its own
defect, split out as B-2026-08-06-24 — it reports an "internal … This is a
compiler bug, please report it" message for an operation that is unsupported by
design.

title: a u64 ARITHMETIC RESULT above i64::MAX renders SIGNED under both compiled backends but unsigned under the interpreter -- `println(u64.MAX - 1u64)` prints -2 on JIT/AOT and 18446744073709551614 on interp. Binding the expression to a `let` first is correct on every surface, so the wrong spelling sits next to a working one. PRE-EXISTING and independent of B-2026-08-06-16 (reproduces entirely through `u64.MAX`, no literal required)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-06-16 (the u64 upper-half
literal) on all four surfaces. The new literals themselves round-trip
IDENTICALLY on interp / JIT / AOT auto-par / AOT KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0; this
divergence is in the print path and predates that change. Established by
reproducing it with `u64.MAX` alone, which needs no new literal at all --
that is the control that separates the two.

SHAPE, and the pattern is sharp:

    let a: u64 = u64.MAX;
    let one: u64 = 1u64;
    println(a);            interp 18446744073709551615   compiled SAME  (ok)
    println(a - one);      interp 18446744073709551614   compiled -2    (WRONG)
    println(a & a);        interp 18446744073709551615   compiled -1    (WRONG)
    println(a | one);      interp 18446744073709551615   compiled -1    (WRONG)
    println(a ^ one);      interp 18446744073709551614   compiled -2    (WRONG)
    println(a / 2u64);     interp  9223372036854775807   compiled SAME  (ok)
    println(a % 10u64);    interp                    5   compiled SAME  (ok)
    println(a >> 1u64);    interp  9223372036854775807   compiled SAME  (ok)
    let b: u64 = a - one;
    println(b);            interp 18446744073709551614   compiled SAME  (ok)

SO THE RULE IS NOT "u64 printing is broken". Two things have to coincide: the
printed expression must be an INLINE BINOP (not an identifier, not a let-bound
name), and its RESULT must exceed i64::MAX. Every op whose result lands below
i64::MAX prints correctly, which is why `/`, `%` and `>>` look fine here -- they
are not special-cased, their results simply fit. The bit pattern is CORRECT in
every case; only the rendering is signed.

f-STRINGS TOO, same split: `f"{a - one}"` prints -2 compiled, and `f"{b}"` with
the same value let-bound prints 18446744073709551614.

THE LET-BOUND SPELLING BEING CORRECT IS WHAT MAKES THIS DANGEROUS -- an author
sees a working example next to a broken one with no reason to suspect the
difference. Exactly the shape of B-2026-08-06-5 (a cast to `char` inside an
f-string), which was also "inline expression loses its type at the print site,
let-bound form is fine".

LIKELY MECHANISM, from the neighbouring row rather than from the source:
B-2026-07-04-8 taught the print sink to recover a `u64` STATIC TYPE from the
printed expression's SPAN so that `u64.MAX` renders unsigned instead of -1
(`test_interp_primitive_const_u64_max` pins it). That recovery evidently
resolves for an identifier and for a let-bound name but NOT for a binop
expression's span, so the sink falls back to signed rendering. NOT VERIFIED
against the code -- stated as the first place to look, not as the diagnosis.

SEVERITY HIGH: it is a silent wrong answer on a default `karac build`, on
ordinary arithmetic, with no diagnostic. It is bounded by needing an
above-i64::MAX result, which is rare in most code -- but B-2026-08-06-16 has
just made such values WRITABLE AS LITERALS, so the surface that can reach it is
larger than it was yesterday. That is a reason to fix it, not a reason to
withhold -16: the same values were already reachable through `u64.MAX` and the
whole upper half of u64 through arithmetic.

FOUR-SURFACE STATUS: interp is the CORRECT one here; JIT and both AOT modes
agree with each other and are wrong together. So this is interp-vs-compiled, not
a JIT/AOT split.

REPRODUCE: the program above, `karac run --interp` vs `karac run` vs
`karac build`.

FILING NOTE: originally numbered B-2026-08-06-17; renumbered on rebase because a
concurrent session claimed that id for an unrelated ffi-docs row.

── FIXED ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

AND THIS ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, which is the part worth carrying.
It guessed: "the span recovery resolves for an identifier and a let-bound name
but NOT for a binop expression's span ... NOT VERIFIED against the code --
stated as the first place to look, not as the diagnosis." The hedge earned its
keep. The first fix followed that guess -- `ExprKind::Binary` and
`ExprKind::Unary` arms added to `expr_is_unsigned_int`
(src/codegen/expr_ops.rs) -- and after a rebuild the probe was STILL BROKEN,
byte for byte.

THE REASON: `a - b` NEVER REACHES CODEGEN AS A BINOP. `rewrite_binary`
(src/lowering.rs) turns every primitive binop into
`Call(Path([<type>, <method>]), args)` before codegen sees it, so the printed
expression is `u64.sub(a, one)`. `expr_is_unsigned_int`'s `Call` arm understood
only an `Identifier` callee (a free function, looked up in
`fn_return_type_names`); a `Path` callee fell through to the `false` default,
which is signed. Every inline binop print has been taking the signed path for
as long as the lowering has existed.

FIX: a `Path`-callee branch in that `Call` arm. A two-segment path whose first
segment is an unsigned type name returns unsigned BY CONSTRUCTION -- `u64.sub`
returns u64 -- with the comparison methods (`eq`/`ne`/`lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge`)
excluded, since those return `bool` and never take the integer print path.

THE SPECULATIVE ARMS WERE THEN DELETED, and that is deliberate rather than
tidying. With the `Path` branch in place they were removed and everything
re-verified -- including `~a`, which also lowers (`rewrite_unary` maps `BitNot`
to `u64.not`) and is therefore covered by the same branch. Nothing regressed,
so they were dead code. Leaving them would have been worse than useless here:
this predicate's entire failure mode is looking more complete than it is, and
two untestable arms reading as load-bearing is how the next person concludes
the shape is handled.

VERIFIED byte-identical on all four surfaces (interp / JIT / AOT auto-par / AOT
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0):

    a - one    18446744073709551614   was -2 compiled
    a & a      18446744073709551615   was -1
    a | one    18446744073709551615   was -1
    a ^ one    18446744073709551614   was -2
    ~one       18446744073709551614   was -2
    f"{a-one}" 18446744073709551614   was -2
    a / 2u64    9223372036854775807   unchanged (result fits i64 -- control)
    a >> 1u64   9223372036854775807   unchanged (control)
    s - 1i64                     -6   unchanged (SIGNED binop -- control)

The two controls that fit i64 and the signed control are what establish this is
a rendering fix and not a blanket "print everything unsigned" -- the bit
patterns were always right, only the format specifier was wrong.

TEST: `e2e_inline_u64_binop_prints_unsigned` (tests/codegen.rs), stash-proven
RED -- without the fix the same program prints
`-2 / -1 / -1 / -2 / -2 / -2 / 9223372036854775807 / 9223372036854775807 / -6`.

SAME CLASS AS B-2026-08-06-5, as this row predicted: a per-syntactic-form
allowlist where an unhandled form silently defaults to the wrong rendering.
That was `expr_is_char`; this is its signedness sibling `expr_is_unsigned_int`,
and the structural criticism recorded there applies verbatim. Worth noting the
two predicates do NOT share the gap: `expr_is_char`'s `Call` arm has the same
Identifier-only limitation, but a lowered binop can never produce a `char`, so
it is not reachable the same way.

FIX SHA: ac3041ce.

GATES: fmt clean, clippy clean, codegen 2828/0, interpreter 1464/0,
typechecker 2146/0, cli 574/0.

fix: FIXED (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs: new `generic_method_return_inst` substitutes the RECEIVER's instantiation into the method's declared return TypeExpr, recovered from the AST the declare loop keeps in `generic_fns`; consulted from `enum_inst_type_of_expr`'s new MethodCall arm — placed BEFORE the span fallback — and from `type_name_of_expr`'s MethodCall tail). Pins tests/codegen.rs `e2e_chained_field_access_on_generic_method_return`, stash-proven RED.
