title: a `Vec[weak N]` push SILENTLY CORRUPTED the target's first field — `w.push(a)` changed `a.v` from 41 to 42, because the weak-target scan never saw through the container and `N` was laid out without its weak-count word
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while implementing B-2026-08-08-4 gap B's read-back; the
read is what made it visible, but the bug is entirely in the STORE half
B-2026-08-08-5 shipped. Reproduced on a stashed tree.

    shared struct N { mut v: i64 }
    fn main() {
        let a: N = N { v: 41i64 };
        println(a.v);              // 41
        let mut w: Vec[weak N] = Vec.new();
        w.push(a);
        println(a.v);              // 42   <-- nothing in the program wrote this
    }

No diagnostic, no sanitizer report, no crash. The push returns and an unrelated
field of an unrelated binding has changed value.

MECHANISM. A shared type that is the target of a `weak` ref is force-headed
with a two-word `{ strong, weak, fields… }` control box; every other shared
type gets `{ strong, fields… }`. The whole-program set driving that decision
(`weak_targeted_types`) was collected by `weak_target_name`, which matches a
field whose type is DIRECTLY `TypeKind::Weak(_)`. A field of type `Vec[weak N]`
is `Path(Vec)` with `Weak(N)` in its GENERIC ARGUMENTS, so `N` was never added
and kept the one-word layout. `karac_weak_downgrade` then incremented the word
it takes to be the weak count -- word 1 -- which in that layout is the struct's
FIRST FIELD.

THE THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE ROOT CAUSE. B-2026-08-08-4 gap A is `check_cycles`
following a field's own type but not its generic arguments; gap B was the
downgrade coercion reaching a field store but not a container-element store;
this is the box-layout scan doing the same thing. Same blindness, three
independent places, and this one is the only one that corrupts memory rather
than leaking or rejecting.

FIX: the collection recurses through generic args, tuples, arrays, refs and
pointers, so `Map[K, weak V]`, `Vec[Vec[weak N]]` and tuple positions are
reached too. It also now walks FUNCTION SIGNATURES and local `let` type
annotations, because the shape that surfaced this has no struct in it at all --
`let mut w: Vec[weak N] = Vec.new();` in a plain function body. Annotations
only; an unannotated `let` whose weak-ness comes from inference is not
reachable at declaration time.

WHY HIGH RATHER THAN MEDIUM: it is a silent wrong answer in already-shipped
code, reachable from a two-line program, and the corrupted word is a live
user-visible field. It leaves no trace for either sanitizer -- the write is
in-bounds for the allocation, just aimed at the wrong word.

tracker: probe: `let mut w: Vec[weak N] = Vec.new(); w.push(a); match w[0] { Some(x) => .. }` under `karac run --interp`
title: the interpreter has no weak CONTAINER element, so a `Vec[weak T]` read-back reports `non-exhaustive match ... the typechecker should have rejected this` where `karac build` and `karac run` are both correct
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the interpreter leg B-2026-08-08-4 gap B's read-back left behind.
Codegen (AOT) and `karac run` (the default JIT, which goes through codegen)
both produce the correct `Some(x)` / `None`; only the explicit `--interp`
backend diverges.

    runtime error: internal error: non-exhaustive match at 7:5 -- no arm matched
    the scrutinee value (the typechecker should have rejected this)

TWO PROBLEMS, and the second is the worse one:

  1. The interpreter models `weak` PER FIELD -- dedicated `weak_immutable_fields`
     / `weak_mut_fields` maps on `SharedStructInner`, upgraded at the field-read
     site. There is no weak VALUE, so a `Vec[weak N]` element is stored as an
     ordinary strong `Value::SharedStruct` and the element read yields a bare
     struct where the typechecker now promises `Option[N]`. Hence no arm matches.
  2. The message BLAMES THE TYPECHECKER for a gap in the interpreter. That is
     the B-2026-08-06-24 class exactly: an internal-error string that sends the
     next reader to the wrong phase. Worth fixing even if (1) is deferred.

WHAT (1) NEEDS: a weak representation at VALUE level rather than at field level
(a `std::sync::Weak` carried in a `Value` variant), so a container element can
hold one and the existing `upgrade_weak_to_option` can run at the element read.
That is a contained change but it touches every exhaustive `match` over
`Value`, which is why it is filed rather than folded into the codegen slice.

NOT A REGRESSION: before f869989f this program failed on BOTH backends
(codegen: `Undefined variable 'x'`). The codegen half is now correct and the
interpreter half is not, which is what makes it a run-vs-build row.

RESOLUTION (f0c47394). Both halves, and the row's own size estimate was wrong
in the helpful direction.

  1. `Value::WeakRef(std::sync::Weak<SharedStructInner>)` is the missing home.
     The row warned this "touches every exhaustive `match` over `Value`, which
     is why it is filed rather than folded into the codegen slice". Measured:
     TWO arms, `Display` and `variant_name`. The worry did not survive contact
     with the compiler, and the change is small enough that filing it
     separately was the more expensive choice.
  2. The misleading message is gone because the condition that produced it is
     gone -- the match now receives the `Option[T]` it was promised. Nothing
     was special-cased in the diagnostic itself.

THE UPGRADE IS ONE POST-STEP IN `eval_expr_inner`, not an arm inside the
`Index` evaluation, and that is the design point worth keeping: `WeakRef` has
exactly ONE producer -- the downgrade at a `Vec[weak T]` push -- so any
expression that yields one is a read of that element and owes the upgrade. The
push's own downgrade runs AFTER `eval_expr_inner` returns, on the
already-evaluated argument, so it is not undone by its own rule. `Display`
renders through the upgrade too (a live target prints as its struct, a dead one
as `None`), so the handle never reaches user-visible output.

THE SITE SETS COME FROM THE TYPECHECKER because the interpreter has no static
element type to consult -- a plain-data span-keyed side channel
(`weak_elem_store_sites` / `weak_elem_read_sites`). Codegen needs neither; it
reads the element `TypeExpr` directly. So these exist purely to keep the two
backends agreeing, which is the opposite of the usual reason for a side table.
The store set is keyed by the ARGUMENT's span rather than the call's: a method
call shares its receiver's span here, so the call span is not unique to the push.

Run now matches build on every probe from the gap-B slice, including the one
that makes this a weak ref rather than an awkward strong one -- `None` once the
target's frame dies.

tracker: src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs (the Vec push element check) + the weak downgrade codegen (B-2026-07-19-8 slices 3-4)
title: the `weak` downgrade store coercion reaches a direct FIELD store but not a container-ELEMENT store, so `Vec[weak N]` cannot be built -- which makes design.md's own worked cycle-breaking example uncompilable and leaves B-2026-08-08-4 with no fix
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-08-4, where it is gap B. Filed separately
because it is independently landable and NON-BREAKING, while its sibling (the
cycle checker looking through containers) is a breaking language change that
cannot land until this one does.

MEASURED, and the contrast is the whole report:

    shared struct P { v: i64, mut kid: Option[C] }
    shared struct C { v: i64, mut parent: weak P }
    c.parent = p;                       // ACCEPTED, and measured LEAK-FREE

    shared struct N { v: i64, mut ns: Vec[weak N] }
    a.ns.push(b);                       // error[typecheck]:
                                        //   expected 'weak N', found 'N'

So `weak` itself is fine -- B-2026-07-19-8 shipped it end-to-end (two-count
control block, downgrade coercion, `Option[T]` read typing) and the field path
reclaims a cycle with no leak. What is missing is the coercion at a CONTAINER
element store.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: design.md § Cycles gives the graph shape as
`mut neighbors: Vec[weak GraphNode]` and writes `b.neighbors.push(a); //
bidirectional, no cycle leak`. That line does not compile. Every real graph
holds its back-edges in a container, so the container store is the ONLY form
that matters for the mechanism's actual purpose, and it is the one form absent.

BOTH HALVES OR NEITHER. The typecheck relaxation alone is worse than the
current error: it would compile a program that stores a STRONG reference into a
slot the author declared `weak`, so the cycle would still leak while the source
says it does not. Codegen must emit the downgrade at the store (and the
matching weak-drop in the container's element drain) in the same commit, gated
on LSan at both opt levels -- the same pairing rule B-2026-08-07-23 established
for frozen containers, and for the same reason.

NOT MEASURED: whether `Map[K, weak V]` / `Set[weak T]` / array and tuple
element stores share one coercion site or several, and whether the container's
per-element drop already routes weak elements to the weak-drop primitive or
would need its own arm. Both decide whether this is one narrow edit or a family
of them, and both should be established before the shape of the fix is
chosen.

-- FIXED (2026-08-08), 1bb5328a. `Vec[weak T]` NOW RECLAIMS A CYCLE --

design.md § Cycles' worked example compiles and is measured leak-free: a
bidirectional 2-node graph and a 4-node / 8-edge one both report "All heap
blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible" under valgrind, where the
strong-`Vec[N]` twin leaks 72 bytes per node (B-2026-08-08-4).

THREE PIECES, not the two this row predicted:
  * typecheck accepts a bare strong handle at a `weak` element;
  * the push emits `karac_weak_downgrade` (`emit_weak_field_init` -- the fresh
    slot sibling, since a push writes `data[len]` with no prior occupant);
  * the push takes NO STRONG COUNT, and the container's scope-exit drain
    weak-drops each element (`__karac_vec_elem_weak_drop`, a new element-drop
    arm in `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` checked BEFORE the name-keyed
    dispatch, which would otherwise hand back the referent's strong `rc_dec`).

THE STRONG-COUNT PIECE WAS NOT IN THE PLAN and is the one worth recording.
With only the store and the drop, the measurement came back "payloads freed,
every control block still leaked" -- the ordinary transfer inc was still
firing, so the strong count never reached zero and the box could not be
released even once weak hit zero. The row's "both halves or neither" framing
was right in spirit and short by one.

NARROWER THAN THE FIELD RULE, DELIBERATELY. A `weak` FIELD also accepts
`Option[T]` and `None`; routing the container store through the same
`check_expr` coercion admitted them and compiled a program that SEGFAULTED at
runtime. The gate is therefore hand-written: a bare strong handle only, with a
diagnostic that names the limitation. The typechecker must admit exactly what
codegen lowers, and the reject row in tests/typechecker.rs is what keeps them
in step. Widening to `Option[T]` is a codegen change first.

-- A VACUOUS-PASS HOLE IN THE ASAN HARNESS, FOUND BY STASH-PROVING THIS --

The new LSan fixture PASSED against a compiler with the fix reverted. Cause:
`run_under_asan_opts` asserted the OWNERSHIP result (`assert_ownership_clean`)
but never the TYPECHECK one, so a fixture whose program fails typecheck was
still handed to codegen and ran. A test written for a not-yet-supported shape
could therefore report `ok` for a program `karac build` REFUSES.

The harness now panics on typecheck errors, the same discrimination the
codegen-failure panic already applies. That exposed SIX existing fixtures in
exactly that state (tensor `ref Tensor[f32,[?]]` vs `Tensor[f64,[N]]`, a
`Vec[u32]`/`Vec[i64]` mismatch, an uninferrable `E`); they are marked
`#[ignore]` with their errors and filed as B-2026-08-08-6, per the harness's own
rule that a gap be visibly deferred rather than silently green.

-- WHAT GATES WHAT, since the answer is not the obvious one --

The LSan fixture gates the TYPECHECK half only. Reverting EITHER codegen half
leaves a program that leaks its entire graph -- 288 bytes, valgrind -- while
LeakSanitizer still reports it clean, even with the stack-churn technique
B-2026-08-08-4 documents. So the codegen halves are gated by an IR assertion
(`tests/codegen.rs
vec_of_weak_push_downgrades_and_takes_no_strong_count`): the downgrade call,
the element weak-drop, and fewer retains than the identical strong-element
build, with a strong-`Vec[N]` control row so the comparison means something.
Each half was proven red with its own change reverted.

STILL OPEN, and both were measured rather than assumed:
  * READ-BACK. `match v[i] { Some(x) => .. }` over a `Vec[weak N]` fails with
    `codegen failed: Undefined variable 'x'` -- the same signature as
    B-2026-08-08-3. The weak FIELD read-back works and is leak-free, so this is
    the container twin of the upgrade, not a missing mechanism. A `Vec[weak T]`
    is therefore STORE-ONLY today, which is enough for cycle-breaking
    back-edges (they exist to not be traversed) and not enough for a
    parent-pointer walk.
  * `Option[T]` / `None` elements, per the narrowing above.
  * `Map[K, weak V]` / `Set` / array / tuple element stores -- untouched, and
    the row's open question about whether they share one coercion site is still
    unanswered.

GATES: typechecker 2157/0, codegen 2836/0, memory_sanitizer 986/0 at -O2 AND
-O0, ownership 416/0, par_codegen 246/0, interpreter 1470/0, concurrency 139/0,

title: a frozen-element container declared INSIDE a closure was still admitted -- `try_admit_container_method` had no `in_closure` gate, so an escaping closure could carry a non-counting handle past its owner; latent until 200fa8d6 removed the typecheck mask, live on main after it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by the negative sweep while re-running kata #133
against `main` after 200fa8d6 (B-2026-08-08-2). Not found by reading the code.
It is the class of hole this family keeps producing -- an admission arm that
never asks whether it is inside a closure -- and it is the fourth one on
B-2026-08-01-33.

SHAPE. Stage 3c (B-2026-08-07-23) admits a local `Vec[S]` as a FROZEN-ELEMENT
container: its elements are non-counting, so the push takes no retain and scope
exit runs no per-element drain. `try_admit_container_method` guards that with
`container_visible_here`, which disqualifies a container declared OUTSIDE the
closure / `defer` / `par` body the push sits in. A container declared INSIDE the
closure passes that test -- while the frozen root pushed into it still comes
from the ENCLOSING frame, and a closure's environment can outlive the call. So
the container carries a non-counting handle past the value whose refcount it
skips, which is exactly the use-after-free property 3 exists to prevent.

    shared struct Node { val: i64, mut kids: Vec[Node] }
    fn leak(n: frozen Node) -> OnceFn() -> i64 {
        return || { let mut v: Vec[Node] = Vec.new(); v.push(n); v.len() };
    }

MEASURED ON `main`, not inferred: that checks CLEAN as of 200fa8d6.

Every other admission in `frozen_escape.rs` is suppressed by `in_closure` --
stage 1's first draft accepted a scalar read inside a closure body and was
closed for this reason at the time. The container arm, added later in 3c, never
got the same gate.

WHY IT ONLY BECAME REACHABLE NOW, which is worth stating because it means
nothing unsound had shipped before: the shape was covered by two unrelated
masks. For a `frozen` PARAMETER the push was a TYPE error first (`expected
'Node', found 'ref Node'`), and for a `freeze`-statement LOCAL the ordinary
borrow-escape analysis catches the returned closure ("closure with `ref` capture
of `g` escapes its scope by being returned"). 200fa8d6 removed the first, and
the second never covered the parameter case. A mask is not a guard.

FIX. `try_admit_container_method` rejects the container outright when
`cx.in_closure`. Rejecting rather than merely declining is deliberate: it takes
the container out of the candidate set, so `c[i]` inside the closure stops being
a frozen place too, and the push falls through to the ordinary walk that reports
it as the capture it is. A container declared inside a `par` branch is
unaffected -- branches join before return, and admitting that sharing is the
point of the feature.

TESTS: tests/ownership.rs `a_frozen_container_store_is_refused_inside_a_closure`
-- three reject rows (an escaping closure holding a `frozen` parameter, a local
closure holding one, and a `freeze`-statement local), each asserting a frozen
diagnostic, plus the control that keeps the gate from being "refuse every
container": the identical push OUTSIDE a closure is still admitted.
Stash-proved red.

title: kata #133's par lane compiles and runs after B-2026-08-01-33, but restoring it is the whole bench pipeline -- the .kara's "DOES NOT COMPILE" header, bench.sh's skip, results.json and the README all still say the lane is withdrawn
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the kata-side half of B-2026-08-01-33, split out so the
task stays tracked now that the compiler half is done.

WHAT IS DONE: kata #133's par lane compiles and runs. Measured on the real file
with two kata-side changes and nothing else -- an index-cursor `Vec` worklist
instead of `VecDeque` + `pop_front` (which is what the C mirror does, so it
moves TOWARD algorithm parity), and graph construction moved into a helper that
returns the root, so the `freeze` source is uniquely bound. It prints 500,
bench.sh's own `expected` sink, and agrees across interp / JIT / AOT /
`KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, and why it is its own item rather than a sentence: restoring
the lane is the whole benchmark pipeline, not a source edit.

  * rewrite `leetcode/101-200/133-clone-graph/bench/clone_bfs_par.kara`, whose
    52-line header currently explains at length why it does NOT compile and
    cites B-2026-08-01-33 -- that header is now wrong end to end;
  * un-skip it in `bench.sh` (which today prints "kara par lane withdrawn") and
    restore the par row;
  * run the bench properly -- one kata, matched karac + lean/full archives,
    `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` for the sequential lane, against the rayon / pthreads-C /
    goroutine-Go comparators already in the tree;
  * regenerate `results.json` and the README through the JSON pipeline rather
    than hand-editing numbers, and re-run the staleness stamper (an ISO date or
    a bare B-ID written inside a `## Benchmarks` section deletes its banner).

A SANITY TIMING EXISTS AND MUST NOT BE QUOTED AS A RESULT: 0.03 s for the
18-branch par lane against 0.17 s sequential, same compiler, auto-par off, user
CPU 0.16 -> 0.44. One build, one machine, no hyperfine, no comparators, no
archive pinning, and `/usr/bin/time -p` resolves to 10 ms on a 30 ms run.

WHY IT LOOKS WORTH DOING, as an expectation to be tested rather than a claim:
the README's existing par row has C-pthreads at 10.1 ms, rust-rayon at 37.0 ms
and go-goroutines at 95.3 ms. A ~30 ms Kara lane would sit between C and rayon
-- ahead of two comparators, behind one. That is a publishable and honest row,
and it is also the outcome that has to be MEASURED before the README is touched.

ALSO WORTH DECIDING in the same slice: `bfs.kara` and `dfs.kara` are the
sequential solution files and need no `frozen` at all, so the only question is
whether the par lane's index-cursor shape should become the kata's canonical
BFS.

-- DONE (2026-08-07), kara-katas 2603167. THE LANE IS PUBLISHED, AND IT IS A TIE
   WITH RAYON RATHER THAN A WIN. --

MEASURED, M5 Pro (6P + 12E = 18 cores), hyperfine `--warmup 5 --runs 30
--shell=none`, all four printing the sink 500, karac 0.1.0-dev.5596+g6bf0dbf6a
with archives rebuilt from the same commit:

    c    clone_bfs (pthreads)     10.1 +/- 0.4 ms    981%
    kara clone_bfs (`par {}`)     35.9 +/- 2.1 ms   1341%
    rust clone_bfs (rayon)        36.9 +/- 2.4 ms   1202%
    go   clone_bfs (goroutines)   97.2 +/- 1.6 ms    731%

THE RAYON ROW IS A TIE, NOT A WIN, and the README says so in those words: a
1.0 ms gap against sigma of 2.1 and 2.4 is inside the noise on both sides. The
honest one-line summary is that C is 3.56x ahead of both and both are ~2.7x
ahead of Go. Kara's own seq -> par speedup is 5.07x (182.1 -> 35.9).

THE PREDICTION ON THIS ROW WAS CLOSE AND THE FRAMING WAS WRONG. It said "a ~30 ms
Kara lane would sit between C and rayon -- ahead of two comparators, behind one".
The number landed at 35.9, and "ahead of rayon" is not a claim the spread
supports. Filed as a reminder that a rough single-build timing predicts the
MAGNITUDE fine and says nothing about whether a gap is real.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THE RESULT, and it is not in the table: Kara shares ONE graph
across all 18 branches; the Rust mirror cannot. `Rc<RefCell<Node>>` is not
`Send`, so rayon has each worker build its own private copy (its header says
so), and the alternative -- `Arc` -- puts an atomic RMW on every handle clone in
an entirely read-only traversal. Those are Rust's only two answers and they are
exactly the Rc-vs-Arc decision Kara exists to remove. Sharing instead of
rebuilding buys a TIE, not a lead; the rebuild rayon pays is O(N*deg) once per
worker against 500 BFS clones, order 3-4% of its work, so it does not explain
the tie away in either direction.

CONTROL FOR THE ONE KATA-SIDE CHANGE THAT COULD HAVE FLATTERED THE NUMBER. The
par file uses an index-cursor `Vec` worklist where the sequential file uses
`VecDeque` + `pop_front`. A/B'd on the SEQUENTIAL lane, where the queue form is
the only variable: 181.4 +/- 2.9 ms cursor vs 183.8 +/- 2.1 ms deque -- within
noise. The par number is not a queue-change artifact. (The change is also what
the C mirror does, so it moves toward parity rather than away.)

AN OBSERVATION LEFT UNCHASED, recorded rather than hidden: Kara burns ~2.7x the
sequential lane's CPU to buy 5.07x wall-clock, where C burns ~1.7x to buy 4.4x
(CPU 1341% vs 981%). Some of that is the 6P/12E split -- an efficiency core
spends more CPU-seconds on the same work -- but not obviously all of it, and
per-branch allocator contention is the other candidate. It is the visible gap
between this lane and C's, and it is a perf lead rather than a defect.

ALSO RETIRED: the BENCHMARKS.md flakiness note. B-2026-07-28-13's ~0.8%
SIGSEGV/SIGTRAP belonged to the stale pre-gate binary that was withdrawn. The
current lane, screened on the same 500-run sample that produced that figure,
gives 0 non-zero exits and 0 bad sinks.

title: a caller-retains struct PARAM whose callee moves a promoted `Option`/`Result` field out has two owners. FIXED by declining per FIELD instead of per struct TYPE: the residual leak the scope condition preserved is closed for every field no by-value callee body can take out, and the moved-out field keeps today's behaviour
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-07-20 when that row landed. Everything
below was measured there, on the disjunct WITHOUT the scope condition.

THE SHAPE. A struct that owns a `shared` field stays CALLER-RETAINS at a call
boundary (B-2026-08-05-32): the callee gets a shallow copy, entry-copies
nothing, and registers no drop. Arm the caller's drop for a promoted
`Option`/`Result` field (B-2026-08-07-20's disjunct) and a callee that moves
that field out double-frees, because the callee's move-out zeroing lands in ITS
copy of the struct and the caller's frame never sees the write.

    shared struct Node { v: i64 }
    struct A { n: Option[Node], m: Option[Map[String, i64]] }

    fn take(a: A) -> i64 { match a.m { Some(x) => { x.len() } None => { 0 } } }

Measured with the disjunct unscoped, 10 iterations, BOTH opt levels:

    match a.m { Some(x) => x.len() }          470 errs / 26 invalid frees
    let mm = a.m; match mm { Some(x) => .. }  470 / 26
    match a.m { Some(x) => x }   (ESCAPES)    470 / 26

TWO REPAIRS ARE ALREADY ELIMINATED, both by measurement rather than by
argument:

  * "GIVE THE CALLEE ITS OWN COPY." The `let mm = a.m` row is exactly the shape
    `deep_copy_owned_struct_param_field_move` exists to handle, and it breaks
    anyway. That helper duplicates a `{ptr,len,cap}` buffer, and a `Map`/`Set`
    HANDLE is the one thing it cannot duplicate — the same fact that closes the
    copy-support arm of the promotion gate in the first place. The band-aid's
    failure is the proof, not a gap to fill.

  * "RETRACT THE CALLER'S BINDING DROP." The first reading was that the caller's
    named binding is the second owner. Measured against a FRESH TEMP argument,
    where there is no binding to retract: still 470 at both levels. The second
    owner exists independently of any named binding — it is a property of the
    caller-retains frame, not of the caller's spelling.

WHAT IT NEEDS. A callee-BODY predicate — "does this callee move this promoted
field out of this param" — in the shape `mono_entry_copies_aggregate_param`
already uses: an answer the CALLEE computes and the CALLER consults, so the two
cannot disagree. That is a different kind of question from every predicate in
this family today, all of which are answered from a TYPE.

Note also that the caller's drop for a shared-owning struct does two jobs —
rc-dec the shared field and free the value fields — and only the value half
should be given up when the callee moves a field out; retracting the whole drop
is what B-2026-08-05-32 measured as stranding the RC box. So the fix is
plausibly a split of the combined drop plus the callee-body predicate that
decides when to take the split.

WHY MEDIUM RATHER THAN HIGH: it is not reachable today. B-2026-08-07-20's scope
condition declines the disjunct for exactly these structs, and
`asan_shared_owning_struct_option_map_by_value_param_single_owner` pins that.
What is live is the RESIDUAL LEAK the scope condition preserves: a shared-owning
struct that IS passed by value still never frees its `Option[Map]` field on the
paths where no callee moves it out. That is the same leak B-2026-08-07-20 fixed
for every other shape, and closing this row closes it here too.

REPRODUCTION: drop the `&& !self.struct_used_as_bare_by_value_param(struct_name)`
conjunct from `shared_owning_struct_sole_field_owner` (`param_own.rs`) and build
the three spellings above under `valgrind --leak-check=full` at
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` and `2`. The scope-guard fixture turns red immediately.

RESOLUTION (9b4abaf0). The callee-BODY predicate this row asked for, at
(type, FIELD) granularity rather than (type) -- which turned out to be the
part worth getting right, and is not what the row's own text proposed.

THE ROW FRAMED THIS AS ONE PROBLEM; IT IS TWO. The double free is real and
stays fenced off. But the scope condition fencing it off
(`struct_used_as_bare_by_value_param`) answers a SIGNATURE question -- "is
this type ever a bare by-value param" -- and then declines the drop for the
WHOLE STRUCT. One callee that could move one promoted field out therefore
also declined every OTHER promoted field, including fields no callee anywhere
mentions. Those leak, and nothing in the program can free them:

    struct Sa { n: Option[Node], m: Option[Map[String, i64]] }
    fn reads_n(a: Sa) -> i64 { match a.n { Some(nn) => { nn.v } None => { 0 } } }

`a.m` is never named at a call boundary at all. Measured at 720 direct /
5,740 indirect bytes over 10 iterations, at BOTH opt levels, under valgrind
and again under LSan. That is the same 720 B / 10 iterations B-2026-08-07-20
measured for the no-call case -- the scope condition simply reintroduced it
for any struct that also happens to be passed somewhere.

WHAT LANDED. `struct_by_value_param_body_takes_field(struct_name, field)`
walks the BODY of every fn / method / owned-`self` receiver that takes the
struct by value and asks whether it could take THAT field out. The drop
synthesis consults it per promoted field, as a SECOND chance for fields the
type-wide gate already refused. `shared_owning_struct_sole_field_owner_core`
is unchanged, so the for-loop strict-shared copy-support site that pairs off
it (`param_own.rs`, the `Option` arm under `copy_support_for_loop_shared_mode`)
is untouched.

CONSERVATIVE AT EVERY STEP, in the direction that keeps today's behaviour:
no program snapshot means assume the worst; a param whose pattern is a
destructure rather than a plain binding means assume the worst; a trait
method's bare param means assume the worst; and the body test treats any use
of the param that is NOT a projection to a different field as taking the
whole struct. A false `true` costs the pre-existing leak, a false `false`
would cost a double free.

`match a.m { Some(x) => .. }` is caught for the RIGHT REASON rather than by
accident. The payload binds BY VALUE, so the match itself is the move -- which
is exactly why the row measured all three spellings (`match`, `let mm = a.m`,
and the escaping `Some(x) => x`) at an identical 470 / 26. All three reach the
predicate through the same `a.m` projection base.

THE PAIRING RULE IS NOT OWED A WIDENING HERE, and this was checked rather
than argued. "Widening the DROP obliges the move sites to widen with it"
binds when the field CLASS changes; B-2026-08-07-20 already paired this drop
with the move sites for exactly these payloads, and this row widens only
WHICH STRUCTS qualify. Verified anyway with a program where the same struct
is a by-value param elsewhere AND the caller does `let mm = y.m` and `match
w.m`: if the newly-armed drop and the move-site zeroing disagreed, that would
double-free rather than leak. Clean at both opt levels.

WHAT IS STILL DECLINED, and why that is the row's remaining open question
rather than a regression: a field a by-value callee's body DOES name keeps
today's behaviour exactly -- the callee owns the move-out, nothing
double-frees, and the non-moving paths through that same field still leak.
Separating those needs the read-vs-move distinction inside the callee body,
which the whole-program AST walk cannot make; the row's "split the combined
drop" note remains the shape for that. What changed is that this now costs
only the fields a callee actually touches, instead of every field of any
struct that is passed anywhere.

tracker: tests/memory_sanitizer.rs — the six `#[ignore]`d fixtures carry their own error text
title: six ASAN fixtures were passing VACUOUSLY — their programs fail typecheck and `karac build` would refuse them, but the harness only ever asserted the OWNERSHIP result, so codegen ran anyway and the tests reported ok. TRIAGED AND CLOSED: five were real inference gaps (three distinct ones), the sixth was the compiler being right
detail:
ID NOTE: filed as -6, renumbered to -7 — a sibling session took -6 for an
unrelated struct-param double-free while this was in flight.

SURFACE NOTE: test infrastructure (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs harness), 
recorded as `other` because the controlled surface vocabulary has no 
test-infra value.

SOURCE NOTE: found while stash-proving B-2026-08-08-5, whose new fixture passed
against a compiler with the fix reverted. Chasing that turned up the harness
hole rather than a problem with the fix.

CAUSE. `run_under_asan_opts` drives the phases by hand: parse, desugar,
resolve, typecheck, lower, ownershipcheck. It called
`super::common::assert_ownership_clean` and never looked at `typed.errors`. A
fixture whose program failed TYPECHECK was still handed to `compile_to_object`,
which emitted something, which ran. So the fixture exercised a program the
compiler REJECTS, and whatever memory behaviour it measured was not the
behaviour its source describes.

FIXED IN THE HARNESS (1bb5328a): typecheck errors now panic with the same
wording and the same reasoning as the existing codegen-failure panic -- a
signal that always means "the compiler rejected the program under test" must
fail loudly rather than slide through.

THE SIX, marked `#[ignore]` with their individual errors so they are visibly
deferred rather than silently green:

    asan_autograd_activations_and_losses
    asan_freshtemp_tensor_ref_arg_assoc_call_no_crash
    asan_freshtemp_tensor_ref_arg_free_fn_no_leak
        -- all three: expected `ref Tensor[f32, [?]]`, found `Tensor[f64, [N]]`
    asan_column_sorted_argsort_narrow_widths_no_leak
        -- expected `Vec[u32]`, found `Vec[i64]`
    asan_with_capacity_zero_no_leak
        -- expected `Vec[i64]`, found `Vec[?T0]`
    asan_unannotated_boxed_optres_let_frees_its_box
        -- cannot infer type parameter `E`

EACH IS A SEPARATE QUESTION, and the split matters for whoever picks this up:
the tensor trio looks like one dtype/shape-inference issue in the FIXTURES
(they are written with `f64` literals against `f32` signatures) and may be a
test-source fix; the `Vec[?T0]` and `E` rows look like real inference gaps that
`karac build` would report to a user too. Nobody has established which are
which -- that is the first step, not the fix.

RESOLUTION (7c7de323). The triage the row asked for was done first, and it
came out BACKWARDS from the guess above. The tensor trio was NOT a
fixture-source dtype problem, and the uninferrable `E` was NOT an inference
gap. Each of the four questions reduced to a 2-4 line probe:

  A. TENSOR TRIO -- real gap. `fn take(v: ref Tensor[f32,[?]])` called with an
     inline `take(Tensor.from([1.0, 2.0]))` failed; the OWNED spelling of the
     identical param passed. At an argument the published expectation is the
     formal param's type VERBATIM, so a `ref` param handed the `Tensor.from`
     element-adoption peek a `Ref(Tensor[..])`, the `Named{"Tensor"}` arm
     missed, and the leaves fell back to their `f64` default. The peek now
     peels `ref`/`mut ref`, as `contextual_scalar_collection_type` already did.

  B. COLUMN -- real gap, and NOT Column-specific. `let c: Column[u32] =
     Column.from_vec([30, 10, 20])` seeded `?T = u32` from the annotation and
     then INFERRED the array literal as `Vec[i64]` anyway, so pass 2 rejected
     the argument pass 1 had just been told to expect. A seeded generic PATH
     call now CHECKS a collection-literal argument against its resolved slot,
     which is what the non-generic call path has always done.

  C. `Vec[?T0]` -- real gap. An expectation reaches a `?` OPERAND but not a
     method RECEIVER, so `Vec.try_with_capacity(0).unwrap()` synth-returned
     `Result[Vec[?T], _]` and the element var had no source. Naming the
     intermediate always worked. Pinned at the receiver in `infer_method_call`.

  D. UNINFERRABLE `E` -- NOT a gap. `let d = Result.Ok(mkres(i))` leaves `E`
     with nothing to infer from, and "cannot infer type parameter 'E'" is the
     correct answer. The fixture was wrong. Its unannotated-`let` shape is
     preserved by binding a call whose declared return type supplies `E`.

THREE THINGS THIS COST, each found by measurement rather than by reading:

  1. Gate 3 on fix B is load-bearing. `check_expr` is not a narrower
     `infer_expr` -- it also runs `check_int_widening_coercion`, which is
     STRICTER than the `check_assignable` pass 2 applies. Running it on an
     arbitrary argument broke `return Some(i)` with `i: i64` into an
     `Option[u64]` -- the exact shape B-2026-08-05-19's own comment promises is
     unaffected "because seeding binds the RETURN type and the payload is then
     an ordinary scalar assignment where numeric coercion stays permissive".
     Three typechecker tests caught it. The gate is now: seeding fired, slot
     fully concrete, AND the argument is a collection literal.

  2. Suppressing pass 2 for a pass-1-checked argument SILENTLY LOST a
     rejection. `Column.from_vec(["a", "b"])` into a `Column[u32]` errored
     before the change and passed after it. Measured against a stashed tree,
     not assumed.

  3. Even with pass 2 restored it still passed -- because check-mode's
     collection-literal adoption (B-2026-08-05-19) stamps the expected type on
     any collection literal WITHOUT reading its elements, so `Vec[String]` was
     overwritten with `Vec[u32]` and sailed through. That hole needs no
     generics to reach (`let v: Vec[u32] = ["a", "b"]` passed on a clean tree)
     and predates this row, but fix B routes generic call arguments through
     check-mode too, so leaving it would have turned a call shape that
     rejected CORRECTLY into one that did not. Adoption now requires a NUMERIC
     source, and refuses the float -> integer direction (`[1.5] : Vec[u32]` is
     a silent truncation) -- which a generic call already rejected and a `let`
     did not, so this also settles that disagreement rather than resolving it
     toward the permissive side.

FIX C IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE, for the same reason B-2026-08-08-5's coercion
had to be narrowed: the typechecker must admit exactly what codegen lowers.
The first cut short-circuited the whole method call in check-mode and returned
the expected type. That typechecked -- and then died with "codegen: no handler
for method 'unwrap' on non-identifier receiver", because the early return
skips the rest of `infer_method_call`, which is what populates
`method_unwrap_inner_types`, which is the table the dispatcher reads. The
pinning is now published on its own channel and consumed at the receiver, so
the ordinary typing still runs.

STASH-PROVED: with the source changes reverted and the repaired fixtures kept,
five of the six go red and the sixth (D) stays green -- exactly the split the
triage predicted.

RESIDUAL, deliberately not fixed here (see B-2026-08-08-8): fix B reaches only
PATH callees and only collection-literal arguments.

tracker: probe: `fn wrap[T](v: Vec[T]) -> Holder[T]` called as `let h: Holder[u32] = wrap([30, 10, 20])`
title: expected-return seeding reaches only PATH callees, and its argument checking only collection literals — a plain generic free fn still rejects a context-adopting argument. FIXED both, and the widening exposed a soundness hole (B-2026-08-08-9) that had to close first
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the residual left standing by B-2026-08-08-7 (7c7de323), which
fixed the seeded-argument path for the shapes its fixtures needed. Filed
rather than folded in because each half has its own regression risk and
neither blocks a test today.

TWO SEPARATE LIMITS, both measured:

  1. SEEDING IS PATH-CALLEE ONLY. `let h: Holder[u32] = wrap([30, 10, 20])`
     over a user-defined `fn wrap[T](v: Vec[T]) -> Holder[T]` still reports
     "expected Holder<u32>, found Holder<i64>". The expectation is never
     published for a bare `Identifier` callee -- `seedable_call` admits
     `ExprKind::Path` plus the three bare enum constructors `Some`/`Ok`/`Err`.
     That restriction is DELIBERATE (B-2026-08-05-19 / -25): a broader gate
     leaked the expectation into a nested call inside an argument, and
     `let b = Bag { items: [..] }` then had its unsolved metavar bound by the
     inner call. So widening it needs the leak addressed, not just the gate
     relaxed. Consequence today: `Type.assoc(literal)` adopts and
     `free_fn(literal)` does not, for the same literal and the same slot.

  2. ARGUMENT CHECKING IS COLLECTION-LITERAL ONLY.
     `let c: Column[u32] = Column.from_vec(Vec.new())` still reports
     "expected Vec<u32>, found Vec<?T1>" -- a constructor argument whose
     element is an UNSOLVED VAR rather than a literal default. Admitting it
     looks safe in isolation (a typevar has nothing to truncate), but the
     gate exists because `check_expr` also runs the integer-widening check,
     which is stricter than pass 2's `check_assignable`; widening it broke
     `return Some(i)` with `i: i64` into `Option[u64]` once already. A fix
     wants to key on the ARGUMENT's inferred type carrying an unsolved var,
     not on its syntactic shape, and that means inferring before deciding.

NEITHER IS A REGRESSION -- both spellings failed before 7c7de323 too. The
workaround for each is the explicit element spelling (`[30u32, ...]`) or a
named intermediate, which is what the affected code already does.

RESOLUTION (a2ce6b79). Both limits fixed. Limit 1 as filed; limit 2 by a
DIFFERENT route than the one this row proposed, and the row's own proposal
would have been wrong.

  LIMIT 1 -- the guard that made the path-only gate necessary is gone.
  `seedable_call` now admits `ExprKind::Identifier` as well as `Path`. The
  nested-call leak the restriction existed for (`let b = Bag { items: [..] }`,
  where the first inner call bound the outer metavar) is blocked by the
  `expectation_is_concrete` condition that was added AFTER the restriction:
  that leak needs an UNANNOTATED `let`, whose expectation is an unsolved
  metavar, and such an expectation is no longer published at all. Re-ran the
  `Bag` shape rather than reasoning about it; it passes.

  LIMIT 2 -- NOT by widening gate 3, which is what this row proposed. Pass 2
  compares a freshly-resolved SLOT against `arg_ty`, which is the snapshot
  pass 1 took at inference time -- and pass 1's own `unify_types` binds that
  snapshot's metavars immediately afterwards. So `Column.from_vec(Vec.new())`
  was told `expected 'Vec<u32>', found 'Vec<?T1>'` while `?T1` was already
  bound to `u32` IN THE SAME MAP. Resolving `arg_ty` the way the slot is
  already resolved fixes it without touching a check-mode path, which
  sidesteps the `check_int_widening_coercion` hazard gate 3 exists for
  entirely. It also reaches further than the proposed fix: `pair(Vec.new(),
  sv)`, where a SIBLING ARGUMENT rather than the expectation fixes the
  element, was equally broken and is equally fixed.

WHAT THE WIDENING EXPOSED. Probing what limit 1 would newly admit turned up a
miscompile, filed as B-2026-08-08-9 and fixed in the same commit because
shipping limit 1 without it would have spread it from path callees to every
generic free function: a slot bound by the EXPECTATION never got the
narrowing check, so `let x: u8 = id(big)` with `big: i64 = 5000000000`
typechecked and printed 5000000000.

THE LOAD-BEARING TEST IS THE CODEGEN E2E, not the typecheck assertions. On a
stashed tree the same program returns "3\n0\n1" -- `h.items[1]` reads 0,
which is a u32-strided read over i64-laid-out data. The typecheck rejection
was masking a real layout disagreement, so "admit the program" and "lower it
correctly" are one change here, not two.

STILL OPEN, found while probing and unrelated to inference: a generic struct
with a `Vec[T]` FIELD returned by value from a generic function fails codegen
outright -- `struct Column[T] { data: Vec[T] }` plus either `fn from_vec[T](v:
Vec[T]) -> Column[T]` or the `impl` spelling dies with `Function return type
does not match operand type of return inst! ret { { ptr, i64, i64 } } %field /
ptr`. A scalar field (`struct Wrap[T] { v: T }`) is fine, and the direct
struct literal is fine. Pre-existing -- reproduces identically on a stashed
tree with a fully concrete `Vec[u32]` argument, no metavar and no seeding
involved. Filed as B-2026-08-08-10.

title: a generic slot bound by the EXPECTATION skipped the narrowing check — `let x: u8 = id(big)` with `big: i64 = 5000000000` typechecked and printed 5000000000
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by probing what B-2026-08-08-8's callee-gate widening
would newly reach, not by a failing test. Fixed in the same commit because
shipping that widening without this would have spread the hole from path
callees to every generic free function.

    fn id[T](x: T) -> T { return x; }
    fn main() {
        let big: i64 = 5000000000;
        let x: u8 = id(big);   // accepted; PRINTS 5000000000
    }

`check_assignable` is permissive between integer types. That is correct when
the slot was fixed by the argument itself -- there is nothing to narrow TO.
But expected-return seeding (B-2026-08-05-19) fixes the slot from the
OUTSIDE, and nothing re-checked the argument against it, so a wide variable
flowed into a narrow slot unchallenged and the call's return type was then
the narrow one. The declared `u8` binding printed a value no `u8` can hold.

NOT A NEW POLICY -- A HOLE IN AN EXISTING ONE. Every other spelling of the
same coercion is already rejected by B-2026-07-09-7:

    let x: u8 = big;                        // rejected
    fn takeu8(x: u8) -> u8 { ... }
    let x: u8 = takeu8(big);                // rejected
    let x: u8 = Boxy.wrap(big);             // ACCEPTED, prints 5000000000

PRE-EXISTING on the path-callee spelling: the `Boxy.wrap` form above builds
and prints 5000000000 on a stashed tree. The identifier-callee form was
rejected there only by accident -- unseeded, `id(big)` infers `i64` and the
`let` narrowing check catches the whole call. Widening the gate made seeding
fire, the return type became `u8`, and the `let` check saw `u8 = u8`.

THE FIX IS DELIBERATELY NARROWER THAN THE GENERAL RULE, and both exemptions
were paid for by measured failures -- a blanket `check_int_widening_coercion`
at the seeded argument broke three existing tests:

  1. SAME-WIDTH reinterpretation stays permissive. `return Some(i)` with
     `i: i64` into an `Option[u64]` is tested and deliberate
     (`generic_numeric_arg_same_layout_and_literals_still_accepted`: "same
     eight bytes, only the interpretation differs"). It DISAGREES with the
     plain `return i` into a `-> u64` fn, which is rejected -- but that
     disagreement predates this row and settling it is a language decision,
     not a bug fix. Only a STRICT width reduction is caught.
  2. A COMPILE-TIME CONSTANT whose value fits stays permissive. `Some(0 - 1)`
     into an `Option[i32]` is arithmetic over literals, so the bare-literal
     exemption inside `check_int_widening_coercion` misses it, but the value
     is known and in range -- the whole point of B-2026-08-05-25.
     Const-evaluated against the TARGET, whose range check IS the fit test; a
     variable of unknown value fails the eval and is caught, which is exactly
     the bug.

fix: f773c317. `llvm_type_for_type_expr` (`src/codegen/types_lowering.rs`) now lowers a user-declared struct through its own (mono) struct type when its name collides with a prelude type, ahead of the hard-coded `name == "Column"` / `"DataFrame"` / `"Tensor"` / `"Interner"` handle arms that keyed on the NAME alone and returned a bare `ptr`. Guarded on `user_shadowed_prelude_types`, the declaration pass's existing record, which excludes `stdlib_origin` items. NOT the generic-struct-return gap this row describes: a non-generic `struct Column { data: Vec[i64] }` fails identically pre-fix, and renaming the struct is a one-token fix. The complement of `reject_shadowed_prelude_types` (B-2026-08-02-13), which still refuses built-in machinery over a user value — all 17 of its tests pass unchanged, as do the 159 built-in Column/DataFrame/Tensor/Interner/Arrow codegen tests. Fixture `user_struct_shadowing_a_prelude_type_name_keeps_its_own_layout`, stash-proven red.
title: a generic struct with a `Vec[T]` FIELD returned by value from a generic function fails codegen — `ret { { ptr, i64, i64 } } %field` against a `ptr` return
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while probing B-2026-08-08-8; unrelated to inference and
left open. Pre-existing -- reproduces identically on a stashed tree.

    struct Column[T] { data: Vec[T] }
    fn from_vec[T](v: Vec[T]) -> Column[T] { return Column { data: v }; }
    fn main() {
        let v: Vec[u32] = [1, 2, 3];
        let c: Column[u32] = from_vec(v);      // codegen failed
        print(c.data.len());
    }

    error: codegen failed: Module verification failed: "Function return type
    does not match operand type of return inst!
      ret { { ptr, i64, i64 } } %field
     ptr"

The returned value is the struct BY VALUE (`{ { ptr, i64, i64 } }` -- a
one-field struct wrapping a Vec control block) while the emitted function's
return type is `ptr`, so the two disagree at the `ret`. Reads like the
generic monomorph picking an indirect/sret return for the signature and a
direct one for the body, or vice versa.

NARROWED, three probes:

  - `struct Wrap[T] { v: T }` with `fn make(x: T) -> Wrap[T]` -- BUILDS and
    runs. So it is not generic-struct-return as such.
  - The `impl[T] Column[T] { fn from_vec(..) }` spelling and the free-fn
    spelling fail IDENTICALLY. So it is not the associated-function path.
  - `let c: Column[u32] = Column { data: v }` (direct struct literal, no
    call) BUILDS and runs. So it is not the struct's layout on its own.

The trigger is the combination: a heap-carrying (multi-word control block)
field in a GENERIC struct returned by value from a GENERIC function. The
argument is a fully concrete `Vec[u32]` here -- no metavar, no seeding, no
inference involvement at all.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE PROBE: this is the shape a user-defined columnar or
wrapper type takes, and the failure is at LLVM module verification -- there is
no diagnostic pointing at the source, just a raw verifier message.

── FIXED f773c317 — AND IT IS NOT WHAT THIS ROW SAYS IT IS ──

The title, the class, the tracker and all three "NARROWED" probes describe a
generic-struct-return codegen gap. There is no such gap. This is a NAME
COLLISION: `Column` is a PRELUDE TYPE (the phase-11 nullable 1-D Arrow column),
and `llvm_type_for_type_expr` keys its built-in HANDLE lowerings on the NAME
alone —

    if name == "Column" { return ptr }   // + DataFrame, Tensor, Interner, …

— so a user's `struct Column[T] { data: Vec[T] }` lowered to a bare `ptr` at its
signature while the body returned the real `{ { ptr, i64, i64 } }` aggregate.
Hence the verifier message, which names the two shapes and nothing else.

ONE COMMAND SETTLES IT: rename the struct to `Kolumn`, change nothing else, and
the identical program builds and prints 3.

THE THREE PROBES ARE ALL CONSISTENT WITH THE COLLISION, which is why they
narrowed to the wrong place:

  * `Wrap[T] { v: T }` builds — `Wrap` is not a prelude name.
  * free-fn and `impl` spellings fail identically — both lower the return type
    through the same hard-coded arm.
  * the direct struct literal builds — that path takes the struct's registered
    `struct_types` entry rather than the return-type lowering, so it never
    consults the built-in arm. (Checked under valgrind: genuinely correct
    pre-fix, not silently corrupt.)

NEITHER GENERICS NOR THE `Vec` FIELD IS THE TRIGGER, measured rather than
argued. A NON-GENERIC `struct Column { data: Vec[i64], name: String }` returned
from a plain `fn make(v: Vec[i64]) -> Column` fails identically on the pre-fix
compiler, and so do `DataFrame` / `Interner` / `Tensor` shadows. The generic
struct in the probe was incidental.

── THE FIX, AND WHY IT IS THIS ONE ──

A single guard ahead of every hard-coded name arm: if the name is in
`user_shadowed_prelude_types` — the declaration pass's own record, which
excludes `stdlib_origin` items so the stdlib is never flagged against itself —
lower through the struct's real (mono) type instead.

This deliberately does NOT make shadowing safe in general, and it is the
complement of machinery that already exists rather than a replacement for it.
`reject_shadowed_prelude_types` (B-2026-08-02-13) refuses to run BUILT-IN
machinery over a user value, with an actionable message. This stops describing a
USER value with the built-in's layout. Both are needed; the 17 `http_client_-
codegen` shadow-rejection tests still pass unchanged.

── MEASURED ──

Pre-fix: the row's repro, the non-generic twin, and the `DataFrame` /
`Interner` / `Tensor` shadows all die at module verification. Post-fix: all five
build, run, and agree with the interpreter, valgrind-clean at `-O0` and `-O2`.
The 159 built-in Column / DataFrame / Tensor / Interner / Arrow codegen tests
pass unchanged, which is the regression that matters — the guard must not
divert a genuine built-in.

Fixture `user_struct_shadowing_a_prelude_type_name_keeps_its_own_layout`
(`tests/codegen.rs`), stash-proven red. It carries the non-generic case and a
no-collision generic control (`Holder[T] { data: Vec[T] }`) specifically so the
next reader cannot repeat this row's misdiagnosis.

── WHAT REMAINS, and it is the real subject ──

One namespace for stdlib and user types (B-2026-08-02-13) is still the
underlying defect. This closes the layout half for a shadowed struct; a user
type shadowing a prelude name still cannot be USED with that prelude type's own
API, and the collision is still discovered at codegen rather than refused with a
source-level diagnostic at declaration.

tracker: src/parser.rs (`frozen T` lowers to `TypeKind::Ref(T)` at parse time)
title: a type error about a `frozen` parameter names its type `ref T` -- the surface keyword and the diagnostic disagree, because `frozen T` lowers to `Ref(T)` at parse time and the typechecker only ever sees the borrow
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while measuring every `frozen` rule for B-2026-08-01-33's
spec adoption. Cosmetic, and filed rather than fixed to keep that change to
documentation.

    fn leak(n: frozen Node) -> Node { return n; }

    error[typecheck]: expected 'Node', found 'ref Node'
    error[ownership]: `frozen` parameter `n` escapes here

The ownership diagnostic is right and actionable. The typecheck one immediately
above it names a type the author never wrote and cannot find in their source,
and the two describe the same parameter.

WHY IT HAPPENS, and it is a deliberate design choice rather than an oversight:
B-2026-08-01-33's RC-suppression slice lowers `frozen T` to `ref T` at parse
time, because non-owning is exactly what `ref` already means and expressing the
mode in the existing borrow vocabulary is what let codegen stay untouched
(`TypeKind::Frozen` is never constructed). The frozen-ness survives on
`Param::is_frozen` for the checking phases. So every phase downstream of the
parser sees a borrow, including the one that formats type names.

FIX SHAPE: the type-mismatch renderer needs to know that a parameter's declared
type was spelled `frozen`, which `Param::is_frozen` already records --
`karac fmt` solves the same problem the same way (it unwraps the borrow so
`frozen N` round-trips rather than printing `frozen ref N`). Scoped to the
renderer, so no lowering changes.

WHY LOW: it is confusing, not wrong -- the ownership error beside it names the
real problem, and no program miscompiles. But `frozen` is new language surface
and this is the first error many authors will see from it.

RESOLUTION (4f32b1e1). The fix shape this row proposed, taken as written: a
span-keyed set records where a `frozen` PARAMETER was read as a value
(`current_fn_frozen_params` already tracked which parameters those are), and
the canonical assignment-mismatch site consults it before formatting. Nothing
about lowering changes -- the type is still the borrow every other phase agreed
on, and only the rendering differs, so `karac fmt`'s existing unwrap and this
now solve the same problem the same way at the two places a user reads a type
name back.

KEYED ON THE PARAMETER HAVING BEEN DECLARED `frozen`, NOT ON THE TYPE BEING A
BORROW. That distinction is the whole content of the fix and is pinned: a plain
`ref P` parameter in the identical shape still renders `found 'ref P'`, because
rewriting every borrow would replace one wrong spelling with another. Covered at
both a RETURN and an ARGUMENT position, since the row's repro is a return and
the argument form reaches the same site by a different route.

tracker: probe: `let p: P = P{..}; let q: Q = Q{..};` in `main` under default auto-par -- read-only in the joining scope gives `Invalid read of size 8` from a block freed in `__par_branch_0_0`; pushed into a container gives a definitely-lost box. Both clean under `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.
title: an RC-bearing `shared struct` published as an auto-par return slot is never adopted by the joining scope -- it LEAKS when the branch suppresses its release and is a USE-AFTER-FREE when it does not; `SlotOwnership` has no RC variant, and auto-par is ON by default
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while probing B-2026-08-08-4's declined "a `Vec[weak N]`
held as a struct FIELD leaks" remainder. It is NOT that item (see the last
section), and it is NOT weak-specific despite being found through a weak probe.

THE SHAPE, and it is an ordinary one:

    shared struct P { v: i64 }
    shared struct Q { a: i64, b: i64, c: i64 }
    fn main() {
        let seed: i64 = env.args().len();
        let p: P = P { v: seed };
        let q: Q = Q { a: seed, b: seed, c: seed };
        let mut w: Vec[P] = Vec.new();
        w.push(p);
        println(w.len());
    }

`p`'s box is never freed. 16 bytes with a strong `Vec[P]`; 24 with a
`Vec[weak P]`, which is the same box one word larger because a weak-targeted
type carries the `{ strong, weak }` header. valgrind `definitely lost`, at both
KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and =2.

THE GATE IS AUTO-PAR, WHICH IS ON BY DEFAULT. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` on the exact
same source is clean, for every fixture in this row. The analyzer splits `main`
into three branches (`__par_branch_0_0/1/2`); `p` is constructed in branch 0.

THE MECHANISM, from an IR diff of the same program with the gate on and off.
Branch 0 constructs `p` (strong=1), stores it into the par returns slot, and
then does `store ptr null, ptr %p` — so its own `rc_cleanup` block loads null,
takes `rc_cleanup_skip`, and correctly declines to release. Control returns to
`main`, which pushes `p` into the container. `main` then suppresses `p`'s
scope-exit release, which is right on its face: the push moved ownership to the
container, and the container's drain is what should complete it. The drain does
run — `__karac_vec_elem_rc_dec_P` is emitted under BOTH settings — but the box
is still never freed. Diffing the two `main`s, exactly ONE `free` is missing
under auto-par:

    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0  main: ... __karac_vec_elem_rc_dec_P, karac_free_buf,
                             free, free, karac_free_buf, karac_free_buf
    auto-par (default) main: ... __karac_vec_elem_rc_dec_P, karac_free_buf,
                             karac_free_buf, karac_free_buf

The branch declines the obligation because it moved the value out; the joining
scope declines it because the container took it; the container's drain does not
complete it. The release falls between the three.

THE CONTAINER IS REQUIRED. A value transferred out of a branch and only READ in
`main` is clean (`x_no_container`, 3 branches, zero lost) — `main` emits the
free normally there. The leak needs the transferred binding to be MOVED INTO a
container in the joining scope.

FOUR THINGS THIS IS NOT, each measured rather than reasoned:

  * NOT weak-specific. The first probes all used `Vec[weak P]`; the strong
    `Vec[P]` twin leaks identically (16 B vs 24 B, the header word being the
    only difference). Any conclusion scoped to `weak` would be wrong.
  * NOT the `let` type annotation. `let p: P = ...` leaks where `let p = ...`
    is clean, but only because the annotation changes whether the auto-par
    analyzer fires. Same for declaration ORDER (a `Vec` declared before the
    structs is clean, after them leaks) and for the presence of a second,
    entirely unused binding. All three are auto-par triggers, not causes.
  * NOT a regression from f869989f. Measured on a tree with that commit's four
    source files reverted to its parent: the same fixtures leak, the same
    blocks, the same annotated-vs-inferred discriminator — at 16 B per box
    instead of 24, because the two-word `{ strong, weak }` header that commit
    correctly restored had not yet been applied. Same leak, smaller box.
  * NOT caught by the existing suite. `asan_vec_of_weak_back_edges_reclaims_a_
    cycle_no_leak` is genuinely green (0 valgrind errors, not the vacuous-LSan
    trap its own doc comment warns about) — it builds its graph in a helper,
    which is a shape the analyzer does not split.

A NOTE ON A VACUOUS CONTROL, because it nearly produced a wrong scope claim: the
first weak-vs-strong control was written without checking that auto-par actually
fired, and it did not (0 branches). It was "clean" because it never exercised the
transfer path. Any control for this row MUST assert the branch count — the
fixtures here count `^define .*@__par_branch` in the emitted IR.

STILL OPEN AND SEPARATE — the probe that started this. A `Vec[weak N]` held as a
struct FIELD, with a mutual weak cycle, leaks 48 bytes with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`,
so it is NOT this row. That is B-2026-08-08-4's own declined remainder
("a `Vec[weak N]` held as a struct FIELD still leaks"), independently confirmed

=== UPDATE, same session: THE SAME MACHINERY ALSO PRODUCES A USE-AFTER-FREE,
=== and two claims made above are corrected by it.

CORRECTION 1 — "THE CONTAINER IS REQUIRED" IS WRONG. It is required for the
leak to be VISIBLE, not for the bug to happen. Without the container, `main`'s
par returns-struct is a STACK alloca still holding the published pointer at
exit, so valgrind's conservative stack scan counts the box as *still reachable*
and reports nothing. Pushing into a container moves the pointer into the heap
buffer, `karac_free_buf` frees that buffer, and only then is the box
unreachable and reported. The container frees the last pointer, it does not
create the defect. This is the same conservative-reachability trap
`asan_vec_of_weak_back_edges_reclaims_a_cycle_no_leak`'s doc comment warns
about, hit from the other direction.

CORRECTION 2 — the no-container shape is not "clean", it is a USE-AFTER-FREE.
`x_no_container` (a transferred binding READ in the joining scope, no container)
reports:

    Invalid read of size 8
       at main
     Address 0x... is 8 bytes inside a block of size 16 free'd
       at free
       by __par_branch_0_0

4 valgrind errors, 0 with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`. It PRINTS THE RIGHT ANSWER — the
freed block had not been reused — which is exactly why it read as a passing
control. I recorded it as evidence that the container was required; it was
evidence of the second failure mode.

SO THE ROW IS ONE DEFECT WITH TWO FACES, chosen by whether the branch's queued
release is suppressed:

  * SUPPRESSED (branch nulls its local after the slot store) → nobody releases
    → LEAK. `u_strong_vec`, `u_weak_vec`, `t_p_first`, `v_ann_1vec`.
  * NOT SUPPRESSED (branch runs its release on the value it just published)
    → parent reads freed memory → USE-AFTER-FREE. `x_no_container`.

Both are the missing half of the same transfer: `SlotOwnership` (state.rs)
enumerates Map / File / Enum / Struct / User / Soa / Column / DataFrame /
Tensor and has NO variant for an RC-bearing shared struct. Those nine kinds are
REMOVED from the branch frame and re-registered against the parent's alloca by
`register_slot_ownership` (par_blocks.rs), which is the shape that makes the
parent the unique owner. The RC cleanup instead takes the sentinel path
(`nullify_local`, par_blocks.rs ~2203) — suppressed in the branch and never
adopted by the parent. The sentinel comment says the parent "receives an intact
pointer", which is true and insufficient: it receives the pointer without the
obligation.

Class raised from `leak` to `use-after-free` accordingly: a silent wrong-memory
read in ordinary auto-par code is the worse of the two faces, and the leak is
the same bug with the pointer still parked on the stack.

=== FIXED in 62619a88.

Both arms now transfer through `SlotOwnership` like every other cleanup kind:
a new `Rc { heap_type }` and a `SharedElided`, produced by the branch-side
transfer loop and re-registered by `register_one_slot_ownership` against the
PARENT's alloca under the same binding name (both actions reload by name at
drain time and carry their pointer only as an out-of-scope fallback). The
sentinel path's own comment already claimed the parent "re-registers the
equivalent cleanup against its fresh alloca" — this makes that true. When the
parent subsequently moves the value on, its ordinary move-suppression now sees
a normally registered cleanup and disarms it, which is why routing through the
parent is the right shape rather than having the branch guess.

Verified: leak 16 B (strong `Vec[P]`) / 24 B (`Vec[weak P]`) -> 0 definitely
lost; the read-only shape's `Invalid read of size 8` -> 0 invalid ops. Both at
KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and =2.

SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-08-15, which existed in shipped

`tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`'s harness compiles each fixture with

defect presenting as a leak in one shape and a use-after-free in another, in

than the "~1000 fixtures could go red" worry that motivated deferring it. Of
those 5:

    * B-2026-08-08-19 (codegen-gap) — a user method on a `shared struct` loses

compiler does not have is as broken as one that hides real ones, and it is
worse for morale — it trains readers to disbelieve the suite. The flip should
not land until the harness's analysis matches `karac build`'s.

    `call_type_subs`; the harness called the bare `karac::effectcheck`. Also a
    real difference, also corrected — same 5 failures.

Neither is the divergence. Something else in the CLI's pipeline (a later phase
that mutates the program before `concurrencycheck`, or a gate `compile_to_object`
applies that the CLI's own call does not) still differs. Finding it is the
remaining work on this row.

plausibly more faithful, but they did not fix the divergence and they change

    KARAC_NO_AUTOPAR=1 karac build ...  -> Built; prints 2 3 4 5 6 7 99

they were never the cause, because there was nothing to cause. The two fixtures
are real, of exactly the same kind as -17 / -18 / -19, and the flip surfaced

Recording how the wrong conclusion was reached, because the check that produced
it is a good check applied to a stale binary: "ZERO `__par_branch` symbols in
the AOT binary" and "identical stdout under both settings" are both true of a
build that never happened — a failed `karac build` leaves the PREVIOUS
executable in place, so re-running it prints the same output and carries the
same symbols. CLAUDE.md's staleness footgun, one level up: not a stale compiler
but a stale ARTIFACT. Checking the build's exit status, or building to a fresh
path, distinguishes them.

THE DEFECT (B-2026-08-08-23): `refs_in_expr` (`src/codegen/closures.rs`), which builds

the scrutinee nor the body contributed a single name; an outlined branch
containing `while let H.Full(v) = next(i) { … i = i + 1; }` never captured

outlined. Every other walker in that file handles `while let`, which is what
makes it an omission rather than a decision. Only the HEAP-payload shape was
reachable (the scalar one was not being parallelized), which is why the gap
looked narrower than it was.

`LabeledBlock` / `Comptime` / `Providers` fall through the same catch-all and
were added with it. Unreachable today, but the failure mode is a MISSED CAPTURE
— a hard error at the outlining site, not a conservative miss — so an
unreachable variant is one par-analysis widening away from the same bug.

THE FLIP: `run_under_asan`, `run_under_asan_counting` and
`run_under_asan_no_leak_check` now all compile with the concurrency analysis.
1000 fixtures pass at -O2 AND -O0. The "~1000 fixtures could go red" worry that
motivated deferring it was, in the end, five defects — all five filed, all five
fixed.

MECHANISM. `refs_in_expr` (`src/codegen/closures.rs`) computes the union of
names an auto-par branch's statements reference; `emit_par_branch_fn` uses it to
build the env struct. It has arms for `if let`, `while`, `for`, `loop`, `match`,

expression hit the `_ => {}` catch-all. Neither the scrutinee nor the body
contributed a name, `i` was never captured, and the branch fn then failed
compiling the statement it had been created for.

EVERY OTHER WALKER IN THAT FILE HANDLES `while let`
(`collect_heap_env_vec_owners`, `block_has_heap_env_misuse`, and one more), so
this is an omission, not a design choice.

WHY IT LOOKED NARROWER THAN IT IS: only the HEAP-payload spelling reproduces.
`while let H.Full(n) = next(i)` with a scalar payload builds fine — not because
the capture set is correct there, but because that shape is not selected for
parallelization at all. The bug is in the walker, not in the payload.

FIXED WITH `LabeledBlock`, `Comptime` and `Providers`, which fall through the
same catch-all. None is reachable today. They are included because the failure
mode here is a MISSED CAPTURE — a hard `Undefined variable` at the outlining
site, not a conservative over-approximation — so a variant that is merely
unreachable is one par-analysis widening away from the identical bug.

=== FIXED in 10659bf4.

ROOT CAUSE: the concurrency analyzer recorded NO WRITE for a call to a
`let`-bound closure. `collect_expr_inner_writes`'s `Call` arm resolves a callee
through `function_bodies` and attributes writes from `mut`-marked arguments and
declared `mut ref` params. A closure binding is in neither: `append(s)` carries
no `mut` marker, `append` is not a program-level function, and — the part that
makes it a different shape from everything that arm already handled — THE WRITE
IS NOT ON AN ARGUMENT AT ALL. It is on a CAPTURE, which is invisible at the call
site. With no write recorded, `append(s)` and `println(buf.len())` looked like
two independent reads, so the analyzer put them in separate concurrent branches
and codegen copied `buf` into the par env by value. The closure wrote through
its env pointer to the real binding; the sibling branch printed the stale
snapshot.

THE FIX: a `closure_bodies` map (binding name -> closure body, collected
program-wide alongside `function_bodies`), and a `Call`-arm expansion that walks
the closure's body so its writes are attributed to the call site. A
`closure_expansion_stack` makes a cycle (`a` calls `b` calls `a`) terminate;
re-entering a name already on the stack is skipped, and nothing is lost because
the outer expansion already collected that body's writes. Keyed by name
program-wide like `function_bodies`, so a same-named closure elsewhere can only
ADD serialization — the safe direction.

The analyzer still parallelizes: the repro went from 3 branches to 2, losing
only the grouping that was wrong.

=== THE ROW UNDERSTATED THIS. It is not only a deterministic lost write.

While checking whether the fix over-serialized, a disjoint-captures probe
(`pa` pushing to `a`, `pb` to `b`, each called several times) showed SIX
parallel branches pre-fix — which means three `pa(..)` calls, all pushing to the
SAME `a`, were running concurrently. That binary is measurably FLAKY: over 40
runs it printed the correct 6 thirty-nine times and 5 once. A dropped push.

So the defect has two presentations from one cause:

  * DETERMINISTIC, on the `String` shape — the write is always lost, because
    the reading branch always restores the stale `{ptr,len,cap}` snapshot.
    This is what the row was filed on.
  * NONDETERMINISTIC, on the `Vec` shape — concurrent `push` calls on the same
    captured Vec, losing an element at whatever rate the scheduler produces.
    The `Vec` arm of the original fixture printed the right answer and was
    recorded above as "correct"; it was correct BY LUCK, at ~97% per run.

Post-fix the same probe is 60/60 correct and no longer splits those calls.

That also revises the row's severity reasoning: a silent wrong answer is bad,
but an intermittent one that passes 39 times in 40 is worse to diagnose in the
field, and it means any existing kata or example that mutates a captured
collection from a closure has been rolling dice.

unannotated `let x = f(..)`, it takes the callee's declared return type as the
binding's surface type name — but only after

`struct_types`, and THE TWO ARE EXCLUSIVE (`if s.is_shared || s.is_par { … }
else { … }`). So the test answered "not a user struct" for every shared type.
`let b = make_bag(..)` crossed the par join with no `var_type_names` entry, and
`b.total()` had no receiver type to dispatch against.

The fix accepts either map. Shared ENUMS come along for free — `shared_types`
holds both — and the test covers that arm so a future narrowing has to break
two assertions rather than one.

THE ERROR MESSAGE IS ACTIVELY MISLEADING and cost the filing its accuracy:

    fell through; this is a codegen bug — add a dispatcher arm in

compiles and runs under `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`. What went missing is the

filed ("the fix belongs upstream of the dispatch table") and that held up. A
reader who follows the message's advice will add a redundant arm and not fix
the bug. Worth revisiting that string separately — it is the

tempting claim is "audit every `struct_types.contains_key`". There are a dozen

detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced by a dogfood probe written to exercise Option/Result
combinators, string ops and SortedMap away from the auto-par cluster — i.e. by
writing ordinary Kāra, which is what the Mend loop is for. The first program
written hit it.

THE MINIMAL REPRO is as idiomatic as Kāra gets:

    let mut v: Vec[String] = Vec.new();
    v.push(f"alpha-{n}");
    v.push(f"beta-{n}");
    println(v.first().unwrap());

    karac check      -> All checks passed
    karac run --interp -> alpha-1                     CORRECT
    karac run (JIT)  -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2
    karac build -O2  -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2
    karac build -O0  -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2

valgrind names it exactly: `Invalid free() / delete / delete[] / realloc()`,
`Address 0x... is 0 bytes inside a block of size 7 free'd` — a clean double
free of the 7-byte element buffer ("alpha-1"), 1 error from 1 context. Not
flaky, not opt-level-dependent, and NOT masked at -O0, which distinguishes it
from the flaky-UAF family (B-2026-07-20-9).

THE ISOLATION MATRIX IS THE DIAGNOSIS. Eight one-line programs, each built
standalone, interp vs AOT:

    v.first().unwrap()                              alpha-1  vs  DOUBLE FREE
    v.last().unwrap()                               beta-1   vs  DOUBLE FREE
    v.first().unwrap_or("none".to_string())         alpha-1  vs  DOUBLE FREE
    v.first().map(|s: String| s).unwrap_or(..)      alpha-1  vs  (empty)
    v.first().map(|s: String| s.to_uppercase())..   ALPHA-1  vs  (empty)
    v.first().map(|s: String| s.len() as i64)..     7        vs  0       <-- SILENT
    ---- clean, and each one narrows it further ----
    v.get(0).unwrap()                               alpha-1  vs  alpha-1  OK
    v[0]                                            alpha-1  vs  alpha-1  OK
    Vec[i64] .first().unwrap()                      42       vs  42       OK
    v.first().unwrap().len() as i64                 7        vs  7        OK
    Option.Some(f"delta-{n}").map(upper)..          DELTA-1  vs  DELTA-1  OK
    Option.Some(f"epsi-{n}").map(identity)..        epsi-1   vs  epsi-1   OK

So it is NOT `map`, NOT `unwrap_or`, NOT `to_uppercase`, and NOT `Option[String]`
— a directly-constructed `Option[String]` goes through the identical
combinators cleanly. It is `Vec[HEAP].first()` / `.last()` specifically, and
only when the borrow is CONSUMED as a value.

THREE SYMPTOMS, ONE CAUSE, AND THE THIRD IS THE WORST. `unwrap`/`unwrap_or`
double-free (loud, memory corruption). `.map(..)` returning a String yields an
EMPTY string (silent wrong output, no diagnostic). `.map(..)` returning a SCALAR
yields 0 (silent wrong ANSWER — `v.first().map(|s| s.len() as i64).unwrap_or(0)`
prints 0 where the interpreter prints 7, with no crash, no warning and no
runtime error). A program can therefore compute a wrong number and exit 0.

THE LEAD, and it is a strong one: `.get(i)` IS CLEAN on the same Vec, same
element type, same consuming expression. `.first()` / `.last()` and `.get(i)`
are the same borrow-accessor family and should be reaching the same consuming
lowering; one of them evidently is not. Start by diffing what `.get(0).unwrap()`
emits against `.first().unwrap()` for an identical `Vec[String]` — the delta
should be small and is likely the whole bug. The `.len()` chain being CLEAN is
a second clue in the same direction: that path has a dedicated intercept
(B-2026-08-01-1), so it bypasses whatever the plain consuming path does.

WHY HIGH. Memory corruption (double free), on maximally idiomatic code, with a
clean `karac check`, on all three codegen backends including -O0, plus a
SILENT wrong-answer sibling. The one mitigating fact is that `--interp` is
correct, so `karac run --interp` and the checker do not mislead — but
