     its only extra guard is the `Client` overload, which cannot apply to
     `first`/`last`. Its wrapper `expr_is_unwrap_of_borrow_accessor` adds only
     the `unwrap`/`expect` test. Both spellings classify identically.

  3. `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` IS NOT IT EITHER. It delegates to
     `is_borrow_returning_call_expr`, which matches only a FREE-FUNCTION call
     with a recorded ref return — it returns `false` for every MethodCall, so
     `get` and `first` get the same answer from it.

  4. THE EXTRA FREE IS NOT A `FreeVecBuffer` REGISTRATION. Instrumented
     `track_vec_var` (the single choke point for that CleanupAction) with a
     backtrace probe and compiled both programs: the registration sites AND
     THEIR COUNTS ARE BYTE-IDENTICAL — 4 assoc-call, 2 stmt, 2 vec-method,
     1 `try_track_len_family_recv_temp`, 4 compile_stmt, in both. So the two
     programs register exactly the same scope-exit cleanups and the second free
     comes from somewhere else.

WHAT THAT LEAVES, and it is a short list. The extra free is emitted OUTSIDE the
`FreeVecBuffer` cleanup channel — an inline release at the consuming site, or a
different CleanupAction variant. And since `get` in the identical position is
clean, the likeliest shape is that the inline-consume path DEEP-COPIES for
`get` (so the temp it frees is independent) and aliases for `first`/`last`.
Several `get`-keyed intercepts exist and were checked — `map_get_unwrap_vec_-
value_te` (`collections.rs`), `unwrap_receiver_is_nonshared_heap_value_map_get`
(`stmts.rs`) — but both are MAP-specific and neither fires for a Vec receiver,
so the Vec equivalent is either missing or lives elsewhere.

NEXT STEP, concretely: repeat the backtrace-probe trick on the OTHER release
channels rather than reading more code — it took one build and one diff to
eliminate the whole `FreeVecBuffer` channel. Instrument the remaining
`CleanupAction` push sites and any direct `karac_string_free` / buffer-release
emission, compile `v_arg_first.kara` against `v_arg_get.kara`, and diff. The
site that appears for `first` and not for `get` is the bug.

REPRO FILES are four lines each and are listed verbatim in the table above; no
corpus, no fixture harness needed.

ROOT-CAUSED AND FIXED 2026-08-08. The bug was a MISNAMED PREDICATE, and the
name is the whole story.

`codegen/calls.rs` zeroes the `cap` field of an unwrapped borrow view so no
consumer's `cap > 0` free-guard can free a buffer the container still owns
(B-2026-07-15-26). It gated that on
`unwrap_receiver_is_nonshared_heap_value_map_get`, whose body tested
`method == "get"`. Read as its name, that means "Map.get". In fact it ALSO
covered `Vec.get`, by accident: the receiver's type is resolved through
`map_receiver_value_type_expr`, which for an identifier receiver reads
`var_elem_type_exprs` -- and that map stores a Vec var's ELEMENT type in the
same slot it stores a Map var's VALUE type. So `v.get(0).unwrap()` was
protected the whole time, invisibly, for a reason nobody wrote down; and
`v.first()` / `v.last()` were not, for no reason at all.

That is exactly why the narrowing table looked like an accessor bug and
wasn't. `first`/`last` and `get` lower IDENTICALLY in `vec_method.rs` -- same
GEP, same shallow `build_load` of the element struct, same
`coerce_to_payload_words(elem_val, 3)`, same `build_option_some_via_phis`.
Reading that code (and `scrutinee_is_borrow_call`, and
`expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp`, and instrumenting the whole `FreeVecBuffer`
channel via `track_vec_var`, which produced BYTE-IDENTICAL registration sites
and counts for both programs) ruled out four mechanisms and found nothing,
because the difference was not in how the accessor lowers -- it was one
`insertvalue` downstream at the shared unwrap site.

WHAT FOUND IT: dumping pre-optimization LLVM IR for the failing and the clean
program and diffing `main`. 250 vs 251 lines; after the block-label renames
the entire semantic delta is one instruction present only in the `get` build:

    %map.get.borrow.cap0 = insertvalue { ptr, i64, i64 } %or.pl.vec.f2, i64 0, 2

and its consequence three lines later, where `%freearg.cap` feeds
`icmp ugt i64 %freearg.cap, 0` -- false with cap forced to 0, so `freearg.free`
is skipped. Without that instruction the `first` build reads the element's REAL
capacity, takes the free branch, and hands `free()` a pointer into the Vec's own
element buffer. The Vec's scope-exit per-element drop then frees it again.
Lesson worth keeping: an IR diff of two programs that differ by one token
answers "which emission site differs" in one build, where reading the emitting
code answers it only if you already suspect the right file.

THE FIX (2 files, mechanical once the diff is in hand): widen the method set
from `get` to `get | first | last` and rename the predicate to
`unwrap_receiver_is_nonshared_heap_borrow_accessor`, which is what it has
always actually meant. The rename is load-bearing, not cosmetic -- the old
name is precisely what made `first`/`last` look out of scope. The IR value
name follows (`accessor.borrow.cap0`).

WHY THE SET IS EXACTLY THOSE THREE. `first`/`last` are Vec/Slice/Array/String
methods only; no Map or SortedMap exposes them (typecheck rejects), so widening
cannot reach a map receiver whose `first()` would mean something else.
`get_unchecked` returns `T`, not `Option[T]`, so it never reaches an `unwrap`
payload. `pop`/`remove` genuinely TRANSFER ownership and must keep their real
cap.

detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found in the same dogfood probe as B-2026-08-08-20, which is the
serious half. This one is cosmetic by comparison and is filed separately
because it is a different class — a declined lowering, not a miscompile.

    let first: Option[String] = out.first().map(|s| s.to_uppercase());

    karac check        -> All checks passed
    karac run --interp -> works
    karac build / JIT  -> error: codegen failed: codegen: Option/Result.map with
                          an un-annotated closure that returns a String/Vec is
                          not yet supported under `karac build`; annotate the
                          closure parameter (`|x: T| ...`) or run with `--interp`

The bail is GOOD as bails go — it names the construct, names the fix, and names
the escape hatch. And the fix works: rewriting the closure as
`|s: String| s.to_uppercase()` builds and runs correctly on both JIT and AOT.

WHAT MAKES IT WORTH A ROW ANYWAY is that `karac check` passes and the
interpreter accepts the bare form, so the annotation requirement is invisible
until you reach the default execution path. For the AI-first wedge that matters
more than it would elsewhere: a model writing idiomatic `.map(|s| ...)` gets a
clean check and then a backend refusal, which is exactly the kind of gap the
Mend loop is supposed to convert into a compiler fix rather than route around.

Note the closure-param inference machinery already exists — B-2026-07-02-12
fixed un-annotated closure params against a declared-`Fn` ABI, and
B-2026-07-15-16 fixed closure-param inference for methods taking a closure. So
this is likely a missing hint-seeding at the `Option/Result.map` call site
rather than new inference, and should be checked against those two before any
new machinery is written.

RESOLUTION (8521c30e). The row's own guess was right, and checking it against
the two rows it named was the whole diagnosis: this was missing hint-seeding at
the call site, not new inference.

`Option/Result.map` inferred its closure argument with a bare
`self.infer_expr(&args[0].value)` and published NO `closure_param_seeds` entry
(B-2026-07-15-16's mechanism). Every sibling that takes a payload closure —
`map_or`, `map_or_else`, `map_err`, `and_then` — seeds through
`infer_closure_ret`; `map` was the one that did not. So the param stayed a
metavar, the closure's surface types were not recoverable at codegen, and the
heap-payload path bailed. THE BAIL WAS DOING ITS JOB over a gap one phase up,
which is why it read as a codegen limitation.

ROOT CAUSE: `infer_closure_return_type`'s `StringLit` arm answered

immediately below it already had this right; a bare literal reaches the same
representation by the same coercion.

operand's type, which is only right when the left already carries the owned
type. `|s| s + "!"` with an UN-ANNOTATED `s` sees `param_types["s"]` as a bare

concatenation yields an owned String, so the aggregate now wins over a borrowed

detail:
THIS ROW WAS FILED WITH A REPRO THAT DOES NOT REPRODUCE, and the correction is
the substance of the fix. As filed it read:

    let s: Option[String] = Some(f"hi");
    match s.map(|x: String| x + "!") { Some(x) => { println(x); } None => {} }

That program is CORRECT, and was correct at dcdad611 -- before B-2026-08-08-22,
the commit the row claimed to have measured against with the fix stashed. The
row was written from a simplified receiver that was never re-measured; the
simplification removed the defect. Bisect: built karac at dcdad611 and at main
and ran a 7-shape matrix through `karac build` + `--interp` at each.

THE REAL TRIGGER IS THE RECEIVER, not the annotation alone and not the concat.
`Vec.first()/.last()/.get()` mint `Option[ref T]`. Over that BORROWED payload an
OWNED parameter annotation was silently accepted, and the failure varies by
payload class -- which is why the empty String read like a String-specific bug:

    out.first().map(|x: String| x.to_uppercase())   -> ""        (interp: HI)
    out.first().map(|x: Vec[i64]| x.len())          -> 0         (interp: 2)
    out.first().map(|x: i64| x + 1)                 -> 140733... (interp: 8)

The scalar case prints a RAW STACK ADDRESS that varies run to run under ASLR --
an address disclosure out of a program `karac check` called clean. That is what
raises this from the medium it was filed at to high. The body shape is
irrelevant (`x.to_uppercase()` fails identically to `x + "!"`), and both legal
spellings -- un-annotated, and `|x: ref String|` -- were correct throughout.

ROOT CAUSE, one line: `src/typechecker/exprs.rs` combined the explicit
annotation with the combinator's param SEED using `.or_else`, so an annotation
won by DISCARDING the seed UNREAD -- no `check_assignable`, no `unify_types`, no
diagnostic. The seed mechanism itself is B-2026-08-08-21's (8521c30e). Two
comments at the seeding sites state 'an explicit annotation still wins' as the
intent; nothing enforced that the annotation was COMPATIBLE. The arm then
records the payload-derived signature at the closure's own span
(`record_expr_type`), so the typechecker published `Fn(ref String) -> String`
for a closure whose surface annotation said `String`, and codegen resolved the
disagreement by reading the borrow AS the owned value.

FIX: when BOTH an annotation and a seed exist, compare them before the
annotation wins; a `ref`/`mut ref` seed under a non-ref annotation is a type
error carrying a machine-applicable fix-it that rewrites the annotation to the
borrow spelling. Verified end-to-end: `karac fix` rewrites `|x: String|` to
`|x: ref String|` unattended and the result then runs correctly on BOTH
backends. Placed at the shared consumption point, so it covers `map` and every
`infer_closure_ret` sibling (`and_then`, `map_or`, `map_err`, `map_or_else`) --
they share the one `.or_else` hole.

WHY REJECT RATHER THAN COERCE: the language already answers this. The
equivalent binding `let s: Option[String] = out.first();` is a type error today,
and so is its SCALAR twin `let s: Option[i64] = out.first();` -- so there is no
auto-deref intent to honour for scalars either, and one uniform rule is right.
Kara has no implicit deep copy and moving out of a borrowed container is
unsound, so no coercion exists to reach for.

DELIBERATELY NARROW, since a false positive here rejects a valid program: fires
only when the seed is a borrow and the annotation is not; skips generic
annotations (`TypeParam`/`TypeVar`), which may still bind to a borrow; and is
hand-rolled rather than delegated to `check_assignable`, whose
`scalar_reads_as_value` peel would wave through `ref i64` -> `i64` -- the very
shape that leaks the address. Corpus check: the only three .kara files carrying
annotated closure params are seedless `let f = |x: T|` closures and still check
clean.

THE IR DIFF WAS RUN, and it says the difference is NOT what "single-owner"
suggested. Ownership-operation signatures of the two `main` bodies are
IDENTICAL -- same 4 `karac_free_buf` sites, same 2 `optpl.suppress.cap` stores.
The clean form is therefore not taking some other ownership path; both forms
ALIAS the payload between source and result, and both emit the same frees.

What differs is WHEN the result's free runs relative to the source's last read.
The `let` extends the result's life to end of scope, which lands its free AFTER
the re-read of `o`; the inline form's temp dies at end of statement, which lands
it BEFORE. That is why one is clean and the other reads freed memory, and it is
why the runtime counts (2 allocs / 2 frees) look correct in the clean shape even
though nothing was cloned.

conclusion from BOTH of this row's candidate designs, and cheaper than either.

GATED ON LIVENESS, which is what keeps this off the ~1000 memory fixtures the row
kept warning about. A consuming match whose source is DEAD afterwards has one
owner and is correct and free on today's transfer path; cloning there would be a
pure `malloc` + `memcpy` tax on a very common shape. `scrutinee_read_after_match`
asks whether any mention of the scrutinee sits at or past the last arm body's
end, over a per-function index of identifier mention OFFSETS built at
`compile_function_body` entry. So the new path fires ONLY on programs that are
broken today.

  Offsets, not a count, because the scrutinee's OWN mention is inside the match
  and must not read as a later use -- that is the whole `match o {…}` (keep the
  transfer) vs `match o {…} … match o {…}` (clone) distinction. Mentions BEFORE
  the match are deliberately ignored: a read that already happened cannot observe
  a buffer freed afterwards. The index is built on `bce_length_pin::block_all`,
  whose walk is exhaustive over `ExprKind` with no wildcard arm, so a new AST node
  breaks the build instead of silently reading as "not mentioned" -- which would
  take the fast path on a live source and dangle it again. Over-approximating
  here costs one `malloc`; under-approximating restores the use-after-free.

NOTE ON `ownership.rs`, because the previous entry's handoff advice was built on
it and it is WRONG. That entry said the ownership pass "already computes
precisely this fact -- it emits `value 'o' moved here, used again here
[UseAfterMove]` on exactly these programs". Measured: it does NOT. On
`o.map(|s| s)` followed by a read, `karac check` prints "All checks passed" with
no diagnostic at all. It emits UseAfterMove for the HAND-WRITTEN `match o {
Some(v) => { let k: String = v; … } }`, and -- stranger -- for the purely
READ-ONLY `match o {…}` twice, which is correct code that this row already fixed.
So the ownership pass currently warns about the safe shape and is silent on the
consuming one. The suggested "plain-data hint over the `OwnershipCheckResult`
channel" would therefore have been plumbed to a fact that is not there. That
diagnostics inversion is worth its own row and is not this one.

PINS: e2e `test_e2e_consuming_match_over_a_live_option_local_keeps_the_source`
(7 cases: the bug, chained consuming mappers, the `Vec[String]` depth case,
the DEAD-source control that must not clone, `None` at runtime, and the
`let`-bound control) and asan
`asan_consuming_match_over_a_live_option_local_frees_each_buffer_once` (all
three directions are memory bugs: no clone = use-after-free + double free,
clone without re-arming the source = leak, clone without the arm's tag zero =
double free). Both STASH-PROVEN red. The e2e deliberately does NOT re-pin the
read-only half: that shape needs an ownership-gate grandfather entry (see the
inversion above) and already has two tests.

STILL OPEN, unchanged and both measured on the fixed tree: leg 2 (`Result.map`,
prints an empty second read, valgrind-clean) and leg 3 (the user-enum channel
through `suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup`, same). The Option-scoped
clone does not reach either. Also not extended to `if let` / `while let`, whose
consuming half goes through the `control_flow.rs` siblings -- the same clone
should apply there, unmeasured as yet.

=== LEGS 2 AND 3 ARE FIXED (df4f33fc). THE ROW IS CLOSED. ===

Each channel had the SAME two halves leg 1 had, and each half had its own
cause. Both were measured, and the framing this row carried for legs 2 and 3
-- "leg 2 = `Result.map`", "leg 3 = the user-enum channel" -- was wrong about
what the axis actually is. Correcting it is most of this entry's value.

LEG 2 IS NOT ABOUT `map`, AND NOT REALLY ABOUT `Result`. The read-only
spelling fails identically:

    let r: Result[String, i64] = Ok(f"hi");
    match r { Ok(v) => { println(v); } Err(e) => { println(f"E"); } }
    match r { Ok(v) => { println(v); } Err(e) => { println(f"E"); } }
                                     -> hi, then an EMPTY line

The discriminator, each line measured:

    Err(_)              binds nothing     clean
    Err(e), e: String   binds HEAP        clean
    Err(e), e: i64      binds a SCALAR    BROKEN

`scrutinee_is_readonly_inline_optres_local` requires EVERY payload-consuming
arm to be the direct-heap shape, so the scalar `Err` binding disqualified the
whole match and sent the `Ok` arm back to the transfer path that empties the
source. The gate's own rationale is about TUPLE payloads, whose bindings own
themselves -- a scalar owns nothing, so the rationale never reached it. That
is the entire reason this looked `Result`-specific: `Option`'s only co-arm is
`None`, which binds nothing and so can never trip the gate.

  THE ROW ALREADY WARNED ABOUT THE TRAP IN FIXING THIS, and the warning was
  exactly right: "no recorded type" cannot be read as "scalar", because a
  DESTRUCTURED tuple payload is untyped in `pattern_binding_types` too. First
  attempt did precisely that and did not work -- a plain `i64` records NO
  entry at all, because that table is a NARROWING record (it stores `u8`/`i32`
  /`f64` and every named type; 64-bit is the default width and is omitted).
  An absent entry is therefore not a witness of anything, and it also covers
  `Some(t)` over `Option[(String, i64)]`, which very much does own heap. The
  exemption is keyed on the scrutinee's own INSTANTIATION instead -- read the
  variant's argument off `enum_inst_var_types` -- which is a positive witness.

LEG 2's CONSUMING HALF IS LITERALLY LEG 1's, one membership test away. The
heap-payload `.map` lowers through `compile_map_via_match_synthesis`, and the
synthesized `match`'s scrutinee is the RECEIVER -- a bare local. So
`clone_escaping_live_local_option` was already the right machinery and simply
gated on `inline_option_payload_vars`. `clone_escaping_live_local_result` is
the twin, on the ref-chain Result leg's clone-slot contract
(`track_inline_result_payload_var` BEFORE the store and the copy, per-arm
`suppress_inline_result_payload_cleanup_at`). Empty rather than garbage, and
valgrind-clean, because the transfer path ZEROES the source's payload words
rather than freeing behind it: one buffer, one free, a source reading {0,0,0}.

LEG 3 HAD BOTH HALVES TOO, and the row only ever described the consuming one.
A user enum's payload rides `field_drop_kinds`, so NO caller-retains
classifier covered it -- `scrutinee_is_readonly_owned_enum_local` is the
missing sibling of the Option/Result and for-loop-element ones. Raising
`pattern_binding_is_borrow` fixes both directions at once, because the arm
loop's whole suppression block is gated on that flag.

  IT REQUIRES A LIVE `EnumDrop` ON THE VARIABLE'S OWN SLOT, not a shape
  inference, because suppressing the arm's registration leaks unless the
  source will really free it. `track_enum_var` declines to register one for a
  shared enum and for an enum with no heap-bearing field -- precisely the
  population where a borrow classification would have nobody to fall back on.

IDENTIFIER SCRUTINEES ONLY -- NOT OWNED `self`, and this is the half that is
easy to get wrong. For `impl E { fn into_id(self) { match self { … } } }` the
source's scope-exit drop is the documented owned-self RESIDUAL: it does NOT
fire, because the caller disarmed the value's payload-bodies walk at the call
(B-2026-08-01-7). The arm is therefore the payload's sole owner, and
classifying it as a borrow drops that owner outright -- caught as a `Drop`
body that simply stopped running (`e2e_owned_self_enum_receiver_single_fire`).
An owned enum PARAM is NOT affected: its entry-registered `EnumDrop` really
does fire, measured byte-identical before and after.

THE ELEMENT-DEPTH TRAP IS REAL FOR THE ENUM CHANNEL, and this row can now say
so from measurement rather than from worry. Leg 1's entry above correctly
recorded that the trap did NOT apply to the Option channel (its clone is
type-directed). It DOES apply here: `deep_copy_enum_heap_payload_in_place`'s
`VecOrString` arm takes an OUTER-buffer copy -- deliberately, mirroring the
enum drop's outer-only free -- so a `Vec[String]` payload comes back with the
element `String`s SHARED. Running the consuming leg without a depth gate
measured TWO invalid reads plus TWO invalid frees on exactly that program:
correct output, memory-unsafe. `enum_payload_deep_copy_is_exact` restricts
the leg to depth-1-exact payloads (a direct `String`, or a `Vec`/`VecDeque`
of trivially-copyable elements), leaving `Vec[heap]` on the wrong-output path
it already had. Trading clean-but-wrong for a use-after-free would be a
severity increase, not a fix. Filed as B-2026-08-09-9 with an `#[ignore]`d pin.

PINS: e2e `test_e2e_live_local_match_keeps_the_source_for_result_and_user_
enums` (9 cases: both halves of each leg, the two co-arm discriminators, a
multi-field variant, the absent variant, and the two liveness controls) and
asan `asan_live_local_match_over_result_and_user_enum_frees_each_buffer_once`.
Both STASH-PROVEN red -- every second read empty on the baseline. This
REPLACES the `#[ignore]`d `test_e2e_consuming_map_over_live_optres_still_open`,
whose two cases are now cases 1 and 4 and pass.

Both new tests needed the ownership-gate grandfather list, for the same
inversion leg 1 recorded: the checker flags the READ-ONLY double match --
safe, and exactly what these legs fixed -- while saying nothing about the
consuming `.map` that genuinely moves the payload out. Leg 1 could delete its
offending case (duplicate coverage); leg 2 cannot, because the read-only
`Result` match IS the diagnosis.

=== THE `if let` / `while let` SPELLING OF LEG 3, read-only half (35629603). ===

The first pass closed leg 3 at the `match` site only. Measured afterwards, the
`if let` spelling of the SAME leg was still broken -- `control_flow.rs` calls
the very same `suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup`, so:

    let e: E = E.A(f"hi");
    if let E.A(v) = e { println(v); }
    if let E.A(v) = e { println(v); }      -> hi, then an EMPTY line

Only the USER-ENUM channel was affected at this site: `Option` and `Result`
were already clean through `if let`, because they had a block classifier
(`scrutinee_is_readonly_inline_optres_local_block`) and the user-enum one
simply did not exist. `scrutinee_is_readonly_owned_enum_local_block` is that
sibling, wired at both the if-let and while-let sites; the shared ownership
witness is factored into `owned_enum_local_that_frees_its_own_payload` so the
match and block forms cannot drift apart on the owned-`self` exclusion or the
live-`EnumDrop` requirement.

WORTH RECORDING AS A PROCESS NOTE: this hole was found by asking what was left
in the thread AFTER the row was marked fixed, not by the work itself. The row's
legs were framed as `match` shapes, so closing them read as closing the row --
while leg 3's own description ("the user-enum channel through
`suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup`") covers a call site the fix never
touched. When a leg is named after a CHANNEL, the close should enumerate that
channel's call sites rather than the spelling the reproduction happened to use.

Pins: cases 10 and 11 of `test_e2e_live_local_match_keeps_the_source_for_
result_and_user_enums`. The CONSUMING half of this same if-let spelling is

tracker: Residual of B-2026-07-31-44 (9013b32), which swept 19 dark llvm-gated targets into codegen-e2e but did not include `cli` -- because `cli` is the one target that LOOKS covered from two directions at once and is covered by neither.
title: `tests/cli.rs` is the dark target B-2026-07-31-44 missed, and it was RED the whole time -- 35 of its 43 `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]` tests run in NO CI job, because `cargo test --all` compiles them to nothing and the only `--test cli` steps filter to five names; one of the 35 (`test_build_text_pad_lever_moves_main_without_changing_behaviour`) has been failing on Linux since it was written
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while running the full `cargo test --features llvm`
suite as the pre-push gate for B-2026-08-08-20. The suite came back with
exactly one failure, in a test that had nothing to do with the change --
and `git stash push -- src/ tests/` confirmed it fails identically on a
clean `origin/main`. CI, meanwhile, was green on every job for that same
commit. Both facts are true, which is the finding.

WHY IT IS DARK. `cli` is covered from two directions and by neither:

  1. `Test (ubuntu-latest)` runs `cargo test --all` -- WITHOUT `--features
     llvm`, so all 43 `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]` tests in the file compile
     to nothing. The job reports 533 cli tests green and never touches them.
  2. Two `codegen-e2e` steps DO run `cargo test --features llvm --test cli`,
     but both filter: `-- test_build_repr_c_enum test_build_repr_c_struct
     test_build_crate_type test_build_auto_boxed test_project_lib_table`.
     By libtest substring matching that reaches 8 of the 43.
  3. The big `codegen-e2e` target list (ci.yml, the `--lib --test codegen
     --test interpreter ...` line) does not name `cli` at all.

35 llvm-gated tests therefore ran in no automated job anywhere. This is the
same failure mode B-2026-07-31-44 fixed for 19 other targets; `cli` escaped
that sweep precisely because a filtered `--test cli` line already existed in
the file and made it look handled.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY BROKEN BEHIND THE GAP -- the point of the row.
`test_build_text_pad_lever_moves_main_without_changing_behaviour` asserts
that `KARAC_TEXT_PAD=16` vs `=80` moves `main` by exactly 64 bytes. On Linux
it moved it by 0. The test's own failure message names the two candidate
causes ("the filler is being dead-stripped or emitted after `main` and the
lever measures nothing"); the second one was true.

    KARAC_TEXT_PAD=16 -> main 0x1280 (size 0x7e), __karac_text_pad 0x1300 (0x11)
    KARAC_TEXT_PAD=80 -> main 0x1280 (size 0x7e), __karac_text_pad 0x1300 (0x51)

The filler is present, correctly sized, and survives `--gc-sections` (the
`@llvm.used` pin works). It is simply AFTER `main`, so it shifts nothing --
the lever silently measures nothing on Linux while looking healthy. That
matters beyond the test: B-2026-08-07-10 / -24 / -25 are all placement rows,
and the next person to reach for this lever on a Linux box would have
gotten a flat curve and concluded placement does not matter.

ROOT CAUSE. Not module order -- `emit_text_pad` is deliberately called at
the top of `compile_program`, ahead of every user function, and the comment
there says so. The reordering happens in the linker. GNU ld's built-in
script places `*(.text.startup)` AHEAD of `*(.text .text.*)`, and LLVM emits
`main` into `.text.startup`. The pad's own `.text.__karac_text_pad` was in a
later output-section group, so no amount of being first in module order
could put it ahead. Mach-O has no such group, which is why the lever worked
where its measurements were taken and only ever failed on ELF.

FIX. Emit the pad into `.text.startup` too on Linux, so both live in one
output-section group where input order does decide. Measured after: main
0x12a0 -> 0x12e0 across 16 -> 80, exactly the requested 64. Linux-only via
`cfg!(target_os = "linux")` -- naming an ELF section on Mach-O would be
wrong, and Mach-O already orders this correctly.

SECOND HALF OF THE FIX: `--test cli` appended to the codegen-e2e target
list, whole rather than filtered, since a name filter is the exact mechanism
that hid this. Measured 577/577 green in 41-45 s warm on a Linux container,
in line with the ~55 s the -44 sweep added to the same job.

LESSON FOR THE LEDGER. A green CI badge and a red local suite are not a
contradiction to explain away -- the delta between them IS the coverage
report. Worth re-deriving periodically rather than trusting that a past
sweep closed the class: -44 swept 19 targets and still left the one target
whose partial coverage made it look done.

tracker: Spun out of B-2026-08-08-26 rather than folded into it: -26 is a coverage-gap row with a landed fix, this is a standing question about whether the remaining dark surface is worth the CI minutes. Needs a measurement, not a debugging session.
title: the dark-llvm-target audit has never been RE-RUN as a check -- B-2026-07-31-44 swept 19 targets by hand and B-2026-08-08-26 found the 20th the same way, so the next gap will also be found by accident unless the audit becomes a script. It is one now, and its first run found a THIRD pocket both hand audits missed: 24 llvm-gated tests across 4 targets, all GREEN, which is why nobody tripped over them
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: filed while fixing B-2026-08-08-26. Both dark-target rows so
far were found the same way -- somebody ran the full suite locally, noticed
a failure CI did not have, and worked backwards. That is luck, twice.

THE GAP. There is no check that answers "which `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`
tests does no CI job run?" The answer is mechanically derivable: parse the
`--test <name>` lists out of `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, subtract from the
set of `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`-gated `#[test]` fns per target, and
report the difference. The `cli` case shows the check must also account for
POSITIONAL FILTERS (`-- name1 name2 ...`) rather than just target names --
a target can be named in the workflow and still be 80% dark.

STILL-EXCLUDED TARGETS, deliberately, as of this row (all documented in
ci.yml's comment block, none are oversights): selfhost_codegen (1 test,
~181 s, wants its own runtime-budget decision), parallax_bench and
relay_bench (bench reproduction is opt-in by design), wasm_codegen
(documented Tier 3, covered by the separate `wasm` job). A checker would
need an explicit allowlist for these or it just reports them forever.

SIZE OF THE PRIZE: unknown, which is itself the argument for measuring. -44
found 554 dark tests; -26 found 35 more. Whether a third pocket exists is
exactly the question nobody can currently answer without redoing the manual
audit.

Low severity: no known defect is hiding behind it today (the whole suite is
green as of this row, on Linux, with -26's fix in). This is about not
finding the next one by accident.

-- RESOLVED (2026-08-08). THE AUDIT IS A SCRIPT NOW, AND ITS FIRST RUN FOUND
   THE THIRD POCKET THIS ROW SAID NOBODY COULD RULE OUT --

`scripts/dark-llvm-tests.py`, wired into the `lint` job. Pure python,
milliseconds, no build: it parses the `--test` lists out of ci.yml, intersects
with the targets that actually contain `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`, and reports
the difference. `cargo test --all` carries no `--features llvm`, so only
llvm-bearing invocations can cover an llvm-gated test -- that one fact is the
whole basis of the check.

THE MEASUREMENT THE ROW ASKED FOR. "SIZE OF THE PRIZE: unknown, which is itself
the argument for measuring." Measured: 32 targets contain llvm-gated code, 26
were named in CI, and after subtracting the four documented exclusions FOUR were
dark:

    example_packages       1 llvm-gated test
    safety_design         21
    safety_design_loop     1
    scaffold               1
                          --
                          24 tests, ~26 s wall clock, ALL GREEN

So a third pocket did exist, and the standing question this row was spun out to
answer -- whether the remaining dark surface is worth the CI minutes -- answers
itself at 26 seconds for 24 tests. All four are appended to the codegen-e2e
job, unfiltered.

THE PART WORTH MORE THAN THE 24 TESTS: they were all GREEN, and that is exactly
why two manual audits walked past them. Both prior rows were found by someone
noticing a local failure CI did not have -- B-2026-07-31-44's 554 tests and
B-2026-08-08-26's 35 -- which means the detection mechanism was "a dark test is
already RED". That mechanism cannot fire until a regression has landed, and it
stays silent for any dark target that is currently passing. A green dark target
is not a lesser problem than a red one; it is the same problem before the bug
arrives. The script reports them while they are still green, which is the only
time the report is cheap.

POSITIONAL FILTERS ARE HANDLED, and stash-proven rather than asserted. The row
flagged that "a target can be named in the workflow and still be 80% dark", the
`cli` case. A target covered ONLY by filtered invocations is reported PARTIAL,
not covered. Run against a reconstructed pre-B-2026-08-08-26 ci.yml (its one
`--test cli` removed from the full-target line, the two filtered arm64 steps
left in place), the script reports:

    PARTIAL -- cli  filters: ['test_build_auto_boxed', 'test_build_crate_type',
                              'test_build_repr_c_enum', 'test_build_repr_c_struct',
                              'test_project_lib_table']

so it would have caught -26 mechanically, at the time, without the red test.

THE ALLOWLIST IS EXPLICIT AND CARRIES REASONS, per the row's own warning that a
checker without one "just reports them forever": selfhost_codegen (1 test,
~181 s, wants its own runtime-budget decision), parallax_bench + relay_bench
(bench reproduction is opt-in), wasm_codegen (Tier 3, separate `wasm` job).
Adding an entry is a visible decision in review, which is the point. The script
also reports allowlist entries that have since become covered, so the list
cannot quietly rot into a list of lies.

TWO MODES, because the gate and the measurement want different things. The
default is the target-level check above -- no toolchain, no build, safe to run
on every push. `--count` additionally diffs `cargo test --features llvm --test T
-- --list` against the same without the feature to get exact per-target test
counts; that needs LLVM and takes minutes, so it is the measurement mode, not
the gate. The 24-test breakdown above came from `--count`.

NO DEFECT WAS HIDING: all 24 pass on Linux with the archives built, consistent
with this row's "no known defect is hiding behind it today" -- which was a
guess when the row was filed and is a measurement now.

tracker: Found while working B-2026-08-08-4's residual (`a Vec[weak N] held as a struct FIELD still leaks`). The leak was the mildest of three symptoms of one missing gate; the other two are a silent wrong answer and a SIGSEGV. Same root cause as B-2026-07-21-21 and as -4's own gap-B read-back fix, one receiver shape further out.
title: a weak ELEMENT read through a struct FIELD (`a.ns[0]` on `mut ns: Vec[weak N]`) skips the balancing acquire and over-releases -- SIGSEGV under JIT and AOT with two owners read, a SILENT WRONG ANSWER with two reads (a live target reads `None`), 48 bytes leaked with one, and `--interp` correct in every case; the identical read through a LOCAL `Vec[weak N]` is clean, which is the whole tell
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: B-2026-08-08-4 closed its gap B (weak container-element
read-back) but left a residual noted on the row: "a `Vec[weak N]` held as a
struct FIELD still leaks (2,264 bytes on the probe). PRE-EXISTING." Probing
that residual showed the leak is the *mildest* of three symptoms of a single
missing gate, and the other two are much worse than a leak.

THE SHAPE IS design.md's OWN GRAPH EXAMPLE, not a corner:

    shared struct N { v: i64, mut ns: Vec[weak N] }

SYMPTOM TABLE, all with `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, all three backends measured. Note
`--interp` is correct in every row -- this is a pure codegen divergence:

    probe                        interp  JIT   AOT     valgrind
    1 read                          2     2     2      48 B leaked (5 allocs, 4 frees)
    2 reads, same element           4     1     1      48 B leaked
    2 reads, two elements           4     1     1      48 B leaked
    2 reads, two owners (a and b)   3   SEGV  SEGV     3 invalid accesses
    CONTROL: same 2 reads, but
    `Vec[weak N]` as a LOCAL         3     3     3      clean

The `1` in the two-read rows is `2 + (-1)`: the FIRST read returns `Some`, the
SECOND read of a plainly-live target returns `None`. That is the silent half,
and it is the one that would have quietly corrupted a graph algorithm rather
than crashing it.

The CONTROL row is the whole diagnosis. Identical program text, identical
number of reads, the only difference being whether the `Vec[weak N]` lives in
a local or in a struct field.

ROOT CAUSE, one predicate. `expr_is_weak_field_read` (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs)
gates the acquire that balances an `Option[shared]` binding's scope-exit
`RcDecOption`. A weak read is a BORROW -- `emit_weak_field_upgrade` hands out a
box pointer with no strong retain -- so without the acquire the dec is
unbalanced and the target is over-released. B-2026-08-08-4's gap-B fix added an
`ExprKind::Index` arm for exactly this, but wrote it as:

    if let ExprKind::Index { object, .. } = &e.kind {
        if let ExprKind::Identifier(name) = &object.kind {      // <-- bare var only
            if self.var_elem_type_exprs.get(name.as_str()) ... Weak => return true

`a.ns[0]` has a `FieldAccess` receiver, so the index arm rejects it -- and the
FIELD half further down never runs either, because it requires `e` ITSELF to
be a `FieldAccess` and `e` is an `Index`. The expression falls through both
halves of a function whose two halves look, between them, exhaustive.

FIX: a small `index_receiver_elem_type_expr` helper that resolves the element
`TypeExpr` for BOTH receiver spellings -- a bare variable out of
`var_elem_type_exprs`, a field through the owning struct's recorded field
type-exprs then `vec_inner_type_expr`. It mirrors `map_receiver_value_type_expr`,
which already does the same two-shape walk for a Map value type. The index arm
now calls it instead of pattern-matching `Identifier` inline.

VERIFIED: all six probes plus the four store-only shapes now agree across
`--interp` / JIT / AOT, and every one is valgrind-clean -- allocs == frees, "0
bytes in 0 blocks" in use at exit, 0 errors. The SIGSEGV probe returns 3 on all
three backends.

REGRESSION PIN: `asan_weak_vec_field_element_read_balanced_no_use_after_free`
(tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), placed beside the gap-B sibling it extends. It uses
the TWO-OWNER shape -- the one that crashed -- because that shape also covers
the other two symptoms: a missing acquire shows up as a UAF long before the
scope-exit accounting is reached. Reads happen in a helper whose frame then
dies, per -4's own note that LSan under-reports when the last handles survive
in an unoverwritten dead frame. Proven non-vacuous: ASAN SEGV (exit 23) with
`src/` stashed, green with the fix.

LESSON, and it is the same one -4 and B-2026-07-21-21 already taught: this
predicate has now been widened three times, each time by one receiver shape
(field, then bare-variable element, now field element). The remaining untested
shapes are named on -4 and are the obvious next place it breaks:
`Map[K, weak V]` / `Set` / array / tuple element reads. A receiver-shape
enumeration would close the class instead of chasing it one spelling at a time.

DOES NOT CLOSE B-2026-08-08-4. That row's remaining item is GAP A (the cycle
checker not looking through containers), which is a breaking language change

detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-08-24, by probing whether the

`|x: ref i64|` panics identically, so it is not annotation-specific: mapping a
borrowed SCALAR payload has no working codegen path at all. The heap twin
(`Vec[String].first().map(|x| x.to_uppercase())`) is correct, which is why this
went unseen -- the whole family reads as working if only String is probed.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A LONE CRASH: B-2026-08-08-24 now rejects the owned
annotation over a borrowed payload and tells the author to drop the annotation
or write `ref T`. For a SCALAR payload BOTH of those spellings land here. The
diagnostic's advice is sound for heap payloads and walks a scalar author from a
silent wrong answer into a compiler panic -- the same advice-into-a-worse-
failure trap B-2026-08-08-22's gate had, so it is worth closing promptly.

A panic also violates the standing rule that every phase emits a structured
diagnostic with a span rather than panicking; even before the lowering exists,
this should be a diagnostic.

NOT NARROWED FURTHER, deliberately: filed at the point of discovery with a
reproduction rather than triaged on a guess. The open question is whether the
borrowed scalar should LOAD at the closure boundary (making this a missing
deref in the mapper's param setup) or whether `Option[ref <scalar>]` should
never reach codegen in the first place.

=== RESOLVED e524f62 ===

The row filed one symptom; there were TWO defects, and defect 1 was masking defect 2. The row's open question ("LOAD at the closure boundary, or keep `Option[ref <scalar>]` out of codegen") turned out to be a false dichotomy: the payload representation was already right, and neither the param ABI nor the Option lowering needed to change.

DEFECT 1 — the closure's declared RETURN type. `infer_closure_return_type` is fed a name -> type map built from the params' SLOT types. For a `ref T` param the slot holds a POINTER, but every read of that name in the body goes through `load_variable`, which DEREFS — so the body's value type is the pointee. The heuristic's `Identifier` arm returned `ptr` and its `Binary` arm propagates the left operand, so `|x| x + 1` declared the closure `-> ptr` while the body computed `i64`: "Function return type does not match operand type of return inst". Fixed by building that map from the DEREFERENCED type for a borrow param (the map only ever feeds return inference; the param ABI is a separate vector and still passes a pointer). The capture leg is fixed too — an enclosing `ref` param read inside a closure hit the same trap through `variables` rather than through the param map.

WHY THE FAMILY LOOKED HEALTHY: this only bites when the mapper's RESULT type IS the payload type. `|x| x > 5i64` returns bool and `|x| x + 1.0` hits the float arm, so both compiled; `Map.get(k).map(...)` is an OWNED `Option[V]` and never had a borrow to mis-type. Only `Vec[T].first()/get()` produce `Option[ref T]`. So probing anything but "scalar in, same scalar out" reported the whole area working.

DEFECT 2 — a LEAKED borrow mark, and the reason this row is reclassified. The closure's `ref` param registration (`ref_params` / `signature_ref_params`) was never restored after the body compile; those two were the ONLY param registries missing from `compile_closure`'s existing "restore outer state" block, which already restores `variables`, `var_type_names`, `owned_vecstr_params` and `for_loop_borrow_vars`. So the enclosing function's NEXT binding of that same name was still marked a borrow. The row saw it as the `Some(x) =>` arm panicking on `into_pointer_value`. That is the benign outcome. When the later binding is a Vec the bogus deref SUCCEEDS and reads the wrong word of the aggregate:

    let v: Vec[i64] = vec![7, 9];
    let q = v.first().map(|x| x + 1);
    let x: Vec[i64] = vec![1, 2, 3];
    println(x.len());        // karac build -> 2      --interp -> 3

A wrong ANSWER with no diagnostic, which is why the fix restores the registries wholesale rather than patching the site that panicked, and why `class` moved from `crash` to `miscompile`. Nothing about the match arm was special: a plain `let x` after the closure reproduces it.

SHAPE OF THE FIX, and the one thing to preserve if it is ever revisited: the registries are CLONED and restored, NOT taken. The body must still see the ENCLOSING fn's borrow marks, because a captured `ref T` keeps its name inside the closure and `load_variable` has to keep deref'ing it. Taking them (the obvious reading of how `variables` is handled two lines up) passes every case in this row and silently un-derefs captured borrows instead — so that case is its own assertion in the regression test.

TESTS: `test_e2e_optres_map_borrowed_scalar_payload` (defect 1, with the `|a| a > 5` / f64 / empty-Vec controls that compiled before, so a regression cannot hide behind them) and `test_e2e_closure_param_borrow_mark_does_not_leak` (defect 2, including the `x.len()` miscompile with its expected VALUE, and the captured-borrow counter-test). Both verified to FAIL on the pre-fix compiler and pass after — not assumed. Full suite green: 116 targets, 13,295 tests, 0 failures.

STILL TRUE AND NOT ADDRESSED: `let s: Option[i64] = out.first();` remains a type error, i.e. the language still does not auto-deref a borrowed scalar. This row only makes MAPPING one work. Whether `Option[ref <scalar>]` should collapse to `Option[<scalar>]` at the surface is a language-design question, not a codegen one, and is left open deliberately.

        inner.push("hello world this is a long string here");

  * TAKE THE BALANCING ACQUIRE. `emit_weak_field_upgrade` hands out a box

payload word after the found/not-found merge, not before it.

-- FIXED (2026-08-09), 68bebfd3. FOUR HALVES, AND THE ROW'S OWN SEVERITY WAS

The row rated this LOW on the grounds that "a REFUSAL, NOT A MISCOMPILE ... the
program does not compile, so nobody ships a wrong answer". That is exactly true
of the state it described and stops being true the moment the typecheck half
lands alone, which is what makes it worth recording rather than a footnote:

    WITH the typecheck relaxation and NOTHING else,
      a LIVE referent   -> correct, BY ACCIDENT (the weak slot holds the box
                           pointer, so reading it as a struct pointer works)
      a DEAD referent   -> prints the freed box's stale field 41 where the
                           interpreter says None; valgrind `Invalid read of
                           size 8`; no diagnostic

So the safe-looking half is the dangerous one to land by itself. This is
B-2026-08-08-5's rule ("the typechecker must admit exactly what codegen
lowers") hit a second time, from the read side, and it was caught only because
the dead-referent probe was written before the accept probe was believed.

THE FOUR PIECES:

  1. TYPECHECK (`stdlib_map.rs`, Map AND SortedMap -- the store gate covers
     both, so the read must too). `get` on a weak-valued map yields
     `Option[V]`. ONE Option, not `Option[Option[V]]`: a missing key and a dead
     referent are both `None`, and collapsing them is honest rather than
     lossy -- a released referent IS a key whose value is gone.
  2. CODEGEN, THE READ (`maps.rs`). Emits the upgrade and builds the Option
     from the niche, reusing the field path's own two helpers
     (`emit_weak_field_upgrade` + `niche_ptr_to_option_value`) so the RC
     behaviour is identical by construction. It bypasses the found/not-found
     phi entirely, which is sound precisely BECAUSE the two Nones collapse.
     The row predicted this would be the hard part -- "the upgrade has to
     happen on the payload word after the found/not-found merge, not before
     it" -- and the merge turned out to be removable instead.
  3. CODEGEN, THE PRE-ZERO (`maps.rs`). On a MISS the runtime leaves the value
     slot untouched, and the upgrade DEREFERENCES that slot to read the
     target's strong count. Without a pre-store the miss path would read an
     uninitialised alloca as a box header and let its contents decide the tag.
     Not defensive tidying: the `m.get(<absent key>)` row of the E2E test is
     what covers it.
  4. CODEGEN, THE ACQUIRE (`expr_ops.rs`) -- the row's second predicted hazard,
     and it was live. `m.get(k)` now joins `expr_is_weak_field_read`. Reached
     through a METHOD CALL, so neither the `Index` arm (B-2026-08-08-4 gap B)
     nor the `FieldAccess` arm saw it.
  5. INTERPRETER (`method_call_seq.rs`). A found `WeakRef` upgrades at the
     `get`. The `eval_expr_inner` post-step that handles the `Vec` element read
     CANNOT reach this one -- it is already sealed inside an `Option.Some`
     payload by the time the post-step runs.

THE ACQUIRE'S SHAPE IS NARROWER THAN THE ROW IMPLIED, and finding which
spelling exercises it took an A/B rather than reading: only the ANNOTATED
`let o: Option[N] = m.get(k)` reaches it. That is binding case (a), the one
that sets `shared_option_info` and queues a scope-exit `RcDecOption`; an
un-annotated `let o = m.get(k)` and a bare `match m.get(k)` queue no dec and
are balanced without it. Measured, with only that arm reverted:

tracker: probe: `impl Drop` on a `shared struct` whose last use is mid-scope, vs the identical program with a plain `struct`
title: a `shared struct` binding's Drop body fires at LEXICAL SCOPE EXIT under codegen but at LIVE-RANGE END under `--interp` -- design.md mandates live-range end, and codegen's own VALUE-struct path already does it, so the RC tier is the lone outlier and the two backends print in different orders
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while verifying B-2026-08-08-29's Map-mediated-cycle fix
with `impl Drop` bodies as the collection oracle. The weak/Map fix is unrelated
-- this reproduces with no `weak`, no `Map`, and no container of any kind, and
it reproduces identically on `main` before that fix.

THE PROBE, and its control, differing in ONE keyword:

    shared struct N { mut v: i64 }          // vs: struct N { v: i64 }
    impl Drop for N { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.v}"); } }
    fn main() {
        let p = N { v: 1i64 };
        let c = N { v: 2i64 };
        println(p.v + c.v);                 // <- last use of both
        println("end");
    }

    plain `struct N`   --interp   -> 3  drop 2  drop 1  end
    plain `struct N`   AOT        -> 3  drop 2  drop 1  end     AGREE
    `shared struct N`  --interp   -> 3  drop 2  drop 1  end
    `shared struct N`  AOT / JIT  -> 3  end     drop 2  drop 1  DIVERGE

WHO IS RIGHT IS NOT A JUDGEMENT CALL HERE. design.md is explicit
(§ "Destructors interleave with `defer` in a single LIFO stack"):

    Destructors fire at each binding's live-range end, not at lexical scope
    end, per the non-lexical-lifetime rule ...; a value whose last use is
    mid-scope is dropped at that use and does not appear in the end-of-scope
    stack at all.

So the interpreter is correct, codegen's VALUE-struct path is correct, and
codegen's RC tier is the single place that defers to the closing brace. That is
what makes this a defect rather than an open design question: the same compiler
implements the spec'd rule for one tier and not the other, and the disagreement
is observable in stdout ordering.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND print ORDER. The whole reason design.md commits to
live-range-end is the lock-held-too-long footgun it names in the same bullet --
a guard whose release the author expects at last use, held to the brace instead.
Any RC-tier resource wrapper (a `shared` connection handle, a `shared` file
wrapper) inherits the wrong hold window under AOT while `karac run --interp`
shows the right one, so the backend that is easiest to test against is the one
that will not reproduce the bug.

WHERE. The RC binding's cleanup is queued as `RcDec` at the `let` and drained
with the end-of-scope stack; the value-struct path already computes a live-range
end for its own-body walk (the B-2026-07-30-11 family's "own-body NLL"). The
question to answer first is whether that existing NLL computation can simply
drive the `RcDec` drain point too, or whether the RC tier needs its own because
a shared handle's live range is genuinely different (an alias taken elsewhere in
the scope must extend it -- the value tier has no such aliasing to account for).
That difference is probably exactly why the RC tier was left conservative, so
the fix is "make the conservative case precise", not "copy the value path".

MEDIUM: no memory error and no wrong VALUE on either backend -- both drop
exactly once. It is a timing/ordering divergence, which is invisible until a
Drop body has an observable effect, and then it is a run-vs-build split on the
tier most likely to hold a real resource.

── LOCALIZED (2026-08-09), NOT YET FIXED ──

Reproduced exactly as filed, both spellings, `--interp` vs AOT:

    struct N         interp / AOT -> 3 drop 2 drop 1 end   (agree)
    shared struct N  interp       -> 3 drop 2 drop 1 end
    shared struct N  AOT          -> 3 end drop 2 drop 1   (diverge)

THE EXCLUSION IS ONE CLAUSE, in `fire_due_user_drops` (runtime.rs ~6029), the
NLL channel that fires a binding's Drop body at its last-use statement:

    CleanupAction::UserDrop { .. } if last_use.get(binding_name) == Some(stmt_idx)
        && (Self::is_container_elem_bodies_fn(*drop_fn)
            || (self.struct_types.contains_key(type_name)
                && !self.shared_types.contains_key(type_name))   <-- HERE
            || ...value enum arm...)

So a shared struct is filtered out by NAME even before the action-kind question
-- and it would fail that too, since an RC binding's cleanup is queued as
`RcDec`, not `UserDrop`, so it is not on this channel at all. Two separate
reasons, both needing an answer; the row's guess that the RC tier "was left
conservative" is confirmed by the explicit `!shared_types` clause.

THE ALIASING WORRY THIS ROW RAISES MAY DISSOLVE, and whoever takes it should
test that argument first because it decides whether the fix is small or large.
The row reasons that an alias taken elsewhere in the scope must extend a shared
handle's live range, unlike the value tier. But `RcDec` is not a drop -- it is a
decrement, and the Drop BODY runs only on the 0 transition. An alias holds its
own +1, so firing THIS name's dec at THIS name's last use cannot drop the count
to zero while an alias is live; the body then fires when the last handle goes,
which is exactly the spec'd behaviour. If that holds, "last use of the name" is
already the right point for the RC tier and `compute_block_last_use` can drive
it unchanged -- making this "let RcDec onto the existing channel" rather than
"build a second NLL".

WHAT TO VERIFY BEFORE BELIEVING THAT: a scope where a second binding aliases
the handle (`let q = p;`) and one where an alias escapes (pushed into a `Vec`,
returned, captured by a closure), each compared against `--interp` on stdout
ORDER, not just on drop counts. The failure mode if the argument is wrong is an
early body -- a resource released while a live alias still uses it -- which is
worse than the current late one, so it needs the both-backends ordering check
and not just memory_sanitizer.

── FIXED (2026-08-09) ──

The RC tier now rides the SAME NLL channel as the value tier. In
`fire_due_user_drops`, an `RcDec` whose binding's last use is this statement
joins the existing due list -- ONE LIFO walk over the frame, so a scope mixing
the two tiers still fires in reverse-introduction order (a two-pass form would
have put every value drop ahead of every shared one regardless of declaration
order). The fired action goes out through `emit_cleanup_action`, the same
per-action emitter the scope-exit drain uses, so the reassignment reload and
the null guard come along for free; then it is retired from the frame, keyed
on (name, slot).

THE ALIASING WORRY DISSOLVED, as the localization guessed it might -- and the
interpreter turned out to already IMPLEMENT the proposed model rather than
merely tolerate it. `invoke_user_drop_if_applicable` runs the body when
`drop_target` reports a strong count of 1, then `remove_local`s the binding
UNCONDITIONALLY, under the comment "To let a *later* alias's drain reach 1,
release THIS binding's Arc from env after handling it". That is a decrement at
each NAME's death with the body on the 0 transition -- exactly what this fix
gives codegen. So the work was "let RcDec onto the existing channel", not
"build a second NLL", and the diff is ~40 lines.

MEASURED, not derived. Every shape below was run on BOTH backends, and every
AOT column was checked at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and -O2 (identical at both):

    shape                       interp             AOT before        AOT after
    the filed probe             3 d2 d1 end        3 end d2 d1       agrees
    alias (`let q = p;`)        1 mid 1 d1 end     1 mid 1 end d1    agrees
    by-value call `eat(p)`      1 d1 end           1 end d1          agrees
    return escape               made 1 d1 end      made 1 end d1     agrees
    loop body                   0 d0 tail 1 d1 …   0 tail d0 1 …     agrees
    early return                d1 1 d1 after 0    (already agreed)  agrees
    shared ENUM                 a 1 dE end         a 1 end dE        agrees
    `defer` naming the binding  P end dP cP        (already agreed)  agrees

The alias row is the load-bearing one: ONE body, at `q`'s last use, not at
`p`'s. Firing `p`'s dec early takes the count 2->1, which runs nothing. The
`defer` row is the pin: `compute_block_last_use` sends a deferred-body name to
the scope-exit sentinel, and the RC tier inherits that unchanged by riding the
same map.

SCOPE, stated so the residual is not mistaken for coverage. Restricted to
shared types carrying their OWN `impl Drop` (`user_drop_wrapper_fns`). A shared
type whose Drop comes only from a FIELD still decs at scope exit -- deliberate,
because there is no oracle to converge on there: `shared struct H { inner: N }`
with the body only on `N` prints `held|1|end|drop 1` under codegen and
`held|1|end` under `--interp`. The interpreter runs that field body not LATE
but NEVER (its own note: a link held in another shared struct's FIELD rather
than by an env binding never reaches a drain; L940 drop-reconciliation).
Retiming toward an oracle that does not fire at all would be motion, not
convergence. A dec with no user body anywhere is excluded for a different
reason: unobservable in output, retimes only a free, and buys nothing to offset
moving a release earlier in the RC machinery's most heavily special-cased path.

ONE EXISTING FIXTURE'S EXPECTATION CHANGED, and it reads as evidence rather
than breakage. `asan_shared_struct_user_drop_recursive_chain_leak_free`
asserted `0 1 2 3` for a 3-link chain whose head `a` is never read. A
never-used binding dies at its own `let` (design.md; the value tier pins the
same rule in `test_ir_user_drops_nll_placement_never_used_bindings`), so the
chain now unwinds at `a`'s declaration, ahead of `println(0)`: `1 2 3 0`.
`--interp` prints `1 2 0` -- the same timing, and its missing `3` is the same
pre-existing field-held gap named above. The old expectation had encoded the RC
tier's scope-exit drain, i.e. the defect this row filed.

TESTS. `test_e2e_shared_user_drop_nll_timing_and_alias` and
`test_e2e_shared_user_drop_defer_pins_to_scope_exit` (tests/codegen.rs) pin the
timing, the alias, and the defer pin. `asan_shared_user_drop_nll_alias_and_
escape_no_uaf` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) puts a live read AFTER every retimed
dec -- through the surviving alias, and through a Vec that owns the escaped
handle -- so a dec that ever frees instead of decrementing is a use-after-free
ASAN catches, not an ordering change a reader has to notice.

ALSO: the early fire calls `record_drop_obs` before `emit_cleanup_action`,
keeping the pairing the scope-exit funnel has. `RcDec` is a name-carrying
variant the drop-differential oracle knows by place, so retiring it here
without recording would have presented a RETIMED drop to the differential as a
MISSING one.

title: `let r = <Option/Result>.map(f)` over a HEAP payload leaks the result's payload once per evaluation — `map_passthrough_armed_source` claimed EVERY `.map` over an armed binding as an ALIAS of the receiver, but the heap-inner lowering (`compile_map_via_match_synthesis`) hands back a result that OWNS both branches, so nothing freed the payload the mapper had just allocated
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by running the sanitizer suite at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 while
gating B-2026-08-09-2, which is not what that row touches. Confirmed
PRE-EXISTING on a clean tree (all B-2026-08-09-2 changes stashed): identical
200 bytes / 40 allocations, so it is not a regression from that slice.

    KARAC_OPT_LEVEL unset (default)  -> ok
    KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0                -> SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 200 byte(s)
                                        leaked in 40 allocation(s)

The fixture came in with 4b941dcd, "feat(codegen): Option/Result.map over heap
payloads (String/Vec) -- via match synthesis (Slice 2)", so the leak is in that
path rather than in the fixture.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A SINGLE RED FIXTURE. The opt level changes only
whether LLVM's optimizer runs; it does not change which cleanups codegen
EMITS. A leak that appears only at -O0 therefore means the -O2 result is being
rescued by an optimization rather than by a balanced emission -- the cleanup is
wrong in both builds and one of them happens to be unobservable. That makes the
default-level green a weaker signal than it looks, for this path and for any
other the same synthesis feeds.

40 allocations for one fixture also suggests a per-iteration leak rather than a
single dropped handle, which should make it cheap to localize: the fixture's
loop trip count is the number to compare against.

NOT CURRENTLY GATED ANYWHERE. Every CI sanitizer job runs at the default opt
level, so nothing in the tree would have reported this. Whether the suite
should run BOTH levels is the second question this raises and is a CI-minutes
decision, not an implementation detail -- the same shape as B-2026-08-08-27's,
and worth answering with a measurement rather than an assumption.

The remaining 1004 fixtures pass at -O0, so this is one path, not a broad -O0
regression.

CORRECTION, 2026-08-09 (different session, found while gating B-2026-08-09-1).
Two claims above are wrong, and both point the next reader at the wrong place.

                 local is a borrow                    (partial fix for B-2026-08-08-25)

   Bisected on CLEAN FULL CHECKOUTS (`git checkout <sha>`, both bins rebuilt,

       e524f62   KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0  ->  same

LEFT TO ITS OWNER rather than fixed here: d530c033 is the in-flight partial fix
for B-2026-08-08-25, which is still open and being worked in another session.
Editing those same lines concurrently is how two correct fixes become one broken
merge. This note is the handoff.

RESOLUTION, 2026-08-09 (same session as the correction above, which is where
the bisect came from).

TITLE REWRITTEN AT CLOSE. The original read "`asan_option_map_heap_payload_no_leak`
leaks 200 bytes in 40 allocations at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 while passing at the
default level, so the `Option.map` heap-payload path has an -O0-only leak no CI
job would catch". Every clause after the byte count turned out to be wrong (see
below), and a fixed row collapses to its title alone in bug-ledger.md, so
leaving it would have left the wrong one-line summary as the permanent index
entry. The original is preserved here.

ROOT CAUSE — not where the original note pointed, and not where the correction
pointed either. d530c033 is a correct bisect of when the leak became
OBSERVABLE; it is not where the defect lives. The defect is in
`map_passthrough_armed_source` (src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs), added one
day earlier by B-2026-08-07-3.

`Option`/`Result` `.map(f)` has TWO lowerings, chosen in calls.rs by
`is_trivially_copyable_te(&inner_te)`:

  * SCALAR inner — hand-rolled. The absent branch compiles as
    `absent_result = recv_struct`, a SHALLOW copy of the receiver's
    `{tag,w0,w1,w2}` words, so a heap `Err`/`None` payload really IS aliased by
    the result. That is the shape B-2026-08-07-3 measured and fixed.
  * HEAP inner — `compile_map_via_match_synthesis`, which compiles
    `match o { Some(x) => Some(f(x)), None => None }`. The present payload is
    produced FRESH by the mapper, the `Err` payload is MOVED out of the receiver
    by its own arm, and the receiver's cleanup is suppressed by the synthesized
    match. The result owns both branches; nothing aliases.

`map_passthrough_armed_source` did not distinguish them. Its own doc comment
says it is "Gated to the SCALAR-inner ... map lowering" — the paragraph was
written, the gate was not. So a heap-inner `let r = s.map(|x| x)` recorded `r`
as a `passthrough_owner_alias` of `s`, which means `r` registered no
`FreeInlineOptionPayload` of its own, and the buffer the mapper had just
allocated had no owner at all. Worth internalising as a review lesson: a doc
comment asserting a narrowing is not evidence the narrowing exists.

WHY d530c033 SHOWED UP IN THE BISECT. Before it, `match r { Some(x) => … }`
handed the payload to the arm binding, which `track_vec_var`'d it and freed it
at arm exit — this leak was masked by an unrelated over-eager transfer.
d530c033 correctly reclassified that arm as a BORROW (`r` stays readable
afterwards), which removed the accidental free and exposed the missing one.
Same lesson as B-2026-08-09-5 one row over: a fix that makes a latent defect
observable is the regression WINDOW, not the regression.

THE "-O0 ONLY" FRAMING IS ALSO WRONG, and the reason is the more useful half of
this row. The fixture's arm is `Some(x) => total + x.len()`, which loads only
the length word — the copied BUFFER is never read, so at `-O2` LLVM proves the
malloc dead and deletes it. Change that one arm to read the bytes and the SAME
program leaks at the default level. So the opt level was never the variable;
the ARM SHAPE was. Measured across a 20-program shape matrix
(interp / AOT-O0 / AOT-O2, each under valgrind):

    let r = s.map(|x| x)                    unused    -O0  5B   -O2   0  (copy DCE'd)
    let r = s.map(|x| x); match r           println   -O0  5B   -O2  5B
    let r = s.map(|x:String| x.to_upper())  match r   -O0  6B   -O2  6B
    s.map(|x| x);            (bare discard)           -O0  5B   -O2   0
    let _ = s.map(|x| x);                             -O0  5B   -O2   0
    let r = <Result[String,String] Ok>.map(|x| x)     -O0  3B   -O2  3B
    ALL of the above, after this fix                  -O0   0   -O2   0

answers the calls.rs question directly (the receiver payload's
`method_unwrap_inner_types` entry, run through `is_trivially_copyable_te`);

LOCALIZED, 2026-08-09 (the session that owns B-2026-08-08-25, per the handoff
above) — and FIXED CONCURRENTLY by another session as 5698333 while this note
was being written. The two agree on the mechanism; the measurements below are
kept because they were taken independently and corroborate that commit's
reasoning from the other direction. Read 5698333 for the fix.

It is one line of registration, and it is NOT the borrow classifier. In
`stmts.rs`, a `let` whose RHS is a `.map` call is registered as a PASSTHROUGH
ALIAS of the receiver (`map_passthrough_armed_source`, B-2026-08-07-3) instead
of getting a cleanup of its own — the source stays sole owner. That is right
when the map result really does alias the receiver's payload, which is what
B-2026-08-07-3 measured on the None/Err branch. It is wrong whenever the MAPPER
ALLOCATES: the new binding then owns a fresh buffer that nothing frees.

Isolated at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0, 8 iterations each, valgrind:

    let same = s.map(|x| x);          match same (read-only)  -> 40 bytes / 8
    let same = s.map(|x| x);          match same (consuming)  -> 40 bytes / 8
    let same = s.map(|x| x.to_uppercase()); match same        -> 48 bytes / 8
    let same: Option[String] = Some(f"hello"); match same     -> clean

5 bytes an iteration is `"hello"`; 6 is `"HELLO"`. The read-only/consuming pair
is the discriminator: BOTH leak identically, so how the arm uses the payload —
the entire subject of d530c033 — does not move this number. The fourth line is
the control: a plain `Some(...)` literal registers its own
`FreeInlineOptionPayload` and is clean.

MEASURED UNCHANGED BY B-2026-08-08-25 LEG 1 (502a598f): identical 40 / 48 bytes
with the leg-1 change stashed and applied, on clean rebuilds of both bins. Leg 1
does fix a DIFFERENT leak on this same fixture that it introduced itself (the
chained `opt.map(|xs| xs.len()).unwrap_or(0)` disarm, 32 bytes an iteration,
pinned as `asan_chained_map_unwrap_or_over_live_option_frees_payload_exactly_once`)
— so the fixture now leaks strictly less, but the 200 bytes this row names are
untouched.

ON THE BISECT TO d530c033: consistent with everything above, but read it as
"the commit after which the fixture leaks", not as "the commit containing the
defect". The passthrough-alias rule predates it. The likely mechanism is that
d530c033 removed the other owner that had been masking the missing registration
— which is exactly the shape a bisect cannot distinguish from authorship.

WHY IT IS NOT FIXED HERE. The fix has to decide whether a mapper's result is a
fresh allocation or an alias of the receiver's payload, and that is a property
of the CLOSURE, not of the call site: `|x| x` deep-copies today (see
B-2026-08-09-5), `|x| x.to_uppercase()` allocates outright, and a borrow-
returning mapper genuinely aliases. Registering a cleanup on the wrong one of
those trades this leak for a double free on a path ~1000 memory fixtures
exercise. It wants its own slice with the mapper-return-ownership question

TWO SOURCES FOR ONE SIGNATURE. `compile_closure` derives the closure's LLVM
return type from the body; `compile_closure_value_call` independently predicts it
from the callee's recorded surface `Fn(..)` type via `closure_abi_fn_type`.
Nothing reconciled them, and nothing catches a disagreement: an indirect call's
callee type is not verified by LLVM. `|s| s` over a borrowed payload is recorded
`Fn(ref String) -> ref String`, so the call site lowered the return as one `ptr`
word while the emitted body deep-copied into the owned `{ptr,len,cap}` aggregate
and returned all three -- `len` and `cap` were dropped on the floor, so the
Option payload carried a pointer and two zeros.

WHY IT SURVIVED e524f62's TEST PASS -- worth internalizing, because the same
trap will recur. The scalar sibling `|x| x` has the IDENTICAL disagreement
(recorded `-> ref i64`, emitted `-> i64`) and is correct only by luck: an `i64`
read back through a `ptr` return keeps its bits, so the payload word survives
intact. Every scalar shape in that row's test therefore passed while the defect
was live. A heap payload is the first place where the word COUNT differs, which
is what makes the disagreement observable at all.

FIX: prefer the signature that was actually emitted. `compile_closure` already
publishes it in `pending_closure_fn_type` (for the surrounding `let` binding to
register), and a closure LITERAL callee is compiled by this very function, so the
call site now compiles the callee first and takes the emitted type over its own
prediction, falling back to the surface lowering for every non-literal callee
(struct field, Vec index, tuple index, call result) where nothing was emitted
here. The pending slot is saved and restored around the compile so an enclosing
`let` still sees its own.

=== FIXED (this commit) — and the filed cause was only the OUTER layer ===

The row diagnosed a phi/extract type mismatch and pointed at the hand-rolled
lowering's absent branch. That was the visible symptom of defect (1); a SECOND,
independent defect sat underneath it, and fixing (1) alone converts a loud panic
into a SILENT WRONG ANSWER — measured, not predicted.

(1) `type_name_of_expr` HAS NO ANSWER FOR A CHAINED COMBINATOR.
    `Option`/`Result` combinators are compiler builtins, so they never reach
    `fn_return_type_names` (whose contract is user fns), and the generic-impl
    recovery below it cannot see them either. `type_name_of_expr(r.map(f))`
    returned `None`, so every caller asking "is this a Result?" silently got
    `false` and the outer `map` built a `Some(..)` for a `Result`.

    Fix (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs): after the `fn_return_type_names` probe, map
    the WRAPPER-PRESERVING combinators back to the receiver's own type name --
    `map`, `map_err`, `and_then`, `or_else`, `filter` on an `Option`/`Result`.
    Listed rather than prefix-matched: the UNWRAPPING siblings (`unwrap_or`,
    `unwrap_or_else`, `map_or`, `map_or_else`) return the PAYLOAD and
    `Result.ok()` changes wrapper, so none of them preserve the name. Placed
    after the user-fn probe, so a user type named `Option`/`Result` still wins.

(2) THE RECEIVER WAS EVALUATED TWICE. `try_compile_option_result_method`
    compiled the receiver eagerly (it is needed by most methods), and
    `compile_map_via_match_synthesis` then compiled the SAME expression again as
    the synthesized match's scrutinee.

    For an identifier receiver that second compile is a dead reload -- which is
    why this never surfaced. For a CHAINED receiver it re-runs the entire inner
    combinator, and the first run has already MOVED the payload out and zeroed
    the source's words (`respl.suppress.w1..w5`), so the second run reads zeros.
    Read straight off the IR: `f(0)=1`, `g(1)=2`, and the program printed `2`
    where the answer is `42`; a heap payload came back as the empty string.

    Fix (src/codegen/calls.rs): hoist the synthesis decision ABOVE the receiver
    compile, so the routed path never compiles the receiver at all. Everything
    the decision needs (`inner_te`, the `method_unwrap_err_types` key) is
    already in hand at that point.

ROOT CAUSE. A bare rebind is a whole-value MOVE that the let-site registration
gate could not see. `rhs_is_fresh_inline_enum` answers false for an identifier
naming an existing binding — correctly, it is not FRESH — and neither
passthrough detector matches a bare identifier either, so the gate was never
entered: `p` got no cleanup and `o` kept its.

That much is balanced on its own, which is why `let p = o; println(p.is_some())`
is clean. What breaks is the SECOND consequence: `p` is absent from
`inline_option_payload_vars`, and that set is the membership test
`scrutinee_is_inline_optres_local` performs — the gate on both caller-retains
classifiers. So `match p` could never be classified read-only, took the OWNED
path, and its arm binding freed the buffer at arm exit while `o`'s untouched
scope-exit action freed it again. The control in the narrowing is exactly this:
without the rebind the scrutinee IS the registered binding, the classifier
fires, and nothing frees at arm exit.

This also explains why the consuming/borrowing split of B-2026-08-08-25 does not
move the number, as the narrowing observed: the classifier never runs at all,
so which half of it would have applied is irrelevant.

    ... x2, x3, chained `let q = p`                  alias: clean   transfer: clean

surviving action reads and the payload is stranded. Transfer also matches the
language — the rebind IS a move, which is why the ownership checker already
calls a later read of `o` UseAfterMove — and mirrors
`transfer_map_handle_on_rebind`, the Map/Set handle sibling (B-2026-07-31-27).

Two guards on the disarm, both load-bearing rather than defensive: it fires only
when the destination ACTUALLY took a registration (each tracker self-skips for a
payload it does not own, and disarming a source whose destination registered
nothing converts this double free into a leak), and a self-shadowing
`let o = o;` is excluded, since source and destination are one slot.

WHY THE FIX FOR THE SIBLING SHAPES DOES NOT EXTEND HERE, measured rather than
predicted. `deep_copy_enum_heap_payload_in_place` is the duplicator the
user-enum clone leg uses, and its `VecOrString` arm takes an OUTER-buffer copy
-- `emit_vecstr_defensive_copy(.., elem_te = None)`, deliberately mirroring the
enum drop's outer-only payload free. For `Vec[String]` that leaves the element
`String`s SHARED between the two copies. Running the leg with the depth gate
REMOVED was measured at two `Invalid read` plus two `Invalid free` on exactly
the program above: correct output, memory-unsafe.

So `enum_payload_deep_copy_is_exact` restricts the clone leg to the payloads
where depth-1 is exact -- a direct `String`, or a `Vec`/`VecDeque` of
trivially-copyable elements -- and this shape keeps the wrong output it
already had. That is a deliberate choice, not an oversight: clean-but-wrong is
strictly better than a use-after-free, and the alternative was to ship the
memory-unsafe version.

  This also confirms, from the other side, a warning B-2026-08-08-25 carried
  and then partly walked back. That row worried a clone would need element
  DEPTH or become a double-free; leg 1 correctly found the worry did NOT apply
  to the Option channel, whose clone is type-directed
  (`emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`). It applies exactly to the ENUM channel,
  which keys on `field_drop_kinds`. Both readings are right about their own
  channel.

WHAT CLOSING IT TAKES: an element-deep copy for the enum channel AND the
matching element-deep free, since copy-depth must equal drop-depth or the
clone leaks. That is a change to the enum drop model rather than to the
match classifier, which is why it is filed rather than forced alongside the
legs it was found beside. A cheaper alternative worth measuring first: route
this payload class through the type-directed `emit_clone_fn_for_type_expr`
(which already handles `Vec[String]` correctly for the Option channel) instead
