=== FIXED (7d9ecce1). Two hazards, not one -- and the second is not a memory bug. ===

WHAT THE FIX IS. `emit_vecstr_defensive_copy` could always go element-deep (it
walks String/Vec/Map/Set inners); the duplicator was simply passing it
`elem_te = None`. So the change is to hand it the inner type -- but only from
callers whose copy has an owner for those elements.

    enum E { A(Vec[String]), B }
    let e: E = E.A([f"aa", f"bb"]);
    match e { E.A(v) => { for s in v { println(s); } } E.B => {} }
    match e { E.A(v) => { for s in v { println(s); } } E.B => {} }

    before -> aa, bb, then NOTHING          (gated off the clone leg entirely)
    ungated + outer-only copy -> correct output, 2 invalid reads + 2 invalid frees
    after  -> aa, bb, aa, bb; 0 errors, 0 leaks, == --interp

DEPTH CANNOT BE THE DEFAULT, and this is the part worth carrying forward.
Making the duplicator element-deep for every caller LEAKED 1990 bytes across
300 allocations in `asan_match_bound_struct_variant_vec_field_reborrow_no_
double_free`, and broke two enum-reassign sequencing tests. The reason is the
mirror image of the original bug: most callers (notably the callee-entry copy
for by-value enum params) produce a copy that is dropped by
`emit_enum_drop_switch` -- outer-only -- so deep element copies have NOBODY to
free them. Copy-depth must equal DROP-depth at each site, and the drop depth
differs per site. Hence `_with_elements` as an opt-in, used by the live-local
match clone alone, which qualifies because it is produced ONLY when an arm's
payload escapes into a consumer whose own binding drains the elements.

THE GATE SURVIVES, WIDENED, because independence is not the only hazard.
Deleting it outright broke `e2e_own_drop_enum_reassign_sequencing`: a
`NestedStruct` payload can carry a user `impl Drop`, and duplicating it runs
that body TWICE. That is perfectly memory-SAFE and still wrong -- a clone is a
compiler-internal artifact the source language never asked for. So
`enum_payload_clone_is_faithful` excludes `NestedStruct` on OBSERVABILITY
grounds regardless of memory safety, excludes `MapOrSet` as unmeasured, and
admits `VecOrString` whose inner is a scalar or a `String` (exactly what the
defensive copy really duplicates -- a `Vec` of user structs would come back
aliased).

  Worth stating plainly because the first attempt got it wrong in both
  directions on the same afternoon: too shallow a copy aliases buffers
  (use-after-free), too deep a copy orphans them (leak), and a faithful-but-
  observable copy is a third failure that neither valgrind nor LSan will ever
  report.

detail:
FOUND while diagnosing B-2026-08-08-25 leg 3's owned-`self` exclusion; it is
NOT that defect. Measured byte-identical before and after that work, so it is
pre-existing and independent.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id} {self.name}") } }
    enum Box2 { Full(Res), Empty }
    fn into_id(b: Box2) -> i64 {
        match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r.id; } Box2.Empty => { return 0; } }
    }
    fn main() {
        let b: Box2 = Box2.Full(Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" });
        let v: i64 = into_id(b);
        println(f"v={v}");
    }

    karac build -> drop 7 e7, v=7      <- fires
    --interp    -> v=7                 <- silent

NOTE THE DIRECTION, which is what makes this worth its own row: the usual
Drop-body divergences on this ledger are codegen MISSING a body the
interpreter runs. Here it is the reverse, so a fix that reasons from "codegen
is the one that forgets" would be aimed at the wrong backend. Codegen's
behavior is the one that matches the language's intent -- the payload is
dropped when the callee-owned enum param dies -- so the interpreter is the
side that needs the fire.

RELATED, and worth reading first: B-2026-08-01-7 covers the owned-`self`
receiver form of this, where the CALLER disarms the value's payload-bodies
walk at the call and the callee's arm becomes sole owner. This is the plain
by-value PARAM spelling of the same call-site transfer. The two differ in
where they end up: the owned-`self` shape is documented as silent on both
backends (the "owned-self residual"), while the param shape is silent on ONE.
Whoever takes this should decide whether the residual is the intended
semantics for both spellings, or whether both should fire -- answering that
is more of the work than the fix.

NOT PINNED as a test yet -- filed at the point of discovery with a measured
reproduction. Severity medium: a `Drop` body silently not running is a
resource-release bug rather than a memory-safety one, but it is a real
backend divergence on ordinary code.

ROOT CAUSE IS NOT WHAT THIS ROW SAYS. It is not about owned enum params, and
the semantics question the row poses was already settled before it was filed.
Both corrections are measured, not argued.

1. THE SEMANTICS QUESTION IS CLOSED. The row says the owned-`self` shape is
"documented as silent on both backends (the owned-self residual)" and that
deciding whether both spellings should fire "is more of the work than the fix".
B-2026-08-01-7 fixed the owned-self shape (a598112) and it now FIRES on both
backends. Measured today, all three spellings:

    owned `self`   -> interp: drop 7 e7, v=7   AOT: drop 7 e7, v=7
    plain local    -> interp: id=7, drop 7 e7  AOT: id=7, drop 7 e7
    owned PARAM    -> interp: v=7              AOT: drop 7 e7, v=7   <- the row

Every sibling already fires on both backends, so "both should fire" is not a
judgment call to make; the param shape is the lone outlier.

2. IT IS A NAME COLLISION, NOT A PARAM RULE. `moved_out_user_drop_bindings` is
a flat `HashSet<String>` with no frame scoping. A callee that moves a payload
out of its own binding inserts that NAME, and an unrelated CALLER binding
spelled the same way is silently disarmed -- its `Drop` never runs. The row's
reproduction spells the caller's local and the callee's param both `b`, which
is why it read as a rule about params.

    fn into_id(b: Box2) ... ; fn main() { let b: Box2 = ...; into_id(b); }
        -> interp SILENT                       (names collide)
    fn into_id(bp: Box2) ...; fn main() { let outer: Box2 = ...; into_id(outer); }
        -> interp fires, both backends agree   (names differ)

Renaming EITHER side fixes it with no compiler change. That is the whole bug.
It is also not enum-specific -- any callee move of a name a live caller binding
shares reaches it; the enum-param shape is just where it was noticed.

RULED OUT ALONG THE WAY, so the next reader does not re-derive them: the early
`return` inside the arm is irrelevant (the same param shape WITHOUT it diverges
identically), and being a param is irrelevant (a LOCAL matched with an early
return in a helper fn is clean on both backends). Param-ness only correlates
because a param is how a caller's name gets reused in a callee frame.

FIX: the callee body evaluates with an EMPTY moved-out set, and the caller's is
restored on the way out, so a move recorded inside a frame can no longer escape
it. Placed beside the existing `owned_param_names_stack` push/pop, which already
establishes frame scoping at that call site. Swapped wholesale rather than made
a stack because the entries are consulted by bare name from many call sites --
replacing the whole map is what makes the isolation total.

CORRECTION TO THE NOTE ABOVE, and the reason this row is harder than it looks.

The frame-scoping diagnosis holds, but scoping `moved_out_user_drop_bindings`
ALONE does nothing -- measured, the divergence is unchanged. The enum payload
walk consults `moved_out_enum_payload_bindings` and
`moved_out_drop_field_bindings`, which are SEPARATE name-keyed sets with the
same missing scoping. All three have to be swapped per frame before the shape
converges.

With all three scoped, every spelling in the family agrees:

    owned param, arm binds + returns id      -> both fire   (was: interp silent)
    owned param, no early return             -> both fire   (was: interp silent)
    owned param, never matched               -> both fire   (unchanged)
    owned struct param                       -> both fire   (unchanged)
    local, early return in arm               -> both fire   (unchanged)

AND IT UNMASKS B-2026-08-09-15 IN THE INTERPRETER, which is the catch. The
payload-RETURNED shape moves the wrong way:

    fn take(b: Box2) -> Res { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r; } ... } }

    before scoping: --interp `got 7, drop 7`        <- ONE fire, and CORRECT
    after  scoping: --interp `drop 7, got 7, drop 7` <- TWO, matching codegen

The interpreter was only accidentally right there: the callee's spurious fire
was being suppressed by the very cross-frame leak this row is about. Restoring
isolation exposes it, and both backends then double-fire.

So the two rows are COUPLED and the scoping should not land alone. On its own it
converges three shapes onto correct behavior and one onto wrong behavior, and --
worse for detection -- it makes B-2026-08-09-15 invisible to the run-vs-build
parity oracle, which is the gate most likely to have caught it. Whoever takes
this should land the frame scoping TOGETHER with the returned-payload disarm
(the callee must not fire a payload whose arm binding escapes by `return`; the
caller's binding is the sole owner after the call), so the family lands correct
rather than merely consistent.


THE COUPLING IS CONFIRMED, AND THE FRAME-SCOPING PATCH IS WRITTEN AND GREEN —
handed off here rather than landed, because the correction above is right that
it must not land alone. Independent session; the scoping diagnosis below was
reached from the other end (a name-collision probe) before that correction was
read, so the two are corroborating rather than copied.

THE ONE-LINE DIAGNOSTIC, if anyone needs to re-confirm this quickly: the defect
is visible as a RENAME. These two programs differ only in the callee's parameter
name, and pre-fix they printed differently:

    fn into_id(b: Box2) -> i64 { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r.id; } … } }
    fn into_id(q: Box2) -> i64 { match q { Box2.Full(r) => { return r.id; } … } }

    caller: let b = Box2.Full(Res{id:7,…}); let v = into_id(b);

    `b`  -> --interp SILENT, karac build fires        <- the reported bug
    `q`  -> both fire                                 <- same program

THE PATCH, verified: in `eval_call.rs`, immediately around the existing
`owned_param_names_stack` push/pop, `std::mem::take` all FOUR moved-out sets
before `eval_body_growing` and restore them after —
`moved_out_container_bodies_bindings`, `moved_out_enum_payload_bindings`,
`moved_out_drop_field_bindings`, `moved_out_user_drop_bindings`. Same boundary,
same lifetime. A callee cannot name a caller's local, so no disarm recorded
inside a body can ever be ABOUT a caller binding; the save/restore is the exact
statement of that. Their shared rationale ("the walks consult this at fire time,
which reaches every frame") is right WITHIN a frame and is precisely what has to
stop at a call boundary.

Measured with that patch: full `--features llvm` suite green (102/102 targets,
exit 0), clippy plain + llvm, fmt. A 9-shape interp/AOT sweep converges — owned
param with early return, owned param without, never-matched param, owned struct
param, local with early return, chained, `is_some`-only, and the un-rebound
control all agree.

`fn take(b: Box2) -> Res { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r; } … } }` goes

(two, matching codegen). So the row should stay open until B-2026-08-09-15 lands

FIXED 128b746 — and the root cause is NOT what this row's title says. It is
neither param-specific nor enum-specific.

The interpreter's moved-out tracking is keyed by NAME with no frame scoping, so
a callee that moves a payload out of its own binding inserts that name and
silently disarms an UNRELATED CALLER binding spelled the same way. This row's
reproduction spells the caller's local and the callee's param both `b`, which is
why it read as a rule about owned params:

    fn into_id(b: Box2)  ... main() { let b: Box2 = ...; into_id(b); }
        -> --interp SILENT                      (names collide)
    fn into_id(bp: Box2) ... main() { let outer: Box2 = ...; into_id(outer); }
        -> both backends agree, body fires      (names differ)

Renaming either side fixed it with NO compiler change. Ruled out on the way:
the early `return` inside the arm (the same shape without it diverges
identically) and param-ness itself (a LOCAL matched with an early return in a
helper fn is clean on both backends).

Three separate sets carry the hazard — `moved_out_user_drop_bindings`,
`moved_out_enum_payload_bindings`, `moved_out_drop_field_bindings` — and scoping
only the first changes NOTHING, which is worth knowing before touching this
again. All three are now swapped for empty ones around the callee body and
restored on exit, beside the existing `owned_param_names_stack` push/pop.

The row's other premise was already stale when filed: it asks whether both
spellings SHOULD fire. B-2026-08-01-7 (a598112) had made owned-`self` fire on
both backends, so every sibling agreed and there was nothing to adjudicate.

(correct)"; the caller's fire is exactly what the name collision was suppressing,

It does not settle the caller-retains vs callee-owns question, which stays open

CORRECTION TO THIS ROW. It predicted that switch would "convert the UAF into a
leak ... because the deep elements are ORPHANED" -- the CLONE's elements having
no owner, which is why it argued the honest close needed an element drain on
the clone slot first. That is not what the residual is. The clone's elements do
have an owner: the arm's `for` loop consumes them, exactly as the leg's escape
gate guarantees. The 2 leaked blocks are the SOURCE's elements, and they are
B-2026-08-09-13's class -- an enum's `Vec[heap]` payload elements are freed by
nothing unless something consumes them. Same count (2) as a bare
`let s = S { e: E.A([f"aa", f"bb"]) }` that is never matched at all.

  So the aliasing was MASKING that pre-existing leak: with the element buffers
  shared, the arm's loop freed the caller's strings too -- wrongly, but it did
  free them. Removing the alias stops the wrong free and exposes the gap
  underneath. Nothing was traded away; the leak was always owed.

program and made the residual look like something the switch had created. The
`-O0` re-measurement is what separated "leak the fix introduced" from "leak the
fix uncovered". B-2026-08-09-13 records the same trap from its own side.

The narrowing table in this row was taken at the DEFAULT opt level, where LLVM
deletes the allocation of any f-string whose buffer is never observed. Reading
`v[0]` is what makes "aa" observable, so the read does not CREATE the leaked
buffer -- it decides whether the buffer is allocated at all. At -O0, where
nothing is optimised away, the leak is CONSTANT:

    shape                                   -O0                 -O2
    plain `let v: Vec[String]`, 2 reads     4/4 clean           3/3 clean
    enum payload, bind, read NOTHING        4 allocs / 2 frees  1/1 clean
    enum payload, 1 index read              4 allocs / 2 frees  2 allocs / 1 free
    enum payload, 2 index reads             4 allocs / 2 frees  3 allocs / 1 free
    CONSUMING match, read nothing           5 allocs / 3 frees  1/1 clean

So, against this row as filed:

  1. NOT "one leaked buffer PER heap-element index read". It is a fixed 2
     blocks (both `Vec[String]` elements) at every read count, including ZERO.
     The row's "bind `v`, read NOTHING -> clean" line is the optimiser, not the
     compiler.
  2. NOT specific to the BORROW path. The consuming match leaks the same 2
     blocks at -O0.
  3. NOT an index-read defect at all. Valgrind with debug info puts both
     leaked blocks at the CONSTRUCTION line, not at any read.

THE ACTUAL MECHANISM, read out of the emitted `__karac_drop_E`: for a
`Vec[String]` payload it frees the Vec's OUTER BUFFER
(`karac_free_buf(data, cap*24)`) and never drains the elements. That is not an
oversight -- `EnumDropKind::VecOrString` (src/codegen/state.rs) documents it:
"For a `Vec[heap-element]` only the OUTER buffer is freed -- per-element heap
is a bounded leak, symmetric with the outer-buffer-only deep-copy-on-entry ...
a deliberate v1 design position."

-- THE LEG-3 CLAIM IS CORRECT, AND THE REGRESSION IS LARGER THAN RECORDED --

Measured against a compiler built from df4f33fc^ (pre-leg-3), same programs,
same opt levels:

    shape                          PRE-leg-3        POST-leg-3
    owned local, read-only match   4/4 CLEAN        4 allocs / 2 frees  LEAK
      (same at -O2)                2/2 clean        2 allocs / 1 free   LEAK
    CONSUMING match, no read       5/5 CLEAN        5 allocs / 3 frees  LEAK
    ref param (0 / 1 / 2 reads)    leaks            leaks (unchanged)

So the row is right that leg 3 moved a new population onto the leaking path,
and UNDERSTATES it: the row scopes the consequence to "the BORROW path" and to
index reads, but a CONSUMING match with zero index reads regressed too --
5 frees to 3. The `ref`-param leak is genuinely pre-existing, as the row says.

WHY LEG 3 DID IT, and it is not a mistake in isolation: leg 3 raises
`pattern_binding_is_borrow`, so `bind_pattern_values` skips the arm binding's
`track_vec_var` and the source's `EnumDrop` becomes the single owner --
"One buffer, one free, at the source's scope exit." That reasoning is exactly
right for the BUFFER and silently wrong for the ELEMENTS, because the arm
binding's `track_vec_var` is what used to drain them and `EnumDrop` never did.
Leg 3 traded a use-after-free for a leak, which is the better end of the trade;
this is the unpriced part of it.

-- WHAT THE FIX IS, AND WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINER --

`EnumDrop` must drain a `Vec[heap-element]` payload's elements. It cannot be
changed alone: `state.rs` requires the drop classification stay SYMMETRIC with
the deep-copy-on-entry ("each must account for exactly the same heap, or a
by-value param copy / a pattern-move-out double-frees or leaks"), and the
default `deep_copy_enum_heap_payload_in_place` is outer-only. Make the drop
element-deep by itself and a by-value enum param -- whose entry copy shares the
element buffers with the caller's -- double-frees every element.

So it is a two-sided slice, and the second side already exists:
B-2026-08-09-9 added `deep_copy_enum_heap_payload_with_elements_in_place`
(param_own.rs) and its doc comment names this exact gap as the reason it is not
the default -- "A copy that is merely dropped by the enum's own `EnumDrop` does
not qualify." Making `EnumDrop` drain is what retires that caveat. The two
edits are:

  * `synth_drop.rs`, the `EnumDropKind::VecOrString` arm -- drain elements
    before `emit_free_buf_call`. Note `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` returns
    `None` for a `String` element (it is for named user aggregates), so the
    String/Vec element walk needs `emit_vecstr_defensive_copy`'s sibling shape,
    not that helper.
  * `param_own.rs` -- flip the default copy to the element-deep variant, so the
    two sides stay symmetric.

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE, deliberately: it changes the enum payload ownership model
on a path the ~1000-fixture memory suite exercises constantly, at both opt
levels, and it is not worth landing with less verification budget than that
needs. Re-scoped and handed back with the measurements above rather than
half-applied.

THE LOAD-BEARING DETAIL, and the reason a naive drain is unsound: the loop sits
INSIDE the `cap > 0` guard. A CONSUMING arm really does take the elements (its
`for s in v` frees each one), and it is `suppress_destructured_enum_payload_
cleanup` zeroing the source's cap that keeps this drop out of the way -- under
the guard, neither the drain nor the buffer free runs, so the arm stays sole
owner. Hoisted above the guard, every element is freed twice. Case 3 of the new
fixture pins exactly that.

    CONSUMING arm (`for s in v`)       4 / 4  clean      4 / 4  unchanged

title: a CONSUMING `while let` arm over a plain enum local whose source is DEAD after the loop double-frees -- the `match` and `if let` spellings of the same shape are clean, and so is the read-only `while let`
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-09-11 and measured PRE-EXISTING: both shapes below
double-free with every change from that slice stashed, so it is not a regression
from it. Re-measured after B-2026-08-09-9's fix (7d9ecce1) landed -- still
reproduces, so it is not that family either.

    enum E { A(String), B }
    fn main() {
        let mut e: E = E.A(f"hi");
        while let E.A(v) = e { let k: String = v; println(k); e = E.B; }
        println(f"done");
    }

    karac build -> hi, then `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
    --interp    -> hi, done

WHAT NARROWS IT, measured rather than guessed:

    while let, CONSUMING arm, source dead    -> double free
    while let, CONSUMING arm, source LIVE    -> clean (B-2026-08-09-11 clone)
    while let, READ-ONLY arm                 -> clean
    match,     CONSUMING arm, + reassignment -> clean
    if let,    CONSUMING arm, + reassignment -> clean

So it is `while let`-specific, and independent of whether the body reassigns the
scrutinee: the `break`-terminated spelling with no reassignment at all
double-frees identically. That rules out the reassignment's drop of the old
value and points at the per-iteration scrutinee handling -- the arm moves the
payload out of a local the loop re-evaluates, and the source's own free is never
suppressed against that move the way the `match` site suppresses it.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED ALONGSIDE B-2026-08-09-11: that row's leg MASKS this
whenever the source is LIVE after the loop, because the clone hands the arm its
own buffer. Dead sources decline the clone by design -- the liveness gate is
what keeps every consuming `if let` / `while let` off a clone it does not need
-- so they land back on the raw transfer path, which is where this lives. The
fix is the per-iteration source suppression, not another clone: cloning for dead
sources would trade a double free for a pointless copy on the common shape.

SEVERITY high rather than medium: a double free is memory-unsafe, unlike the
wrong-output rows in this family.

FIXED at a2e1f42. NOT while-let-specific, which the narrowing above made it look:
it is the missing WHILE-LET leg of B-2026-07-23-13. That row added the
owned-enum-local cap suppression to `if let` (`compile_if_let`'s `else if
optres_bindings_owned` arm) and left the loop form behind;
`compile_while_let` carried only the FRESH-TEMP arm
(`suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup_at`) and never gained the named-
local `else if`. `match` had it from the start. So all five narrowing rows are
explained by which sites got that one arm, and the per-iteration scrutinee
handling the note above suspected is not involved.

The row's own prediction was right about the remedy — the source suppression,
not another clone. One line of dispatch, plus the gate capture:

    let optres_bindings_owned = !self.pattern_binding_is_borrow;   // before the restore
    …
    if let Some((alloca, enum_name)) = &freshtemp_enum {
        self.suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup_at(*alloca, enum_name, pattern);
    } else if optres_bindings_owned {
        self.suppress_destructured_enum_payload_cleanup(value, pattern);
    }

Emitted in `body_bb`, so it runs per MATCHED iteration and the miss edge stays
unsuppressed (the drop frees the source whole there), which is the same
contract the if-let site documents. Re-zeroing an already-zero cap is a no-op,
and an iteration that REASSIGNS the source re-arms it: the assignment's drop of
the old value reads the zeroed cap and skips the payload the binding owns, then
the next iteration's store re-populates and this store re-fires.

title: codegen runs a `Drop` body TWICE when a match arm RETURNS a Drop-carrying payload out of an owned enum param -- once in the callee, once at the caller's binding; `--interp` runs it once
detail:
FOUND while characterising B-2026-08-09-10's owned-param family, and it points
the OPPOSITE way on the opposite backend, which is why it is its own row.

    struct Res { id: i64, name: String }
    impl Drop for Res { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.id}") } }
    enum Box2 { Full(Res), Empty }
    fn take(b: Box2) -> Res {
        match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r; } Box2.Empty => { return Res { id: 0, name: f"z" }; } }
    }
    fn main() {
        let b: Box2 = Box2.Full(Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" });
        let r: Res = take(b);
        println(f"got {r.id}");
    }

    karac build -> drop 7, got 7, drop 7      <- TWO bodies for one value
    --interp    -> got 7, drop 7              <- one, and it is the correct one

The payload ESCAPES the callee via `return r`, so the callee must not fire: the
value's sole owner after the call is the caller's `r`, whose own death runs the
body. The interpreter has this right. Codegen fires the arm-bound payload at the
callee's frame exit ANYWAY and again at the caller's binding.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT. B-2026-08-01-7 was the same doubled observation for the
owned-`self` RECEIVER spelling, fixed at a598112 by disarming the receiver's
payload-bodies walk at the call. This is the by-value PARAM spelling with the
payload leaving by RETURN rather than the receiver moving in, and that disarm
does not reach it. B-2026-08-09-10 is the third member and points the other way
again (interp silent where codegen fires), so the three should be read together
and NOT assumed to share a fix.

NOT A REGRESSION: measured identical before the B-2026-08-09-10/-11 work, and
again after B-2026-08-09-9's fix landed. Memory is valgrind-clean -- bodies
only -- so the defect is a doubled observable side effect, not a double free.

ALSO PRESENT IN THE INTERPRETER, masked. Measured while working B-2026-08-09-10:
the interpreter's single (correct) fire here depends on that row's cross-frame
name-collision leak suppressing the callee's spurious fire. Scope the moved-out
sets per frame -- the fix that row needs -- and `--interp` double-fires too. So
this is a both-backends defect wearing a one-backend disguise, and the two rows
must land together or the parity oracle stops seeing this one.


RE-MEASURED FROM A SECOND SESSION, and two things about this row's shape change.

1. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE OWNED PARAM, NOT THE `return`. A local source with
   the identical returning arm is CORRECT on both backends:

       fn take() -> Res {
           let b: Box2 = Box2.Full(Res { id: 7, name: f"e7" });
           match b { Box2.Full(r) => { return r; } … }
       }
       -> both backends: `got 7`, `drop 7 e7`      ONE fire, correct

       fn take(b: Box2) -> Res { match b { … } }   (param)
       -> both backends: `drop 7 e7`, `got 7`, `drop 7 e7`

   So the extra fire is the CALLER's payload-bodies walk for the argument, at
   the moved-from binding's live-range end — the very fire B-2026-08-09-10 is
   about restoring. When the callee returns the payload that fire is wrong,
   because the value's sole owner after the call is the caller's NEW binding.
   Both rows are the same question asked from opposite sides.

2. ONE SPELLING IS MEMORY-UNSAFE, so "memory is valgrind-clean — bodies only"
   holds for the reported program but not for the family. Routing the return
   through a local inside the arm:

       match b { Box2.Full(r) => { let k: Res = r; return k; } … }

       karac build -> `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`
       valgrind    -> Invalid read of size 1 + Invalid free(),
                      ERROR SUMMARY: 3 errors from 2 contexts
       --interp    -> drop 7 e7, got 7, drop 7 e7   (doubled body, no abort)

   The direct `return r;` spelling is 0 valgrind errors as filed; adding the
   intermediate `let` makes it a double free. Severity is worth revisiting on
   that basis.

THE MODEL QUESTION, which is what actually needs deciding, and why this is
bigger than a disarm. Three shapes, one root:

    owned param, payload NOT returned   -10  caller fires   (correct)
    owned param, payload RETURNED       -15  caller fires   (WRONG — callee's
                                             return handed ownership on)
    owned param, FRESH ctor argument    ---  nobody fires under codegen
                                             (no caller binding to retain)

All three follow from CALLER-RETAINS being the model for a by-value param. The
language says the opposite: a bare `T` param is OWNED, so the callee owns the
value and the callee's arm binding is the one whose live-range end should fire.
Under CALLEE-OWNS all three fall out correctly with no interprocedural
reasoning — the returning arm suppresses its own fire because the binding
escapes (the existing escape machinery), the non-returning arm fires in the
callee, and a fresh argument is owned by the callee like any other.

Caller-retains was chosen deliberately (B-2026-08-01-13, and codegen's
`pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`) to stop a double fire against the
caller — but the double it was avoiding is the same one this row reports, which
suggests the gate treated a symptom. Worth pricing the inversion before writing
a targeted disarm: a disarm needs the caller to know whether the callee returns
the payload, which is interprocedural, while callee-owns needs none of that.

Not attempted here: the inversion touches both backends and the Drop-body
expectations of a large fixture corpus, and this family is being actively worked
in another session. The measurements above are the handoff.

INVERSION PRICED BY BUILDING IT (2026-08-09, third session), THEN THE DIAGNOSIS
CORRECTED (same day, fourth session). The measurement table below is real data
and stands. The conclusion drawn from it -- that this row needs a
caller-retains -> callee-owns inversion, blocked on the disarm channel -- was
wrong on BOTH halves. Correction at the bottom.

WHAT WAS BUILT (codegen only, both halves the second note proposed):

  2. callee owns the arm binding's body -- delete the
     `!pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param` clause at both registration
     sites in pattern_binding.rs (the inline `track_user_drop_var` gate and the
     `rehome_src` filter).
  3. caller disarms the moved argument -- `suppress_user_drop_for_var` on any
     by-value Identifier argument, in call_dispatch.rs's arg loop next to the
     existing `move_declined_copy_struct_arg`.

MEASURED, every line `karac build`:

    shape                                        before        after
    param, arm RETURNS payload (this row)        drop,got,drop  got,drop   FIXED
    param, arm returns payload via `let k = r`   drop,got,drop  got,drop   FIXED
    LOCAL source, arm returns payload (control)  got,drop       got,drop   same
    param, payload NOT returned (-10's shape)    drop,v=7       v=7        ZERO
    param, matched, no early return              drop,v=7       v=7        ZERO
    param, NEVER matched                         in,drop,end    in,end     ZERO
    owned STRUCT param (Drop type directly)      drop,v=7       v=7        ZERO

So halves 2+3 fix exactly this row and silence FOUR sibling shapes. REVERTED
rather than half-landed, which was right. But the reason those four went silent
was misdiagnosed as "nothing in codegen makes a callee own its by-value params."

THAT IS FALSE, and it is the load-bearing correction. `src/codegen/param_own.rs`
(#14) IS that mechanism, and `compile_function` calls it for every bare-`Path`
by-value aggregate param: it entry deep-copies the param's heap payload and
registers a scope-exit drop, so the callee owns buffers INDEPENDENT of the
caller's retained originals. It engages for this row's `Box2` param. PROOF --
mutate the payload inside the callee before returning it:

    Box2.Full(r) => { let mut q: Res = r; q.id = 99; q.name = f"MUT"; return q; }

    -> drop 7 e7 / got 99 / drop 99 MUT       (identical on both backends)

Two fires carrying TWO DIFFERENT VALUES. The callee's copy is genuinely
independent and the caller's original is still alive and still runs a body.
That is a complete explanation of the doubling, and it is why memory is
valgrind-clean and the defect is bodies-only.

SO THE GAP IS ONE AXIS, NOT ONE MODEL. `param_own.rs` transfers the MEMORY axis
(`EnumDrop` / `StructDrop`) and never the BODY axis -- it never calls
`track_user_drop_var`. The caller therefore keeps the argument's payload-bodies
walk (`__karac_dropelems_*`) and fires it on the ORIGINAL at `b`'s live-range
end, while the returned COPY's body fires at the caller's `r`. One body per
buffer, two buffers, one logical value.

The second note's stated prerequisite is answered already, too:
`suppress_struct_cleanup_for_tail_identifier` (call_dispatch.rs:5283) retracts
`StructDrop` by ALLOCA and is in production as the caller half of
B-2026-08-05-33's own-by-transfer. The functions.rs ~2158 comment that was read
as blocking is about the NAME-keyed `suppress_user_drop_for_var`, and about
`StructDrop`-ONLY params -- a set this row is not in, since `Res` carries a real
`impl Drop` and sits in `drop_method_keys`.

CORRECTED ORDER, for whoever takes it:

    a. CALLEE HALF -- in param_own.rs's enum arm, beside the existing
       `track_enum_var`, also register the payload-bodies walk when a variant
       payload's type has a real `impl Drop`. The entry copy one line above is
       what makes that body legitimate: the callee has its own buffer to run it
       on. functions.rs:2167 is the precedent -- the same registration, gated
       today to `is_coroutine_compiled` fns only.
    b. CALLER HALF -- retract the argument binding's payload-bodies walk at the
       call: the bodies-axis twin of `move_declined_copy_struct_arg`. Must land
       WITH (a) and never before; alone it is exactly the four-shapes-go-silent
       column measured above.
    c. INTERPRETER TWIN. Both backends now double-fire after B-2026-08-09-10's
       fix (measured on the mutation probe above), so the parity oracle agrees
       in error here and only the `#[ignore]`d pin catches this row.
    d. Halves 2+3 above are NOT needed once (a)+(b) land -- they treat the arm
       binding as the owner when the param already is one. Re-measure the seven
       shapes before adding anything at those sites.

The struct-param row of the table (`owned STRUCT param ... ZERO`) is the same
story one level down: param_own.rs already owns that param's memory as well.

ALSO, THE SEVERITY NOTE ABOVE IS STALE. The `let k: Res = r; return k;` spelling
that this row records as `free(): double free detected in tcache 2` plus 3
valgrind errors is CLEAN as of B-2026-08-09-12's fix (9a15e07c): both that
spelling and the direct `return r;` measure 0 errors from 0 contexts. What
remains here is the doubled Drop BODY only -- bodies-only, memory-clean -- so
the medium severity as filed is right and the "worth revisiting" note can go.

FIXED (2026-08-09, fourth session) -- but NOT by the callee-owns inversion the
note above prices. That was built a second time, measured against the whole
suite, and REVERTED. What landed is one level down on the rule the family
already runs on.

WHY THE INVERSION LOST, with the evidence a matrix of hand-written probes could
not produce. Registering the payload-bodies walk on the callee's entry copy
(param_own.rs) and retracting the caller's does fix this row AND keeps all seven
shapes of the table above correct -- and then breaks three established E2E tests:

    e2e_owned_enum_arg_payload_body_single_caller_fire   `drop 55 x55` TWICE
    e2e_owned_self_enum_receiver_single_fire
    e2e_assign_param_rebind_and_displaced_bodies

The failing shapes are FRESH-TEMP args -- `check(E2.B(Res { .. }))`. There is no
caller binding there at all, so nothing is doubled by a caller NLL fire; the
caller-side temp drop is the single owner, which is exactly what B-2026-08-01-13
established. Give the callee a body too and that shape doubles. Worse, for an
own-`Drop` enum the parent body stays caller-side while the payload walk moves
callee-side, so `Loud`'s `loud drop` and its payload body swap order -- the
parent-then-fields sequence design.md mandates, broken by construction.

WHAT LANDED INSTEAD: `crate::ast::fn_returns_param_payload`, the payload sibling
of `fn_returns_param`. The earlier note's premise -- "a disarm needs the caller
to know whether the callee returns the payload, which is interprocedural" -- is
true but was never an obstacle: the caller ALREADY reads the callee's AST here
(B-2026-08-02-23 leg 2 calls `fn_returns_param`). This is the same query one
level down. Not "is the param returned" but "is something a `match` arm bound
OUT of it returned".

  * src/ast/items.rs -- the predicate. Walks for a `match` / `if let` /
    `while let` whose scrutinee IS the param, takes the bindings its patterns
    introduce, and asks whether any leaves the frame. Follows `let` ALIASES
    (`let k: Res = r; return k;`, the spelling most code writes) and counts a
    return of a bare binding or one moved into a returned aggregate. A FIELD
    projection (`return r.id`) deliberately does not count -- the payload stays
    behind. CONSERVATIVE-TRUE on a mixed-path callee, the same trade
    `fn_returns_param` documents: a missed body, never a double drop, and never a
    memory fault, since nothing on this channel frees.
  * src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs -- `callee_returns_enum_arg_payload` widens the
    existing `flows_into_return` retraction by it.
  * src/codegen/method_call.rs -- the same at the method arg loop.
  * src/interpreter/eval_stmt.rs -- `record_passthrough_arg_moves` ORs the new
    predicate in beside `fn_returns_param`. One line. The interpreter needed no
    new machinery at all, where the inversion needed a param drop-slot channel
    plus a change to `owned_param_names_of_fn`'s caller-retains set.

THE METHOD SPELLING IS FIXED TOO, and it is why the indices needed care: the
method path counts the receiver as declared slot 0 while the AST keeps `self` out
of `Function::params` entirely. The first wiring passed the declared index
straight through, read past the end of a one-arg method, and answered "does not
escape" for EVERY method in the program -- silently, with nothing failing. Only
instrumentation caught it; the predicate now shifts by one itself when
`self_param` is present, and the method pin exists to make that fail loudly.

    param, returns payload via `let k = r`     got,drop      was drop,got,drop
    LOCAL source, returning arm (control)      got,drop      unchanged

    NO-HEAP payload, returned                  got,drop      unchanged

detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-09-15, by writing that row's method-spelling pin.

(B-2026-08-09-12 closed it at 9a15e07c). Moving the same body into an

method path does not reach it. That fix was in the duplicator used by

CORRECTED ON INVESTIGATION, twice, and the row as filed was wrong on both
counts.

1. IT IS NOT A METHOD BUG. The free-function spelling has it identically:

       fn take(b: Box2) -> Res { match b { Box2.Full(r) => { let k: Res = r; return k; } .. } }
           -> free(): double free detected in tcache 2

   The reason it was filed as method-only is the SECOND correction, and it is
   the same trap this family has now sprung three times.

2. THE "CLEAN" FREE-FUNCTION MEASUREMENT WAS A DCE MASK. The probe it came from
   spells its `Drop` body `println(f"drop {self.id}")` -- the payload `String` is
   never read, so at the default opt level LLVM deletes the allocation together
   with BOTH of its frees and the double free evaporates. The identical program
   at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, or with a body that reads `self.name`, aborts. That
   also means B-2026-08-09-15's second pin was passing over a program that
   double-freed underneath; its `Drop` body now reads the string, and the ASAN
   fixture below covers the same shape.

MEASURED, `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`, `Drop` body reading the payload:

    shape                                         before         after
    free fn, arm `return r;`                      clean          clean
    free fn, arm `let k = r; return k;`            DOUBLE FREE    clean
    method,  arm `return r;`                      clean          clean
    method,  arm `let k = r; return k;`            DOUBLE FREE    clean
    LOCAL source, arm `let k = r; return k;`       clean          clean

So the discriminators are the owned enum PARAM and the `let` ALIAS; the call
shape is irrelevant. All five valgrind-clean after, 0 errors from 0 contexts,
nothing leaked.

ROOT CAUSE, read off the IR. Both spellings emit the arm binding's memory drop
on the return path:

    call void @__karac_drop_struct_Res(ptr %r)

`return r;` survives it because the tail-return move-suppression cap-zeroes the
RETURNED slot, which in that spelling IS `%r`. With the alias the returned slot
is `%k`, so `%k` gets zeroed and `%r` keeps a live `{ptr,len,cap}` -- the callee
frees the payload the return value is carrying, and the caller's binding frees it
again.

The `let` move-suppression did run; it just did half the job. Its `has_user_drop`
arm called `suppress_user_drop_for_var` and stopped, which is sufficient ONLY
when the source's memory rides that action's `karac_drop_<T>` wrapper (body +
fields + memory in one `UserDrop`). A match-arm payload binding taken off an
OWNED ENUM PARAM is precisely the shape where it does not: the owned-param gate
in `pattern_binding` withholds the wrapper -- the caller runs the body,
B-2026-08-09-15 -- and the binding carries a plain `StructDrop` instead, which
`suppress_user_drop_for_var` cannot see. The `has_field_user_drop` arm one branch
up already pairs both retractions for exactly this reason (B-2026-07-29-39); this
arm needed the same pairing.

RETRACTION, NOT CAP-ZEROING, and the choice is deliberate. Both stop the free;
only retraction leaves the source's bytes intact. Kāra does not reject a read
after a move -- `let k = r; println(f"{r.id}")` compiles, and `karac check` emits
an ownership WARNING rather than an error -- so zeroing would trade the double
free for a silently empty string, the same trade
`suppress_container_elem_bodies_for_var` documents choosing against.

NOT A REGRESSION from B-2026-08-09-15: measured at that fix's parent commit,
identical (3 valgrind errors from 2 contexts).

tracker: src/codegen/call_dispatch.rs (the shared move-out suppressor carried a `FreeMapHandle` arm but no `FreeFileHandle` arm)
title: a `File` MOVED out of its binding (into a `Vec`, a struct, or a return) is still closed by the origin binding at scope exit, so the new owner holds freed memory and the next method call blocks forever on a Mutex inside it -- the interpreter runs the same program correctly
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while designing streaming integration for the Cumulus
dogfooding app (kara-katas apps/cumulus). Streaming needs N subs open at once
so each output strip can be gathered from every frame without holding whole
frames in memory, and `Vec[File]` is the natural way to carry the handles.
This bug BLOCKS that design -- there is no workaround that keeps the I/O
sequential, because the alternative is reopening every file per strip.

REPRO (hangs forever under AOT, correct under `--interp`):

    fn main() with reads(FileSystem) writes(FileSystem) {
        let mut hs: Vec[File] = Vec.new();
        match File.open("a.txt") {
            Ok(f) => { hs.push(f); }
            Err(e) => { println("open failed"); }
        }
        let mut buf: Array[u8, 4] = [0u8; 4];
        println("about to read via hs[0]");
        match hs[0].read(mut buf) {
            Ok(n) => { println(f"read {n}: {buf[0]}"); }
            Err(e) => { println("read failed"); }
        }
        println("done");
    }

    $ karac run --interp v3.kara
    about to read via hs[0]
    read 4: 65
    done

    $ karac build v3.kara -o v3 && ./v3
    about to read via hs[0]
    <hangs>

`karac check` passes. Run unbuffered (`stdbuf -o0`) to see the last println --
stdout is block-buffered when redirected, so a naive capture shows NO output
at all and reads like a hang before `main` starts, which is misleading.

SCOPE, measured by bisection:

  - `Vec[File]` push + `len()`, no method call            OK
  - repeated `f.read()` on a handle NOT in a container    OK (position advances)
  - `File` in a STRUCT FIELD, then `h.f.read(buf)`        OK
  - `hs[0].read(buf)` where `hs: Vec[File]`               HANGS
  - `hs.pop()` then `f.read(buf)` on the moved-out value  HANGS
  - `hs[0].flush()`                                       HANGS

Two things narrow it. First, moving the handle back OUT with `pop()` does not
help, so this is not about an index expression as a method receiver -- the
handle is already damaged by having been stored. Second, a struct field holding
the same handle works, so it is not `File` in aggregates generally; it is the
Vec element path specifically. Every File method hangs, not just `read`, so it
is the receiver rather than the operation.

LIKELY MECHANISM (hypothesis, not verified in the IR). Codegen represents a
`File` as a pointer to a runtime `KaracFile` (`self_val.into_pointer_value()`
in `compile_file_read`), and `KaracFile` wraps `Mutex<std::fs::File>` with
every entry point doing `file.inner.lock()`. A `std::sync::Mutex` blocks
rather than faulting, so if the pointer read back out of the Vec is not the
pointer that went in, the runtime locks whatever the bytes at that address
happen to be and waits forever. That is consistent with every observation
here: a hang rather than a crash, every method affected, and the struct case
-- which stores the pointer in a field of known type -- being unaffected.
It predicts the Vec element type for an opaque handle is being mapped to
something that does not preserve a pointer.

WHY HIGH: it is a run-vs-build divergence that HANGS rather than producing a
wrong answer, with no diagnostic from any phase, in a pattern (a collection of
open handles) that any program doing multi-file I/O will reach. The
interpreter running it correctly is what makes it expensive -- the natural
debugging move is `--interp`, which says the program is fine.

RELATED: `File` has no `seek` (`src/interpreter/method_call_file.rs`: "Seek /
metadata are deferred to a follow-on slice"). Seek would not fix this, but
the two together are what make streaming file access hard to express today: no
seek forces sequential access, and sequential access across many files forces
many concurrently-open handles, which is exactly the shape that trips this.

RESOLUTION (fdc874b), AND A CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN DIAGNOSIS.

The scope recorded above is WRONG. This row claimed the defect was
Vec-element-specific because a `File` in a struct FIELD appeared to work -- but
that probe read the handle while the origin binding was still in scope, so the
close had not fired yet. Re-probed with the read moved past the origin's scope:

    Vec[File], read after the arm closes              HANGS
    Vec[Holder] where Holder { f: File }              HANGS
    struct returned from a fn, no Vec, no match arm   HANGS   <- no container
    control: Vec[i64] in a struct, same shape         OK      <- not File

Containers were never the discriminator. OUTLIVING THE ORIGIN BINDING is. The
hypothesis about a Vec element type failing to round-trip a pointer was wrong
too; the pointer round-trips fine. What actually happens is that the origin
binding's queued `FreeFileHandle` fires at its own scope exit even though the
handle was moved, `karac_runtime_file_close` reconstructs the Box and drops it,
and the new owner is left holding freed memory. The Mutex prediction was right
for the wrong reason: the lock sits inside a freed allocation, not at a garbage
address.

`FreeFileHandle` is queue-driven exactly like `FreeMapHandle`, which has carried
move-out suppression since B-2026-07-15-25 and simply had no File arm. The fix
adds it to the shared suppressor, retracting the action for the moved binding's
slot from EVERY live frame -- the same rationale the Map arm documents, since a
move site can fire with a transient arg/method-eval frame above the frame that
owns the action. One arm covers all ~20 existing move sites instead of
duplicating them.

Both shapes are pinned as regression tests, and both were confirmed to FAIL
without the fix by taking the full 15s watchdog timeout -- they reproduce the
hang and are killed, rather than merely asserting. The Vec test reads TWICE and
requires the second read to continue where the first stopped: a reopened handle
or a struct copy would restart at byte 0 and still look healthy, so the
advancing file position is what distinguishes the same LIVE handle from merely a
non-crashing one.

NOT FIXED HERE: nothing closes the handle once moved -- see B-2026-08-09-20.

fix: FIXED by bb46a68d -- `eval_method_call` short-circuits on `pending_cf` immediately after evaluating the receiver, so a faulted receiver propagates its own runtime error instead of being dispatched on as a `Unit` poison. Placed at the single receiver-eval site rather than in the arm that reported it: the receiver assertions are per-method (`len`, `chars`, ... each have their own; `is_empty` has none), so one check covers every method on every builtin receiver. Pinned by `test_faulted_method_receiver_reports_the_fault_not_an_ice` plus a healthy-receiver over-fire control.
title: Interpreter ICEs (`internal error: entered unreachable code`) on a METHOD CALL whose RECEIVER faulted, instead of reporting the receiver's runtime error. `let n = v[3].len();` on an empty `Vec[Vec[i64]]` panics with `len() receiver at L:C was Value::Unit; either an interpreter codepath produced the wrong receiver variant or the typechecker accepted .len() on a type without one` -- the assertion's own two hypotheses are both wrong: the typechecker is right and no codepath produced a wrong variant. The out-of-bounds index set pending_cf and yielded the Unit POISON value, and the method-call receiver path dispatches on it without first checking pending_cf. The bare index `v[3]` with no method call reports correctly (`runtime error: index 3 out of bounds (len 0)`), so it is purely the receiver position. RUN-VS-BUILD: interp ICEs; `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` both report cleanly (`panic ...: vec index out of bounds`), so this is an interpreter-only diagnostics divergence, not a miscompile. SAME CLASS AS an already-fixed row: B-2026-06-19-13's 'BONUS BUG' gave `match` SCRUTINEE position exactly this treatment ('the Match arm now short-circuits on pending_cf before eval_match, mirroring the Binary/Unary operand-fault short-circuits'); Binary, Unary and Match all short-circuit on pending_cf and the METHOD-CALL RECEIVER was never given the same guard. FIX DIRECTION: check pending_cf before method dispatch in method_call_seq.rs and propagate the pending fault, mirroring the Binary/Unary/Match arms; then the assertion at :74 becomes genuinely unreachable and its misleading message can stay. REPRO (4 lines): `fn main() { let mut v: Vec[Vec[i64]] = Vec.new(); let n = v[3].len(); println(f"{n}"); }` under `karac run --interp`.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while authoring kata #251 (Flatten 2D Vector) -- specifically while PROVING that the `and` in `while v.row < v.data.len() and v.col >= v.data[v.row].len()` is a load-bearing bounds guard. Swapping the operands so the guard no longer runs first was expected to produce a clean out-of-bounds runtime error; it produced the ICE instead. The kata itself is unaffected (the correct operand order never faults) -- this was surfaced by a deliberate negative probe, which is the same way B-2026-06-19-13's sibling ICE was found. -- SURFACE NOTE: interpreter runtime-error propagation, method-call receiver position.

-- FIXED by bb46a68d (2026-08-09), the fix direction as filed --

ONE guard at the single receiver-eval site in `eval_method_call`
(method_call.rs, right after `let obj = self.eval_expr_inner(object)`):
`pending_cf` set means the receiver already failed, so return the poison and
let the caller propagate.

WHY THERE and not in the arm the ICE named, which is the part worth keeping:
the receiver assertions are PER-METHOD. `len` (:74) and `chars` (:101) each
carry their own `unreachable!`; `is_empty` instead falls through to a tolerant
default and reported the fault correctly all along. So which arm the program
happens to land in decides whether you get an ICE or the truth -- and that is
not a property of the program. Checking once covers every method on every
builtin receiver, and leaves the arms' assertions meaning what they say: a
NON-faulted receiver of the wrong variant really is a compiler bug. The row's
closing note ("then the assertion at :74 becomes genuinely unreachable and its
misleading message can stay") holds, and now holds for every sibling assertion
too, not just that one.

WIDER THAN THE ROW RECORDED, both axes measured under `karac run --interp`:

    receiver expression                     BEFORE            AFTER
    `v[3].len()`, empty Vec[Vec[i64]]       ICE (:74)         index 3 out of bounds
    `o.unwrap().len()`, o = None            ICE (:74)         called unwrap() on None
    `v[2].chars()`, empty Vec[String]       ICE (:101)        index 2 out of bounds
    `v[0].len()`, empty Vec[Map[..]]        ICE (:74)         index 0 out of bounds
    `v[1].is_empty()`                       already clean     unchanged
    `v[0].get()`, user-struct method        already clean     unchanged
    `w.push(v[5])` -- faulted ARG, not rcvr already clean     unchanged

So the trigger is not the index operation the repro used: ANY fault in the
receiver position does it (`unwrap` of `None` is the second one measured).
Arg position was never affected.

Exit code is 1 after the fix, matching `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build`,
which reported cleanly throughout. Their message text still differs from the
interpreter's (`panic ...: vec index out of bounds` vs `runtime error: index 3
out of bounds (len 0)`), but that wording gap is interpreter-wide and
pre-existing -- visible on the `is_empty` shape that never ICEd -- so it is NOT
part of this row.

PINNED: `test_faulted_method_receiver_reports_the_fault_not_an_ice`
(tests/interpreter.rs) -- two faults across two asserting arms, plus the
tolerant `is_empty` arm as the converse control, each case asserting both the

VERIFIED: interpreter 1474, cli 577, lowering 137, example_packages 28, plus
comptime / comptime_ast / comptime_derive / comptime_reflection, json, closures,

title: SIBLING OF B-2026-08-09-18, NOT CLOSED BY bb46a68d: a faulted operand still ICEs the interpreter in THREE more positions, all with the same shape (`unreachable!` whose message proposes two causes and both are wrong -- the typechecker is right and no codepath produced a bad variant; the operand faulted, set pending_cf, and yielded the `Unit` poison, which is then asserted against). bb46a68d guarded the METHOD-CALL RECEIVER only. Still ICEing: (1) `if v[3] > 0i64 and true {}` -> eval_ops.rs:140 `short-circuit `And` LHS ... was Value::Unit not Bool`; (2) same with `or` -> same site, ``Or` LHS`; (3) `if true and v[3] > 0i64 {}` -> interpreter.rs:1966 `condition was Value::Unit not Bool` (the RHS fault escapes the short-circuit evaluator and poisons the enclosing `if` condition instead). So the guard is missing on the short-circuit operator's LHS, its RHS, and the if-condition consumer. NOTE the earlier row's fix note asserted `Binary, Unary and Match all short-circuit on pending_cf` -- that holds for the NON-short-circuit Binary path; `eval_short_circuit` is a separate evaluator with its own operand assertions and was never given the guard. RUN-VS-BUILD: interpreter-only in all three; `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` report `vec index out of bounds` cleanly at the right span. FIX DIRECTION: same one-line-per-site treatment as bb46a68d -- check pending_cf after evaluating each operand in `eval_short_circuit` and before the enclosing condition test -- or, better, hoist the check to the single place a `Value` is consumed as a Bool, since this is now the third distinct site found for one root cause.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found by re-running the SAME negative probe that produced B-2026-08-09-18 after that row was closed -- the 4-line minimal repro (`v[3].len()`) is fixed, but the real kata-shaped case that originally surfaced it (`while v.col >= v.data[v.row].len() and v.row < v.data.len()`, kata #251's skip-empty guard with its operands deliberately swapped) still ICEs, now at eval_ops.rs:140 instead of method_call_seq.rs:74. Worth noting as process: verifying a closed row against the ORIGINAL finding case, not only against the minimised repro that was filed, is what exposed the incompleteness. -- SURFACE NOTE: interpreter runtime-error propagation, short-circuit operator operands and if-condition.

FIXED at 512f59a, with the hoist the row asked for rather than one guard per
reported site — and that choice closed a FOURTH position the row does not list.

TWO guards, not three:

  - `eval_short_circuit`, right after the LHS eval: propagate the poison
    instead of asserting it is a Bool. This covers sites (1) and (2), which
    were always one site with two operators. Returning early also preserves
    the short-circuit's own guarantee: a faulted LHS must not evaluate the RHS.

  - `is_truthy`, the single place a `Value` is consumed as a Bool: answer
    `false` when `pending_cf` is set. This covers site (3), where the RHS fault
    escapes the short-circuit evaluator and poisons the enclosing condition.
    `false` is safe for every caller — the fault is already pending, so the
    enclosing block unwinds and reports the operand's real error at its own
    span before the not-taken branch can be observed.

THE FOURTH SITE. `is_truthy` has exactly three callers: the `if` condition, the
`while` condition, and a MATCH GUARD. The guard consumes its Bool through the
same helper and ICEd identically on

    match n { x if v[3] > 0i64 => { … } _ => { … } }

which nobody had reported. Hoisting to `is_truthy` fixed it for free; guarding
the two condition sites named in the row would have left it, and this defect
has now been found three times by exactly that pattern of fixing the reported
spelling. Worth stating as the general lesson: the assertion sites are where
the ICE surfaces, but the CONSUMERS of a poisoned value are where the guard
belongs.

WHY THE EARLIER NOTE'S CLAIM WAS RIGHT BUT IRRELEVANT. B-2026-08-09-18's fix
note said "Binary, Unary and Match all short-circuit on pending_cf". True — of
the NON-short-circuit `Binary` evaluator (B-2026-07-15-7). `and`/`or` are
routed away from it precisely so the RHS stays unevaluated, so `eval_short_
circuit` never saw that guard and needed its own.

VERIFIED. All five shapes report the operand's own fault at the right span,
with `--interp`, `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` agreeing — including the
row's source case, kata #251's `while it.col >= it.data[it.row].len() and
it.row < it.data.len()`, which still ICEd after -18 closed. Full `--features
llvm` suite green (102/102), clippy `--all-targets`, fmt.

TESTS. `test_faulted_short_circuit_operand_reports_the_fault_not_an_ice` pins
all three reported sites plus the match guard plus the kata shape; reaching its
assertions at all is the no-ICE half, since the old failure was a Rust
`unreachable!` that aborts before the errors can be inspected.
`test_short_circuit_still_skips_its_rhs_and_evaluates_healthy_operands` is the
converse control for the two things these guards could plausibly break: a
false `and` and a true `or` must still leave a FAULTING RHS unevaluated (the
program completing is the assertion), and conditions reached with no pending
fault must still decide normally.

PROCESS NOTE, seconding the row's own. It was found by re-running the ORIGINAL
finding case against the closed row rather than the minimised repro that was
filed. The minimisation dropped the short-circuit that turned out to be the
whole point.

tracker: src/codegen/synth_drop.rs (`vec_element_drain_fn`) and the struct drop glue -- neither emits `karac_runtime_file_close` for a `File` element/field
fix: FIXED by cc48dcca -- two arms, one per container kind: a `File` element arm in `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` (new `emit_file_slot_close_fn`, threaded as `elem_agg_drop` so every `track_vec_of_aggs_var` site picks it up) and a `FieldDrop::FileHandleClose` in the struct drop glue; `te_recursive_drop_fully_supported` admits `File` so `Vec[Vec[File]]` leaves the one-level fast path. Both null the slot after closing, because `karac_runtime_file_close` is not idempotent, and both defer to a user type that shadows the name `File`. Also fixes two shapes the row did not record -- a handle read back out of a container into a fresh binding (`let g = hs[0]` / `let g = h.f`) leaked identically. Pinned by four ASAN fixtures including an over-fire control. The row's unverified `DropChannelEnd` sibling risk was probed and does NOT reproduce.
title: a `File` moved into a `Vec` or a struct is never closed -- the container has no element/field drop for the handle, so the fd leaks until process exit (253 of 400 opens succeed under `ulimit -n 256`)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the other half of B-2026-08-09-17, split out because the two have
different severities and different fixes.

B-2026-08-09-17 stopped a moved-out `File` being closed by its ORIGIN binding,
which is what made the handle usable at all. Nothing took over the closing. A
`Vec[File]`, or a struct holding a `File`, has no element/field drop that emits
`karac_runtime_file_close`, so the fd (and the `Box<KaracFile>` behind it) lives
until process exit.

MEASURED, under `ulimit -n 256`:

    handle opened and dropped, never moved        3000 of 3000   closes fine
    Vec[File] built and dropped per iteration       253 of 400    LEAKS
    struct holding a File, dropped per iteration    253 of 400    LEAKS

253 is the limit minus the standard streams. The failure is SILENT: the program
does not crash, `File.open` simply starts returning `Err`, and a caller that
ignores the error arm just stops making progress.

This is a strictly better failure mode than the use-after-free hang it replaced,
and for the streaming design that motivated the work it is immaterial -- those
handles are held for the program's lifetime by construction. But a long-running
program that opens files in a loop and parks them in a container will exhaust
its descriptors.

FIX SHAPE: teach the container drop paths about `File`, the way `FreeMapHandle`
already carries `val_drop_fn` / `key_drop_fn` for per-entry drops.
`vec_element_drain_fn` is the Vec-side hook; struct fields need the equivalent
in the struct drop glue.

SIBLING RISK, unverified: `CleanupAction::DropChannelEnd` (`track_channel_var`)
is registered the same queue-driven way and has no suppression arm either, so a
`Sender`/`Receiver` moved into a container is likely to reproduce the ORIGINAL
B-2026-08-09-17 shape rather than this one. `FreeGpuBuffer` is explicitly safe:
its comment records that `karac_runtime_gpu_free_soa` is idempotent, which is
exactly the property `karac_runtime_file_close` lacks. Not probed -- noted so the
next person starts from the pattern rather than from a single symptom.

-- FIXED by cc48dcca (2026-08-10), the fix shape as filed --

TWO arms, one per container kind, because they are two code paths that merely
shared a symptom -- the same trap B-2026-08-09-17's first diagnosis fell into
when it read "struct field works, Vec element fails" as a statement about
containers:

  (a) `vec_elem_agg_drop_for_type_expr` gains a `File` element arm returning a
      new `emit_file_slot_close_fn` (`__karac_file_slot_close`). It is threaded
      as `elem_agg_drop`, so EVERY `track_vec_of_aggs_var` registration site --
      let-binding, for-loop iterable, pattern binding, par block, method result
      -- picks it up at once rather than one site at a time.

  (b) The struct drop glue gains `FieldDrop::FileHandleClose`, classified by
      declared field type name in a post-pass beside the HTTP handle-field
      override, which is the same shape of gap: an opaque runtime-owned handle
      no layout-driven classifier can see.

  (c) `te_recursive_drop_fully_supported` admits `File`, which is what keeps a
      `Vec[Vec[File]]` off the one-level buffer-only fast path. Without it (a)
      alone would not have reached the nested shape.

MEASURED under `ulimit -n 256`, before -> after:

    Vec[File] built and dropped per iteration       253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    struct holding a File, per iteration            253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    Vec[Vec[File]], per iteration                   253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    handle read out of a Vec by index               253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    handle read out of a struct field               253 of 400  -> 400 of 400
    handle opened and dropped, never moved         3000 of 3000 -> unchanged
    element popped out (`Some(g)` binding owns it)  400 of 400  -> unchanged

Rows 4-5 were NOT in the row as filed: reading a handle back out of a container
into a fresh binding (`let g = hs[0]` / `let g = h.f`) gave that binding no
cleanup either, so those shapes leaked for the same reason and are fixed by the
same owner. Rows 6-7 are the controls -- `pop` already had an owner, and the
drain walks `0..len`, so a popped element is outside the walk.

NEITHER arm guards on null: `karac_runtime_file_close` returns early on null, so
a branch would only restate the runtime's own check in IR. Both NULL the slot
after closing, and that IS load-bearing -- close reconstructs the `Box` and
drops it, so it is not idempotent (precisely the property the row noted
`karac_runtime_gpu_free_soa` has and this lacks), and the null is what makes a
second drop of the same storage inert. Both are also guarded against a user type
named `File` shadowing the builtin: the element arm sits AFTER the
struct/enum/shared checks so a shadowing type is claimed by those, and the field
arm additionally requires the LLVM field to be the `ptr` the handle lowers to.

PINNED: four fixtures in tests/memory_sanitizer.rs --
`asan_file_moved_into_a_vec_is_closed_by_the_vec`,
`asan_file_moved_into_a_struct_field_is_closed_by_the_struct`,
`asan_file_inside_a_nested_vec_is_closed_at_every_level`, and
`asan_file_handed_to_a_second_owner_is_closed_exactly_once` (the over-fire
direction: three shapes that hand the handle to a second candidate owner).
All four stash-proven RED, leaking 468 B/39, 480 B/40, 480 B/40 and 960 B/80
respectively. The fourth's count is itself evidence rather than decoration: 80
of its 120 opens leaked, and the 40 that did not are exactly the popped ones --
the measurement that shows `pop` was already covered.

LSan is the right gate here even though the user-visible symptom is descriptor
exhaustion: fd counts are awkward to assert portably, and the leaked
`Box<KaracFile>` behind each fd is the same defect one level down.

SIBLING RISK -- PROBED, DOES NOT REPRODUCE. The row flagged
`CleanupAction::DropChannelEnd` as likely to reproduce the ORIGINAL
B-2026-08-09-17 UAF shape. It does not, in either direction: a `Sender[i64]`

fix: FIXED by 4f3d6921, BOTH halves. READ: `compile_nested_index_read` gained a struct-FIELD arm -- `nested_index_field_base_elem` resolves the element `TypeExpr` from the field's DECLARED type and the container pointer via `lower_field_access_ptr`, then rejoins the existing synth-identifier tail (factored out as `finish_nested_index_read`). The name-keyed lowering was split into a by-POINTER core, `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_vec_at`, so the field base reuses the identical bounds check and GEP. title: A NESTED index whose base is a STRUCT FIELD (`h.data[i][j]`) is rejected by codegen -- `codegen: nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable in v1 (got non-identifier inner expression)` -- while the interpreter runs it. RUN-VS-BUILD: `karac run --interp` prints the right value; `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` both fail. LOUD, not a miscompile, and the JIT failure carries an actionable `--interp` hint. BOUNDARY (probed): `d[i][j]` on a named local BUILDS; `h.data[i][j]` FAILS; `let row = h.data[i]; row[j]` BUILDS; `h.data[i].len()` (single index on a field, then a method) BUILDS; the nested WRITE `h.data[i][j] = v` FAILS the same way. So it is specifically the DOUBLE index rooted at a field access, read and write alike -- single-index-on-field and double-index-on-local are both fine. CAUSE: `compile_nested_index_read` requires `inner_object` to be `ExprKind::Identifier` because it recovers the element TypeExpr from `var_elem_type_exprs[outer_name]` and registers a synthetic identifier for the element slot; a field access has no entry in that map. FIX DIRECTION: resolve the element TypeExpr from the FIELD's declared type (struct field type -> Vec/Slice/Array element) rather than from the variable map, and compile the base to a pointer via the existing place-expression path, so the synthetic-element machinery can stay as-is. Sibling deferral in the same function: chained `a[i][j][k]` is rejected by an explicit MR5 guard, so any fix should decide whether it generalises to arbitrary place expressions or only to field bases. REPRO (9 lines): `struct H { data: Vec[Vec[i64]] } fn main() { let mut i: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); i.push(1i64); let mut d: Vec[Vec[i64]] = Vec.new(); d.push(i); let h = H { data: d }; println(f"{h.data[0][0]}"); }`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while authoring kata #251 (Flatten 2D Vector). An iterator over a 2D vector naturally stores the data as a struct field and reads `v.data[v.row][v.col]` -- that is the canonical spelling of the whole problem, so 3 of the kata's 4 programs (the lazy two-cursor solver, the prefix-offset solver, and the differential) cannot AOT-build. The eager-flatten solver builds because it copies through a named local. Per the kata policy the natural spelling is KEPT rather than rewritten around the gap: the kata's README records that its `karac build` leg is blocked on this row. -- SURFACE NOTE: codegen nested-index lowering, field-access base.

=== FIXED (4f3d6921). Two halves, two different gates, and one gate choice that
decided whether the fix was worth anything. ===

THE WRITE HALF WAS A SEPARATE DEFECT with its own error string. The row records
`h.data[i][j] = v` as failing "the same way"; it does not -- the read dies on
`nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable`, the
write on `Index assignment target must be a variable`, from
`compile_index_store` in collections.rs, a different function the row's tracker
never points at. Same user-visible gap, two edits.

  The write half needed no new lowering at all. `compile_index_store` already
  has a nested arm (named outer) and a field arm (single index); this shape fell
  between them. Resolving the field to a synth identifier and recursing hands it
  to the existing nested arm unchanged, so the store logic keeps one
  implementation.

THE GATE CHOICE THAT MATTERED, and the row's suggested one would have missed
the case the row itself cares about. The obvious base-pointer helper is
`field_chain_place_ptr` -- and it DELIBERATELY returns `None` for a `ref`-param
root, because the slot holds a pointer rather than the aggregate. Built that
way first and measured: `h.data[i][j]` worked for an owned local, and still
failed for `fn read(h: ref H)` and for every `ref self` / `mut ref self`
method. That is the shape the motivating kata actually writes -- a 2D cursor
keeps its grid in a field and reads `self.data[self.row][self.col]` from a
method -- so the fix would have left the reported use case broken while looking
green on the filed reproduction. `lower_field_access_ptr` is the right helper:
it derefs a `ref` param, loads the handle for a shared struct, and normalises
`SelfValue`. Both halves use it.

  GENERAL LESSON, not specific to this row: when a repro is a `main`-level
  program but the reported SOURCE is a method on a struct, verify the borrowed
  spelling before believing the fix. The two differ by exactly one deref, and
  only one of them is in the reproduction.

MEASURED BOUNDARY on the fixed tree, `--interp` vs `karac build`, all matching:
owned local field base (read + write), `ref self` / `mut ref self` methods,
`ref` / `mut ref` params, `shared struct` receiver, `Vec[Vec[String]]` heap
elements, computed indices in nested loops, and OOB on the outer index still
panicking through the same checked helper.

STILL DEFERRED, deliberately: the TRIPLE index `a[i][j][k]` remains refused by
the separate MR5 guard, loudly. The row asked whether a fix should generalise
to arbitrary place expressions -- it does not, and the pin's case 5 holds that

on the pre-change tree via the already-supported local spelling

title: a NESTED indexed store that overwrites a heap element (`d[i][j] = <String>`) leaks the old value -- the single-index store frees it, the nested one does not
detail:
FOUND while fixing B-2026-08-09-21 (nested index rooted at a struct field). NOT
introduced by it: measured identical on the pre-change tree using the local
spelling, which has always compiled.

    let mut r: Vec[String] = Vec.new();
    r.push(f"aa"); r.push(f"bb");
    let mut d: Vec[Vec[String]] = Vec.new();
    d.push(r);
    d[0][0] = f"zz";        -> "aa" is never freed

NARROWED, each line measured at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 with `--leak-check=full`:

    r[0] = f"zz"            single index, local        clean
    h.data[0] = f"zz"       single index, field        clean
    d[0][0] = f"zz"         NESTED, local              1 leak
    h.data[0][0] = f"zz"    NESTED, field              1 leak

So the single-index store already frees the displaced element and the NESTED
one does not -- the gap is the nested store path
(`compile_nested_vec_vec_index_store`), independent of whether the base is a
name or a field. The field-base half only reaches it because B-2026-08-09-21
now routes there, which is why this is filed rather than treated as that row's
regression.

WHY IT IS ONLY VISIBLE AT -O0: at the default level the overwritten element is
frequently a dead allocation LLVM deletes outright, so a default-level valgrind
run reports clean. Same trap as B-2026-08-09-13 and B-2026-08-09-4. Any
measurement on this path must be taken at -O0.

FIX DIRECTION: the single-index store's displaced-value free is the model --
whatever it does before overwriting a heap element, the nested store should do
at the same point. Worth checking whether the nested path can simply delegate
to it once the inner element pointer is known, rather than growing its own
copy of the release logic; the two would then not drift again.

NOT PINNED as a test yet -- filed at the point of discovery with the narrowing
above. Note that an ASAN fixture for it needs `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` (the -O0 leg)
to witness anything.

FIXED at __SHA__, by DELEGATION rather than a second copy — the row's own
preferred shape ("worth checking whether the nested path can simply delegate to
it once the inner element pointer is known").

The displaced-release-then-store logic is now
`emit_elem_store_releasing_displaced(elem_ptr, elem_ty, elem_te, val,
rhs_is_fresh)`, taking an ALREADY-COMPUTED element slot so it is indifferent to
how the caller got there. `compile_vec_index_store` calls it after its single
GEP; `compile_nested_vec_vec_index_store` calls it after its leaf GEP, passing
the inner element `TypeExpr` it already had to derive in order to GEP at all.
The four shape rules — vec-struct buffer free, tensor block free, `shared` /
`Option[shared]` refcount release, scalar width coercion — now live in one
place. The nested path also threads `rhs_is_fresh`, so the refcount shapes get
the same retain-new → store → release-old ordering that keeps a self-alias
safe.

Worth stating why the diff is small but not trivial: two of the four shapes
(tensor, shared) do the STORE themselves and return early, so the extraction
had to take the store with it rather than leaving it at the call sites.

VERIFIED at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 with `--leak-check=full`, since per the note
above a default-level run cannot see this class:

    d[0][0] = f"zz"           the row's repro          clean (was 1 block)
    h.data[0][0] = f"zz"      struct-FIELD base        clean (was 1 block)
    d[0][0] = 9i64            scalar leaf, control     clean, value correct
    d[0][0] = d[0][0]         SELF-alias               clean, no invalid free
    d[0][0] = d[0][1]         sibling alias            clean, value correct
    o[j][0] = f"n{j}" in a loop                        clean (was 4 blocks)

All six match `--interp`. Full `--features llvm` suite green (102/102), clippy
`--all-targets`, fmt.

ONE CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN GUIDANCE, measured rather than assumed. The
row says any measurement on this path must be taken at -O0, and that is right
for a bare `d[0][0] = f"zz"` probe. But it is NOT true of the ASAN fixture
written here: measured against the pre-fix compiler it leaks 24 B in 8 blocks
at `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` **and the same at the default -O2**, because the
loop-derived labels (`f"r{i}a"`) keep the displaced buffers from folding into
the dead allocations LLVM deletes. So this fixture does not depend on the -O0
leg the way B-2026-08-09-13's and -4's do. That is recorded in the fixture's
doc comment specifically so nobody "simplifies" the labels to constants and
silently turns it into a vacuous pass.

TESTS. `test_e2e_nested_index_store_releases_the_displaced_element` (codegen)
pins the values for the four shapes above — it cannot see the leak, but it
catches the opposite error, a release that frees a still-live buffer, as a
wrong or empty string. `asan_nested_index_store_frees_the_displaced_element`
carries the memory half, with the self-alias row present as the
invalid-free direction (over-eager release) against the leak direction
(missing release).
