title: a generic struct's method whose parameter is the TYPE PARAMETER leaks a fresh TEMPORARY argument's buffer -- `s.push([1i64,2i64])` on a `Stack[T]` leaks while the same call with a NAMED binding is clean. The row's original framing (a `Vec[T]` field's element resolution at drop, char/element-type specific) is REFUTED by measurement: the drop synthesis already resolves the monomorph correctly, and `Vec[String]` leaks too
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found dogfooding a generic container + trait-dispatch program
(`Stack[T]` instantiated at `i64`, `String`, and `Vec[i64]`, plus a
`describe_all[T: Describe]`). Output matched the oracle on all three backends;
LSan caught 16 bytes in 1 allocation that no oracle could see.

MINIMAL REPRODUCER -- 11 lines, leaks on `karac build`:

    struct Stack[T] { items: Vec[T] }
    impl[T] Stack[T] {
        fn new() -> Stack[T] { Stack { items: Vec.new() } }
        fn push(mut ref self, v: T) { self.items.push(v); }
        fn len(ref self) -> i64 { self.items.len() }
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut s: Stack[Vec[i64]] = Stack.new();
        s.push([1i64, 2i64]);
        println(f"{s.len()}");
    }

    LeakSanitizer: 16 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s)

THE GENERIC IS REQUIRED, which is the discriminator worth having: the
non-generic twin with the SAME concrete field type is clean.

    struct Stack[T] { items: Vec[T] }   at T = Vec[i64]   LEAKS
    struct Holder { items: Vec[Vec[i64]] }                clean

WHICH MONOMORPHS LEAK, measured:

    Stack[i64]        clean      (scalar element owns no buffer)
    Stack[String]     clean      (the String monomorph IS resolved)
    Stack[Vec[i64]]   LEAKS      (the nested-Vec monomorph is not)

So this is not "generic struct drops are broken" -- the `String` monomorph works,
which is exactly what B-2026-07-15-11 and B-2026-07-15-24 fixed. The gap is the
NESTED container element: `Vec[T]` where `T` itself resolves to a `Vec`.

PER-ELEMENT PATTERN -- the whole buffer of every unconsumed element goes:

    push([3i64])                     clean   (1-element payload does not heap-allocate)
    push([1i64, 2i64])               16 B in 1 alloc
    push([1i64, 2i64, 3i64, 4i64])   32 B in 1 alloc
    push([1,2]) + push([3])          16 B in 1 alloc   (the [3] has no allocation to leak)

The 1-element case being clean is an allocation artifact, not a partial fix --
there is simply nothing on the heap for that element. Read the rule as "every
heap-allocated element buffer leaks".

CONSUMED ELEMENTS ARE FINE. Popping every element out before the container dies
is clean, because the popped `Some(v)` binding owns and frees the buffer:

    push([1,2]); push([3]); pop(); pop();   clean
    push([1,2]); push([3]); pop();          LEAKS (the un-popped one)

So the defect is squarely the container's DROP path, not `push` and not the
monomorph's construction.

UNBOUNDED IN A LOOP, and invisible without a sanitizer: the program is correct on
all three backends and prints the right answers. A long-running program that
builds a generic container of collections leaks one buffer per element per
iteration.

FIX SHAPE: `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_mono` already threads the concrete
`param -> arg` substitution so a `Vec[T]` field resolves its element before
picking a per-element drop -- that is what makes the `String` monomorph correct.
Extend that resolution to a `T` that is itself a container, so the element drop
becomes the recursive `emit_vec_drop_fn` rather than the buffer-only fast path.
Worth checking `Stack[Map[..]]`, `Stack[Set[..]]` and `Stack[VecDeque[..]]` in
the same pass rather than one dogfooding session at a time; `Vec` and `String`
differing already shows the resolution is per-shape rather than general.

=== RE-DIAGNOSED 2026-08-11 (not yet fixed) ===

The headline reproducer still reproduces EXACTLY as filed (16 bytes, 1 allocation, and 32 bytes at four elements). Everything this row concluded ABOUT it is wrong, and the FIX SHAPE it proposes would have been a no-op. Re-measured on a tree ~100 commits later; each row below is valgrind on `karac build`, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`.

REFUTED (1) -- "the nested-Vec monomorph is not resolved". It is. `emit_struct_drop_synthesis_impl`'s `FieldDrop::VecOrString` arm was instrumented to print the resolved element and whether a per-element drain fn was selected. Both monomorphs resolve and both select one:

    Stack[Vec[i64]]    PROBE struct=Stack field=0 elem="Vec_i64"  drain=true
    Stack[String]      PROBE struct=Stack field=0 elem="String"   drain=true

So the container's drop path is correct for the leaking case, and extending "that resolution to a `T` that is itself a container" — the row's FIX SHAPE — would have changed nothing.

REFUTED (2) -- "which monomorphs leak". The `String`-vs-`Vec` split was an artifact of how the two probes were WRITTEN, not of the element type. Holding the element type fixed and varying only the ARGUMENT FORM:

    Stack[Vec[i64]]    s.push([1i64, 2i64])            LEAKS 16 B
    Stack[Vec[i64]]    let v = ...; s.push(v)          clean
    Stack[Vec[String]] s.push(["a long string ..."])   LEAKS 24 B
    Stack[Vec[String]] let v = ...; s.push(v)          clean

`Vec[String]` leaks just as readily; the original `Stack[String]`-clean row used a string LITERAL, whose buffer is static.

REFUTED (3) -- "consumed elements are fine / pop-all is clean". It is not, and popping makes it WORSE: with two pushes, no pop leaks 16 B in 1 block, one pop leaks 24 B in 2, and popping BOTH leaks 40 B in 3. (Measured with a `pop` method added to the row's own `Stack`.) So the drop path is not where this lives, which is consistent with (1).

THE ACTUAL DISCRIMINATOR, isolated by holding the argument a fresh temporary and varying only the callee:

    generic struct's method, param is bare `T`   s.push([1i64,2i64])       LEAKS
    non-generic struct's method, param Vec[i64]  h.push_one([1i64,2i64])   clean
    free fn, param Vec[i64]                      take([1i64,2i64])         clean
    GENERIC free fn, param bare `T`              take([1i64,2i64])         clean
    builtin Vec.push                             items.push([1i64,2i64])   clean
    non-generic struct, same field type          h.items.push([...])       clean

So it needs ALL THREE: a generic STRUCT, a METHOD on it (a generic free function is clean), and a parameter typed as the bare type PARAMETER, called with a temporary. A named binding is clean because the move is tracked; the temporary's buffer is what goes.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE NEXT ATTEMPT. Look at the caller-side cleanup for the argument temporary of a mono'd generic method, not at drop synthesis. The container ends up owning a live buffer (the program prints correct answers and the element is readable), so the temp is either deep-copied with the original never freed, or moved with the caller's cleanup still armed on a slot it no longer owns — the pop numbers going UP rather than down suggests the former. Note the sibling family already in flight: B-2026-08-10-21 (the `UseAfterMove` defensive copy) and B-2026-08-07-12 (a heapless boxed envelope counting as heap for the caller-temp gate) are both about caller temporaries, and this may be a third facet of the same gate rather than its own mechanism.

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE, deliberately: the sibling containers the row asks about (`Stack[Map[..]]`, `Stack[Set[..]]`, `Stack[VecDeque[..]]`) were measured CLEAN, but every one of those probes used a named binding, which is now known to be the clean arm — so they prove nothing and must be re-run with temporaries before anyone concludes the shape is Vec-specific.

=== FIXED 2026-08-11 ===

The re-diagnosis above was right about WHERE and wrong only in not going one step
further. Root cause, confirmed in the emitted IR:

A parameter written as the BARE TYPE PARAMETER (`fn push(mut ref self, v: T)`)
is resolved to its concrete type by the mono prologue
(`subst_monomorph_type_params`), which enters it in `owned_vecstr_params` —
B-2026-07-11-35's "push leg". That registration makes every RETAINING CONSUME
SITE in the mono body deep-copy the argument: `self.items.push(v)` emits a
`dcopy` malloc + memcpy and stores the COPY into the container. That is the
caller-retains convention, so the callee never frees the caller's buffer. A
fresh TEMPORARY argument had no owner in any frame and leaked; a NAMED binding
was clean only because its own let-drop still owned the original.

That is why every earlier conclusion pointed the wrong way. The container's
per-element drain is correct AND fires — it frees the callee's independent copy,
which is exactly why instrumenting it showed `drain=true` and changing it would
have been a no-op. Confirmed by allocation accounting: the leaking and clean
programs make the SAME number of allocations and differ by exactly one free.

B-2026-07-11-35's own comment names three legs — "paired with per-monomorph
struct-drop synthesis (so the now-deep-copied element buffers are freed at the
container's drop) and caller-side fresh-owned-temp cleanup". The first two
shipped; the third never did. This is the third leg.

FIX: `compile_generic_call` (mono.rs) materializes a fresh heap Vec temp into
the caller's scope when the callee's param at that index is written as a bare
type param, via the new `generic_param_is_bare_type_param`. Deliberately
narrower than `compile_call`'s #20 arm, which materializes EVERY fresh heap Vec
temp. Borrow forms (`ref T` / `mut ref T` / `mut Slice[T]`) are excluded — they
never enter `owned_vecstr_params`. Collection literals are admitted explicitly
because `expr_yields_fresh_owned_temp` is Call/MethodCall-only and the headline
reproducer passes a literal.

THE PASSTHROUGH GUARD, and the near-miss that produced it. The first version of
this fix gated only on "param is a bare type param" and was WRONG — it aborted
`e2e_return_owned_generic_param_no_double_free` and
`test_e2e_generic_forward_owned_string_param_no_double_free` with a real
`free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. B-2026-07-14-12's note ("a `Vec[T]`
param temp MOVES/aliases into the callee's sink, so materializing it would add a
spurious second free") was RIGHT, and the reasoning that a bare-`T` gate could
not disturb it was wrong: `fn echo[T](x: T) -> T { x }` IS a bare type param,
and it hands the argument straight back out, so the caller's binding for the
RESULT already owns that buffer.

So the gate additionally requires that the callee's declared RETURN TYPE not
mention the same type param anywhere (`-> T`, `-> Vec[T]`, `-> Option[T]` all
reject). The test is deliberately syntactic rather than a body walk, because
`fn_returns_param` is NOT sufficient here: it recognizes a param reaching a
return site bare or inside an aggregate literal, so it answers false for a
FORWARDING tail — `fn pick[T](a: T, b: T) -> T { id(a) }` and
`fn nest[T](x: T) -> T { id(id(x)) }` both slip past it, and both were measured
aborting. An unrecognized return-type shape answers "mentions it", so the
conservative direction is a leak, never a double free. The leak this fix targets
lives on a `push`-shaped sink whose return type is unit, which the rule admits.

Worth stating plainly for the next person: `llvm_ty_is_vec_struct` admits
`String` as well as `Vec` (both lower to `{ptr,len,cap}`), and
`string_typed_exprs` does NOT cover every String-valued expression — a String
temp produced by a nested generic call inside a mono is absent from it. So an
arm that means "Vec" cannot be spelled as "vec-struct shaped and not in
`string_typed_exprs`"; the return-type guard is what makes it safe, not the
String exclusion.

MEASURED, 12 probes under valgrind, `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0`, before vs after. Nine
leaked before; all twelve are clean after, with byte-identical output under
`karac run`, `karac build`, and the default auto-par build:

    Stack[Vec[i64]]      literal arg          16 B / 1 blk   -> clean
    Stack[Vec[String]]   literal arg          24 B / 1 blk   -> clean
    Stack[Vec[i64]]      + one pop            32 B / 2 blk   -> clean
    Stack[Vec[i64]]      + both popped        32 B / 2 blk   -> clean
    Stack[Vec[i64]]      50-iteration loop   800 B / 50 blk  -> clean
    Stack[VecDeque[i64]] fn-result temp       32 B / 1 blk   -> clean
    Stack[Vec[i64]]      fn-result temp       24 B / 1 blk   -> clean
    Stack[Vec[Vec[i64]]] nested literal       48 B / 1 blk   -> clean
    Stack[Vec[i64]]      repeat literal       48 B / 1 blk   -> clean
    Stack[String]        String elem          clean          -> clean
    Stack[Map[..]]       fn-result temp       clean          -> clean
    Stack[Set[..]]       fn-result temp       clean          -> clean

SIBLING CONTAINERS, the question the row left open and the re-diagnosis flagged
as unproven (the original readings used named bindings, the clean arm). Re-run
with TEMPORARIES: `VecDeque` DID leak and is fixed; `Map` and `Set` never leaked
— they are handle-backed, so they are not the `{ptr,len,cap}` LLVM shape
`llvm_ty_is_vec_struct` admits and were never on this path at all. So the shape
is "the Vec/String LLVM representation", not "Vec specifically".

REGRESSION TEST: `asan_generic_struct_method_bare_type_param_temp_arg_no_leak`
in `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`, 50 iterations so LSan sees accumulation. It
pushes a TEMPORARY and a NAMED binding side by side on purpose: the temporary is
the defect, and the named binding is the double-free control — a caller-side
free that over-fired would abort under ASAN. Verified to FAIL on the pre-fix
compiler and pass after.

NOT the same defect as B-2026-08-10-21 / B-2026-08-07-12, which the
re-diagnosis flagged as a possible shared gate: those are caller-temp cases in
`compile_call`'s surface, while this one is the generic-mono path's missing
third leg. The family resemblance is real but the mechanism is distinct.
investigation: 2026-08-11: found by LSan on a generics+traits dogfood program whose oracle was clean on all three backends. Bisected 5 ways: Stack[i64] clean, Stack[String] clean, Stack[Vec[i64]] leaks, trait dispatch over Vec[Point] clean, trait dispatch over Vec[Tag] (String field) clean. title: `v.cast()` on ANY primitive receiver passes `karac check` and then fails at run time -- `cast` sits on the PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS exemption but is not implemented on any backend, so the exemption guards nothing and only holds the hole open
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while closing B-2026-08-11-2, which routed `char`/`bool`
onto the same scalar-primitive arm the numeric receivers use. This is the one
hole that arm still has, and it predates that change on every receiver.

MEASURED, all four receivers, identical:

    i64    All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'i64'
    f64    All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'f64'
    char   All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'char'
    bool   All checks passed.   ->  runtime error: method 'cast' not found on type 'bool'

WHY IT SURVIVES. `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` exists for a real reason: the baked
stdlib `Ord`/`Eq` impls on primitives carry a `(self, other)`-shaped signature
that impl-table dispatch mis-counts (`a.cmp(b)` -> "expects 2 args, found 1"), so
those names are held off the dispatch path AND off the `NoMethodFound` error.
`cmp`/`eq`/`ne`/`lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` all genuinely dispatch and need the
exemption. `cast` does not: grepping `src/` and `runtime/src/` finds the method
name in that list and nowhere else. The other `cast` hits are the `as` operator's
internals (`cast_value` in the interpreter, `build_signed_int_to_float` in
codegen, `cast_ctor` in the WGSL backend) -- none of them a `.cast()` method
dispatch arm. No test, example or `.kara` source calls `.cast()` either.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, both small:
  - the typo `v.cast()` is check-green/run-red, the class this family keeps
    closing;
  - a USER impl named `cast` on a primitive (`impl i64 { fn cast(self) -> f64 }`)
    is unreachable, because the exemption short-circuits before the impl lookup.

FIX SHAPE: drop `"cast"` from `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS`. It then takes the normal
path -- a real impl candidate routes to impl-table dispatch, no candidate errors
`no method 'cast' on type 'i64'`. Deliberately NOT bundled into B-2026-08-11-2:
that row is scoped to `char`/`bool`, and this changes behavior for every numeric
receiver too, so it wants its own commit and its own suite run.

CONFIRMED AS FILED, and the fix is the one-token removal the row proposed. Two
things worth adding.

1. BOTH PREDICTED CONSEQUENCES VERIFIED, not just the one that motivated the
   row. `v.cast()` is now `no method 'cast' on type 'i64'` (and f64 / char /
   bool / u8) at typecheck. And the second, which mattered more than it looked:

       impl i64  { fn cast(self) -> f64 { return self as f64 } }
       impl char { fn cast(self) -> i64 { return self as i64 } }
       let a: f64 = x.cast();   let b: i64 = c.cast();   // -> 7 65

   Pre-fix that program was unreachable -- the exemption short-circuits ahead of
   the impl lookup, so `cast` was the ONE method name in the language you could
   not define on a primitive. Its return type is now enforced too
   (`let a: String = x.cast()` -> expected 'String', found 'f64').

2. THE SAME LIST HAS A SECOND DEAD REGION, found while writing the regression
   guard, and it is NOT `cast`-shaped. Mapping every exempted name against every
   primitive receiver:

       recv    cmp    eq     ne     lt     le     gt     ge     cast
       i8..i64 runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   (fixed)
       u8..u64 runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   (fixed)
       char    runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   (fixed)
       bool    runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   (fixed)
       f32     RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED (fixed)
       f64     RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED (fixed)

   (every name). This row fixes the column; the row is filed as B-2026-08-11-9.

   The float cause is different from `cast`'s, which is why it is a separate row
   rather than a widening: `cast` names no method anywhere, whereas `cmp`/`eq`/…
   are real baked impls that are DELIBERATELY not registered for floats --

title: EVERY parse-phase diagnostic raised inside an f-string interpolation hole is DISCARDED. Two consequences: (a) a hard syntax error degrades SILENTLY to literal text -- `println(f"typo={n.}")` passes `karac check` and prints `typo={n.}` on all three backends; (b) recoverable errors go unenforced -- `f"{takes(ref xs)}"` compiles clean while the identical call outside an f-string is a hard parse error.
tracker: src/parser/exprs.rs:771 -- `let result = crate::parse(&wrapper);` consumes only `result.program.items`; `result.errors` and `result.fix_edits` are dropped on the floor.
detail:
ROOT CAUSE (single site, both legs). An f-string interpolation hole is not parsed inline: `parse_primary`'s InterpolatedStringLit arm re-parses the hole's source by wrapping it in a synthetic function -- `format!("fn __interp__() {{ {}; }}", expr_src)` -- and calling `crate::parse(&wrapper)` recursively (exprs.rs:770-771). The returned `ParseResult` has three fields (`program`, `errors`, `fix_edits`); the arm reads ONLY `program.items`, pattern-matching out the single `StmtKind::Expr`. `errors` and `fix_edits` are never touched, so every diagnostic the nested parse raised is destroyed at the call site.

LEG A -- HARD parse error becomes SILENT literal text (the severe leg). When the hole does not parse, the `find_map` yields `None` and the `else` branch (exprs.rs:792) pushes `ParsedInterpolationPart::Text(format!("{{{}}}", raw))` -- i.e. the malformed source is re-emitted as the literal characters it was written as, braces included. `karac check` reports `All checks passed.` and `karac check --output=json` reports `"diagnostics":[]`. All three backends then agree on the wrong output:

    fn main() {
        let n = 3;
        println(f"good={n}");
        println(f"typo={n.}");
        println(f"trunc={n * }");
    }

  interp / JIT / AOT all print:
    good=3
    typo={n.}
    trunc={n * }

Because all three backends agree, the 3-backend differential oracle CANNOT see this class -- it is unanimous silent-wrong-output, found only by reading program output against an intended result.

LEG B -- RECOVERABLE parse errors go unenforced. When the nested parser recovers, a well-formed expression IS produced, so the program compiles and behaves correctly, but the diagnostic that should have rejected it is gone. The cleanest instance is the call-site borrow-marker rule (design.md Feature 4 Part 1.5, `ref` is never legal at call sites): `println(f"{takes(ref xs)}")` and the `mut ref` twin both pass `karac check` and run, while `let s = takes(ref xs);` is a hard parse error with a machine-applicable fix-it. So a documented language rule is enforced in statement position and unenforced one character inside an f-string.

BOUNDARY -- the loss is exactly the PARSE phase, no wider. Post-parse phases walk the real AST (whose spans `shift_expr_spans` has already rebased to absolute coordinates), so they are unaffected: an undefined name in a hole IS reported (`f"{nope()}"` -> `error[resolve]: undefined name 'nope', did you mean 'name'?`, correct line:column into the hole), and so is a typecheck error (`f"{if x { 1 }}"` -> `condition must be 'bool', found 'i64'`). Measured 6-shape in-hole vs outside-hole table, `karac check` first line each:

    expression        in-hole                       outside
    Vec<i64>.new()    All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected expression, found Dot
    x as              All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected type, found Semicolon
    [1,2              All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected RightBracket, found Semicolon
    x.0.              All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected field name or tuple index after '.'
    foo(,)            All checks passed.            error[parse]: Expected expression, found Comma
    if x { 1 }        error[typecheck]: ...         error[typecheck]: ...        <- parses fine, so survives

5/6 swallowed; the only survivor is the one that is not a parse error.

MEND-LOOP CONSEQUENCE. `karac check --output=json` emits `"diagnostics":[]` for Leg A, so the Mend loop has nothing to feed back and `karac fix` has nothing to apply -- a typo inside an interpolation hole is unrepairable by the AI-first path, not merely unreported. Leg B compounds it: the nested `fix_edits` map is discarded alongside `errors`, so even after B-2026-08-10-2 taught the marker diagnostics to emit a deletion edit, that edit cannot reach `cmd_fix` from inside a hole.

FIX SHAPE. The rebasing machinery this needs already exists and is already applied to the expression on the success path. `span_visitor::shift_expr_spans(&mut e, offset, line, column)` computes `offset_delta = hole_offset - PREFIX_LEN` and `col_delta = hole_column - (PREFIX_LEN + 1)` where `PREFIX_LEN = "fn __interp__() { ".len()` = 18, then maps line 1 of the wrapper onto `hole_line`. The same two deltas rebase a `ParseError`'s span and a `fix_edits` `SpanKey`/`TextEdit`. So: (1) rebase `result.errors` with those deltas and append them to the enclosing parser's error list; (2) rebase and merge `result.fix_edits` into the enclosing `ParseResult`'s map; (3) on the `None` arm, stop falling back to `Text` -- an unparseable hole must be an error, since with (1) in place the nested parse has already produced the precise diagnostic and the `Text` fallback would only re-hide it. Guard against double-reporting: the wrapper's own trailing `;` and closing brace must not manufacture spurious errors for a hole that parsed cleanly.

NOT a duplicate of the prior f-string entries: B-2026-06-09-1 was the LEXER's hole EXTRACTOR miscounting braces/quotes (which hole text is extracted); this is the PARSER discarding the result of re-parsing an already-correctly-extracted hole. B-2026-07-15-12 / -07-12-5 / -06-14-15 are codegen/auto-par behaviour on holes that parsed fine.

exact -- single site, both legs, correct fix in three parts -- so this is a

1. THE `fix_edits` HALF HAS A TRAP THE ROW DID NOT NAME, and the first attempt
   at this fix fell into it. The map is keyed by the DIAGNOSTIC's span, not by
   the edit's own range: `record_call_site_mode_deletion` deletes the `ref`

   deriving a fresh key from it therefore compiles, merges, and silently loses

   the identical construct outside a hole carries its edit. Key and edit must be
   rebased SEPARATELY. Caught by diffing `--output=json` for the same program in
   and out of a hole, which is the check worth repeating for any future

title: A bare TYPE NAME in call position -- `i64(42)`, `F64(1.5)`, `bool(1)`, `String("hi")`, `Vec(1)`, or a named-field user struct `P(1)` -- is accepted by EVERY checking phase, then breaks downstream: the interpreter panics on an `unreachable!` (or raises its own 'This is a compiler bug' internal error) while the compiled backends silently evaluate it to `0`.
tracker: src/interpreter/eval_call.rs:2101 (the `unreachable!` whose message already says 'the typechecker accepted a non-callable callee'); the missing rejection belongs in the typechecker's call-callee resolution.
detail:
`karac check` reports `All checks passed.` for a bare type name applied to arguments. Nothing downstream can honour it, and the three backends fail three different ways -- none of them a diagnostic.

    fn main() {
        let a = i64(42);
        println(f"val={a}");
    }

    karac check       All checks passed.
    karac run --interp  runtime error: internal: name 'i64' resolved but has no binding at run time.
                        This is a compiler bug (the resolver should have rejected or bound it)
                        -- please report it with the source.   at u.kara:3:13
    karac run (JIT)   val=0
    karac build (AOT) val=0

Measured matrix (`karac check` was `All checks passed.` for every row):

    expression       interpreter                          JIT / AOT
    i64(42)          runtime error: internal (compiler bug)  prints val=0
    bool(1)          runtime error: internal (compiler bug)  prints val=0
    String("hi")     runtime error: internal (compiler bug)  codegen refuses (struct-Display msg)
    F64(1.5)         PANIC, unreachable! eval_call.rs:2101   prints val=0
    F32(1.5)         PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    F16(1.5)         PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    Bf16(1.5)        PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    Vec(1)           PANIC, unreachable!                     -
    P(1)  (struct P { x: i64 } -- NAMED fields, not a tuple struct)
                     PANIC, unreachable!                     -

The panic text is self-diagnosing: "call target at 2:28 was Value::TypeVal (not Function, not an enum-variant constructor); either an interpreter codepath produced the wrong variant or the typechecker accepted a non-callable callee". It is the second disjunct. The typechecker resolves the callee to a type and then types the call without ever asking whether that type has a callable (tuple-struct / enum-variant) constructor form.

THE SILENT LEG IS THE WORSE ONE. On JIT and AOT the argument is simply discarded and the binding takes `0`; there is no diagnostic at any stage. `let a = i64(42); println(f"val={a}")` prints `val=0` on both compiled backends. A user who writes a C/Java-style conversion cast gets a zero, not an error.

REACHABILITY -- this is not an exotic typo. It is the shape a user lands on by following the compiler's own advice. `max(1.5, 2.5)` is correctly rejected with a diagnostic that says "use the total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`)"; `F64.from` does not exist (B-2026-08-11-8), and `F64(1.5)` is the next thing anyone tries -- and it is the row that PANICS the interpreter.

STRUCTURAL PRECEDENT: B-2026-08-02-5 (tuple-element assignment targets accepted by every checking phase, unimplemented downstream) is the same shape -- a construct that no phase rejects and no backend implements. Same fix discipline applies: reject at the typechecker, since neither backend can be made to mean anything sensible here.

CONFIRMED AS FILED -- the matrix reproduces exactly -- with the ROOT CAUSE
CORRECTED and one leg added.

1. THE CAUSE IS NOT WHERE THE TRACKER POINTS. Not the interpreter's
   `unreachable!`, and not "the typechecker's call-callee resolution": it is
   `resolve_identifier_type`'s closing fallback, whose comment reads "likely a
   name the resolver already handled -- return Error silently (resolver already
   reported it)". True for a typo; FALSE for a type name, which resolves
   perfectly well and simply is not a value. `infer_call` then took its silent
   `Type::Error` arm rather than the `NotCallable` arm immediately below it --
   the rejection the row wanted was already there, unreachable.

2. A LEG THE ROW DID NOT HAVE: the same fallback made `let x = i64;` pass, with
   no call involved. Any fix confined to call position would have left it.

3. THE LEGAL SET IS SMALLER THAN THE ROW ASSUMES. It refers to the
   "(tuple-struct / enum-variant) constructor form", but KARA HAS NO TUPLE
   STRUCTS -- `struct T(i64)` is a parse error. Enum variants and distinct
   types are the whole list, which is what makes a blanket rejection safe.

4. THE REMEDY HAD TO BE PER-FAMILY, and the ordering is load-bearing. The baked

   authors to write `F64 { … }` and `Vec { … }`, neither of which exists.
   `F64`/`F32` -> `.from(x)` (which now exists, B-2026-08-11-8, and is exactly
   the remedy this row's REACHABILITY paragraph said was missing); numeric
   primitives -> the cast; `String` -> `String.from` / `to_string`; prelude
   containers -> `.new(…)`; a user struct -> a literal naming a real field.

TWO COLLATERAL PATHS, both found by the suite rather than by inspection, and
both now pinned because they are where a future refactor reintroduces this:

title: `Vec[f64].sort()` bypasses the `Ord` gate that design.md § Float semantics REQUIRES -- the spec's own verbatim counter-example compiles. With a NaN present, `sort()` silently leaves the Vec UNSORTED (all three backends agree), so a percentile/statistics program yields wrong answers with no diagnostic. `.sorted()`, `.max()`, `.min()` and `.contains()` on `Vec[f64]` are ungated the same way, while `Map[f64,_]`, `Set[f64]`, `SortedSet[f64]` and free `max(f64,f64)` all gate correctly.
tracker: src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs:1436 -- the Vec `"sort" | "reverse"` arm calls `expect_no_args` and returns `Type::Unit` with NO element-type Ord check; the Slice twin at :1164 checks mutability only. Working gate to copy: stdlib_map.rs:516/633 (SortedSet/SortedMap element+key Ord).
detail:
design.md § Float semantics (around line 2263) is explicit and gives this exact example:

    let scores: Vec[f64] = [1.0, f64.NAN, 2.0];
    scores.sort()                 # compile error: f64 does not implement Ord
    scores.map(F64.from).sort()   # OK

The first line compiles. The spec's stated rule -- `f32`/`f64` implement `PartialEq`/`PartialOrd` but NOT `Eq`/`Ord`/`Hash`, so "`f64` cannot be used ... in any context requiring `Ord`" -- is enforced in some contexts and not others.

GATED CORRECTLY (measured, `karac check` first line):
    Map[f64, String]   error[typecheck]: key type does not implement `Hash + Eq`
    Set[f64]           error[typecheck]: element type does not implement `Hash + Eq`
    SortedSet[f64]     error[typecheck]: element type does not implement `Ord`
    max(1.5, 2.5)      error[typecheck]: trait bound `T: Ord` is not satisfied ...
                       (with the good note pointing at the F64 wrapper)

NOT GATED (all report `All checks passed.`):
    Vec[f64].sort()      <- design.md's verbatim counter-example
    Vec[f64].sorted()
    Vec[f64].max()       <- note the asymmetry: free `max(a,b)` IS rejected
    Vec[f64].min()
    Vec[f64].contains(x) <- an Eq context; f64 has PartialEq only

So the machinery exists and is wired up for the Sorted* containers and for the generic trait-bound solver; the Vec method arms just never consult it. The `max`/`v.max()` split is the sharpest instance -- the same ordering question is rejected as a free call and accepted as a method.

THE HARM IS A SILENT WRONG ANSWER, not just a missing message. Because `value_compare` is not a total order over NaN, `sort_by` is free to leave elements where they are, and it does -- observed identical on interp, JIT and AOT:

    let nan = 0.0 / 0.0;
    let mut b: Vec[f64] = [3.0, nan, 1.0, 2.0];
    b.sort();
    // prints: 3 NaN 1 2      <- COMPLETELY unsorted; even 3/1/2 are untouched

    let e: Vec[f64] = [5.0, nan, 4.0, 6.0];
    let f = e.sorted();
    // prints: 5 NaN 4 6

    let c: Vec[f64] = [3.0, nan, 1.0];
    c.max() -> Some(3)   c.min() -> Some(1)     <- NaN silently skipped

No panic, no diagnostic, no divergence between backends -- so the 3-backend differential oracle cannot see this either. The realistic failure is exactly the program this was found in: a latency-percentile reporter that sorts its samples and reads p50/p90/p99 off the sorted Vec. One NaN in the input (a division by a zero count, a failed parse defaulted to `0.0/0.0`) and every percentile is read from unsorted data, silently.

FIX SHAPE. Add the element-type Ord check to the Vec/Slice `sort`/`sorted` arms and the Ord/Eq checks to `max`/`min`/`contains`, reusing the SortedSet/SortedMap diagnostic text (which already names the `F64` fix). Note the ordering dependency: the diagnostic and design.md both direct users to `F64.from(x)`, which does not exist -- B-2026-08-11-8 must land first or the gate will send users into a dead end, and the obvious next thing they type (`F64(1.5)`) panics the interpreter (B-2026-08-11-6).

JUDGEMENT CALL worth recording: `contains` is the one leg where rejection is arguable, since `contains` needs only `PartialEq`, which f64 does have. The spec's blanket wording ("not `Eq`") says reject; a narrower reading says allow. Whoever fixes this should decide deliberately rather than inherit it -- `sort`/`sorted`/`max`/`min` are not ambiguous. -- FIXED 2026-08-11 in e51d3e7, PARTIALLY AND ON PURPOSE; the residual is B-2026-08-11-15. -- PREMISE RE-VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY rather than inherited, and it is worse than filed: `[3.0, NaN, 1.0, 2.0].sort()` does not merely fail to place the NaN, it returns the sequence COMPLETELY UNTOUCHED (`3 NaN 1 2`) — the 3/1/2 do not move either — identically on interpreter and compiled backends. NaN-free float data sorts correctly, which is why this survived: the failure needs a NaN to appear. (Probed through a generic `fn gsort[T](v: mut ref Vec[T])`, which incidentally documents a HOLE IN THE GATE: the element type at a generic call site is a TypeParam, so `Ord` passes and monomorphization does not re-check. A `Vec[f64]` laundered through a generic sorts unchecked. Narrow, but real, and it is the shape a stdlib helper would have.) -- WHAT WAS GATED AND WHAT WAS NOT, since this departs from the filed fix shape. Gated: `sort`, `sorted`, `binary_search` (the last NOT named in the row — found ungated while fixing its siblings; binary search over unordered data is meaningless). Not gated: `reverse` (compares nothing; it shared a match arm with `sort`, which is part of why the check was never added), `contains`, and `max`/`min`. -- THE `contains` JUDGEMENT CALL, which the row explicitly asked the fixer to make deliberately: ALLOW. It needs only `PartialEq`, which design.md says `f64` does implement, and measured behaviour is IEEE-correct and identical across backends — it finds elements positioned after a NaN, `contains(NaN)` is correctly `false` (NaN != NaN), and `-0.0` finds `0.0`. There is no silent wrong answer to prevent, so gating it would break correct code for no soundness gain. The spec's blanket 'not Eq' wording is about Eq/Ord/Hash CONTEXTS; a linear scan is not one. -- WHY `max`/`min` WERE DEFERRED rather than gated: they ARE broken (NaN first makes BOTH answer NaN; NaN in the middle is silently skipped), but every remedy measured worse than the disease, and shipping a gate whose advice dead-ends is exactly what B-2026-08-11-8 was filed for. `Vec[F64].max()` typechecks only if the iterator arm's numeric-or-String test is widened, and then FAILS IN CODEGEN ('no handler for method max'), trading a wrong answer for a run-vs-build gap; `Stats.max(v)` is itself wrong and BACKEND-DIVERGENT on the same input. Both measurements are in B-2026-08-11-15. -- THE GATE KEYS ON FLOATS, NOT ON `!type_supports_ord`, and that distinction is load-bearing: `type_supports_ord` is STRICTER than what the sort comparators actually implement, because `Vec` is a baked stdlib struct with no `#[derive(Ord)]`, so it answers false for `Vec[Vec[String]]` — whose sort is supported and tested (B-2026-06-30-15's recursive lexicographic comparator). The first version gated on it and broke that ASAN fixture. Scoping to 'element type reaches an IEEE float' (recursing through tuples, arrays, slices, Vec/Option, refs) cannot reject a sort that works today. Anyone widening this gate to other non-Ord element types must first check what the comparators support, not what the predicate says. -- ORDERING DEPENDENCY HONOURED: the diagnostic prescribes `F64.from(x)` and a copy-pasteable `xs.iter().map(F64.from).collect()`, both verified end-to-end on all three backends. That remedy only became real in B-2026-08-11-8 (d8ddc56), landed first for exactly this reason.

`Vec[F64]` gives max 3 / min 1; `[NaN, 3.0, 1.0]` AND `[3.0, NaN, 1.0]` both

title: `Vec[f64].max()` / `.min()` return an ORDER-DEPENDENT element instead of erroring, and there is currently no working remedy to point users at -- which is why B-2026-08-11-7 gated `sort`/`sorted`/`binary_search` but deliberately left these alone. Measured: `[3.0, NaN, 1.0].max()` silently skips the NaN and answers 3, while `[NaN, 3.0, 1.0]` makes BOTH `max()` and `min()` answer NaN -- the result depends on where the NaN sits. The two obvious remedies are both broken: (a) `Vec[F64].max()`, the wrapper -7's own sort gate prescribes, is rejected at typecheck by the iterator arm's numeric-or-String element test, and when that test is widened to admit the wrapper it then FAILS IN CODEGEN with 'no handler for method max on non-identifier receiver' -- i.e. it would trade a wrong answer for a run-vs-build gap; (b) `Stats.max(v)`, the f64-shaped alternative, is itself wrong AND BACKEND-DIVERGENT -- on `[NaN, 3.0, 1.0]` the interpreter answers 3 and the JIT answers NaN. Fixing (a) is the real task: add the codegen max/min-over-wrapper arm, then widen the element test, then gate. That makes `F64` a COMPLETE answer instead of a partial one.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-11-7 (fixed in e51d3e7) when the gate for these two was written and then WITHDRAWN. Recorded in full because the withdrawal was a judgement call with measurements behind it, not an oversight, and because re-deriving those measurements is the expensive part. -- WHY NOT JUST GATE THEM. The gate is one line and the bug is real, but a diagnostic is only worth shipping if the fix it names exists and works -- that is the entire lesson of B-2026-08-11-8, where design.md and the compiler both prescribed `F64.from(x)` for two months while it did not exist, and the natural next guess (`F64(1.5)`) panicked the interpreter. Gating max/min today would recreate that one row later: the user follows the advice to `F64`, and either typecheck rejects it or codegen does. Meanwhile the status quo is at least CONSISTENT across backends and correct on NaN-free data, which is the overwhelmingly common case -- so gating without a remedy would break far more working code than it protects. -- THE STATS DIVERGENCE IS ITS OWN BUG and is arguably worse than the max/min one, since a run-vs-build split cannot be reasoned about from the source at all. It is recorded here rather than filed separately only because the fix is likely shared (one total-order float reduce that both surfaces call); split it out if that turns out not to be true. -- RELATED: B-2026-08-11-13 (the wrapper's own NaN ordering depends on the NaN's sign bit, which no source construct controls) should probably land FIRST, since it decides what 'correct' even means for a NaN-bearing max/min over `F64`. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 shared cloud container; the NaN-sign behaviour that drives the Stats split is architecture-specific, though the order-dependence of max/min is not.

fix: d8ddc56 (three parts: an ordinary Kāra `impl <W> { fn from }` in each of runtime/stdlib/{f32,f64,f16,bf16}.kara makes the call typecheck; a codegen intercept in assoc_call.rs BUILDS the wrapper struct, because codegen does not route path-calls to baked stdlib impls and the call was otherwise reaching the unknown-callee tail as a const i64 0; and type_name_of_expr in expr_ops.rs types the call-result temp so a direct `F64.from(x).value` chain resolves its field. Display is a fourth part: one seam in build_struct_display_parts covering both println and f-strings.)
title: `F64.from(x)` / `F32.from(x)` -- the total-order wrapper constructor that design.md AND the compiler's own `T: Ord` diagnostic both name as THE fix for `f64` in an Ord/Eq/Hash context -- is unimplemented: `no associated function 'from' on type 'F64'`. Every spelling a user would try next fails, and one of them (`F64(1.5)`) panics the interpreter.
tracker: the `F64`/`F32` stdlib surface; the diagnostic that prescribes it is the `T: Ord` bound message (it renders "use the total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`)"), and design.md § Float semantics line ~2264 writes `scores.map(F64.from).sort()  # OK`.
detail:
design.md § Float semantics introduces `F32`/`F64` as the sanctioned total-order wrappers -- "Implement `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash` -- usable as `Map`/`Set` keys, in `TreeMap`, and anywhere `T: Ord` is required" -- and shows construction as `F64.from`:

    scores.map(F64.from).sort()  # OK

The compiler agrees in prose. `max(1.5, 2.5)` is rejected with a genuinely good note: "`f64` is not totally ordered (IEEE-754 NaN), so it does not implement `Ord` -- use the total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`) in `Ord`/`Eq`/`Hash` contexts, or drop the `Ord` bound if you only need arithmetic".

Then the prescribed call does not exist. Measured, every construction spelling:

    F64.from(1.5)   error[typecheck]: no associated function 'from' on type 'F64'
    F64.new(1.5)    error[typecheck]: no associated function 'new' on type 'F64'
    F64.of(1.5)     error[typecheck]: no associated function 'of' on type 'F64'
    1.5 as F64      error[typecheck]: cannot cast 'f64' to 'F64'
    F64(1.5)        All checks passed  -- then PANICS the interpreter (B-2026-08-11-6)
                                       and evaluates to 0 on JIT/AOT

So there is NO working way to construct an `F64` from an `f64`. The type is reachable enough to annotate (`let mut v: Vec[F64] = ...`, `Map[F64, String]` both typecheck) but not to populate.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE MISSING METHOD. It makes a correct diagnostic actively harmful: the user hits the (correctly-firing) `Ord` gate, follows the advice verbatim, hits a second error, and the most natural next guess is the one shape that crashes the compiler. For the Mend loop this is worse than silence -- `karac fix` and any LLM reading the diagnostic are steered toward an API that is not there, so the repair attempt cannot converge.

Second-order Display gap noticed while probing and worth folding into the same slice: with `F64` values obtained any way at all, `f"{v[0]}"` on a `Vec[F64]` element reports "type 'F64' does not implement Display; cannot interpolate in f-string". If `F64` is to be the recommended wrapper it needs Display too, or the recommendation costs users their `println`s.

FIX SHAPE: implement `F64.from(f64) -> F64` and `F32.from(f32) -> F32` (plus the inverse accessor to get the bits back out as `f64`/`f32`), give both `Display`, and keep the bit-level total order design.md specifies (`-Inf < ... < -0.0 == 0.0 < ... < +Inf < NaN`, `NaN == NaN` true). Sequencing: this should land BEFORE B-2026-08-11-7's Ord gate, or that gate will start rejecting `Vec[f64].sort()` and point users at an API that still does not exist. -- FIXED 2026-08-11 in d8ddc56. WHAT IT ACTUALLY TOOK, vs what the row predicted. The row's fix shape asked for `from`, the inverse accessor, and Display. The inverse accessor ALREADY existed and needed nothing — unwrap is the plain field read `x.value`, verified on all three backends — so the round trip is `F64.from(v).value`. The wrapper itself was also already built (B-2026-07-22-11 shipped total-order compare, Map/Set keys, sort and `.value` across all three backends), which made this a much smaller slice than the row reads: the type was reachable enough to annotate and to construct via the `F64 { value: x }` STRUCT LITERAL, just not via the constructor the docs and diagnostics name. -- THE INTERPRETER ALREADY IMPLEMENTED `F64.from`: eval_call.rs has carried a hardcoded `"F32.from"`/`"F64.from"`/`"F16.from"`/`"Bf16.from"` arm for a long time, and tests/interpreter.rs has carried PASSING tests for it (test_f64_from_constructor et al). They passed because that harness's `run()` bypasses the typechecker, which is exactly what hid the bug: the feature worked and was tested, but no CHECKED program could reach it. A test that skips a gate cannot see a gate-shaped bug. -- DISPLAY RENDERING WAS A REAL CHOICE, recorded because it is not recoverable from the code. Both `println(x)` and `f"{x}"` rejected every wrapper, so the type the compiler RECOMMENDS for Ord contexts was unprintable, and no rendering was reachable — meaning the `F64(3.14)` form in the interpreter's `Display for Value` had never been observable from checked Kāra. It now renders as the bare inner float (`3.14`), on the reasoning that the wrapper is an ORDERING CONTRACT, not a distinct textual form: a percentile report that wraps its samples to sort them should print numbers, and `Vec[F64]` should print `[1, 2, 3]`. Java's `Double` makes the same choice. Three interpreter tests asserted the old form and were updated; because the form was unreachable, this changes no reachable behaviour. -- KNOWN ADJACENT LIMITATION, pre-existing and NOT wrapper-specific: Display of a struct in a non-place position (`println(v[0])`, `f"{F64.from(x)}"`) is a standing codegen restriction for ALL user structs — 'bind a struct literal or call result to a `let` first'. Wrappers inherit it. -- FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, filed separately: B-2026-08-11-13 (the wrapper's NaN ordering diverges across backends and optimization levels — directly relevant to B-2026-08-11-7, which steers users to `F64` for exactly the NaN case) and B-2026-08-11-14 (design.md says `-0.0 == 0.0`, every backend implements `-0.0 < 0.0`). Also noticed: design.md's example writes `scores.map(F64.from)`, but the compiler requires an explicit `.iter()` and says so in a good diagnostic; the spec line is stale.

Found by following B-2026-08-11-7's own remedy: after establishing that `Vec[f64].sort()` should be rejected per spec, I wrote the spec-blessed alternative `scores.map(F64.from).sort()` to confirm it works, and it does not compile. Probed five construction spellings and the Display path. Filed, not fixed, per the hunting-only remit.

fix:
FIXED by 284d44a4, by canonicalizing NaN at CONSTRUCTION in all three backends --
the row's own preferred shape ("doing it at construction is the stronger
invariant"), chosen over normalizing in the comparison key.

1. Codegen: `canonicalize_wrapper_nan` (src/codegen/assoc_call.rs) emits
   `select(fcmp uno x, x, <canonical quiet NaN>, x)` and runs inside
   `compile_total_order_wrapper_from`.
2. Codegen: `F64 { value: x }` previously fell through the GENERIC struct-init
   path and stored raw bits. It is now intercepted at the top of
   `compile_struct_init` and routed through that same
   `compile_total_order_wrapper_from`, so the literal and `.from` are ONE
   lowering rather than two that can drift apart.
3. Interpreter: `canonical_wrapper_f64` / `_f32` (src/interpreter/helpers.rs)
   applied at both producers -- the four `X.from` arms in eval_call.rs and the
   struct-literal arm in interpreter.rs.

The canonical value is spelled as an explicit bit pattern on both sides
(0x7FF8000000000000 / 0x7FC00000, plus the 16-bit siblings) rather than
`f64::NAN`, so the interpreter and the compiled backends are provably the same
bits instead of the same by convention.

WHY CONSTRUCTION AND NOT THE COMPARISON KEY. The key-side fix is narrower per
site but has MORE sites -- cmp, eq, the two sort-key paths in vec_method.rs, and
the Map/Set hash -- and a site that forgot would fail SILENTLY: `eq` calls two
keys equal while `hash` sends them to different buckets. Construction gives one
invariant ("no wrapper ever holds a non-canonical NaN") that every consumer
inherits, at two sites per backend. The producer set is closed and small, which
is what makes that tractable: there is no `F64.NAN` constant (it does not
exist -- see B-2026-08-11-14) and the wrapper has no arithmetic, so `X.from` and
the struct literal are the ONLY ways to make one.

`-0.0` is deliberately NOT normalized. Unlike a NaN's sign it is a distinct,
well-defined point of the total order that all three backends already agreed on,
with a pin (`test_e2e_total_order_float_wrappers`) asserting it.

WHAT THE ROW UNDER-STATED. It reported a 3-way split; measured here it is 4-way,
and the extra leg is the sharpest evidence: the default `-O2` AOT build and
`KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` disagree on the SAME source, because -O2 inlines the call and
constant-folds the division while -O0 leaves a real one. Two further findings the
row did not have, both worse than a split:
  - `Vec[F64].sort()` under the JIT returned NaN at BOTH ENDS (`NaN -1 1 NaN`).
    That IS correctly sorted under raw totalOrder -- -NaN precedes -Infinity,
    +NaN follows +Infinity -- and completely unreadable, since both print `NaN`.
  - A two-NaN `Map[F64, i64]` had a different LEN per backend (interp 1, JIT 2,
    AOT -O2 1, AOT -O0 2), so a collection silently gained or lost an entry
    depending on how the program was run.

MEASUREMENT TRAP WORTH RECORDING. The first codegen pin PASSED pre-fix. At -O2
LLVM folds both the constant NaN and the nominally-runtime one to the same
positive NaN, so AOT agreed with the correct answer by luck, and the bug is only
visible where a NaN genuinely survives to run time. The pin now sources its zero
from `env.args().len()`, which the optimizer cannot see through; that made it red
at every opt level. A codegen E2E test that exercises constant-foldable
arithmetic is testing the folder, not the backend.

Pins: twin tests asserting the SAME string in tests/interpreter.rs
(`test_total_order_wrapper_nan_canonicalized_interp_parity`) and tests/codegen.rs
(`test_e2e_total_order_wrapper_nan_canonicalized`) -- the pairing IS the
contract, run == build. Both stash-proven red.
tracker: the total-order float wrappers: total_order_key / compile_total_order_wrapper_cmp in src/codegen/assoc_call.rs, and the `TotalFloat*` arms of value_compare in src/interpreter/helpers.rs (both correct in isolation — see detail)
title: `F64`/`F32` ordering and equality depend on the SIGN BIT of a NaN, which is not stable across backends or optimization levels -- so `Vec[F64].sort()` on NaN-bearing data puts NaN FIRST under the interpreter and LAST under both compiled backends, and `F64 { value: nan } < F64 { value: 1.0 }` is `true` interp / `false` compiled. Measured three ways on one program: a NaN from a constant `0.0 / 0.0` gives interp true / JIT false / AOT false, while a NaN computed at runtime (`z / z` behind a fn call) gives interp true / JIT true / AOT FALSE -- i.e. the same source expression flips answer with optimization level, because AOT inlines the call and constant-folds the division. NOT a comparator bug: both backends implement the same documented IEEE-754 totalOrder key and agree on every non-NaN value. The divergence is in WHICH NaN gets produced -- x86 runtime division yields a NEGATIVE NaN (sign bit set) while LLVM's constant folder yields a POSITIVE one, and totalOrder sorts -NaN before -Infinity but +NaN after +Infinity.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-11-8 (fixed in d8ddc56) against design.md's own `scores.iter().map(F64.from).collect()` example, which sorts a NaN-bearing Vec and printed `NaN 1 2` on interp vs `1 2 NaN` compiled. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING and independent of that fix by reproducing with only constructs that already worked (`F64 { value: nan }` struct literals and a `.value` read, no `F64.from`, no wrapper Display). -- WHY IT IS A SPEC VIOLATION AND NOT JUST A SPLIT. design.md § Float semantics states the wrapper contract as `NaN == NaN` is TRUE and the ordering `-Infinity < ... < +Infinity < NaN` -- i.e. NaN is ONE value that sorts last. Bit-level totalOrder does not give that: it distinguishes NaNs by sign (and by payload), so -NaN sorts FIRST, and two NaNs with different payloads compare UNEQUAL, contradicting the stated `NaN == NaN`. `a == a` only holds today because both sides are the same bits. So the compiled backends are not 'right' either -- they happen to match the spec's ordering only for positive NaN. -- FIX SHAPE: CANONICALIZE NaN in the wrapper rather than picking a winner between the backends. At construction (`F64.from`, the struct literal, and any other producer) or in the comparison key, map every NaN bit pattern to one canonical quiet NaN. That makes `NaN == NaN` true as specified, makes NaN sort last regardless of sign or payload, and makes the order independent of whether a NaN was folded at compile time or produced at run time -- which is the property that actually matters, since otherwise the same program changes answer between `karac run` and `karac build`. Doing it in the comparison key alone is cheaper but leaves the raw bits observable through `.value`; doing it at construction is the stronger invariant. -- COUPLING, and the reason this is worth doing before or with B-2026-08-11-7: that row adds the `Ord` gate that REJECTS `Vec[f64].sort()` and directs users to `F64` precisely so their NaN-bearing data sorts predictably. Landing it while the wrapper's own NaN order is backend-dependent would move the silent wrong answer rather than remove it -- the user follows the diagnostic, wraps, and gets a different sort order from `karac run` than from `karac build`. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 shared cloud container. The NaN-sign behaviour of hardware division is architecture-specific, so the exact interp/JIT/AOT pattern above may differ on arm64 -- but the CLASS of bug (order depends on a bit no source-level construct controls) is architecture-independent.

FIX VERIFICATION (2026-08-11). One program, four execution paths, before and
after (`c` = constant-folded NaN, `r` = NaN from an optimizer-opaque runtime
division via `env.args().len()`):

                    c==r    c<one   r<one   sort              map len
    BEFORE
      interp        true    true    true    NaN NaN -1 1      1
      JIT           false   false   true    NaN -1 1 NaN      2
      AOT -O2       true    false   false   -1 1 NaN NaN      1
      AOT -O0       false   false   true    NaN -1 1 NaN      2
    AFTER
      all four      true    false   false   -1 1 NaN NaN      1

Verified identical across interp / JIT / AOT -O2 / AOT -O0 for all four wrapper
types (F64, F32, F16, Bf16). `-0.0 < 0.0` and `-0.0 != 0.0` unchanged in every
leg, as intended.

Full `--features llvm` suite green (102 binaries, 13418 tests, 0 failures);
clippy `--all --all-targets` and `cargo fmt --check` clean; `scripts/asan-o0-leg.sh`
exit 0 with the quarantine list matching exactly.

fix:
FIXED by 284d44a4, in the same commit as B-2026-08-11-13 and for the reason this row
gave: once NaN is canonicalized, the bullet can be stated CORRECTLY as a whole
instead of patched in place. Doing this row alone was not actually possible
honestly -- writing today's raw-totalOrder NaN behaviour into the spec would have
documented a run-vs-build divergence as intended semantics.

The `F32`/`F64` bullet list in docs/design.md § Float semantics now reads:
  - Ordering `-Infinity < ... < -0.0 < 0.0 < ... < +Infinity < NaN`, with `-0.0`
    and `0.0` called out as DISTINCT adjacent values and `-0.0 == 0.0` stated
    explicitly as `false`, contrasted against the `f64` primitive where it is
    `true`. That is the correction this row asked for.
  - Equality is bit-equality, with the reason attached: it is what makes `Hash`
    sound, since equal keys have identical bits and cannot hash apart.
  - NaN is ONE value, canonicalized at construction -- now true of the code as
    well as the spec.
Plus a paragraph on why canonicalizing is not cosmetic, since a reader who
assumes raw totalOrder would reasonably expect the sign to matter.

THE CODE BLOCK WAS ALSO WRONG, in three ways this row did not list, each found by
RUNNING it rather than reading it:
  - It used `#` for comments. Kāra's comment is `//`; `#` begins an attribute, so
    every commented line was a parse error. This was the ONLY `#`-commented kara
    block in design.md, against 600 `//` comments elsewhere.
  - `F64.NAN` does not exist -- no associated constants are implemented on the
    wrapper (`no associated function 'NAN' on type 'F64'`). Rewritten as
    `F64.from(f64.NAN)`.
  - `scores.map(F64.from)` is rejected: iterator adaptors require an explicit
    `.iter()`. Rewritten as `scores.iter().map(F64.from).collect()` -- which is
    also verbatim what B-2026-08-11-7's new `Ord`-gate diagnostic tells users to
    write, so the spec and the compiler's own advice now agree.

Every line of the replacement block was executed on interp, JIT and AOT before
being written down, including the two claims stated as compile errors
(`Map[f64, String]` and `Vec[f64].sort()`).
tracker: docs/design.md § Float semantics, the `F32`/`F64` total-order bullet list
title: design.md § Float semantics specifies the `F32`/`F64` total order as `-Infinity < ... < -0.0 == 0.0 < ... < +Infinity < NaN`, but ALL THREE backends implement `-0.0 < 0.0` (and `-0.0 != 0.0`) -- the IEEE-754 totalOrder / Rust `total_cmp` behaviour, verified interp/JIT/AOT agreeing. The implementation is the more standard reading and is already shipped with tests (test_e2e_total_order_float_wrappers asserts `-0<+0` true and `-0==+0` false), so the SPEC LINE is what should change, not the code.
detail: SURFACE NOTE: filed under `other` because the defect is in docs/design.md, not a compiler phase; the ledger's surface vocabulary has no `docs` value. SOURCE NOTE: noticed while implementing B-2026-08-11-8 (fixed in d8ddc56) -- had to know which order was authoritative before writing the constructor. Recorded rather than silently picking a side. -- WHY THE CODE IS RIGHT: bit-level totalOrder makes the wrapper's equality exactly bit-equality, which is what makes it sound as a `Map`/`Set` key and a `Hash` impl (equal keys must hash equal; `-0.0 == 0.0` with distinct bits would need explicit normalization in the hash to stay consistent). It also matches Rust's `f64::total_cmp`, which is the reference every reader will have in mind. -- SCOPE: this is a one-line doc correction, EXCEPT that it interacts with B-2026-08-11-13: if that row's fix canonicalizes NaN at construction, the spec bullet should be rewritten as a whole to state the real contract (bit-equality for finite values and -0/+0 distinct, all NaNs canonicalized to one value that sorts last) rather than patched in place. Prefer doing both together.

title: the seven comparison-op names are exempted from method-existence checking by NAME rather than by whether the receiver carries the baked impl, so `f.cmp(g)` / `f.eq(g)` / `f.lt(g)` on a FLOAT receiver pass `karac check` and then fail at run time -- floats are deliberately excluded from the Eq/Ord registration
tracker: the PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS list in src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs, against eq_ord_targets in src/typechecker/env_build.rs
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found closing B-2026-08-11-4 (which removed the dead `cast`
entry from the same list), while writing the regression guard that the REMAINING
entries still dispatch. They do -- except on floats.

MEASURED, every exempted name against every primitive receiver, `karac check`
then `karac run --interp`:

    recv      cmp    eq     ne     lt     le     gt     ge
    i8..i64   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    u8..u64   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    char      runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    bool      runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs   runs
    f32       RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED
    f64       RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED RUNRED

RUNRED = `All checks passed.` then `runtime error: method 'cmp' not found on
type 'f64' (no interpreter dispatch arm)`. A clean dead ROW; `cast` (fixed in
B-2026-08-11-4) was the dead COLUMN of the same table.

THE FLOAT EXCLUSION ITSELF IS CORRECT AND IS NOT THE BUG. `env_build.rs`'s
`eq_ord_targets` registers the baked `Eq`/`Ord` impls for the integers, `bool`,
`char`, `String` and the F32/F64 WRAPPER types, and carries the comment "Floats
(f32/f64) deliberately excluded -- IEEE NaN breaks Eq/Ord". That matches Rust
(`f64: PartialOrd` but not `Ord`) and should stay. The operators `==` / `<` /
`>` work on floats and are unaffected -- this is only about the METHOD
spellings.

THE DEFECT IS THE KEYING. `PRIMITIVE_VALUE_METHODS` holds a name off BOTH the
impl-table dispatch and the `NoMethodFound` error. It is keyed on the name
alone, so it shields the float receivers just as strongly as the integer ones
that actually have the impl. The exemption exists for a real reason -- the baked
impls' `(self, other)` signature mis-counts under impl-table dispatch (`a.cmp(b)`
-> "expects 2 args, found 1") -- but that reason only applies where the impl
exists.

FIX SHAPE: gate the exemption on the receiver carrying the baked impl rather
than on the name. Practically, do not exempt `Type::Float(_)`. Since floats have
NO baked candidate, `find_methods_with_args` comes back empty and the existing
error branch produces exactly the right message with no new code: `no method
'cmp' on type 'f64'`. Verified there is no mis-count risk on that path -- the
mis-count only arises when a baked `(self, other)` impl IS found, which is
precisely the case floats do not have.

SEE ALSO B-2026-08-11-7 (`Vec[f64].sort()` bypasses the `Ord` gate) and -8
(`F64.from` unimplemented) -- the same `f64`-Ord-gating family, found the same
day from an unrelated dogfood. Those two are about the COLLECTION surface and
the wrapper constructor; this row is about the direct method spelling, and the
three fix sites are disjoint.

A `total_cmp` / `partial_cmp` surface for floats is a SEPARATE question and is
deliberately not part of this row; rejecting the name that does not work is
correct whether or not a working one is ever added.

CONFIRMED AS FILED and fixed with the proposed shape. Four things the row did
not have.

1. THE ROW MEASURED ONLY `--interp`. All three paths are broken, and the AOT one
   is worse than run-red -- it is the FALSE COMPILER-BUG REPORT that motivated
   B-2026-08-11-2, verbatim:

       karac check   All checks passed.
       --interp      runtime error: method 'cmp' not found on type 'f64'
                     (no interpreter dispatch arm)
       build         error: codegen failed: codegen: no handler for method 'cmp'
                     on variable 'a' (method dispatch fell through; this is a
                     codegen bug - add a dispatcher arm in `compile_method_call`
                     or mark the test `#[ignore]` if the method is genuinely
                     deferred)

   So this row belonged to that same class and not merely to the run-vs-build
   one: `f.cmp(g)` told the author to go patch the compiler. Checked the codegen
   side too -- its `cmp` arm is guarded `if let (IntValue(l), IntValue(r))`, so a
   float operand falls straight through to the "no handler" panic. Nothing was
   ever going to dispatch.

2. THE BOUND SURFACE WAS ALREADY CORRECT, which is what makes this a leak rather
   than a missing feature. A `T: Ord` instantiation at `f64` has always been
   rejected, with a diagnostic that is genuinely good:

       trait bound `T: Ord` is not satisfied; `f64` does not implement `Ord`;
       trait `Ord` is implemented by: Bf16, F16, F32, F64, String, bool, char,
       i16, i32, i64, i8, u16, u32, u64, u8, usize; note: `f64` is not totally
       ordered (IEEE-754 NaN), so it does not implement `Ord` - use the
       total-order wrapper `F64` (`F64.from(x)`) in `Ord`/`Eq`/`Hash` contexts

   So `pick(1.0, 2.0)` under `T: Ord` was a hard error while a bare `a.cmp(b)`
   on the same `f64` typechecked clean. The two surfaces disagreed; this aligns
   them. Pinned as `test_generic_ord_bound_still_gates_floats_the_same_way`.

3. THE SECOND-ORDER WIN REPEATS. Exactly as with `cast` (B-2026-08-11-4), the
   exemption short-circuits AHEAD of the impl lookup, so while it applied to
   floats these seven names were undefinable on a float receiver. A user
   `impl f64 { fn cmp(self, other: f64) -> i64 }` now dispatches (verified: -1)
   and its return type is enforced. That pattern -- an exemption meant to protect
   a builtin also blocking every user impl of the same name -- has now shown up
   twice in this one list.

4. ONE THING NOT VERIFIED END-TO-END, stated rather than implied. The F32/F64
   WRAPPER types keep their baked `Eq`/`Ord` impls and are untouched, but I could
   not exercise them, because an `F64` value cannot currently be constructed at
   all -- `F64.new` and `F64.from` are both unimplemented (that is
   B-2026-08-11-8, filed independently the same day). The wrapper is nonetheless
   unaffected BY CONSTRUCTION: `F64` is a `Type::Named`, so it resolves on the
   named-receiver arm and never reaches the scalar-primitive fall-through this
   change lives in.

SCOPE, unchanged from the filing: the comparison OPERATORS `==` / `!=` / `<` /
`<=` / `>` / `>=` on floats are a separate lowering and keep working -- that is
the point, `a < b` is how floats are compared -- as do `abs` / `to_string` /
`clone`, which are handled by the early scalar intercept and never reach here.
A `partial_cmp` / `total_cmp` surface for floats remains a separate question;
rejecting the spelling that does not work is right either way.
