title: ACCEPTED COST, not a pending fix: `Vec[(i64,i64)].sort_by` on SHUFFLED-UNIFORM input is ~1.30x Rust's `sort_by` (karac ~11.1 ms vs driftsort 8.2-8.9, 150k pairs, this host). Residual of B-2026-08-10-19. FIVE DIRECTIONS WERE MEASURED AGAINST IT AND NONE CLOSES IT -- merge-kernel tweaks, RUN tuning, the bounds-check hoist, a 3-way quicksort run-builder and a 2-way one; do not reopen any of them without new information. The last and most promising, a stable 2-way branchless quicksort run-builder, was BUILT IN FULL, verified correct (98/98 pattern x size, element-type coverage across AOT/LLJIT/interp) and measured: random 11.11 -> 11.73 ms (0.95x, i.e. SLOWER) with instructions 74.05M -> 82.18M (+11%); sawtooth 2.82 -> 3.22 (0.87x). A sweep of the configuration space (span 512/2048/8192/16384/65536, base 16/32/64) found NO setting that beats main on random -- the best, span 16384 base 64, reaches 11.17 vs main's 11.11, i.e. parity. Not merged; the implementation was reverted. This is the cost of the algorithm karac has. The one direction that DID pay, few-unique, is split out as its own open row B-2026-08-11-10. Full write-up in docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-10-19 (fixed in 31485cd). Reshaped five times on 2026-08-11 as measurements landed; this is the terminal state. -- WHY THE BUDGET CHECK POINTED THE WRONG WAY, the methodological lesson and the most reusable thing here. The probe measured 14.38 instructions per element per partition level against the merge's 26.93 and that number was correct, but it was measured the wrong way round: the probe partitioned the FULL 150k array at every level, so every loop had a huge trip count, unrolled well, and amortised its per-range setup to nothing. It captured the kernel's ASYMPTOTIC cost. A real quicksort spends most of its work on SMALL ranges -- recursing from 16384 to a base of 16 makes roughly 2*span/base ranges, most near base size, each paying a fixed cost (pivot xorshift plus a 64-bit urem, stack push/pop, block dispatch, two helper calls) over very few elements with loops too short to unroll. The merge has no such problem: every pass is one long loop per run pair, so it already sits at its asymptotic cost. GENERAL RULE: when costing a kernel for a RECURSIVE algorithm, measure it at the range sizes the recursion actually produces (a geometric mix from span down to base), never on one range of n. -- WHAT WAS BUILT, if anyone revisits for the few-unique win: `__vec_<m>_qs_<id>(data, scratch, lo, hi)`, a stable 2-way count-then-scatter partition into alternating buffers that borrows PHASE 2's OWN SCRATCH at matching indices and so needs no allocation at all (the 3-way attempt needed a fourth malloc). Progress without a 3-way equal block comes from making the split predicate `cmp(x,pivot) < t` with `t` loop-invariant and re-running with t=1 when nlt==0: the retry cannot return 0 because the pivot is <= pivot, so the left half is then the block of elements equal to the pivot, already sorted and stable and needing no recursion, and two passes restore buffer parity so nothing downstream knows a retry happened -- ONE kernel, not two. Phase 1 accumulates only CONSECUTIVE short runs, so a long run ends the accumulation and is recorded untouched, which is what keeps nearly-sorted input from being destroyed. -- ALL FIVE DIRECTIONS, with the data that closed them: (1) contained merge-kernel tweaks -- unconditional branchless merge is 2x worse on ordered-ish shapes, cached merge heads 3-5%, ordered-run bulk copy helps only already-sorted; (2) RUN tuning -- flat within ~3% across 4/8/16/32/64 under BOTH the branchy and branchless kernels; (3) bounds-check hoist -- net-neutral, -9.1% instructions bought only +3-4% wall clock, proving the merge is latency-bound not throughput-bound; (4) 3-way quicksort run-builder -- ~47 instructions/element/level, MORE than the merge pass it replaced; (5) 2-way quicksort run-builder -- this row, parity at best on random across the whole configuration sweep. -- ALSO STILL TRUE: not a codegen-quality gap (karac is 5-8% faster than rustc compiling the identical algorithm); karac now runs 1.53x driftsort's instructions and 0.82x its mispredicts, i.e. it mispredicts LESS OFTEN than driftsort. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 Xeon @2.80GHz 4-vCPU shared cloud container, NOT the canonical Apple-silicon bench host. Instruction counts are host-independent; the wall-clock figures and anything resting on cache or unrolling behaviour are not. -- SEVERITY LOW and should stay there: ~1.30x on one input shape, where karac is 7x FASTER than driftsort on sorted and reverse-sorted input, 1.85x faster on sawtooth, and the parent rows were 54x and 1.66x. -- DISPOSITION 2026-08-11: moved from `open` to `wontfix`. `open` is the work queue (bug-curve.py renders open rows in full precisely because you are expected to act on them), and this row has no action left, so leaving it open would have parked a permanent no-op in the queue. It is NOT `invalid` -- the 1.30x is real and reproduces on demand; `invalid` in this ledger means the premise was refuted (see B-2026-07-17-14, B-2026-07-29-8) and claiming that here would be false. The `wontfix` status was added to the lint enum and to the rollup for exactly this case. The live remainder of the investigation moved to B-2026-08-11-10.

fix:
FIXED — the full-array stable partition of § Direction 7 was budget-checked,
built, and measured. On the pattern this row filed as 3.3x behind driftsort,
karac now runs FEWER INSTRUCTIONS THAN DRIFTSORT and lands at wall-clock
parity. Fixed in 3d77cc60; emitter in `emit_sort_by_mono` (src/codegen/vec_method.rs); write-up in
docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md § Direction 7.

Before/after on the same container, baseline reproducing this row's own
recorded checksum (48.8M / 22.5M) exactly:

    pattern         instructions           driftsort   was            now
    few-unique      48.8M -> 13.2M  3.70x     14.2M    3.44x behind   1.08x AHEAD
    sawtooth        22.5M -> 23.4M  0.96x     31.6M    1.40x ahead    1.35x ahead
    random          72.3M -> 72.1M  1.00x     48.2M    1.50x behind   unchanged
    nearly-sorted   31.5M -> 32.9M  0.96x
    sorted           1.0M ->  1.0M  1.00x
    reverse          1.8M ->  1.8M  1.00x

Wall clock on the target, same session and slope method: 4.760 -> 1.742 ms
(2.73x), against driftsort's 1.514 ms best / 1.764 ms bulk average. Wall clock
on the other five rows is noise -- it swings several percent in BOTH directions
against IDENTICAL instruction counts, and sorted/reverse sit at 0.03-0.4 ms,
under the slope method's floor. Argue from the instruction column.

THE 4% ON SAWTOOTH AND NEARLY-SORTED IS REAL AND IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE, and
three candidate explanations were each measured and killed. Not the probe:
sorted and reverse call it on every sort and did not move off 1.0M / 1.8M, which
bounds it under 0.05M. Not the partition running: neither pattern passes the
gate. Not the call-graph change: the obvious suspect was that `qpart` calling
back into the merge gives the merge a second caller, but DELETING that call (a
deliberately incorrect build, valid to measure because neither pattern ever
reaches `qpart`) made both WORSE, 24.4M and 34.4M. What is left is codegen
jitter -- perturbing the module around a 60-block function moves these two
patterns a few percent either way, and the shipped arrangement is the better end
of the measured range. Also measured and rejected: hoisting the probe into its
own function changed nothing (13.2/23.4/72.1/32.9 identical), so it is kept out
of line on structure, not on evidence of a win.

THE DESIGN, and the two things that made it work where six earlier directions
did not. (1) It occupies the OTHER END OF THE RECURSION from the bounded
run-builder that was built and reverted for B-2026-08-10-20: partition from n
DOWN to a span and merge below, rather than merge above a span and partition
below. So it removes the TOP passes, and every partition runs on a large range
rather than paying a fixed per-range cost near its base size. (2) It STOPS
EARLY, which no merge can -- a range whose every element ties with the pivot is
sorted and stable and is finished. Instrumented on few-unique: 8 all-equal exits
for 8 distinct keys, and NOT ONE merge pass over the array.

GATE PLACEMENT WAS MOST OF THE WORK, because ungated this is 11-13x WORSE on
sorted and reverse. Both full-pass placements lose: a counting pass BEFORE phase
1 costs ~1.3M, which is 42% of sorted's entire budget; AFTER phase 1 it is free
for sorted/reverse but costs few-unique 19.4M -> 33.9M, because phase 1's RUN=32
insertion padding spends ~14.5M on an input whose natural runs are ~2 long and
the partition then discards it -- no better than the 34.25M run-builder this row
already rejected. So the entry gate is O(1): 512 samples estimating BOTH
cardinality (ties with a random pivot) and existing orderedness (ordered
adjacent pairs). Both are needed -- cardinality alone would partition an input
that is ALREADY SORTED over few keys. The in-recursion gate is exact and free:
`neq = nle - nlt` is already computed by the partition's own counting pass, so
each range re-decides for nothing and a mixed input partitions the part that
pays and merges the part that does not.

FOUR KERNEL DETAILS, NONE OPTIONAL. (a) The pivot must be RANDOMISED; a
fixed-position median-of-3 is degenerate on periodic input -- on the sawtooth
lo/lo+len/2/hi-1 hold 0, 0, 999, the median is 0, and 0 is the range MINIMUM, so
each level peels only the copies of the minimum: measured 2328.7M instructions,
~100x the merge. (b) ONE counting pass tallies both `< pivot` and `<= pivot`,
which picks the split predicate without a second pass and folds the old t=1
retry into it. (c) Count-then-scatter, two cursors over one in-order walk --
the whole stability argument. (d) `allow_part` on the merge sort's signature:
without it an abandoned range is re-probed, accepted by the sampling estimate
that the exact tie count just rejected, and handed straight back -- same range,
same pivot, forever. A depth limit of 64 keeps the worst case O(n log n) after
introducing a randomised pivot.

GATE THRESHOLD VALIDATED AGAINST A MEASURED CROSSOVER, not tuned to the
benchmark. With the partition forced on, so the crossover is a property of the
algorithms: distinct keys 2/8/32/64/128/256/512 -> partition 7.6/22.4/30.7/36.8/
60.6/64.8/67.0M against merge 38.7/49.7/53.0/52.0/51.0/50.5/50.5M, i.e. the
crossover is between 64 and 128. The arithmetic predicts d < 68 (a partition
level costs two passes against the merge's one, so it wins while 2*log2(d) <
log2(n/RUN) = 12.2). GATE = 64 sits just on the winning side of both.

VERIFICATION. A 756-case sweep -- 6 patterns x 14 sizes x 9 cardinalities,
sizes straddling the probe floor (4095/4096/4097) and cardinalities straddling
the gate (63/64/65/129) -- asserting sorted AND stable, with the ORACLE ITSELF
VALIDATED by poisoning it (two deliberately unsorted cases produce 27,500 FAIL
lines, so a silent pass means something). Element types i64, all-int struct and
heap String. Full `cargo test --features llvm` green; ASAN clean at the default
level and on the `-O0` leg (1032 passed, quarantine list matched exactly).
`should_use_mono_vec_sort_by_for` admits only i64 and all-int structs, so no
heap-owning element ever reaches this path -- the memory-safety class here is
bounds, not ownership. Pins: `test_e2e_vec_sort_by_partition_path_low_cardinality`
(tests/codegen.rs, strict assert_eq so a stale archive fails loudly) and
`asan_vec_sort_by_partition_path_in_bounds` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs), both
checking sortedness, stability, and the all-equal early exit -- that branch
returns a range declaring it sorted WITHOUT writing it, so only stability can
catch it having moved anything.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLOSE: B-2026-08-10-20, the shuffled-uniform 1.50x, which
remains `wontfix`. Random is untouched here (72.3M -> 72.1M) by design -- the
gate rejects it after one 512-sample probe.
title: `Vec[(i64,i64)].sort_by` on FEW-UNIQUE input (150k pairs over 8 distinct keys) is 5.93 ms / 48.8M instructions vs driftsort's 1.81 ms / 14.2M on this host -- a 3.3x gap, NOT the 1.3-1.5x originally filed. The stable 2-way quicksort run-builder built for B-2026-08-10-20 is a real 1.43x (to 34.25M / 4.15 ms) but is NOT a route to parity as this row first claimed: it still leaves 2.4x on instructions and 2.3x on wall clock. Both previously proposed options (pay down the sawtooth regression; gate on a cardinality signal) only bank that 1.43x, and the sawtooth one defends the pattern karac ALREADY WINS (22.5M vs 31.6M). Any future attempt should be budgeted against driftsort's 14.2M -- ~95 instructions per element against karac's ~325 -- before a line is written.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: split out of B-2026-08-10-20 on 2026-08-11 when that row was closed as `wontfix`. The parent is about SHUFFLED-UNIFORM input and is finished; this row exists because the same experiment produced one genuine unexploited win on a DIFFERENT input shape, and burying an actionable finding inside a closed row is how it gets lost. -- WHY IT IS SEPARATE AND NOT A REOPENING: the parent's five dead ends were all attempts on random input, where the run-builder reaches parity at best. Few-unique is the one shape where it is decisively ahead, and it is ahead for a legible reason -- 8 distinct keys means the partition resolves the array in ~3 levels while the merge still pays all 12 passes, and the comparisons become almost perfectly predictable (the 10x mispredict drop). -- WHAT EXISTS ALREADY: the full emitter was written and verified (98/98 pattern x size combinations, element-type coverage on i64, a mixed-width (i64,i32,i64) tuple and a named struct, agreeing across AOT, LLJIT and the interpreter) and then REVERTED, so there is no code on main. Recover it from the B-2026-08-10-20 investigation rather than rewriting: `__vec_<m>_qs_<id>(data, scratch, lo, hi)`, a stable 2-way count-then-scatter partition into alternating buffers that borrows phase 2's own scratch at matching indices and so needs no allocation; progress without a 3-way equal block comes from a loop-invariant threshold t in `cmp(x,pivot) < t` with a t=1 retry when nlt==0. Design notes and the configuration sweep are in docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md. -- MEASURE OPTION (a) FIRST: it is the cheaper experiment and it is the one that would let the win land unconditionally, whereas (b) adds a cardinality probe to every sort and has to earn its own keep. -- CAVEAT: x86_64 Xeon @2.80GHz 4-vCPU shared cloud container, NOT the canonical Apple-silicon bench host. Instruction and mispredict counts are host-independent; the wall-clock figures are not, and branch-prediction-sensitive results are the most likely to move on a different microarchitecture. -- SEVERITY LOW: it is one input shape, karac is already 7x faster than driftsort on sorted and reverse-sorted input and 1.85x faster on sawtooth, and nothing here is a correctness or codegen-quality defect.

PREMISE CORRECTED 2026-08-11 -- THE ROUTE IS NOT TO PARITY, AND THE GAP IS
BIGGER THAN FILED. Re-measured with a rebuilt harness, now checked into
docs/spikes/sortbench/ (the original was lost with its session scratchpad,
which is why this row had to be re-measured from scratch at all).

THE HARNESS WAS VALIDATED BEFORE IT WAS BELIEVED, on host-independent numbers
this row's own spike already recorded: karac few-unique 48.8M instructions
(recorded 48.85M), karac sawtooth 22.5M (recorded 22.53M), clone-only slope
1.13-1.24 ms (recorded 1.13-1.23). Three significant figures from an
independently written harness, so what follows is not a harness artifact.

WHAT CHANGED IS THE DRIFTSORT SIDE:

    pattern      karac              filed driftsort   RE-MEASURED driftsort
    random       10.92 ms / 72.3M   8.2-8.9 ms        8.65 ms / 48.2M
    few-unique    5.93 ms / 48.8M   3.6-4.1 ms        1.81 ms / 14.2M
    sawtooth      3.58 ms / 22.5M   6.0-6.5 ms        4.50 ms / 31.6M

Random lands inside the filed range -- that is the control, and it says the two
measurements are of the same thing. Few-unique does not: driftsort is 1.81 ms,
not 3.6-4.1, and its 14.2M instruction count corroborates that on a metric that
does not move between hosts. The filed figure appears never to have been
cross-checked against instructions.

(Method note, because it nearly produced a wrong correction: without `black_box`
on the Rust timing loop, random measures 6.77 ms instead of 8.65 and flatters
driftsort by 28%. The mismatch against the spike's own recorded 8.2-8.9 is what
caught it. The Rust input generator is now mirrored line-for-line from the Kara
one, per the spike's own caveat 3.)

CONSEQUENCES FOR THIS ROW, both halves of the title:

stable sorting -- timsort's, therefore Java's and CPython's -- and karac's merge
does not have it. Anyone picking this row up tries it first. It is also the one
lever that attacks the property this document already identified as the real
bottleneck: the bounds-check hoist showed the merge is LATENCY-bound on its
loop-carried chain (-9.1% instructions bought +3.5% wall clock), and a bulk
memcpy has no such chain at all.

checksum (few-unique 48.8M, sawtooth 22.5M, random 72.3M -- reproduced exactly):

is measuring a different loop.

INSTRUCTIONS -- the bounds-check-hoist signature again, and for the same reason:
a gallop's binary search has a WORSE dependency chain than the streaming merge
it replaces, since each probe address depends on the previous comparison.

NOT A DUD IMPLEMENTATION, AND NOT A TUNING MISS. Instrumented: few-unique
bulk-copies 1,619,133 of ~1.76M merge outputs (92%) across 35,145 copies, and
random correctly self-disables (693 galloped of 1.9M). A MIN_GALLOP sweep is
flat -- 40.3/40.3/40.3/40.1/40.1/41.1M at thresholds 1/2/3/4/7/12 -- while
threshold 1 costs random 27%.

THE ARITHMETIC, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Every phase-2 pass writes all n
elements, so with RUN=32 and n=150k the sort does ceil(log2(150000/32)) = 13
passes ~= 1.8M merge outputs, AND THAT VOLUME IS INDEPENDENT OF KEY CARDINALITY.
Galloping makes an output cheaper; it cannot make one fewer of them. It also
only reaches the TOP passes -- with 8 keys a run of length L holds ~8 blocks of
L/8, so a gallop pays only once L/8 clears the threshold, while the bottom
passes contribute exactly as many outputs and are untouched (measured average
bulk copy: 46 elements, not hundreds).

Against that, driftsort's 14.2M is ~95 instructions per ELEMENT. Spread over 13
passes that is 7.9 instructions per merge output -- less than one
compare-and-move. Driftsort is not running a cheaper merge; it is running about
THREE PASSES. And the pass count cannot be bought by raising the insertion base,
because phase 1 is O(n*RUN) -- measured RUN 32/64/128/256/1024 -> 13/12/11/10/8
passes -> 50.5/58.2/76.8/116.0/362.4M. RUN=32 is already optimal.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS ROW'S FIX SHAPE. Four of the six measured directions --
merge-kernel tweaks, RUN tuning, the bounds-check hoist, and now galloping --
optimize COST PER MERGE OUTPUT, and n*log2(n/RUN) outputs is fixed, so that
whole family provably cannot reach 14.2M at any per-output cost. The other two
(the 3-way and 2-way quicksort run-builders) were pass-count reducers but
bounded the partition to a `span` and merged above it, removing only
log2(span/RUN) passes -- which is why the better of them landed at 34.25M.

So the requirement on any future attempt is now specific: IT MUST REDUCE THE
NUMBER OF FULL PASSES OVER THE ARRAY, AND BOUNDING THE PARTITION TO A SPAN
FORFEITS MOST OF THAT. A full-array stable partition is the only shape left that
qualifies.

WHY IT REDUCES PASSES WHERE THE BOUNDED RUN-BUILDER COULD NOT. Same kernel as
the reverted B-2026-08-10-20 attempt -- stable 2-way count-then-scatter into
alternating buffers, borrowing phase 2's own scratch, still no extra allocation.
The inversion is which end of the recursion it occupies: the bounded one merged
ABOVE a span and partitioned BELOW (removing log2(span/RUN) passes off the
bottom, and paying a partition's fixed per-range cost on ranges near its base
size); this one partitions from n DOWN to a span and merges below, so it removes
the TOP passes and every partition it performs is on a large range. And it can
STOP EARLY, which no merge can: a range whose every element ties with the pivot
is sorted and stable and is finished. Instrumented on few-unique:
partitions=12, all_equal_exits=8, merged=0 -- eight all-equal exits for eight
distinct keys, and not one merge pass over the array.

TWO KERNEL DETAILS, NEITHER OPTIONAL. (1) The pivot must be RANDOMISED, not a
fixed-position median-of-3: sampling lo, lo+len/2, hi-1 is degenerate on
periodic input -- on the sawtooth those hold 0, 0, 999, the median is 0, and 0
is the range MINIMUM, so each level peels only the 150 copies of it. Measured
2328.7M instructions, ~100x the merge. (2) ONE counting pass tallies both
`< pivot` and `<= pivot`, which chooses the split predicate without a second
pass and folds the old t=1 retry into it: nlt == 0 means the left block is
exactly the elements equal to the pivot, already sorted and stable, no recursion.

THE TWO GATES, AND WHY PLACEMENT WAS MOST OF THE WORK. Ungated, this is
UNSHIPPABLE: 11-13x worse on sorted and reverse (3.1M -> 40.2M, 3.7M -> 39.7M)
and 1.3-2.7x worse on random, sawtooth and nearly-sorted. Two plausible
placements both lose. A full counting pass BEFORE phase 1 costs ~1.3M, which is
42% of sorted's entire 3.1M (sorted -> 4.4M, reverse -> 5.0M) -- and those are
the patterns karac beats driftsort 7x on. AFTER phase 1 it is free for
sorted/reverse but few-unique goes 19.4M -> 33.9M, because phase 1's RUN=32
insertion padding costs ~14.5M on an input whose natural runs are ~2 long and
the partition then discards that work -- no better than the 34.25M run-builder
already rejected. So the entry decision must PRECEDE phase 1 and be O(1) in n.
256 random samples settle both halves: distinct keys among the sample estimate
cardinality (8 true keys reads 8, 1000 reads 231, all-distinct reads 256), and
the fraction of sampled ADJACENT PAIRS already in order estimates what phase 1
would find (sorted 100%, nearly-sorted 99%, shuffled 57-61%). Both are needed --
cardinality alone would partition an input that is ALREADY SORTED over few keys.
Inside the recursion the gate is exact and genuinely free: part_once's counting
pass has already computed neq = nle - nlt, so len/neq is an unbiased cardinality
estimate available BEFORE a single element is written; a range that fails it
abandons having moved no data and is merged as today. The decision is therefore
per-range, not a global mode.

WHERE THE THRESHOLD BELONGS, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Sweeping cardinality
with the partition forced on, so the crossover is a property of the algorithms
and not of the gate:

    distinct keys      2     8    32    64   128   256   512
    merge          38.7M 49.7M 53.0M 52.0M 51.0M 50.5M 50.5M
    partition       7.6M 22.4M 30.7M 36.8M 60.6M 64.8M 67.0M
    ratio           5.1x  2.2x  1.7x  1.4x  0.84x 0.78x 0.75x

Crossover is between 64 and 128 distinct keys. The analytic prediction is that
partitioning wins while 2*log2(d) < log2(n/RUN) = 12.2 -- two passes per level
against the merge's one -- i.e. d < 68. Measurement and arithmetic agree, which
is the corroboration worth having before trusting either. GATE = 64 therefore
sits just on the winning side of a crossover it was not tuned to.

SOURCE NOTE: found dogfooding a ~100-line log aggregator (parse a

into a `Vec[Stat]`, report sorted by total). The interpreter matched the
hand-computed oracle exactly; AOT printed the right NUMBERS with a garbage

THE INVARIANT THAT IS BROKEN is stated in the compiler itself, at
`src/cli.rs:1477` (`is_fatal_ownership_kind`):

    `UseAfterMove` -- codegen defensive-copies the reuse, so the binary is
    memory-safe; the diagnostic carries a machine-applicable `.clone()` fix
    precisely because the program compiles and runs. Keeping it non-fatal for
    `build` is deliberate ...

B-2026-07-19-3 reached the same conclusion explicitly ("build's leniency is
intended, NOT a soundness hole") and that is the conclusion this row narrows:
the defensive copy is real for the sources those investigations looked at, and
does not exist for a container element read. For that subset the leniency IS a
soundness hole -- `karac check` exits 0 with "All checks passed", `karac build`
exits 0, and the emitted program reads freed memory.

MEASURED. Identical 10-line shape each time -- first owner dies in an inner
block, second copy read after it -- varying ONLY where the doubly-moved String
came from:

    source of the doubly-moved String        interp     AOT
    plain local binding (`let s: String`)    alpha      alpha      copy emitted
    struct field (`h.name`)                  alpha      alpha      copy emitted
    Map value (`m.get(k)` payload)           alpha      GARBAGE    no copy
    Vec element (`names[0]`)                 alpha      GARBAGE    no copy

The minimal reproducer is 10 lines with no function boundary at all:

    fn main() {
        let names: Vec[String] = ["alpha"];
        let mut out: String = f"";
        {
            let n = names[0];
            let _keep: String = n;
            out = n;
        }
        println(out);
    }

    interp: alpha        AOT: JofY (garbage)

THE INNER BLOCK IS THE INSTRUMENT, not incidental. Without it the same program
prints correctly -- but only because the read happens BEFORE the first owner's
scope exit frees the shared buffer. That is why this looked at first like an
escape-analysis bug (it reproduces through a returned `Vec[Stat]`, through a
returned bare `String`, and across a by-value or `ref` Vec parameter, and NOT
when the value is consumed in the same scope). All of those are the same defect
seen through different lifetimes: the two owners always alias, and whether you
observe it depends only on whether the first one has died yet. Any "working"
case here is timing, not a copy.

THREE BACKENDS, THREE BEHAVIOURS, which is the sharpest symptom:
  - `--interp`  correct
  - `run` (JIT) ABORTS: "unsafe precondition(s) violated:
    ptr::copy_nonoverlapping requires that both pointer arguments are aligned
    and non-null" at `karac_string_clone` (runtime/src/clone.rs:80)
  - `build` (AOT) silently prints garbage bytes

`.clone()` at the move site -- what the diagnostic prescribes -- does fix it, so
the escape hatch works. That is the mitigation, not the fix: the whole reason
the diagnostic is a warning rather than an error is the promise that you do not
have to take it.

WHY THE CORPUS NEVER HIT IT, and this is the actionable part beyond the fix
itself: `tests/common/mod.rs`'s ownership gate (`assert_ownership_clean`)
REFUSES any fixture whose program has ownership errors, `UseAfterMove`
included, on the stated grounds that "`karac check` would reject it, so codegen
is being fed input it never sees in production". That premise is false for this
one kind -- `karac check` exits 0 on it BY DESIGN (`is_fatal_ownership_kind`
excludes `UseAfterMove` and `RcFallbackNote`). So the ~1000-fixture
memory_sanitizer suite, the codebase's primary memory gate, structurally cannot
contain a single test of the defensive-copy mechanism, which is exactly the
mechanism whose correctness `UseAfterMove`'s non-fatal status depends on. Any
fix here needs the gate widened (or a grandfathered lane) or it will not be
regression-testable under ASAN.

    let s: String = f"alpha";

    interp  alpha        build  garbage        run (JIT)  garbage

    String            garbage
    Vec[i64]          garbage (prints 8475182884243973504)

WIDENING THE GATE WAS THE PREREQUISITE, not housekeeping. `assert_ownership_clean`
failed on any ownership error, justified by "`karac check` would reject it, so
codegen is being fed input it never sees in production". For the two ADVISORY

`karac build` compiles them. The gate now mirrors that function. Until it did,
the ~1000-fixture memory suite could not hold a single test of the
defensive-copy mechanism -- which is exactly how the copy could be ENTIRELY

THE TWO HALVES, and the measured reason they are welded together. The copy
alone leaks the source; the disarm-skip alone turns the use-after-free into a
DOUBLE free. That is not a hypothetical -- the first build keyed the disarm skip

title: a `Vec[char]` INDEX used directly as a method receiver (`cs[0].to_string()`) loses its `char` type and dispatches to the INTEGER method, so codegen silently prints `120` where the interpreter prints `x` -- the same root gap hard-errors on `VecDeque[char]` and `Array[char, N]`
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found dogfooding a ~180-line recursive-descent expression
evaluator (tokenizer building identifier names character by character, then a
`Map[String, i64]` variable lookup). The interpreter matched the hand-computed
oracle on all 8 expressions; JIT and AOT agreed with each other and returned
`ERR:unknown variable` for every expression that referenced a variable. The
numbers-only expressions (`1 + 2 * 3`, `100 / 7`) were correct, which is what
pointed at the identifier text rather than at the parser.

ROOT CAUSE, and the `Array` arm states it outright. An index expression used
DIRECTLY as a method receiver has no resolved element `TypeExpr`, so method
dispatch falls back to the LLVM representation. `char` lowers to an integer, so
instead of failing it silently resolves to the INTEGER `to_string()` and
produces the code point:

    let cs: Vec[char] = "x".chars().collect();
    let mut acc: String = f"";
    acc.push_str(cs[0].to_string());
    println(f"len={acc.len()} val=[{acc}]");

    interp: len=1 val=[x]          AOT/JIT: len=3 val=[120]

120 is `'x'`. That is the whole bug: not a corrupted buffer, a correctly-built
string of the WRONG THING.

THE SAME GAP, THREE SURFACES -- and only one of them is silent:

    Vec[char]        cs[0].to_string()   ->  "120"   SILENT WRONG ANSWER
    VecDeque[char]   d[0].to_string()    ->  hard error, "no handler for method
                                             'to_string' on variable
                                             '__indexed_elem_0' ... this is a
                                             codegen bug"
    Array[char, 2]   a[0].to_string()    ->  hard error, "indexed-receiver method
                                             'to_string' on 'a' -- element
                                             TypeExpr unknown (outer is not a
                                             tracked Vec/Slice/Array variable)"

The `Array` message names the mechanism exactly, and note it fires on a variable
that IS an Array -- so the "tracked Vec/Slice/Array" set has a hole for `Array`
too. `Vec` is the dangerous one precisely because it is the best-supported
container: dispatch succeeds, on the wrong type.

MEASURED BOUNDARY -- both ingredients are required, and either one alone is
clean:

    let c: char = cs[0]; c.to_string()      x        BOUND FIRST -> correct
    'x'.to_string()                         x        literal receiver -> correct
    cs[0].to_string()                       120      index + method -> WRONG
    f"{cs[0].to_string()}"                  [120]    same in an f-string
    f"{cs[0]}"                              [x]      no method call -> correct
    cs[0] == 'x'                            true     operator, not method -> correct
    Map[i64, char] value .to_string()       x        Map read -> correct
    Vec[String] index .len()                3        String element -> correct

So it is specifically METHOD DISPATCH on an INDEX expression, and specifically a
`char` element. A `String` element is fine because its mis-dispatch has nowhere
wrong to land; a `char` element is not, because `char` and `i64` share a
representation.

NOT push_str-specific and not argument-position-specific -- my first framing was
wrong. `let s: String = cs[0].to_string();` reproduces on its own.

FAMILY: this is the same shape as B-2026-08-10-13, where a `sort_by` comparator
parameter lost its element type and method dispatch fell through with "no
handler for method 'len'". That fix registered the params in `vec_elem_types` /
`var_elem_type_exprs`. The index-expression receiver was not covered by it, and
here the failure is worse than the one that motivated that fix: loud there,
silent here.

FIX SHAPE: resolve the element `TypeExpr` for an indexed receiver before method
dispatch, from the same side-tables B-2026-08-10-13 used. Worth covering
`VecDeque` and `Array` in the same pass rather than one container at a time --
all three are the one lookup, and two of them are already erroring with messages
that blame codegen for a resolution gap.

=== RESOLVED 7372313 ===

THREE root causes, not one, and the row's framing ("the indexed-receiver element-TypeExpr lookup") was right about only the middle one. Each was stashed independently and the regression test goes RED for every one, so all three are load-bearing.

(1) THE SILENT ONE, and it was not in the indexed-receiver path at all. `register_var_from_type_expr` records `var_type_names` for structs, shared types, enums and INTEGER primitives -- and not for `char`. `expr_is_char` reads exactly that map, so a binding with no recorded name is INDISTINGUISHABLE from an `i32` downstream and the renderer emits the code point. The int-prim arm sitting immediately above carries a comment describing this same bug class in another skin (a `for b in vec_u8` element rendering 255u8 as -1, self-hosted lexer, 2026-06-12); `char` was never added beside it.

Fixing it THERE rather than at the call site is what makes it general: every binding form routing through that registrar gets the name -- the `__indexed_elem_N` synth the indexed path mints, for-loop elements, destructured elements, and function params. It also explains the row's own boundary table without further work: `let c: char = cs[0]` was always correct because `stmts.rs` records the annotation directly, which is precisely what made the defect look like it belonged to indexing.

(2) ARRAY, and it is not char-specific. `Array[T, N]` records its element TypeExpr into `array_elem_type_exprs`, a deliberately separate table (B-2026-07-30-3) because `var_elem_type_exprs` has ~170 readers that treat a present entry as "this binding is a Vec/Slice/Map". The indexed-receiver lookup read only the shared table, so it errored on a variable that IS an Array while its message named "Vec/Slice/Array". Fixed by reading the array table as a FALLBACK at that one site -- one new reader, no widening. Measured: `Array[i64, N]` and `Array[String, N]` failed identically before the fix, so EVERY indexed-receiver method on an Array was unreachable, not just the `char` one the row probed.

(3) VECDEQUE, and it is a TYPECHECKER bug, which is why the row's codegen-only framing could not have found it. The scalar integer-index arm in `infer_expr` resolves `Type::Array` / `Type::Slice` / `Type::Vector` / `Type::NamedVec` and their Ref/MutRef forms -- `VecDeque` is absent, so `d[i]` infers `Type::Error`. Most uses survive that, which is why it hid: `d[0] + 1` and `let x: i64 = d[0]` both work because the operator and the annotation recover the type. METHOD DISPATCH cannot: an `Error` receiver produces no `method_callee_types` entry, so codegen's `dispatch_key` is `None`, `recv_is_scalar_primitive` is false, and the scalar `to_string` arm is never reached. Measured discrimination: on a VecDeque index, `abs()` and `is_alphabetic()` WORK and only `to_string` fails -- because only `to_string` is gated on the dispatch key. The range-index arm two hundred lines above already pairs `Vec`/`VecDeque`; the scalar arm now does too, in both the direct and the borrowed position.

CORRECTED FROM THE ROW: the `Array` diagnostic was read as evidence that "the tracked Vec/Slice/Array set has a hole for Array", which is true, but the hole is a second TABLE rather than a missing entry -- and the VecDeque failure is not the same gap wearing a different message, it is a different phase entirely. The three surfaces genuinely needed three fixes; treating them as one lookup, as the FIX SHAPE section proposed, would have fixed Array alone and left both the silent `char` render and the VecDeque error standing.

TEST: `test_e2e_indexed_receiver_char_element_method` (tests/codegen.rs) runs all three containers across `char` / `i64` / `String` elements and carries the row's own measured-boundary table as controls -- bound-first, literal receiver, f-string without a method, `==`, a Map value, a `Vec[String]` element, a for-loop element. Those controls were all correct BEFORE the fix, so they are what stops it over-reaching. The expected VALUES are the assertion rather than the fact that it compiles: `char` and `i64` share a representation, so a regression in this area is silent by nature.

detail:
SOURCE NOTE: hit while rebuilding the sort benchmark harness for
B-2026-08-11-10 (docs/spikes/sortbench/). Reading an element back out of a
`Vec[(i64,i64)]` is the whole of the workload, and there is no spelling that
does it through `get`.

MEASURED, all four on the same two-line program:

    let e = v.get(0).unwrap(); e.0
        error[typecheck]: tuple index on non-tuple type 'ref (i64, i64)'
    let (a, b) = v.get(0).unwrap();
        error[typecheck]: tuple pattern used but type is `ref (i64, i64)`
    let e: (i64,i64) = v.get(0).unwrap();
        error[typecheck]: expected '(i64, i64)', found 'ref (i64, i64)'
    let e = v.get(0).unwrap().clone(); e.0
        All checks passed.  ->  runtime error: method 'clone' not found on
                                type 'unknown' (no interpreter dispatch arm)

THE CONTRAST IS WHAT MAKES IT A BUG AND NOT A DESIGN CHOICE. The identical
shape on a struct element works:

    struct P { a: i64 }
    let e = v.get(0).unwrap(); e.a          // All checks passed

Field projection through a `ref` is supported; tuple-index projection through
the same `ref` is not. Those are the same operation on two aggregate kinds, so
the tuple side reads as an unimplemented case rather than a rule. Indexing
sidesteps it entirely -- `v[0].0` works -- which is the available workaround and
is what the harness uses.

THE `.clone()` ARM IS A SEPARATE, SMALLER DEFECT IN THE SAME SPOT, and is the
run-vs-build class this ledger keeps closing (B-2026-08-11-2 / -4 / -9). Note
the receiver prints as `'unknown'`, not as `'ref (i64, i64)'` -- so the method
lookup for a ref-to-tuple receiver is not merely missing an arm, it has lost
the receiver type by the time it reports. That is worth looking at first: it
may be the same root cause as the three rejections above.

WHY MEDIUM: no wrong answers and no unsoundness -- three of the four spellings
are honest compile errors. But `Vec[tuple]` is a common shape (it is the
canonical pair/record before a struct is worth declaring), `get` is the safe
accessor the language steers people toward over indexing, and the failure hits
on the first thing anyone tries. The check-green/run-red `.clone()` is the part
that could actually mislead.

=== FIXED (bf43b275). Wider than filed, and the first fix attempt missed. ===

WIDER THAN THE ROW RECORDED: this is not Map-specific. `Vec[String].get(i)
.unwrap_or(d)` double-frees identically, and a nested value
(`Map[String, Vec[String]]`) showed FOUR invalid accesses rather than one. The
common factor is the ACCESSOR, not the container: `get`/`first`/`last` return an
`Option` whose payload words alias the container's storage, and `unwrap_or`
handed that back as an owned result.

THE FIRST ATTEMPT LOOKED RIGHT AND DID NOTHING, which is the part worth keeping.
The obvious move is to reuse the match path's predicate wholesale --
`borrow_get_payload_clone_te(object)` -- since that path has been correct on
this shape all along. Measured with a debug print, the receiver classified as a
borrow call (`borrow_call=true`) and the predicate still returned `None`,
because it resolves the payload type through the SPAN-keyed
`enum_inst_type_exprs`, which is populated at match-SCRUTINEE sites and has no
entry for a receiver in argument position. The fix therefore takes the payload
type from `unwrap_or`'s own `inner_te` and borrows only the SHAPE GATE, which is
now split out as `borrow_payload_clone_te_gate`.

  Generalisable: a predicate that answers "is this expression X" can be reusable
  while its data lookup is not, because the side table it reads may only be
  populated at the syntactic position the predicate was written for. Checking
  that the reuse actually FIRED -- rather than that it compiled -- is what
  caught it, and cost one instrumented build.

MEASURED after, `--interp` vs `karac build` at both opt levels, 0 leaks and 0
invalid accesses: `Map[String, String]`, `Vec[String].get`,
`Map[String, Vec[String]]` (element-deep), plus the two controls that must NOT
clone -- a scalar value (nothing to alias) and an ABSENT key, where the result
is the caller's own default and cloning would leak it once per call.

OPT LEVEL DISAGREES ABOUT SEVERITY here, as the row noted: a hard double-free
abort at the default level, a single silent invalid read at -O0. Both pins carry
it; the ASAN fixture reports `attempting double-free` pre-fix.

SCOPE CORRECTED ON INVESTIGATION -- THIS ROW OVERSTATED THE BUG AND MISDIAGNOSED
IT. Running the same four spellings against a STRUCT element, which the row
cited only as a passing contrast, settles which are defects:

    spelling                struct                       tuple
    projection .field/.0    works                        REJECTED   <- defect
    annotated by-value      expected 'P', found 'ref P'  same shape <- BY DESIGN
    pattern destructure     struct pattern ... is ref P  same shape <- BY DESIGN
    .clone()                honest 'no method' error     check-green/run-red

So TWO of the four spellings this row listed as part of the bug are not bugs at
all: a borrow does not implicitly deref-copy, struct and tuple agree on that,
and rejecting them is correct. The row should have run the contrast on all four
before filing rather than on one.

THE REMAINING TWO ARE REAL, BUT THEY ARE NOT ONE BUG, AND THE SECOND IS NOT
ABOUT `ref` AT ALL:

  - The PROJECTION asymmetry is genuine and is exactly as filed.

  - The `.clone()` arm is the B-2026-08-11-2 CLASS, fourth instance. A BY-VALUE
    tuple behaves identically: `let t = (7, 8); t.completely_bogus()` was
    check-green, and the poison unified freely -- `let s: String = t.bogus()`,
    `let n: i64 = ...`, `let v: Vec[i64] = ...` all passed. `ref` was a red
    herring; every tuple method call poisoned.

THE ROW'S PROPOSED ROOT CAUSE WAS WRONG. It read the interpreter's "method
'clone' not found on type 'unknown'" as the typechecker losing the receiver type
before lookup. It does not: `receiver_for_method_lookup` peels `Ref`/`MutRef`
correctly (types.rs:575). The actual cause is that `method_callee_type_name`
returns `None` for `Type::Tuple`, so the scalar-primitive arm -- the one
`char`/`bool` joined in B-2026-08-11-2 -- skips tuple receivers entirely and
they fall to the silent-poison branch. The `'unknown'` was the interpreter
naming a type it has no case for, not evidence about the typechecker.

That also dictated where the fix goes. Giving tuples a name in
`method_callee_type_name` would have been the small change, but that function
feeds the `method_callee_types` side-table codegen's `dispatch_key` reads, so it
would point dispatch at a name no impl can ever be registered under. An early
return in the method-call path keeps the fix inside the typechecker.

ONE MORE THING THE ROW DID NOT HAVE: `to_string` -- the single method that
worked on a tuple -- was ALSO poisoned. It merely happened to have a runtime
dispatch arm, so `let n: i64 = t.to_string()` type-checked exactly as readily as
the `String` binding. Probed the surface exhaustively (`clone`, `to_string`,
`eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `cmp`, `hash`, `len`, `first`, `second`): `to_string` is the
whole of it, and it now types as `String`.

script matched on `B-2026-08-11-11`, which by then belonged to a DIFFERENT bug
filed minutes earlier by another session (the tuple-receiver row). The write
landed on that row, so this bug's title and fix ended up attached to the wrong
detail and this bug had no row of its own anywhere in the ledger. -11 has been
restored to the tuple row; this row carries the title and fix VERBATIM from the
original close, under the next free id.

WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED AND WHAT IS NOT. The `title` and `fix` fields are exactly
as the fixing session wrote them. Everything below is drawn only from that
session's own commit message (3c2e4dc) and is marked as such; the original
`detail`, `investigation`, `source` and `severity` fields were never written to

double-free` are inferred from the fix's own description of an ASAN pin proving

FROM THE ORIGINAL COMMIT MESSAGE, verbatim in substance:

  - THE BUG IS WIDER THAN IT WAS FILED. Not Map-specific:
    `Vec[String].get(i).unwrap_or(d)` fails identically, and a nested value
    shows four invalid accesses. The common factor is the ACCESSOR, not the
    container.

  - THE NEAR-MISS, recorded as the transferable part: reusing the match path's
    whole predicate compiled and did nothing. The receiver classified as a
    borrow call while the predicate still returned `None`, because it resolves
    the payload type through a SPAN-KEYED TABLE populated at match-scrutinee

    be reusable while its data lookup is not, and verifying that the reuse
    actually FIRED rather than merely compiled is what caught it.

PROCESS NOTE, because this will happen again: ledger ids are allocated by
reading the max id in the file, so two sessions that file within the same window
both compute the same next id, and a close script keyed on id then writes into
whichever row landed first. Filing and closing in the same push narrows but does
not close the window. A close script should verify the row it is about to
overwrite still matches the bug it thinks it is closing -- e.g. compare a
fingerprint of the title or source -- and refuse rather than clobber.

This row exists because that session's close was written onto another session's row through an id collision, leaving the bug unrecorded; title and fix are carried over verbatim and the remaining prose comes solely from commit 3c2e4dc.

fix:
FIXED by 7fe2b6dd — one condition in `classify_loop_body`
(src/concurrency.rs). The induction-step skip was tied to a SHAPE when it
needed to be tied to a NAME.

    // before
    if induction_step_via_assign(value, &name) {
        // i = i + const_lit -- loop-counter step; ignored.
    } else { ...reduction... }

    // after
    if induction_step_via_assign(value, &name) && induction_var == Some(name.as_str())
    { ... }

THE COMMENT ABOVE THAT LINE ALREADY STATED THE INTENT CORRECTLY -- "an explicit
`while`-loop counter would be tagged as the reduction accumulator" -- so the
defect was that the test never checked the write was against the loop's OWN
counter. `x = x + <literal>` is the counter's shape, but it is also any
literal-step accumulator's shape, so `a = a + 1` was swallowed by a branch
written for `i = i + 1`: neither classified as a reduction nor rejected, just
dropped on the floor. The fan-out lowering then rebinds only the accumulator and
the loop variable per worker and captures everything else, so `a`'s writes went
into per-worker copies and the parent kept its pre-loop value.

A new helper `loop_induction_var(expr)` names the counter -- the `for` pattern
binding, or the variable in a `while k < end` condition via
`par_cost::parse_lt_condition`, which is the SAME matcher the cost model and the
fan-out lowering use, so the analysis agrees with the shape codegen will
actually lower. The same one-name rule was applied to the `+=` arm, which had
its own copy of the skip.

WITH THE NAME CHECK, A NON-COUNTER LITERAL-STEP WRITE BECOMES A REDUCTION
CANDIDATE -- which is what it is, `+` with a constant delta -- and the existing
"two distinct accumulators decline the loop" rule three lines below then rejects
the mixed loop by itself. No new rejection logic was needed; the bug was that
these writes never reached that rule.

CORROBORATION THAT THIS WAS THE ODD ONE OUT, not a new restriction: the SAME
statement wrapped in a conditional (`if cond { a = a + 1; }`) was always
classified as a reduction by `conditional_acc_update_shape`, with no
induction-shape exclusion at all. The bare form was the only spelling that
vanished.

TWO BEHAVIOUR CHANGES, both measured, neither a correctness risk:
  - A loop whose ONLY accumulator is literal-step (`while i < n { a = a + 1;
    i = i + 1; }`) is now a recognized reduction where before it was invisible.
    That is a legitimate reduction (identity 0, associative, commutative) and
    the codegen cost gates still decide whether to lower it. Verified correct.
  - A `while` whose counter cannot be named -- e.g. `i <= n`, which
    `parse_lt_condition` does not match -- now treats its counter as a reduction
    candidate, so a loop with a real accumulator alongside it DECLINES instead
    of lowering. That is perf-only and fail-safe, and `while k < hi` is the
    shape the reduction lowering supports anyway. Verified the answer stays
    correct.

PINS. Three in tests/concurrency.rs (analysis level): the mixed loop must
decline, the `+=` spelling must decline, and the ordinary single-accumulator
loop must STILL be recognized -- that last one is the guard against fixing this
by breaking auto-par generally. One in tests/par_codegen.rs (value level):
asserts `4 6 3`, and pre-fix produces `1 0 3`.

THE VALUE PIN HAD TO MOVE, and the reason generalises. It was written first in
tests/codegen.rs, where it PASSED PRE-FIX and so asserted nothing: that
harness's `run_program` compiles without `concurrency_analyze`, so auto-par
never fires there and the sequential fallback happens to give the right answer.
tests/par_codegen.rs has its own `run_program` that threads the analysis into
codegen -- its doc comment says exactly this -- and there the pin fails pre-fix
with `left: Some("1 0 3\n")`. AN AUTO-PAR E2E ASSERTION PLACED IN
tests/codegen.rs IS VACUOUS; it must go in tests/par_codegen.rs. Checked by
stashing the fix and re-running, which is the only reason the vacuous placement
was caught.

VERIFICATION. The 12-line repro and every variant from the row's boundary map
now give the right answer, as does the original 648-case harness this was found
in (`combinations=648`, was 0). Full `cargo test --features llvm` green; ASAN
clean at the default level and on the `-O0` leg. Also re-ran the sort sweep the
harness was built for: 648 combinations, 0 failures.
title: Auto-par (ON BY DEFAULT) silently DROPS every LITERAL-step accumulator in a `while` loop that also contains a NON-literal-step one: `while i < n { b = b + f(x); a = a + 1; }` leaves `a` at its PRE-LOOP value, with no diagnostic and no crash -- just wrong arithmetic. MIXING IS THE TRIGGER: two literal-step accumulators are fine, two non-literal ones are fine, and a bare call that feeds no accumulator is fine. Interpreter is CORRECT; `karac build` and `karac run` (JIT) are wrong at BOTH -O0 and -O2, so it is karac's own transform and not an LLVM pass. `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` fixes it. `for` loops are unaffected.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while writing a correctness harness for B-2026-08-11-10
(docs/spikes/sortbench/). The harness counted its own test cases in a nested
loop and reported `combinations=0` after 648 cases demonstrably ran -- the
counter was the dropped accumulator. It cost a bisection to establish the sort
work was not at fault, which is the shape of the risk here: the wrong value
looks like a bug in whatever you were actually testing.

MINIMAL REPRO -- 12 lines, no Vec, no sort, no generics:

    fn one(x: i64) -> i64 { return 1; }
    fn three() -> i64 { return 3; }
    fn main() {
        let n = three();
        let mut a = 0;
        let mut b = 0;
        let mut i = 0;
        while i < n {
            b = b + one(1);   // non-literal addend -> SURVIVES
            a = a + 1;        // literal addend     -> DROPPED
            i = i + 1;
        }
        println(f"a={a} b={b}");
    }

    karac build   -> a=0 b=3      WRONG
    karac run     -> a=0 b=3      WRONG (JIT)
    --interp      -> a=3 b=3      correct
    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 build -> a=3 b=3   correct
    KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 build -> a=0 b=3  WRONG, so it is not an LLVM pass

`a` reads its PRE-LOOP value, not zero: initialise it to 1 and it reads 1 after
three iterations. Printing `a` INSIDE the loop shows 1, 2, 3 correctly -- the
value is right during the loop and reverts on exit. That is the signature of a
variable being privatised per chunk and then never merged back.

BOUNDARY, mapped over ~20 variants (each one line different from the repro):

    b = b + one(1);  a = a + 1;      a WRONG      mixed
    b = b + n;       a = a + 1;      a WRONG      mixed; NO CALL NEEDED, just a
                                                  non-literal addend
    b = b + one(1);  a = a + 2;      a WRONG      literal step need not be 1
    let mut a = 1 ... a = a + 1;     a WRONG      reads 1 (its pre-loop value)
    c=c+one(1); a=a+1; b=b+2;        a,b WRONG    every literal-step one drops
    a = a + one(1);  b = b + one(2); both OK      two NON-literal: fine
    a = a + 1;       b = b + 2;      both OK      two literal: fine
    let r = one(1);  a = a + 1;      OK           bare call, feeds no accumulator
    b = one(1);      a = a + 1;      OK           assignment, not accumulation
    i = i + one(1) + 1;  a = a + 1;  OK           call in the COUNTER update
    for x in xs { ... }              OK           `for` is unaffected
    while i < 3 { ... }              OK           CONSTANT bound; a runtime bound
                                                  is required
    let n = xs.len(); while i < n    WRONG        so it is the runtime bound, not
                                                  `.len()` in the condition

Order does not matter (literal-first and non-literal-first both fail), and the
Vec is irrelevant -- the repro above has none.

HYPOTHESIS, NOT ESTABLISHED, and it should be checked before it is believed: an
accumulator whose step is a LITERAL looks exactly like the loop's own induction
variable (`i = i + 1`), so the auto-par analysis may be classifying it as one --
privatising it per chunk and recomputing/discarding it at the join, the way it
legitimately does for `i` -- while an accumulator with a runtime addend is
classified as a true reduction and gets its merge. That would explain all four
of: literal steps drop, non-literal survive, all-literal is fine (no reduction
present, so presumably no parallel dispatch is emitted at all), and all
non-literal is fine (every one is a real reduction). A first cut was WRONG and
is recorded so it is not re-run: `src/codegen/accum_overflow.rs` recognises
exactly `acc = acc + <literal>` with `acc` initialised to literal 0 and elides
its overflow check, which made it the obvious suspect -- but variants that
analysis must REJECT (`let mut a = 1`, `a = a + 2`) still fail, so it is not the
cause. The emitted IR from `compile_to_ir` (which takes no concurrency analysis)
is CORRECT and stores to `%a` normally; the divergence only appears once the
auto-par path is in play, which is what localises this to auto-par rather than
to the assign lowering.

WHY HIGH. It is a silent wrong ANSWER, not a crash or a diagnostic, in a shape
that is completely ordinary -- count something while accumulating something else
over a runtime-bounded `while` loop. Auto-par is ON BY DEFAULT (`Codegen`'s gate
defaults to auto-par enabled; `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` is the only way to turn it off
in v1, and there is no `--sequential` flag yet), so a default `karac build`
produces the wrong number. It is also a run-vs-build divergence, so `--interp`
agrees with the programmer and the shipped binary does not -- the class this
ledger keeps closing (B-2026-08-11-2 / -4 / -9), but those were check-green /
run-red; this one is check-green, run-green, and quietly WRONG.

NOT MEASURED: whether the loop actually executes in parallel at n=3, or whether
the transform is emitted with a runtime trip-count guard that keeps it
sequential while still losing the merge. Either way the answer is wrong at n=3,
so the defect does not need real parallelism to fire.
investigation: 2026-08-11: bisected from a 648-case harness that reported 0 cases down to a 12-line repro, over ~20 single-line variants, establishing that the trigger is MIXING a literal-step and a non-literal-step accumulator in a runtime-bounded `while` loop -- not the call, not the Vec, not `.len()`, not the loop nesting. Confirmed interp-correct / build-wrong at both -O0 and -O2 and under the JIT, and confirmed `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` fixes it, which localises it to auto-par. Checked and REFUTED the obvious suspect (accum_overflow.rs's literal-step overflow elision): variants that analysis must reject still fail.

fix: c6c34c3 (two independent causes in one expression: the interpreter's `value_compare` float arm went from `partial_cmp(..).unwrap_or(Equal)` to `total_cmp`, which fixes the incoherence; and BOTH that arm and the runtime's `karac_float_cmp` now canonicalize NaN first, which fixes the provenance split `total_cmp` alone left behind.)
title: The INTERPRETER's `sort_by_key` with a float key returns a COMPLETELY UNSORTED sequence when a NaN is present, while both compiled backends sort correctly with NaN last. Measured on one program, `[3.5, NaN, 1.2, -2.0, 2.7].sort_by_key(|x| x)`: interp gives `3.5 NaN -2 1.2 2.7` (not sorted in any order -- 3.5 stays first), JIT and AOT both give `-2 1.2 2.7 3.5 NaN`. A silent wrong answer AND a run-vs-build divergence. The typechecker deliberately ALLOWS float keys here (stdlib_seq.rs documents the concession) on the grounds that the backends implement bit-level total-order semantics via `karac_float_cmp` -- that is true of codegen and NOT of the interpreter, which appears to use IEEE partial comparison, so NaN makes its sort incoherent. A shipped codegen test (test_e2e_vec_sort_by_key_float_nan_sorts_largest) pins the COMPILED behaviour on this exact input; the interpreter side was never asserted, which is why this survived.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while measuring B-2026-08-11-15's NaN behaviour, not while working on sort_by_key. -- Distinct root from B-2026-08-11-13: that one was the NaN SIGN BIT differing between backends and was fixed by canonicalizing at construction; this reproduces AFTER that fix (re-verified on 284d44a) and is about the interpreter using a different COMPARATOR, not a different NaN. -- The f64 path is the one still exposed: B-2026-08-11-7 gated `sort`/`sorted`/`binary_search` on `Vec[f64]` and B-2026-08-11-15 gated `max`/`min`, but `sort_by_key` with a float KEY is allowed by design, so this is now the remaining way to get an incoherent float ordering out of the interpreter without a diagnostic.
 -- FIXED 2026-08-11 in c6c34c3. TWO INDEPENDENT CAUSES, and the row only names the first; the second was invisible until the first was fixed, so anyone re-deriving this should expect the fix to look wrong halfway through. (1) INCOHERENCE. `value_compare`'s float arm was `partial_cmp(..).unwrap_or(Equal)`, so EVERY comparison involving a NaN answered "equal". That does not misplace the NaN by one slot -- it makes the order intransitive, so the sort is incoherent rather than merely wrong: on the row's input 3.5 never moves. `total_cmp` fixes it. (2) PROVENANCE. With `total_cmp` in place the interpreter sorted coherently but still disagreed with AOT, because `total_cmp` is SIGN-sensitive -- a negative NaN sorts before -Infinity, a positive one after +Infinity -- and nothing at the source level chooses which you get: an x86 runtime `z / z` yields a negative NaN, LLVM's constant folder a positive one. Measured mid-fix: NaN-first under interp and JIT, NaN-LAST under AOT, which inlines the producing call and folds the division. Fixed by canonicalizing NaN in BOTH `value_compare` and the runtime's `karac_float_cmp`. This is the same shape as B-2026-08-11-13 (which canonicalized the F64 WRAPPERS); this row is the plain-`f64` path that fix did not reach, so the two together mean no float ordering anywhere is sign-of-NaN dependent. -- WHY THE GLOBAL `value_compare` CHANGE IS SAFE, since it is a bigger blast radius than the row implies. `value_compare` is only ever asked for a TOTAL order: sort keys, binary_search, SortedSet/SortedMap ordering, is-sorted checks, and derived-`Ord` aggregate comparison. IEEE `==` / `<` on bare floats does NOT route through it -- eval_ops.rs compares `Value::Float` operands directly -- so `NaN != NaN` on `f64` is untouched, which design.md § Float semantics requires and the new tests assert. The only behavioural change on NaN-FREE data is that `-0.0` now sorts before `+0.0` instead of tying under a stable sort; that is what `total_cmp` and `karac_float_cmp` both already did, so it moves the interpreter toward the compiled backends. -- WHY IT SURVIVED, worth keeping: a shipped codegen test (test_e2e_vec_sort_by_key_float_nan_sorts_largest) pinned the COMPILED behaviour on this exact input and there was no interpreter twin. A one-sided test on a run-vs-build class asserts the half that works. The twin now exists and asserts the same order on the same input, and a second test on BOTH backends puts a runtime NaN and a folded NaN in one program -- the existing test used only a constant-folded NaN, which is precisely the provenance that did NOT expose cause (2). -- SCOPE NOTE: `sorted_by_key` (the non-mutating twin) is fixed in the interpreter by the same change but is NOT supported in codegen at all ("Vec/String method 'sorted_by_key' is not yet supported in codegen"), a pre-existing gap unrelated to this row.

fix:
FIXED by e23bf9e, in `src/codegen/expr_ops.rs`.

`type_name_of_expr`'s `MethodCall` arm gains the UNWRAPPING siblings, and a new
`unwrap_receiver_inst` resolves the receiver's wrapper instantiation with
generic args intact.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is a deliberate exclusion rather than an oversight.
B-2026-08-09-7 taught this same arm the wrapper-PRESERVING combinators
(`map`/`map_err`/`and_then`/`or_else`/`filter`), which return the receiver's own
type, and its comment explicitly lists the unwrapping siblings as NOT covered
because they return the PAYLOAD -- for which `recv_ty` ("Option") is the wrong
answer. That reasoning was right. What was missing is the payload's own name,
which needs the receiver's generic ARGS, and `fn_return_type_names` keeps only
the bare head segment. The full-TypeExpr table (`fn_return_type_exprs`) already
existed for exactly this reason -- `declare_function`'s comment names the
`Option[T]` / `Result[T, E]` generic arg it recovers -- it was simply never
consulted from this path.

Two parts:

1. `unwrap_payload_idx` -- which generic arg the method returns. Arg 0 for
   `unwrap` / `expect` / `unwrap_or` / `unwrap_or_else` (`T` in both
   `Option[T]` and `Result[T, E]`); arg 1 for `unwrap_err` (`E`, `Result`-only
   -- `Option` has no error arm). `map_or` / `map_or_else` are excluded because
   they return the CLOSURE's result, which the receiver's instantiation does
   not name at all. The lookup sits after the `fn_return_type_names` probe, so
   a user type named `Option` with its own `unwrap` still wins.

2. `unwrap_receiver_inst` -- the receiver's instantiation. A CALL receiver
   resolves through the callee's declared return TypeExpr, and that probe runs
   FIRST, before `enum_inst_type_of_expr`, whose last resort is a span lookup:
   the parser gives a `MethodCall` its RECEIVER's span, the collision
   B-2026-08-06-19, -12 and B-2026-08-05-28 all trace to, so consulting it
   first on a call receiver risks a neighbouring record instead of a clean
   miss. An IDENTIFIER receiver still goes through `enum_inst_var_types`.

THE ROW'S CHARACTERIZATION WAS TOO BROAD and the correction matters, because it
is what localizes the bug. The row said "the gap is specifically the un-bound
temporary receiver". Measured, it is not about temporaries at all:
`plain().x` (a struct-returning fn) and `P { x: 11 }.x` (a struct literal) are
both un-bound temporaries and both always compiled, and
`get().unwrap().double()` -- a METHOD call on the very same receiver -- also
always worked, because method dispatch resolves through a different path. Only
FIELD access on an unwrap-family result failed. All three are carried in the
test as live controls.

TWO THINGS THE ADVERSARIAL PASS CHANGED, both found by trying to break the fix
rather than by confirming it:

  * `unwrap_err` was excluded in the first version, on the reasoning that its
    payload sits at a different index. That was SAFE -- it failed loudly rather
    than resolving wrongly -- but it left the same gap one method over, so the
    index was made method-dependent instead. This is the case worth being
    careful about: answering arg 0 for `unwrap_err` would read `T`'s field
    layout out of an `E` value, a miscompile rather than a failed lookup.
    `Result[P, Q]` with `Err(Q { y: 99 })` reading 99 is the assertion that
    pins it.
  * The nested `Option[Option[P]]` chain failed, because the intermediate
    payload is itself a wrapper and the first gate admitted only structs.
    `unwrap_receiver_inst` now recurses through a chained unwrap, and the gate
    admits `enum_layouts` too. The recursion lives in the instantiation
    resolver rather than the name lookup on purpose: the next link needs the
    full `Option[P]`, and a head name would drop the `[P]`.

MEASURED on interpreter / JIT / AOT, all identical: single unwrap 6, `expect`
6, `unwrap_or` 6, `Result` Ok 10, `unwrap_err` 100, nested chain 43, identifier
receiver 4, plus the three controls. Before the fix the six chained forms
failed `karac build` while the interpreter ran every one of them.

Test: `e2e_chained_field_access_on_option_result_unwrap` (tests/codegen.rs),
on the default codegen leg because the divergence is run-vs-build. Full
`--features llvm` suite green (102 targets, 13431 passed); fmt and clippy
--all-targets clean.
title: Chained field access on an Option-unwrap TEMPORARY fails in codegen while working in the interpreter: `get().unwrap().x` where `get() -> Option[P]` errors with 'codegen: cannot resolve field 'x' on this receiver (its type was not recorded for codegen)'. Reproduces with a plain `struct P { x: i64 }` -- no iterator, no generics, no float wrapper. Binding the unwrap first (`let p: P = get().unwrap(); p.x`) compiles and runs correctly on all three backends, so the gap is specifically the un-bound temporary receiver. A loud failure rather than a silent one, but still a run-vs-build divergence: the interpreter prints 5 and codegen refuses to build.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: hit while writing B-2026-08-11-15's E2E test, where the natural spelling `w.iter().max().unwrap().value` failed. Confirmed pre-existing and unrelated by reproducing it with a plain struct and no iterator, so B-2026-08-11-15 landed with the `let`-bound spelling and this was split out rather than worked around silently. -- Practical impact is on copy-pasteable remedies: the wrapper advice that several float diagnostics print is most naturally written as a chain, and the chain is exactly the form that does not compile.

fix:
FIXED by cb3d9015 — the desugar gate was reading a side table through a key that CANNOT
distinguish the calls in a chain.

THE ROW'S PREMISE WAS WRONG, and the correction is the useful part. This is not
about string concatenation and not about "position". `let s =
xs.max().unwrap().to_string();` fails with no concat anywhere, while
`println(xs.max().unwrap() + 1)` — a binary operand, the shape the row blamed —
works fine. THE TRIGGER IS ONE EXTRA METHOD CALL CHAINED ONTO THE RESULT.
Measured across seven positions: bare statement, `let`-bound then concatenated,
arithmetic operand, f-string interpolation, struct-literal field and call
argument all work; every spelling that chains a further call onto the terminal
failed.

MECHANISM, PROVEN RATHER THAN INFERRED. Dumping `method_callee_types` for the
working and failing programs shows ONE entry, at the SAME key:

    println(xs.max().unwrap())               SpanKey(48, 2) -> Vec.max
    let s = xs.max().unwrap().to_string()    SpanKey(48, 2) -> i64.to_string

The parser sets a MethodCall's span equal to its RECEIVER's span, so every call
in a chain hashes to one key and the last write wins. `src/lowering.rs` gated
the `.iter()` insertion on that entry's head being "Vec"/"VecDeque"; with
`.to_string()` chained the entry read `i64.to_string`, the head test failed, no
`.iter()` was inserted, and the backends met a raw `Vec.max()` they do not
implement. Hence the misleading nouns this row was filed for: interp "method
'max' not found on type 'Vec'", codegen "Vec/String method 'max' is not yet
supported" — both blaming `max`, which was never the problem.

THE FIX IS TO STOP RE-DERIVING THE DECISION. `infer_method_call`'s Vec/VecDeque
narrowing arm is the one place that actually decides a call is a direct
iterable-collection terminal, so it now records the site itself, in a dedicated
`TypeCheckResult::direct_iter_terminals` set, and the lowering asks that instead
of reconstructing the answer from a receiver-type NAME. The two sides can no
longer disagree about what the narrowing means.

The new table is keyed by `SpanKey::for_method_call` — the CLOSING-PAREN span,
a leaf no outer expression aliases. Both halves of that were already in the
codebase and simply unused here: `SpanKey::for_method_call` is documented as the
key "that disambiguates chained calls", and `infer_method_call`'s own
`args_close_span` parameter carries a doc comment describing precisely this
aliasing ("`span` ... the parser sets equal to the receiver's span, so ... any
outer chained `MethodCall` clobbers `expr_types[span]`"). The infrastructure was
there; this side table just wasn't using it.

DELIBERATELY NOT RE-KEYED GLOBALLY. `method_callee_types` has 6 insert sites and
7 readers (monomorphization, codegen/method_call, codegen/lazyframe x2,
unsafe_lint, must_use_lint x2), any of which may depend on today's
last-write-wins behaviour. Re-keying it is a strictly larger change than this
row, and the collision remains latent for those consumers.

VERIFIED, both backends: all four terminals (`sum` / `product` / `max` / `min`)
on `Vec` and on `VecDeque`, chained; and the narrowing is intact —
`SortedSet.max()` / `.min()` keep their own surfaces and are NOT rewritten
(pinned separately, since moving the decision into the typechecker could have
widened it).

TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT FIX, both pre-existing and both confirmed independent
of the desugar:
  - `Vec[String]` iterator terminals are unsupported in codegen. The error now
    names `iter` rather than `max`, which still reads oddly for someone who
    wrote neither — but the USER-WRITTEN explicit `v.iter().max()` produces the
    identical error, which is what proves the desugar is not the cause.
  - Chaining onto a SCALAR's `.to_string()` breaks codegen in two ways, both
    interp-correct: `n.to_string().len()` is a clean error ("no handler for
    method 'to_string'") for i64 / f64 / bool, and `n.to_string().to_string()`
    PANICS the compiler at src/codegen/method_call.rs:2683 ("Found IntValue but
    expected the StructValue variant") — it loads the i64 and treats it as a
    String struct. Same chained-call span-aliasing family as this row, different
    table. Filed separately.
    (Measured twice: a first pass reported these as silent wrong ANSWERS —
    printing a constant 3, and once printing a string from an unrelated
    program. Both were artifacts of a probe script that fell through to a STALE
    binary when the build failed without the word "error" on stderr. Checking
    the exit code instead showed rc=101, a panic. Worth recording because the
    false reading was the more alarming one and would have gone into the ledger
    as a miscompile.)
title: The DIRECT-on-Vec iterator terminals (`v.max()` / `v.min()`, desugared to the `.iter()` chain) are POSITION-SENSITIVE: they compile in statement/argument position but FAIL when the call is nested inside a string-concat expression. Measured on `let fs: Vec[f64] = [1.5, 2.5, 0.5]`: `println(fs.max().unwrap())` answers 2.5 on interp / JIT / AOT, while `println("max=" + fs.max().unwrap().to_string())` fails on BOTH backends -- interp 'runtime error: method 'max' not found on type 'Vec' (no interpreter dispatch arm)', codegen 'Vec/String method 'max' is not yet supported in codegen'. Both backends agree, so this is a gap rather than a divergence, but the DIAGNOSTIC IS ACTIVELY MISLEADING: it blames `max` for not existing when `max` is fine and the problem is the surrounding expression shape.
detail: SOURCE NOTE: this diagnostic cost real investigation time on B-2026-08-11-15. The misleading message led to the conclusion that `Vec.max()` did not exist at all, which was written into that row as a correction before being caught and reversed -- a shipped ASAN fixture (asan_direct_vec_iterator_terminals_and_string_join_no_leak) had been compiling the direct form the whole time. Recorded with that history because the cost here is not the missing lowering, which has an easy workaround, but the wrong noun in the error: anyone who trusts it concludes the method is absent and stops looking. -- Same misleading shape presumably applies to the other direct-on-Vec terminals (`sum`/`product`); only max/min were measured.

fix:
FIXED by 1597660. `expr_is_unsigned_int` (`src/codegen/expr_ops.rs`) gains a
`to_bits` / `to_bits32` arm returning `true` unconditionally, alongside the
existing `abs_diff` one -- the two methods whose result signedness is fixed by
the METHOD rather than the receiver. Recursing on the receiver (what the
Self-returning methods below it do) is wrong here precisely because the
receiver is a float, so it answered `false` and codegen emitted `%lld`.

Pin: `e2e_to_bits_renders_unsigned` in `tests/codegen.rs` -- negative, negative
non-power-of-two, a positive control, `to_bits32`, and the bare `println` path
alongside the f-string one.
title: `f64.to_bits()` is declared `-> u64` by the typechecker but its value renders as a SIGNED i64 on all three backends: `(-1.0).to_bits()` prints -4616189618054758400 rather than 13830554455654793216 (0xBFF0000000000000). Consistent across interp / JIT / AOT, so not a divergence -- the declared type and the printed value simply disagree whenever the high bit is set, i.e. for every negative float.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while using `to_bits()` to identify which NaN each backend produces for B-2026-08-11-13/-15. It did not confound that measurement (the two NaN bit patterns differ regardless of how they are rendered) but it made the output harder to read, which is how it was noticed. -- Low severity because all three backends agree; the bug is the u64/i64 mismatch, not a split.

CORRECTED ON INVESTIGATION -- IT IS A BACKEND SPLIT, WHICH RAISES WHAT THE ROW
CONCLUDES FROM IT. The row records the signed rendering as "Consistent across
interp / JIT / AOT, so not a divergence", and closes with "Low severity because
all three backends agree". The interpreter never agreed. Measured on the row's
own program, pre-fix:

    interp   13830554455654793216      <- the declared unsigned value, correct
    JIT      -4616189618054758400
    AOT      -4616189618054758400

So it was an interp-vs-compiled divergence for every float with the sign bit
set -- exactly the class the 3-backend differential oracle exists to catch, and
the reason it was NOT caught is below.

THE EXISTING E2E WAS PINNING THE DIVERGENCE. `e2e_float_to_bits_codegen`
asserted `-9223372036854775808` for `(-0.0).to_bits()` while its own doc comment
claimed every value in it is "byte-identical to the interpreter oracle". The
interpreter prints `9223372036854775808` for that line and always did. `-0.0`
was the ONE value in that test with the high bit set -- every other line agrees
under either rendering -- so the test both encoded the bug as expected output
and asserted, in prose, the opposite of what it was doing. Expectation and
comment are now corrected.

WHAT THE FIX DOES NOT COVER, and it is bigger than this row. `to_bits` was one
instance of a general defect: codegen's `expr_is_unsigned_int` is a SYNTACTIC
classifier over expression shapes, and an identifier's answer comes from
`var_type_names`, which is not populated for an un-annotated `let`. So every
inferred binding of an unsigned value prints signed under both compiled
backends, `to_bits` or not. Measured post-fix:

    let a = 18446744073709551615u64;        interp OK    AOT -1
    let b = u64_fn();                       interp OK    AOT -1
    let c = 9223372036854775808u64 + 0u64;  interp OK    AOT -9223372036854775808
    let d = x.to_bits();                    interp OK    AOT -4616189618054758400
    let e = (…u64).reverse_bits();          interp OK    AOT -1

An explicit annotation fixes all of them (`let a: u64 = …` prints correctly via
the identifier arm), and so does interpolating the call DIRECTLY rather than
through a binding -- which is why this row's own repro, `(-1.0).to_bits()`
inline, is genuinely fixed while `let b = (-1.0).to_bits(); f"{b}"` is not.
That is a distinct defect at a distinct site (let-binding type registration,
not the classifier's method arm), it is higher severity than this row, and it
is filed as B-2026-08-11-21.

INTERPRETER SIBLING, also separate and also filed under -21's sweep: `u64`'s
`to_string()` renders SIGNED in the interpreter (`hi.to_string()` ->
-9223372036854775808, `mx.to_string()` -> -1) while `f"{hi}"` on the same value
is correct, and while codegen gets both right. So the two backends are wrong in
OPPOSITE directions on the same type, which is worth stating plainly: there is
no single "unsigned rendering is broken" story here, there are three separate
sites.

VERIFICATION. Full non-llvm suite green (100 binaries, 0 failures). Codegen E2E
(2893), asan (1032), par_codegen (580) and cli (255) green under
`--features llvm`. The row's own repro now prints 13830554455654793216 on all
three backends.

fix:
FIXED by cacd93e1, both legs, and they turned out to be the SAME defect seen from two sides:
a type recorded against a span that something else overwrites.

LEG 1 (codegen, the inferred `let`) — fixed UPSTREAM of the classifier, which is
what the row asked for. Codegen's un-annotated `let` path already ends in
`record_var_type_name` for whatever surface it finds in `pattern_binding_types`;
the gap was that the TYPECHECKER never wrote an entry there for a scalar. It
records Tuple, Map/Set, Option/Result and generic user structs, and primitives
fell straight through. One arm in `bind_pattern_types`
(`src/typechecker/patterns.rs`) recording `Type::Int(_) | Type::UInt(_)` via the
existing `method_callee_type_name` therefore fixes every consumer of
`var_type_names` at once, rather than patching the `%llu`/`%lld` classifier
alone -- so the narrow-int widening and coercion paths the row flagged are
covered by the same entry. Signed sizes are recorded alongside unsigned on
purpose: the classifier now answers "not unsigned" from a PRESENT entry instead
of from an absent one, so no future consumer can mistake "unrecorded" for
"signed".

LEG 2 (interpreter, `u64.to_string()`) — the interpreter ALREADY had an unsigned
arm; it was asking the wrong span. `span_type_is_unsigned64(&object.span)` reads
