`expr_types`, and the parser sets a MethodCall's span equal to its RECEIVER's,
so by the time the interpreter runs that entry holds the CALL's result. Measured
directly rather than inferred: for `hi.to_string()`,
`expr_types[SpanKey(66, 2)] = Str`. That is also exactly why `f"{hi}"` was
correct all along -- its interpolated expression is the bare identifier, whose
span nothing aliases -- which is the asymmetry the row found so surprising.

The typechecker now stashes an integer receiver's type at the CLOSING-PAREN span
for `to_string`, and the interpreter reads there first, falling back to the
receiver span for unaliased shapes. That hatch is not new: `args_close_span`
exists for precisely this, its doc comment on both `infer_method_call` and
`eval_method_call` describes this clobber, and `pow` plus the bit intrinsics
already read through it via `int_width_at`. `to_string` simply never opted in.

VERIFIED interp == JIT == AOT, character for character, on all five producing
shapes from the row (suffixed literal, fn return, binop, `to_bits`,
`reverse_bits`) plus `to_string` on both a bound and an annotated u64, `usize`,
and the two controls that were already correct and had to stay so: an annotated
binding, and interpolating the producing expression directly. A SIGNED binding
is the control in the other direction -- a fix that simply rendered every
`Value::Int` unsigned would turn -1 into 2^64-1, and both pins assert it stays
-1.

TWO CONSEQUENCES THE SUITE SURFACED, both worth recording.

  1. TWO EXISTING TESTS WERE PINNING THE BUG AS EXPECTED OUTPUT.
     `test_codegen_primitive_const_u64_max_bit_pattern_preserved` and
     `..._usize_max` asserted "-1" for `let x = u64.MAX; println(x)`, with a
     comment calling the signed rendering "a separate concern; the constant
     value is correctly emitted". It was not separate -- it was this bug, and
     `let x = u64.MAX` is exactly the un-annotated shape leg 1 is about. Both
     now assert 18446744073709551615. This is how the row's "invisible for over
     a month" happened: the wrong answer had a green test defending it. Both
     were also on the tolerant `if let Some(out)` form, which asserts NOTHING
     when the runtime archive is missing, so they were tightened to strict
     `assert_eq!` while being corrected.

  2. THE COROUTINE STATE-STRUCT LAYOUT WANTS THE ABSENCE, uniquely.
     `state_struct_layout_primitive_typed_bindings_have_none_type_name`
     documents a real contract -- codegen falls through to its primitive-sizing
     path on an ABSENT entry, so a present "i64" would send it down the
     named-type path instead. Recording scalar names broke that assertion, and
     the assertion was RIGHT: this was a genuine risk of miscompiled coroutine
     state, not a stale expectation. Every other consumer of the map wants the
     scalar name, so the narrowing was put at that one reader (a filter in
     `record_entry`, src/cli.rs) rather than at the recording site.

FOURTH INSTANCE OF ONE ROOT CAUSE, which is now the thing worth carrying
forward. B-2026-08-11-19 (the direct-Vec iterator desugar), B-2026-08-11-22
(both `to_string` routing gates), and now this row's leg 2 are all the same
mechanism: a side table keyed by `SpanKey::from_span` on a method call, whose
span the parser aliases to the receiver's, so a chain -- or merely a call
wrapping an identifier -- collapses to one key and the last write wins. Each has
been fixed by giving that ONE consumer a different signal: a dedicated
collision-free table (-19), the receiver's own static type (-22), the
closing-paren stash (here). None re-keyed `method_callee_types` or `expr_types`,
so the collision is still latent for every other consumer. The recurrence rate
suggests the next one is a matter of when.
title: EVERY un-annotated `let` holding an unsigned value prints SIGNED under both compiled backends while the interpreter prints it correctly -- `let a = 18446744073709551615u64; println(f"{a}")` is -1 under JIT/AOT and correct under `--interp`. An explicit `let a: u64` fixes it, so the value is right and only codegen's signedness classifier is wrong. Separately and in the OPPOSITE direction, the INTERPRETER's `u64.to_string()` renders signed while its f-string of the same value is correct
tracker: var_type_names population for un-annotated `let` (src/codegen/stmts.rs) against expr_is_unsigned_int (src/codegen/expr_ops.rs); interpreter to_string for unsigned ints
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found closing B-2026-08-11-20, which fixed the `to_bits` arm of
codegen's signedness classifier. `to_bits` turned out to be ONE INSTANCE of
this; the row below is the general case, and it is not float-specific.

LEG 1 -- CODEGEN, the inferred `let`. Codegen chooses `%llu` vs `%lld` from
`expr_is_unsigned_int`, a SYNTACTIC classifier over expression shapes. For an
identifier it consults `var_type_names`, which is not populated for a `let`
without a type annotation. So the binding is classified signed regardless of
what it holds. Measured, same program, `--interp` vs AOT:

    let a = 18446744073709551615u64;        interp OK    AOT -1
    let b = u64_fn();                       interp OK    AOT -1
    let c = 9223372036854775808u64 + 0u64;  interp OK    AOT -9223372036854775808
    let d = x.to_bits();                    interp OK    AOT -4616189618054758400
    let e = (…u64).reverse_bits();          interp OK    AOT -1

The first line is the one to look at: a plainly SUFFIXED u64 literal, bound and
printed, disagrees between backends. No floats, no method calls, no inference
subtlety -- `let a = 18446744073709551615u64` is about as explicit as Kāra gets
short of writing the type.

TWO THINGS NARROW IT, and both point at the same place:
  - an explicit annotation is correct (`let a: u64 = …` prints unsigned), because
    the annotation IS what populates `var_type_names`;
  - interpolating the producing expression DIRECTLY is correct
    (`f"{x.to_bits()}"`), because that reaches the classifier's own arms rather
    than the identifier arm.
So the runtime VALUE is always right; only the binding's recorded type is
missing, and only the print path consults it.

LEG 2 -- INTERPRETER, and it is wrong in the OPPOSITE DIRECTION on the same
type. `u64.to_string()` renders signed where the f-string does not:

    let hi: u64 = 9223372036854775808u64;
    f"{hi}"            -> 9223372036854775808   (correct)
    hi.to_string()     -> -9223372036854775808  (wrong)
    (18446744073709551615u64).to_string() -> -1 (wrong)

Codegen gets BOTH of these right. So this is not one "unsigned rendering is
broken" story: there are three distinct sites (codegen's classifier arms, fixed
for `to_bits` in B-2026-08-11-20; codegen's `var_type_names` population, Leg 1;
the interpreter's integer `to_string`, Leg 2), and the two backends fail on
opposite halves of the surface.

WHY HIGH. Silent wrong output with no diagnostic on the most ordinary spelling
there is (`let x = <unsigned>` then print it), and the two backends disagree, so
a program validated under `karac run --interp` prints different numbers once
built. It is only invisible because a u64 whose high bit is set is uncommon in
test programs -- every value below 2^63 renders identically either way, which is
also why B-2026-08-11-20's E2E managed to pin the divergence as expected output
for over a month without anyone noticing.

FIX SHAPE (leg 1): populate `var_type_names` for an un-annotated `let` from the
typechecker's inferred binding type, the same way the annotated path does --
`record_var_type_name` already normalizes aliases and is the single write point.
Failing that, have the identifier arm of `expr_is_unsigned_int` fall back to the
typechecker's recorded expression type for the binding. The first is better: the
classifier's other consumers (narrow-int widening on the print and coercion
paths) have the identical gap and would be fixed with it.

FIX SHAPE (leg 2): route the interpreter's integer `to_string` through the same
signed/unsigned decision its f-string interpolation already makes correctly.
investigation: 2026-08-11: found closing B-2026-08-11-20. Probed five un-annotated `let` shapes (suffixed literal, fn return, binop, to_bits, reverse_bits) plus annotated and direct-interpolation controls across `--interp` and AOT; all five diverge and both controls are clean, isolating var_type_names population as the site. The interpreter's `to_string` leg was found in the same sweep and points the other way.

fix:
FIXED by 13b4814d — and the row's HYPOTHESIS WAS RIGHT: it is the same span-aliasing
mechanism as B-2026-08-11-19, in the two gates that route a `to_string` call.

CONFIRMED BY INSTRUMENTATION, not by reading. Printing the gate's inputs for
`n.to_string().to_string()`:

    outer link  obj=MethodCall  dispatch_key=Some("String.to_string")  string_like=true
    inner link  obj=Identifier  dispatch_key=Some("String.to_string")  string_like=false

The inner link is reading the OUTER's key. The parser sets a MethodCall's span
equal to its receiver's, so both links share one `method_callee_types` entry and
the last write wins. There IS already a chained-call collision guard where
`dispatch_key` is computed -- it separates links by requiring the key's method
segment to match this call's method -- but it cannot help here, because BOTH
links are named `to_string`. That is the specific reason this shape slipped
through a guard written for exactly this class.

TWO GATES WERE READING THAT KEY, which is why the row had two arms:

  1. The String-copy path (`method_call.rs`) tested the key's type segment for
     "String"/"StringSlice". The inner link passed it with an `i64` receiver,
     compiled `n` to an IntValue, and unwrapped it as a struct: the compiler
     panic.
  2. `recv_is_scalar_primitive` tested the same key for a scalar type name. With
     the key shadowed to "String.to_string" it declined too, so once the panic
     was vetoed the call fell through to the catch-all as "no handler for method
     'to_string'". Fixing only the first arm converts a panic into a wrong
     error, which is why both had to move.

BOTH NOW CONSULT `type_name_of_expr(object)`, which is keyed by the receiver
EXPRESSION and so cannot be shadowed. It separates the two links exactly -- the
inner reports Some("i64"), the outer None -- so nothing that previously worked
changes. It is also a static lookup, which preserves the property the scalar
gate was written for: the receiver is NOT pre-compiled, so a side-effecting
receiver is still evaluated once. The veto is applied ONLY to the span-keyed
half of the String test; `expr_is_string_like` reads the receiver expression, so
it is left alone.

SECOND LEG, found while building the ASAN fixture and fixed here because leaving
it would have made the surface MORE irregular, not less: `x.clone()` as a
receiver in a chain had no resolvable type, so the same shadowed key broke
`s.clone().to_string().len()` (String receiver) and `n.clone().to_string()
.len()` (scalar). `clone` preserves its receiver's type, so `type_name_of_expr`
now resolves it by recursion, and `expr_is_string_like` does the same. Recursion
rather than adding `clone` to the neighbouring string-like NAME list, because
that list deliberately excludes `sorted`/`replace`/`repeat` for naming Vec
methods too -- a blanket `clone` entry would misroute `v.clone().to_string()` on
a Vec into the String-copy path. `v.clone().len()` is pinned as that control.

VERIFIED build == interp on i64 / f64 / bool / char, for `.to_string()
.to_string()` and `.to_string().len()`, and for identifier, struct-field and
call-result receivers. Controls that must keep their existing routing all hold:
String and literal receivers, `trim()` / `to_uppercase()` / `clone()` chains,
and `Vec.clone()`.

ASAN, which the value pins cannot cover: the String-copy path both mallocs a
fresh buffer and frees the intermediate receiver when it is a fresh owned
String, and this fix changes WHICH calls reach it -- so a routing fix with the
ownership wrong is a per-iteration leak or a double free. The new fixture loops
both sides of the veto (a scalar receiver that must now allocate its own String,
and a String receiver chained through a builtin that must still free the
intermediate) and is clean at the default level and on the -O0 leg.

STILL LATENT, and worth stating plainly since this is now the third row in this
family: `method_callee_types` is still keyed by `SpanKey::from_span`, so a chain
still collapses to one entry for its 6 writers and 7 readers. B-2026-08-11-19
fixed one consumer by giving it a collision-free side table; this row fixed two
more by having them consult the receiver's own type instead. Neither re-keyed
the map. A consumer that needs the key and cannot use either workaround will hit
this again.
title: CHAINING ONTO A SCALAR'S `.to_string()` BREAKS CODEGEN TWO WAYS, both check-green and both interpreter-correct: `n.to_string().to_string()` PANICS the compiler at src/codegen/method_call.rs:2683 ("Found IntValue ... but expected the StructValue variant" -- it loads the i64 and treats it as a String struct), and `n.to_string().len()` is a clean but wrong error ("codegen: no handler for method 'to_string'"). Measured on i64, f64 and bool. Breaking the chain with a `let` fixes both, and a String-typed receiver (`s.to_string().to_string()`) is fine -- it is specifically a further call chained onto a SCALAR's to_string. Same chained-call span-aliasing family as B-2026-08-11-19, different table.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while fixing B-2026-08-11-19, whose repro used
`xs.max().unwrap().to_string()`. Probing whether `.to_string()` chaining was
itself sound turned this up; it is independent of that row's desugar (it needs
no Vec and no iterator terminal).

MEASURED, `karac build` vs `--interp`:

    let n: i64 = 12345;
    println(n.to_string().to_string());     build: PANIC rc=101   interp: 12345
    println(n.to_string().len());           build: error rc=1     interp: 5
    println(n.to_string());                 build: 12345          interp: 12345
    let a = n.to_string(); println(a.to_string());
                                            build: 12345          interp: 12345
    let s: String = "hello".to_string();
    println(s.to_string().to_string());     build: hello          interp: hello

So: the receiver must be a SCALAR (i64 / f64 / bool all reproduce), the chain
must be at least two calls deep, and binding the intermediate to a `let` is the
workaround. A String-typed receiver is unaffected. Curiously
`n.to_string().to_string().to_string()` (three deep) also panics -- the arity is
not the discriminator, the scalar receiver is.

THE PANIC, which localises it:

    thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/codegen/method_call.rs:2683:48:
    Found IntValue(IntValue { ... llvm_value: "  %n1 = load i64, ptr %n" ...
    llvm_type: "i64" }) but expected the StructValue variant

Codegen has decided the receiver of the OUTER `to_string` is a String (correct
-- it is), then emitted a load of the INNER receiver `n`, an i64, and unwrapped
it as a String struct. That is the signature of a receiver-type side table
answering for the wrong call in the chain, which is exactly the mechanism proven
in B-2026-08-11-19: the parser sets a MethodCall's span equal to its RECEIVER's
span, so every call in a chain hashes to one `SpanKey::from_span` key and the
last write wins. HYPOTHESIS, NOT VERIFIED HERE -- the fix for -19 was scoped to
the one table it needed and deliberately did NOT re-key `method_callee_types`
globally (6 writers, 7 readers), so if this is the same key collision it is one
of the latent cases that row predicted. Whoever takes this should check the
side table read at method_call.rs:2683 before assuming it.

WHY MEDIUM AND NOT HIGH: no wrong answers -- one arm is a compiler panic and the
other an honest-if-misdirected error, so nothing silently computes the wrong
number. But `n.to_string()` chained is an ordinary thing to write, `karac check`
passes both spellings, and a compiler PANIC (with a Rust backtrace) is a bad
failure mode for a user who has written valid code -- the interpreter runs it
correctly.

METHOD NOTE, recorded because the first measurement was WRONG and the wrong
answer was the more alarming one. A probe script reported these as silent
miscompiles -- `n.to_string().to_string()` "printing a constant 3 for every
input", and one case "printing a string from an unrelated program". Both were
artifacts: the script decided a build had failed by grepping stderr for
"error", and a PANIC does not print that word, so it fell through and ran a
STALE binary left by the previous case. Checking the exit code instead (rc=101)
showed the truth. A probe that infers failure from message text rather than exit
status will manufacture miscompiles out of stale artifacts.
investigation: 2026-08-11: found while fixing B-2026-08-11-19. Measured across i64/f64/bool receivers, chain depths 1-3, and the let-bound workaround; captured the panic site (method_call.rs:2683). Re-measured after an initial probe misreported it as a silent wrong answer -- that reading came from a script that detected build failure by grepping for 'error' and so ran a stale binary on a panic.

fix: a243f2a (folded into the existing `sorted_by` arm in src/codegen/vec_method.rs rather than copied — the two are one desugar with a different inner method)
tracker: the Vec/String method dispatch in codegen — the arm that serves `sorted_by` has no `sorted_by_key` twin; interpreter side is method_call_seq.rs "sorted_by_key"
title: `Vec[T].sorted_by_key(f)` PASSES `karac check` and then fails at build: "Vec/String method 'sorted_by_key' is not yet supported in codegen". It is the ONLY hole in the six-method sort family -- measured on one `Vec[i64]` program, `sort` / `sort_by` / `sort_by_key` / `sorted` / `sorted_by` all check AND compile, and `sorted_by_key` alone checks-but-does-not-compile. The interpreter implements it correctly (it shares the precompute-keys path with `sort_by_key`, and got the B-2026-08-11-17 float-ordering fix for free), so the program runs under `karac run --interp` and fails under both `karac run` and `karac build`. Fails LOUDLY with an actionable message naming `--interp`, so this is a missing feature rather than a miscompile -- hence low severity despite being a check-vs-build divergence.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: noticed while verifying B-2026-08-11-17 (fixed in c6c34c3) -- the interpreter fix covered `sorted_by_key` automatically, and probing whether the backends agreed showed codegen does not implement it at all. Not part of that row's bug and not fixed with it. -- EVIDENCE, one program per method, `let mut v: Vec[i64] = [3,1,2]`: `v.sort()` check=OK codegen=OK; `v.sort_by(|a,b| a.cmp(b))` OK/OK; `v.sort_by_key(|x| x)` OK/OK; `v.sorted()` OK/OK; `v.sorted_by(|a,b| a.cmp(b))` OK/OK; `v.sorted_by_key(|x| x)` OK/GAP. -- WHY IT IS PROBABLY SMALL: the immutable twins are the same shape as the in-place ones (build the keyed pairs, sort, return a NEW Vec instead of writing back), and BOTH of its neighbours already exist in codegen -- `sorted_by` was implemented by B-2026-07-20-8 and `sort_by_key` carries the float-key `karac_float_cmp` dispatch. The likely fix is routing `sorted_by_key` through the existing `sort_by_key` lowering with the `sorted_*` copy-then-mutate wrapper that `sorted_by` already uses, not new sort code. -- WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING METHOD USUALLY WOULD: `karac check` is the primary tool in the Mend loop, so a construct that CHECKS CLEAN and then fails at build wastes an entire repair cycle -- the model has no diagnostic to act on until it tries to build. Either implement it or reject it at typecheck; passing check is the one thing it should not do. -- WORKAROUND: `let mut c = v.clone(); c.sort_by_key(f);` compiles and is equivalent.
 -- FIXED 2026-08-11 in a243f2a. The row's guess was right: no new sort code was needed. `sorted_by` already desugars to `{ let mut tmp: Vec[E] = <recv>.clone(); tmp.sort_by(<f>); tmp }`, and the immutable key-sort is that same desugar with `sort_by_key` as the inner method, so the two now SHARE one match arm parameterized on the method name. Everything the in-place `sort_by_key` lowering supports therefore carries over through the clone for free -- including the float-key `karac_float_cmp` dispatch and its own loud errors for shapes it cannot handle -- and the arm cannot drift, because there is only one of it. -- WHAT THE TESTS COVER AND WHY EACH ONE, since the obvious test (sort some ints) proves the least. (a) The IMMUTABLE contract: the receiver must be observably unsorted afterwards, which is the only thing distinguishing this from `sort_by_key`. (b) A key that is NOT the element (`|p| p.age`) -- the entire point of `by_key`, and the one thing a `sorted`/`sorted_by` test structurally cannot exercise. (c) A FLOAT key, which routes through `karac_float_cmp`: NaN must still sort last, proving B-2026-08-11-17's fix survives the clone desugar. (d) A String key on a heap-bearing element, under ASAN (asan_vec_sorted_by_key_heap_elements): the clone makes a SECOND owner of every String and then returns it while the receiver stays live, which is precisely the shape that leaks or double-frees when a clone's element ownership is wrong -- and it was covered by neither the in-place `sort_by_key` tests (no clone) nor `sorted_by` (never reads a field for a key). Clean under Linux LSan. -- SCOPE NOTE: `String.sorted_by_key` is NOT implemented and needs no codegen guard, because the typechecker rejects it outright ("no method 'sorted_by_key' on type 'String'"); its `sorted_by` sibling does carry such a guard only because `String.sorted_by` typechecks. -- VERIFIED on all three backends (interp / LLJIT / AOT) agreeing byte-for-byte on every case above.

fix: 7239101 (one arm in src/codegen/exprs.rs: extend the surface-`Binary` fresh-owned-operand free from `Add` to `Eq`/`NotEq`, gated on the OPERANDS being String-shaped since a comparison yields i1)
title: A String EQUALITY comparison between an unbound TEMPORARY and a `ref String` PARAMETER leaks the temporary, every evaluation. `hay.substring(0, 4) == needle` inside `fn f(hay: ref String, needle: ref String)` leaks; the same comparison against a LOCAL, or with the temp `let`-bound first, or with an OWNED `String` param, is clean. The leak is unbounded in input size -- the ordinary `substring(i, i+n) == needle` scan loop leaks one allocation per iteration.
tracker: the String `==`/`!=` lowering in codegen (the operand-cleanup decision). NOT the RC-elision hint and NOT optimization-dependent -- both ruled out by measurement, see detail.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO -- two lines, 4 bytes leaked in 1 allocation under LSan:

    fn f(hay: ref String, needle: ref String) -> bool { hay.substring(0, 4) == needle }
    fn main() { let h = "abcdefgh"; let n = "abcd"; println(f"{f(h, n)}"); }

THE RULE -- three conditions, all necessary (each row is a separate one-shape fixture measured under the Linux LSan harness):

    shape                                                          verdict
    temp == ref-param            (inside a fn)                     LEAK 4 B / 1 alloc
    ref-param == temp            (operands swapped)                LEAK 4 B / 1 alloc
    temp != ref-param            (`!=` as well as `==`)            LEAK 4 B / 1 alloc
    mk(hay) == ref-param         (temp from a USER fn, not substring)  LEAK 4 B / 1 alloc
    temp == LOCAL                (`let n = "abcd"` in the fn)      clean
    temp == local, in `main`     (no params at all)                clean
    let s = temp; s == ref-param (temp `let`-BOUND first)          clean
    temp == OWNED `String` param (mode is owned, not `ref`)        clean
    let s = temp; s.len() + needle.len()  (no comparison at all)   clean

So it needs, simultaneously: (1) one operand is an UNBOUND temporary String -- a call result, not a binding; (2) the other operand is a `ref String` PARAMETER -- a local or an owned-mode param is fine; (3) the operation is a String equality comparison. Side does not matter, `!=` behaves like `==`, and the temp's producer does not matter (builtin `substring` or a user fn returning `String` both leak). Reading the same two values without comparing them is clean, so it is the comparison's operand cleanup that is wrong, not the temp's construction.

LIKELY SHAPE OF THE DEFECT: the equality lowering appears to suppress the temp-operand drop whenever an operand is borrowed, rather than suppressing it only for the borrowed operand. A `ref` param is correctly not-dropped (the caller owns it); the fresh temp on the other side is then also not-dropped, and nothing else ever frees it. That predicts every measured row above, including why an owned-mode param is clean (no borrowed operand, so no suppression) and why `let`-binding the temp is clean (a binding gets ordinary scope cleanup instead of the comparison's temp path).

TWO PLAUSIBLE CULPRITS RULED OUT BY MEASUREMENT, so the fixer need not chase them:
  - NOT the RC-elision hint. `KARAC_RC_ELIDE_REF_PARAMS=0` (B-2026-07-15-21's opt-out) still leaks 4 B / 1 alloc. The name is a near-miss -- that hint is about skipping balanced retain/release on read-only `ref` `shared`/`Option[shared]` params -- but it is not this.
  - NOT optimization-dependent. `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0` leaks identically (4 B / 1 alloc), so this is not a case of a drop being optimized away.

MAGNITUDE -- this is not a 4-byte curiosity. The leak is per-evaluation and the triggering shape is the standard substring-scan inner loop:

    fn find_from(hay: ref String, needle: ref String, start: i64) -> i64 {
        ...
        while i + n <= h {
            if hay.substring(i, i + n) == needle { return i; }   // <- leaks EVERY iteration
            i = i + 1;
        }
        -1
    }

Measured in the dogfood program this came from -- a `{{key}}` template renderer over a single ~120-character template -- LSan reported 290 bytes leaked in 145 allocations, i.e. one allocation per scan step. A real template engine or tokenizer running over a document leaks proportionally to input size, with no bound. Note the early `return` is NOT required and is not the mechanism: a `hits = hits + 1` accumulator variant leaks exactly once per iteration too (28 B / 14 allocs over 14 iterations).

INVISIBLE TO EVERY NON-LSAN CHECK. The renderer's output is byte-identical and correct on interp, JIT and AOT (verified against a hand-checked oracle covering adjacent placeholders, a missing key, an empty key, an unterminated placeholder and bare single braces), and `karac check` is clean. Only the Linux LSan leg sees it. Per CLAUDE.md this class also needs an arm64 cross-check before any fix is trusted, since B-2026-07-12-29 established that leaks are not always architecture-independent.

FIXTURE SUGGESTION: the nine-row table above is exactly the permanent test matrix this wants -- four leaking shapes as regression pins and five clean shapes as over-fire controls, since a fix that simply always drops the temp would break the borrowed-operand cases the current code is trying to protect.

SCOPE CONFIRMED NARROW (measured after filing). The same 'unbound temp vs `ref` param' pairing does NOT leak for any other operation tried, so this is local to the String equality lowering and not a general borrowed-operand cleanup bug:

    shape                                                            verdict
    `hay.substring(0,4) + suffix`   (CONCAT, `suffix: ref String`)   clean
    `other.contains(mk(hay))`       (temp as a method ARGUMENT)      clean
    `mk() == other`  where the type is a `#[derive(Eq)]` STRUCT      clean
                     with a String field and `other: ref P`

Those three double as over-fire controls: a fix must leave them clean. (`Vec[i64]` equality could not be tested -- `Vec` does not implement `Eq`, and the diagnostic for it suggests `add #[derive(Eq)]`, which is not something a user can do to a builtin. Minor, noted here rather than filed separately.)
 -- FIXED 2026-08-11 in 7239101. THE ROW'S HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG IN A USEFUL WAY, worth recording because the real cause is simpler and already had a precedent. The row predicted that the equality lowering SUPPRESSES the temp's drop when an operand is borrowed. Nothing is suppressed: String `==` normally desugars to a `String.eq` assoc call whose route DOES free fresh-owned operands, but `rewrite_binary` SKIPS that desugar when an operand is ref-typed, so the comparison stays a surface `Binary`, lands in exprs.rs, and meets a free that was gated to `BinOp::Add` only. The free was never written for this operator. B-2026-07-21-12 closed precisely this hole for CONCAT ("a string concat that STAYED a surface Binary ... never went through the assoc-call route's operand frees") and left `Eq`/`NotEq` open; this is its equality sibling. -- The two predictions are observationally identical on the nine-row table, which is why the row could not distinguish them: both explain why a `ref`-mode param is required (with a local or an owned param the desugar fires and the assoc route frees), why side does not matter, and why `let`-binding the temp is clean. They differ only in where you go to fix it. -- GATE DETAIL: on the OPERANDS being String-shaped, not the result -- the `Add` arm above can test its result because concat yields a String, whereas a comparison yields i1. `free_fresh_owned_str_arg` self-gates to fresh-owned Call/MethodCall shapes with a `cap > 0` runtime backstop, so the borrowed operand and any identifier / place / rodata literal is left alone; that is what makes the swapped-operand and owned-param rows safe rather than double-frees. -- THE ROW'S "SCOPE CONFIRMED NARROW" IS CORRECTED, by measurement. Its derived-struct control was read as clean, but that fixture built the struct's String field from a LITERAL, which allocates nothing and therefore cannot leak -- the operand pairing was right and the payload was not. Rebuilt with `P { name: s.substring(0, 4) }` it leaks 4 B / 1 alloc every time. Split to B-2026-08-11-33 rather than fixed here: it is a different lowering (`compile_struct_eq`), and its fix is to materialize the fresh temp into a slot and register a STRUCT DROP (the `track_freshtemp_field_access_object` pattern from B-2026-07-22-2), not to free a buffer -- different machinery, different double-free risk, own matrix. Pinned as an `#[ignore]`d ASAN fixture that still reproduces under `--ignored`. -- The row's suggested nine-row matrix is now a permanent fixture, plus the scan loop (the unbounded case) and the literal-field struct control that documents why the original scope call read clean. Its concat and method-argument controls are kept as over-fire guards: a fix that simply always freed the temp would break them. -- ARM64 NOTE: per CLAUDE.md this leak class is not guaranteed architecture-independent (B-2026-07-12-29 was arm64-only), so the arm64 CI leg should be checked before treating this as fully cleared; the fix is a straight missing-free with no RC or index-assign involvement, which is the class least likely to be arch-specific.
investigation: 2026-08-11 (hunt, domain 7 -- string/text processing dogfood). Found by putting a template renderer (placeholder substitution, word wrap, padded table) under the ASAN/LSan harness after it had already passed the 3-backend differential oracle: 290 bytes / 145 allocations. Bisected in nine fixtures -- `split_ws` alone clean, `pad_right` alone clean, the substring-scan comparison in `main` clean, the same comparison inside `find_from` leaking -- down to the two-line repro, then pinned the three necessary conditions with the one-shape-per-fixture matrix above rather than a bit-coded single program (a first attempt that encoded shapes by allocation SIZE mis-decoded, because allocation size does not track substring length reliably at small sizes; the separate-fixture rerun is the trustworthy measurement). Filed, not fixed, per the hunting-only remit.

fix:
FIXED by 970dadfd — the Assign arm never called the field-move-out suppressors the Let arm
has called since B-2026-08-03-8 / B-2026-08-01-31. Three lines of dispatch, not
new machinery.

WHAT THE DIAGNOSIS TURNED ON: the row's own control table already said the
`let` form of the identical read is clean, INCLUDING through a Vec index. So
`suppress_place_field_struct_move_source` — the deeper-place suppressor that
resolves the owner through `field_chain_place_ptr` / `place_chain_type_name` —
already handled `stats[0].region` exactly. It had simply never been reachable
from an assignment: grepping its call sites (plus
`suppress_struct_field_move_into_literal` and `disarm_struct_field_move_bodies`)
finds the Let arm and struct-literal field init, and nothing else. The
ASSIGNMENT path compiled the RHS and stored it while leaving the field live in
its owner, so the owner's drop freed the buffer the target now owned.

That is why the row's three necessary conditions are what they are, and each is
now explained rather than just observed: the read must be an ASSIGNMENT (the
`let` arm calls the suppressors), the struct must be reached through a Vec INDEX
(a plain binding or `self` takes the SHALLOW suppressor, which the Let arm also
calls but which a deeper place never reaches), and the field must be heap-owning
(there is nothing to double-free otherwise).

The fix mirrors the Let arm's block verbatim — same three calls, same gates
(`owned_struct_params` sources are deep-copied instead, shallow forms take the
dedicated suppressor, deeper places take the place-chain sibling) — so the two
arms cannot drift apart again. Gated on the assignment TARGET being a
heap-shaped local, which is the Let arm's `vec_elem_types` gate.

ORDERING IS LOAD-BEARING and is commented at the site: the calls go AFTER
`compile_expr(value)`, because they cap-zero the SOURCE in place. Emitting them
first hands the target a cap of 0 and converts the double free into a leak —
the same bug wearing different clothes, and one the value pins cannot see.

VERIFIED on the row's full eight-row table: the four aborting shapes (String
field, `Vec[i64]` field, an unrelated earlier read of the same field, a source
built by `+` instead of `push_str`) and the four over-fire controls that were
already clean and that a broad fix would regress (the `let` form, a plain struct
binding, a tuple element, a `Vec[String]` with no struct). All eight now agree
with the interpreter. The row's real-world shape — a max-by-revenue scan
assigning `best_region = stats[j].region` in a loop — runs correctly too.

ASAN IS THE GATE THAT DISTINGUISHES A FIX FROM A RELABELLING, since the repair
is precisely "stop the owner freeing". The new fixture loops 40 iterations so a
per-iteration leak accumulates, and covers String fields, a `Vec[i64]` field and
a `+`-built source. Clean at the default level and on the `-O0` leg; pre-fix it
reports `AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free`. The value pin pre-fix
returns `Some("")` — the abort beats the stdout flush, which is exactly the
"appears to produce NO output" failure mode the row warns sends debugging in the
wrong direction.

FIXTURE HAZARD, carried forward from the row because it is easy to re-introduce:
every payload in both pins is built at RUN TIME (`String.new()` + `push_str`, or
`a + b`). A `String` LITERAL field is static, so the second free lands on a
non-heap pointer and the fixture passes while the bug is present.
title: DOUBLE FREE on both compiled backends: a heap field of a struct held as a Vec ELEMENT, read back by ASSIGNMENT to an existing binding (`out = stats[0].region`), aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. The `let` form of the same read is clean (that leg was fixed), a plain struct BINDING is clean, and a tuple element is clean -- it is specifically the Vec-element + assignment pair. `karac check` passes and the interpreter is correct.
tracker: the field-move-out cap-zeroing path for an ASSIGNMENT whose source is `<vec>[i].<heapfield>`. Family: B-2026-08-03-8 / B-2026-08-01-31 fixed the `let x = h.f` form; B-2026-08-04-19 is the precedent for an assignment twin of a fixed `let` bug.
investigation: 2026-08-11 (hunt, domain 8 -- iterator/closure pipelines over heap-bearing structs). Found by a sales-report dogfood: fold/filter/map pipelines, a group-by into a Map, a Vec of summary structs, then a max-by-revenue scan. Interpreter printed the full correct report; AOT aborted with a double free and the JIT exited 1 with no output. Bisected by building cumulative PREFIXES of `main` -- every prefix passed, so the trigger needed the final scan plus something earlier -- then by deleting one optional section at a time, which never helped, isolating the mandatory core. From there ~15 variants took it to the 10-line repro and pinned the three necessary conditions, including the literal-payload false-clean noted above. Filed, not fixed, per the hunting-only remit.

fix:
FIXED by 883fcbe1 — `jit_dispatch` now takes the `OwnershipCheckResult` the harness ALREADY computes a few lines above the dispatch, and forwards it to `compile_to_ir_with_options`, so the JIT leg's codegen arguments match its AOT twin's `compile_to_object_with_options(..., Some(&ownership), None, ...)` argument for argument.

`concurrency` stays `None` on BOTH legs, deliberately, and that is parity rather than a second half-fix: `tests/codegen.rs` is the SEQUENTIAL lane by design and `tests/par_codegen.rs` is the auto-par one (its own comments name the split — "`tests/codegen.rs`'s harness compiles without `concurrency_analyze`"). The bar for this lane is its AOT twin, not cli.rs.

VERIFIED both legs, full suite, on the same tree:
    KARAC_TEST_JIT=1 cargo test --features llvm --test codegen  →  2902 passed, 0 failed
                     cargo test --features llvm --test codegen  →  2902 passed, 0 failed
Before the fix the JIT leg was 2900 passed / 2 failed with the AOT leg at 2902 / 0 — and the 2900 that passed anyway are why this sat undetected: only a test whose outcome DEPENDS on an ownership hint can see the starvation, and until B-2026-08-10-21 landed its two pins, the suite had none.
tracker: `tests/codegen.rs` `jit_dispatch` (was `compile_to_ir_with_options(program, None, None, filename, None)`); its AOT twin in `run_program_capturing_inner`, which passes `Some(&ownership)`; `src/cli.rs:5462` for what the PRODUCTION JIT does (`pipeline.ownership.as_ref()`, with the comment "run them now so the emitted IR matches `karac build`'s")
title: the codegen suite's JIT lane — the ONE lane whose stated job is run==build parity — fed codegen `ownership: None` while its AOT twin fed `Some(&ownership)`, so every ownership-derived codegen decision was dead on it; B-2026-08-10-21's two new pins then failed on that lane ALONE and made `main` red on both x86-linux and macOS-arm64, reading as a JIT miscompile when the JIT was fine and the harness was starving it
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found during a project-health review, from CI rather than from a
program. `Codegen E2E (LLVM 18)` and `Codegen E2E (macOS arm64, LLVM 18)` were
both failing on `main` (run 2860, ff002b20/5c5fcad9 window) at step "Codegen E2E
via LLJIT (run==build parity)" — every other step of both jobs green, including
the AOT `Codegen E2E + interpreter + typechecker + self-host oracle` step
immediately before it.

    codegen_tests::test_e2e_use_after_move_defensive_copy_vecstr_family
        left: Some("\\e\u{8}\n")   right: Some("alpha\n")
    codegen_tests::test_e2e_use_after_move_defensive_copy_map_set_struct
        left: Some("")                right: Some("7\n")

Both are B-2026-08-10-21's pins. Reproduced locally on x86-linux, and the AOT
leg passes the same two tests on the same tree — so the divergence was
lane-shaped, not arch-shaped, which is what pointed at the harness instead of at
codegen.

THE PRODUCTION JIT WAS NEVER BROKEN. That row's own minimal repro, through the
shipped CLI:

    fn main() { let s: String = f"alpha"; { let keep: String = s; } println(s); }

    karac run --interp   alpha
    karac run  (JIT)     alpha
    karac build          alpha

All three correct. `cli.rs` runs `pipeline.ownershipcheck()` before
`compile_to_ir_with_options` and passes the result, under a comment that states
exactly why ("so the emitted IR matches `karac build`'s"). The harness passed
`None` and matched NEITHER shipped path.

THE RULE WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, FORTY LINES ABOVE THE BUG. The comment on the
harness's own `ownershipcheck` call says a harness passing `None` "leaves the
entire RC-fallback boxing surface dead across the suite and systematically
diverges from shipped binaries", cites the collision it hid (b027fc15 bug 3:
"every real build of the prepend-builder shape segfaulted while 1100+ E2E tests
stayed green"), and closes with "The suite tests what ships." The AOT leg obeys
it. The JIT leg, added later as a separate dispatch function, silently did not —
so the fix that comment describes was applied on one leg and the identical blind
spot re-opened one lane over.

WHAT THE FALSE RED COST, ordered by what actually matters:

  1. Not the red. A red `main` is loud, and this one was already visible.
  2. The COVERAGE. This lane is the only one that runs the JIT across the whole
     ~2900-program corpus, so it is the only broad detector of a real
     ownership-dependent run-vs-build divergence — the exact class of divergence
     the LLJIT-productionization spike exists to keep closed, and the class
     Phase 12's bootstrap loop rests on (`karac run`/`test` are its execution
     path). Starved of the hint, it could not have caught one.
  3. The MISREADING. A parity lane failing where AOT passes is, by construction,
     read as "the JIT miscompiles" — the most expensive wrong diagnosis
     available here, since it points investigation at the backend and at a
     just-landed memory fix rather than at the harness.

AND THE COVERAGE META-CHECK CANNOT SEE THIS CLASS. `scripts/dark-llvm-tests.py`
(CI's "Dark llvm test targets" step, built for B-2026-07-31-44 / B-2026-08-08-26)
answers "which llvm-gated test TARGET does no CI job run?" and reports OK here —
correctly, since this target is run, twice. The question it does not ask is
"which lane runs with DEGRADED INPUTS?", which is the shape of both this row and
b027fc15 bug 3. A lane can be fully scheduled, fully green, and testing a
compiler configuration that ships to nobody.

A SEPARATE OBSERVATION, not fixed here and not folded into this row's scope:
`tests/par_codegen.rs` — the lane that DOES thread `ConcurrencyAnalysis` into
codegen — has no JIT leg at all (no `KARAC_TEST_JIT` reference in the file). So
the auto-par codegen surface currently has no run==build parity coverage of any
width. Worth its own row and its own decision; auto-par is on by default in
`karac build`, so the shipped configuration is the one uncovered.

fix:
FIXED by 7dfc17c. `collect_expr_inner_writes`'s `Call` arm
(`src/concurrency.rs`) now records a write on an argument whose parameter is a
SHARED type AND whose callee body writes that parameter, alongside the existing
`mut`-marker and `MutRef` gates. Two helpers: `type_is_shared` (against the
`shared_type_names` set the checker already builds) and `callee_writes_param`
(walks the callee body with the existing `collect_block_inner_writes`, which
covers both the `s.f[i] = …` assignment spelling and the `s.f.push(…)` method
spelling; re-entry guarded through the closure walk's name stack).

Pins: two tests in `tests/concurrency.rs` -- the mutation case, stash-proven red
against the pre-fix analysis, and the read-only case as the over-serialization
guard. Both use a plain `Vec[i64]` shared struct.
tracker: the auto-par admission decision for `go(s)`'s body and the `Tensor` element clone it hoists into `__par_branch_0_1` — the ASAN frame is `karac_clone_Tensor_f32` called from `__par_branch_0_1` on a `karac_runtime::worker_loop` thread, so the question is why this body was admitted, not how the clone is emitted. Start at the three auto-par admission changes in the window: 7fe2b6dd (2026-08-11, induction-step skip tied to the loop counter by name), 4e01841e (2026-08-08, a closure call writes what the closure captured), eb21d86e (2026-08-05, auto-par admits `frozen` values). NOT bisected — see the detail.
title: NONDETERMINISTIC SILENT WRONG ANSWER on the DEFAULT `karac build`: a 13-line program that overwrites a `Vec[Tensor]` element through a `shared struct` (`s.grads[0] = old + g`) prints `0` instead of `1` on ~2% of runs and SEGVs on ~1.3%, measured over 300 runs of one binary. Auto-par is the trigger — `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` is 0 failures in 200 — and the crashing frame is `karac_clone_Tensor_f32` inside `__par_branch_0_1` on a runtime worker thread. The wrong answer is the worse half: the program exits 0 and lies
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced from CI, not from a program. The `Memory sanitizer -O0
(unoptimized allocations)` job was RED on `main` (run 31540330997, 76abf839)
with the ratchet reporting `asan_vec_tensor_element_overwrite` as a NEW failure
not on the quarantine list. Reproduced locally, then carried off the ASAN
harness and onto the plain shipped CLI, which is where it got much worse than
the ASAN report suggested.

THE FIXTURE, unchanged from `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` (added 2026-07-17 in
87443eda, so the SHAPE is nearly a month old — it is the failure that is new):

    shared struct S { mut grads: Vec[Tensor[f32, [?]]] }
    fn go(s: S) {
        let z: Tensor[f32, [?]] = Tensor.zeros([2]);
        s.grads.push(z);
        let g: Tensor[f32, [?]] = Tensor.ones([2]);
        let old = s.grads[0];
        s.grads[0] = old + g;
    }
    fn main() {
        let s = S { grads: Vec.new() };
        go(s);
        let r = s.grads[0];
        println(r[0]);
    }

MEASURED on the SHIPPED path — plain `karac build`, DEFAULT opt level, DEFAULT
auto-par, one binary, x86_64 Linux, no sanitizer involved:

    300 runs:  290 correct (`1`)   ·   6 WRONG ANSWER (`0`)   ·   4 SEGV

THE WRONG ANSWER IS THE FINDING. A crash is loud and a user files it; `0` for
`1` from a numeric kernel exits 0, prints a plausible value, and propagates.
Two percent is also the worst possible rate — frequent enough to corrupt a real
run, rare enough that a developer checking their work three times sees three
passes. Any earlier probe of this shape that ran the binary ONCE recorded a
pass.

AUTO-PAR IS THE TRIGGER, isolated by rebuilding the same source both ways:

    default (auto-par on)   7 / 200 non-zero exits   ·   `nm` shows 2 `__par_branch` symbols
    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0        0 / 200 non-zero exits   ·   `nm` shows 0 `__par_branch` symbols
    karac run --interp      correct
    sequential binary       correct

So this is not the Tensor element-ownership work per se (that path is clean
sequentially); it is that `go(s)`'s body is being admitted to a parallel branch
when it is not safe to run there.

THE ASAN FRAME names the site precisely — from the -O0 leg, `exitcode=23`:

    ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x503000010000
        #0  karac_clone_Tensor_f32.19
        #1  __par_branch_0_1
        #2  core::ops::function::FnOnce::call_once{{vtable.shim}}
        #3  karac_runtime::execute_task
        #4  karac_runtime::worker_loop

A `Tensor` clone running on a worker thread, reading an address that is not
mapped. Combined with the `0`-instead-of-`1` result, the shape is the parallel
branch racing the main thread over the `s.grads[0]` slot that the overwrite
frees and replaces — sometimes reading the displaced block after it is gone
(SEGV), sometimes reading the pre-overwrite zeros (`0`).

IT DOES NOT GO ON THE -O0 QUARANTINE LIST, and this is worth stating because
the ratchet's own failure message offers that as one of two options. That list
is contractually for fixtures that "FAIL at KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0 and PASS at the
default -O2" — this one fails at BOTH, on the shipped default build, so listing
it would write a false claim into the file. It would also break the ratchet's
other direction: the leg fails when a LISTED fixture passes, and at a ~1-in-3
per-run failure rate this fixture passes most of the time.

CONSEQUENCE FOR CI SIGNAL, flagged rather than fixed: because the failure is
nondeterministic, the `memory-sanitizer-o0` leg will now flip red and green on
identical trees. Until this row closes, a green -O0 leg is not evidence.

NOT BISECTED, deliberately, and handed back with the window instead. The shape
is a month old and the failure is new, so something changed underneath it —
most plausibly an auto-par ADMISSION change rather than anything in the Tensor
path, since the sequential lowering of the same source is clean. Three
candidates landed in the window and each widened what auto-par accepts:
7fe2b6dd (2026-08-11), 4e01841e (2026-08-08), eb21d86e (2026-08-05). Attributing
it needs a rebuild-and-run-200x per candidate, which is a real bisect rather
than a spot check, and guessing between three plausible causes on a race is how
a wrong attribution gets written down as fact.

RELATED COVERAGE GAP, filed separately as B-2026-08-11-26: `tests/par_codegen.rs`
— the lane that threads `ConcurrencyAnalysis` into codegen — has no JIT leg, so
the auto-par surface has no run==build parity coverage of any width. Auto-par is
on by default in `karac build`, so the shipped configuration is the uncovered
one, and this row is an example of what lives there.

CONFIRMED AS FILED, and the row's own instinct was right: it is the auto-par
ADMISSION, not the Tensor path. The concurrency report names the group without
any bisection needed:

    function main (line 9):
      parallel_group {
        [11] go(...)        // mutates s.grads
        [12] <expr>         // let r = s.grads[0]
        reason: independent effects on different resources
      }

A write and a read of the same object, admitted as a parallel group. Branch 1
is the `karac_clone_Tensor_f32` frame from the ASAN report -- it clones the
Tensor out of `s.grads[0]` while branch 0 pushes and reallocates the Vec under
it, which is both the SEGV (block freed mid-clone) and the `0` (pre-overwrite
zeros observed).

THE CAUSE, exactly one gap. `collect_expr_inner_writes`'s `Call` arm recorded an
argument write only for a call-site `mut` marker or a `MutRef`/`MutSlice`
parameter. A `shared struct` is REFERENCE SEMANTICS passed BY VALUE: mutating
the parameter mutates the caller's object, but there is no marker (markers are
the `mut ref T` rule) and no `MutRef` in the signature, so neither gate fires
and `go(s)` recorded no write at all.

NO BISECTION WAS NEEDED, and the three candidates the row handed over are all
innocent. The gap is not new -- it is the shape of the `Call` arm since it was
written -- so the correct reading is that the fixture's admission became
reachable rather than that an admission rule broke. That also explains the row's
puzzle of a month-old fixture failing only now, without attributing it to
7fe2b6dd / 4e01841e / eb21d86e, which is exactly the wrong-attribution-on-a-race
the row declined to guess at.

MEASURED, shipped path, default opt level, default auto-par, one binary:

    pre-fix    300 runs:  283 correct  ·  10 WRONG  ·   7 SEGV
    post-fix   400 runs:  400 correct  ·   0 WRONG  ·   0 SEGV   (0 `__par_branch` symbols)
    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, pre-fix   200 runs: 200 correct (isolates admission)

THE GATE DISCRIMINATES, verified against the pre-fix binary rather than argued.
A minimal shape without any Tensor reproduces it -- `shared struct S { mut vals:
Vec[i64] }`, `writes_it(s); let n = s.vals.len();` -- and:

    read-only shared arg   pre-fix: not grouped     post-fix: not grouped
    writing  shared arg    pre-fix: GROUPED         post-fix: not grouped

So the fix costs no parallelism it was not already costing, and the read-only
surface (passing a shared handle to a function that only reads it -- common)
stays open. Blanket-serializing every shared argument would have closed the race
by surrendering that surface, which is why the gate is keyed on the callee's
body writing the parameter.

TENSOR IS INCIDENTAL. The row's fixture uses `Vec[Tensor[f32, [?]]]` and the
crash frame is a Tensor clone, which invites reading this as Tensor
element-ownership. It is not: the `Vec[i64]` shape above admits the identical
bad group. Tensor only made the failure LOUD -- a big heap payload turns the
race into a SEGV often enough to reach CI, where an i64 element would more often
have produced a quiet wrong number.

CI SIGNAL. The row flags that `memory-sanitizer-o0` will flip red/green on
identical trees until this closes, and that a green -O0 leg is not evidence
meanwhile. That caveat lifts with this commit; `asan_vec_tensor_element_overwrite`
passes, and it correctly never went on the -O0 quarantine list (it failed at
BOTH opt levels, so listing it would have written a false claim).

VERIFICATION. Full non-llvm suite green (100 binaries, 0 failures), including
`tests/concurrency.rs` at 145 with the two new pins. Codegen E2E (2902), asan
(1034), par_codegen (580) and cli (255) green under `--features llvm`.

fix:
WONTFIX -- real and reproducible, measured to a standstill, and the SAME
residual B-2026-08-10-20 already closed as `wontfix` from the other lineage
(this row came up B-2026-08-10-9 -> -28, that one B-2026-08-10-9 -> -19 -> -20).
No code change; the deliverable is the measurement and the disposition. Recorded
in docs/spikes/sort-algorithm-gap.md § "Where shuffled-uniform stands after
Direction 7".
title: RESIDUAL of B-2026-08-10-9, split out per the live-remainder rule: on SHUFFLED-UNIFORM input the mono `sort_by` is still ~1.6x Rust's driftsort. 50a50e8 replaced the fixed-32-run merge sort with a natural-run merge sort, which was the right fix and moved the ORDERED patterns enormously (sorted and reverse went from 39-54x behind to roughly 2x AHEAD -- measured here at 0.47x and 0.52x). It deliberately did not move the shuffled case, and the closing note records that in its own numbers: `random 14.91 -> 14.60 ms (UNCHANGED)`, because shuffled input has ~2-element natural runs so the RUN padding reproduces the old run length and the old pass count. MEASURED FRESH (hyperfine, 10 runs each, clone subtracted via an identical kernel minus the sort call; 25 rounds x 150k (i64,i64) pairs, x86 container): kara pure sort 260.6 ms vs rust 159.0 ms = 1.64x. Same kernel by pattern: shuffled 1.51x total / 1.64x pure, sorted 0.47x, reverse 0.52x. SEVERITY LOW deliberately -- shuffled-uniform is the regime where an adaptive sort has least to exploit, driftsort is a strong baseline, and 1.6x on the hardest pattern while beating it 2x on ordered input is a defensible place to sit. Filed so the remainder is visible in the work queue rather than only inside a closed row's prose, NOT as a claim that it must be closed. CAVEAT: single host, x86_64 shared container, not the canonical Apple-silicon bench host. NEXT STEP if picked up: compare the emitted merge inner loop against driftsort's on shuffled input; the run-detection phase is already known not to help there, so any remaining gap is in the merge itself.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: surfaced while verifying 50a50e8 against the isolated kernel that produced B-2026-08-10-9's original evidence. That verification also corrected my own filing: I had measured shuffled-uniform ONLY (both source katas shuffle their input), and shuffled turned out to be the MILDEST manifestation -- the same defect was 39-54x on ordered input, which I never generated. The operation was isolated correctly; the input SHAPE was not sampled. Recorded here because it generalises: for a comparison-driven algorithm, input pattern is a first-class axis and an adaptive sort must be measured across patterns, not just across sizes. -- SURFACE NOTE: codegen, mono sort_by merge phase on unordered input.

CLOSED WONTFIX ON MEASUREMENT, 2026-08-11. The residual is real and reproduces;
what is refuted is that there is an action left, and specifically the one this
row proposes.

FIRST, IT IS A DUPLICATE SUBJECT. B-2026-08-10-20 is the same thing --
`Vec[(i64,i64)].sort_by` on shuffled-uniform input against driftsort, same
operation, same pattern, same baseline, same host class -- and it is already
`wontfix` with five directions measured and an explicit "do not reopen any of
them without new information". The two rows reached it by different lineages
(-9 -> -28 here; -9 -> -19 -> -20 there), which is how the queue ended up
tracking one residual twice. Recorded so it does not become three.

SECOND, THERE WAS GENUINELY NEW INFORMATION SINCE BOTH WERE FILED, and it was
checked rather than assumed: Direction 7 (the full-array stable partition,
3d77cc6) landed. Re-measured on current `main`, instructions:

    pattern       karac before D7   karac after D7   driftsort
    few-unique         48.8 M           13.2 M         14.2 M   <- karac now AHEAD
    sawtooth           22.5 M           23.4 M         31.6 M   <- karac ahead
    random             72.3 M           72.1 M         48.2 M   <- 1.50x, UNCHANGED

Direction 7 did exactly what the arithmetic predicted on exactly the pattern it
predicted: few-unique fell 3.7x and passed the 14.2 M target set when the
driftsort baseline was corrected in B-2026-08-11-10. Shuffled-uniform did not
move -- 72.3 -> 72.1 M is noise. A full-array partition collapses the array at 8
distinct keys; at 150 k distinct keys it still leaves ~log2(n) passes, so the
pass-count reduction that carried few-unique has nothing to give here. The new
information exists and it points AT the standstill, not away from it.

THIRD, THIS ROW'S OWN NEXT STEP IS ALREADY REFUTED. It proposes "compare the
emitted merge inner loop against driftsort's ... any remaining gap is in the
merge itself". That is the cost-per-merge-output family, and § Direction 6
retired the WHOLE family by arithmetic rather than by trying its members:
`n · log2(n/RUN)` outputs is fixed, so no per-output constant reaches the
target. Seven directions have now been measured against this residual, and the
only one with the required property -- reducing full passes -- is the one that
landed and does not apply to shuffled input.

FOURTH, A CORRECTION THAT OUTLIVES THIS ROW. Three rows now quote three ratios
for this one residual: -20 says 1.30x, this row says 1.64x, and a fresh
wall-clock pass in a single sitting produced 1.26x and then 1.71x from the same
binaries. None of them disagree about the code; they disagree about the host.
The slope method (subprocess spawns) and best-of-N in-process timing respond
differently to contention on a shared container -- driftsort's random figure
alone moved 8.65 -> 5.80 ms between two measurements an hour apart while karac's
moved 10.92 -> 9.90. QUOTE INSTRUCTIONS FOR THIS RESIDUAL, NOT WALL CLOCK:
72.1 M vs 48.2 M reproduces to three significant figures across sessions; the
wall-clock ratio is not stable to two.

WHAT WOULD REOPEN IT: a design that reduces the NUMBER OF FULL PASSES on input
with ~n distinct keys. That is the single property § Direction 6 isolated, it is
not satisfied by anything in the merge, and Direction 7 shows a partition
bounded by cardinality does not supply it either. Absent that, karac sits at
1.50x on the hardest pattern while beating driftsort on sawtooth (23.4 M vs
31.6 M) and on the ordered patterns -- a defensible place, which is what this
row said when it filed itself severity `low`.

fix:
FIXED by 8e1f96dc — the row's hypothesis was the right family but the wrong member. It is
not a missing Map/Set half on a promotion arm; it is the WHOLE-BINDING sibling
of `wrapper_arm_moves_heap_field_to_free_fn`, which had only ever detected a
moved FIELD.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS, read off the IR and confirmed by valgrind rather than
inferred. The Ok arm binds the struct and passes it BY VALUE, so the callee owns
it and ends with `__karac_drop_struct_S`, which frees the Map. The arm's source
payload drop stayed armed, so `main`'s `respl.ok` block called
`karac_drop_Map_String_i64` on the same handle: valgrind reports an invalid read
inside `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` over a block already freed by `main`, from
a `karac_map_new` allocation. Not a double free at two call sites — a
use-after-free with both ends inside `main`.

Two false leads are worth recording because each looked decisive:

  - `take()` appeared to free nothing. Grepping its IR for `drop_Map`/
    `karac_map_free` returns zero hits — the callee's free is spelled
    `__karac_drop_struct_S`, one level up. The by-value param IS callee-owned.
  - `main` appeared to hold only ONE Map drop, which argued against a double
    free at all. It does hold one; the other free is the callee's, inlined.

WHY THE EXISTING GATE MISSED IT. The arm-suppression condition is
`!(borrow_only && wrapper) || heap_field_moved_to_free_fn || binding_owns_
payload`. For `Ok(s) => take(s)`: `wrapper` is true; `borrow_only` is
SPURIOUSLY true, because `consume_class` scores a free-fn argument as
entry-copied (the exact blind spot the `heap_field` override was added for);
`heap_field_moved_to_free_fn` is false because the arm passes `s`, not `s.a`;
and `binding_owns_payload` is false because `field_copy_supported` excludes
`Map`/`Set`, so the struct is not entry-copy supported. Nothing fired.

That last clause is also the whole explanation for the row's sharpest control:
a `Vec[String]` field IS entry-copy supported, so `binding_owns_payload` is
already true and suppression already fires. Verified in the IR before touching
anything — the Vec variant emits `respl.suppress.at.*` on BOTH arms (20
occurrences), the Map variant only on the Err arm (10). The new condition is
therefore additive on the shape that already worked, which is what keeps the
control clean rather than merely appearing to.

THE FIX: `wrapper_arm_moves_whole_binding_to_free_fn`, gated to a non-shared
user struct binding, plus `consume_class::bindings_passed_whole_to_free_fn_arg`
(bare identifier arguments only — `take(s.a)` is the field case and
`take(s.a.len())` reads rather than moves). Added as one more override on the
same condition, so both move shapes are handled at one site.

VERIFIED on the row's seven-row table plus an Err-arm variant: both crashing
shapes (Map, Set) now agree with the interpreter, and all five over-fire
controls stay clean — `Option` instead of `Result`, no wrapper, a bare Map
payload, inline use, and the `Vec` field. Under valgrind with `--leak-check=full`
the fixed Map, Set and Vec binaries report 0 errors and no leaks, which is the
direction that matters here: the repair is "stop the SOURCE freeing", so
over-suppressing would leak instead of crash.

TEST-INFRA NOTE, filed separately: a single program combining all seven shapes
fails MODULE VERIFICATION inside `tests/codegen.rs`'s harness ("Function return
type does not match operand type of return inst") while `karac build` and
`karac run --interp` both compile and run that same program correctly, with and
without this fix. The pin is therefore written as one small program per shape.
That divergence is not this bug and is not caused by it, but it means the E2E
harness can reject a program the compiler accepts.
title: SEGV (exit 139) on a DEFAULT `karac build`: a struct with a `Map`/`Set` field, bound out of a `Result`'s `Ok(..)` match arm and then passed BY VALUE to a function, dereferences a wild pointer in `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec`. `karac check` is clean and the interpreter prints the right answer. Five conditions, all necessary -- `Option` instead of `Result` is clean, a `Vec` field is clean, using the value inline instead of passing it is clean.
tracker: `karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` -- the ASAN frame is `#0 karac_map_free_with_drop_vec` called directly from `main`, on `SEGV on unknown address 0x0b`, i.e. the Map handle slot holds a non-pointer when the drop runs. Family: B-2026-08-07-19 (`struct { s: Result[Map,E] }`) is the INVERSE nesting and is fixed.
detail:
MINIMAL REPRO -- 6 lines, no loops. `karac check` reports no errors; `--interp` prints `1`; the compiled binary dies:

    enum E { Missing(String) }
    struct S { a: Map[String, i64] }
    fn mk() -> Result[S, E] { let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new(); m.insert("k", 1); Ok(S { a: m }) }
    fn take(s: S) { println(f"{s.a.len()}"); }
    fn main() { match mk() { Ok(s) => take(s), Err(_e) => println("e") } }

    karac check          no errors
    karac run --interp   1                       (correct)
    karac run  (JIT)     no output, exit 1
    karac build (AOT)    Segmentation fault, exit 139
    KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0    Segmentation fault      (not an optimizer artifact)
    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0     Segmentation fault      (not auto-par)

Under ASAN the failure names itself:

    ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x0000_0000_000b
      #0 karac_map_free_with_drop_vec
      #1 main
    SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV in karac_map_free_with_drop_vec

Address 0x0b is 11 -- not a mapped pointer at all. The drop path is handed a slot that holds a scalar (or a stale tag) where a Map handle is expected, and dereferences it.

FIVE NECESSARY CONDITIONS, each with a measured clean control (all built with a default `karac build`, run, exit code recorded):

    variant                                                              verdict
    baseline (above)                                                     SEGV 139
    ... field is `Set[String]` instead of `Map[String, i64]`              SEGV 139
    `Option[S]` + `Some(s) => take(s)` instead of Result                  ok
    no wrapper: `fn mk() -> S`, `take(mk())`                             ok
    no struct: `Result[Map[String,i64], E]`, `Ok(m) => take(m)`           ok
    used INLINE in the arm: `Ok(s) => println(f"{s.a.len()}")`           ok
    field is `Vec[String]` instead of a Map/Set                          ok

So it needs, together: (1) a `Result` wrapper specifically -- `Option` is clean, which is the sharpest clue since the two share most of this machinery; (2) a STRUCT payload -- a bare `Map` payload is clean; (3) that struct's field is a `Map` or a `Set` -- `Vec` is clean; (4) the struct is bound out of the `Ok(..)` arm; (5) it is then passed BY VALUE to a function -- consuming it inline in the arm is clean.

RELATION TO B-2026-08-07-19 (fixed): that row is `struct S { s: Result[Map[K,V], E] }` -- a Result INSIDE a struct field, leaking at the struct's own field drop with no call involved. This is the INVERSE nesting -- a struct inside a Result -- and it crashes rather than leaks, and it requires the by-value call. The fix for that row (`result_field_map_or_set_half_ok` routed to `emit_result_drop_fn`) is on the promotion loop's Result arm; worth checking whether the same Map/Set half is missing on the arm-binding + by-value-argument path, which would make this its mirror image.

SEVERITY: a SEGV on a default build from source every checking phase accepts. The interpreter disagreeing (correct answer) means `karac run --interp` cannot be used to reproduce or debug it, and the JIT gives no output at all rather than a diagnostic.

SUGGESTED FIXTURES: the seven-row table -- two crashing pins (Map and Set) and five over-fire controls. The `Option` and `Vec` controls matter most: they are the two shapes an over-broad fix would most plausibly regress.
investigation: 2026-08-11 (hunt, domain 9 -- Result chains with heap error payloads). Found while bisecting a 549-byte leak in a config-validator dogfood: narrowing the leak's payload shape reached `Result[struct-with-Map-field]`, and one variant of that -- passing the unwrapped struct to a function -- aborted under ASAN instead of leaking. Confirmed outside ASAN on a plain `karac build`. The seven-variant matrix was run with `karac build` + exit code rather than the ASAN harness, which made each iteration seconds instead of a minute. Filed, not fixed, per the hunting-only remit.

fix:
FIXED by 19d0e9a.

Own by transfer for the two built-in enums, mirroring B-2026-08-05-33's struct
arm one type-class over. `compile_function` (src/codegen/functions.rs) now
registers the inline Option / Result / Option-Map payload drops on a by-value
`Option`/`Result` param's slot, gated on the param NEVER ESCAPING
(`nonescaping_param_names`). No entry copy: the caller has already transferred,
which the emitted IR shows directly as a whole-slot `store zeroinitializer` into
the source binding, so there is no original left to protect.

That gate keeps exactly one owner in each direction. A param that reaches a
return hands ownership back, and the caller's arg-site zeroing is itself
suppressed for that shape (`!call_arg_flows_into_return`), so the caller kept
its drop and the callee must not add one. A param used only as a match
scrutinee is consumed in place, and the standard local move-suppression retracts
this registration exactly as it already does for the entry-copied user-enum
params that share the path.

Verified over the row's own -O0 matrix under valgrind, 200 iterations: all seven
leaking shapes go to zero (String and Vec payloads, fresh-temp and let-bound
arguments, Option and Result, struct and bare-container payloads) and all
thirteen controls stay clean -- discard, inline-match, let-match, arg-match,
bare-struct, bare-Vec, user-enum, let-unused and double-pass.

The two repros this row landed are un-ignored as regression pins, and
`asan_by_value_optres_arg_passed_twice_no_double_free` pins the safety property
the copy-free form rests on: the second pass of the same binding arrives all
zeros, so every `cap > 0` guard skips instead of double-freeing. It reads the
payload in the callee so a drop that fired twice would surface as a
use-after-free rather than passing quietly.

NOT fixed by this, and deliberately so: B-2026-08-12-1, the wrong-variant read
on that second pass. It is the caller-side half of the same split and is
unchanged here.
title: A by-value `Option`/`Result` parameter that the callee never DESTRUCTURES is dropped by NO frame, so the entire `Ok`/`Some` payload leaks: the caller retracts its own cleanup on the pass-as-arg move while `param_own.rs` bails on `Option`/`Result`. The argument form (fresh temp vs let-bound) and the payload field type are BOTH irrelevant -- the row's original Vec-leaks/String-is-freed asymmetry was an -O2 artifact. A user enum in the same shape is clean, which is what localises the defect.
tracker: Shares one root cause with B-2026-08-12-1 (the same caller-retracts/callee-bails split, surfacing as a wrong answer instead of a leak); the two halves have to move together. Leg A was split out to B-2026-08-12-2 -- it is a different bug. Same code area as B-2026-08-11-29 (SEGV).
detail:
Filed separately from B-2026-08-11-29 because the necessary conditions do NOT match that row's, so a fix for the SEGV will not obviously cover these, and vice versa. All measurements are Linux LSan via the `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs` harness on a default build.

LEG A -- `Map`/`Set` field, leaks when the Result is LET-BOUND. Counterintuitively the `let` is what triggers it; the inline form is clean, which is the opposite polarity from most temp-vs-binding bugs in this ledger:

    enum E { Missing(String) }
    struct S { a: Map[String, i64] }
    fn mk() -> Result[S, E] { let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new(); m.insert("k", 1); Ok(S { a: m }) }

    fn main() { match mk() { Ok(s) => println(f"{s.a.len()}"), Err(_e) => .. } }        clean
    fn main() { let r = mk(); match r { Ok(s) => println(f"{s.a.len()}"), .. } }        LEAK 600 B / 3 allocs
    fn main() { let r = mk(); take(r); }   (take(r: Result[S,E]) matches inside)       LEAK 600 B / 3 allocs

The same struct built and dropped WITHOUT the Result wrapper is clean in every form tried -- in `main` directly, and returned by value from a function -- so the wrapper is required here too.

LEG B -- `Vec` field, leaks one allocation per Vec field, and ONLY alongside another heap field. Measured over a struct inside a fresh-temp `Result` passed by value to a function that matches it:

    struct field layout                        verdict
    { a: String }                              clean
    { a: Vec[String] }                         clean
    { a: Vec[i64] }                            clean
    { a: Vec[String], n: i64 }                 clean      <- a scalar companion is not enough
    { n: i64, a: Vec[String] }                 clean
    { a: String, b: String }                   clean      <- two heap fields, but no Vec
    { a: String, b: Vec[String] }              LEAK 96 B / 1 alloc
    { a: Vec[String], b: String }              LEAK 96 B / 1 alloc
    { a: Vec[String], b: Vec[String] }         LEAK 192 B / 2 allocs   <- one per Vec

So leg B needs a `Vec` field AND at least one other HEAP-owning field; a scalar companion does not do it, and two Strings with no Vec do not either. The leaked size is ~96 B per Vec field regardless of element count, i.e. the Vec's own allocation, not its elements -- and element heapness is irrelevant (literal and `String.new()`-built elements behave identically).

Leg B also needs the FRESH TEMP -- `take(mk())` leaks, `let r = mk(); take(r)` is clean. That is the exact opposite of leg A's polarity, which is the main reason these are one row and not merged into B-2026-08-11-29.

MEASUREMENT HAZARD worth recording: several early single-field probes read CLEAN and were not informative, because a one-container-field struct appears to take a different (working) drop path. Anyone reducing this must keep the companion field or the shape stops reproducing -- the minimal repro is genuinely two fields, not one.

    { a: String, b: String }       clean                   clean

buffers it "can't soundly duplicate" and therefore leaves "on caller-retains"
-- and `Result` is on that list. So the callee never takes ownership of a
`Result` parameter. That predicts every polarity above: a `let`-bound argument
has a caller binding that drops it, an inline match keeps it in `main`, and a
FRESH TEMP argument has no owner on either side.

String alike). The suspect is the dedicated inline-`Result`-payload path

`result_field_struct_enum_payload_ok` / `option_payload_struct_or_enum_drop_ok`
in `src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs`), which decides per-half whether a
Result's payload drop is admitted at all.

is the tool that ends the guessing on this row -- every earlier pass argued

WHAT THE TRACE SAYS, for the same `Result[S, E]` under `take(mk())`:

    String payload:   fn=mk  action=FreeVecBuffer  slot=fstr.acc
    Vec payload:      fn=mk  action=FreeVecBuffer  slot=v
    (main: NO cleanup actions at all, in either case)
    (take: NO cleanup actions at all, in either case)

THREE THINGS FALL OUT.

1. NOBODY IN THE CALLER OWNS THE TEMP -- empirically, not just from
   param_own.rs's prose. `main` registers zero actions for `take(mk())`. That
   confirms the bail directly.

2. THE SECOND PASS'S "only the ARGUMENT path is short" IS INCOMPLETE, and the
   producer is where the ownership is actually lost. `mk` registers a
   `FreeVecBuffer` on `v` -- the local it MOVED into `Ok(S { b: v })`. The
   local is REQUIRED for the leak:

       return Ok(S { b: Vec.new() });                       clean   <- no local
       let mut v = ...; return Ok(S { b: v });              LEAKS
       let mut v = ...; let s = S { b: v }; return Ok(s);   LEAKS

   (`fn mk2() -> S { return S { b: v } }`), so it is the enum-variant wrapping
   in return position that loses it, not the move itself.

   rescues it only on the `let` / discard paths (which register
   `track_inline_result_payload_var`). The argument path registers nothing, so
   that is where the orphaning becomes VISIBLE -- but the argument path is not
   where the ownership is dropped.

   worry was that `mk` freeing `fstr.acc` might be freeing the very buffer the
   struct now holds, which would read clean to LSan only because nobody touches
   the field. Made `take` actually PRINT `s.b` and ran it under ASAN: clean, and
   the value is correct on both backends. So the String and Vec paths really do
   differ in the producer, and `fstr.acc` is not the struct's buffer.

payload's buffer. It is not a `CleanupAction` in `main`, `take` or `mk` -- the

side is now fully mapped.
