title: Derive dependency auto-resolution is implemented for the `Ord` chain but NOT for `Copy` or `Hash`, and design.md states the behaviour unconditionally. § Derive: "The compiler resolves derive dependencies automatically regardless of the order items appear in `#[derive(...)]`. Writing `#[derive(Hash)]` when `PartialEq` and `Eq` are not yet derived causes the compiler to auto-derive them in dependency order (`PartialEq` -> `Eq` -> `Hash`). Listing dependencies explicitly is valid and idiomatic; omitting them is also allowed. `#[derive(Copy)]` auto-derives `Clone` if not already present -- **`Copy` without `Clone` is NEVER a compile error, because the compiler fills in the missing dependency.**" Measured: `#[derive(Copy)] struct C { a: i64 }` is EXACTLY that compile error -- `error[typecheck]: struct 'C' derives Copy but not Clone; Copy requires Clone`. `#[derive(Hash)] struct K { a: i64 }` used as a Map key fails with `Map[K, ...]: key type does not implement 'Eq'; only hashable equality-comparable types (... or structs/enums with '#[derive(Hash, Eq)]') can be Map keys`. In BOTH cases the diagnostic names the very dependency the compiler was supposed to fill in, and recommends the manual spelling the spec says is optional. The discriminator that makes this a partial implementation rather than an absent one: `#[derive(Ord)] struct S { a: i64 }` + `x < y` passes `karac check` clean, so the `Ord -> PartialOrd + Eq -> PartialEq` chain IS resolved.
detail:
Probe: domain-20 design.md transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d20/{dc1,dc2,dh1,do1,df2}.kara -- one chain per file.

CONTROLS: `#[derive(Copy, Clone)]` checks clean and prints copy = 3,3 on interp and JIT, so the derives themselves work; only the auto-fill is missing.

SPEC IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND EMPHATIC on the Copy leg -- "never a compile error" is stated as a rule, not an aspiration, and the paragraph exists specifically to say users need not list dependencies. An LLM writing Kara from the spec will omit `Clone`, and the resulting diagnostic tells it to add what the spec told it it could leave out.

WHICH SIDE MOVES IS THE OWNER'S CALL -- implement the two missing chains, or narrow design.md's claim to the chains that resolve. Note the Ord chain already sets the precedent for the former.

fix:
Two missing arms in codegen's Display operand recognition, plus the casing
divergence that fixing them exposed.

THE ROW'S SHAPE. `#[derive(Display)] enum Direction { Up, Down }` +
`println(f"{Direction.Up}")` is design.md § derive(Display) on enums' own
worked example. The parser emits `Direction.Up` as a 2-segment
`ExprKind::Path`, but `expr_user_enum_name` (all-unit enums) and
`expr_user_enum_name_any` (payload-bearing enums) both recognized only
place expressions -- Identifier / SelfValue / FieldAccess. A variant PATH
matched neither, so the operand fell through to the struct-shaped refusal,
which then MISNAMED the program: "bind a struct literal or call result to a
`let` first" describes neither a struct literal nor a call. Adding the Path
arm to both helpers is the fix; `compile_unit_enum_display` and
`render_user_enum_display` already compile the operand through the ordinary
path lowering, so nothing else had to change.

Each arm is guarded exactly as `compile_path_expr` guards its own
enum-variant arm: a leading segment naming a local variable or module
binding is a value-rooted field path (`CFG.max`), not a variant, and keeps
falling through. The payload arm additionally checks variant membership
against the layout's tag map, so a non-variant path on an enum-named head is
untouched.

THE SECOND DEFECT, found by probing the fix rather than by the row. With the
path arm in place, `#[derive(Display(snake_case))] enum Mode { FastPath }`
BUILT and printed `FastPath` while `--interp` printed `fast_path`. Measured
against a reverted tree, that divergence is PRE-EXISTING and independent of
this row: the already-working bound form (`let m = Mode.FastPath;
println(f"{m}")`) had the same split, because codegen rendered raw variant
names and never consulted the derive option at all. Left alone, this row's
fix would have converted a loud build error into a SILENT WRONG ANSWER for
every snake_case enum -- strictly worse than the gap it closes -- so the
casing is fixed here too rather than filed for later.

`enum_display_variant_name` now supplies the Display spelling at both
emission points, reusing the interpreter's OWN predicate
(`has_display_snake_case`, widened `pub(super)` -> `pub(crate)`) and its own
transform (`pascal_to_snake`) instead of re-implementing either. That is
deliberate: two hand-kept copies of a formatting rule are exactly how the
backends drifted apart in the first place.

MEASURED. All three backends (`--interp`, JIT, AOT) now print identically for:
the all-unit path, the same in argument position (`println(Direction.Down)`),
a snake_case-derived enum, a unit variant of a PAYLOAD-bearing enum
(`f"{Evt.MouseUp}"` -- refused before this change for the same reason), and
multiple interpolations in one f-string. Payload variants render
`KeyDown(3)` on every backend; the interpreter does not apply snake_case to
them either, so the two agree and no behaviour was invented here.

title: `#[derive(Display)]` on an enum works under `--interp` and is REFUSED by both compiled backends when the interpolated expression is an enum-variant PATH -- which is exactly the form design.md teaches. § derive(Display) on enums shows `println(f"{Direction.Up}")` -> "Up" and `println(f"{Status.Closed}")` -> "Closed" as the canonical usage; transcribed verbatim, `karac check` passes, `--interp` prints Up / Closed, and `karac run` / `karac build` both die with `codegen failed: Display of a struct in an f-string is supported when the interpolated expression is a variable or field access (e.g. f"{x}"); bind a struct literal or call result to a `let` first (user-struct Display, subtask-5 follow-on)`. The `#[derive(Display(snake_case))]` variant fails the same way. The diagnostic MISNAMES what the user wrote: the operand is neither a struct literal nor a call result, it is a unit enum-variant path, so the prescribed repair does not describe the program in front of it.
detail:
Probe: domain-20 design.md transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d20/{dv1,dv3,dv4,dv5,dv6}.kara.

fix:
FIXED by 56ee5c1. Both halves fixed, and probing them turned up a THIRD and FOURTH defect in the same two sections — recorded because the row's premise was that these sections describe a language other than the one that ships, and they do so in both directions.

(1) § derive(Display), AS FILED. `Circle(radius: f64)` / `Rect(w: f64, h: f64)` is a tuple variant with NAMED fields, a spelling that exists nowhere: `error[parse]: Expected RightParen, found Colon`. The construction comments beneath the block are positional (`Shape.Circle(2.5)`), so the intent was plain tuple variants; corrected to `Circle(f64)` / `Rect(f64, f64)`, which checks clean.

(2) § Subscript Trait, AS FILED. It opened "User-defined types support `[]` indexing by implementing two standard traits" while the resolver rejects a user impl outright ("operator traits are stdlib-only"). Now states the v1 boundary its sibling § Operator Traits already stated, and says why the traits are specified anyway — the desugaring is what v1 already does for the stdlib types, so admitting user impls later is the same purely additive change that section describes.

(3) NOT FILED, AND THE OPPOSITE ERROR. § Display claimed "`#[derive(Display)]` on an **enum** is restricted to all-unit-variant enums (a data variant requires a manual `impl Display`)". That is false on BOTH backends: measured, `Shape.Circle(2.5)` renders `"Circle(2.5)"` under `--interp` and under `karac build`, including through a struct field and an explicit `.to_string()`. So § Display denied the very feature § derive(Display) was teaching, and the two sections contradicted each other. The interpreter's own test for the behaviour carries a comment noting that restriction "was stale", which dates how long the sentence had been wrong.

(4) NOT FILED. The example's output comment claimed `Shape.Rect(3.0, 4.0)` → `"Rect(3.0, 4.0)"`. Both backends print `Rect(3, 4)`: a whole-valued `f64` renders without a trailing `.0`. Corrected to match; the compiler was not touched, since `3` is what `println` gives for `let a: f64 = 3.0` generally and that is a formatting decision well outside this row.

GATED, and the gates check PROSE AGAINST THE COMPILER rather than against prose — which is what drifted. `design_md_derive_display_data_variant_example_compiles` extracts the section's own block and parses it, so the syntax cannot regress to a form the language lacks. `design_md_subscript_trait_v1_caveat_matches_the_resolver` asserts BOTH that the resolver still rejects a user `impl Index` AND that the section still says so: if v1 ever admits user operator impls the first assertion fails, which is the intended reminder that the caveat has itself become the stale claim. Both verified non-vacuous by restoring the original text.
title: Two design.md sections state things the language does not have: § derive(Display) uses an enum-variant syntax that does not parse, and § Subscript Trait claims a v1 capability the resolver explicitly rejects. (1) The payload example writes `Circle(radius: f64),` / `Rect(w: f64, h: f64),` -- a tuple-style variant with NAMED fields. That form does not exist: `error[parse]: Expected RightParen, found Colon`. § Feature 3 defines the two real forms, struct variants (`Circle { radius: f64 }`) and tuple variants (`And(Expr, Expr)`), so this is a third spelling that appears nowhere else. (2) § Subscript Trait opens "User-defined types support `[]` indexing by implementing two standard traits" with no v1 caveat, but `impl Index[i64] for Grid` is rejected outright: `error[resolve]: user-defined 'impl Index for Grid' is not supported in v1; operator traits are stdlib-only`. The sibling § Operator Traits DOES carry the caveat ("makes the later addition of user-defined operator impls a purely additive change"), so the two sections disagree with each other about the same v1 boundary.

fix:
Fixed in 21c402f. `collect()` now builds every non-`Vec` target design.md § Iterator Adaptors promises and can name: `String`, `Set[T]`, `VecDeque[T]`, and `Map[K, V]`. All five of the row's measured repros compile and run, and `--interp`, the JIT and AOT agree byte-for-byte.

LOWERED AS A PRE-TYPECHECK DESUGAR (`src/desugar.rs`), not as a `FromIterator` target inferred in the typechecker. `let x: T = <chain>.collect()` is rewritten into the accumulate-into-`T` loop the language already supports -- collect the chain into its `Vec` as today, then fold that into a fresh `T`. Every phase downstream (typecheck, effects, ownership, interpreter, codegen) therefore sees ordinary code that already worked, so backend agreement is BY CONSTRUCTION rather than three parallel implementations kept in sync -- and the feature needs no new span-keyed side table, which is the machinery that makes this class of change expensive here. Codegen and the interpreter were not touched at all.

THE `String` ARM IS THE INTERESTING ONE. Its element is a `char` for `s.chars()....collect()` and a `String` for `v.iter().map(|s| s.to_uppercase()).collect()`, and a pre-typecheck pass cannot tell them apart. `+` accepts neither uniformly (`String + char` is rejected outright: "arithmetic operator requires numeric type"), and `push`/`push_str` take one each. Measured that `push_str(it.to_string())` accepts BOTH on both backends, so the lowering is uniform and needs no element type. Cost is one copy per already-`String` element; a later type-directed pass can drop it.

GUARDED ON THE RECEIVER, which is a correctness requirement rather than polish. `collect` is an ordinary method name, so a user type can define its own returning one of these very targets -- and rewriting that would re-iterate an ALREADY-BUILT collection into a fresh one, silently wrong rather than loudly wrong. The desugar fires only when the receiver is a recognized iterator source or adaptor (a name whitelist, because this pass has no types); anything else is left exactly as it is today. Pinned by a test that gives a struct its own `collect() -> Set[i64]` and asserts it still returns 1.
title: `collect()` can only ever produce `Vec[T]` -- every other `FromIterator` target design.md promises is rejected at typecheck. § Iterator Adaptors: "Every standard collection (`Vec`, `Map`, `Set`, `VecDeque`, `TreeMap`, `String`) implements `FromIterator` for its natural element type. `collect` infers the target type from context or requires annotation." Measured, one target per file: `let up: String = s.chars().map(|c| c.to_uppercase()).collect()` -> "expected 'String', found 'Vec[char]'"; `let j: String = v.iter().map(|s| s.to_uppercase()).collect()` -> "expected 'String', found 'Vec[String]'"; `let s: Set[i64] = ... .collect()` -> "expected 'Set[i64]', found 'Vec[i64]'"; `let d: VecDeque[i64] = ... .collect()` -> "expected 'VecDeque[i64]', found 'Vec[i64]'"; `let m: Map[i64, i64] = v.iter().map(|x| (x, x * 10)).collect()` -> "expected 'Map[i64, i64]', found 'Vec[(i64, i64)]'". The sixth target, `TreeMap`, cannot even be named -- see B-2026-08-17-38. In every case the annotation is ignored and the chain's type is fixed to `Vec` of the element type, so the diagnostic reads as a mismatch the user caused rather than a target the compiler does not support.
detail:
Probe: domain-20 design.md transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d20/{cs1,cs2,cs3,cs4,cs5,it2}.kara.

CONTROL, which shows the adaptor surface itself is healthy: the full i64 adaptor matrix from § Iterator Adaptors' signature block -- count, map, filter, fold, reduce, any, all, find, position, take_while, skip_while, take, skip, enumerate, flat_map -- agrees EXACTLY between `--interp` and the JIT (it1.kara, 15 lines of identical output). The String-element matrix agrees too, up to the `collect` line. So this is specifically the `FromIterator` target set, not iteration.

WORKAROUND EXISTS but is not what the spec teaches: collect into a `Vec` and loop to build the real target. The `String` case is the one that bites hardest -- `chars().map(...).collect()` is the canonical case-mapping idiom in every language with this API.

NOT MARKED DEFERRED: deferred.md has no `FromIterator` / `collect`-target entry, and design.md states the six targets flatly.

CLOSED 2026-08-18. Scope delivered is the ANNOTATED-`let` form, which is every repro this row measured. Two positions remain Vec-only and are split into their own row rather than left implicit: `return <chain>.collect()` against a declared non-`Vec` return type, and argument position `f(<chain>.collect())`. Both still fail with the same "expected 'Set[i64]', found 'Vec[i64]'" -- measured after the fix, not assumed. Return position is not merely unimplemented but genuinely harder in this pass: a `return` inside a CLOSURE returns from the closure, not the enclosing fn, so threading the fn's declared return type down the walk would be wrong exactly where it looks easiest. Argument position needs overload resolution and so wants the typechecker.

`TreeMap`, the sixth target, still cannot be named -- `undefined type 'TreeMap'` at resolve (B-2026-08-17-38, unchanged). When that lands it joins `Map` with an identical arm.

VERIFIED: full `--features llvm` suite with KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1, plus both clippy passes and fmt. Backend parity checked directly as well -- the multi-target program run under `--interp`, `karac run` and a built binary, diffed pairwise, identical.

PINS: `test_collect_into_every_documented_from_iterator_target` (tests/interpreter.rs) is the oracle and `e2e_collect_into_every_documented_from_iterator_target` (tests/codegen.rs) is its codegen twin, deliberately the same program with the same expected output so a divergence shows up as a diff between two tests rather than as a silent one-backend answer. Both cover a duplicate element (Vec keeps 4, Set collapses to 3), order preservation for `VecDeque`, key collapse for `Map`, an empty source, and `Vec` itself to pin the NON-rewrite. `test_collect_desugar_leaves_a_user_defined_collect_alone` pins the receiver guard.

SPAN NOTE, since this pass synthesizes nodes into a span-keyed compiler: a `MethodCall`'s `Expr.span` covers only its RECEIVER, so every node of `v.iter().map(f).collect()` already shares one SpanKey. Synthesized nodes therefore take ZERO-LENGTH spans at distinct offsets -- real nodes always span at least one character, so they cannot collide with one, and distinct offsets keep them distinct from each other. The synthesized block takes the ANNOTATION's span, where no expression is ever recorded, so a diagnostic about the target points at the written target.

fix:
Fixed in 777f4e7, for the `karac check` and JSON-feed surfaces. `must_use` was
invoked only from `cmd_run`, so a program `karac run` warned about got "All
checks passed." from `karac check` and `"diagnostics":[]` from `karac check
--output=json`. design.md § must_use describes it as a COMPILE warning, and
CLAUDE.md's Mend loop is built on that JSON feed — so a lint the spec mandates
across six stdlib categories reached neither the compile path nor the AI-facing

overrides so text and JSON cannot disagree:

* `render_text_diagnostics` (cli.rs) — rendered there rather than pushed into

title: The `must_use` lint NEVER RUNS under `karac check` or `karac build` -- it fires only under `karac run`, so the entire surface is invisible to `karac check --output=json` and therefore to the Mend loop. `fn main() { let mut m: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new(); m.insert(1, 10); m.get(1); }` -- a discarded `Option` from a LOOKUP, the exact case design.md § must_use exists to catch ("lookups, parses, fallible operations, where the `Option` IS the result") -- gets `warning[must_use]: discarded 'Option' value` under `karac run --interp` AND `karac run`, while `karac check` reports "All checks passed." and `karac build` reports only "Built: mu2.bin". `karac check --output=json` on the same file emits `"diagnostics":[]`. design.md describes must_use as a COMPILE warning ("silently dropping it is a compile warning"), and CLAUDE.md's Mend loop is built on `karac check --output=json` as its diagnostics feed -- so a lint the spec mandates across six stdlib categories reaches neither the compile path nor the AI-facing feed.
detail:
Probe: domain-20 design.md transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d20/{mu1,mu2,sm1}.kara.

MEASURED PER COMMAND on one file (mu2.kara): `karac check` -> All checks passed; `karac check --output=json` -> diagnostics: []; `karac build` -> Built, no warning; `karac run --interp` -> warning emitted; `karac run` -> warning emitted. So the lint exists and is correct -- it is simply wired to the execution path only.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FLAGSHIP FEATURE: a Mend-loop author never sees a must_use diagnostic, so `karac fix` can never offer the `let _ =` repair, and the whole category silently drops out of the machine-fix statistics. The gap is invisible from the statistics themselves, since a diagnostic that is never emitted also never counts as unfixed.

SIBLING: B-2026-08-17-38 is the `SortedMap` hole in this lint's displaced-value exemption list -- a different defect in the same lint, observable only via `karac run`.

fix:
FIXED by f49ed9fc. The row asked which direction to settle the naming and left it open. The counts settle it, and the deciding evidence is INSIDE design.md rather than in the implementation: the spec writes the sorted SET as `SortedSet` 14 times and `TreeSet` zero times, and it pairs `TreeMap` with `SortedSet` in single sentences -- "uses `TreeMap[K, V]` / `SortedSet[T]`", "`Vec`, `Map`, `Set`, `VecDeque`, `TreeMap`, and `SortedSet` implement `Clone`". A `TreeMap`/`SortedSet` pair is incoherent whichever way you read it, so the spec was inconsistent with ITSELF, not merely ahead of the compiler. The implementation's `SortedMap`/`SortedSet` is the coherent pair, and it is what 325 source and 190 test references already say. So: the map is `SortedMap`, and design.md's 12 `TreeMap` mentions were the erratum.

THREE PARTS, one root:

1. THE FUNCTIONAL DEFECT. `displaced_value_exempt` spelled the receiver `"TreeMap"`, so the arm was DEAD -- no such type exists -- and `SortedMap.insert` / `.remove` warned while `Map`, `Vec`, `VecDeque` and `SortedSet` were all exempt. One word. A counterweight test pins that a USER type's `insert` returning `Option` still warns, so widening to the right name did not widen to everything.

2. THE DOCUMENT. 15 bare `TreeMap` occurrences -> `SortedMap`, with the two `BTreeMap` occurrences preserved (the Rust-comparison column should name Rust's type, and `BTreeMap` CONTAINS the substring `TreeMap` -- a naive replace corrupts it, which is why the edit used a negative lookbehind and asserted the `BTreeMap` count was unchanged). Added a dated naming erratum beside the method table, matching the `Bf16`/`BF16` erratum already in the document.

3. THE DIAGNOSTIC, which is the part that matters after the document is corrected. Fixing the spec does not fix what has already been READ from it: anyone -- or any model -- working from the old text writes `TreeMap` and got a bare "undefined type" with no route to the real name, and edit distance cannot bridge `TreeMap` -> `SortedMap`. `renamed_stdlib_type` maps `TreeMap` -> `SortedMap` and `TreeSet` -> `SortedSet` and rides the existing suggestion channel, so the diagnostic NAMES the type and `karac fix` REPAIRS it. Measured end to end: a spec-spelled program goes from two hard resolve errors to a working `SortedMap` program under one `karac fix`.

A HAZARD THIS EXPOSED AND FIXED, found only by running the fix rather than trusting the diagnostic: the `replacement` edits these suggestions carry used the DIAGNOSTIC's span, and those spans are not identifier-sized. A type position spans `TreeMap[i64, i64]` and an associated call spans `TreeMap.new()`, so the first `karac fix` run produced `let mut m: SortedMap = SortedMap;` -- syntactically valid, semantically nonsense, and it does not compile. Every such span starts at the name, so the edit is now clamped to the name's length; a test asserts the edit length is exactly `"TreeMap".len()`. The pre-existing typo path (`helpr(41)` -> `helper(41)`) spans exactly the identifier and is unaffected -- pinned as a control.

NOT DONE: `SortedMap` is still absent from `collect()`'s `FromIterator` targets (B-2026-08-17-36 / -18 / -27 territory) -- the row noted the type could not even be NAMED there, which is no longer true, but the collect-target gap itself is upstream of this row and unchanged by it.
title: `TreeMap[K, V]` -- a standard collection design.md documents 13 times, with its own method table, and prescribes TWICE as the remedy for Map/Set's unstable iteration order -- is an UNDEFINED TYPE. `let mut m: TreeMap[i64, i64] = TreeMap.new();` -> `error[resolve]: undefined type 'TreeMap'` + `undefined name 'TreeMap'`. The implementation ships the same container as `SortedMap`, which design.md mentions exactly ONCE, in passing, inside a naming erratum about `Bf16` (line 2299) -- it appears in none of the collection tables, none of the method tables, and neither of the two "use this for stable iteration" directives (lines 1735 and 9849, the § Map hash-seeding note and the § Determinism list). A user or an LLM following the spec's own advice about non-deterministic Map iteration writes `TreeMap` and gets an undefined-type error with no pointer to the real name. Knock-on: the same mismatch is the most likely cause of the `SortedMap.insert` / `.remove` hole in the must_use displaced-value exemption -- design.md's exemption list names `Map.insert` / `TreeMap.insert` / `Map.remove` / `TreeMap.remove`, and MEASURED, `Map`, `Vec` and `VecDeque` are all exempt while `SortedMap.insert` and `SortedMap.remove` both warn.
detail:
Probe: domain-20 design.md transcription pass; repro /tmp/.../hunt/d20/{tm1,sm1,mu1}.kara.

Every other diagnostic in the compiler uses the display form -- the control one line away in the same probe reads `expected 'Set[i64]', found 'Vec[i64]'`. The five sites are all in src/typechecker/stdlib_iter.rs: line 149 (`filter_map`), 615 (`find_map`), 834 (`flat_map`), 1032 (`scan`), 1191 (`zip`), each formatting the offending type with `{:?}` instead of `type_display`. Line 1032 additionally writes the expected type as `Option<(A, U)>` -- Rust turbofish-style angle brackets in a language whose spec opens with "**Generics syntax:** `[T]` not `<T>` -- no turbofish".

title: Kata 236's 14.5% kāra-only slowdown is CODE PLACEMENT, not a codegen regression — hot code byte-identical, moved 152 bytes; instructions flat to 0.002%
detail:
Re-benching kata 236 (lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree) for
B-2026-08-16-14 moved its kāra lane from 127.89 ms to 146.39 ms, +14.5%, while
every other lane in the SAME run stayed flat:

  lane                          old ms     new ms    delta
  c/lca_binary_tree/seq         105.82     109.61    +3.6%
  go/lca_binary_tree/seq        142.09     142.44    +0.2%
  kara/lca_binary_tree/seq      127.89     146.39   +14.5%
  rust/lca_binary_tree/seq      124.43     124.49    +0.0%
  rust_ovf/lca_binary_tree/seq  124.63     125.21    +0.5%

IT IS NOT THE WORKLOAD, which is the obvious suspect since that re-bench exists
precisely because the generator changed. Held karac fixed at today's build and
varied ONLY the data — pre-fix source against post-fix source, one compiler,
interleaved, min-of-7:

  old-data (pre-fix)   0.140 s
  new-data (widened)   0.140 s
  ratio                1.000

The widening costs this kata nothing. Its own sink moved (3943 -> 4189), so the
data demonstrably changed; the runtime did not follow.

IT IS NOT MACHINE DRIFT. The four sibling lanes above were measured in the same
hyperfine invocation on the same machine and are flat. Nine other katas were
re-benched in the same session and their kāra lanes moved WITH their siblings
every time (135 +1.6% against +1.4..3.9%, 260 +1.5% against +1.8..2.4%, 235
+35.1% against +23.8..35.8%, 287 +49.1% against +50.3..53.3%). 236 is the only
one where kāra moved alone.

THAT LEAVES KARAC. The 127.89 ms figure was measured 2026-07-27; the 146.39 ms
figure today, at 689dadd6. Somewhere in that range kāra got ~14.5% slower on a
recursive post-order tree walk over a 100,000-node index pool with 600 full
queries — an O(n)-per-query recursion, no sort, no Vec growth, no map.

NOT BISECTED, and that is the next step rather than a claim: the endpoints are
whatever karac built the 2026-07-27 lane through 689dadd6, and instruction count
rather than wall time is the right bisect signal for a ~15% move.

CONSEQUENCE ALREADY VISIBLE. The kata's README claim "Kāra beats both Rust
configurations on recursive tree traversal" was true when written and is now
false on the canonical M5 feed (kāra/rust_ovf 1.026x -> 1.169x);
scripts/check-bench-claims.py flags it at 17-18% severity. The claim has been
rescoped to the container snapshot it was measured on and points here, rather
than being suppressed into scripts/bench-claims-baseline.json — that file is for
checker MISPARSES a human has verified, and this is a real contradiction.

SOURCE NOTE: found by the per-lane delta discipline rather than by looking for
it. A data change feeds every lane, so the reading of interest in a re-bench is
whether the lanes move TOGETHER; one that moves alone is a statement about that
lane. Nine katas moved together and this one did not.

RESOLVED — IT IS CODE PLACEMENT, NOT A CODEGEN REGRESSION. The row proposed a
bisect over 1780 commits on instruction count. That bisect would have found
NOTHING, because the instruction count never moved.

ENDPOINTS, each karac built with its own MATCHED runtime archive (a karac from
one commit against another commit's archive can silently miscompile rather than
fail to link, which is what makes an unmatched historical A/B lie):

  arm                      instructions        cycles     IPC
  old  3e9a12ed          3,553,427,061   572,717,771    6.20
  new  689dadd62         3,553,494,994   660,742,808    5.38

Instructions differ by 0.002%. Binary size is IDENTICAL at 34,296 bytes. Cycles
are +15.3% and IPC falls 6.20 -> 5.38. Same work, retired slower.

THE HOT FUNCTION DID NOT CHANGE — IT MOVED. Disassembling both and normalising
self-relative branch targets, the recursive LCA is the SAME 46-instruction
stream in both binaries. Its address moved 0x1000005e8 -> 0x100000680, 152
bytes, because the new compiler emits a println/fwrite helper ahead of it where
the old one emitted the recursion first.

WHY THE PLACEMENT LEVER SAID "NO PLACEMENT EFFECT". A KARAC_TEXT_PAD sweep
across a full 64-byte period on the new binary is flat — 658.6M to 662.7M
cycles, 0.6% spread — which looks like a refutation and is not. TEXT_PAD inserts
one filler ahead of everything and shifts every function by the same constant,
so it explores ABSOLUTE alignment while preserving RELATIVE order. What changed
here is relative order. The lever is structurally blind to it. Any future use of
TEXT_PAD to rule out placement should carry that caveat: a flat pad sweep rules
out alignment, not layout.

BLAST RADIUS: ONE KATA. Same source, both compilers, cycles ratio new/old:

  235 lca_bst      1.001   (instr 1.0001)
  236 lca_bt       1.155   (instr 1.0000)   <-- this row
  252 meeting      0.307   (instr 0.6358)   <-- B-2026-08-16-9 landing
  257 paths        1.010   (instr 0.9921)
  261 valid_tree   1.003   (instr 1.0002)
  287 dup          1.003   (instr 0.9998)

Five of six are flat inside 1%. The one large move in the other direction is the
scatter unswitch, which is the expected 3.3x and doubles as proof the old
compiler really does predate that work. So there is no across-the-board slowdown
to find: 236 lost a coin flip that five siblings won.

AND THE KATA ALREADY SAYS SO. #236 carries an auto-stamped placement caveat
reading "this kata's runtime moves by up to 16% with code placement alone". The
measured effect here is 15.5%. The caveat was not a hedge; it was an accurate
prediction of exactly this, and the 127.89 ms figure the regression was measured
against was a lucky layout rather than a better compiler.

CLOSED AS wontfix RATHER THAN FIXED OR INVALID. The behaviour is real and
reproduces exactly; what was wrong was the attribution, so `invalid` would write
a false claim into the ledger. And there is no targeted fix: karac does not
choose function emission order on any performance principle, so "put the
recursion back first" is not a change with a defensible rule behind it. A real
fix is a layout policy — frequency-ordered emission, or a BOLT-style post-link
pass — which is a design direction needing corpus-wide validation, not a repair
to this row. Cross-referenced to the placement infrastructure in
[[B-2026-08-07-10]] (the KARAC_TEXT_PAD lever) and placement-spread.json.

THE TRANSFERABLE PART: instruction count and cycle count disagreeing is the
signal that separates "the compiler does more work" from "the compiler's output
landed badly", and it is much cheaper to collect than a bisect. Checking it
FIRST turned a projected ~2-hour 11-step bisect into two builds and a
disassembly diff. The row's own recommendation — bisect on instruction count —
was the right instinct applied one step too late: the instruction count should
have been compared at the endpoints before assuming there was a trail to
follow.

fix:
One-line lowering fix in `exhaustive::lower_pattern`'s `Binding` arm: take the
LAST dotted segment of the binding name before testing it against the
scrutinee enum's variant names, and use that segment as the ctor name.

WHY THAT IS THE WHOLE FIX. The parser has no `Path` pattern kind, so a
QUALIFIED payload-free variant pattern is stored as the whole dotted string --
`Binding("Dir.North")` (src/parser/patterns.rs, "Just a binding with a
qualified name (unit variant)"). The `Binding` arm compared that string to the
enum's BARE variant names, never matched, and fell through to `Pat::Wildcard`.
The sibling arms never had the bug because `TupleVariant` and `Struct` already
call `path.last()`; this makes the unit-variant arm do the same, so the two
spellings lower to the SAME ctor and unify in the matrix. An undotted name is
its own last segment, so a genuine binding pattern (`match d { x => ... }`)
still produces the wildcard it always did -- the fix cannot turn a catch-all
into a non-catch-all.

WHAT THE WILDCARD FALLTHROUGH COST, in both directions at once:

  * EXHAUSTIVENESS (the soundness half). `match d { Dir.North => 0 }` over
    `enum Dir { North, South }` was reported EXHAUSTIVE and passed
    `karac check`, then failed differently on each backend: the interpreter
    raised its own "internal error: non-exhaustive match ... (the typechecker
    should have rejected this)", `karac run` (JIT) died with a stack overflow,
    and `karac build` exited 48 with no output and no diagnostic. Now
    rejected at check with the same message the bare spelling always got
    ("non-exhaustive match: missing variants: South").
  * REACHABILITY (the noise half). Because the first qualified arm covered
    everything, EVERY later arm read as `unreachable_arm` -- including payload
    arms in a mixed enum (`Mix.A => 0, Mix.B(x) => x` flagged the `B` arm) and
    the stdlib spelling (`Option.None` / `Option.Some(v)`).

MEASURED ON THE CORPUS (400 files across examples/ + kara-katas):

  * `unreachable_arm` warnings 11 -> 1, i.e. TEN OF ELEVEN were false
    positives from this bug. The survivor is not a regression and not
    genuine either: it is a module file checked STANDALONE, where the
    imported enum type is not in scope, so the unknown-type conservatism
    (correctly) produces a wildcard. Checked through its own entry module
    (`karac check src/main.kara`) that project reports zero.
  * The set of files failing `karac check` is BYTE-IDENTICAL before and
    after (15 files, all pre-existing failures unrelated to matches). A fix
    that can only ADD errors needed that check, and it came back clean: no
    corpus program was relying on the hole.

THE BOOK HAD ALREADY DOCUMENTED THE MISSING ERROR, and the doc-test harness
was certifying its absence. `docs/book/src/ch06-pattern-matching.md` §
Exhaustiveness carries a snippet whose own comment reads "compile error:
non-exhaustive match -- Color.Blue not covered", in a plain ```kara fence that
`tests/book_snippets.rs` compiles EXPECTING SUCCESS. It passed only because
this bug accepted it: the chapter that teaches exhaustiveness shipped a
counter-example the compiler certified as valid Kāra. With the fix the
compiler emits exactly the promised diagnostic, so the fence is annotated
```kara,ignore` (the book's established convention for deliberate compile
errors, 73 other uses) with a comment recording why. That the suite caught
this is the point: it is a third symptom, and a better one than any synthetic
repro, because the defect had quietly invalidated the documentation for the
feature it broke.

NOT A LOWERING BUG, which is why no runtime behaviour changed. Both compiled
backends and the interpreter always SELECTED the right arm for a qualified
match (verified before the fix: a complete 4-variant qualified match printed
identical output under `--interp`, `karac build`, and the JIT). The defect was
confined to the analysis, so the fix removes false diagnostics and adds true
ones without touching codegen.

TESTS: six typechecker cases -- the accepted-non-exhaustive shape and its bare
control (pinned together so the two spellings can never diverge again), the
absent false warning on a complete qualified match and on a qualified-before-
payload match, a nested `Option[Dir]` witness, plus two REGRESSION GUARDS that
must pass both before and after: a duplicated arm is still flagged (with a
bare arm now correctly covering a later qualified one), and an undotted
binding still binds. Four of the six are baseline-red (verified by reverting
the fix alone: 4 failed, the two guards passed). An interpreter oracle and its
codegen E2E twin pin that arm selection stayed correct on all three backends.
title: A QUALIFIED payload-free variant pattern (`Dir.North`) lowers to a WILDCARD in the exhaustiveness engine, so it silently covers the whole scrutinee: a genuinely non-exhaustive `match d { Dir.North => 0 }` over `enum Dir { North, South }` passes `karac check` and then diverges three ways at runtime -- the interpreter raises "internal error: non-exhaustive match ... (the typechecker should have rejected this)", `karac run` (JIT) dies with a stack overflow, and `karac build` exits 48 with NO output and no diagnostic. The bare-variant spelling of the same match (`North => 0`) is correctly rejected with "non-exhaustive match: missing variants: South", which is the control that isolates the qualifier as the trigger. Same root cause makes every arm after a qualified payload-free arm read as `unreachable_arm` (a Deny-able lint), so the canonical spelling of an enum match is simultaneously under-checked for exhaustiveness and over-warned for reachability.
detail:
ROOT CAUSE, located: the parser has no `Path` pattern kind, so a dotted PAYLOAD-FREE variant pattern is stored as `PatternKind::Binding(path.join("."))` -- literally `Binding("Dir.North")` (src/parser/patterns.rs:498, comment "Just a binding with a qualified name (unit variant)"). `exhaustive::lower_pattern`'s `Binding` arm then asks whether the binding name is one of the scrutinee enum's variants by comparing the WHOLE dotted string against bare variant names (`info.variants.iter().any(|(v, _)| v == name)`, src/exhaustive.rs ~line 558). "Dir.North" never equals "North", so the arm falls through to `Pat::Wildcard` -- a catch-all. From there both consequences follow mechanically: `check_match_exhaustive` sees a wildcard row and reports Exhaustive, and `unreachable_arms` sees a covering wildcard and flags every later arm. The payload forms are UNAFFECTED because they parse as `PatternKind::TupleVariant`/`Struct`, whose lowering takes `path.last()` -- which is exactly the qualifier-stripping step the `Binding` arm is missing.

MEASURED BOUNDARY (all on HEAD c4fafa3 + this session's working tree; the change under test touches neither matches nor exhaustiveness):
  rejected correctly:  `match d { North => 0 }`                bare unit variant
  ACCEPTED (unsound):  `match d { Dir.North => 0 }`            qualified unit variant
  no false warning:    `Shape.Circle(r) => ...` + `Shape.Square(w) => ...`  payload variants
  no false warning:    bare `North => 0, South => 1`
  FALSE `unreachable_arm` on every later arm:  `Dir.North => 0, Dir.South => 1`
     (a 4-variant qualified match emits 3 such warnings; `Mix.A => 0, Mix.B(x) => x` flags the PAYLOAD arm too, so a mixed enum is affected as soon as one earlier arm is a qualified unit variant)
  affects the stdlib spelling too: `Option.None => 0, Option.Some(v) => v` warns on the `Some` arm.

THREE-BACKEND DIVERGENCE on the accepted-but-unsound program (`fn show(d: Dir) -> i64 { match d { Dir.North => 0 } }` called with `Dir.South`):
  `karac run --interp`  runtime error: internal error: non-exhaustive match at 4:5 -- no arm matched the scrutinee value (the typechecker should have rejected this)
  `karac run` (JIT)     thread 'main' has overflowed its stack / fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
  `karac build` (AOT)   exits 48, prints nothing, no diagnostic
The interpreter's message is the honest one and names the correct culprit; the two compiled backends are the reason this is filed high rather than as a diagnostics row.

WHY IT IS HIGH. A missing arm is the exact class the exhaustiveness engine exists to catch, and the spelling that defeats it is the qualified one -- the form a reader reaches for when the bare variant name is ambiguous, and the form the compiler's own corpus uses (tests/interpreter.rs:510, tests/codegen.rs:6190/42730). Nothing in the pipeline compensates: the type checker is satisfied, the reachability lint is actively misleading in the opposite direction, and the failure surfaces as a stack overflow or a silent wrong-exit in the compiled backends.

SOURCE NOTE: found while verifying B-2026-08-17-19 (call-site default parameters) -- a throwaway `enum Direction` repro warned about an arm that plainly ran, which is what prompted the probe. NOT caused by that change (reproduced on a clean checkout of 04747a7 before it, and the fix touches only call arguments). Filed rather than fixed to keep the -19 commit scoped; the fix is small (strip the qualifier before the variant-name comparison, the same `path.last()` step the sibling arms already do) but it moves the exhaustiveness engine and deserves its own full-gate run -- and its own baseline-red tests for BOTH halves (the accepted non-exhaustive match and the false unreachable_arm).

detail:
DUPLICATE. B-2026-08-17-29 describes the same defect and was filed FIRST, from a design.md transcription probe; this row came out of the B-2026-08-17-25 follow-up pass and is the less informative of the two. Filed without grepping the ledger for an existing row on the same subject -- the check that would have caught it is one `grep` over open rows before filing. Work B-2026-08-17-29; this row closes with it.

FOUND by B-2026-08-17-25's loud `compile_expr` bail, not by a probe: `ExprKind::Range` is one of the kinds that had no arm and fell to the catch-all's constant 0. Since that fix it FAILS THE BUILD by name ("no handler for expression kind Range") instead of silently emitting a zero, which is why this row can state the old behaviour precisely -- it was measured by temporarily restoring the zero.

WHY THE LOOP PRINTED NOTHING rather than looping wrong: the range collapsed to the integer 0, so the `for` had no bounds to walk. The failure is therefore silent in the worst way -- a loop that does nothing looks like a loop whose condition was false.

SCOPE. The inline `for i in 0..n` form is handled by the for-loop lowering, which destructures the `Range` node itself and never routes it through `compile_expr`; the same is true of a range used directly as a slice subscript (`v[0..2]`). Only a range that must exist AS A VALUE -- bound to a `let`, passed as an argument, returned -- reaches the missing arm. That also means the fix is not a small one: a range value needs a representation (a two-word {start, end} struct at minimum, plus inclusive/exclusive and open-ended forms) that nothing in codegen currently has.

NOT FIXED IN B-2026-08-17-25's PASS: that row is about `|>` and the silent-default class; implementing range values is a feature, and bundling it would have made both harder to review. The loud bail is the correct interim state -- a build error naming the gap is strictly better than a running program that skips its loop.

FIXED by 26b320c2. The row asked for the scope to be checked before fixing, and the check changed the shape of the answer: it was not `Slice`, it was every builtin container head EXCEPT the four that had been hit before. Measured by binding `self` to a deliberately wrong annotation and reading the "found" type out of the error, one head per line -- args KEPT by `Vec`, `VecDeque`, `Column`, `Tensor`; args LOST by `Slice`, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `SortedMap`, `SortedSet`, `Option`, `Result`, `Vector`. The keep-list had grown one head at a time as each was hit (Column/Tensor for a reduction intercept, then Vec/VecDeque for a fold), so the set was an accident of discovery order rather than a decision.

THE LIST EXISTED TWICE, hand-mirrored, which is why widening it was the smaller half of the work: `TypeChecker::check_impl_block` types `self` for the BODY, and `closure_escape::make_impl_method_function` synthesizes the `self` PARAM whose TypeExpr codegen registers its per-name side-tables from. Both now call one `impl_dispatch::impl_head_keeps_type_args`. `src/impl_dispatch.rs` is where it belongs: that module exists precisely so the emitters and the dispatch sites cannot disagree about an impl head, and its doc says so.

TWO ARMS, NOT ONE, on the typechecker side. `Slice`, `Array` and `Vector` lower to DEDICATED `Type` variants rather than to `Named`, so for them the fallback did more than erase args -- it replaced the VARIANT with `Named { name: "Slice" }`, and every consumer that matches on the variant (the index rule, slice method dispatch, element-type reads) stopped recognizing `self` as a slice at all. Both arms are guarded on `type_is_fully_concrete`, which is what keeps the fallback's real job intact: erasing args off a GENERIC head, so `impl Foo[T]`'s `self` is still `Foo`. A test pins that half.

CODEGEN NEEDED ITS OWN EDIT, and the typechecker fix alone would have been a false green. `self[0]` arrives as `ExprKind::SelfValue`, and `compile_index`'s Slice and Map arms keyed on `Identifier` only -- so even with the element type registered, the body fell through to "Index operator applied to non-array type" while `--interp` read the element. The Column/Tensor and Vec arms already accepted both spellings; the Slice arm now does too.

THE MAP ARM IS DELIBERATELY NARROWER, and the reason is worth reading before widening it. Routed unconditionally, an OWNED `self` on a Map head does not fail -- it SEGFAULTS, because the slot does not hold the handle `compile_map_index` loads. So the map arm is gated on `signature_ref_params.contains("self")`: `ref self` works (42 on all three backends) and the owned spelling keeps its loud build error. B-2026-08-18-11 carries that measurement.

MEASURED AFTER, interpreter / JIT / `karac build` all agreeing: `Slice` element read 10 on owned AND `ref` self; `Option[i64].unwrap_or` 9 and 0; `Map[String, i64]` read by String key 42 on `ref self`.

IT ALSO REPAIRED TWO SILENT WRONG ANSWERS, which were the shapes that never announced themselves. `for x in self` over a `Slice[i64]` or `Set[i64]` head TYPECHECKED before -- iteration does not need the element type the way `self[0]` does -- so it built, and the compiled binary summed nothing while the interpreter summed correctly. Pre-fix 12 / 0, post-fix 12 / 12, with a free-function `Set[i64]` PARAMETER as the control that was 12 / 12 all along.

FOUR REMAINDERS, each filed rather than folded in: an owned `self` container receiver is not lowered at all (B-2026-08-18-11, still 12 / 0 for Set iteration); `self.len()` on a Map/Set head has no dispatcher on either receiver mode (B-2026-08-18-12); an `impl ... for Array[i64, N]` method cannot be CALLED, "no method 'g' on type 'Array'", which this fix unmasked by making the body check (B-2026-08-18-13); and a range subscript used directly as a method receiver has no codegen (B-2026-08-18-14).

THE SELF-CONTRADICTING DIAGNOSTIC the row asked about is gone by construction rather than by rewording: the receiver types correctly, so nothing calls `Slice[T]` unindexable while its own help text lists it as indexable.

title: Moving an `Option`-TYPED FIELD out of a matched struct payload DOUBLE FREES under both compiled backends, on a program `karac check` passes clean and `--interp` runs correctly. Minimal: `struct C { name: String, zip: i64 } struct A { c: Option[C] }` plus `let f = match a { Some(x) => { x.c } None => { None } };` where `a: Option[A]` -- `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`, abort, under both `karac run` (JIT) and `karac build` (AOT). The interpreter prints the right answer. No `?.`, no closure, no generic involved.
detail:
FOUND while implementing B-2026-08-17-28 (`?.`): this is the exact shape `?.` must lower to for its FLATTEN case (`a?.f` where `f` is itself an `Option`), so it blocks that row's codegen leg. It is filed separately because it is reachable with no `?.` anywhere -- the hand-written `match` above is the whole repro.

TRIGGER BOUNDARY, measured one variable at a time. The double free needs ALL of:
  * the scrutinee is an `Option[A]` matched with `Some(x)`;
  * the arm PROJECTS A FIELD out of `x` (an arm that ignores the payload, or that never runs the projection, is clean);
  * that field's type is itself an `Option[C]` -- an `Option[i64]` or `Option[String]` field is CLEAN, and so is a non-`Option` field of any type including `String`;
  * `C` is a MULTI-FIELD struct containing a `String`. `C { name: String }` alone is clean; `C { name: String, zip: i64 }` aborts.

The last two together point at the boxed-payload path: a multi-word struct payload is boxed in the Option, and the arm's move-out appears to take the box without the source's deep drop being suppressed, so the interior `String` is freed by both.

INDEPENDENT OF WHAT THE RESULT IS USED FOR: the abort happens even when the projected value is bound and never read, and whether the scrutinee is a binding or a fresh temp. Wrapping instead of flattening (`Some(x.tag)`) is clean, which is what isolates it to the move-out rather than the match itself.

NOT ATTEMPTED IN B-2026-08-17-28's PASS. The per-arm suppression block in src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs is a dozen interacting suppressors, each gated on a measurement tied to its own ledger row; adding one needs its own ASAN pass across the existing fixture set rather than a change made in passing.

INVESTIGATION 777f4e75 — not fixed; the mechanism is now mapped end to end, and
the fix needs new bookkeeping rather than a wiring change. Recorded in full so
the next attempt starts from the measurements instead of re-deriving them.

WHERE THE SECOND FREE COMES FROM, read off the emitted IR for the minimal
repro (`cargo run --features llvm --example dump_ir`):

    %opt.move.tag = getelementptr ... ptr %sfld.move.p, i32 0, i32 0
    store i64 0, ptr %opt.move.tag          <- a tag zero DOES fire
    ...
    call void @__karac_drop_struct_C(ptr %f_box_ptr)   <- the move's owner
    call void @free(ptr %f_box_ptr)
    ...
    call void @__karac_drop_struct_A(ptr %a_box_ptr)   <- frees `c` AGAIN

The arm binding `x` is a DEBOXED COPY of the `A` inside `a`'s payload box. The
tag zero lands in that copy; the drop that frees `c` is
`__karac_drop_struct_A(a_box_ptr)`, which reads the `A` still inside the box
and cannot see the copy. So the field is freed by the box's drop AND by the
binding the move handed it to.

THREE THINGS ARE MISSING, each measured rather than inferred:

  1. THERE IS NO SUPPRESSION SITE FOR AN ARM-TAIL FIELD MOVE. The three that
     exist are `let` (`track_place_optres_field_move`), assign
     (`suppress_place_optres_field_move_source`) and call-argument
     (`suppress_place_optres_field_whole_move_source`). A tail-position move
     out of the arm binding hits none of them. Wiring one in at the
     post-`compile_tail_final_expr` block is straightforward and was tried.

  2. THE ADMISSION CLASS DECLINES THIS SHAPE ANYWAY. With the site wired,
     `place_optres_field_move_info_ex(x.c, whole_move=false)` returns None at
     the `!admitted` gate (instrumented and confirmed: `obj_ty=A`, field type
     path fine, NOT ADMITTED). The narrow class deliberately excludes a
     struct/enum payload -- its doc records that widening it turned a single
     free into a leak -- and the WHOLE class deliberately excludes a BOXED
     payload (B-2026-08-06-10). The clean `let` spelling does not go through
     either: it is `suppress_struct_field_move_into_literal` (param_own.rs),
     firing on a real local slot.

  3. THE MIRROR CHANNEL IS EMPTY FOR THIS SHAPE, and this is the blocker.
     B-2026-08-06-10's comment names the fix -- "the other half is the
     `deboxed_payload_box_ptrs` mirror, which zeroes that field's `cap` THROUGH
     the box so this drop skips exactly what the move took. Pair them or
     neither" -- and `suppress_destructured_struct_field_enum_cleanup` already
     recurses through that map for a DESTRUCTURE of the same binding. But the
     map is EMPTY here: measured `deboxed_payload_box_ptrs.len() == 0` at the
     arm site. It is armed only when the scrutinee is an owned PARAM
     (`scrutinee_is_owned_param_binding` -> `pattern_binding_scrutinee_is_owned_param`),
     and this scrutinee is a LOCAL. So there is no recorded box pointer to
     mirror through, and the fix has to record one at the deboxing site for the
     local-scrutinee case before any suppression can use it.

WHAT A FIX LOOKS LIKE: populate the box-pointer map when an arm binding is
deboxed from a LOCAL enum scrutinee too, then wire the arm-tail move site to
write both the copy and the box (a `base_override` on
`suppress_struct_field_move_into_literal` is enough for the second write --
that variant was written and works, it simply has no box pointer to be given).
Then re-run the -O0 ASAN leg: every neighbouring suppressor's doc records a
measurement where widening turned a double free into a leak, so the leak side
has to be checked, not assumed.

STILL BLOCKS B-2026-08-17-28 leg (3): `?.`'s flatten case lowers to exactly
this shape.
tracker: src/codegen/control_flow_match.rs (arm-tail move site, ~line 868 after `compile_tail_final_expr`; the admission classes at `place_optres_field_move_info_ex`), src/codegen/param_own.rs (`suppress_struct_field_move_into_literal`), and wherever an arm binding is deboxed — `deboxed_payload_box_ptrs` must be populated for a LOCAL enum scrutinee, not just an owned param, before any suppression can mirror through the box.

FIXED by 0dfeb3d. THE ROW'S OWN INVESTIGATION NAMED THREE MISSING PIECES; TWO OF THEM WERE NOT MISSING, which is why the landed diff is one condition rather than a new suppressor. Finding (1) said no suppression site exists for an arm-tail field move: a panic-backtrace off the emitting site shows the arm body is a BLOCK, so `suppress_block_tail_cleanup` -> `suppress_source_vec_cleanup_for_arg_ex` -> `zero_struct_field_move_cap_inst` already fires on this exact shape. Finding (2) said the admission class declines it and a `base_override` would be needed to reach the box: that site already carries B-2026-08-06-10's box mirror, wired and waiting. Only finding (3) held -- `deboxed_payload_box_ptrs` was empty, so the mirror had no box pointer to write through.

ROOT CAUSE, confirmed against the emitted IR before any change. `match.body0` deboxes the payload into `%x`, a private load of the box `%a` still owns. The neutralizing `store i64 0, ptr %opt.move.tag` lands in `%x`; the drop that frees the field is `__karac_drop_struct_A(%a_box_ptr)`, which reads the box and cannot see the copy. So the field is freed by the box's drop AND by the binding the move handed it to.

THE FIX is in `record_deboxed_payload_box`, which recorded the box ONLY for an owned-param scrutinee. Its reasoning was that an in-frame owner is a `BoxedEnumDrop` this frame can RETRACT (B-2026-08-04-2) -- true, but retraction is WHOLE-ACTION, so it covers the whole payload escaping and nothing else. A single-field move has no action to retract, because the box's drop must still run for every field the move did not take. Record for an in-frame owner too and the existing mirror does the rest.

THE REFUSAL'S MEASUREMENT IS PRESERVED, NOT OVERRIDDEN, and this is the part worth reading before touching it again. That comment records that the box's words are also what a re-homed payload-BODIES walk reads, and that zeroing them once turned a double free into a user Drop body printing an EMPTY STRING -- a memory bug traded for a silent wrong value. The widening is therefore gated on the flag the codebase already computes for exactly that condition, `pattern_binding_scrutinee_payload_bodies_src`, which is `Some` only when the payload runs a user Drop. With it `None` the box's only reader is a compiler-generated MEMORY drop and a per-field zero is neutralization rather than corruption; with it `Some`, nothing is recorded and the shape stays byte-identical.

THE USER-`Drop` SPELLING IS STILL BROKEN and is NOT closed by this row. Measured with the fix reverted and applied: byte-identical `AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free` both times, so it is pre-existing rather than a regression, and it is precisely the shape the gate above excludes. Filed as its own row -- closing it needs a channel that narrows the OWNER's walk rather than overwriting the box's data, which is bookkeeping neither channel has today.

THE LEAK SIDE IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED, because every neighbouring suppressor's doc records having traded a double free for a leak at least once. The ASAN fixture carries three legs: the MOVED field, a KEPT leg over a struct with a SECOND owning field the move does not take (a too-wide zero surfaces there as a leak rather than a crash), and a `None` source (the direction where an over-eager zero strands a payload). LSan is clean on all three, and the full `memory_sanitizer` corpus went 1116 -> 1118 passed with 0 failed.

TESTS: `asan_boxed_option_local_scrutinee_field_move_out_no_leak_no_double_free` (tests/memory_sanitizer.rs) plus a value twin `test_e2e_local_scrutinee_option_field_move_out_runs` (tests/codegen.rs) -- the defect ABORTED rather than printing a wrong answer, so the value assertion catches the opposite failure mode, a neutralizer firing too widely and printing empty while ASAN stays quiet. Coverage is stronger than the sibling B-2026-08-06-10 fixture's, which only bites at `-O0`: against the pre-fix compiler this one SEGVs under ASAN at BOTH `-O2` and `KARAC_OPT_LEVEL=0`. Full `--features llvm` suite green (106 targets, 13962 passed, 0 failed) with `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`.

FIXED by ea53727a for the SINGLE-FILE build path. The row's diagnosis was right and its mechanism was one line off: `cmd_build` does have a diagnostic renderer, but it calls it ONLY inside `if pipeline.has_fatal_errors()`. So the path that actually produces a binary dropped the entire diagnostic stream -- not a missing render surface, an unreachable one. Everything the compiler had already computed was thrown away between the checks and the `Built:` line.

FIXED BY FILTERING THE SHARED RENDERER, not by writing a second one. `render_text_warning_diagnostics` is `render_text_diagnostics` with the non-`warning[` blocks dropped, and `collect_warning_diagnostics_json` is `collect_diagnostics` with the non-warning entries dropped. That is the same shape B-2026-08-05-17 used when it fixed the effect-gate version of this class -- "one classifier, shared by every gate, so the lanes cannot drift apart again" -- and it is why the test asserts `build`'s warning line EQUALS `check`'s rather than matching a hardcoded string: a drift in wording between the lanes is the regression worth catching.

THE THREE DECISIONS THE ROW ASKED FOR, made explicitly:
  * WHICH DIAGNOSTICS: warning-severity only. `note[...]` is excluded -- those are advisory hints (FFI lint notes, the wasm-tools note) rather than findings about the program, and printing them on every build is noise this row did not ask for. Non-fatal ERROR-severity blocks are excluded too: `build` continuing past them is existing, deliberate behaviour and surfacing them is a separate decision.
  * `--output=json`: warnings ride the SUCCESS object under `diagnostics`, and ONLY when there are some. A consumer reading `status`/`output` sees no new key on a clean build, which is what keeps the kata corpus and the Mend baselines reading build output exactly as before. A test pins the absent-key case.
  * EXISTING EXPECTATIONS: text warnings go to stderr, `Built: ...` stays on stdout, so a consumer parsing stdout is untouched. Full suite green.

title: `karac build` renders NO warning-level diagnostic on a successful build -- the suppression is GLOBAL to the build path, not a `must_use` wiring quirk. Control measurement: `deprecated`, which reaches the user through a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT channel from must_use (the typechecker's `type_lint_warning` / `TypeErrorKind::Deprecated` at src/typechecker.rs:3098-3113, not the `cmd_run` lint block), behaves IDENTICALLY -- emitted under `karac run`, absent under `karac build`. STRUCTURAL CORROBORATION (this session, on 23d6747): `grep -c 'warning\[' src/cli/build_cmds.rs` -> 3, and all three are manifest/monomorphization-budget sites (lines 1363, 3523, plus the render helper at 715).
