Three were Rust path syntax in expression position -- `host::close`, `File::open`, `log::error` -> `.` -- which design.md itself specifies as `.` (§ Modules, `myapp.db.UserDB`); each was reported AS an `Expected Semicolon` (`found ColonColon`) and blocked the terminator measurement of its block. The fourth is `unsafe { *out = parse(s).unwrap() }` -> `...unwrap(); }`: a genuine terminator, but on a statement INSIDE a single-line block, so it goes before the `}` rather than at end-of-line and no line-based pass can place it.

THE SCAN WAS ALSO WIDER THAN THE ROW'S. The original harness anchored its fence match at column 0 and never saw INDENTED ```kara fences (blocks nested in list items). The new gate finds them, which is how the § structured-logging block -- a missing `;` on an `import`, where every other import in the document carries one -- was caught at all.

GATED by `design_md_statements_carry_their_terminating_semicolon` in tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs, which calls `karac::parse` in-process rather than shelling out, and reports both the line to fix and the line the parser stopped at. It checks that ONE diagnostic rather than "every block parses", because most blocks are deliberate fragments. Its allow-list is two entries, each naming its row, and a sibling test asserts every entry still fires -- so a fixed row cannot leave a stale entry silently covering a future regression. Verified non-vacuous: removing one `;` fails the gate with the right line.

ONE MORE ROW CAME OUT OF DOING THIS BY HAND: B-2026-08-18-43. Writing a parser-driven fixer raised the question of why the compiler was not doing it, and `Expected Semicolon` turns out to carry no machine-applicable `replacement`, so `karac fix` reports it and changes nothing -- while a sibling parse diagnostic (stray comma in a `with` clause) does emit one and gets applied. That is the most actionable of the three follow-ups: the insertion offset is exact at the raise site, and this is the most common parse error in the corpus.

title: `compile_method_call`'s `args_close_span` parameter is now a REDUNDANT second key: it exists only to disambiguate side-table reads across a chain, and B-2026-08-18-24 made `call_span` unique per chain step, which is the job it was hired for.
detail:
Its own doc states the premise -- "parser sets `MethodCall.span == receiver.span`, so `call_span` collides across a chain" -- and that premise is false as of B-2026-08-18-24. The parameter threads through ~12 sites in `src/codegen/method_call.rs` plus `method_call_key`, and the `method_unwrap_*` tables still INSERT under it, so it is not a free deletion: producer and consumer have to move together, exactly as the four postfix-span rows did. Collapsing the pair back onto `call_span` is mechanical but wants its own change and its own suite run. The comment at the parameter has been corrected in the meantime, so nobody re-derives the obsolete rationale.

A sibling of the same kind: `try_compile_freshtemp_user_method` carries a fallback whose comment says "the chained-call span collision leaves only ONE `method_callee_types` entry per chain". That collision is gone too; the fallback is now dead weight rather than load-bearing. Worth auditing in the same pass -- and worth CHECKING rather than assuming, since a fallback that is dead for the reason stated may still be live for another.
tracker: src/codegen/method_call.rs (the `args_close_span` parameter and its ~12 call sites); `method_call_key`; `try_compile_freshtemp_user_method`.
fix:
REFUTED by af6c5a70. PREMISE REFUTED, and the refutation is the deliverable. The row says `args_close_span` is "now a REDUNDANT second key". It is not. Its METHOD-CHAIN rationale did expire with B-2026-08-18-24, exactly as the row states -- but the parameter has a second, live client the row did not enumerate, and collapsing the key breaks it.

MEASURED, not argued. `method_call_key` was collapsed to the receiver span (the whole change the row asks for, in one line) and the suite run:

    passed=14057 failed=0

A green suite, and the change is WRONG. `outer(1) ?? mid(5) ?? -1` fails to build under it:

    codegen: Option/Result method 'unwrap_or' expected struct receiver,
             got IntValue(... %uo.val = phi i64 ...)

while the pristine build compiles it and agrees with the interpreter (11 / -1 / -1).

THE CLIENT IS `??`. `NilCoalesce` still copies its LHS's span, so both nodes of `a ?? b ?? c` carry `a`'s span, and `ast::desugar_nil_coalesce` passes the FALLBACK's span in the args-close slot precisely because that is what differs per node. Drop the args-close preference and the outer `??` reads the INNER's payload type -- `i64` where `Option[i64]` was due.

WHY THE SUITE MISSED IT. The only chained-`??` coverage in the tree is `tests/typechecker.rs:6374`, `find(1) ?? (find(7) ?? -1)` -- PARENTHESIZED, which puts the inner node inside the parens and gives the two distinct spans anyway, and it asserts no runtime value. A left chain is also awkward to reach: `a ?? b` already unwraps one layer, so `find(2) ?? find(3) ?? -1` over `Option[i64]` is a type error rather than a chain. The smallest genuine chain needs a nested `Option` payload, which is why nobody had written one.

LANDED INSTEAD OF THE COLLAPSE:

  * `chained_nil_coalesce_keeps_its_two_nodes_apart` (tests/codegen.rs) -- the gate that was missing. Verified in both directions: green on the current tree, and it reproduces the exact "expected struct receiver, got IntValue" failure under the collapsed key. A future attempt now gets a red suite instead of a false green.
  * The two docs that encoded the obsolete model are corrected -- `token.rs`'s `method_call_key` and the `args_close_span` parameter comment in `compile_method_call`. Both now say what is true: the method-chain reason is gone, `??` is the live client, and retiring the parameter means widening `NilCoalesce` FIRST.

THE FULL INVENTORY, since the family kept discovering its own members one at a time. SEVEN parser arms still copy `lhs.span`: `Cast`, `TupleIndex`, `Call`, `Path`, `Pipe`, `NilCoalesce`, `Range`. Five were fixed (`?.`, `?`, `Index`, `MethodCall`, `FieldAccess`); these seven were never enumerated anywhere. Filed as B-2026-08-18-33, which is the row that actually unblocks this one.

NOT WONTFIX: the cleanup is still wanted, it just has a prerequisite the row did not know about. Closed as invalid because the stated premise -- "redundant" -- was tested and is false.

title: `FieldAccess` nodes still copy their object's span -- a FIFTH postfix arm with the identical defect the four-row family (`?.`, `?`, `Index`, `MethodCall`) just finished closing. `v[0]` and `v[0].second` share one SpanKey.
detail:
NOT in the family's inventory, and found only because closing the fourth arm exposed it. While `MethodCall` also copied its object's span, three nodes of `v[0].second.len()` shared one key and whichever wrote last was what every consumer read. B-2026-08-18-24 removed one writer, and the survivor at that key became `v[0].second`'s `Vec[i64]` -- so `receiver_struct_inst`, asked about `v[0]`, answered with its FIELD's type. `resolve_generic_field_te` then found a head of `Vec` where it wanted `Pair`, skipped the generic substitution, and the synth field element registered as the bare param `B`: `v[0].second.len()` loud-bailed with "no handler for method 'len' on variable '__field_elem_0'" -- the exact diagnostic B-2026-07-15-20 fixed, reappearing through a different door.

FIXED AT THAT CONSUMER, not at the parser: `receiver_struct_inst` now asks the structural walk first and the span table second (the discriminator B-2026-08-18-14 established). So there is no known live victim today. The row stays open because the collision itself is still there, and the family's whole record is that such a collision is a trap for the NEXT consumer keyed on a postfix node's span, not a bug in the current ones.

WHAT THE FOUR PRIOR ROWS SAY THE ATTEMPT COSTS, in order: record producer and consumer on one key FIRST, widen SECOND; re-measure the fallout rather than trusting a stale count (B-2026-08-18-24 was filed at 21+16 failures and measured 42); and budget for the two self-host oracles, which compare Kara-vs-Rust span for span and so break on any seed-parser span change -- `selfhost/src/parser.kara`'s `finish_dot` FIELD arm is the twin to widen.
tracker: src/parser/exprs.rs (the `Token::Dot` field-access arm, `span: lhs.span`); selfhost/src/parser.kara `finish_dot`; src/codegen/expr_ops.rs `receiver_struct_inst` for the consumer that already compensates.
fix:
FIXED by 399c7a68. The FIFTH and final postfix arm. `FieldAccess` now spans lhs-start -> past the field name, joining `?.` (B-2026-08-18-7), `?` (B-2026-08-18-9), `Index` (B-2026-08-18-21) and `MethodCall` (B-2026-08-18-24). No postfix node in the seed parser copies its object's span any more.

TWELVE FAILURES, against 42 for the `MethodCall` arm -- and the shape of the difference is the useful part. `MethodCall`'s fallout was spread across four unrelated mechanisms (fresh-temp dispatch, for-loop ownership, generic field resolution, slice borrows). This one was a SINGLE mechanism, hit through three doors: 6 codegen + 4 memory_sanitizer tests, all in the B-2026-08-13-14 use-after-move defensive-copy family, plus the customary 2 self-host oracles.

ONE PRODUCER, THREE READERS, ONE WRONG KEY. `use_classifier`'s `record_place_at_root` states its contract in its own name and doc -- a place consume is recorded "against the ROOT identifier's span", so `let t = b.a;` records at `b`, not at `b.a`. All three place-shaped readers in `src/codegen/runtime.rs` -- `uam_defensive_copy_field`, `uam_reclone_source_field`, `uam_defensive_copy_tuple_elem` -- looked the site up at their OWN node's span instead, which resolved only because `FieldAccess` and `TupleIndex` copy their object's. Separate them and every lookup misses: no defensive copy is made, the source disarm still fires, and the reused field is a stale alias. Measured on `test_e2e_field_bound_out_of_local_is_a_copy`: `hi1 hi1 1 1 x1 1 0 panic: vec index out of bounds` against an expected `... 1 y1 7`.

The fix is one shared helper, `uam_consume_root_span`, walking a place to its root, plus `uam_consume_site_at_root` wrapping the lookup -- so all three readers ask the question the producer answers, and none can drift back onto the node's span. The IDENTIFIER reader needed no change: its `expr.span` already IS the root's, which is why that arm never broke and why the defect stayed invisible. Per-use-site precision is unaffected: each mention of a root is its own span, so `let t = b.a;` and a later `let u = b.n;` still key separately.

`uam_copied_sites` -- the sibling table the source-disarm skip keys on -- is written AND read at the node's span, entirely inside codegen, so it is self-consistent either way and was left alone. Worth noting because the two tables sit next to each other and only one of them crosses a phase boundary; that is the whole difference.

THE TUPLE ARM IS FIXED THOUGH `TupleIndex` WAS NOT WIDENED. `uam_defensive_copy_tuple_elem` reads through the same helper now, so it is correct whether or not `TupleIndex` ever gets a span of its own -- and `test_e2e_tuple_elem_bound_out_of_local_is_a_copy` was among the twelve, because a tuple index over a field access (`b.a.0`) inherits the widened span through its object. Fixing the reader rather than only the arm that happened to break is what makes the remaining arm's future widening a non-event here.

`receiver_struct_inst` needed nothing: B-2026-08-18-24 already reordered it to ask the structural walk before the span table, which was the compensation filed on this row. That prediction held.

FIXED by 982ce8c, resolving the row's OPEN LANGUAGE DECISION in favour of its
second option: `+` BORROWS. The owner made the call; the row correctly declined
to.

WHY THAT OPTION. It matches what both backends already do, so no emitted code
changes and the diff is confined to the checker, the builtin signature and the
spec line. The alternative — teaching the backends to consume — is defensible
(it is what Rust's `String + &str` does, and an owned receiver is what would let
`a + b` reuse `a`'s buffer instead of allocating) but is real work in both
backends to make natural code an error.

MECHANISM, a known shape rather than a new one. `+` on `String` lowers to
`Call(Path(["String", "add"]), [lhs, rhs])` — a free-call of an INSTANCE trait
method, which never gets a `callee_param_modes` entry because that table is
static-methods-only, so the receiver fell to the consume default.
B-2026-07-02-23 fixed exactly this for the comparison operators;
`callee_is_string_concat` is the sibling of its `callee_is_relational_operator`.

NARROWER THAN THAT SIBLING ON PURPOSE: comparisons borrow BOTH operands,
concatenation only the RECEIVER. The fix frees argument 0 alone, so the right
operand keeps whatever mode its own position gives it — `e + eat(f)` followed by
`f.len()` still warns, and that is a test.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE ROW, both from a 955-file sweep of examples/ +
kara-katas rather than a sample:

(1) PREVALENCE. The row says "a scan of 40 corpus files ... turned up exactly
one that trips it (kata 278's differential)". The full sweep finds 7 move
warnings and NONE is a String `+`: all are ordinary argument moves
(`consume(t)`, `drain_cursor(lists)`, `tos.push(cur)`) or a `let` rebind. 278's
is `d_ans` moved into `is_valid_answer(...)`. Kata 282, the row's source, was
never landed. So the true corpus prevalence is ZERO and this change alters no
existing diagnostic — it removes a warning on a shape nobody had committed yet,
which is the cheapest moment to fix it.

(2) THE MIRROR-LANGUAGE ARGUMENT. The row says borrowing "matches ... what every
mirror language does". Go and Python treat strings as immutable values so reuse
is free, but RUST'S `String + &str` CONSUMES `self` exactly as the old signature
did — the Rust mirrors avoid the question by using `push_str`. The mirrors are
split, so that argument does not carry the decision; the backends-already-agree
argument does.

WHAT CHANGED: `callee_is_string_concat` (lowering.rs) + one disjunct in the
classifier's arg-mode decision; the typechecker's builtin `Add` impl for String
now carries a `Type::Ref` receiver instead of the shared owned `binop` sig
(which stays owned for the scalar types, where the receiver is a register copy);
design.md's row 1824 becomes `fn add(ref self, other: ref String)` with a note
that the left operand survives.

VERIFIED on all four surfaces (check / interp / JIT / AOT / AOT under
KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0). Three tests: the row's repro accepted, plus two anti-vacuity
guards — a plain rebind and a move through the right operand both still report,
so the fix cannot degrade into blanket suppression for `String`.

Gates: fmt clean, clippy --all --all-targets --features llvm clean, 14,060
passed / 0 failed / 18 ignored across 107 suites.

NOT ADDRESSED, and still true: the O(n^2) cost of building a string by repeated
`+`. design.md's own note on the same line says "prefer `push_str` in loops",
and borrowing the receiver does not change that — if anything it removes the
clone that made the quadratic shape look even worse than it is.
title: THE OWNERSHIP CHECKER AND BOTH BACKENDS DISAGREE ABOUT WHETHER `String + ` CONSUMES ITS LEFT OPERAND. design.md gives `+` the signature `fn add(self, other: ref String)` — bare `self`, i.e. OWNED — so the checker warns "value moved here, used again here" on a second use. Neither the interpreter nor codegen enforces the move: the value is intact and correct afterward. The suggested `.clone()` is a real cost for a problem that does not exist at runtime.
tracker: The `+` operator's declared receiver mode. design.md:1821 says `fn add(self, other: ref String) -> String`; the ownership checker reads that as a move, and neither backend implements it as one. One of the two is wrong and it is a language call, not a bug-fix call.
detail:
FOUND authoring kata 282, whose backtracking search builds `expr + "+" + piece`
three times from the same `expr` in consecutive branches — the natural shape for
this problem, and the shape the C, Rust and Go mirrors all use too.

MINIMAL REPRO:

    fn main() {
        let e: String = "ab";
        let x = e + "x";
        let y = e + "y";
        println(f"{x} {y} {e}");
    }

    karac check       warning[ownership]: value 'e' moved here, used again here
                                          (moved at line 3:13)
                        help: clone 'e' at the move site (`e.clone()`), ...
                      All checks passed.
    --interp / JIT / build / AUTO_PAR=0      ->  abx aby ab

`e` is still `"ab"` and usable after both concatenations, on every surface.

THIS IS NOT A FALSE POSITIVE, which is what it looks like at first and is worth
stating so the next reader does not file it as one. design.md:1821 specifies

    | `+` | `fn add(self, other: ref String) -> String` | Concatenation operator |

and a bare `self` is the OWNED receiver mode (design.md § ownership tiers). By
the spec the checker is right and the program is using a moved value twice. The
backends are the ones out of step — they treat the left operand as borrowed.

SO THE DEFECT IS THE DISAGREEMENT, and either resolution is coherent:

  * If `+` is meant to CONSUME (the current signature), the backends should
    enforce it and this should be an ERROR, not a warning that everything then
    ignores. The corpus would need reworking — this shape is everywhere.
  * If `+` is meant to BORROW (`fn add(ref self, ...)`), the signature is wrong
    and the warning should not fire at all. This matches what the backends
    already do and what every mirror language does.

The second looks right to me, but it is a language decision and I am not going to
make it in a bug row.

WHY LOW: it is a warning, `All checks passed` still prints, and the program is
correct on every surface. The cost is that the recommended remedy — `e.clone()` —
is a real deep copy on what is usually a hot path, offered for a problem that does
not exist at runtime. A newcomer following the help text makes their program
slower for no reason.

PREVALENCE, measured rather than guessed: a scan of 40 corpus files declaring a
`String` binding turned up exactly one that trips it (kata 278's differential).
It is not widespread — it needs a `String` binding reused across two `+`
expressions, which most code does not do.

NOT AT ISSUE: the O(n^2) cost of building a string by repeated `+`. That is
documented and intended — design.md's own note on the same line says "allocates a
new buffer; prefer `push_str` in loops" — and it is why kata 282's differential
had to be sized down for the `--interp` leg. Recorded here only so it is not
conflated with the ownership question.

  NilCoalesce  0 failures   3b417d29
  TupleIndex   1 failure    678b00d7

THREE ZEROS WERE ABSENT WITNESSES, NOT PROOF, and each got a real test instead. `selfhost_parser_matches_rust_parser` compares the two parsers span-for-span and caught `TupleIndex` and `Call` -- so a clean run reads like coverage. title: SEVEN parser arms still copy their LHS's span -- `Cast`, `TupleIndex`, `Call`, `Path`, `Pipe`, `NilCoalesce`, `Range` -- and the postfix-span family never enumerated them. `NilCoalesce` is the one with a MEASURED consequence: it is why `method_call_key`'s args-close preference cannot be retired (B-2026-08-18-30).
tracker: Seven parser arms still copy their LHS's span. `NilCoalesce` is the one with a measured consequence -- it blocks B-2026-08-18-30's cleanup -- and the other six (`Cast`, `TupleIndex`, `Call`, `Path`, `Pipe`, `Range`) are unmeasured. Widen one arm per change with its own suite run; the five already done cost 3, 42 and 12 test failures and each needed a different fix.
detail:
THE FAMILY FIXED FIVE ARMS AND NEVER LISTED THE REST. B-2026-08-18-7 (`?.`), -9 (`?`), -21 (`Index`), -24 (`MethodCall`) and -31 (`FieldAccess`) each discovered the next member by breaking something, and -31 was found only because closing -24 exposed it. A `grep -n 'span: lhs.span' src/parser/exprs.rs` gives the whole remaining set in one line, and it is seven: `Cast`, `TupleIndex`, `Call`, `Path`, `Pipe`, `NilCoalesce`, `Range`. Recorded here so the next member is looked up rather than stumbled into.

`NilCoalesce` IS THE ONE WITH A MEASURED CONSEQUENCE TODAY. Both nodes of `a ?? b ?? c` carry `a`'s span, and `ast::desugar_nil_coalesce` works around it by passing the FALLBACK's span in the args-close slot, which is what `method_call_key` keys on. That workaround is the ONLY thing keeping the two `method_unwrap_inner_types` entries apart, so B-2026-08-18-30's cleanup -- retiring the args-close key now that no method chain needs it -- is blocked on widening this arm first. Measured there: collapsing the key with `NilCoalesce` unwidened fails the build on `outer(1) ?? mid(5) ?? -1` with "'unwrap_or' expected struct receiver, got IntValue", while all ~14k tests pass. `chained_nil_coalesce_keeps_its_two_nodes_apart` now guards that.

ORDER, which the family has paid for five times: put producer and consumer on one key FIRST, widen SECOND. For `NilCoalesce` the producer is `infer_nil_coalesce`'s `SpanKey::for_method_call(span, &right.span)` and the consumer is the `unwrap_or` lowering; once the node has a span of its own both collapse to `SpanKey::from_span(span)` together, and `method_call_key` plus the `args_close_span` parameter can go with them.

THE OTHER SIX ARE UNMEASURED, deliberately: no consequence is claimed for them here. `Call` and `Path` are the interesting ones to check next -- a call's span collides with its callee's, which is the same shape as the five that turned out to matter. `Range` also feeds the index/slice tables. Whoever takes this should widen ONE arm per change with its own suite run, as -21/-24/-31 each did, rather than widening the set: the fallout was 3, 42 and 12 tests respectively, and each needed a different fix.

SEVERITY LOW because nothing is known to miscompile TODAY -- the workarounds hold and the new test pins the one that matters. The cost is that every span-keyed table added from here inherits a collision the author cannot see.

NILCOALESCE ARM LANDED 2026-08-18 in 3b417d29; this row stays OPEN for the other six. Widening it cost ZERO test failures (14,059 passing), and with it in place the collapse B-2026-08-18-30 could not make now succeeds -- so that row's cleanup landed here too: `method_call_key` and `SpanKey::for_method_call` are deleted outright, their ~13 call sites key on the span directly, and the compiler plus clippy found the six destructuring bindings and five parameters that went dead as a result.

THE `args_close_span` AST FIELD SURVIVES, and that is a deliberate finding rather than an omission: its other consumers are real. `method_numeric.rs` calls `record_expr_type` at that span, and `concurrent_shared.rs` derives a `karac fix` edit range from it. Only the COMPOSITE-KEY concept was dead weight. Anyone retiring the field itself needs to rehome those two first.

REMAINING SIX: `Cast`, `TupleIndex`, `Call`, `Path`, `Pipe`, `Range`. Still unmeasured -- no consequence is claimed for any of them. `Call` and `Path` remain the interesting pair to check next (a call's span collides with its callee's, the shape that turned out to matter five times). One arm per change with its own suite run: the arms so far cost 0, 3, 42 and 12 failures, and each needed a different fix, so the cost is not predictable from the arm.

title: `map.entry(k).or_insert(default).push(v)` FAILS ON ALL THREE BACKENDS when the map is a struct FIELD, while `karac check` accepts it: interpreter says "method 'push' not found on type 'unknown' (no interpreter dispatch arm)", codegen says "no handler for method 'push' on non-identifier receiver". The identical chain over a LOCAL map works everywhere. This is the idiomatic way to mutate a container nested in a container, and a struct holding a map is its common home.
detail:
FOUND by writing LeetCode #895 (Maximum Frequency Stack) as a kata -- the textbook solution is `freq: Map[i64, i64]` plus `buckets: Map[i64, Vec[i64]]` on a struct, and `push` appends to the bucket for the new frequency. That one line is unusable.

THE VARIABLE IS THE RECEIVER'S ROOT, not `self` and not the method:
    let mut m: Map[i64, Vec[i64]] = Map.new();
    m.entry(1).or_insert(Vec.new()).push(7);              // WORKS, all backends

    struct Holder { buckets: Map[i64, Vec[i64]] }
    h.buckets.entry(1).or_insert(Vec.new()).push(7);      // FAILS, all backends
    self.buckets.entry(k).or_insert(Vec.new()).push(v);   // FAILS (same shape)
The field form fails from `main` exactly as it does inside a `mut ref self` method, so it is the FIELD-ROOTED receiver, not the method context.

`karac check` passes all three, so this is a check/run divergence rather than a rejected program: the typechecker resolves `or_insert`'s `mut ref Vec[i64]` result and is happy to call `push` on it; both executors then fail to dispatch a method on that non-identifier receiver. The interpreter's "type 'unknown'" says its dispatch never learned what `or_insert` handed back.

SEVERITY HIGH despite being a loud failure rather than a wrong answer, because of what it costs: `Map[K, Vec[V]]` on a struct is an ordinary shape (grouping, bucketing, adjacency lists, any multimap), and the workaround is the get/modify/insert round-trip -- `let mut b = m.get_or(k, Vec.new()); b.push(v); m.insert(k, b);` -- which is three lines, copies the bucket out and back, and turns an O(1) append into an O(n) one. The kata ships that spelling as `freq_stack_explicit.kara` precisely because the idiomatic one does not run.

BOTH EXECUTORS AGREE it is unsupported, so this is a missing lowering on a shape the typechecker admits, not a divergence between them.

CLOSED 2026-08-18. Every claim in the row held up: `karac check` accepted all three spellings, the local map worked everywhere, the field root (not the method context, not `self`) was the variable, and both executors failed for the same missing-lowering reason.

SCOPE CONFIRMED WIDER THAN THE REPRO, deliberately: `or_insert`, `or_insert_with` and `and_modify` on a field all work now, from `main` and from a `mut ref self` method. LeetCode 895 (Maximum Frequency Stack), the kata that found this, runs its textbook solution on all three backends and no longer needs the get/modify/insert workaround the row describes -- so `freq_stack_explicit.kara` can be retired as the primary spelling when that kata is next touched.

ONE SIBLING FOUND AND FILED SEPARATELY, not folded in: a nested indexed read through a struct field (`h.buckets[3][1]`) fails codegen with "nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable in v1" while `--interp` returns the right element. It involves no entry chain -- an `insert` plus two index reads reproduces it -- so it predates this fix and is independent of it.

VERIFIED: full `--features llvm` suite with KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1, both clippy passes, fmt. Backend agreement checked directly as well: the multi-shape program run under `--interp`, `karac run` and a built binary, compared pairwise.

PINS: interpreter oracles (`test_entry_chain_on_a_map_field_mutates_the_real_map`, `test_entry_chain_on_a_self_map_field`) with a codegen twin (`e2e_entry_chain_on_a_map_field`). Because the row was a CHECK/RUN divergence rather than a rejected program, each pin keeps the LOCAL spelling beside the field one, so the property under test is that the two agree -- a regression that broke only the field path would otherwise look like a passing test with a smaller number in it. The E2E's expected values were taken from `--interp` rather than from codegen's own output.
tracker: The interpreter's method-dispatch arm for a borrow-returning builtin result (`src/interpreter/method_call.rs`), and codegen's `compile_method_call` non-identifier-receiver routing (`src/codegen/method_call.rs`) -- the same 'materialize the receiver and re-dispatch' family as `try_compile_freshtemp_mapset_read_method`, except here the receiver is a `mut ref` INTO the map and must not be copied, or the append lands on a temporary.
fix:
Fixed in 4e49246, both executors. `map.entry(k).or_insert(d).push(v)` now works with the map in a struct field, from `main` and from a `mut ref self` method alike, on `--interp`, JIT and AOT.

ONE CAUSE, TWO SURFACES: every map reference the entry chain builds is keyed on a BINDING NAME, and a struct field has none. Codegen's `emit_entry_chain` needs a slot holding the handle plus the K/V LLVM types, all from per-binding registries; the interpreter's `Value::Entry` / `Value::MapSlotRef` carry a `map_var: String`. So both refused the same shape for the same reason, which is why the row correctly read it as a missing lowering rather than a divergence between them.

CODEGEN — the fix is ONE rewrite, not three. Three separate places peel an entry chain down to an `ExprKind::Identifier` root (`try_compile_entry_chain` for the terminal, `compile_entry_chain_receiver_method` for the trailing `.push`, `entry_chain_or_insert_map_name` for deref-writes). The new arm binds the field's address to a synth identifier and rewrites the chain's root once, so all of them run unmodified. The synth slot is the field's OWN ADDRESS, never a materialized copy -- the hazard the row named; a copy would append to a temporary.

INTERPRETER — map references resolve as a PLACE: a plain binding or a dotted field path (`h.buckets`, `self.buckets`). A dot cannot occur in a Kāra identifier nor in the `__`-prefixed synthetic names, so it unambiguously marks a path. Only value structs are walked: a `shared struct` field returns `None` and behaves exactly as before rather than being half-supported, since its fields carry interior mutability and the write would need to go through the cell. Resolving in place also removes the whole-map clone-and-write-back that `or_insert` performed on every call, including the local case.

A DIVERGENCE THE FIX ITSELF EXPOSED, found by probing the sibling terminals rather than stopping at the filed repro: with the rest corrected, `and_modify` on a field gave `7 107` under codegen and `7 7` under `--interp` -- codegen applied the modification while the interpreter silently skipped it and left the `or_insert` default. That arm was still name-keyed. Both now agree with the local-map oracle.

FIXED by 502d6279. The multi-shot host producers' node timers are now unref'd, and both test harnesses have had their `process.exit()` removed rather than rescheduled. The row was filed as an intermittent V8 teardown fatal; the cause is a user-facing hang underneath it. `std.web.time.every` (setInterval) and `animation_frames` (a setTimeout fallback outside a browser) re-arm forever and were never unref'd, so under node the producer's timer is the reason the process stays alive and a program that finishes its work and returns from `main` never exits — measured on a plain program with no harness: before, it printed its output and hung until killed at 10s; after, same output and exit 0 in 0s. Every harness using these producers force-exited to get out, and since the harnesses are async modules an inline `process.exit()` runs inside the module's own continuation, which is the frame V8 aborts in. The force-exit was load-bearing, so the teardown race could not be removed without first removing the need for it; `unref` restores the browser's meaning (feed the channel while the program runs, never be the reason it keeps running) and the browser rAF path is untouched. What replaces the force-exit is a bound, not an exit path: an unref'd 5s timer that cannot hold the loop open itself and so only fires if something else is, which keeps a future regression a failing test rather than a hung suite. Verified across 10 runs of the 71-test wasm E2E set with zero failures, zero skips and zero occurrences of the V8 signature, plus a full suite of 108 binaries / 14,157 tests.
title: Multi-shot host producers (`every`, `animation_frames`) never unref their node timers, so a wasm program HANGS after completing its work — and the force-exit every harness needed is what produced the intermittent V8 teardown fatal this row was filed for
detail:
FOUND while gating B-2026-08-18-32 on the merged tree. NOT caused by that change: the same working tree passed a full suite run immediately before the merge (14,060 / 0 failures) and again immediately after the failure (14,065 / 0 failures), and the change alters no emitted code — it moves `String +` from an owned to a borrowed receiver in the ownership checker, which the backends already treated as a borrow.

WHY IT IS WORTH A ROW RATHER THAN A SHRUG: the failure mode is a GREEN TEST BODY followed by a crash in the runtime's exit path, so it is indistinguishable at the `cargo test` exit code from a real regression. Every session that hits it has to spend the same evidence — re-run in isolation, re-run the suite, check the ledger — before it can rule its own change out. Recording the signature makes that a grep instead of an investigation.

SIGNATURE TO GREP FOR: `Check failed: (location_) != nullptr` together with `SourceTextModule::ExecuteAsyncModule`, in `tests/cli.rs`'s raf harness.

WHAT IS NOT YET KNOWN: whether it is load-dependent (it appeared under a full parallel suite and not in isolation, which is suggestive but 3 isolated runs is weak evidence), whether other node-driven wasm E2E tests share it, and whether the node version in this container is implicated. A fix probably starts by making the harness await module settlement before letting node exit, rather than by retrying.

CLAUDE.md's rule that "flaky is not a diagnosis" applies and is the reason this is filed rather than dismissed: the test body ran, so a re-run is not the fix — the exit path is.

--- INVESTIGATION 2026-08-18 (row STAYS OPEN: the flake is not fixed) ---

NOT REPRODUCED. 32 isolated runs of `wasm_threads_animation_frames_recv_e2e` and 24 parallel runs of the whole wasm E2E suite, all clean.

THE FIRST 32 OF THOSE RUNS PROVED NOTHING, and finding out why was the useful part of this investigation: they were SKIPS, not passes. `wasm_test_dir` rooted its scratch dir at `std::env::temp_dir()`, so karac's wasi-sysroot probe ran under the default rustup toolchain rather than the `rust-toolchain.toml` pin, and every wasm E2E test in the file took its skip path while reporting `ok`. That is filed and fixed separately -- it is a much larger problem than this flake (36 tests, whole surface). Only AFTER that fix did the re-runs above actually execute the test. The 24 parallel-suite runs are real.

HARNESS CHANGE LANDED ALONGSIDE, HONESTLY LABELLED: the raf harness's terminal `process.exit(0)` now defers by one macrotask (`setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 0)`). Rationale from the V8 signature: the harness is an async module (top-level `await`), so an inline `process.exit()` runs inside the module's own continuation -- the frame V8 aborts in (`SourceTextModule::ExecuteAsyncModule`). Deferring lets the module settle before the process leaves.

THIS IS REASONING, NOT A MEASUREMENT. With no reproduction there is no before/after, so the change cannot be claimed as the fix and the row is not closed. It is safe on its own terms (every assertion has already run by that line; the rAF loop re-arms every ~16ms so exit stays prompt), and it makes the next occurrence more informative: if the signature reappears WITH the deferral in place, the async-module-teardown hypothesis is refuted and the next investigator can skip it.

STILL UNKNOWN: whether the original observation was load-dependent, and whether the container's node version is implicated (the one sighting predates the skip fix, so it happened on a run where the OTHER wasm tests were all skipping -- i.e. under LESS load, not more, which weakens the load-dependence guess).

--- ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-18 (502d6279) ---

THE FLAKE WAS A SYMPTOM OF A USER-FACING HANG. Two prior investigations treated
this as test infra and could not reproduce it. The question neither asked was
why the harness had to call `process.exit()` AT ALL — and the answer is that
without it, nothing exits.

A MULTI-SHOT host producer re-arms forever and its node timer was never unref'd:
`std.web.time.every` (setInterval) and `animation_frames` (a setTimeout fallback
outside a browser). Under node that timer is the reason the PROCESS stays alive,
so a program that finishes its work and returns from `main` never exits.
Measured on a plain program with no test harness around it — no `process.exit`,
a 10s alarm as the bound:

  before   before / after / RAN threaded=true ... then HUNG, killed at 10s
  after    same output, exit 0, 0s

So every kāra program using `every` or `animation_frames`, compiled to wasm and
run under node, hung after completing its work. The test suite never saw it
because every harness that uses these producers force-exits.

AND THE FORCE-EXIT IS WHAT PRODUCED THIS ROW'S SIGNATURE. The harnesses are
ASYNC modules (top-level `await run(...)`), so an inline `process.exit()` runs
inside the module's own continuation — the frame V8 aborts in with
`Check failed: (location_) != nullptr` in
`SourceTextModule::ExecuteAsyncModule`. The previous investigation reasoned its
way to exactly that mechanism and deferred the exit by one macrotask, but could
not verify it and correctly declined to close the row. The deferral treated the
symptom; the exit was load-bearing, so the race could not be removed without
first removing the NEED for it.

THE FIX. `unref` the producers' node timers, which restores the browser's
meaning: a browser page keeps itself alive and the producer is never the reason
the tab is open, so in node — where there is no page — the producer should feed
the channel while the program runs and never be the reason it keeps running. The
primary worker stays ref'd, so frames keep arriving while the guest lives, and
node leaves on its own once the guest is done. Browsers return a number from
setInterval/setTimeout with no `unref`, hence the guard; the browser rAF path is
untouched, since `requestAnimationFrame` is still used directly when present.

BOTH HARNESSES NOW HAVE NO FORCE-EXIT, which is what actually retires the flake
— the hazardous call is gone rather than rescheduled. What replaces it is a
BOUND, not an exit path: an unref'd 5s timer, which cannot hold the loop open
itself and so only fires if something else is. Natural exit wins whenever it is
available; otherwise the test fails with a message instead of hanging the suite.
Keeping a `process.exit()` would have preserved the hazard AND hidden a
regression — if the unref ever stops working, a force-exit makes the test pass
while users hang.

VERIFIED: the wasm E2E set (71 tests) run 10x — zero failures, zero SKIPS, zero
occurrences of the V8 signature. Skips are counted explicitly because a skip
reports `ok`, which is how this whole surface once passed vacuously. Full suite
108 binaries / 14,157 tests / 0 failures. fmt and clippy clean.

RE-CLASSED. Filed low/other/other as test-infra; it is a defect in emitted glue
that hangs user programs, so surface becomes `codegen` and severity `high`. The
V8 signature stays in this row rather than moving to a new one because it has no
independent existence — it was only ever reachable through the force-exit this
change deletes. If it is ever seen again WITH no `process.exit()` in the
harness, that is a genuinely new bug and deserves a fresh row.

WHAT THE THREE INVESTIGATIONS COST, since the lesson is cheaper than the
repetition: 56 no-reproduction runs and one unverifiable mechanism fix, all
spent on the crash rather than on the line that made the crash possible. The
question "why does this harness need to force-exit?" was available from the
first reading and answers in one command — run the program without one.

fix:
FIXED by ffb3f76. The nested-index lowering resolved a struct field's ELEMENT type through `vec_inner_type_expr`, which returns the FIRST generic argument. That is right for `Vec[T]` / `VecDeque[T]` and wrong for a map, whose element is the SECOND argument (the VALUE type) -- so the map case never got as far as a container arm and fell out to the "outer container must be a named variable" diagnostic. The head is now matched BEFORE the element type is resolved rather than after, which is the only ordering under which a map can supply its own element type.

Reaching the entry then needed a Map lowering that is not keyed on a binding name. `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_map` resolved exactly three things from name-keyed side tables -- the slot holding the handle, the key LLVM type and the value LLVM type -- and everything after that is name-independent. A field has none of those registry entries but can supply all three from its declared type and its place-expression pointer, so the function splits at precisely that boundary: the named path keeps the lookups and delegates the rest to a new pointer-keyed twin, `lower_indexed_elem_ptr_map_at`. Same split B-2026-08-09-21 made for the Vec arm, and no second copy of the key-coercion and hash-probe logic to drift.

Verified on all four surfaces (`--interp`, JIT, AOT default/auto-par, AOT with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0), byte-identical, for a Map field, a SortedMap field with a String key, and a Vec-of-Vec regression control that pins the reordering.
title: A NESTED INDEXED READ through a struct field -- `h.buckets[3][1]` where `buckets: Map[i64, Vec[i64]]` -- fails codegen with "nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable in v1 (got non-identifier inner expression)", while `--interp` returns the right element. `karac check` accepts it. Binding the inner container first (`let b = h.buckets[3]; b[1]`) works, so the gap is the CHAIN, not the types.
tracker: the nested indexed-read path in src/codegen (the 'nested indexed read requires the outer container to be a named variable in v1' diagnostic); cf. try_compile_field_rooted_entry_chain in src/codegen/calls.rs for the materialization pattern

fix:
FIXED by c80c62f. The `ExprKind::Index` arm evaluated both operands and went straight to matching them against the container arms, with nothing checking whether either evaluation had FAULTED. A short-circuit on `pending_cf.is_some()` -- the interpreter's standard fault protocol, read at roughly 125 other sites -- now sits between the two, returning `Value::Unit` and letting the pending `ControlFlow::RuntimeError` carry the real diagnostic up.

Placed AFTER both operands are evaluated rather than between them, so a faulting object still evaluates its index and left-to-right evaluation order is preserved.

That restores the precondition the catch-all `unreachable!()` always assumed but never enforced: it is only sound for operand pairs produced by successful evaluation. The fix is therefore container-agnostic, which matches the defect -- the nested Vec out-of-bounds case ICE'd identically and is fixed by the same line.

Third visit to this arm; B-2026-08-18-3 taught it one more legal operand shape (a let-bound range), and this is the complementary half.

Verified: the map miss through a struct field, the same miss through a local, and a nested-Vec out-of-range now all report the real user-facing error with exit 1 under `--interp`, matching what JIT and AOT already did. The error is reported ONCE, not compounded by the outer subscript re-reporting against the `Unit` placeholder. Anti-vacuity pinned in the test: the present-key and in-range spellings still evaluate to the right elements, and the test fails with the original ICE when the fix is stashed.
title: A NESTED SUBSCRIPT whose INNER index FAULTS panicked the interpreter with an internal `unreachable!()` -- `m[missing_key][0]` printed "internal error: entered unreachable code: index expression at 4:13: obj=Value::Unit, index=Value::Unit" on top of the user's own correct "key not found in map" diagnostic. Both compiled backends faulted cleanly on the identical source, so it was a run-vs-build divergence as well as a crash.
tracker: the ExprKind::Index arm in src/interpreter/eval_expr.rs and its catch-all unreachable!(); cf. B-2026-08-18-3 which reached the same arm from the other direction

title: The ENTIRE wasm E2E surface in `tests/cli.rs` passed VACUOUSLY on any machine whose default rustup toolchain is not the pinned one: 36 tests took their "rustup target wasm32-wasip1 not installed" skip path and reported `ok`. `wasm_test_dir` rooted its scratch directory at `std::env::temp_dir()`, and the wasm builds run with `current_dir` set there; rustup resolves a toolchain from the CURRENT DIRECTORY, so karac's `rustc --print target-libdir --target wasm32-wasip1` probe ran under the DEFAULT toolchain instead of the `rust-toolchain.toml` pin -- and the pin is the only toolchain that declares `targets = ["wasm32-wasip1", "wasm32-wasip1-threads"]`.
detail:
FOUND while investigating B-2026-08-18-35 (the flaky raf test): 32 isolated runs of that test all reported `ok` in ~0.02s, which is not a runtime for a test that builds a wasm module and runs it under node. They were skips.

MEASURED, by stashing the fix and re-running `cargo test --features llvm --test cli` with skip notices captured:
  before:  36 skips "rustup target wasm32-wasip1 not installed" + 10 "wasm-tools not installed"
  after :   0 spurious skips + the same 10 (wasm-tools genuinely absent here), and 71 wasm tests PASS

PROOF IT WAS TOOLCHAIN RESOLUTION AND NOT A MISSING TARGET: forcing `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.94.1-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` on the unfixed tree changed the skip reason from "target not installed" to "wasm runtime archive not built" -- i.e. the target was there all along, under the pin, and only the pin.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS CONTAINER: `rust-toolchain.toml`'s own comment promises that "a fresh checkout can build them without a separate `rustup target add`". That promise holds only while the build's CWD is inside the checkout. Any machine with a different default toolchain -- which is every machine that has ever run `rustup default stable` -- silently lost the whole wasm surface, in exactly the shape CLAUDE.md already warns about for the runtime archives: a skip reports `ok`.

FIX: root the scratch dir at `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/target/wasm-e2e` instead of `std::env::temp_dir()`. The pin then applies, and the directory is already gitignored and cleaned by `cargo clean`.

REMAINING GAP (deliberately not closed here): there is still no opt-in gate for the wasm skips equivalent to `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1`. A future skip regression would be just as silent. Worth adding when someone next touches this harness.

fix:
FIXED by f3fb56b. CAUSE. `SlotOwnership` — the branch→parent transfer for auto-par return slots — did not carry `BoxedEnumDrop`. The `retain` loop that lifts a branch's ownership-bearing cleanup actions out of its frame matched thirteen kinds and fell through to `_ => None` for that one, so the branch ran it on the value it had just written into the parent's return struct and the parent's first read was of a freed box. Identical in shape to `FreeColumn` (B-2026-07-03-32), `RcDec` / `FreeSharedElided` (B-2026-08-08-15) and `FreeClusterWalkOption` (B-2026-08-14-28) — the fourth time this loop has been found short an arm. Fixed by adding `SlotOwnership::BoxedEnum` and wiring both ends, keyed on the alloca like the other slot-reloading kinds.

THREE OF THE ROW'S FINDINGS WERE WRONG, and each mattered to the diagnosis:

(1) `?.` IS NOT AN INGREDIENT. The row inferred that from "`match` on the identical bindings is correct, which is what rules out the fork itself being the whole story". Measured: the `match` spelling PRODUCES NO PARALLEL GROUP AT ALL (`--concurrency-report`: `<no parallelization opportunities detected>`), so it never exercised the fork and ruled nothing out. An ordinary by-value function call — `first(a)` — keeps the group and was corrupted exactly like `?.`.

(2) THE `Vec` FIELD IS NOT AN INGREDIENT EITHER; the trigger is PAYLOAD WIDTH. `Option`'s inline payload area is 3 words, and a payload wider than that spills behind a `malloc`'d box (`coerce_to_payload_words`) — only the box POINTER reaches the slot. Swept 1/2/3/4 `i64` fields: 1-3 correct, 4 corrupted. The row's `{val: i64, mut kids: Vec[i64]}` is i64 plus a 3-word Vec header = 4 words, so the `Vec` mattered only by making the struct one word too wide. A 4-field all-scalar struct with no heap anywhere reproduces it identically.

(3) THE CORRUPTION IS PARTIAL, NOT TOTAL, and reading that pattern is what identified the mechanism. With sentinel field values the first TWO words come back as pointer-shaped noise while the rest are intact (`f0=Some(34344714240) f1=Some(-5908575129709856518) f2=Some(2222) f3=Some(3333)`). That is the free-list metadata an allocator writes over the head of a returned chunk — a use-after-free READ signature, not uninitialised memory.

NOT REPRODUCIBLE, checked in the same pass: the sibling `NestedBoxedEnumDrop` (a box resting inside `Result[Option[T], E]`'s inline area) — correct before the fix and after.

ASAN DOES NOT CATCH THE ORIGINAL DEFECT, which is worth recording before someone tries. The first ASAN run of the repro returned a wrong value and reported nothing, because the freed chunk is still mapped and the read lands inside it. The regression gate for the use-after-free is therefore an OUTPUT-VALUE assertion (tests/par_codegen.rs), with the ASAN fixture guarding only the "freed exactly once" half of the repair.

LEAVES A LIVE REMAINDER, filed as B-2026-08-18-48 rather than buried here: if the joined binding is then MOVED into a by-value call, the move-out sentinel zeroes the parent's slot so the adopted drop no-ops, and a by-value enum parameter does not adopt the box — 2000/2000 boxes leak in a loop repro. That hole is older than this row and independent of it; sequentially the same program is clean only because the box never escapes a single function and LLVM deletes the allocation outright, so nothing was freeing it there either. Before this fix that program had a use-after-free instead of a leak, so the change is strictly an improvement, but it is not the whole story and the ASAN fixture deliberately uses a READING consumer and says so.
title: `?.` ON TWO LET-BOUND CALL RESULTS MISCOMPILES UNDER AUTO-PAR, RETURNING MEMORY THAT VARIES BETWEEN RUNS. Two independent `let`s from Option-returning calls, consumed by `?.`, print `Some(23092184781)` where the answer is `Some(5)` — a different value on every execution. `--interp` and `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0` are correct; the JIT and the default build each give their own garbage.
tracker: Unknown. The SHAPE is B-2026-08-16-1's family — two independent `let`s form an auto-par fork group and a later expression reading them gets no return slot — but that row's cause (a missing `refs_in_expr` arm) is NOT it here: `ExprKind::OptionalChain` IS handled, at closure_escape.rs:2362, recursing into both `object` and `args`. Checked before filing so the next reader does not repeat it.
detail:
FOUND on the FIRST probe of `?.`, which landed the same day (b76912a, "lower
`?.` to the match it stands for"). The kata was deliberately aimed at
newly-landed surface after two consecutive katas found nothing; this took one
program.

REPRO — the divergence needs exactly two calls:

    struct P { val: i64, mut kids: Vec[i64] }
    fn get(v: ref Vec[P], k: i64) -> Option[P] {
        let mut i = 0i64;
        while i < v.len() { if v[i].val == k { return Some(v[i]); } i = i + 1i64; }
        return None;
    }
    fn main() {
        let mut ns: Vec[P] = Vec.new(); ns.push(P { val: 5i64, kids: [1i64] });
        let hit = get(ns, 5i64);
        let miss = get(ns, 9i64);
        println(f"{hit?.val} {miss?.val}");
    }

    --interp             Some(5) None          correct
    KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0     Some(5) None          correct
    karac run (JIT)      Some(34130739200) None
    karac build          Some(22987285108) None

AND THE COMPILED VALUE IS NOT STABLE. Three consecutive runs of the same binary:
`Some(34337259520)`, `Some(23045798656)`, `Some(34204696576)`. Values in that
range read like pointers, so this is uninitialised or freed memory rather than a
wrong constant — which is why it is filed as a miscompile at high severity and
not as a wrong-answer bug. The `None` arm is unaffected throughout.

BOUNDED BY EXPERIMENT — three ingredients, and dropping any one of them fixes it:

    FAILS   two let-bound calls, consumed by `?.`
    OK      ONE let-bound call, consumed by `?.`      (a 1-statement group never forks)
    OK      two let-bound calls, consumed by `match`  (the same bindings, read another way)
    OK      `?.` on a call result directly, not via a let
    OK      struct with no Vec field / Option[i64] / no struct at all

So it needs (1) enough independent `let`s to form a fork group, and (2)
consumption by `?.` specifically. `match` on the identical bindings is correct,
which is what rules out the fork itself being the whole story.

WHAT I CHECKED AND RULED OUT, recorded so it is not re-checked: the obvious
theory is B-2026-08-16-1's — `refs_in_expr` missing an arm, so the binding never
enters the outside-reads set and gets no return slot. That row's fix made the
walker exhaustive precisely to stop a new ExprKind reading as "mentions
nothing". `ExprKind::OptionalChain` is present and recurses into `object` and
`args` (closure_escape.rs:2362), and its sibling walker has it too
(par_capture_classify.rs:558). So a missing arm is NOT the cause, and I did not
establish what is. The `?.` LOWERING (ast.rs `OptionalChainLoweringTable`) is the
obvious next place to look, since the walker sees the pre-lowering form while
codegen emits the lowered match — but that is a hypothesis, not a finding.

WHY HIGH: silent wrong data, varying per run, on the DEFAULT build path, from a
feature days old. Nothing traps and nothing warns — `karac check` passes. A
program using `?.` on more than one Option-returning call is the ordinary way to
write "look up two things and use whichever exist", and it produces garbage
that changes between runs, which is the hardest possible failure to diagnose from
the outside.

NOT AFFECTED, measured in the same pass: default arguments and `PartialEq`
derived through a `Vec` field — both landed in the same window and both agree on
all four surfaces.

fix: FIXED across four increments — 7e373aa9 (immutable `let` locals), f700fabf (`while` + `let mut` + assignment and compound assignment), 34800a15 (`for` over an exclusive or inclusive range), 6a41f79c (value `match` as a nested `select` chain) — which together take a `#[gpu]` kernel body from a single expression to a statement sequence. Reductions, accumulators, nested counted loops and table lookups compile and run. The remainder was split out as B-2026-08-18-49 (statement-form `if`, itself since fixed) rather than tracked here.
title: A `#[gpu]` KERNEL BODY COULD NOT LOOP, BIND A LOCAL, OR BRANCH ON A VALUE — it had to be a SINGLE EXPRESSION. All four increments LANDED 2026-08-18: immutable `let`, `while` + mutable locals + assignment, `for`-over-range, and value `match`. Reductions, accumulators, nested counted loops and table lookups now compile AND run (each verified on lavapipe against the interpreter). REMAINDER SPLIT OUT AS B-2026-08-18-49: statement-form `if` is unsupported (and a value-`if` branch cannot hold a local) — wider than this row's original "locals inside an `if` branch" wording, which understated it.
tracker: docs/implementation_checklist/phase-10-targets.md § GPU codegen cluster (CG-1…CG-7); the slice-0 scope decision is docs/spikes/gpu-wgsl-slice0.md. Not a regression — an unlifted slice-0 floor. Sibling of the CG-5 assessment (docs/spikes/gpu-llvm-offload-assessment.md finding 4), which is where it surfaced.
detail:
MEASURED 2026-08-18 with the release `karac check`, one construct per probe:
  • `x * 2.0`                      → accepted
  • `if x > 0.0 { x } else { -x }`  → accepted
  • `x.sqrt()`                      → accepted
  • `let y: f32 = x * 2.0; y + 1.0` → REJECTED
  • `while` loop with accumulator   → REJECTED
Both rejections carry the same clean, correctly-spanned diagnostic:
  error[E_GPU_DISPATCH_KERNEL]: cannot lower `k` to a GPU shader — a
  slice-0 GPU kernel body must be a single expression (no locals)
So this is NOT a diagnostics defect — the error names the limit precisely
and fires at the `gpu.dispatch` call site. It is a capability ceiling,
reported honestly.

ROOT: `src/gpu_wgsl.rs` (2,329 lines) is an AST→WGSL *text* emitter that
handles fourteen ExprKinds — Binary, Block, Call, Cast, FieldAccess,
Float, Identifier, If, Index, Integer, MethodCall, Path, Return,
StructLiteral, Unary — with zero occurrences of ExprKind::While / For /
Loop / Match, and a single-expression body contract on top.

SCOPE NOTE: slice-0 documented its SIGNATURE contract (`fn k(x:T)->U`
over `[T]`→`[U]`) but not this BODY restriction; the CG-5 assessment's
finding 4 first stated it as "no loops or match" and understated it — the
real limit also forbids `let`. Corrected in that doc alongside this row.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: real GPU kernels are reductions,
stencils, tiled matmul, prefix sums — essentially all of them need locals
and loops. The element-wise map is the demo case. Lifting this is also
the only route to better kernels on MACOS/METAL, the dogfooding path: an
LLVM-IR kernel backend (the CG-5 direction) would inherit codegen's full
expression coverage, but it can only feed PTX/HSA — our LLVM has no
SPIR-V backend, so it cannot feed wgpu. WGSL is the only road on Metal,
and extending this emitter is the only way down it.

SUGGESTED SHAPE (not started): lift in the order locals → `while` → `for`
over a range → `match`. WGSL has `var`, `let`, `loop`/`while`/`for`, and
`switch`, so each is a direct structural lowering, not a research
problem. The `#[gpu]` effect gate + GpuSafe already guarantee the body is
allocation-free, panic-free and heap-free, so no runtime-support question
rides along. Every increment is testable GPU-lessly: kernels compile to
WGSL text at typecheck time, and `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu` (lavapipe) runs
the real pipeline on a GPU-less host.

--- INCREMENT 1 LANDED 2026-08-18: immutable `let` locals ---
The scalar `emit_kernel` path now accepts leading `let` bindings before the tail
expression, each lowering to a WGSL `let` inside `main`, in source order, with the
kernel parameter resolving to `input[i]` and later bindings seeing earlier ones.

KEY FINDING that made this small: the SoA/stencil emitters ALREADY supported locals
via `kernel_body_parts` — only the scalar path had never adopted it. The fix
generalized that shared helper (parameterized tail wording) rather than writing a
second body walker, and deleted the now-dead `kernel_return_expr`.

Two guards were added to `kernel_body_parts`, benefiting BOTH paths — each converts
a shader that would only fail inside the GPU driver at dispatch into a clean
compile-time diagnostic:
  • SHADOWING (`let a = ...; let a = a + 1;`) — WGSL has no same-scope
    redeclaration, so the second binding would emit invalid WGSL.
  • RESERVED NAMES — a local spelled `i`/`gid`/`input`/`output`/`main` collides with
    the generated wrapper's own declarations; WGSL keywords are covered too.
`let mut` is rejected with a diagnostic naming this row and pointing at loop support.

VALIDATED BY EXECUTION, not by inspecting shader text. `mesa-vulkan-drivers` turns
out to be apt-installable in the cloud container, so `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu`
(lavapipe) ran the real naga+Vulkan pipeline: a two-local kernel returned 9 and 25,
byte-identical to `--interp`. **This contradicts the CG-7 assumption that GPU work
cannot be validated here** — the software-adapter lane works in a GPU-less container
and is worth a CI job.

Two tests that pinned the old floor were inverted rather than deleted:
`gpu_wgsl::tests::rejects_body_with_locals` -> `accepts_body_with_locals`, and
`gpu_dispatch_rejects_unsupported_kernel_body` now guards `let mut` (so the
E_GPU_DISPATCH_KERNEL surfacing path stays covered) beside a new acceptance test.

REMAINING (increments 2-4): `while`, `for`-over-range, `match`, and the mutable
locals + assignment that loops need. Also still open: locals inside an `if` branch —
the emitter lowers value-`if` to WGSL `select()`, so branches must stay expressions;
that needs statement-form `if`, a larger change.

--- INCREMENT 2 LANDED 2026-08-18: `while` + mutable locals + assignment ---
The scalar kernel body is now a STATEMENT SEQUENCE, not `let`s-then-expression:
`let` / `let mut` / assignment / compound assignment / `while`, then the tail.
`let mut` lowers to WGSL `var`, `while c { .. }` to `while (c) { .. }`, and `+= -= *=
/= %=` to their WGSL spellings. The accumulator shape every reduction needs works:
  let mut acc: f32 = 0.0; let mut i: i32 = 0;
  while i < 4 { acc = acc + x; i = i + 1; }  acc * 2.0

DESIGN NOTE — the scalar path now has its OWN statement walker (`scalar_body_stmts` +
`KStmt` + `Scope`) rather than sharing `kernel_body_parts` with the SoA/stencil
emitters, which still take only `let` bindings. Widening a helper two of its three
callers cannot use would have been worse than the duplication.

THE RESERVED-NAME REJECTION FROM INCREMENT 1 IS REPLACED BY RENAMING on this path,
and that is a CORRECTNESS property, not ergonomics. A loop counter called `i` is
idiomatic, but `i` is the generated wrapper's THREAD index — the kernel parameter
lowers to `input[i]`. Rejecting was user-hostile; silently letting a local `i` win
would make every thread read the wrong element. `Scope::bind` renames a colliding
local (`i` -> `i_k`, walking to a free name), so `acc = (acc + input[i])` keeps
reading the thread's own element. A pinned test asserts exactly this.
Shadowing is likewise now SUPPORTED rather than rejected: the scope stack gives the
inner binding a distinct WGSL name, the inner RHS still sees the outer value, and the
tail sees the innermost — Kara's own semantics. (The SoA/stencil paths keep the
increment-1 rejections; only the scalar path grew a scope stack.)

VALIDATED BY EXECUTION on lavapipe again, not by reading shader text: the accumulator
kernel returned 8 and 24, and a compound-assign kernel with a loop-body-scoped `let`
returned 9 — each byte-identical to `--interp`.

TEST-CHURN LESSON worth keeping: `gpu_dispatch_rejects_unsupported_kernel_body` has
now been re-anchored TWICE (a `let` local, then `let mut`) because each anchor became
supported one increment later. It is now anchored on assigning to the kernel
PARAMETER — a permanent boundary, since the param is a read-only storage load and can
never be a place — so it guards the E_GPU_DISPATCH_KERNEL surfacing path instead of
chasing the frontier.

REMAINING (increments 3-4): `for`-over-range and `match`. Still blocked separately:
locals inside an `if` branch, because value-`if` lowers to WGSL `select()` so both
branches must stay expressions; that needs statement-form `if`.

--- INCREMENT 3 LANDED 2026-08-18: `for` over a range ---
`for v in a..b { .. }` lowers to a native WGSL `for (var v = a; v < b; v = v + 1)`,
and `a..=b` to `v <= b`. Loops nest, and the loop variable is scoped to its own loop:
two sequential `for n in ..` loops both emit `var n` rather than accumulating rename
suffixes, because the scope stack is truncated at loop exit.

Kara's loop variable is IMMUTABLE, so it binds non-mutable and assigning to it is
rejected, even though WGSL needs a `var` to carry the increment. Both range bounds are
lowered in the ENCLOSING scope before the variable is bound, so `for i in 0..i` reads
the outer `i` rather than the one being declared.

REJECTED with named diagnostics: iterating a non-range (there is no collection inside
a scalar kernel — the buffer element IS the parameter), a destructuring loop pattern,
and a `for` body that produces a value.

Validated on lavapipe: a kernel with an exclusive and an inclusive loop returned 11
and 23, byte-identical to --interp.

TESTING NOTE: the open-ended-range guard (`for n in 0.. {`) has no test because that
syntax does not parse in Kara — the `..` runs into the block. The guard stays as a
defensive arm because the AST carries both bounds as Options.
A second sloppy-assertion lesson: `!wgsl.contains("n_")` failed spuriously because
the entry point's `@builtin(global_invocation_id)` contains that substring. Assert on
the declaration (`var n_`), not a bare identifier fragment.

REMAINING: `match` (increment 4, WGSL has `switch`), and locals inside an `if` branch —
still blocked because value-`if` lowers to WGSL `select()`, so both branches must stay
expressions; that needs statement-form `if`, a larger change than either loop form.

--- INCREMENT 4 LANDED 2026-08-18: value `match` ---
A `match` lowers to a NESTED `select()` CHAIN, the same branchless shape value-`if`
already used. WGSL's own `switch` is a STATEMENT and cannot produce the value a Kara
`match` is; `select` can, and lowering it as an expression made it compose into every
position at once — a `let` initializer, an assignment RHS, a loop body, the tail —
with no statement-position work at all.
  match x { 0 => 4, 1 | 2 => 2, _ => 1 }
  -> select(select(1, 2, ((input[i] == 1) || (input[i] == 2))), 4, (input[i] == 0))
Supported: integer and bool literal arms, `|` alternations of those, and `_`.
Rejected with named diagnostics: guards, binding arms (the branchless lowering has
nowhere to introduce a binding), and float-literal arms (exact float equality is not a
reliable selector).

WHY EVALUATING EVERY ARM IS SOUND — the load-bearing point, and it is the effect
system that buys it. `select` is not short-circuiting, so all arms are evaluated. That
is safe precisely because the `#[gpu]` effect gate has already proven the kernel's
whole transitive call graph free of allocation, host I/O, channel traffic and explicit
panics, so an unselected arm can have no observable effect. The implicit trap sources
FE-4b deliberately keeps permitted (integer division by zero, indexing) are DEFINED,
non-trapping operations in WGSL, so they cannot fault an unselected arm either.
Branchless is also what a GPU wants: no per-lane divergence.
The LAST arm is the fallback and its pattern is not tested, which is sound without
inspecting it because the typechecker has already proven the match exhaustive.

ORDERING BUG FOUND BY ITS OWN TEST: bodies were lowered before patterns were checked,
so a binding arm `n => n` reported "unknown identifier 'n'" — the symptom, from the
body — instead of naming the unsupported pattern. Every arm's pattern is now validated
first, INCLUDING the fallback's (whose condition is discarded but whose shape must
still be supported).

Validated on lavapipe: a table-lookup kernel returned 40, 20, 10 across the literal,
alternation and wildcard arms — byte-identical to --interp.

SEVERITY LOWERED to low: the kernel language now covers the shapes real compute needs.
The remaining gap (locals inside an `if` branch) has a workaround — hoist the binding
above the `if`, or use `match` — and needs statement-form `if`, which is a larger
change than any of these four increments and deserves its own row if pursued.

--- REMAINDER SPLIT OUT 2026-08-18 as B-2026-08-18-49 ---
Re-probing every `if` position (rather than only the one this row named) showed the
remainder is WIDER than "locals inside an `if` branch": statement-form `if` is
rejected outright, even when neither branch declares a local — `if c { acc = x; }
else { acc = 0.0-x; }` does not compile. Filed with its own measurements, root cause
and a two-step suggested shape. This row keeps only the four landed increments; do
not track the `if` work here.


--- VALIDATED ON METAL 2026-08-18, and closed ---

All four increments had landed but the row was left open. Re-validating them on
the M5 before closing turned up the reason that was worth doing: every one of
them had been verified on LAVAPIPE ONLY (naga -> SPIR-V), because
`tests/gpu_e2e.rs` pinned `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu` and macOS has no software
adapter, so on this machine all fourteen execution fixtures SKIPPED while the
suite reported `ok`. Filed and fixed as B-2026-08-19-9.

With the backend resolved rather than pinned, the fixtures run on an Apple M5
Pro through naga's MSL backend, and each increment's own fixture agrees with the
interpreter:

  increment 1  gpu_executes_let_locals
  increment 2  gpu_executes_while_loop_with_thread_index_shadowing_local
               gpu_executes_compound_assignment
  increment 3  gpu_executes_for_range_exclusive_and_inclusive
  increment 4  gpu_executes_match_as_select_chain

The MSL leg matters most for increment 2's RENAME and increment 4's `select`
chain, which are the two lowerings whose failure mode is a shader that compiles
and looks right while computing the wrong answer. Both are now confirmed on two
different shader languages rather than one.

CLOSING NOTE ON SCOPE — this row's title was rewritten twice as the frontier
moved, and its remainder was restated once (by B-2026-08-18-49) after re-probing
found it wider than described. The durable lesson is the one -49 recorded: probe
EVERY position, not the one the previous row happened to name. This close adds a
second: a row whose work has landed still has an unmeasured claim in it if the
validation lane was never checked on the platform that ships.

fix:
FIXED by 641d6df (the generic bound; see below for the multi-bound half). design.md:6071's `effect resource RequestCh: Channel[Request];` now parses, and -- the half that matters -- the argument MEANS something: the trait's own generic params are brought into scope when the method signature is lowered (otherwise `T` lowers to `Type::Named` and no substitution can reach it, since `substitute_type_params` rewrites `Type::TypeParam` only), then bound positionally from the declared args. Both steps are gated on the resource having declared arguments, so a plain `: Trait` bound lowers byte-identically to before.

ARITY IS CHECKED AT THE DECLARATION, both directions -- the substitution zips, so too many args were dropped and too few left the trait's remaining params free to unify with anything. A MISSING argument list counts as zero, which gives this row's motivating diagnostic a home: `effect resource RequestCh: Channel;` against `trait Channel[T]` now reports at the declaration and names the fix rather than surfacing as "expected 'T', found 'i64'" at the first call site. The uniform rule was measured against the full corpus before adopting it -- nothing regressed, because no existing program declares a bare bound on a generic trait.

CODEGEN NEEDED NOTHING: the vtable is keyed on the trait NAME and its method-declaration order, neither of which depends on the arguments. An E2E test dispatches through `impl Channel[i64] for Echo` to hold that claim rather than assert it. The formatter (which silently DROPPED the args, rewriting a declaration into one that no longer typechecks), the resolver (arg types now existence-checked), the catalog and the span walker are all plumbed.

design.md's example gained its missing `;`, and the NON_TERMINATOR allow-list is now EMPTY. That entry had been masking a second defect: no terminator gate could see the missing `;` while the parser was failing earlier on the same line at `[`.

MULTI-BOUNDS (`: A + B`) IS SPLIT OUT to B-2026-08-19-3 rather than left here, with a cost this row understated. It is not "a Vec and a union of the method sets": codegen resolves a resource to exactly ONE trait to pick ONE vtable and ONE method order, across nine call sites, so two bounds need per-bound vtables plus a method-to-bound map at every dispatch site. Separately measured and filed as B-2026-08-19-4: `with_provider` does not check that the provider implements the declared bound AT ALL, at arity 1 -- a program whose provider has a matching method but no `impl Trait for U` passes every check and dies in codegen blaming the vtable. That is a pre-existing hole the multi-bound work would inherit, not part of it.
title: TWO `effect resource` declaration forms design.md specifies normatively do not parse: a GENERIC trait bound (`effect resource C: Provider[Request];` -> "Expected Semicolon, found LeftBracket", design.md:6071) and MULTI-BOUNDS (`effect resource UserDB: DatabaseProvider + HealthCheckable;` -> "found Plus", spec'd at design.md:7216 under the normative line "Multiple trait bounds are allowed on a resource declaration:" at :7213). The third form this row was filed with -- PARAMETERIZED resources, `effect resource UserDB[user_id: i64];` -- is FIXED (see below); only `effect resource X;`, `effect resource X: Trait;` and the parameterized form parse.
detail:
FOUND while closing B-2026-08-18-29 (design.md statement terminators). One of that row's two residual `Expected Semicolon` diagnostics was `effect resource RequestCh: Channel[Request]` at design.md:6071 -- reported as a missing terminator, actually the parser stopping at `[`. Probing the neighbouring forms turned up two more.

MEASURED, each as a standalone file against `karac check --output=json`:
    effect resource RequestCh;                                  PARSE-CLEAN
    effect resource UserDB: DatabaseProvider;                   PARSE-CLEAN
    effect resource C: Provider[Request];                       Expected Semicolon, found LeftBracket
    effect resource UserDB: DatabaseProvider + HealthCheckable; Expected Semicolon, found Plus
    effect resource UserDB[user_id: i64];                       `user_id` is Value-class ...

TWO OF THE THREE ARE SPEC'D WITH NORMATIVE PROSE, not merely shown in passing. design.md:7213 reads "Multiple trait bounds are allowed on a resource declaration:" immediately above the `A + B` example, and "Any provider passed to `with_provider` must implement all declared bounds plus `Send + Sync`" immediately below -- so the multi-bound form has semantics attached, not just syntax. Parameterized resources have their own section heading and a worked conflict-analysis example (`writes(UserDB[id])` conflicts for equal ids and parallelizes for different ones), plus a design decision at :7268 explaining why individual instances cannot be bound with `with_provider`.

SO THIS IS AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT A DIAGNOSED DEFECT, and that is why the severity is low. Either the parser is missing three declaration forms the spec commits to, or the spec commits to more than v1 intends and the three sites need the v1 caveat the sibling § Operator Traits carries. Deciding which is the work; both outcomes are cheap, and the wrong guess writes a false claim into either the compiler or the corpus.

WORTH NOTING FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP: the two richer examples sit in BARE ``` fences, not ```kara, which is why no design.md block gate has ever flagged them -- the corpus harness only scans kara-tagged blocks. The generic-bound one at :6071 is in a kara block and IS gated (allow-listed by id in tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs, with a sibling test that fails if the entry stops firing, so closing this row surfaces the stale entry rather than hiding it).

--- RESOLVED 2026-08-18: the row's open question is answered, and one of the three forms is fixed. Row stays OPEN for the other two. ---

THE QUESTION WAS "missing parser forms, or a spec that overcommits?" It is the first, for all three, and that is measured rather than argued.

PARAMETERIZED RESOURCES ARE ALREADY IMPLEMENTED -- everywhere except the declaration. `Resource::param` in the AST carries `writes(UserDB[id])`; the use site parses and checks clean today against a BARE `effect resource UserDB;`; and `concurrency/effects_collect.rs::apply_parameterized_keys` substitutes call arguments into the callee's declared keys and records `StmtEffect::key`, with literal keys proven distinct and variables left conservatively conflicting. The spec's own worked example behaves exactly as § Parameterized Resources says, verified through `karac query concurrency`:
    update_profile(42); update_settings(42);  -> serialization_points: "writes(UserDB) conflicts with writes(UserDB)", no parallel group
    update_profile(42); update_settings(99);  -> parallel_groups: [[0, 1]], "no data or effect dependencies"
So the declaration was the one missing piece of a working feature, not the tip of an unimplemented one. FIXED in b58fa25.

THE SLOT WAS FREE, which is what made that fix clean rather than an ambiguity. `EffectResourceDecl::generic_params` was parsed and read by NOBODY but the formatter; design.md declares no generic effect resource; and the key at :7124 is the only `[...]` written after a resource name anywhere in the spec. So `[...]` is the key's outright, and `[user_id: i64]` no longer has to survive a Type-class naming rule meant for type parameters.

THE GENERIC TRAIT BOUND IS NOT DECORATION EITHER, which is the strongest evidence against the spec-overcommits reading. A generic provider trait declared WITHOUT its argument is unusable, not merely imprecise:
    trait Channel[T] { fn send(ref self, v: T); }
    effect resource RequestCh: Channel;      // parses
    fn push(v: i64) with sends(RequestCh) { RequestCh.send(v); }
    -> error[typecheck]: expected 'T', found 'i64'
`Provider[Request]` is the only syntax that binds that parameter. Its absence is why the diagnostic names an unbound type parameter the user never wrote.

WHAT THE TWO REMAINING FORMS COST, so whoever picks this up is not surprised. Both need more than a parser edit, because `provider_trait: Option<String>` is a bare NAME and four phases consume it as one (`resolve_items.rs` existence check, `effectchecker/inference.rs` trait-method seeding, `typechecker/expr_ops.rs` `resource_dispatch_signature`, and codegen's `provider_trait_methods` table). The generic form needs the field to carry generic args AND `resource_dispatch_signature` to substitute them; the multi-bound form needs a Vec and a UNION of the method sets, plus the spec's "must implement all declared bounds" check at `with_provider`. Parsing either and dropping the extra information would be worse than not parsing it -- accepting syntax whose meaning is ignored.

ALSO STILL OPEN, and worth its own attention: nothing typechecks a partition KEY against its declared type. `effect resource UserDB[user_id: i64];` records the type, and a use site `writes(UserDB[k])` for a `String` k is accepted. The typechecker does not walk effect lists at all today, so this needs a new hook rather than an extra assertion; filed separately rather than bolted on here.
tracker: the `effect resource` declaration parser (src/parser.rs) vs design.md:6071, :7216 (multi-bound, prose at :7213) and design.md:7124 (§ Parameterized Resources, heading at :7121); allow-list entry in tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs NON_TERMINATOR

fix:
FIXED by 9b6e1b1. All eight sites corrected, and the two the row said needed "a language answer" got one each rather than a guess.

`panic!` x 6 -> `panic(...)`. The row already measured this as the safe drop-in; `panic()` with no argument checks clean too, which the `panic!()` sites at design.md:556-557 need.

`matches!` -> a plain `match` expression yielding a bool:
    let is_lit = match parent.left { AstNode.Lit { .. } => true, _ => false };
No language decision was needed after all -- the row read `matches!` as requiring one because its second argument is a PATTERN with no bare-call equivalent, which is true, but a `match` expression takes patterns natively and returns a value.
