So the harness accepted input the CLI rejects. The test was corrected to `reads` before landing; the harness gap is what this row is for.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The harness is explicitly built to mirror `karac build` -- `run_program_capturing_inner` calls `karac::prepare_for_resolve` as "the `karac build` front end between parse and resolve, as one call shared with cli.rs" precisely because hand-spelling those passes had already drifted from the CLI once (B-2026-08-11-34), and `assert_check_clean` exists because a program that flunks the check phase "is input production never compiles". Effects are the third phase of that same gate and are simply absent, so the stated invariant is not the enforced one. A codegen test can therefore encode -- and permanently pin -- a program shape no user can compile, and the divergence surfaces only if someone copies the test source into a file.

SEVERITY LOW because the failure direction is permissive: it admits extra programs rather than rejecting valid ones, so no correct test is at risk and nothing miscompiles. The cost is that codegen E2E coverage silently includes non-programs, and an effect-checker regression is invisible to the suite that exercises the most real binaries.

SHAPE OF THE FIX: run `karac::effectcheck` alongside resolve/typecheck in `run_program_capturing_inner` and extend `common::assert_check_clean` to take its errors. Expect to fix a handful of existing test sources -- the same `pub fn ... with <wrong verb>` shape is easy to write and has never been caught here. Worth checking whether the sibling harnesses (`tests/par_codegen.rs`, `tests/memory_sanitizer.rs`) share the omission.
tracker: tests/codegen.rs::run_program_capturing_inner; tests/common's assert_check_clean; cf. B-2026-08-11-34 (the prepare_for_resolve drift this gate was hardened against)

title: `i128` / `u128` are CARRIED AS 64-BIT and wrap there silently: `let a: i128 = 9223372036854775807; a.wrapping_add(1)` prints `-9223372036854775808` instead of `9223372036854775808`. The types parse, type-check and run — they are simply not the width they claim, so any value above the 64-bit range is silently wrong rather than rejected.
detail:
FOUND while widening `wrapping_*` to the narrow integer widths for B-2026-08-19-1. That work deliberately left 128-bit out, and a test was drafted asserting `i128.wrapping_add` is REJECTED. It failed — and failed identically on the pre-change binary, so this is pre-existing and independent of that widening.

MEASURED (`karac run --interp`, and the same under codegen):
    let a: i128 = 9223372036854775807;   // i64::MAX
    a.wrapping_add(1)   ==>  -9223372036854775808     (wrapped at 64 bits)
    expected for a true i128:  9223372036854775808

So the interpreter's `Value::Int(i64)` model backs `i128` directly, with no diagnostic. The comment at `src/typechecker/method_numeric.rs` was accurate that 128-bit is 'not yet i64-representable in the interpreter' — but the consequence is not that 128-bit methods are refused, it is that the TYPE silently behaves as 64-bit everywhere.

WHY IT MATTERS. This is the same failure shape as B-2026-08-19-1 one level down: a value that is quietly wrong rather than a program that fails. design.md's overflow rationale (§ Arithmetic Overflow) argues at length that silent wraparound is a live logic-bug and CVE class; a type whose declared width is a fiction is that argument's premise violated by the type system itself. The AI-first wedge sharpens it — a model that reaches for `i128` is specifically reaching for range it will not get.

OPTIONS: (a) reject `i128`/`u128` at type-check with a clear 'not supported in v1' diagnostic — honest, cheap, and matches how other unimplemented surface behaves; (b) implement them properly (interpreter needs an i128 value carrier, codegen already has LLVM `i128`); (c) leave and document. (a) is the obvious near-term move: the current state is strictly worse than not having the types, because it looks like it works.

NOT ATTEMPTED HERE — out of scope for the GPU row it was found under, and filed rather than folded in so the width-widening slice stayed reviewable.

ID NOTE: first written as B-2026-08-19-2 and renumbered before push — another session allocated that id concurrently (its row is the `--interp | head` Rust-panic one). Caught at the rebase: resolving the ledger conflict with `--theirs` during a REBASE takes the commit being applied, not upstream, so the naive resolution would have overwritten their row's content under a shared id — precisely the clobber `scripts/bug-close.py --expect` exists to prevent on the close path, which has no equivalent guard on the FILE path.
fix:
FIXED by b62cd33. `i128` / `u128` are now REJECTED as runtime value types, at the point the type is named, with a diagnostic that names this row.

THE WRONGNESS IS THE CARRIER, NOT ONE METHOD — which is why the fix is not where the row was filed. The row was written against `wrapping_*`, where it was noticed. Measured across the family before choosing the shape, on `a: i128 = i64::MAX`:

    a.wrapping_add(1)     -> -9223372036854775808   (want  9223372036854775808)
    a.saturating_add(1)   ->  9223372036854775807   (saturated at i64::MAX)
    a.checked_add(1)      ->  None                  (want Some(2^63))
    (-1i128).count_ones() ->  64                    (want 128)

So `saturating_*`, `checked_*` and the bit intrinsics were silently wrong too. Fixing `wrapping_*` alone would have left three families and the intrinsics quietly wrong while looking addressed; a program that cannot NAME the type cannot observe any of them.

THE ROW'S TITLE OVERSTATED THE BLAST RADIUS, and the correction matters for anyone reading this later. Not everything 128-bit was silent: checked arithmetic already TRAPPED at the 64-bit boundary ("integer overflow") rather than wrapping, shifts trapped, and an out-of-range literal was a parse error. Those are loud, and were never the bug. CONST EVALUATION IS GENUINELY 128-BIT — it computes in Rust `i128` at compile time and never reaches a runtime carrier — so `Array[T, 100i128 + 200i128]` and 128-bit const params keep working, untouched, and `test_const_eval_i128_arithmetic_resolves` passes unchanged. Only the runtime value type is rejected. Option (b) from this row (implement properly) was costed and declined for this slice: `Value::Int` has 480 occurrences in the interpreter alone, so a real 128-bit carrier is a sweeping change, not a bug fix.

THREE ENTRY PATHS, because the first two leave a hole worth recording. The annotation (`let x: i128`) and the literal suffix (`let x = 1i128`, which has no `TypeExpr` for the annotation guard to see) are the obvious ones; casts fall out of the first. The third is the float conversion family — `(3.7f32).trunc_to_i128()` names the type in the METHOD NAME only, so unannotated it type-checked clean and produced a 64-bit carrier claiming to be 128. Diagnostics dedupe by source offset because `lower_type_expr` re-runs for a single annotation under generic instantiation and trial typing.

design.md gets a STATUS NOTE, not a scope change (owner-directed). The spec normatively promises 128-bit in v1 — § `checked_*`/`wrapping_*`/`saturating_*`/`overflowing_*` families, the widening-cast table, the primitive-numeric lists, Portable SIMD element types — and rejecting the type without saying so would have traded a soundness bug for the spec/impl divergence class of B-2026-08-18-41. The promise stands; the note records that the compiler does not deliver it yet. Deleting that note is what "implement 128-bit" looks like, and B-2026-08-19-8 tracks it.

FALLOUT, recorded rather than papered over. Four tests asserted the opposite and were REPLACED, not deleted: `test_integer_suffix_{i,u}128_accepted`, `test_const_eval_u128_literal_typechecks`, and the 128-bit lines of `test_float_to_int_conversion_methods_typecheck`. They pinned that 128-bit was NAMEABLE — true, and never in doubt — and read as pinning that it WORKED. `tests/simd_report.rs::require_simd_rejects_unsupported_128bit_element` used `Vector[i128, 4]`, design.md's own example of a lane type no vector unit supports; it no longer type-checks, so the test moves to `f16` (same `UnsupportedElement` classification, still spellable) and the classifier's `bits >= 128` arm is kept and unit-tested on `Type` values for when 128-bit lands. The `Vector` element-type diagnostic stopped advertising `i128` as permitted. No `.kara` file in examples/, stdlib/ or kara-katas uses either type — consistent with a type that never worked.

FIXED by 15a11aa. `karac_jit_runner` restores the DEFAULT SIGPIPE disposition at the top of `main`, before any path that runs user code, and `cmd_run` forwards a signal death as `128 + signal` instead of collapsing it to 1. All three surfaces now end a closed-reader run the same way: status 141, empty stderr.

THE ROW'S "LIKELY FIX" WAS WRONG ABOUT THE LOCATION, and the correction is the useful part of this close. It proposed one shared helper over "the five `stdout().lock()` sites in `runtime/src/lib.rs`". Those five sites are all `BOUND_PORT=<n>` diagnostics emitted by the HTTP servers on bind — nothing to do with the program's output. A karac program's `println` never passes through Rust at all: codegen emits `__karac_write_console`, whose body is a direct libc `fwrite(data, 1, len, stdout)` for any non-parallel module (it routes through `karac_runtime_write_console` ONLY when the module contains a `karac_par_run` / `karac_par_reduce` site, so that par-branch writes can be captured and replayed in source order). A runtime-side write helper would therefore have missed every sequential program — which is to say, the entire reported case.

THE ACTUAL DIVERGENCE IS ONE PROCESS PROPERTY, not a write path. A karac AOT binary's `main` bypasses Rust std's `lang_start`, so it inherits the default SIGPIPE disposition and the kernel kills it at the first write to a closed pipe. `karac_jit_runner` IS a Rust program, so `lang_start` installs `SIG_IGN` before the JIT'd code runs; the emitted `fwrite` then gets EPIPE, and codegen's wrapper discards the return value, so the program runs on. Restoring `SIG_DFL` in the runner makes the JIT'd process start in the same state an AOT binary starts in — which is the runner's whole job.

WHY THIS DOES NOT BREAK SERVERS, the obvious objection, and it is already handled by the design rather than by this fix: the runtime masks SIGPIPE for exactly the programs that need it, from the network reactor's one-time init (`event_loop.rs`, `event_loops()`), NOT from process startup — deliberately network-scoped so compute-only binaries stay off that path. A socket-writing program therefore re-installs `SIG_IGN` itself the moment it registers its first fd, under the JIT exactly as under AOT, through the same code. VERIFIED rather than assumed: a `Server.serve` program under `karac run` survived 40 aborted client connections and was still answering afterwards.

MEASUREMENTS, before -> after, on a 2,000,000-line program with the reader closed after two lines (`PIPESTATUS[0]`, not `$?` — the parent pipeline's status is `head`'s either way):

    AOT binary          3 ms / 141      3 ms / 141   (the reference, unchanged)
    karac run (JIT)   272 ms /   0    116 ms / 141
    karac run --interp                 36 ms / 141   (fixed by the sibling)

The JIT's remaining 116 ms is compile-plus-spawn, not program execution: the same program under the JIT writing everything to /dev/null takes 260 ms, so the closed-reader run is no longer doing the work.

THE UNBOUNDED CASE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERED. `karac run prog | head -3` on a `while true` program did not terminate at all before this. It now ends in 108 ms with status 141.

GATED by `jit_broken_pipe_stops_the_program_like_a_native_binary` (tests/cli.rs, `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]`), deliberately built on an UNBOUNDED program: a finite one exits on its own and would pass even fully broken, whereas `while true` cannot, so a regression hangs instead of passing quietly. Verified red before the fix — and the failure mode IS the hang, which is why the test asserts by completing at all. It also asserts status 141, which is what pins the `cmd_run` half: without that change the runner dies by signal and `code()` returns None, so `unwrap_or(1)` would report a generic failure.

ONE CLIPPY NOTE for whoever touches this next: `exit_code_of` needs `#[cfg(feature = "llvm")]` because its only caller is inside the JIT path. Ungated it is dead code in the DEFAULT build, which is the leg CI runs — the exact trap CLAUDE.md documents, hit again here.
title: `karac run` (JIT) IGNORES A CLOSED READER ENTIRELY: with `| head -2` it runs the whole program to completion, discarding every failed write, then exits 0 — while the AOT binary for the same source dies at the first broken write with status 141. MEASURED on a 2,000,000-line program: 541 ms with the pipe closed after two lines vs 547 ms writing everything to /dev/null (statistically identical), against 5 ms for the AOT binary. 100x the work here, and unbounded for a long-running program.
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-19-2 when that row's interpreter half landed. Same trigger, different component and different failure: the interpreter PANICKED (loud, wrong, now fixed to exit 141 quietly); the JIT is SILENT AND WRONG, which is why it went unnoticed and why it is worth its own row.

MECHANISM, and it is the same root cause as its sibling seen from the other side. An AOT binary is the process, so it inherits the default SIGPIPE disposition and the kernel kills it. `karac_jit_runner` is a Rust program, so Rust sets SIGPIPE to SIG_IGN at startup and the runtime's write gets EPIPE instead — and the runtime's stdout path discards write errors, so the program simply keeps running. `cmd_run` then reports the runner's own clean exit: `Ok(s) => s.code().unwrap_or(1)` yields 0, because nothing died.

THE STATUS IS THE SMALLER HALF. `karac run prog | head -1` on a program that streams indefinitely does not terminate when the reader goes away — it runs forever, writing into a pipe nobody is reading. That is the shape worth fixing, and it is invisible to the corpus's A/B rule because that rule compares stdout, which is identical (both truncated by the reader).

LIKELY FIX, in the same spirit as the interpreter's: have the runtime's stdout write recognise EPIPE and exit 141 rather than discard the error. The interpreter's fix is one call site because `write_stdout` is its single choke point; the runtime has several stdout writers (`runtime/src/lib.rs` has five `stdout().lock()` sites), so this wants one shared helper rather than five edits. `cmd_run`'s `unwrap_or(1)` should also forward a signal-death as `128 + signal` instead of collapsing it to 1, so a runner that IS killed reports faithfully.

SEVERITY LOW on the same grounds as its parent: stdout is byte-identical, so no program computes a wrong answer. What it costs is a status a harness cannot trust and, for a streaming program, a process that will not stop.

fix:
FIXED by 7561b5d (stage 5 of 5). 128-bit integers are usable: bindings, parameters, returns, struct fields, Vec/Map elements, the arithmetic and comparison surface, wrapping_*/saturating_*/overflowing_*, the bit intrinsics, casts, literals in every radix, and println / f-string / to_string formatting — all agreeing between karac run and karac build. Vector[i128, N] is spellable again and scalarizes, which is design.md § Portable SIMD's own worked example.

THE FIVE STAGES, and what each actually cost against what this row first estimated:
  1 (22b3bf3) interpreter carrier widened to i128. The row argued for a parallel Int128 variant; measurement reversed that — the variant produced 2 compile errors against 480 Value::Int sites, so ~478 catch-alls would have swallowed a 128-bit value silently, which is B-2026-08-19-6's own shape. Widening produced 229 compiler-identified sites. PERF GATE PASSED: interleaved A/B, -1.7%, ranges overlapping. It also exposed that the i64 carrier had been doing 64-bit overflow DETECTION for free, and that MIN % -1 needs an explicit width check because its result (0) fits.
  2 (ebcd3ca) AST/token literals widened, lexer admits 128-bit magnitudes behind an explicit suffix. The gate is load-bearing: the (i64::MAX, u64::MAX] band must keep its own token kind or every u64 literal's wrapped encoding changes.
  3a (b0c61ec) codegen. The row called this "the architectural stage" from 832 i64_type() occurrences; a vertical slice refuted it — widen_int_to_i64 returns its input unchanged at >= 64 bits, so the carrier is an AT-LEAST-i64 carrier and the arithmetic paths were already correct once the LLVM type was. Five changes, 88 lines.
  3b (f536190) the method families, both backends. The divergence FLIPPED SIDES mid-fix: fixing the interpreter's width lookup left codegen wrong for the families that coerce a RESULT back to i64. Only running both surfaces found it.
  4 (18522f8) runtime formatting. %lld read 64 bits and 2^100's low word is zero, so printing it produced "0" — a plausible wrong answer. First stage verified on printed DIGITS rather than boolean comparisons.

ONE SHAPE REMAINS REFUSED and is split out to B-2026-08-19-19: a 128-bit ENUM PAYLOAD (Option[i128], Result[i128,E], and checked_* which returns Option[Self]). A payload word is 64 bits and a 128-bit scalar needs two. Unchecked it MISCOMPILES SILENTLY — Option[i128] holding 2^100 read back as 0 — so it is refused loudly rather than shipped. The fix was attempted, five sites deep, and REVERTED when the match arm still read 0: that means the model of the path was incomplete, and a half-applied change to machinery 3000+ codegen tests depend on is worse than none. The layers are written into that row.

ALSO FIXED IN STAGE 5, found by exercising the newly-usable type: the interpreter PANICKED on a narrowing "as" cast (2^100 as i64) where codegen correctly truncated. design.md § numeric cast defines "as" as bitwise/truncating with no runtime check, so the interpreter was the wrong one.

design.md's status note NARROWS to the remaining exception rather than disappearing; deleting it is what closing B-2026-08-19-19 looks like. The four tests B-2026-08-19-6 flipped are restored as their inverses, not deleted.
title: IMPLEMENT 128-bit integers for real: `i128` / `u128` are specified normatively in design.md as v1 primitives (all four overflow method families, the widening-cast table, the primitive-numeric lists, Portable SIMD elements) and the compiler now REJECTS them, because no runtime carrier is 128 bits wide. Deleting design.md's 'Implementation status — 128-bit integers are NOT YET IMPLEMENTED' note is the definition of done.
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-08-19-6 when that row's rejection landed. -6 stopped the silent wrongness; this row is the capability it deferred.

COST RE-MEASURED 2026-08-19, AND THE FIRST ESTIMATE IN THIS ROW WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Read this section before planning the work — the original text understated the total by missing codegen entirely, and overstated the part it did name.

(1) INTERPRETER CARRIER — decided: WIDEN `Value::Int` to `i128`, do NOT add a parallel `Int128` variant. Both were probed by making the edit and counting what the compiler caught:
      separate `Value::Int128(i128)` variant  ->   2 compile errors (both in value.rs)
      widen `Value::Int(i64)` -> `Value::Int(i128)` -> 229 compile errors (219 are E0308)
    The 2-error option is the DANGEROUS one and that is the whole finding: `Value::Int` has 480 occurrences and only two of those matches are exhaustive, so a new variant falls into ~478 catch-alls with no compiler complaint. That is precisely the shape of -6 itself — 128-bit added to the type system with nothing enforcing that the value paths kept up. Widening is more edits and no silent path: every site is compiler-identified, 219 of them plain type mismatches, concentrated in value.rs (160), method_call.rs (39), eval_ops.rs (24), eval_expr.rs (24).
    Size is NOT an objection: `size_of::<Value>()` is already 184 bytes (align 8) because of the `String` variant, so a 16-byte payload is free. The residual cost of widening is that EVERY interpreter integer becomes i128 arithmetic (i128 div/rem call compiler-rt). That is UNMEASURED and is stage 1's gate, not a reason to prefer the unsafe option.

(2) CODEGEN — THE ORIGINAL ESTIMATE'S BIG MISS. This row previously said codegen 'lowers both to LLVM i128_type ... and LLVM does 128-bit arithmetic natively', implying the backend was nearly ready. It is not. Codegen emits ZERO 128-bit instructions. Measured by dumping IR for `let a: i128 = 9223372036854775807; a.wrapping_add(1)`:
        %a = alloca i64, align 8
        store i64 9223372036854775807, ptr %a
        %wadd = add i64 %a1, 1
        call snprintf(..., ptr @fst.fmt_i, i64 %wadd)     ; %lld
    `grep -c i128` over the whole emitted module returns 1 — the `i128:128` datalayout string. The `types_lowering.rs` I128 mapping is not reached for locals.
    This is by DESIGN, not oversight, which is what makes it architectural: `codegen/method_call.rs` states it outright — 'codegen's narrow-int model normalizes to an i64 carrier (`compile_narrow_int_binop`) ... matching the interpreter, which is i64-backed', and the reduction step is skipped for `bits >= 64`. That guard is literally why an i128 wraps at 2^63. `i64_type()` appears 832x in codegen, though most are lengths/indices/ABI rather than the value carrier; the arithmetic-carrier helpers proper are narrow (`widen_int_to_i64` 8, `compile_narrow_int_binop` 11, `receiver_int_kind` 10), so the change is deep rather than wide.

(3) STILL MISSING, unchanged from the original text: the LEXER rejects any integer literal above `i64::MAX`, so a 128-bit value cannot be WRITTEN; and the RUNTIME has no 128-bit formatter (f-strings/println go through snprintf `%lld`).

STAGED PLAN. Each stage is independently testable and NONE of stages 1-4 makes the type nameable again — the -6 rejection stays in place until stage 5, and the -6 tests (`integer_suffix_128bit_is_rejected_as_a_runtime_type`, `float_to_128bit_conversion_methods_are_rejected`) fail loudly if that order is broken, which is intended.
  1. Interpreter carrier: widen `Value::Int` to i128, fix the 229 sites, MEASURE interpreter throughput before/after on an arithmetic-heavy program. If the regression is unacceptable, that is the moment to reconsider — not after codegen work is sunk.
  2. Lexer: admit the full 128-bit literal range for suffixed/annotated forms.
  3. Codegen: a width-parameterized carrier instead of forced-i64 — i128 alloca for 128-bit declared types, arithmetic in the carrier width, and every `bits >= 64` guard restated as `bits >= carrier_bits`. This is the architectural stage.
  4. Runtime: 128-bit integer formatting.
  5. Remove the -6 rejection (`typechecker.rs::reject_128bit` and its three call sites), restore the four flipped tests, restore `Vector[i128, N]` in `tests/simd_report.rs`, and DELETE design.md's 'Implementation status — 128-bit integers are NOT YET IMPLEMENTED' note. That deletion is the definition of done.

WHAT IS GENUINELY ALREADY THERE: `IntSize::I128` / `UIntSize::U128` flow through the typechecker; `ConstValue::I128/U128` exist and CONST EVALUATION IS ALREADY TRUE 128-BIT (Rust `i128` at compile time, never a runtime carrier), so `Array[T, 100i128 + 200i128]` works today and is untouched; `simd_report`'s `bits >= 128 -> UnsupportedElement` arm is retained and unit-tested on `Type` values so the SIMD classification stays correct for when the type becomes spellable again.

STAGE 1 LANDED in 22b3bf3 — the interpreter carrier is now i128. No user-visible change and no new capability: 128-bit is still rejected at type-check. What it bought is the answer to the question that could have invalidated the plan.

PERF GATE PASSED, NO MEASURABLE REGRESSION. Interleaved A/B (both binaries built release, alternated within each round to avoid drift), 7 rounds, 400k iterations of add/sub/mul/div/rem/compare: best-of-7 1796ms before vs 1766ms after (-1.7%), per-round ranges 1796-1970 vs 1766-2002 — fully overlapping. Tree-walk dispatch dominates so completely that the arithmetic width is invisible, INCLUDING the i128 div/rem that call compiler-rt, which was the specific worry. `Value` did not grow either (already 184 bytes from its `String` variant). The objection this row recorded against widening does not survive measurement.

THE CARRIER HAD BEEN DOING OVERFLOW DETECTION FOR FREE — the one piece of real semantic work in stage 1, and something neither this row nor B-2026-08-19-6 anticipated. `narrow_oob` range-checked only the NARROW widths and was documented as "a no-op for i64/u64/usize/isize", because a 64-bit overflow was caught by the i64 carrier itself (`checked_add` returning None). Widening removed that silently: `i64::MAX + 1` fits in an i128. Width now comes from the declared type at every width, and an unrecorded span defaults to i64's range rather than to no-check (`karac run` populates `expr_types` sparsely and those spans used to trap via the carrier). Five tests failed on the first build, which is exactly the compiler-and-suite-enforced feedback the separate-variant option would not have produced.

`MIN % -1` NEEDED MORE THAN A RANGE CHECK and had no test. Its result is 0 — fits every width — so nothing about the value says overflow; the old carrier reported it because the intermediate division overflowed the carrier. `div_overflows_at_width` now makes it explicit for `/`, `%`, `div_euclid`, `rem_euclid`. Only the euclid pair had coverage; the `%` case was found by asking what else the carrier had been doing for free.

WORKLIST FOR STAGE 3/5: `grep -rn narrow_to_i64 src/` — ~100 sites where a value leaves the i128 carrier for an i64-only consumer. It is a HARD check, not a `debug_assert`, and it fired during stage 1 catching the overflow case above; a silently-truncating release build would have reproduced the very defect this work removes.

STAGES 2-5 UNCHANGED and still ordered so the type stays unnameable until the end.

STAGE 2 LANDED in ebcd3ca — `ExprKind::Integer` and `Token::Integer` carry i128, `Token::IntegerOutOfRange` carries u128, and a magnitude past `u64::MAX` lexes with an explicit 128-bit suffix in all four radices. Still unusable by design: the type stays rejected, so such a literal lexes, parses, and is then refused on the type.

THE LEXER THRESHOLD IS GATED ON THE SUFFIX, and that gate is load-bearing rather than conservatism. The `(i64::MAX, u64::MAX]` band must keep producing `IntegerOutOfRange`, because the parser encodes that band as a WRAPPED bit pattern on the signed carrier and the typechecker reads it back through the suffix. Widening the thresholds unconditionally reroutes every `u64` literal into `Token::Integer` and silently changes that encoding — a test pins the band precisely because that is the simplification a later reader reaches for.

THE WRAP SURVIVES ON PURPOSE, and stage 5 owns retiring it. With an i128 node a `u64` magnitude fits positively and the wrap looks obsolete — but the INTERPRETER still represents unsigned runtime VALUES the same wrapped way (`(a as u64) as i128` at several sites in `method_call.rs`). Retiring one without the other splits the encoding between literal and value, so both move together.

COST: 40 compiler-identified sites for the node widening (AST 30, +10 for the token), plus 32 more in codegen that the DEFAULT feature leg does not compile — the default build was clean while `--features llvm` had 32 errors. CLAUDE.md warns about the two legs and it still took the second run to surface; anyone continuing this work should build both legs after every stage.

WORKLIST ADDITION: `grep -rn narrow_literal_to_i64 src/` — ~30 AST-layer sites, the sibling of stage 1's `narrow_to_i64` (~100 value-layer sites). Both are hard checks, both are what stage 5 must revisit.

STAGE 3a LANDED in b0c61ec — codegen emits real 128-bit IR (`alloca i128` / `add i128` / `icmp sgt i128`, against `alloca i64` / `add i64` and a whole-module i128 count of 1 before). Still inert: the type stays rejected.

THIS ROW'S STAGE-3 ESTIMATE WAS WRONG, AND WRONG IN THE EXPENSIVE DIRECTION. It called codegen 'the architectural stage', reasoning from 832 `i64_type()` occurrences and from `method_call.rs`'s own comment that the backend 'normalizes to an i64 carrier'. A vertical slice refuted it: `widen_int_to_i64` RETURNS ITS INPUT UNCHANGED at `>= 64` bits, and reduction is skipped for `bits >= 64` — so the carrier is an AT-LEAST-i64 carrier and every arithmetic path was already width-correct for 128 bits once the LLVM type was right. The whole stage was FIVE focused changes, 88 lines across 10 files:
  1. `llvm_type_for_name` had no `i128`/`u128` arm — both fell to the unknown-name i64 default, which is why an `i128` local allocated as `alloca i64`.
  2. `const_int_for_suffix` used single-word `const_int` (sign-extends one u64, truncates anything wider) — now `const_int_arbitrary_precision`.
  3. `receiver_int_kind` had no 128 arm, so width-sensitive intrinsics answered for 64: `(-1i128).count_ones()` returned 64, now 128.
  4. PARSER GAP the slice found: a 128-bit-suffixed literal in the `(i64::MAX, u64::MAX]` band was rejected outright, because that band routes to the wrapped-bit-pattern arm whose unsigned list excludes `i128`. 128-bit suffixes now take the magnitude positively; the wrap stays with the widths that need it.
  5. `bce_length_pin` and `int_const_locals` FAIL CLOSED on a 128-bit literal rather than narrowing — both are i64 constant tables feeding bound elision, and declining costs a bounds check while truncating would cost an OOB.
VERIFIED BY DISCRIMINATION rather than by a comparison that could pass with both sides wrong: `2^63 > 0` (the 64-bit wrap is negative) and 2^100 arithmetic across `+ - * / %`. `i128::MAX + 1` traps in both backends.

REMAINING — STAGE 3b, INTERPRETER PARITY. Measured on the same programs: codegen is 128-bit correct while `karac run --interp` still wraps at 64 for `wrapping_*` and panics in `narrow_to_i64` for `count_ones`. Stage 1 widened the VALUE CARRIER but not the width-sensitive METHOD paths, which still narrow their operands to i64 (`eval_wrapping_arith`, the bit intrinsics). Nothing observes the divergence today because the type is rejected, but stage 5 must not lift the rejection until interp and codegen agree. That is now the next slice, and it is the same `grep -rn narrow_to_i64 src/interpreter/` worklist.

STAGE 3b LANDED in f536190 — the method families are 128-bit correct on BOTH backends, and interp/AOT agree. Verified as a matrix on the same programs, 11 cases all matching: wrapping / checked / saturating add, pow(2,100), count_ones, leading_zeros, rotate and byte/bit permutation chains, `+ - * / %` at 2^100, and the `i128::MAX + 1` trap. The parity constraint stage 3a recorded is satisfied.

THE DIVERGENCE FLIPPED SIDES MID-FIX, which is the part worth keeping. The interpreter's `int_width_at` had no 128 arms, so every width-sensitive method fell to its signed-64 default (`wrapping_*` wrapped at 2^63, `count_ones` panicked in `narrow_to_i64`). Fixing that made the interpreter right and left CODEGEN wrong for `checked_*`, `saturating_*`, `pow`, `rotate_*` and the bit permutations — each computed at the correct width and then coerced its RESULT back to i64. `int_carrier_type_for_bits` now names the distinction: a result rides the receiver's carrier, a COUNT (`count_ones` -> u32) does not. Neither side was visible from the other; only running both found it.

A CHAINED CALL WAS THE LAST HOLE, and its origin is not 128-specific. The parser aliases a chain's `MethodCall.span` to its receiver's, so `method_callee_types` holds one entry for the whole chain (B-2026-07-18-36) and the outer call fell through to `receiver_int_kind`'s 64-bit default. `a.swap_bytes().swap_bytes()` on an i128 round-tripped through a 64-bit swap and lost the top half while the same expression UNCHAINED was correct — which is what made it findable at all. `type_name_of_expr` now resolves a Self-returning integer method to its receiver's type. That changes chain resolution at EVERY width, so the narrow widths carry an E2E test; they are what the change puts at risk today. Also corrected: `receiver_int_kind`'s literal-suffix arm mapped `I128`/`U128` to 64 outright.

REMAINING: stage 4 (runtime 128-bit formatting — `println`/f-strings still go through snprintf `%lld`, which is why the stage-3 probes compare values instead of printing them) and stage 5 (lift the rejection, restore the four flipped tests and `Vector[i128, N]`, delete design.md's status note). Stage 5's gate list is now: formatter done, and the interp/AOT matrix above still green.

STAGE 4 LANDED in 18522f8 — `println` and f-strings render 128-bit integers correctly under AOT. They went through snprintf `%lld` before, which reads 64 bits, and the failure was not conspicuous: `2^100` has an all-zero low word, so printing it produced `0`.

THE INTERPRETER ALREADY DID THIS RIGHT — its carrier has been an i128 since stage 1, so `format!("{v}")` was exact and only AOT needed work. `karac_runtime_i128_to_str` is the same arrangement `karac_runtime_f64_to_str` uses for floats: Rust's `Display` is the reference both surfaces agree on. The value crosses the ABI as two 64-bit WORDS rather than by value, since `extern "C"` i128 is not uniformly defined across this runtime's targets.

VERIFIED AS PRINTED VALUES, not boolean comparisons — 12 cases, interp vs AOT, every digit matching: 2^100 with its double and seventh, `i128::MAX`, `i128::MIN`, 0, +/-1, `2^64` and `2^64 - 1` (the word boundary), multi-hole f-strings, and the stage-3 method matrix re-run in printing form. Stages 1-3 could only compare values; this is the first stage where the digits are on screen.

TWO GAPS IT SURFACED, both found by running rather than reading. `u128` literals past `u64::MAX` hit `literal_as_i128`'s wrap read-back and tripped its own debug assertion — stage 3a had made 128-bit suffixes store POSITIVELY while that read-back still applied the u64 wrap, so `u128` leaves the wrapped list. And `to_string()` on an `i128`/`u128` fell through method dispatch entirely because `is_scalar_primitive_name` never listed the 128-bit names (a loud codegen error, not a wrong answer).

ARCHIVE NOTE FOR ANYONE PICKING THIS UP: `karac_runtime_i128_to_str` is a NEW runtime symbol, so every archive built before it is stale and fails the link with `undefined reference`. The lean and full archives were rebuilt here and the two targets that link them — `codegen` (3071 tests) and `memory_sanitizer` (1130) — were run under `KARAC_REQUIRE_RUNTIME_ARCHIVE=1` so a soft-skip could not hide it. The OPTIONAL gpu archive is absent in this container as it always has been and will need the same rebuild wherever it exists; the symbol is not feature-gated.

ONLY STAGE 5 REMAINS: remove `reject_128bit` and its three call sites, restore the four tests B-2026-08-19-6 flipped plus `Vector[i128, N]` in `tests/simd_report.rs`, retire the `narrow_to_i64` / `narrow_literal_to_i64` worklists where they now block real values, revisit `u128`'s `i128::MAX` ceiling (the carrier is signed), and DELETE design.md's 'Implementation status — 128-bit integers are NOT YET IMPLEMENTED' note. That deletion is the definition of done.
tracker: docs/design.md § checked_*/wrapping_*/saturating_*/overflowing_* method families (the status note — deleting it is done); src/typechecker.rs::reject_128bit; src/interpreter/value.rs::Value::Int; src/codegen/method_call.rs (the i64-carrier comment + the `bits >= 64` reduction guard)

fix: FIXED by 7c862b7d. `gpu_probe` now RESOLVES a backend — explicit `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND`, then the platform's default adapter, then a forced software one — instead of pinning `cpu` on every fixture, so the execution suite runs on Metal here and on lavapipe in a GPU-less container. The `NoAdapter`-only fallback and the no-fallback-when-forced rule were both verified (the first by mutating the emitter to produce invalid WGSL and confirming the `Broken` arm still panics on Metal), and the candidate order is pinned by a pure test that runs on GPU-less hosts. 16 passed / 0 skips on Metal, up from 15 passed / 14 skips.
title: `tests/gpu_e2e.rs` PINNED `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu`, so all fourteen execution fixtures SKIPPED ON macOS — the project's primary dev machine — while reporting `ok`. macOS has no software adapter, so the one suite that actually runs shaders had never run on Metal, and every `#[gpu]` increment to date was validated on lavapipe only. FIXED: the probe now RESOLVES a backend (explicit env, then the host's own device, then software) instead of pinning one.
detail:
FOUND while validating B-2026-08-18-40's four kernel-body increments on the M5,
which is the whole reason it was found: the container that landed them has no
Metal device and could not have noticed.

MEASURED on macOS 25.5 / Apple M5 Pro, with libkarac_runtime_gpu.a built:

  $ ./probe                          # default adapter
  1
  2
  $ KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu ./probe    # what the suite pinned
  runtime error: KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu: no software (CPU) adapter is
  available. ... Available adapters:
    KARAC_GPU=0: Apple M5 Pro [Metal, Integrated]

The device is RIGHT THERE and named in the error. `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu` asks
`select_adapter` for a `DeviceType::Cpu` adapter (runtime/src/gpu.rs); Apple
ships no software Metal device, so on macOS there is never one. That error
matches `is_no_adapter`, so the probe classified a fully working host as
`NoAdapter` and all fourteen execution fixtures took the soft-skip:

  test result: ok. 15 passed; 0 failed  ... finished in 1.41s
  $ ... | grep -c 'gpu_e2e: skipping'
  14

1.41s for fourteen fixtures that each build and run a binary is the tell; the
suite reported green having executed no shader at all.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A MISSING TEST. It is precisely the vacuous-pass hole
this file's own header was written to close (and which B-2026-08-18-51 already
had to re-close once for the archive case), reintroduced by the mechanism meant
to make the suite portable. The skip message compounded it — it advised
installing `mesa-vulkan-drivers`, which does not exist on macOS, so the honest
reading of a local run was "this machine can't do GPU work", which is false.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE GPU WORK TO DATE: every `#[gpu]` increment (B-2026-08-18-40
increments 1-4, B-2026-08-18-49 steps 1-2, B-2026-08-19-1) was validated on
lavapipe, i.e. naga -> SPIR-V, only. macOS goes naga -> MSL. Those are different
backends with different validation rules, so a lowering valid in one shader
language and not the other would have been invisible. That gap was live for the
entire GPU push.

THE FIX. `gpu_probe` now RESOLVES a backend instead of pinning one, in order:
an explicit `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND` from the caller, then the platform's default
adapter, then a forced software adapter. macOS lands on Metal, a GPU-less Linux
box still lands on lavapipe, and pinning the software lane stays one env var
away. `build_and_run_on_gpu` takes the resolved backend and `env_remove`s the
variable for the default case, so an exported value in the parent `cargo test`
process cannot leak into the child and quietly override the choice.

TWO CONTRACTS WERE PRESERVED DELIBERATELY, and both were verified rather than
argued:

  1. THE FALLBACK IS REACHED ONLY FROM `NoAdapter`. Retrying on ANY failure
     would let a host with a working device mask a genuinely broken shader as a
     skip — exactly what the four-way split exists to prevent. Verified by
     MUTATION: emitting `arrayLength(input)` (naga rejects the non-pointer
     form) makes the suite PANIC through the `Broken` arm on Metal, not skip.
  2. AN EXPLICIT `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND` DOES NOT FALL BACK. Forcing the software
     lane on a host that has a device is a legitimate thing to want (it is how
     a CI job pins lavapipe), and silently falling back to the real GPU would
     report a pass for a lane that never ran. Verified: `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu`
     on this M5 still skips rather than quietly running on Metal.

The skip/panic wording now follows what was actually TRIED, so a forced-lane
skip on a machine that HAS a GPU no longer reads as "this host has no adapter".

PINNED BY A PURE TEST (`backend_order_prefers_the_hosts_own_device`), in the
style of the classifier test beside it, because re-pinning the backend is a
one-line change that looks harmless and silently un-runs fourteen tests on a
whole platform. It asserts the candidate ORDER and both wordings, takes its
input as an argument rather than reading the ambient environment (an earlier
draft did read it, and failed under `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND=cpu`), and therefore
runs and asserts on hosts with no GPU at all — the hosts where nothing else in
the file asserts anything.

RESULT ON METAL: 16 passed, 0 skips, 3.9s (was 15 passed / 14 skips / 1.4s).
All fourteen fixtures agree with the interpreter on Apple Silicon, so every
kernel construct shipped so far is now confirmed through naga's MSL backend as
well as SPIR-V.

--- FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-19: THE MSL LEG IS NOW A CI LANE (4cd574ce) ---

Fixing this row made the Metal lane RUNNABLE; it still only ran when someone ran
it locally. `gpu-e2e-macos` (macos-latest, non-required until it has a green
streak) makes naga -> MSL permanent alongside the Linux `gpu-e2e` job's
lavapipe / naga -> SPIR-V.

VIABILITY WAS MEASURED FIRST, on a throwaway branch-scoped probe, in two rounds
— the cheap question before the expensive one:

  ROUND 1 (~2 min, no LLVM, no karac — just the runtime's own GPU unit tests):
    arch: arm64, macOS 26.5.2
    system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType  ->  (nothing at all)
    test result: ok. 10 passed; 0 failed
    adapter-missing skip lines: 0

  ROUND 2 (~8 min, the real candidate job end-to-end):
    gpu_e2e (Metal):         16 passed; 0 failed   9.36s
    runtime GPU unit tests:  10 passed; 0 failed
    gpu_e2e skip lines:      0
    gpu_e2e: running on the platform's default adapter

THE MISLEADING SIGNAL, which is the part worth keeping: a hosted macOS runner is
HEADLESS, so `system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType` prints NOTHING. Probing "does
this runner have a GPU" that way returns the opposite of the truth — wgpu
enumerates and dispatches on a Metal adapter perfectly well. Only wgpu's own
enumeration answers the question.

ROUND 2 EXISTED BECAUSE ROUND 1 DOES NOT PROVE THE JOB. An adapter being present
says nothing about Homebrew LLVM 18, the gpu archive build, or the suite itself
on that host. Running the real job on the probe branch first is what kept a
red job off main; the version committed is substance-identical to the proven one
(runs-on, env and all eight steps compared programmatically rather than by eye).

TWO DETAILS IN THE JOB ARE LOAD-BEARING:
  • `KARAC_GPU_BACKEND` is deliberately NOT set — leaving it unset is what
    selects Metal. Setting it to `cpu`, as the Linux lane does on purpose, would
    reintroduce THIS BUG inside the job created to prevent it.
  • A final step asserts the suite EXECUTED (zero `gpu_e2e: skipping` lines plus
    the backend banner), because a green exit code is not evidence here: skips go
    to stderr and the suite still reports `ok`. That is the whole failure mode
    this row was filed for, so the lane refuses to trust its own exit code.

COST: public repo, so macOS runner minutes are free; ~8 minutes wall-clock.
tracker: `gpu_probe` / `build_and_run_on_gpu` / `backend_candidates` in tests/gpu_e2e.rs; `select_adapter` in runtime/src/gpu.rs (the `DeviceType::Cpu` requirement that makes `=cpu` unsatisfiable on macOS); cf. B-2026-08-18-51, the previous vacuous-pass hole in the same probe.

title: A GPU REDUCTION (N inputs -> 1 result) CANNOT BE WRITTEN AT ALL. `gpu.dispatch` is the entire user-facing GPU surface and it is map-shaped ([T] -> [U], one output per input); the WGSL emitter has ZERO workgroup-memory or barrier support. So sum / dot / min / max / argmax / prefix-sum / any tiled matmul have nowhere to go, which is most of what GPUs are bought for.
detail:
MEASURED 2026-08-19. Both natural spellings are rejected at the dispatch site:

  #[gpu] fn k(v: Vec[f32]) -> f32   { ...sum v... }
      E_GPU_DISPATCH_KERNEL: the GPU kernel parameter must be f32, i32, or u32 in slice-0

  #[gpu] fn k(x: f32, acc: f32) -> f32 { acc + x }
      E_GPU_DISPATCH_KERNEL: a GPU kernel takes exactly one parameter in slice-0, found 2

And `src/gpu_wgsl.rs` contains no `var<workgroup>` and no `workgroupBarrier()` — zero occurrences — so even a hand-written reduction body has no cross-lane mechanism to lower to. The seven runtime entrypoints (`karac_runtime_gpu_{map, map_multi, dispatch_soa, upload_soa, dispatch_resident, download_soa, free_soa}`) are all map/element shaped; none returns a scalar.

WHY THIS IS NOW THE BINDING CONSTRAINT. B-2026-08-18-40's original text said no reduction could be written because the kernel BODY was a single expression. That was lifted on 2026-08-18 (locals, while, for-range, match) and B-2026-08-18-49 (statement `if`), so an accumulator body compiles and runs today. The blocker moved rather than cleared: the body can express a fold, the DISPATCH SHAPE cannot express one. Anyone reading the older entry will believe reductions were unblocked; they were not.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE FEATURE LIST. The CG-5 assessment (`docs/spikes/gpu-llvm-offload-assessment.md`) frames Kara against a rustc/LLVM-Offload paper benchmarked on RAJAPerf, which is largely reductions and stencils. Kara currently cannot express that benchmark class at all, so there is no honest comparison to make regardless of hardware. This gap, not CG-7's missing discrete GPU, is what stands between us and a comparable number.

SHAPE OF THE WORK (not started, sketched only):
  1. A dispatch form that returns a scalar rather than a buffer — surface, typecheck, and a runtime entrypoint whose readback is one element.
  2. Workgroup memory + barriers in the emitter (`var<workgroup> arr: array<f32, N>;` plus `workgroupBarrier()`), which is the first time the emitter needs a construct with no expression-level Kara counterpart.
  3. The standard two-stage tree reduction: per-workgroup partial into workgroup memory, then a second pass (or an atomic) over the partials. Slice 1 can be single-workgroup only — a buffer that fits one workgroup — which proves the whole path end to end without the second stage.
  4. Testable GPU-lessly through `tests/gpu_e2e.rs` on lavapipe, and on Metal via the resolving probe, so the two naga backends both get exercised.

ALTERNATIVE WORTH PRICING FIRST: expose the associativity requirement honestly. A float reduction on a GPU is NOT the same number as the interpreter's left fold — the tree order differs — so the A/B rule (`run` == `build`) that kara-katas/CLAUDE.md calls non-negotiable cannot hold bit-exactly for f32 sums. That has to be decided BEFORE the feature ships, not after: either the oracle tolerates a documented epsilon for reductions, or the reduction is specified as tree-ordered and the INTERPRETER changes to match. The second is more defensible and is the smaller surprise for users, but it is a semantics decision, not an implementation detail.

REMAINDER SPLIT OUT, NOT BURIED HERE: what shipped is `Sum` and `Prod` over `Vec[f32]`. The Ord family (min / max / argmin / argmax), the two-pass statistics (mean / var / std), dot products, prefix sums and tiled matmul are still unwritable, and integer reductions are blocked on an overflow rule rather than on effort. Those are B-2026-08-19-13, filed against this row rather than left implicit in it.
fix:
FIXED by 63870ee0 (the last of three commits, 2026-08-19): the premise — "a GPU reduction cannot be written at all" — is now false.

  * `gpu.sum(buf)` / `gpu.prod(buf)` are a surface form, reusing the existing `ReduceOp` vocabulary rather than inventing a second one. Typechecker, interpreter, codegen and runtime are all wired; `karac_runtime_gpu_reduce_f32` is the scalar-returning entrypoint item 1 of the sketch asked for.
  * The emitter grew `var<workgroup>` + `workgroupBarrier()` (item 2) — its first construct with no expression-level Kara counterpart, as predicted.
  * Two-stage tree reduction (item 3), BOTH stages: each dispatch collapses every workgroup's 64-wide chunk to one partial at `output[workgroup_id]`, and the host re-dispatches the same shader over the partials until one value remains. Any length, not the single-workgroup slice the sketch was willing to settle for.
  * Verified on lavapipe through `tests/gpu_e2e.rs` (item 4) with real AOT binaries: 64-, 65-, 4096-element and empty fixtures, each asserting interpreter == GPU bit-for-bit.

THE ALTERNATIVE THE ROW ASKED TO PRICE FIRST WAS PRICED FIRST, AND THE ROW'S OWN RECOMMENDATION WAS TAKEN. The tree order is now specified and the INTERPRETER changed to match, rather than the oracle tolerating an epsilon. So the A/B rule holds bit-exactly for f32 reductions instead of being weakened for them: `reduce_kernel::tree_reduce_f32` reproduces the shader step for step (pad to 64 with the op's identity, halve at strides 32..1), and a buffer past one workgroup recurses through the same chunking the host dispatch performs — a TREE OF TREES whose grouping is observable in f32 and therefore part of the specified answer. Sixty-four copies of 0.1 sum to 6.400000 on both legs where a left fold gives 6.399996; 4096 copies give 409.6000061035156 on both.

Two things worth knowing that the row could not have anticipated:

  * The tree order is also the MORE ACCURATE one — pairing keeps partial sums at similar magnitudes — so specifying it costs nothing in precision.
  * An empty buffer never reaches a device, so the runtime has to be TOLD the identity; it was hardcoded to 0.0, which would have made `gpu.prod([])` print 0 under `karac build` and 1 under `karac run`. Found by writing the multi-workgroup fold, not by any reduction test that existed at the time.

FIXED by f4340ba. SPEC EDIT, as the row's own closing paragraph guessed it might be -- but for the opposite reason. The row expected the spec to be right and the compiler behind it; the truth is the compiler was right and the SPEC was four lines out of date.

design.md now says, at every one of the five spots that touched this:

- :7223 "must implement all declared bounds plus `Send + Sync`" -> "must implement all declared bounds, and its concrete type must be cross-task-safe", with a pointer to the enforcement paragraph and an explicit note that Kara has no Send/Sync auto-traits (item 61).
- :7230 the signature itself: `P: R.Provider + Send + Sync` -> `P: R.Provider`. This is verbatim what docs/deferred.md's "Updated design shape" paragraph said the signature should be -- the decision was recorded in deferred.md on 2026-05-02 and never propagated into design.md, which is the authoritative document.
- :7236 "`Send + Sync` is enforced at the call site ... the constraint is visible in `with_provider`'s signature" -> rewritten to say thread-safety is enforced structurally against the resolved concrete `P`, and is NOT a bound in the signature at all.
- :7244 / :7245 the two bullets that described providers as "satisfying `Send + Sync`" / "satisfying `Sync`" -> cross-task-safety and concurrent-access wording.

:7274 keeps its Send/Sync mentions on purpose: that paragraph is the one EXPLAINING the replacement, and its deferred.md cross-reference is the historical record.
title: design.md's `with_provider` signature demanded `Send + Sync`, a guarantee Kara had already DECIDED NOT TO SHIP under that name -- four stale spec lines corrected to the structural cross-task-safe set that in fact enforces it (the row's "NOTHING checks it" was refuted by measurement; see detail)
detail:
MEASURED while closing B-2026-08-19-3 (multi-bound `effect resource R: A + B`). That row wired up the FIRST half of design.md:7223 -- "Any provider passed to `with_provider` must implement all declared bounds" is now checked, per bound, with its own diagnostic. The `plus Send + Sync` half is untouched and is deliberately NOT claimed by that row's fix prose.

THIS IS NOT A MULTI-BOUND REGRESSION, which is why it is filed separately rather than left as a caveat on -19-3. It was equally unchecked at arity 1, before multi-bounds existed, and `check_provider_satisfies_declared_bound` (B-2026-08-19-4) did not check it either. A provider that is neither Send nor Sync passes every phase today and runs.

THE COST IS NOT A CHECK, IT IS A TRAIT SYSTEM. `Send` and `Sync` appear NOWHERE in `src/` -- not in the prelude's trait list, not as auto-derived marker traits, not in `type_satisfies_bound`. So this cannot be closed by adding two `type_satisfies_bound` calls beside the declared-bound loop: there is nothing for them to resolve to, and inventing user-declarable `Send`/`Sync` traits would be the wrong shape (they are AUTO traits -- structurally derived from a type's fields, not written by hand). Whoever picks this up should decide whether v1 wants auto traits at all before touching the provider check; the provider surface is one consumer of that decision, not the reason to make it.

SO THIS MAY WELL BE A SPEC EDIT RATHER THAN A COMPILER CHANGE -- the same open question B-2026-08-18-41 answered in the compiler's favour for the three declaration forms, asked here about a concurrency guarantee. The sibling § Operator Traits carries a v1 caveat for exactly this situation. Deciding which is the work; the wrong guess writes a false claim into either the compiler or the corpus.

WHY IT MATTERS AT ALL, given the low severity: the provider stack is a RUNTIME stack (`karac_provider_push` / `_lookup`), and a `with_provider` body that spawns or runs under `par {}` reaches the same frame from more than one thread. `Send + Sync` on the provider is what design.md offers as the guarantee that this is safe. Nothing enforces it, so the guarantee is currently prose.

CORRECTION (2026-08-19, at close). The row's central factual claim is FALSE and was refuted by running the compiler, not by reading it. "A provider that is neither Send nor Sync passes every phase today and runs" -- it does not. The guarantee is enforced, and has been since Phase 6 line 170 slice 3c; it is simply not spelled Send/Sync, which is why the row's `grep '"Send"' src/` came back empty and was read as absence of enforcement rather than absence of that NAME.

MEASURED. A `shared struct` provider is rejected at the call site in all three surface forms -- inline `with_provider[R](SharedDB { .. }, || ..)`, a let-bound provider, and `providers { R => .. } in { .. }` -- each with `error[E_NOT_CROSS_TASK]: provider for resource `UserDB` (type `SharedDB`) cannot cross a task boundary`, a type-path note, and a `par`-form fix-it. src/typechecker/expr_call.rs:678 and src/typechecker/exprs.rs:5215 are the two call sites; tests/typechecker.rs already carried with_provider_shared_struct_provider_rejected and with_provider_provider_with_raw_pointer_field_rejected.

The design question the row posed -- "decide whether v1 wants auto traits at all before touching the provider check" -- was ALREADY ANSWERED, in three places the row did not reach: design.md:7274 (the paragraph three below the one it cites), design.md:3519 (item 61, No Auto-Traits), and docs/deferred.md:425, whose title literally ends "-- Superseded by Structural Cross-Task-Safe Set (item 48)". There was no decision left to make and none was made here.

WHAT THE ROW WAS RIGHT ABOUT: design.md:7223 does say `Send + Sync`, and that IS wrong -- it contradicts design.md's own :7274, contradicts item 61, and contradicts deferred.md's recorded "the signature is no longer ... + Send + Sync". A reader following the spec would write a bound the language does not have. That defect was real, and fixing it is what this row closed.

WHAT PROBING IT TURNED UP, which is worth more than the row was: two live compiler bugs, both found by writing the provider the spec's own fix-it tells you to write. B-2026-08-19-13 (`shared struct` / `par struct` could not satisfy ANY trait bound anywhere -- `impl_table_key` had no `Type::Shared` arm) and B-2026-08-19-14 (the `providers {}` block form never checked the declared provider trait at all). Together they made the provider surface a catch-22: the cross-task check tells you to replace `shared struct` with `par struct`, and doing so produced "ParDB does not implement DbProvider". Both fixed alongside this row.

METHOD NOTE, third in three days. This row, like B-2026-08-19-12, was filed from a plausible mechanism rather than a run -- a grep for a NAME was read as absence of a BEHAVIOUR. The cheap guard is the one that worked here: write the four-line program the row says should be accepted, and run it. Both rows would have been caught in under a minute.
tracker: design.md:7223 (`with_provider` signature at :7225, `P: R.Provider + Send + Sync`); src/typechecker/expr_call.rs::check_provider_satisfies_declared_bound

title: RETRACTED CLAIM: that ~100 E2E harness sites passing a bare `karac::effectcheck` into the auto-par / concurrency tables diverge from `karac build`'s typecheck-threaded form. Measured on three shapes (unique-name effectful method, SAME method name on two types, polymorphic effect slot): the effect sets, diagnostics, `callee_effectful` table and `concurrency_analyze` output are IDENTICAL. Only `call_effect_subs` differs, and all six sites that build it already use the threaded form.
detail:
FOUND while closing B-2026-08-19-5 (which wired the effect checker into the same harnesses as a GATE). That row's fix needed a build-faithful effect run and got one; this row is the observation that ~100 OTHER call sites in the same files still use the bare form for a different purpose, and that the difference is not cosmetic.

WHAT DIVERGES. `Pipeline::effectcheck` (cli.rs) calls `effectcheck_with_typecheck_data`, threading the typechecker's `method_callee_types` and `call_type_subs`, and then builds `Program.callee_effectful`, `callee_network_yield_effect`, `call_effect_subs` and `callee_purely_polymorphic_effects` from the result. Codegen uses those to narrow the par-branch cooperative cancel-check, and `concurrency_analyze` consumes the same effect table for disjointness. The harnesses rebuild those tables by hand from `karac::effectcheck(&parsed.program)` -- the no-argument form, with an EMPTY `method_callee_types`.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS DOCUMENTED, from a prior incident in a different consumer of the same API. `tests/cli.rs::test_query_effects_resolves_instance_method_network_effect` records it verbatim: the Effects query arm "ran `effectcheck()` without `typecheck()`, so `method_callee_types` was empty and an effect reaching a caller *through an instance method* (`c.get(...)`) was invisible -- `inferred_effects` came back `[]` even though `build`/`test` correctly propagate `sends`/`receives(Network)`." Threading the table is the documented PURPOSE of the richer entrypoint, so any harness program whose effects flow through a method call gets a table production does not use.

DIRECTION OF THE ERROR: under-reporting. A missing entry in `callee_effectful` means the par-branch cancel-check is narrowed AWAY in the test where production would keep it -- so the tests can be greener than the shipped binary, on precisely the concurrency surface `par_codegen`/`parallax` exist to cover. That is the same "suite tests what ships" invariant `assert_ownership_clean`'s comment defends, one phase over.

NOT FIXED IN -19-5 DELIBERATELY, and this is the scope note that matters: switching the bare calls is a BEHAVIOUR change to the auto-par analysis across ~100 tests, not a gate addition. It could legitimately change which branches get cancel-checks and therefore what those tests assert. It wants its own change, its own measurement of which tests move, and a decision about each that moves -- rather than being folded into a test-infra commit as a silent rider.

SITE COUNT by file (grep `karac::effectcheck(&parsed.program)`): par_codegen 59, codegen 6, parallax 6, parallax_lite 6, memory_sanitizer 4, effectchecker 9 (those are legitimate -- unit tests OF the bare checker), disjoint_differential 2, wasm_codegen 2, concurrency_report / http_server / park_and_wake / scaffold / spawn_e2e / tcp_listener / tcp_stream / parallax_bench 1 each. The `effectchecker.rs` ones are testing the entrypoint itself and are correct as they stand; the harness ones are the subject.

SHAPE OF THE FIX: reuse `common::effectcheck_as_build_does(&parsed.program, &typed)` (added by -19-5, already the build-faithful call) at the harness sites, run the suite, and triage every test whose behaviour moves. Expect the movement to be concentrated in `par_codegen`.

SEVERITY MEDIUM rather than low: nothing miscompiles and no user-facing behaviour is wrong -- the compiler does the right thing, the tests measure the wrong thing -- but the blind spot sits on the concurrency surface, where the suite is the only oracle and B-2026-07-12-29 already showed a leak class that only one architecture's run could see.
fix:
INVALID — the premise was refuted by measurement, in b5e1ffae. Filed on 2026-08-19 while closing B-2026-08-19-5; retracted the same day.

WHAT THE ROW CLAIMED: that the ~100 harness sites passing a bare `karac::effectcheck(&parsed.program)` into the auto-par / concurrency tables diverge from `karac build`, which threads the typechecker's `method_callee_types` + `call_type_subs`, and that effects reaching a caller THROUGH AN INSTANCE METHOD are therefore missing from the table those tests analyze.

WHY IT LOOKED TRUE, AND WHY THAT WAS NOT ENOUGH. It reasoned from a real, documented incident in a DIFFERENT consumer: `tests/cli.rs::test_query_effects_resolves_instance_method_network_effect` records that the Effects query arm "ran `effectcheck()` without `typecheck()`, so `method_callee_types` was empty and an effect reaching a caller *through an instance method* (`c.get(...)`) was invisible -- `inferred_effects` came back `[]`". That is a genuine defect, and threading the table is the documented PURPOSE of the richer entrypoint. The inference was that the same omission must have the same consequence in the harnesses. It does not: the query arm ran NO typecheck at all, while the harnesses run the full resolve -> typecheck -> lower front end first and only skip passing the side tables. Reasoning from a neighbouring bug's mechanism is not measurement, and this row is the record of that difference mattering.

MEASURED (bare vs threaded, both after a full front end, on the three shapes most likely to break):
  * an effectful instance method with a UNIQUE name;
  * two types declaring the SAME method name where only one is effectful, so name-based lookup alone is ambiguous and the receiver's resolved type is the only disambiguator -- the closest analogue of the query-arm repro;
  * a polymorphic effect slot (`fn run[with E](ref self, f: Fn() -> i64 with E)`) reached through a method call, the shape `call_type_subs` exists for.
In all three, `inferred_effects`, `declared_effects`, the diagnostics, the `callee_effectful` table AND `concurrency_analyze`'s full output are IDENTICAL. Also checked without `lower` in between, in case lowering was what made the bare form sufficient: still identical.

ONE REAL DIFFERENCE, and it is already handled everywhere it matters: `call_effect_subs` is EMPTY under the bare form and carries the `E := sends(Net)` entry under the threaded one. That table feeds `Program.call_effect_subs` via `build_call_effect_subs_table` and codegen reads it. All SIX sites in `tests/` that build it -- codegen (3), coro_e2e (2), relay_bench (1) -- already call `effectcheck_with_typecheck_data`. So the hazard the row was groping toward is real but was never live.

WHAT LANDED INSTEAD OF A HUNDRED-SITE REFACTOR: two tests in tests/effectchecker.rs. `call_effect_subs_needs_the_typecheck_threaded_effectcheck` pins the real difference, because an empty substitution table is indistinguishable from "this program has no polymorphic calls" and would fail silently if a future site got it wrong. `effect_sets_agree_with_and_without_the_threaded_tables` pins the negative result over all three shapes, so the next reader does not re-derive this row from the same cli.rs comment.

A METHODOLOGICAL NOTE, since this is the second row in two days whose cost estimate was wrong in the same direction: B-2026-08-19-3 predicted a dispatch redesign that a closer look at the actual invariant made unnecessary, and this one predicted a divergence that measurement refuted. Both were filed from a plausible mechanism rather than from a run. Filing on suspicion is fine -- that is what the ledger is for -- but the suspicion belongs in the row as a QUESTION, not as a stated consequence with a site count attached.

CLASSIFIED `invalid` rather than `not-reproduced`: this is not a finding that failed to recur, it is a claim whose stated mechanism was checked and does not hold.

title: GPU reductions still lack TILED MATMUL (2-D workgroup indexing the 1-D model lacks); integer `prod` / `dot` are blocked on WGSL lacking a widening multiply; and `variance` / `stddev` are f32-only (the integer form needs a decision, not just work — the deviations are formed on-device in f32, so `mean`'s promote-late trick does not carry over). A SAMPLE (÷ n-1) form is decided against rather than pending. Everything else has shipped: sum / prod / min / max / mean / dot / argmin / argmax / variance / stddev / prefix_sum over `Vec[f32]`, and sum / min / max / mean / argmin / argmax over `Vec[i32]` and `Vec[u32]`.
detail:
SPLIT OUT OF B-2026-08-19-10 (fixed 63870ee0), which asked that a live remainder get its own row rather than be buried in a closed one.

WHAT SHIPPED: `gpu.sum(buf)` / `gpu.prod(buf)` over `Vec[f32]`, any length, bit-identical between `karac run` and `karac build` because the tree order (and, past one workgroup, the CHUNKING) is specified in `reduce_kernel::tree_reduce_f32` and reproduced by the shader.

WHAT DOES NOT, AND WHY EACH IS ITS OWN SLICE RATHER THAN A LOOP OVER THE SAME CODE:

  * INTEGER REDUCTIONS (`Vec[i32]` / `Vec[u32]`). The emitter can already produce the shaders — `emit_reduce_kernel` takes `elem` and handles i32/u32 — and is deliberately WIDER than the typechecker here. Two blockers, both semantics: (a) the runtime entrypoint is `karac_runtime_gpu_reduce_f32`, and an integer routed through the f32 core loses precision above 2^24 (`[16777217, 1]` sums to 16777216 — measured, and the reason the first cut of this feature was reverted); (b) an integer reduction can OVERFLOW, and WGSL wraps where Kara traps. B-2026-08-19-1 just settled that question for kernel BODIES with a narrow `wrapping_*` escape hatch; a reduction has no expression to write `wrapping_add` on, so the trap-vs-wrap decision has to be made at the reduction's own surface. Do not inherit it by accident.

  * THE ORD FAMILY (min / max / argmin / argmax). `argmin`/`argmax` need an INDEX carried alongside the value through every halving step, so the scratch array is a pair, not a scalar — a different shader shape, not a different `infix` string. `min`/`max` alone are close to free once the identity is `+inf`/`-inf`, but NaN handling has to match `reduce_kernel`'s existing f64 twin or the two disagree.

  * TWO-PASS STATISTICS (mean / var / std). `mean` needs a count division after the fold; `var`/`std` need the mean first. Expressible as two dispatches, but the emitter currently produces one shader per call.

  * DOT / PREFIX-SUM / TILED MATMUL. Dot is a map-then-reduce and the cheapest of these — two dispatches, or one shader that multiplies on load. Prefix-sum is a genuinely different algorithm (Hillis-Steele or Blelloch, not a halving fold). Tiled matmul needs 2-D workgroup indexing, which `emit_reduce_kernel`'s 1-D `local_invocation_id.x` model does not have.

WHY IT STILL MATTERS AT THIS SIZE. The CG-5 assessment (`docs/spikes/gpu-llvm-offload-assessment.md`) benchmarks Kara against a rustc/LLVM-Offload paper measured on RAJAPerf, which is largely reductions and stencils. `sum` alone covers some of that class; `dot` and `min`/`max` would cover much more of it, and they are the two cheapest items on this list. If the goal is an honest comparison rather than feature breadth, do those two first.

ORDERING SUGGESTION: dot, then min/max, then the integer overflow decision, then argmin/argmax. Prefix-sum and matmul are separate projects.

PROGRESS 2026-08-19 — the two items this row named as cheapest, and as the ones that move the RAJAPerf comparison, are DONE:

  * `gpu.min` / `gpu.max` (1b564fee) → `Option[f32]`, matching `Stats.min` and `Vec.min`: an empty buffer has no extremum, and the runtime's empty short-circuit returns the shader's padding identity, so answering +inf there would be exactly the plausible-wrong number this family must avoid. The NaN question the row did not anticipate turned out to be the real work: WGSL's `min` builtin tie-breaks POSITIONALLY (`e1` unless `e2 < e1`, and every comparison against NaN is false), which is harmless in a left fold and fatal in a tree where the grouping decides the position. The emitted shader spells out a NaN-ignoring combine instead, matching `f32::min`, which makes the op associative and therefore grouping-independent. Proven on lavapipe in both NaN orders, not just argued.
  * `gpu.dot(a, b)` (36fce374) → `f32`, fused: the level-0 shader forms the product on load and runs the identical halving tree, and every level after it IS the sum shader. So `gpu.dot(a, b)` and `gpu.sum(a * b)` agree bit-for-bit by construction rather than by matching. Mismatched lengths trap on both surfaces (truncating to the shorter would silently answer a different question).

WHAT THIS ROW NOW TRACKS. Argmin/argmax still need an index carried alongside the value through every halving step — a scratch of PAIRS, a different shader rather than a different combine string. Mean needs a count division; var/std need two passes. Prefix-sum is a genuinely different algorithm (Hillis-Steele or Blelloch, not a halving fold). Tiled matmul needs 2-D workgroup indexing, which the 1-D `local_invocation_id.x` model does not have. Integer reductions remain blocked on the trap-vs-wrap decision at the reduction's own surface — B-2026-08-19-1's kernel-body `wrapping_*` escape hatch does not reach them, because a reduction has no expression to write `wrapping_add` on.

REVISED ORDERING: mean (cheapest remaining — one division after the fold), then the integer overflow decision, then argmin/argmax. Var/std, prefix-sum and matmul are separate projects.

PROGRESS 2026-08-19 (second batch) — `gpu.mean` (4db566db), the item the revised ordering above named as cheapest. It is the first reduction whose SURFACE op and SHADER op come apart: mean has no tree-shaped kernel and never will, because a shader cannot know it is running the last level of the fold, so a division inside it would divide once per level. It runs the SUM kernel unchanged and the host divides once after the fold converges — no new shader, no new runtime symbol, one `fdiv`. `gpu.mean(v)` and `gpu.sum(v) / n` are therefore the same number to the last bit, so mean inherits the sum's grouping and adds exactly one further rounding. Returns `Option[f32]` for the same reason min/max do.

REVISED ORDERING AGAIN: the integer overflow decision is now the cheapest remaining item (it is a decision, not an implementation), then argmin/argmax. Var/std are no longer 'cheap after mean' — they need a second pass over the buffer with the mean in hand, which is a two-dispatch shape the surface has never had. Prefix-sum and tiled matmul remain separate projects.

PROGRESS 2026-08-19 (third batch) — THE INTEGER OVERFLOW DECISION, which this row named as the cheapest remaining item because it is a decision rather than an implementation. It turned out to be DETERMINED BY PRECEDENT rather than taste: `v.sum()` over a `Vec[i32]` whose total exceeds i32 already fails with `integer overflow` on both surfaces, so `gpu.sum(v)` traps too (5a008604 machinery, daad01cc surface). Anything else would silently convert a trap into a wrong answer the moment a reduction moved to a GPU — the class B-2026-08-19-1 closed for kernel bodies.

THE CONSEQUENCE THE ROW DID NOT ANTICIPATE, and the reason it is in design.md rather than a comment: THE TREE ORDER DECIDES WHETHER AN INTEGER REDUCTION TRAPS, not merely what it returns. Overflow is a property of the intermediate sums, and a tree forms different intermediates than a line. Both directions are reachable, with MAX = i32::MAX:
    [MAX, MAX, -MAX, -MAX]   tree -> 0        left fold -> traps
    [MAX, -MAX, MAX, -MAX]   tree -> traps    left fold -> 0
So `gpu.sum(v)` and `v.sum()` may legitimately disagree about FAILING on the same buffer. Specified, not a divergence — but it means replacing `v.sum()` with `gpu.sum(v)` is NOT a pure speedup on integer data. Float reductions have no analogue, because float addition saturates rather than trapping.

MECHANISM. WGSL has no trapping arithmetic and no overflow flag — its integer ops are DEFINED to wrap — so the emitted shader computes the flag itself (`((a ^ s) & (b ^ s)) < 0` for a signed add; `s < a` for an unsigned carry) and OR-folds it through the same halving tree as the value, so one overflowing lane at any stride reaches lane 0. Validated on lavapipe: `[i32::MAX, 1]` comes back as the wrapped i32::MIN WITH the flag set, and the bit survives from both stride 1 and stride 32. The runtime REPORTS the overflow rather than aborting so codegen can raise Kāra's own panic at the call site (same message, exit code and span as `v.sum()`); a runtime-side abort would be a bare SIGABRT with no span.

HAZARD CLOSED IN PASSING: the float emitter accepted i32/u32 and would have produced a silently-WRAPPING reduction the moment anything wired it up. It now refuses them outright, so the wrong shader is unreachable rather than merely undocumented.

WHAT THIS ROW NOW TRACKS. Argmin/argmax (an index carried alongside the value through every halving step — a scratch of PAIRS, a different shader). Var/std (a second pass with the mean in hand — a two-dispatch shape the surface has never had). Prefix-sum (a different algorithm: Hillis-Steele or Blelloch, not a halving fold). Tiled matmul (2-D workgroup indexing the 1-D `local_invocation_id.x` model lacks). Plus four integer deferrals, each a DECISION rather than effort: `u32` (mechanical — the runtime entry point is byte-transparent — but its identity and result would travel through an i32-typed slot, and sign confusion there is the plausible-wrong-number failure this family must avoid); integer `prod` (a checked multiply needs a widening intermediate WGSL lacks, and the usual `s / a != b` substitute is unsound there because `i32::MIN / -1` is indeterminate in WGSL — it would misfire on exactly the input it exists to catch); integer `mean` (truncate or promote?); integer `dot` (same checked multiply).

REVISED ORDERING (fourth pass): `u32` is now the cheapest — one decision about a slot type and a near-copy of the i32 twin — then argmin/argmax. Integer `prod`/`dot` are blocked on WGSL itself rather than on us, and are worth leaving alone until there is a caller who wants them.

PROGRESS 2026-08-19 (fourth batch) — `u32` (916e699f). CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN TEXT: the deferral above says u32 was blocked because "its identity and result would travel through an i32-typed slot, and sign confusion in that slot is exactly the plausible-wrong-number failure this family must not have". That was WRONG about where the hazard lived. The runtime entry point is genuinely bit-transparent — it casts the input straight to `*const u8`, writes the output from raw little-endian bytes, and only copies the identity on the empty path — so signedness never reaches it, and the shader does the interpreting.

THE REAL HAZARD was one instruction away: codegen SIGN-extended the 32-bit result into the i64 carrier, which turns any u32 at or above 2^31 negative. Measured by reverting the fix: `gpu.sum` of `[2147483647, 1]` prints 18446744071562067968 instead of 2147483648. Worth recording that a `max` fixture does NOT catch this — the print path masks an Option payload back to 32 bits and hides the sign extension — so the discriminating E2E fixture is the bare sum.

SECOND FINDING, subtler and the reason this was not purely mechanical: THE INTERPRETER CANNOT INFER SIGNEDNESS FROM THE VALUES. A `Value::Int` carries no width or sign, and a `Vec[u32]` of small values is indistinguishable from a `Vec[i32]` by inspection. Range-sniffing would fold such a buffer with the SIGNED overflow rule and trap somewhere past 2^31 that the compiled path sails through — a run/build divergence reachable only on large data, which is the worst shape it could take (small tests all pass). The interpreter therefore reads the same typechecker hint codegen reads. The hint now carries the element SPELLING rather than an is-integer bit, because the extend needs three states (f32 / i32 / u32).

The overflow RULE differs as well, which is why the twin is a separate function rather than generic: a signed add overflows on a shared-sign-then-flip, an unsigned one on a carry. The i32 rule would call `u32::MAX + 1` fine; the u32 rule would miss `i32::MAX + 1`. Both directions pinned.

REVISED ORDERING (fifth pass): argmin/argmax is now the cheapest remaining item — it needs an index carried alongside the value through every halving step, i.e. a scratch of PAIRS, which is a genuinely different shader rather than a different combine string, but it needs no new decisions. Var/std need a two-dispatch shape the surface has never had. Integer `prod`/`dot` remain blocked on WGSL itself (no widening multiply; `i32::MIN / -1` is indeterminate there, so the usual checked-multiply substitute would misfire on exactly the input it exists to catch) and are worth leaving alone until a caller wants them. Integer `mean` needs one decision — truncate or promote.

PROGRESS 2026-08-19 (fifth batch) — the ARG FAMILY (abef0226). The one reduction whose tree carries (value, index) PAIRS: an index alone cannot be compared and a value alone cannot be reported. It needed no new decisions, only a different shader, which is why it kept sliding down the ordering behind things that needed answers.

SHAPE: two shaders, one index space. Level 0 seeds every element as its own candidate; every level after it takes the surviving candidate INDICES and re-reads their values from the ORIGINAL buffer, which stays bound throughout. Indices are absolute at every level, so no value ever crosses a dispatch boundary — the host never ships values back and forth. The combine is lexicographic (strictly better value wins; exact tie goes to the SMALLER index), hence a semilattice, hence grouping-independent like min/max.

NaN DIVERGES FROM `Stats.argmin`, necessarily. That one seeds its best with element 0 and displaces only on a strict comparison, so a LEADING NaN is never displaced: `Stats.argmin([NaN, 3.0, 1.0])` is 0 while `[3.0, 1.0, NaN]` is 1. Position-dependence cannot survive a halving tree, where the grouping decides positions. `gpu.argmin` makes NaN always lose (answering 2 for the first buffer; 0 for an all-NaN buffer, where nothing wins and the leftmost survives). Same trade as `gpu.min`, documented beside it in design.md.

DESIGN POINT WORTH KEEPING: padding is marked by the INDEX sentinel, not by a value.
